learning_outcomes: Evaluate the key historical and contemporary themes that have shaped Australian foreign policy and their impact
Consider Australia’s key relationships and engagements and the ways that they contribute to the achievement of Australia’s national interests
Assess the actors and issues that are relevant to Australian foreign policy and their impact on the construction of Australia’s interests and its international practices
Summarise and apply different theoretical approaches to the study of foreign policy, including the different models of foreign policy decision making
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Australian Studies, Policy, Power and Government, Politics and International Relations, or Security Studies

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: How to start a revolution: activism, social movements and political change
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: How to start a revolution and change the world? In a world of growing inequality, environmental pollution, and conflict this question seems more important than ever. In this course, you examine this question from a Politics and International Relations perspective, examining processes of, and the actors involved in, political change. From the #metoo movement, to Black Lives Matter, to the Alt Right, to the Arab spring protests and Occupy and Indignado movements: all around the world citizens are mobilising, some because they want political change, others because they want to maintain the status quo. What is change? Why do some people want radical and others moderate change? What explains the success of advocates for non-change, i.e. the status quo? What kind of change do political actors seek to achieve? In this course you will further explore these questions comparing processes of political change and actors involved in generating political change in Australia and other countries around the world. You will learn about the role of power, legitimacy, and insider and outsider positions in making political change work (or not). You will leave this course with a better understanding of what political change is, how it can be achieved, and what your own role can be in changing the world.
learning_outcomes: Explain the contested nature of political inquiry and the dimensions of ethical scholarship in the disciplines of Politics and/or International Relations in relation to processes of political change and non-change.
Describe and evaluate the main theories and concepts used in the study of political change
Critically evaluate and contrast research about processes of political change and actors involved in political change (and non-change) in national and international contexts
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations: Politics and International Relations or Working with Communities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Politics of Identity in the 21st Century
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Encompassing a variety of timely, globally relevant topics, reflected through various identity ‘lenses’, including those of race, culture, gender, sexuality, and class, you will look closely in this course at the intersection of identity, politics, and governance. In this seminar we will focus on cultural identities – national, ethnic, racial, religious, and linguistic – and examine a range of scholarly and public debates provoked by these identities. How should cultural identity fit within liberal democratic states? Does a nation-state have a right to protect its ‘national identity’ through restrictive immigration policies? Are liberal democratic states obliged to recognise the cultural identities and practices of its minorities? Should Indigenous groups be distinguished from immigrant groups in this regard? Should religious identity be treated differently from ethnic identity? Is multiculturalism bad for women, children, and animals? Should citizenship still be the foundation for addressing identity claims in democracies? By exploring how identities are constituted and situated in today’s highly mobile and interconnected world, you will be equipped to think analytically about the importance and implications of the politics of identity in the twenty-first century.
learning_outcomes: Identify and outline the contested and diverse character of the politics of identity in global, national, and local politics.

Locate, prioritise and apply appropriate information in and to the analysis of the politics of identity in a sophisticated and persuasive manner, using clear and effective independent research, critical reasoning, and scholarly writing skills.
Evaluate contending scholarly arguments on questions of identity in twenty-first-century politics, using relevant concepts, theories and categories of analysis.
Employ self-reflexive, critical research and writing practices.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Politics and International Relations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: United States Politics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the main institutions, actors, and practices of the United States political system. You will explore the historical evolution and contemporary powers of the Presidency, Congress, and the judiciary; the US electoral system; US federalism; and the key political issues, challenges, and dilemmas that the US faces. You will consider the contemporary turbulence of US politics, including the controversies of the Trump administrations, political polarisation, and the ongoing conflicts and struggles over race and racialisation within American politics and society. The course actively encourages you to assess the promises of US democracy and concepts of freedom and liberty against the lived realities of American peoples, particularly First Nations and Black Americans. You will also evaluate the resilience of US democratic institutions and conventions in the context of contemporary populist and authoritarian trends.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impacts of race and racialisation on US politics, particularly in relation to minority groups such as First Nations and Black Americans
Evaluate the main institutions of the US political system and their historical development, including Congress, the President, and the Supreme Court
Employ key concepts and theories to analyse US politics and its specific forms of representative democracy and federalism
Assess contemporary issues, challenges, events, and debates in US politics, including those associated with the Trump and Biden Administrations
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in a specialisation in Politics and International Relations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Thinking Like a Social Scientist
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: How does social and political science differ from other kinds of social or political analysis, for example, journalism? In what sense are the social and political sciences scientific? How do theories, evidence, positionality, and value commitments come together in the social and political sciences to produce knowledge? In this course you will consider fundamental questions about what social and political knowledge is and how it is acquired. You will be introduced to the disciplinary debates around these questions. You will then learn how rival theoretical traditions variously emphasise the individual, groups, institutions, classes, systems, and culture in explaining social and political phenomena. To this end, you will examine landmark works in social and political science that have sought to explain real-world social and political phenomena, from the micro to the macro (e.g. voting behaviour, ‘glass ceilings’ and ‘glass cliffs’, social revolutions, the Holocaust). This course will enhance your understanding in your other Arts & Social Sciences subjects, equip you to conduct theoretically sophisticated social and political inquiry, and empower you to assess knowledge claims about social and political life in general.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate a variety of advanced debates about and approaches to the study of social and political sciences, informed by a self-reflexive awareness of the reasoned views of others

Identify and outline the contested character of approaches to studying and analysing political and social phenomena and the different visions that the social sciences disciplines have of their mission
Locate, prioritise and apply appropriate methodology and methods to the study of social and political phenomena
Employ self-reflexive, critical research and writing practices
Recognise the different analytical traditions and perspectives in social and political science and their contrasting interpretive implications
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Politics and International Relations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Violence, Resistance, Change
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores ‘violence’ as a social phenomenon. What is violence, what are its different forms and expressions? How does violence manifest in our social histories, experiences, and relations? What purpose does violence serve in the social? In this course, you will explore experiences of violence throughout history and the present day, by examining connections between historical and contemporary episodes of violence, and the range of cultural values and perceptions that surround violence as social structure. You will learn about conceptualisations of violence, issues of political and cultural violence, trauma, and the aftermath of violence. You will learn how violence is expressed, concentrated, enacted, and resisted.
learning_outcomes: Examine violence as a socio-cultural phenomenon
Contribute to a vibrant learning community through class discussions
Apply sociological approaches to understand violence and social problems both past and present
Differentiate debates on violence to assess the potential for recovery and restoration
Articulate a coherent and well-substantiated argument using a range of communication skills
prerequisites: Prerequisites: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, International Studies, or Sociology & Anthropology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Intimacy and Relationships: Social Perspectives, Critical Questions
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: You will engage key debates on intimacy to appreciate the complexity of relationships in their historical and socio-cultural contexts. You will consider challenges to family formation and intimate relationships through questions such as: How are relations of care and caring experienced, and how do socio-demographic contexts mediate such experiences? How are digital intimacies, unequal and parasocial relationships understood in everyday life? And, how are connectedness, belonging and loneliness – along with vulnerability, disadvantage and difference - felt by families and communities? Through a series of critical case studies, you will examine how diverse forms of intimacy and relationships are felt and understood through the life course. In doing so you will draw on a range of approaches to researching themes such as the relational and the affective, social and individual, self and other, and technologies and power. This course will apply theory to practice relevant social issues, and provide opportunities for research training and project management in the social sciences.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical skills to research based on course themes and debates.
Develop the capacity for independent research.
Critique and analyse social issues that shape contemporary relationships and forms of intimacy
Examine key concepts and approaches to sociological thinking on intimacy and relationships
Contribute to a vibrant learning community through class discussions, dialogue, and debate
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 units of credit overall, including ARTS1870 and ARTS2871.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Crisis and the Social
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will explore the multiple dimensions of crisis through a sociological lens. You will examine the different temporal and spatial elements of crisis such as time, memory, geography, place and history. You will investigate the intersections of crisis through historical and contemporary examples that focus on the experiential, emotional and social implications of crisis. Themes and topics may include but are not confined to climate crisis and extinction, economic and socio-political crisis and revolt, effects of pandemics as well as the multiple framings of power, justice and humanitarian response in times of crisis. By examining these various themes and cultural practices, you will focus on how crisis is lived and experienced, and you will examine the consequences of accelerated change in our everyday lives and communities, and how we can navigate the future for human and non-human worlds.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate classic and contemporary sociological theories and apply them to the analyses of social justice and crisis.
Demonstrate a capacity for independent research.
Apply critical skills to research, writing and discussion on course themes such as social justice and crisis.
Develop implications of concepts raised in the course to lived and theoretical existence.
Contribute to a vibrant learning community through class discussions, dialogue, and debate.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, International Studies, Policy, Power and Government, or Sociology & Anthropology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Feminist and Queer Theory: Histories and Debates
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course offers an interdisciplinary survey of key thinkers, debates and developments in feminist and queer theory, in the Anglophone world and beyond it. You will have the opportunity to engage closely and critically with the ideas of influential scholars such as Gloria Anzaldúa, Sara Ahmed, Judith Butler and Eve Kosofsky Sedgwick, as well as innovative thinkers whose work deserves to be more widely known. We will consider the overlaps and differences between feminist and queer theories and their emergence as part of, and in response, to social movements. You will also be encouraged to make connections between feminist and queer theories and critical race theory, trans studies and Indigenous feminisms. Above all, this course aims to demonstrate the ongoing relevance of feminist and queer theory to gender studies and to the wider world we live in.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate teamwork and leadership skills, including through sensitive engagement with diverse cultural and social perspectives.
Communicate effectively both orally and in writing, using a variety of media, for diverse audiences and purposes.
Display initiative and self-direction to continuously acquire knowledge and skills in gender studies and analysis.
Apply high-level skills in feminist and queer theory to address complex problems in professional practice, society and/ or scholarship.
Articulate how gender is a constitutive feature of societies and cultures and how it intersects with other categories such as race, class and sexuality.
Apply feminist and queer theory within disciplinary, interdisciplinary and/ or trans-disciplinary contexts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Gender Studies or History.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Security in Asia: Politics Meets Economics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will examine the complex and dynamic relationship between political and economic processes and outcomes in Asia. You will be challenged to ask: How have geopolitical concerns shaped economic development trajectories across the region? How have domestic and geo-political dynamics within the region been transformed by economic developments? And what are the implications of the region’s rapid rise for the global economic and security landscape? Through a theoretically informed analysis of such questions, you will develop an understanding of the the interdependencies between economic and political developments in the region, and the possible trajectories of future economic and political developments.
learning_outcomes: Assess the implications of the region’s rapid rise for the global economic and security landscape, from a theoretically grounded point of view.
Analyse and evaluate key debates about how domestic and geo-political dynamics within the region have been transformed by economic developments
Explain the various ways in which geopolitical concerns have shaped economic development trajectories across the region
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, International Political Economy, Politics and International Relations, or Security Studies

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Media, Culture and Power
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will explore broad sociological understandings of media and theories of power and knowledge that exist in the public sphere and social life. By introducing you to different ways of theorising media practices, this course prepares you for the analysis of the changing media landscape and new forms of social feeling and popular culture. Topics are likely to include: ideas of memory, time and technology; the social relationship between 'public' and 'private' in the context of hyperpublicity today; changing media devices and the role of social media; digital cultures, film and visual cultures; the relationship between revolutions in media technology and public debate; the role of different media in shaping ideas of citizenship and belonging.
learning_outcomes: Engage with and evaluate theories around the sociology of media and new forms of social feeling and popular culture.
Contribute to a vibrant learning community through class discussions, dialogue, and debate.
Apply critical skills to research, writing, and conversations on the sociology of media.
Act with integrity, responsibility, and respect, demonstrating ethical conduct in all contexts including class discussion, assessments, and thoughtful and accountable use of digital technologies.
Apply concepts raised in the course to everyday life and experience of media cultures.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations: Digital Social Sciences, International Studies, or Sociology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Culture and Human Rights
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Human rights are commonly understood to be universal, but is this really the case? What does the idea of human rights, as legal and policy mechanisms, international principles, and values, tell us about how the human is understood? Through critiques of conventional approaches to human rights, and exploring the tensions between individual and group rights, and between State actors and individuals, groups, and other non-state actors, this course thinks about human rights and their limits. You will engage in critiques of law as a reductionist discourse on the social by exploring the relationships between human rights and cultural differences such as gender, ethnicity, religion and indigenous cultures. You will be introduced to the fundamentals of human rights, the global human rights machinery, and think about how human rights are articulated or challenged through cultural artifacts such as poetry, art, storytelling, songsand literature. Finally, this course asks, who is the human in human rights, and consequently, who isn’t the human?
learning_outcomes: Critically apply a knowledge of human rights to various local, national and transnational contexts.
Contribute to a vibrant learning community through class discussions, dialogue, and debate.
Interrogate how human rights frameworks and institutions produce particular understandings of the social and the human.
Act with integrity, responsibility, and respect, demonstrating ethical conduct in all contexts including class discussion, assessments, and thoughtful and accountable use of digital technologies.
Develop, research, and produce work that critically considers the contested theories of, and perspectives on, human rights.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Australian Studies, Geographical Studies, Global Development, International Studies, Sociology, or Working with Communities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Race and Gender
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: We often understand knowledge as a neutral, disinterested point of view: as purely rational, untainted by partiality or prejudice, and detached from the social and political entanglements that cloud objectivity. In recent decades, however, theoretical feminism, critical race theory, and postcolonial theory have questioned this view of knowledge. In this course you will consider how race and gender is expressed in modes and styles of theorising. By claiming to be neutral, does a philosophy or theory exclude certain positions marked by social difference? If western traditions of thought are typically ‘masculine’ and ‘white,’ then (how) can academic philosophy accommodate the experiences of women and non-Europeans? How have philosophers historically represented racial and sexual difference? And what contributions can philosophy make to theorising race and gender in the contemporary world?
learning_outcomes: Recognise how historical and social contexts (such as race and gender) inform philosophical writing
Critically appraise particular feminist, race critical, and/or postcolonial theoretical positions within the context of the course materials
Identify and explain key concepts in gender and feminist studies, critical race theory, and postcolonial theory
Recognise where and in what ways gender studies is applicable in Philosophy
Construct arguments using critical race, postcolonial, and feminist analysis in written and/ or verbal form
Collaborate ethically and responsibly with others to increase written communication skills
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in one of the following specialisations, Gender Studies

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Honours-level Thesis Writing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: This Honours-level seminar course is designed to introduce you to higher-level academic research and writing in the disciplines of Creative Writing, English, Film, Media, Music, and Theatre & Performance Studies. It will extend the writing skills developed in the first three years of the degree to support the preparation and completion of your first major piece of independent research – the Honours thesis and/or production project. It will introduce you to core issues in and approaches to research which will help you consolidate and extend their understanding of their chosen discipline and of the place of their research within it. The course is organised around a structured seminar series, beginning with a consideration of the nature of disciplinary research in the Humanities and moving on to consider the genre of the Honours thesis, and to developing a Research Plan and Thesis and/or project timetable.
learning_outcomes: Present an outline of specific research questions developing out of their research, and identify research methods suitable for their project.
Develop a formal research proposal for their Honours thesis and/or project.
Engage with peers' and colleagues' research critically and in the spirit of intellectual openness and generosity.
Analyse critically the structure, argumentation and quality of a thesis and/or practical project, and identify the methodological approaches employed.
Work independently to develop a complex research project.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a School of the Arts and Media honours program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Skills in the Humanities
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will help you to develop a range of higher-level research skills. It will cover such areas as research methodology, research questions, the literature review, presentation skills, and academic writing. It will help you to identify and develop your research proposal, articulate its point and purpose, and present it in oral and written form. It will thereby support you in the skills you need to produce a sustained research project such as the Honours thesis. The content is delivered through seminars and workshop.
learning_outcomes: Construct and articulate a clear and coherent research proposal
Locate, analyse and evaluate research relevant to a specific topic
Evaluate the key principles of high-quality quality research in a relevant discipline
Articulate the ethical obligations generated by research in the humanities
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a School of Humanities and Languages honours program or Nura Gili Indigenous program completing honours (ATSIAH specialisation).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advances in the Humanities
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: This is a 12 UOC course. You will enrol in 6 UOC in each of two successive terms with a result reported by a single grade at the end of the second 6 UOC course. This course aims to immerse you in advanced topics in the Humanities and equip you with skills to embark on a research inquiry. You will critically evaluate and synthesise current knowledge, determine a need for new knowledge, and communicate knowledge with an awareness of ethical, social and cultural issues. You will benefit from guest lectures by leading scholars in the field. You will also have the opportunity to debate ideas, learn how to do archival and fieldwork research, and discuss the challenges you encounter in your chosen field and discipline.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate perspectives in your discipline and situate them in relation to broader developments in the Humanities
Analyse different epistemological and cultural traditions within the Humanities and their influence on the wider world
Communicate effectively and present work in a manner that conforms to scholarly conventions and subject guidelines
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a School of Humanities and Languages honours program or Nura Gili Indigenous program completing honours (ATSIAH specialisation)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Methodologies in the Social Sciences: Questions and Quandaries
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: This is a 12 UOC course. You will enrol in 6 UOC in each of two successive terms with a result reported by a single grade at the end of the second 6 UOC course. This is a core course for Honours candidates in the School of Social Sciences and the main focus will be the question of methodology. Each seminar will look at different approaches to research across the sub-disciplines and will explore what we might call the ‘so what’ of a particular methodology’s analytical leverage. Why do the Social Sciences break into myriad, competing methodologies? Can we describe our methodologies as scientific, and if not, then how do we best secure a notion of accuracy and usefulness? How does our understanding of evidence actually change our research methods as well as the outcomes and conclusions that we might reach?
learning_outcomes: Effectively deploy a particular theory or methodological approach
Identify and apply the ethical requirements and responsibilities of researchers
Apply critical thinking and analytic skills
Develop and demonstrate effective oral presentation skills
Design and sustain an argument, or point of view
prerequisites: Enrolment in a School of Social Sciences Honours Program or one of the following Honours Programs: Asian Studies, Criminology, or European Studies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Puzzles, Planning, and Presentation for Honours in the Social Sciences
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This is a compulsory course for Social Sciences honours students in the School of Social Sciences. It will introduce you to the practice of thesis writing and support you in the early stages of developing your honours argument. This course includes topics such as: using library resources for honours students including research consultation and access to databases; the role of methods in research and the use of theory in framing and conducting a research project in the social sciences; your ethical responsibilities as a researcher; and planning and managing a research project; working effectively with your supervisor; time and data management skills. The course introduces you to the idea of framing your research as an intervention in a disciplinary debate (or series of debates). A particular focus of the course is introducing students to the thesis form. This includes learning about the component parts of a minor-thesis, and thinking about how you might construct your own thesis, for maximum impact.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively with colleagues to share skills and knowledge relevant to producing a minor thesis
Verbally present material in an engaging and informative way.
Identify the features of an outstanding thesis or dissertation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a School of Social Sciences Honours Program or one of the following Honours Programs: Asian Studies, Australian Indigenous Studies, Criminology, or European Studies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Intellectual Foundations and Methods of Research
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Through a sequence of readings, seminars, and discussions, this course will introduce you to the intellectual foundations of research. The goal of this course is to provide you with a basic working knowledge of systematic and rigorous research in the humanities and social sciences. A sound understanding of research is underpinned by an understanding of: the intellectual traditions that inform debates (i.e. research disciplines in the humanities and social sciences and cross-disciplinary work); how knowledge is produced (i.e. the economic, social, political and human motivations that drive discoveries and innovations); and what research might be able to achieve in democratic contexts, according to sound ethical principles (i.e. ethics of research, management of knowledge in a just society). Upon completion, you will be able to understand debates about research methods, epistemology, paradigm wars, the social and political contexts of research, and the contributions of the humanities and social sciences to the improvement of human and environmental well-being. These insights will help you develop capabilities and skills for producing thoughtful and impactful research.
learning_outcomes: Propose solutions to methodological issues in their disciplinary research
Situate research in a historical and theoretical context
Evaluate the appropriateness, ethics and quality of research, its paradigm and methods
Articulate methodological issues relevant to their disciplinary research
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Master of Philosophy (2364)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Knowledges and Ethical Practices
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: What is knowledge and how is it socially organized and ethically produced? Are there different forms of knowledge and/or ways of knowing? How is knowledge created, and what are its conditions? This course introduces you to different perspectives on knowledge production in the humanities and social sciences. It will introduce you to different conceptions of what knowledge is and expose you to current debates about the way that knowledge is produced. You will also learn different modes of inquiry that draw on diverse traditions and understandings of knowledge and its production.
learning_outcomes: Assess the consequences of different knowledge traditions for the production of ethical research
Apply relevant concepts of knowledge production to contemporary problems and concerns
Distinguish between approaches to the construction of knowledge
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Knowledges and Ethical Practices specialisation in the Master of Philosophy (2364)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global and First Nations Studies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The increasing pace of interactions in the global sphere prompt critical inquiries into human society and culture. How do we understand identity, time and place? What is the nature of power and how it is exercised? How do we learn from knowledges and experiences of first nations peoples? Our appreciation of these questions is enhanced by bringing together multifocal theoretical and methodological approaches drawing from historical, literary, subaltern, anthropological, and sociological disciplines. This specialisation will develop your skills in cross-cultural inquiry through engagement with multiple narratives and voices.
learning_outcomes: Negotiate cross-disciplinary forms of knowledge through a variety of critical approaches and methodologies.
Formulate a persuasive argument in writing that applies critical and cultural theories.
Develop research skills in the collection and critical management of primary and secondary sources of information.
Describe and analyse a range of theoretical materials concerning knowledge, history, culture and representation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Global and First Nations Studies specialisation in the Master of Philosophy (2364)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research and the Creative Arts
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course develops observational, critical, and analytical tools for application to research in the creative arts. It begins with a focus on art and artists; understanding the materials and processes of creative practice in historical, disciplinary and aesthetic contexts. An understanding of the role of research, theory, and criticism within the arts is developed, alongside ethical processes for undertaking such work. You will be introduced to media-specific and trans-disciplinary forms of compositional analysis, with specific attention to the practices and processes of the artist. Beyond the terms of the work of art and the role of the artist, analytical and theoretical methods drawing on disciplines within and beyond the arts will be covered and may include empirical, formal, post-structural, phenomenological, material and cultural approaches. There is a focus on Australian content, including indigenous artists, and their place within important international networks
learning_outcomes: Apply writing skills to the analysis and critique of creative practices and associated discourses
Hone research skills, gathering primary and secondary sources of information about case studies, and critically assessing such resources
Recognize and analyze key theories of creativity across a variety of artistic disciplines
Apply diverse critical lenses to creative work including interpretative, formal, aesthetic, phenomenological, empirical, pedagogical, sociological
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Creative Arts specialisation in the Master of Philosophy (2364)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Social Approaches to Researching Health and Well-Being
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Although health and well-being research may appear dominated by biomedical disciplines, the humanities and social sciences extend our understanding of how these normative concepts are viewed, expressed and promoted in a variety of social contexts and communities. Drawing on the insights of faculty researchers who employ a range of innovative social and critical approaches to health and well-being research, we will consider the intersections and tensions between established and emerging theoretical and methodological traditions. Looking across a range of health issues critical to governments and communities today, our understandings of what counts as research data will be expanded beyond the foundational methods of interviewing and observation to encompass digital data, policy and legal texts, social media interactions, as well as participatory and arts-based methods. By the end of the course you will be better equipped to explain the value of and build a rationale for incorporating social approaches into research on health and well-being.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the benefits and limitations of taking social approaches to researching health and well-being to non-HASS-informed audiences
Describe health and well-being as socially complex, culturally located and politically contested subjects
Apply specific frameworks, methods and techniques from the humanities and social sciences (HASS) to the design of research projects examining experiences of and responses to health and well-being
Explain the value of interdisciplinary social approaches to understanding health and well-being
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Health and Well-being specialisation in the Master of Philosophy (2364)

faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This core course of the Master of Philosophy in Arts and Social Sciences provides you with the opportunity to work closely with academic leaders in your field of specialization within the Humanities and Social Sciences to gain in-depth knowledge of current developments, problems and debates. The specialisation enables you to hone your discipline-specific research skills, gain experience with relevant research methods and deepen your understanding of the field in its historical and intellectual context, its theories and approaches, as well as its cutting-edge debates in the literature. Ultimately it also assists you with writing your research proposal
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and apply theories and methods to drive relevant discipline-specific innovation in a global context
Synthesize disciplinary knowledge purposefully to drive convincing argument
Hone written and verbal communication skills
Demonstrate advanced research and information retrieval skills

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Academic Writing for the Humanities
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: This course will assist you to develop your capacity to write academic essays according to the conventions of the Humanities. It provides the knowledge and vocabulary by which you can critically analyse the work of others as well as your own. The course focuses sustained attention on various modes of academic writing that are used in essay writing and shows how these may be deployed to present a strong argument. The course includes analysis of a range of exemplars as well as essays from academic journals researched by students and related to their disciplinary interests. This study will be accompanied by writing exercises, writing workshops and detailed feedback from both peers and staff. The course is offered as a Prescribed Elective in the Master of Journalism and Communication and the Master of Public Relations and Advertising. Students enrolled in other Postgraduate Coursework Programs in UNSW Arts and Social Sciences, may take the course as an additional elective, but it will not contribute credit toward those programs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate facility with grammar, sentence construction and conceptual exposition, associated with expectations of academic writing in the humanities.
Structure, edit, and present a piece of writing according to conventions of academic writing in the humanities, and in conjunction with inquiry based/research based learning.
Apply the primary modes of academic writing in the humanities, including exposition, description, narrative and argumentation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a postgraduate Arts and Social Sciences program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Languages of Australia
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: By taking this course, you will gain an appreciation of Australia’s rich and complex Aboriginal linguistic heritage in contemporary and traditional contexts. You will delve into a curated range of topics including language and the land, kinship and social organisation, narrative and conversation, language acquisition, language contact, language and education, language maintenance and revival. Each of these topics will be discussed with reference to engaging case studies of current research and current community-based projects. Through the exploration of these topics, you will learn about the characteristic linguistic properties of Australian languages and apply analytical skills to the description of Australian language data. There will be a focus on how new ways of speaking are created, how languages are lost, and the ways in which Aboriginal speakers are teaching and reviving their traditional languages today. You will work with a selection of authentic NSW Aboriginal language material from State Library of NSW collections. In doing so, you will have hands-on experience in how to find and utilise rich archival linguistic material and the ethical practices in the management and use of Aboriginal language materials. You will take away from this course a deepened understanding of social and cultural diversity as seen through the lens of language, analytical methods and critical thinking skills, and knowledge of research ethics and intellectual integrity.
learning_outcomes: Recognise common linguistic features of Australian languages
Master research ethics and archive protocols in the management of Aboriginal language material
Discern current debates and issues in the study of Australian languages
Employ comprehensive principles of language analysis and description to Australian language data

In this course, you will be guided to develop a personal project that meets your needs and implement it in a warm and safe environment being supported not only by the teachers but also by peer mentors. In addition, you will learn a number of important skills needed for life-long learning, including reflective thinking and time management.
learning_outcomes: Communicate critical personal learning insights and outcomes with peers
Develop a personal project tailored to individual linguistic needs, utilising tools and resources for language enhancement supported by relevant literature
Critically analyse and identify specific linguistic areas that need improvement within a professional and academic context
Critically evaluate personal and professional development through reflective practice, demonstrating advanced critical thinking and self-directed learning
Demonstrate advanced communication skills by implementing a sustainable personal project that enhances linguistic proficiency in a professional or academic context

The submitted thesis is examined by two academic leaders in the field, at least one of whom is external to the university. Students must also pass an oral defense of the thesis. The thesis represents 54UoC of the total 72 UoC for the MPhil program
learning_outcomes: Synthesise complex concepts and express them in a logical, articulate form
Demonstrate a deep understanding of the global body of knowledge of a discipline or a cross-disciplinary field
Communicate with advanced writing skills the analysis and critique of past literature related to the thesis topic
Demonstrate advanced knowledge and application of research principles and methods appropriate in investigations in the Humanities and Social Sciences.
Apply specific frameworks, methods and techniques from the humanities and social sciences to the delivery of an interdisciplinary research project
Demonstrate cognitive, technical and creative skills in generating and evaluating complex ideas and concepts pertaining to humanities and social sciences.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Personalised English Language Enhancement for HDR
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Personalised English Language Enhancement for HDR (HDR PELE) is a self-directed learning course designed to help postgraduate research students in all faculties enhance their communication skills in English. In this course, you will be guided to develop a personal project that meets your linguistic needs and implement it with strong support from the lecturer, tutors, as well as peer mentors, in a warm and safe learning community. You will learn a number of essential skills needed by all research students, including reflective thinking and time management. This course best suits you if you are in the early stages of candidature. You are required to have your supervisor's permission to enrol. More information about the course can be found on the ADA Faculty website: https://www.unsw.edu.au/arts-design-architecture/our-schools/humanities-languages/student-life/resources-support/personalised-english-language-enhancement
learning_outcomes: Design and carry out a personal project based on the analysis of personal language needs
Reflect on and assess their own progress to sustain personal and professional language enhancement
Apply tools and resources for language enhancement
Analyse and identify personal language needs
Communicate critical personal learning outcomes with peers

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Atomic Energy
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides the basic background knowledge, understanding and vocabulary that is unique to nuclear engineering. In doing so, this course also provides the foundations for later courses in the Nuclear Engineering specialisation. The course will introduce a wide breadth of topics. These include nuclear fission and fusion, the historical context of nuclear engineering, the impact of radiation on matter, fuel fabrication and the fuel cycle, radioactive wastes and storage methods, reactor accidents, and nuclear safety and licensing.
learning_outcomes: Define and interpret units, nomenclature and concepts specific to nuclear engineering.
Describe the impact and sequence of events within historical nuclear accidents.

Analyse the techno-socio-economic challenges of nuclear energy, considering factors such as engineering limits of nuclear materials and system, safety, sustainability, public perception, and regulatory frameworks.
Classify and discuss main reactor design features and components of nuclear technologies.
Relate how the strengths and drawbacks of nuclear energy affect our ability to meet each of the United Nations sustainable development goals.
Collaborate effectively with team members to develop technical communication and problem-solving skills in a nuclear engineering context
prerequisites: Prerequisites: MATS1110 and (PHYS1121 or PHYS1131)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Neutronics
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an introduction to the key elements of neutron physics within a nuclear reactor. Students completing this course will be able to discuss aspects of reactor physics and the implications that reactor physics has on the engineering and safety of nuclear systems. Students will be able to perform analyses on simple reactor geometries and describe and understand the main kinetic mechanisms, and their significance, on reactor design and control. Analytical and computational techniques will be used by the student to solve neutron physics problems. A review of the accident at the Chernobyl nuclear power plant is presented to highlight the link between neutron physics and reactor safety. Key concepts such as neutron flux and diffusion are first introduced. These are then utilised to demonstrate multiplication and criticality. The neutron life cycle in thermal reactors is described along with fast and delayed neutron production. Reactor kinetics are discussed including doubling times, reactivity feedback mechanisms, power and temperature coefficients, and Xenon poisoning. The course material is highly technical in nature. Students taking this course are expected to have the mathematical skills of second year engineering students, so that they are able manipulate and solve the mathematical expressions inherent to neutron physics problems. Students are expected to be familiar with coding principles so that they can operate codes on high performance computers to solve neutron physics problems. Students must also have completed an introductory course on Nuclear Engineering prior to this course, as the material builds on the physical processes at work during fission including neutron flux, criticality, moderation, reactor dynamics and transients.
learning_outcomes: Analyse reactor component designs to ensure criticality control and radiation safety under dynamic operating conditions.
Use software on high performance computers to solve complex problems in nuclear engineering applications.
Assess reactor power, stability and safety by calculating flux distributions and criticality in nuclear reactors.
Solve equations to describe the kinetic and spatial behavior of neutrons in practical nuclear engineering applications.
Evaluate fuel burnup and reactor behavior over time by predicting isotopic composition changes in materials under neutron flux.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: (ATOM2000 or ENGG3741 or ENGG9741) and (MATH2018 or MATH2019) and ENGG1811 and PHYS2117

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nuclear Reactor Coolants
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an in-depth understanding of the thermophysical properties, selection criteria, and performance characteristics of various coolant materials used in nuclear reactors. Students will investigate the heat transfer and hydraulic mechanisms that transmit power from the fuel to the turbine, enabling the safe and efficient operation of a power plant. Two-phase fluid flow and nucleate boiling will be discussed, with students examining strategies for managing coolant system integrity and reliability under normal and accident conditions.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and compare the thermophysical properties of different coolant materials to determine their influence on reactor performance, efficiency, and safety.
Apply thermal–hydraulic models of single‑ and two‑phase flow to determine heat removal performance in reactor coolant systems.
Analyse deviations in power plant thermal–hydraulic behaviour to determine their underlying causes and assess their implications for system integrity and safety.
Apply steady-state and transient heat transfer principles to assess temperature distribution and reactor cooling performance
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ATOM2000 and MMAN2700 and (ENGG2500 or MMAN2600)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reactor Engineering and Control
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course integrates in-depth knowledge of neutron physics and thermohydraulics to examine the complexities of reactor dynamics, control theory, and the safety protocols essential for the safe operation of a nuclear reactor. Students will be introduced to linear control system theory, employing block diagrams and frequency analysis to model the reactor's state, stability, and optimal design. Practical experience will be gained through the operation of a reactor simulator, demonstrating the impact of reactor design and operator actions on the reactor's response. Students completing this course will be able to confidently address the challenges of reactor system control by comprehending, configuring, and utilizing the feedback mechanisms inherent within a nuclear reactor.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate reactor operation against its design specifications, identifying discrepancies and proposing corrective actions where necessary.
Assess system performance by monitoring, analyzing, and reporting key operating parameters of a nuclear reactor simulator to identify deviations and inform operational decisions.
Deliver, interpret and apply technical briefings to operate a nuclear reactor simulator, demonstrating an understanding of safety protocols and reactor response.
Assess nuclear reactor behavior by developing and applying linear mathematical models, using analytical methods to evaluate stability and control.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ATOM3001 and ATOM3002

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nuclear Reactor Degradation and Lifecycles
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an understanding of the degradation mechanisms that must be accounted for in nuclear energy. The course will explore the life cycle of nuclear materials from production to disposal, with a specific focus on in-core usage and the effects of radiation damage. Students will be encouraged to evaluate the sustainability and environmental impact of nuclear materials throughout their entire lifespan, from cradle to grave. Students will gain knowledge of the materials used in nuclear reactors, their properties and their interactions within a nuclear environment. By examining the degradation of materials in extreme environments, students will gain an appreciation for the most pressing material challenges in the nuclear industry.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and optimize strategies to minimise corrosion taking place in a PWR plant.
Relate the evolution of structure and properties of materials used in nuclear reactors to fundamental processes of radiation damage.
Monitor and characterise the corrosion taking place in PWR plant using a range of chemical and electrochemical techniques.
Compare the degradation mechanisms that limit the life and/or the performance of nuclear components.
Describe and justify the materials used in nuclear reactors.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: MATS1110 and (ATOM2000 or ENGG3741 or ENGG9741)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Topic in Nuclear Engineering
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will involve a detailed examination of novel, emerging or advanced topics in the broad field of nuclear technology. Its content will change each time the course is run to allow for presentation of the content by visitors with recognised expertise in the topic. Comprehensive details of the course content will be made available on the School's website in advance of each offering. It should be noted that the course may not be available every year, hence you are encouraged to check the website for updates on upcoming offerings.
learning_outcomes: Communicate nuclear technology concepts and methodologies to technical stakeholders through written reports and mathematical analysis.
Analyse the technical application of advanced disciplinary nuclear knowledge as specified by the topic.
Evaluate technical literature, data, and methodologies to asess real world applications of the nuclear technology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nuclear Engineering Design
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Nuclear Engineering Design is a capstone course in the Nuclear Engineering Honours specialistion which gives students an opportunity to integrate their knowledge and nuclear engineering skills from preceding courses to design a nuclear fission reactor. Working in small groups, students divide the key elements of reactor design - reactor physics, thermal hydraulics and nuclear materials – among team members and produce a combined design report, backed up by individual reports on the rationale for design choices in their area of specialization. Various offerings of the course have targeted reactor designs for powering space missions, naval propulsion, and small and modular microreactor designs for disaster response and remote power systems, such as mines and forward operating army base. Students are assisted by the detailed functional requirements specification for the reactor design, provided in week one, lectures on key topics, and guidance from teaching staff specialized in each of the three topic areas. The assessments encourage students to self-evaluate justify their design choices, leading to technical contestability as an important outcome.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced techniques in nuclear engineering to analyse reactor dynamics, thermal-hydraulic performance, or fuel cycle planning, based on operational scenarios.
Communicate nuclear engineering concepts and design decisions to technical stakeholders through written reports, presentations, and peer discussions.
Develop a nuclear fission reactor and thermal power plant design that meets mission objectives while balancing constraints.
Evaluate technical decisions in reactor design and defend proposed solutions by applying principles of reactor physics, thermal hydraulics, and materials science.
Specify safety margins in nuclear reactor design to address engineering uncertainties and human error.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ATOM3003 and ATOM4001 and DESN3000

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aboriginal Sydney
syllabus_overview: In this course students are introduced to Aboriginal Sydney through local written and oral histories, as well as notable works in film, performance, television and art, seeking to make visible Aboriginal experiences, lives and connections to place in the city. Different approaches to urban history and to understanding the relationship between identity, memory and place are discussed against the broader context of imperial and colonial history and the marginalisation of Aboriginal land and heritage. With a specific focus on doing place-specific research, students are encouraged to get outside of the classroom and visit the places they are learning about.
learning_outcomes: Explain and reflect on different approaches to writing about Aboriginal histories, lives and connections to Sydney as an Aboriginal place: particularly in areas of spatial history, critical geography and oral history.
Deploy your critical, scholarly and historical investigations to write a short paper that communicates the value of place-specific research
Evaluate the Aboriginal Sydney archive in relation to imperial and colonial practices of history-making and Australian historiography

Identify and relate central course concepts, including identity, memory and power, to interpret the cultural and political significance of objects, symbols, and stories associated with specific sites in Sydney.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Australia
syllabus_overview: Indigenous Australia is the gateway course to the Indigenous Studies Major. In this course students will gain an understanding of the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, peoples and societies. A central focus of the course is the ways in which the philosophical frameworks of Indigenous knowledge systems continue to inform contemporary Indigenous practice that continues to shape Indigenous identities today. Taught from a range of perspectives, students will develop an understanding of social, cultural, political, economic, and ecological aspects of Indigenous Knowledge, which are key foundational elements to the Indigenous Studies Major.
learning_outcomes: Explain the diversity and complexity of Indigenous Australian knowledge, cultures and identities;
Identify arguments and key concepts in Indigenous Studies literature;
Critically consider the impact of different disciplinary approaches to the study of Indigenous Australia;
Describe the changing contexts in which Indigenous knowledge and culture are developed and practiced;
Communicate respectfully and responsibly about Indigenous knowledge systems and traditions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: What's this, then? Blak pop culture!
syllabus_overview: There’s been something of a renaissance in Blak pop culture in recent decades. From children's TV shows to literary fiction, through film and music in every genre, sports broadcasting, memes and viral protest movements, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander creatives have made the most of changing media environments to find and reach new audiences. In this course, we’ll engage with a range of Blak pop culture. We’ll listen to music and watch cartoons. Along the way, you’ll learn to critically interpret and analyse popular culture and constructively engage in debates involving the politics of representation. You’ll learn about the entanglement of popular culture and power. We’ll focus especially on how Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander creatives have leveraged this complex to advance Indigenous interests.
learning_outcomes: Communicate respectfully and effectively using digital tools, platforms and/or media appropriate to a range of audiences
Evaluate the impact of the production and circulation of Indigenous-authored popular culture on advancing collective Indigenous interests
Critically analyse popular representations of Indigeneity in Australia
Explain relationships between popular culture and power
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Political Thought in 20th Century Australia
syllabus_overview: Indigenous Political Thought explores the history of Indigenous resistance, activism and political organisation in Australia during the twentieth century, and its ongoing legacies. It studies ideas and ideologies, such as self-determination and Black Power, that influenced Indigenous political leaders and movements, situating these within wider contemporary social, political, and economic contexts. During the course, students analyse relevant contemporary texts produced by Indigenous political activists revealing recurring themes, directions, tensions, successes and legacies of Indigenous political thought and activism.
learning_outcomes: Communicate research findings orally and/or in writing accurately and effectively in diverse media.
Examine how Indigenous political thought and activism responded to its contemporary sociopolitical and economic environment.
Analyse, critically read and draw from primary and secondary sources, and synthesize research findings to produce a well-supported and coherent argument.
Identify political ideas and ideologies that influenced Indigenous political leaders and movements and describe their continuing relevance.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 30 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reclaiming Material Culture
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is on the role of museums and art galleries in the representation of Indigenous peoples and their cultures. The course begins with an introduction to Indigenous material culture, in both pre-contact and contact Australia. Students will also learn about the collection, study and display of Indigenous objects by museums and galleries. In this context disciplines of anthropology, ethnography, archaeology and museology are examined. Particular attention is given to the ways in which we can study objects and their different meanings as they journey from Indigenous contexts to non-Indigenous institutions. Students undertake an excursion to one or more local museums and participate in interactive seminar discussion as part of this course.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the representation of Indigenous material culture held in museums and collecting institutions.
Locate, assess, and analyse a variety of sources about Indigenous material culture, and synthesise research findings into a simple, logical and coherent argument.
Communicate research findings and views, individually and in groups, accurately and effectively using a variety of techniques (written, spoken, visual).
Evaluate methods used by collecting institutions to display Indigenous material culture, and assess their overall effect on various audiences.
Illustrate the role of Indigenous material culture in representing Indigenous peoples and cultures in the past and present museums and institutions.
Analyse the way in which objects change in purpose and function as they move through, and within varying Indigenous cultural and non-Indigenous institutional contexts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 30 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Issues in Indigenous Politics
syllabus_overview: Contemporary Issues in Indigenous Politics examines contemporary debates in Australian Indigenous affairs, placing an emphasis on the political contexts within which these debates take place. Students will learn to analyse political debates in Indigenous affairs in terms of the history of state strategies to transform Indigenous populations and Indigenous peoples' strategies to retain control over their collective cultural, political and economic development. The course encourages students to consider the impact of powerful interests, ideology and political institutions in constraining and enabling political participation by Indigenous people and communities. It also explores different models of political representation and engagement in the context of contemporary debates around recognition, sovereignty and treaty.
learning_outcomes: Examine, critically read and synthesize research findings from a range of sources;
Analyse the role of interests and institutions in shaping political decision making affecting Indigenous Australians;
Develop and effectively communicate an argument which is persuasive and substantiated.
Identify and evaluate the role of political ideology in contemporary debates in Indigenous affairs;
Critically analyse contemporary Issues in Indigenous politics in terms of structure and agency;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 30 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous People and Public Policy
syllabus_overview: This course aims to develop student understanding of the role of public policy in shaping Indigenous communities. It considers case studies of policy development by Australian Commonwealth, State and Territory authorities. It provides students with a theoretical framework for understanding policy and policy development processes and observing how key actors and institutions shape policy outcomes. The course considers opportunities for participation and engagement in policy formulation, and reflects on past policies which have contributed to Indigenous disadvantage and marginalisation. Students will critically analyse past and current policies and develop their understanding of the important role that policy plays in shaping community.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively with others to analyse policy development for and with Indigenous peoples
Explain key elements of the policy making process and describe the political, cultural and historical contexts in which policy is developed
Critically analyse policy documents and relevant texts in relation to their potential impact on Indigenous people and communities and formulate appropriate policy recommendations
Identify and assess key mechanisms of participation and engagement in the policy process
Analyse the role of key actors and institutions in shaping policy for Indigenous people and communities in Australia
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 30 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Science of Indigenous Knowledges
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the history, philosophy, theory, and methods of Western science and ethnoscience. Students will critique the development, application, and dissemination of traditional Indigenous knowledge about the natural world, including astronomy, weather, medicine, geography, and mathematics. ATSI2015 Science of Indigenous Knowledge provides a framework for students to explore the history and development of science in both Western and Indigenous contexts by learning how knowledge systems are developed and how this knowledge is passed down to successive generations through oral tradition and material culture. Students learn about the history of colonial "scientific" practices that disempowered Indigenous people and led to environmental damage and unsustainable practices. Students will discover ways in which Indigenous Knowledge can inform and benefit Western science, and investigate how scientists and Indigenous communities are now collaborating to provide new technologies and developing sustainable practices that are beneficial to all. Students will use the tools they learn to benefit their careers and practices to move toward a sustainable and mutually beneficial future.
learning_outcomes: Think critically, independently, reflectively and analytically about the nature of science and Indigenous Knowledges;
Understand how scientific knowledge is encoded in Indigenous cultures by analysing oral and material culture;
Demonstrate ways in which the students' fields of study can be enhanced and informed by Indigenous Knowledges;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 30 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Gender, sexuality, and colonialisms
syllabus_overview: The course explores the ways in which gender, sexuality and variants of colonialism intersect in the past and present both in Australia and elsewhere. It encourages students to reflect on the entanglements between heteronormativity, colonialism, and settler colonialism. The course material covers a range of issues involving gender, sexuality, including land, art and popular culture, activism, Indigeneity, feminism, violence, and race. Particular attention is paid to gender and gender roles in colonial processes.
learning_outcomes: Appraise, reflect on and interpret different kinds of evidence about gender and race from a range of sources, and construct from research findings a nuanced and persuasive argument.
Articulate and interrogate concepts such as gender, gender roles, sexuality, masculinity and feminism in the context of Indigenous Studies.
Communicate ideas and research findings effectively in an informed and respectful manner using different techniques (written, spoken, visual).
Debate about different facets and complexities of gendered and inter-racial relations in contemporary Australia.

Analyse historical and popular media representations of gender and race, and consider the way in which these representations reflect and influence Indigenous and inter-racial gender relations in contemporary Australia.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 36 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Cultural Heritage and the Environment
syllabus_overview: This course explores Indigenous perspectives on, and aspirations for the management of Country, waterways, culture and heritage in Australia. The course is designed to refine student understandings of traditional ecological knowledge, Indigenous knowledge and its relationship to western natural resource sciences and ecology. By exploring intersections between cultural heritage management practices, the environment, Indigenous knowledges and the contemporary space, students will gain an insight into best practice models for cultural heritage management and associated practices of sustainability and maintenance of Australia's rich cultural heritage and the environment. A compulsory field trip for this course incurs an additional cost.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an understanding of Indigenous philosophies, knowledges, and perspectives in Indigenous cultural heritage and natural resource management practices, and their complex interface with Western science disciplines.

Critically analyse cultural heritage, environmental conservation and natural resource management laws, policies, and programs within Australia and describe the implications for Indigenous initiatives and aspirations for Country and Culture.
Demonstrate an appreciation of Indigenous knowledge and Indigenous relational ontological perspectives within an Aboriginal community context through a multidisciplinary setting.
Analyse the social, legal and political tensions and connections between Indigenous knowledge systems and contemporary land/environment conservation practices.
Apply self-reflexive skills that facilitate culturally based, place specific engagement with Indigenous cultural heritage and natural resource management practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 36 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Working with Indigenous Communities
syllabus_overview: This course helps you develop the skills and knowledge required to engage respectfully and effectively with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities. It builds your cultural and professional capability to work in diverse Indigenous contexts by fostering critical self-reflection and cultural awareness. The course introduces you to key principles of ethical engagement, consultation, collaboration, and co-design, essential when working in partnership with Indigenous communities and organisations. During the course we will explore strategies for enhancing strengths-based and culturally responsive policies that support self-determination and positive outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, communities and organisations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate Indigenous-led strategies for enhancing strengths-based and culturally responsive policies that support self-determination.

Articulate principles and practices required for respectful and meaningful communication with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities in a range of social, professional, and institutional contexts.
Critically reflect on your own prior learning and assumptions about working with Indigenous communities.
Apply principles of culturally responsive consultation and co-design to plan and develop projects with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in diverse contexts.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Race and Colonialism
syllabus_overview: There are (at least) two sides to the colonial relationship. In this class we focus on the ways in which colonialism is enmeshed with White knowledge traditions and cultures so that we can better understand the complex relationship between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australia. Students will be introduced to key concepts and thinkers in the fields of Critical Race and Whiteness theory and together we will apply them to everyday experience and popular culture. At the theory and application learning stage of the Indigenous Studies Major, this course will help students develop their understanding of identity politics that are deeply entangled with a variety of political and intellectual debates in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the construction and representation of race and ethnicity in both global and Australian social and political discourse;
Appraise, reflect on and interpret different kinds of evidence about race and ethnicity from a range of sources, and construct from research findings a nuanced and persuasive argument.
Analyse the social positioning and privileging of White knowledge, culture and identities;
Demonstrate the ability to lead and participate in respectful and productive discussions about race and ethnicity;
Demonstrate an appreciation of the significance of one's own social identity and position in relation to debates involving race and ethnicity;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 36 units of credit.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Studies Capstone
syllabus_overview: This is the Capstone course for students completing the Indigenous Studies Major. The course draws on content, themes and theories from all levels of the Indigenous Studies Major to consolidate understandings of the convergences that characterise the relations between Indigenous and non-Indigenous Australia. Students in this course will learn how to explore the deeper complexities of their chosen disciplines and Indigenous Australia, and practise ways to productively engage their boundaries, limits and agendas. Students will have the opportunity to refine their analytical and communicative capacities to navigate these boundaries as their preparation for professional practice or further study.
learning_outcomes: Organise and communicate research findings for an audience
Critically reflect on and analyse your personal and intellectual position in relation to Indigenous Studies as a field of scholarly inquiry
Differentiate between different theoretical traditions in the history of the field
Evaluate scholarly arguments about the aims and goals of Indigenous Studies scholarship
Apply knowledge and skills from across the major to independently construct a research question
