prerequisites: Prerequisite: 120 units of credit overall, enrolment in a major in Indigenous Studies and enrolled in the final semester of an Arts Faculty single or dual degree program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Resistance and Self-Determination in 19th Century Australia
syllabus_overview: This course explores Indigenous histories in Australia and their contemporary resonance. It offers students an overview of relationships between Indigenous peoples and settlers, centring Indigenous experiences and tracing some of the ways Indigenous people have enacted self-determination and made their own histories in varied contexts of settler colonialism. The course covers nineteenth century Indigenous travellers and entrepreneurs, examines violence and friendship, studies reserves and resistance, and historicises displacement and the many novel articulations of land rights. Students will also engage with debates about the representation of Indigenous pasts in the present, as well as completing in-depth and independent historical research.
learning_outcomes: Identify continuity and change in the context of Indigenous resistance and self-determination in 19th century Australia.
Review Indigenous histories in the context of the 19th century colonial world and in particular the British Empire.
Accurately and effectively communicate research findings in diverse media.
Examine, critically read and infer from relevant primary and secondary sources, and synthesise research findings to produce well supported and coherent accounts of Indigenous pasts.
Debate Indigenous and non-Indigenous perspectives on the colonial past, such as those over Indigenous agency, resistance, self-determination and accommodation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 36 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Indigenous Studies: Issues and Debates
syllabus_overview: The course is designed to build on and extend knowledge of Indigenous Studies developed over an undergraduate degree. The course will engage critically with current theoretical and conceptual debates and will introduce students to key international and Australian authors in the discipline. The course is designed to develop critical thinking and analytical skills in preparation for thesis work, and to help students to position their own research within the discipline of Indigenous Studies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and apply key concepts, theories and approaches in Indigenous Studies.
Locate and analyse relevant research literature related to a specific research topic.
Plan, design and execute self-directed research into a specific topic in Indigenous Studies..
Demonstrate effective, clear, and informative written communication skills.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise the work of key authors in Indigenous Studies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Studies Honours I
syllabus_overview: A 6 UOC thesis in Indigenous Studies to be completed as part of the 30 UOC of thesis component in the Honours Program. Students are also required to complete 18 UOC of coursework.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective, clear, and informative written communication skills.
Design, develop, and manage a major research project.
Identify and make an original contribution to research in Indigenous Studies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Studies Honours III
syllabus_overview: A 12 UOC thesis in Indigenous Studies to be completed as part of the 30 UOC of thesis component in the Honours Program. Students are also required to complete 18 UOC of coursework.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective, clear, and informative written communication skills.
Identify and make an original contribution to research in Indigenous Studies.
Design, develop, and manage a major research project.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Design in Indigenous Studies
syllabus_overview: This course is a core component of the Honours year in Indigenous Studies. It includes an intensive workshop on research design and methodology at the start of the academic year, and regular workshops through terms 1 and 2 which will develop skills in research, analytical and writing.The course as a whole is designed to prepare students for designing and carrying out an Honours thesis project in Indigenous Studies. Students will be exposed to research methods and practices in the field in the context of approaches in the social sciences and humanities. They will have the opportunity to discuss and explore some of the major contemporary approaches to Indigenous Studies and some of the key issues raised by academic research and writing in the field, including ethical implications of research. Students will be well prepared to complete an Honours thesis, and will have the necessary basis for further research. Note: This is a 12 UOC course. You will enrol in 6 UOC in each of two successive terms with a result reported by a single grade at the end of the second 6 UOC course.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate theoretical and methodological approaches which are used in Indigenous Studies.
Identify and respond appropriately to ethical issues raised by research on Indigenous issues, culture and people.
Locate, critically analyse, evaluate and synthesise relevant research literature related to a specific research topic
Design and defend a complex extended research project in Indigenous Studies.
Demonstrate effective, clear, and informative written and oral communication skills.
Critically analyse and apply key concepts, traditions, theories and approaches in Indigenous Studies

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Business Program (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Indigenous Pre-Business course is an intensive four-week residential course for prospective Indigenous students wanting to enrol in an undergraduate degree in the Australian Business School at UNSW. The course has been designed to assess your academic potential and to provide a realistic environment within which you can develop the knowledge and skills to manage your undergraduate studies effectively. The Pre-Business course will engage you in learning activities associated with the following business disciplines: Accounting; Business Finance; Business Law; People and Organisational Management; Economics; Information Systems and Marketing. There is a strong focus on the acquisition of the study and learning skills required to undertake Business studies at the university level. Students are also given opportunities to apply their learning through case studies, written and oral presentations and site visits. Entry into the Indigenous Pre-Business course is based on a completed application form and an interview with staff from Nura Gili and the Australian School of Business. On successful completion of the course, measured through participation, assessments and a final interview, students may then be offered a place in a Business degree at UNSW. For further information please contact Nura Gili at UNSW.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their ability to collaborate actively and respectfully in class and group activities
Understand how to analyse and structure arguments within various business disciplines
Understand the different components an academic task for a variety of business disciplines
Understand a range of fundamental concepts within a variety of business disciplines.
Understand how to structure, write, and orally present, academic information in various business disciplines
Understand the importance of time-management and planning skills, and self-directed learning for success in a business discipline
prerequisites: Prereq: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Law Program (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Indigenous Pre-Law course is an intensive three-week residential course for prospective Indigenous students wanting to enrol in a Bachelor of Laws at UNSW. The course has been designed to assess students’ academic potential and provide a realistic environment for them to develop the knowledge and skills to manage their undergraduate studies effectively. The course focuses on teaching students a broad range of academic skills and legal knowledge. Skills include critical thinking, reading, writing and oral presentations, so that students are well prepared to undertake tertiary studies. The course is also directed at ensuring that students are equipped with foundational knowledge about the Australian legal system that will support their learning in first year law courses. Entry into the Indigenous Pre-Law course is based on a completed application form and lodgement of supporting documentation, which is then assessed by Nura Gili and Faculty staff. On occasion, applicants may be required to attend an interview as part of this assessment process. On successful completion of the course, measured through participation, assessments and a final interview, students may then be offered a place in a Law degree at UNSW. For further information please contact Nura Gili at UNSW.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on different ways law is practised in the community
Discuss basic legal reasoning and problem-solving techniques relevant to first-year law studies.
Use basic tools to locate legal materials to support tertiary law studies
Describe the origins, structures, and functions of the Australian legal system, including its historical and ongoing impact on Indigenous peoples and communities.
Apply critical thinking, time-management skills, and communication skills in both academic and legal contexts to support success in future tertiary law studies.
Use client interview skills to prepare and deliver submissions in a legal advocacy setting
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Medicine and Health Program (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Pre-Medicine and Health Program (PMHP) is an intensive academic program that runs for three weeks at the University of New South Wales in Sydney. The program will introduce you to some of the content covered in first year Medicine and Health Faculty undergraduate courses in Dietetics, Exercise Physiology, Medicine, Pharmacy, Physiotherapy and Optometry (Vision Science). The program will also develop your academic skills to enable you to more effectively engage with this content.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of interprofessional communication for effective multidisciplinary healthcare, in the context of First Peoples primary health care.
Apply reflective skills to explore how your cultural, lived experiences and personal attributes will influence your professional identity and future practice as a health professional.
Identify and describe the fundamentals of human structure and function in health and disease.
Demonstrate effective academic written and oral communication and research skills.
prerequisites: Prereq: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Social Work Program (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Indigenous Pre-Social Work course is designed for Indigenous students wanting to enter the Bachelor of Social Work or any of the combined Social Work degrees. Students will undertake a variety of seminars and activities designed to assist them to prepare for entry into social work and to develop an understanding of the social work course and the social work profession.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate basic academic skills in writing, speaking and the starting skills of critical thought. Demonstrate an understanding of the social work course and also what is required to be a practicing social worker
prerequisites: Prereq: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Teacher Education Program (Secondary) (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Pre-Teacher Education Program is an academic preparatory and enabling program designed for Indigenous students to undertake further undergraduate degree studies in education for the pupose of becoming secondary school teachers. The program focuses on the following topics: an introduction to teaching academic literacy and classroom interaction how students learn the social context of schooling Indigenous perspectives in education
learning_outcomes: Use the UNSW Library website for introductory research
Demonstrate academic skills in writing, comprehension and critical thinking
Give a short oral presentation to a class
Understand and apply the time management skills required of university students
Demonstrate an understanding of the teacher education program and what is required for the profession
prerequisites: Prereq: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Pre-Science and Engineering Program (Indigenous)
syllabus_overview: The Indigenous Pre-Science/Engineering course is an intensive four-week residential course for prospective Indigenous students wanting to enrol in an undergraduate degree in the faculties of Science or Engineering at UNSW. The course has been designed to assess your academic potential and to provide a realistic environment within which you can develop the knowledge and skills to manage your undergraduate studies effectively. The Pre-Science/Engineering course will engage you in learning activities associated with the following disciplines: Mathematics, Chemistry, Biology, Psychology, Sustainable Engineering, Computer Science. There is a strong focus on the acquisition of the study and learning skills required to undertake studies at the university level. Students are also given opportunities to apply their learning through fieldwork, written and oral presentations. Entry into the Indigenous Pre-Science/Engineering course would require students to apply through Nura Gili. Students would have to: Attach documentation to confirm their Aboriginal and/or Torres Strait Islander descent as part of the application process. Lodge an application with the Universities Admissions Centre (UAC) for the UNSW undergraduate degree program that they wish to study Complete the online Nura Gili, UNSW Indigenous Preparatory Programs application and attach all supporting documentation. On successful completion of the course, measured through participation, assessments and a final interview, students may then be offered a place in a relevant degree at UNSW. For further information please contact Nura Gili at UNSW.
learning_outcomes: Develop critical thinking skills around key concepts, challenges and developments in Science and/or Engineering
Begin to work independently and in teams to explore their understanding of the fundamentals of biology, chemistry, psychology, sustainable engineering and computer science
Verbally present information to peers and provide critical feedback to peers
Generate questions for research and discussion
Grow in their capacity to learn new and complex information and skills and reproduce it in a variety of formats
Have developed lab skills and be able to produce a lab report
Begin to develop skills in reflective writing describing accurate and neutral descriptions of own behaviours, strengths and weaknesses, emotions, and intentions.
Develop further skills in core competency areas such as Mathematics
Begin to identify questions and learning needs arising from lectures, tutorials and other teaching activities.
Have developed skills in academic writing and information searching strategies
Have an understanding and an awareness of individual skills and knowledge required to study Science and/or Engineering
prerequisites: Prereq: Enrolled in 7019

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aeronautical Knowledge for Aviation Managers
syllabus_overview: Aviation management involves the overseeing of various aviation departments and being able to communicate, coordinate and manage readily and effectively when addressing many complex aviation challenges and scenarios. Therefore, to be a successful aviation manager, you must have a solid foundational understanding of key aviation concepts from which to draw upon during the various stages of your career and day-to-day responsibilities. This course explores concepts including the principles of flight; aeroplane performance, components, and systems; regulations; meteorology; and threat and error management. There is also a direct emphasis on the aspects of operational aeronautical knowledge relevant to aviation managers which will be taught through a combination of lectures, tutorials, and scenario-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Describe aeroplane components, systems, and principles of flight for normal and transport category aeroplanes, including calculating solutions to aeroplane performance problems.
Access typical operational regulatory documents and explain their application to fatigue, safety, drug and alcohol, security, and compliance management
Explain meteorological concepts, interpret weather forecasts and reports, and determine their effect on flight, including flight planning.
Categorise operational and systemic threats, errors, and undesired aircraft states, and nominate appropriate countermeasures.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aeronautical Knowledge
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students with no prior aviation flight experience who are enrolled in programs that include airborne flying training for the award of flight crew licences. Through the use of face-to-face lectures and instruction, students will undertake all aeronautical knowledge training in the units of competency specified in the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998, Part 61 Manual of Standards, for the Recreational and Private Pilot Licences.
learning_outcomes: Define and explain basic meteorological concepts and describe their effect on flight.
Explain the components, methods of operation and, applicable cockpit indications in relation to single engine aeroplane systems.
Define and explain basic aerodynamic concepts and describe how these apply to single engine aeroplanes in flight.
Define and apply visual navigation concepts to day flying and calculate solutions to navigation problems after interpreting navigation data.
Maintain, interpret, and apply the relevant regulatory documents to safely conduct Day Visual Flight Rules private flight operations.
Define and explain basic human factors problems that affect Day VFR flying.
Calculate take-off and landing performance, and determine weight, and balance solutions using typical performance and loading systems.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998, Part 61 Manual of standards, for the Recreational and Private Pilot Licences.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolled in Aviation Program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Airworthiness Management
syllabus_overview: Safety is paramount in aviation and core to this is airworthiness . With a focus on Transport Category Aircraft, the Airworthiness Management course introduces the concepts of risk and safety assessment, before exploring key aircraft design principles, the establishment of initial airworthiness, through-life continuing airworthiness management and aircraft maintenance. Case studies are used to illustrate airworthiness responses from manufacturers, regulators, operators and maintenance organisations to incidents and accidents. Students learn first-hand from an airworthiness management industry expert, who will take them through real-life examples destined to build foundation knowledge for a career in aviation.
learning_outcomes: Describe how airworthiness issues may arise during design, manufacture, operations, and maintenance, and how deficiencies in airworthiness may be corrected by actions from manufacturers, regulators, operators, and maintenance organisations.
Identify the Australian Civil Aviation Safety Authority Regulations which govern airworthiness standards and certification, continuing airworthiness, and maintenance.
Describe the concepts of initial airworthiness and continuing airworthiness.
Describe various continuing airworthiness management activities and types of aircraft maintenance tasks, and have awareness of different contemporary airworthiness management issues.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Human Factors: The Safety Science of Human Performance
syllabus_overview: Human performance is highly dependent on a number of factors, some of which are under our direct control while others are outside our sphere of control. Nonetheless, with the correct application of knowledge, planning and design, systems can be designed with the human in mind to facilitate human performance. This course examines human behaviour from a theoretical perspective, with the intent to optimise the relationship between humans and their environment. With the focus primarily on the individual, this course examines basic human cognition, including perception, memory, information processing, and decision-making. These principles are then applied to various industries, including aviation to understand the design of systems (i.e., flight deck, consoles, aircraft, etc.) for human use.
learning_outcomes: Appraise individual and operational factors capable of affecting human performance in aviation.
Discuss the cognitive aspects of human performance.
Apply and appropriately adapt writing and communication skills and strategies for various stakeholders, needs and contexts.
Evaluate the effectiveness and intuitiveness of physical objects/apparatuses used within aviation, and redesign those which are not considered user-friendly.
Assess existing systems, processes, and design, from a human factors perspective, and translate these to the aviation industry.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Transport Economics
syllabus_overview: This course covers the economics of airlines, and starts by introducing students to the language and data of the aviation business before analysing the economics of the demand for, and supply of aviation services. The analysis of airline demand focuses on the drivers of demand, travel purposes, mode of transport substitution, destination substitution, demand complements and the various price elasticities of demand. The course then explores the supply-side of the aviation business, which involves an investigation of airline revenue in the short and medium runs, airline cost and profitability. Students will investigate the curvature of the airline profit function and how it may be optimised. The course then moves onto additional topics in aviation economics such as airline relationships and the economics of oil and jet fuel markets. Students are provided with a variety of learning opportunities during the course through a combination of online and face-to-face lectures, and case-based activities that align the course material with current issues in aviation and foster meaningful discussion.
learning_outcomes: Explain why airlines form relationships and the impact of those relationships.
Describe the drivers of unit cost, yield and revenue and the impact of changes in the passenger seat factor and capacity on airline profitability.
Identify and access key information sources for aviation operational and financial data.
Recall and appropriately use aviation business language and terminology, and the metrics used to describe airline operational and financial performance.
Build economic models of the historical movements in oil and jet fuel prices for understanding their future values.
Describe the forces that drive the demand side of the aviation market and the price elasticity of demand.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Human Factors
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students a detailed understanding about ‘why individuals behave the way that they do’, from a safety perspective. This will be achieved by providing students with an advanced-level of understanding of current theories, and key conceptual and applied models relating to human performance and decision-making. This information will be used in a variety of applied settings (I.e., aviation, road, maritime, and research laboratories) to understand the safety implications of human behaviour, and importantly methods to prevent and or reduce the implications of unsafe acts.
learning_outcomes: Classify human performance based on various applied taxonomies
Apply and demonstrate advanced learning, writing and communication skills consistent with graduate attributes
Describe the cognitive processes that lead to unsafe acts, including the impact of moderating factors
Explain how individuals process information and formulate decisions, including associated theories
Assess the viability and utility of methods to reduce unsafe acts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Airborne Drone Management
syllabus_overview: Whether known as airborne drones, unmanned aerial vehicles or remotely piloted aircraft systems, this form of flight is permeating the civil aviation sector across recreational, commercial and research activities. Drones come in varying shapes and sizes and can perform processes for numerous industries such as medicine, military, humanitarian aid, retail, and construction in safer and more efficient ways than crewed air flight. By extension, the drone industry is also an entrepreneurial frontier that calls for a diverse set of skills, current knowledge, and experience to manage high value enterprise operations. In this course, students will develop a holistic, systematic understanding of commercial drone operations, engaging in experiential learning and teamwork. They will develop the basis for a company that uses drones for safe, legal, and effective commercial operations. This culminates in a project planning every aspect of a commissioned job set by an industry client. The course is delivered fully online with asynchronous, interactive, self-paced content each week, and regular synchronous online meetings with course instructors to support the project activities. This course is suitable for students across a variety of disciplines who wish to develop drone operations skills and knowledge to support their future career.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the operational feasibility of a given remotely piloted aircraft mission under varying circumstances.
Explain the basic aeronautical principles relevant for remotely piloted aircraft systems (RPAS).
Critique the advantages and limitations of remotely piloted aircraft for data collection and research in relation to other existing airborne methods.
Describe the human factors principles relevant for safe and efficient remote piloting and remotely piloted aircraft systems.
Describe the legislative and regulatory framework guiding the governance of remotely piloted aircraft in Australia.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Navigation
syllabus_overview: The course covers all the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS CASR 91 MOS & CASR 135 MOS for Commercial Pilot Licence level Navigation, specifically the PNVC and CNVC units of competency. Through a combination of lectures, tutorials and individual briefing, students learn about operational situations and problems related to commercial flying operations, and skills for relating theoretical aspects of airborne navigation to practical aviation contexts.
learning_outcomes: Relate theoretical concepts to practical aspects of visual and instrument airborne navigation.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the PNVC and CNVC units of competency.
Calculate numerical solutions to navigation problems using operational data and a circular navigation computer.
Define and explain concepts applicable to airborne navigation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and enrolment in Program 3980 or 3928

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Meteorology
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to all of the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for commercial pilot licence level meteorology, specifically the PMTC and CMTC units of competency. The course explores key concepts of aviation meteorology, with a focus on understanding legislation relating to aviation meteorology, and information in aviation weather forecasts and reports. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to assess retention and understanding of student learning.
learning_outcomes: Amend and keep up to date a personal copy of current legislation versions, interpret and apply legislation relating to aviation meteorology.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the PMTC and CMTC units of competency.
Decode and apply aviation weather forecasts and reports for various flight contexts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and Enrolment in Program 3980 or 3928

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Human Factors, Flight Rules and Air Law
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to all of the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for commercial pilot licence level Human Factors, Flight Rules and Air Law, specifically, the CHFC, CFRA and CFRC units of competency. The course explores key concepts of commercial human factors, flight rules, and air law, with a focus on understanding human factors applicable to flight crew, the relationship between theoretical human factors concepts and conditions found in piloting aircraft, and the theoretical and practical aspects of aviation law relating to flight crew and Pilots in Command of commercial Visual Flight Rules (VFR) flight. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the CHFC, CFRA & CFRC units of competency.
Explain theoretical and practical aspects of aviation law as it relates to flight crew and Pilot in Command of commercial VFR flight.
Relate theoretical Human Factors concepts to conditions found in piloting aircraft.
Define and explain Human Factors concepts applicable to flight crew.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and Enrolment in Program 3980 or 3928

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Aircraft General Knowledge
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to all of the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for commercial pilot licence level Aircraft General Knowledge (Aeroplane), specifically the PAKC, PAKA (Section 2), CAKC (Sections 2.1 – 2.5) and CAKA units of competency. The course explores key concepts of commercial aircraft, with a focus on understanding the components, method of operation, and applicable cockpit indications in relation to aeroplane systems, and the relationship of theoretical concepts and practical systems information in Aircraft Flight Manuals. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Relate theoretical concepts to the practical systems information found in Aircraft Flight Manuals.
Explain the components, method of operation and applicable cockpit indications in relation to aeroplane systems.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the PAKC, PAKA (Section 2), CAKC (Sections 2.1 – 2.5) and CAKA units of competency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and enrolled in 3980

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Aerodynamics
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the aeronautical knowledge training required by Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 Part 61 Manual of Standards for commercial pilot licence level Aerodynamics, specifically the Commerical Aerodynamics - all aircraft categories (CADC) and Commercial Aerodynamics - aeroplane (CADA) units of competency. The course explores key concepts of commercial aerodynamics, with a focus on understanding aerodynamic concepts applicable to low-speed propeller driven aeroplanes, and the relationship between theoretical aerodynamics concepts and design features, controls and limitations found in low-speed propeller driven aeroplanes. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Relate theoretical aerodynamic concepts to design features, controls and limitations found in low speed propeller driven aeroplanes.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the CADC and CADA units of competency.
Define and explain aerodynamic concepts applicable to low speed propeller driven aeroplanes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and enrolled in 3980

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Operation, Performance and Planning
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to all of the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the grant of a Commercial Pilot Licence specifically POPC, POPA, COPC and COPA units of competency. The course explores key concepts of commercial operation, performance, and flight planning with a focus on planning and operating flights under day Visual Flight Rules (VFR) conditions and performing key calculations for performance and typical loading scenarios for different aeroplanes. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Calculate weight and balance solutions for typical loading scenarios that apply to light aeroplanes.
Define and explain concepts used in planning and operating flights under day VFR conditions.
Calculate take-off, landing, enroute, climb and descent performance for piston engine aeroplanes.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the POPC, POPA, COPC and COPA units of competency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1111 and enrolled in 3980

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Drone Operations Management
syllabus_overview: The use of drones for applications like environmental and wildlife monitoring, logistics, security, and more is a rapidly-evolving frontier. A diverse set of entrepreneurial skills, industry knowledge and technical insight is needed to manage high value enterprise operations. Through interactive sessions and project-based learning, students will gain a broad understanding of current and emerging commercial drone operations, covering topics such as safety and regulations, operational planning, analysis software and workflows, and creating viable financial models. Students will learn how to address real-world challenges with solutions that involve drones, developing the basis for a mock company that works through the step-by-step planning of every aspect of a commissioned job set by a real industry or internal (UNSW) client, and presenting a comprehensive job proposal to their stakeholder. Students from Engineering, Science and elsewhere in the university are encouraged to contact the course convenor regarding suitability of the course for their studies and career. It is designed to be an accessible introduction to commercial drone operations. There will be an introductory drone flying session and other hands-on work, though the course focus is on industry-standard operations planning and management.
learning_outcomes: Create external-facing materials that demonstrate an industry-standard level of planning for a commercial job.
Compare and contrast different financial and business models for drone services or technologies.
Explain the regulatory frameworks for governance of drones in Australia and how they influence practical commercial operations.
Assess the challenges of guidance, navigation, and data acquisition approaches for specific autonomous/remote piloted system scenarios.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: MATH1041 OR equivalent (as reviewed and approved by the Course Convenor)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Instrument Rating
syllabus_overview: This course is for students undertaking flight training at UNSW within the Bachelor of Aviation (Flying) program and Bachelor of Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems) program. The course focuses on equipping students with the ability to fly in all-weather operations, in multi-engine aeroplanes, and during commercial operations. The course consists of face-to-face lectures and synchronous online lectures. Relevant subject topics, IREX and GNSS, from the CASR 1998, Part 61 MOS are designed to help students achieve the aeronautical knowledge requirements for the issue of an Australian Instrument Rating.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of single pilot threat and error management to the conduct of Instrument Flight Rules flying operations;
Amend and keep up to date a personal copy of current legislation versions, interpret and apply the comprehensive set of regulatory publications applicable to the instrument flight rules.
Apply the aeronautical knowledge that underpins flying operations undertaken by night and in Instrument Meteorological Conditions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolled in 3980 OR 3928, and completion of AVIA2111-2113

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Drone Imagery and Sensing
syllabus_overview: This course features hands-on, learn-by-doing with drones for the capture and processing of remote sensing data and photographic/video imagery for applications such as aerial surveying and mapping, search and rescue, cinematography, environmental monitoring and more. Students from Engineering, Science and elsewhere in the university are encouraged to contact the course convenor regarding suitability of the course for their studies and career. It is designed to be an accessible introduction to work involving applied robotics for anyone with an interest in drones/UAVs and the impact they are having on our understanding of the world around us. Students will complete projects that cover essential workflows for aerial imaging and data-gathering such as risk management, flight planning for manual and autonomous flight, and the outputs of image-based data using different techniques including AI-enabled analysis and visualisation. Through a combination of interactive lectures, tutorials, and fieldwork, students will learn how to apply the introduced knowledge to their own real-world flights and post-processing for specific challenges like a creative self-directed videography assignment, making detailed 3D models of buildings and terrain, and scientific analysis of Sydney’s coastline.
learning_outcomes: Assess the safety, economic and technical viability of an end-to-end drone information system workflow.
Explain the capabilities of common drone-mounted sensors, and the type of practical problems these can solve.
Explain and demonstrate the basic scientific principles of photogrammetry and data-based visualisation.
Describe and demonstrate the main factors determining the quality of aerial photography and cinematography.
Design and implement flight plans to achieve safe and efficient real-world mapping and remote sensing tasks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH1041

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Drones and Society
syllabus_overview: Drones and related robotic/autonomous platforms of wildly-varying shapes and sizes are permeating society across recreational, commercial, defence and scientific uses. This is due to their ability to use autonomy and AI to perform processes for numerous industries such as humanitarian aid, logistics, and infrastructure and environmental monitoring in far safer and more efficient ways than crewed air flight - in many sectors, drones save lives or achieve exceptional improved outcomes for communities. Yet, they can also have applications that raise important ethical and privacy questions to be discussed. This course will cover historical, current, and future uses of drones and the legal/regulatory, ethical, and technological considerations that drive the evolving acceptance or resistance to their use. The course is delivered online with asynchronous, interactive, self-paced content each week. In addition, course staff will be available online for weekly student interaction and assistance for project work, with synchronous discussion and presentation sessions related to assessment. Fun hands-on sessions flying drones (<2kg) on the UNSW Aviation Kensington campus will be available as an option to any students enrolled in this course at no additional cost. Through these sessions, students can gain practical in-person experience to complement their learning in this course.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the operational and economic feasibility of a specific “drones for good” mission.
Discuss the use of drones and related emerging technologies for solving societal challenges while analysing the social, ethical, and safety considerations involved.
Critically evaluate the implications and consequences of using drones and other AI-enabled robotics for a variety of applications.
Describe the legislative and regulatory framework guiding the governance of drones in Australia and globally.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Law and Regulations
syllabus_overview: The aviation industry is a highly regulated and legislated sector. In alignment with this, an aviation professional should be conversant with, and knowledgeable of, the law as it applies to the aviation industry. However, although aviation professionals are highly trained technicians or managers, their training does not necessarily include significant knowledge and skills development in the law and legal systems. In fact, most sections of the aviation industry there are no formal requirements for training in the law or legal systems. Of course, there is a myriad of rules and regulations in aviation that must be known but that does not equate to training in statutory interpretation or the like. Aviation Law and Regulations focuses on providing a comprehensive overview of the regulatory structure of civil aviation in Australia and also an understanding of this structure within a legal context. Topics include the Australian legal system, contract law; employment law and administrative law; criminal law and commercial law; and airline operations. The course provides students with the opportunity to start developing the skills needed to become an aviation professional knowledgeable in both aviation and the law through case-based learning delivered by industry experts and assessments exploring current aviation and legal issues. Development of these skills, knowledge and confidence will empower students to make appropriate decisions for addressing aviation challenges in their careers, whilst accommodating the changing needs of society with consideration of aviation regulations and the law.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the law and its relationship to the aviation regulatory regime, legal principles and concepts, when considering various aviation industry situations.
Recall and describe the way in which the Australian legal system has been developed.
Describe the regulatory structure of aviation in Australia and how it operates within the legal system.
Explain the legal implications associated with various aviation personnel including the pilot-in-command.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Operations Research
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on modelling and data analytics in aviation and will explore these ideas from the viewpoint of practices in the aviation industry. Data analytics and Python programming skills are included to provide students with problem-solving skills in data preparation, data exploration and data modelling. Students are provided with computer programming training in the Python language. Tutorial sessions are an essential and significant part of this course. Major aviation models are introduced including regression models, clustering models and classification models. Assessments are based on aviation data projects to bring the relevance of model building and machine-learning practices to aviation data.
learning_outcomes: Implement data visualisation techniques and apply these to aviation data exploration.
Apply Python programming language proficiently to process data and conduct data exploration tasks.
Recall data modelling skills and statistical learning algorithms to build data models.
Develop mathematical models to investigate business challenges and create effective solutions.
prerequisites: MATH1041 OR equivalent experience (approval required from Course Authority)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Airline Marketing Strategies
syllabus_overview: This course begins with a classic approach to marketing management but focused on marketing within the airline industry. The approach is a practical one, addressing airline market research, product development, pricing and revenue management, distribution (a key area), and promotion. Theory is positioned in current airline marketing issues, and reinforced through synchronous learning and collaborative discussion facilitated by industry experts who provide a practical industry framework in which to test the subject content.
learning_outcomes: Conduct market segmentation analysis, using government and commercial databases for the purpose of optimising airline marketing.
Discuss the role of intermediaries in airline distribution.
Develop marketing planning and strategic planning processes from both a generic and an airline perspective.
Apply promotion and advertising techniques to develop campaigns, and sales or marketing pitches appropriate to the business model or market position of an airline.
Evaluate the use of airfare and pricing strategies as part of the broader aviation marketing context.
Explain how airline promotional tools, including advertising, online distribution, and social media, can be used effectively to enhance brand awareness and market dominance.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Security and Airport Management
syllabus_overview: This course is split into two parts: Aviation security; and Airport management Aviation is a complex set of procedures and activities that when brought together results in a secure and efficient transport system. Any interruption to that system, can and will have far reaching effects on public confidence and their expectations, government oversight, delays and costs to industry, and the potential for loss of life and suffering. Aviation security as applied to airlines and airports, must be risk based and outcomes focused. It must be tailored to the specifics of the airline or airport. Whilst it is conceded that approximately 80% of risks are known and common to all airports and airlines, the location, operating environment, brand and political stability will all provide unique challenges to the aviation security professional. Aviation security takes a layered approach to protecting an aircraft, passengers and crew. There is no one single measure that can be applied to mitigate the risk to zero. All risks must be identified and mitigated to an acceptable level. Aviation security is about reducing the risk whilst adding these elements to the aircraft. This course provides an insight into contemporary security issues of airlines and airports, aviation security standards and recommended practices, and aviation security principles and procedures. It will also develop your skills to ask, “What is the desired security outcome and can it be achieved in different ways?”. Unless otherwise stated, the Australian examples used throughout the course are typical of international practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify the difference between a prescriptive and outcomes based regulatory framework for the management of aviation security.
Ask appropriate security questions when dealing with security threats and/or risks and exploring potential security outcomes.

Describe the various aspects of airport management, including a consideration of how airports work, the critical elements that make airports successful and key issues with the current airport management climate.
Apply different regulatory approaches when dealing with modern day airport and aviation security challenges.
Recall and apply the principles of dealing with aviation security risks to a variety of aviation scenarios.
Describe the historical development of airports and aviation security and the international and Australian frameworks underpinning the aviation regulatory environment;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Quantitative and Qualitative Research Methods in Aviation
syllabus_overview: Research design, data collection and analysis are imperative for understanding key areas of aviation such as economic trends, ground operation efficiency, sustainability and environmental impact and passenger satisfaction. Where quantitative data can allow us to measure, assess and predict trends such as levels of safety in an aviation environment, qualitative data can give us insights such as first-hand accounts and non-numerical findings such as passenger perception and customer satisfaction. Both quantitative and qualitative data are necessary to gain business intelligence in aviation, and the combination of the two provides a holistic perspective to address challenges in the aviation industry. In this course, students are taught designing research projects for typical real-world questions, various methods of collecting quantitative and qualitative data and ways to analyse them efficiently and effectively as well as ethical pitfalls and their avoidance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate quantitative and qualitative aviation-centric data, and effectively communicate findings and recommendations to various stakeholders in the aviation industry.
Identify and evaluate sources of bias and limitation in various quantitative and qualitative research methodologies and project design.
Identify and appropriately use quantitative and qualitative research methods to achieve reliable research design and data collection approaches for investigating aviation-based challenges.
Apply various data analysis skills and software to perform data analyses on diverse sets of data relating to different scenarios and challenges in aviation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Security and Air Freight Logistics
syllabus_overview: This course is split into two parts - Aviation Security and Air Freight Logistics. Aviation is a complex set of procedures and activities that when brought together results in a secure and efficient transport system. Any interruption to that system, can and will have far-reaching effects on public confidence and their expectations, government oversight, delays and costs to industry, and the potential for loss of life and suffering. Aviation security as applied to airlines and airports must be risk-based and outcomes focused. It must be tailored to the specifics of the airline or airport. Whilst it is conceded that approximately 80% of risks are known and common to all airports and airlines, the location, operating environment, brand, and political stability will all provide unique challenges to the aviation security professional. Aviation security takes a layered approach to protecting an aircraft, passengers and crew and is about reducing the risk whilst adding these elements to the aircraft. Driven by the ever-increasing demand for speed, transparency, and efficiency in global trade, the air freight logistics industry has become a critical pillar of aviation management. It plays a vital role facilitating the movement of essential goods like pharmaceuticals, manufactured products, and humanitarian aid across borders. While air freight accounts for only a small fraction of global trade by volume, it carries a significant 35% of its total value, highlighting its importance in today's economy. This rapid and efficient transportation of high-value, time-sensitive goods relies on a complex network of interconnected stakeholders, including airlines, freight forwarders, ground handling agents, border agencies and more. Each participant in the supply chain plays a crucial role in ensuring the seamless and timely movement of cargo shipments. This part of the course delves into the core principles, operations, and regulations governing the air cargo industry, exploring its supply chain, commercial aspects, operational practices, and emerging trends. This course provides insight into contemporary security issues of airlines and airports, aviation security standards and recommended practices, and aviation security principles and procedures. It will also develop your skills to ask, “What is the desired security outcome, and can it be achieved in different ways?”. The course also introduces the framework for understanding how airfreight is moved and managed, the many demands placed upon the industry by a wide range of stakeholders, and what is needed for the airfreight industry to be successful at both an operational and business level. Unless otherwise stated, the Australian examples used throughout the course are typical of international practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain the air cargo supply chain in comprehensive detail, including key stakeholders, their roles and interactions.
Explain the historical development of aviation security and the international and Australian frameworks underpinning the aviation regulatory environment and its management.
Implement different regulatory approaches and frameworks for the management of various aviation security and air freight challenges.
Recall and apply the principles of dealing with aviation security risks correctly in a variety of situations.
Investigate potential security outcomes for dealing with security threats and/or risks through appropriate enquiry.
Evaluate the operational and commercial aspects of air cargo management, identifying current challenges and emerging trends that influence the industry.
Analyse the critical role of air cargo logistics in the global economy, emphasising its contribution to speed, transparency, and efficiency in international trade.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Airport Management
syllabus_overview: The modern airport manager is no longer someone with just a skill set in operations. It is someone who can contribute to the ongoing rapid growth of non-traditional airport commercial activity and commercial revenue streams, especially in understanding the growth and importance of non-aeronautical revenue. This course provide students an opportunity to gain an in-depth understanding of key issues within the airport management context. This includes learning about the regulatory environment, and licensing and obligations, and exploring an evaluation of various ownership models. Students also learn about the economics of running the airport as a commercial business, including costs, revenues, subsidies and key performance indicators to evaluate performance. The course teaches students about customer relationships, especially the importance of the airport-airline relationship and how airport route marketing helps set the airport for growth. Lastly, students learn about the shifting focus in airports deploying greater technology and how this translates to improved guest and customer experience provided within their terminals and airports.
learning_outcomes: Use measurement and analysis processes to assess airport performance, and to propose appropriate airport management strategies.
Apply high level insights when discussing the current key issues impacting airports for the management of diverse local and global scenarios.
Develop and present solutions for addressing the complexities of various airport management issues and challenges.
Explain how airports can be successful at both the commercial and strategic level, and apply this knowledge to effectively manage an aviation operations environment.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Airline Financial Analysis and Decision Support
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the financial tools that are used to make critical decisions in the commercial air transport industry. Specifically, this course examines (1) the tools for financial decision-making, and (2) the use of those tools to solve problems faced by airlines. Topics include aviation financial statements, yield and revenue management, estimating long run growth rates, route financial performance, aircraft investment decisions, and fuel and foreign exchange (FX) hedging by airlines.
learning_outcomes: Use capital budgeting analysis when making investments and decisions.
Identify the tools for evaluating air transport financial decisions and evaluate the financial viability of aircraft investments.
Discuss financial derivatives and how they can be used to hedge risks in fuel price and currency movements.
Implement capital asset pricing, weighted average cost of capital, and return on invested capital models when undertaking project evaluation for airline financial analysis and decision making.
Evaluate airline route network, and yield and revenue management decisions by applying the appropriate analytical methods and techniques.
Effectively use financial statements when making financial decisions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Multi-Crew Cooperation
syllabus_overview: This Multi-Crew Cooperation course is intended for third-year UNSW Bachelor of Aviation (Flying) students who are already licensed pilots. Multi-crew cooperation is the set of procedures, techniques, and interactions that enable pilots to operate, as a crew member, on transport category aeroplanes in the safest and most efficient way. This course builds on the knowledge and skills gained from single-pilot operations, by expanding the scope to multi-crew operations skills that are essential for students who aspire to a career as a professional pilot. Students are provided with the opportunity to learn the foundational knowledge and practical flight instruction required for the award of the multi-crew cooperation course completion certificate, which is required by legislation to operate as a pilot in multi-crew operations. Key topics are non-technical skills, including human factors; crew resource management; standard operating procedures; transport category aeroplane systems; and the practical techniques and crew interactions necessary to achieve safe and efficient flight. These topics are explored through interactive lectures and guided discussions for underpinning knowledge plus simulated flights in a Boeing 737 PS4.5 fixed base, fully enclosed Flight Training Device. The course is intensive mode to provide the best learning outcomes and provides a high level of practical experience guided by experienced airline pilots. All learning is conducted at the UNSW Aviation Flying Operations Unit at Bankstown Airport.
learning_outcomes: Apply transport category systems principles and methods of operation to normal and emergency scenarios typical to transport category aeroplane operations.
Explain and implement standard operating procedures applicable to aircraft operation, flight path management, checklist execution, and crew interaction.
Apply non-technical skills to multi-crew decision making processes.
Communicate clearly and confidently during normal and emergency scenarios typical to transport category aeroplane operations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolled in 3980.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Transport: Economics and the Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to develop non-economics majors’ economic literacy in the understanding of the key drivers of the commercial air transport industry and the industries’ impact on society. The course builds on the principles of economics to examine contemporary and prominent issues in the aviation-environment nexus such as aircraft noise and climate change. Students will be encouraged to apply concepts and techniques learnt in class through a short field excursion and series of tutorials on basic econometrics. The course will encourage students to think about air transport from varying perspectives on sustainable development.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in analytical numeracy to undertake causal econometric modelling such as hedonic pricing method.
Describe how air transport interacts with broader socio-economic and environmental issues in Sydney using experiences from field research.
Apply market economic theory to compare and evaluate key environmental economic policy options to manage aircraft noise and aviation-induced climate change.
Recall and apply economic literacy developed in the marginalist paradigm to evaluate the economic and environmental impacts of the aviation industry.
Explain how air transport interacts with aspects of society using neoclassical economic tools such as supply and demand.
Appraise the spatial (un)evenness of the costs and benefits of air transport, and the relevance and limitations of economic methods.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1901

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Aviation Safety Management Systems
syllabus_overview: Modern aviation transport systems now enable people to travel vast distances at high-speed, within a highly hazardous environment, yet paradoxically with minimal risk. A primary enabler for this is the development of Safety Management Systems (SMS). Successful completion of this course is expected to equip the student with the theoretical knowledge of the requirements of a SMS as described by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) Australia. The theoretical knowledge acquired in this course will be applied to a variety of real-world safety scenarios and examples across a variety of high reliability industries including aviation, nuclear, and oil and gas.
learning_outcomes: Be able to apply and demonstrate advanced learning, writing and communication skills consistent with graduate attributes.
Describe the principles of a Safety Management System and the accepted pillars which form a Safety Management System.
Evaluate and describe how to implement a Safety Management System.
Apply the knowledge and skills necessary to undertake the functions and responsibilities of a Safety Manager
Compare and contrast the international and domestic requirements for a Safety Management System in an aviation context.
Describe the concept of safety and the origins of Safety Systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Factors Tools and Methods
syllabus_overview: Understanding human factors is critical to improving complex systems, so that systems, tasks, systems and interfaces need to be designed with consideration of the abilities and limitations of humans. A range of tools and methodologies are used in human factors practice to proactively identify these issues to inform task and system design, or to retrospectively analyse these issues to improve future performance. This course outlines human factors tools and methods from task analysis techniques to complex systems analysis methods and discusses their advantages, disadvantages, intended applications, and limits in practice and interpretation. Students will have opportunities to apply elements of the tools to examples from different industries tasks and systems, analyse their results, and formulate recommendations for task and system re-design.
learning_outcomes: Identify the main features and intended uses of a range of human factors tools and methods
Evaluate the relative advantages and disadvantages of a range of human factors tools and methods
Apply elements of one or more human factors tools or methods to incidents, tasks or systems to help identify potential system-level changes
Outline factors that may affect the implementation of human factors tools and the interpretation of their results

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing Safety and Risk at Work
syllabus_overview: The ways in which work can affect people's health, safety and well-being are important considerations for all organisations. Accordingly, an understanding of workplace safety issues is important for students pursuing careers in any industry. This course explores current methodologies, frameworks and issues of best practice in the prevention and management of workplace hazards. The course uses a variety of media for course material and assessment, including websites, videos and case studies, and builds on students’ own workplace experiences. It is anticipated that students will gain an appreciation of current legislation and codes of practice, identify different types of workplace hazards and understand how they can affect people; and be able to apply the risk management approach to workplace hazards. Important notes: This course is jointly taught with GENS5013, with Science students required to take the AVIA3013 version of the course. Both Aviation and non-Aviation based examples are used in the course.
learning_outcomes: Apply the generic process of hazard identification, risk assessment, risk control and review to a range of workplace scenarios and case studies.
Outline systems and strategies to help manage and promote workplace health and safety, including the hierarchy of controls, safety management systems and improving safety culture.
Differentiate and describe the basic concepts of hazard and risk, and identify relevant examples.
Contextualise personal experiences of workplace safety in wider events relevant to safety at work, including recent incidents, case studies, court cases, and other students' experiences.
Locate and evaluate information and statistics relevant to workplace hazards and risks in a range of industries.
Outline the general requirements and foundations of workplace safety legislation, and elements of best practice in workplace safety

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Drone Programming and Applications
syllabus_overview: A multi-drone air traffic environment is fundamental to scalable remotely piloted aircraft systems (RPAS) management. Through hands-on programming modules, students will develop an understanding of the sources of complexity in environment-drone interactions and multi-drone operations. This course is available to Bachelor of Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems) students as well as those with interest in drone air traffic management, and can be taken by students with little or no programming experience. As a laboratory project, students will have the opportunity to test their programmed solutions in a simulation platform before implementing them in the field.
learning_outcomes: Apply drone programming techniques and appropriate digital literacy skills to address real-world challenges in the aviation industry.
Compare and contrast the common principles of multicopter flight and multi-drone traffic management, drawing on real-life aviation examples to contextualise their use and function.
Prepare and implement risk management strategies to safely trial the developed drone flight automation programs in the field.
Trial and appraise the efficacy of an agent-based model of automated multi-drone flight using programming skills.
Design programs to mitigate the impact of the physical environment on a programmed drone flight.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA2225 OR equivalent (as reviewed and approved by the Course Convenor)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Airline Management
syllabus_overview: Airline Management is a vast topic – few people can become subject matter experts across the broad spectrum that encompasses airline management in its entirety within a lifetime. This is also the case in teaching such a subject over a 10 week term. With an array of possible subject matter, this course has as its focus, the main facets of corporate airline management and begins with airline organisational practice, management's visions and objective setting. It proceeds with the main corporate processes of business planning, network and fleet planning, schedule planning, revenue management and consideration of key external factors, such as the prevailing regulatory environment. Financial analysis, performance benchmarking and business model options are also addressed The course is uniquely structured and delivered in such a way to allow students to be exposed to a diverse range of industry subject matter experts, through the inclusion of guest speakers on a week-to-week basis during the scheduled lecture time. These guest lecturers are currently working in industry and in various locations nationally and internationally. In order to allow for these guest speakers to share their knowledge in real time with the students, lectures are delivered online. During these lectures, students also have the opportunity to directly engage with these industry experts, which in itself, differs from some other subjects offered in the school. Another unique component of the course, is the airline simulation tool provided by SIMULATE.AERO, which is a software program that will involve students running and managing their own startup airline over the course of the term. The simulation will form the basis of one of the assessments, which students will work on during the weekly tutorials. As with the guest speakers, we will work closely with the software provider and for this reason, tutorials will be a combination of online instruction, as well as person participation and held in the allocated classroom.
learning_outcomes: Explain the critical factors that contribute to the commercial and strategic success of an airline.
Develop and justify strategic solutions to complex airline management challenges and effectively communicate these solutions.
Identify and describe key contemporary issues affecting airline operations and management.
Apply appropriate metrics to measure airline performance and analyse data to evaluate strategic issues.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA1901

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Transport Flight Planning
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the aeronautical knowledge training required by the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 Part 61 Manual of Standards to achieve the competencies of Air Transport Flight Planning, specifically the Air Transport Pilot Flight Planning - Common and Air Transport Pilot Flight Planning - Aeroplane units of competency. The course explores key concepts of air transport flight planning, with consideration of the various factors that contribute to effective flight planning, and the need to accurately extract and interpret performance data to inform key planning decisions. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 Part 61 Manual of Standards for the Air Transport Pilot Flight Planning - Common and Air Transport Pilot Flight Planning - Aeroplane units of competency.
Interpret and extract data from cruise, climb and descent planning tables and charts using the performance handbook.
Define and explain concepts used in planning flights in pressurised, multi-engine turbojet aeroplanes operating under Instrument Flight Rules.

Construct flight plans accounting for weight, payload and fuel limitations, route requirements, optimal altitude considerations, weather conditions and engine, pressurisation and other system failures.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA2117

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Transport Performance and Navigation
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the Air Transport Pilot Licence level Navigation, and Performance and Loading, specifically the APLC, APLA and ANVC units of competency. The course explores key concepts of air transport performance and navigation, considerations and data interpretation relating to take-off, enroute and landing performance; weight and balance calculations, and limitations; and principles and practical techniques involved in route navigation. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Explain weight and balance concepts, take-off, enroute and landing performance considerations applicable to multi-engine jet transport aeroplanes.
Complete B727-200 load and trim sheets and extract take-off and landing performance data from the performance manual.
Explain the principles of navigation charts, time zones, flight instruments and compasses, radio wave propagation, radio navigation aids, radar, area navigation systems and route navigation.
Practically apply chart plotting techniques involved in route navigation.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the APLC, APLA and ANVC units of competency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA2117

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Transport Air Law, Meteorology and Human Factors
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the aeronautical knowledge training required by Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 Part 61 Manual of Standards for the Air Transport Pilot Licence level Air Law, Meteorology and Human Factors, specifically the AFRC, AFRA, AHFC, AMTC and AMTA units of competency. The course explores key concepts of air transport air law, meteorology and human factors through a combination of synchronous face-to-face and online learning and discussion to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes to assess retention and understanding of students’ learning.
learning_outcomes: Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the AFRC, AFRA, AHFC, AMTC and AMTA units of competency.
Maintain current versions of, interpret and apply legislation relating to aviation meteorology, in particular relating to high altitude flight.
Explain theoretical and practical aspects of aviation law as it relates to flight crew conducting multi-crew IFR operations.
Decode and apply information in aviation weather forecasts and reports to operational scenarios, in particular relating to high altitude flight.
Define and explain advanced Human Factors concepts applicable to multi-crew operations.
Relate theoretical Human Factors concepts to conditions found in piloting high altitude capable aircraft.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: AVIA2117

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Drone Entrepreneurship
syllabus_overview: The use of drones across the global economy is seeing exponential growth. With new opportunities emerging all the time, entrepreneurial activity is high and new economic and societal value in many industrial and government sectors is being enabled all the time by small companies and startups. This course involves experiential learning as teams develop the initial basis for viable new commercial or non-profit ideas related to drone technologies or services. It is aimed at students with an interest in drones or related areas of applied robotics, and/or students with a broader interest in startups and companies enabled by emerging hardware and software technologies. Students will research company structures, business ideas, and technology opportunities, iterating evidence for potential economic and social impact with their new “company” via intensive customer discovery and competition analysis, culminating in a final pitch.
learning_outcomes: Identify gaps in markets by testing assumptions and examining evidence from customer discovery interviews and research.
Develop, iterate, and justify concepts for a new enterprise involving drones or drone-related technology.
Create external-facing materials that support the refinement of a chosen business concept.
Analyse and explain different financial and business models for drone services or technologies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Transport Aerodynamics and Aircraft Systems
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the aeronautical knowledge training required by the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the Air Transport Pilot Licence level Aerodynamics and Aircraft Systems, specifically the AAGC and AAGA units of competency. The course explores key concepts of air transport aerodynamics, and aircraft systems, with a focus on the components, methods of operation and indications relating to transport aeroplane systems, and the relationship between theoretical aerodynamic concepts and practice systems in various operational contexts. A combination of synchronous learning and discussion is used to teach key concepts, knowledge and skills, and homework and class quizzes are also provided to students to assess retention and understanding of their learning.
learning_outcomes: Relate theoretical aerodynamic concepts to design features, controls and limitations found in high-speed propeller and jet aeroplanes.
Explain the components, method of operation and applicable cockpit indications in relation to transport aeroplane systems.
Relate theoretical concepts to the practical systems information found in transport aeroplane Aircraft Flight Manuals.
Satisfy the theoretical knowledge requirements of the CASR 1998 Part 61 MOS for the AAGC and AAGA units of competency.
