institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Writing the City
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Democracy hinges on the principle of popular debate, and questions of demotic engagement in the shaping of the built environment are more topical, and more controversial, than ever. Yet fewer and fewer newspapers (and almost no broadcast media) employ architecture critics in any form or role. Where criticism does happen, further, it is generally relegated to the ‘arts’ pages or time-slots, effectively minimizing its exposure and greatly narrowing its demographic. This course aims to give you an understanding of the different genres of architectural and urban writing, differentiating according to purpose, style, audience and lexicon. It aims to impart an understanding of how words are used in shaping cities, how media and publishing work in relation to the built environment and some of the essential skills in producing publication-quality text.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the various forms of architectural and urban writing: scholarship; criticism; exegesis; reportage; promotion and polemic

Create new work that demonstrates a capacity to analyse, evaluate, articulate and synthesise complex ideas and concepts about the concepts, patterns and evolution of architectural and urban fabric as coherent written text
Apply theory to advanced understanding of the roles of different media, genres and players in the culture-building and city-building process
Develop publication-quality text across genres of architectural and urban writing

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Housing Typologies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Housing Typologies explores the complex and diverse discussions around the design, innovation, planning, policies and economics of various Australian housing types. Housing design, whether considered as a reflection of social policy, a commodity, or a site of social struggle, plays a significant part in our everyday life. The debates concerning Australian housing typologies reflect ideologies that affect our society and shape our built environment. Through this course, you will gain an understanding of the long history of the ‘housing question’ and the key concepts that have underpinned such discussions in the Sydney and Australian context. You will document exemplary housing typologies with the aim of contributing to the construction of an Atlas of Australian housing. Through the cross-institutional collaboration you will exploration of relationships between design, regulatory frameworks and housing policy, and you will develop tools for critical analysis and participation in the production of this significant and ever-evolving typology.
learning_outcomes: Undertake independent historical, archival and contextual architectural research.
Document and present architectural research data and analysis according to professional standards.
Critically analyse the planning and design of various housing typologies in the context of the economic, social, and political dimensions of city-making.
Explain design concepts and theories to select housing typologies.
prerequisites: Enrolled in the following BE post graduate design programs: architecture, landscape architecture, city planning

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Programmable Cities
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Programmable Cities focuses on the fundamentals of computer programming and the technical skills needed to design and implement programming solutions to automate urban data analytics. Using a given programming language and working with a live urban project, you will learn how to automate repetitive tasks, accurately document and quickly repeat or modify analytical processes. By focusing on the foundational concepts and fundamental skills needed to operate a single programming language, this course develops your ability to work with diverse computer programming languages and adapt to new technologies.
learning_outcomes: Apply programming knowledge and skills appropriate to the aims of specific practical urban projects and real data.
Demonstrate an understanding of programming concepts, methods, and approaches.
Design and implement solutions in advanced programming languages to automate geoprocessing tasks.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Data Visualisation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Contemporary cities have grown extraordinarily complex and can be described and analysed through an increasing variety of social, economic and environmental data in different dimensions. In this course you will learn about new 3D tools that have been created to cope with the large availability of urban data and models. Visualisation is a critical component of modelling, analysing and understanding the built environment, and visual statements can play a key role in shaping opinions, supporting planning, and helping policy and decision-making. This course will equip you with the theory and techniques to harness the power of 3D visualisation.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise data and insights to achieve the visualisation aims for specific projects and scenarios.
Critically assess the theory and processes of urban data visualisation.
Apply theoretical insights and practical urban data visualisation skills to urban problems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geodesign
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be introduced to the fundamental theory, concepts and frameworks of geodesign. Geodesign is a design and planning method which tightly couples the creation of design, landscape and city planning with simulations informed by geographic contexts, systems thinking and digital technology. You will develop a greater understanding of data driven decision support tools to support city planning, and will engage with the geodesign process by reviewing case studies including specific case study applications.
learning_outcomes: Describe the basic historic and contemporary foundations of geodesign theory.
Define “geodesign” and its goals.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of the geodesign process through via collaborative project development.
Identify a geographic problem and propose a method for solving the problem.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geocomputation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students the skills to undertake sophisticated spatial (statistical) analysis and simulation. GeoComputation is in part the continuing development and application of analytical statistics that can be applied to clustering, search and measures of association over space and through time. The course will provide students with the theoretical and mathematical background behind numerous spatial analytical techniques, and also to select and integrate these methods in a way that it is appropriate for the problems addressed and the data available. Ultimately, the course will enhance the intellectual and methodological capacity of students in the domain of urban problem-solving. The course will use varied analytical environments, including software and R programming.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts and methods for geocomputational analysis through interaction with real-world data.
Demonstrate computationally-oriented independent research applied to the urban context.
Select and employ a range of data analysis tools and methods including demonstrating understanding of the appropriateness of different geocomputation methods for different data.
Manipulate and analyse data in a reproducible fashion using computational techniques.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Cities
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Digital Cities, you will explore the breadth of data available to urban designers, planners, and policymakers, using real projects undertaken within the City Futures Research Centre and the School of Built Environment at UNSW. You will become familiar with a range of innovative spatial datasets and investigate how they can be used to improve policymaking. Australian cities (especially Sydney) will be our laboratory, but international perspectives will also be incorporated. Importantly, you will also critically engage with the politics and power dynamics embedded in the emergence of the Smart City and the complexity associated with data access, knowledge production, and dissemination.
learning_outcomes: Identify new technologies and how best to use them in the social planning and management of a contemporary city
Use digital technology platforms such as data portals, GIS, digital planning tools, BIM, and 3D visualisations to support the planning process for future developments
Assess the benefits and disadvantages of new data platforms and innovative technologies for analysing spatial and temporal data
Critique and apply cutting-edge public involvement methodologies, techniques and tools for enabling an effective smart city strategy

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Smart Cities and Urban Informatics Major Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The Smart Cities and Urban Informatics Project represents the culmination of studies in the Smart Cities and Urban Informatics. Students will work closely with the Director of the Program to develop a proposal. Projects which tap into current ‘live’ projects, building upon existing partnerships internationally through the PLuS Alliance and with industry and government organisations including Department of Planning and Environment, the Greater Sydney Commission, Urban Growth, Sydney Water, and the Department of Finance, Services and Innovation, along with partnerships with local councils including the City of Sydney, Randwick City Council and Parramatta., will be encouraged. This might take the form of a discrete element or task within its ongoing strategic development or implementation, or a more general critical analysis of the Smart City agenda. The major project report can take the form of a research thesis or a practice-oriented report. Each student will be assigned a supervisor, and it is expected that many students will also benefit from engagement with industry partners. The final thesis/report will be 10-12,000 words long. Where partners have been directly involved, students will be encouraged to provide a short debrief to the relevant organisations. The production of the thesis will explore and provide new insights into one or more of the challenges facing cities through the integration of research and/or practical insight.
learning_outcomes: Critically review existing literature, and available data, tools and techniques a means of refining the research question(s) and supporting data driven methodology.
Produce a research thesis or practice-research led project which is underpinned through the application of digital data and technological.
Identify the role of research and its contribution to future work in the field of smart cities and urban informatics.
Apply critical and analytical thinking to a significant challenge facing our cities.
prerequisites: Currently enrolled in program 8151 City Analytics or 8152 City Analytics (Extension)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Healthy Built Environments
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Healthy Built Environments is a postgraduate elective that focuses on the role of the built environment in supporting healthy behaviours that reduce major risk factors for chronic diseases across the life course for diverse communities. The course examines the ways in which health and built environment professionals are collaboratively addressing the epidemic of chronic disease associated with sedentary and socially isolated urban living. Current research, legislative and policy frameworks, together with best practice from Australia and abroad, are presented and critically evaluated. The challenges of inter-disciplinary research, policy development and implementation are considered. This course is specifically designed for students undertaking post graduate studies in built environment and health. Classes involve a mixture of lectures, participant discussion and critical review, hands-on experience with different tools, field trip and group presentation.
learning_outcomes: Development of written communication skills (thematic organisation of material and critical commentary) for research projects
Critical awareness of the latest research on healthy cities and the needs of diverse communities
Familiarity with, and an ability to use audit tools and checklists
Development of succinct written communication skills for professional practice
Appreciation of the differing approaches, research traditions and ways-of-working within the health and built environment sectors
Content knowledge of healthy built environments - understanding of chronic disease, relationship between built environment and health, best ways of addressing the issues
Development of analytical research skills
Understanding and experience of collaborative and inter-disciplinary ways-of-working to achieve equitable healthy environments

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geographical Information Systems and Urban Informatics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Geographical Information Systems and Urban Informatics introduces a series of fundamental and advanced GIS and GeoAI concepts and methods and their applications in urban studies, planning, public health, environmental planning, and business contexts. You will also learn about types of spatial data and their uses, GIS software functions used for applying spatial analysis methods, and spatial storytelling techniques.
learning_outcomes: Create a spatial storymap including embedded interactive web maps.
Evaluate Geographical Information Systems (GIS) open data and spatial analysis results.
Explain Geographical Information System (GIS) and GeoAI concepts, principles/methods, open data, and open software.
Analyse location data and apply spatial analysis methods in Geographical Information Systems (GIS) environments.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Documentation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will learn the technical and legal aspects involved in the successful completion of a comprehensive set of construction documents for major buildings. You will use architectural documentation technologies, primarily Building Information Modelling (BIM) to prepare and assess working drawings, including design details, specifications and schedules. You will develop knowledge of the relevant design information technologies including CAD, BIM and Artificial Intelligence (AI), Australian Standards, and their application to the design and construction of a major building.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively in the preparation of design documentation and the production of building information
Specify and apply the relevant Australian Standards related to access and mobility in the documentation of major buildings
Document a given design, inclusive of construction methods and materials, using professional standard drawings and building information modelling

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design and Technology-Timber
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Design and Technology-Timber focuses on the conception and structural resolution of a clear-span timber public building and associated works constructed in timber. The course aims to develop your knowledge of materials, structure and construction in order to enhance the architectural design process. You will learn about the conception and structural resolution of a clear-span timber public building and associated works constructed in timber.
learning_outcomes: Assess durability issues in timber construction.
Develop a conceptual design of a timber structure informed by the material’s unique mechanical properties.
Design timber joints that explore aesthetic possibilities.
Evaluate timber as a sustainable material.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Fabrication Techniques
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This elective will focus on one of architectures primary modes of investigation; the model. As a critical part of the design process the model expresses ideas and concepts in three dimensions with concern for materials, lighting, space and, nowadays, interactivity; in other words the model literally presents all of the components of a finished architecture. Traditionally architectural models have been hand-made which both reflected the building process of the time and a cultural longing by architects to be more directly involved in the production of their work (many architects design products, especially furniture, for the same reason). But for some time now architecture has been tending towards the assembly of factory made components; and, as can be seen across the world, factories tend towards automated machine-made production. It’s worthwhile to point out at this stage that beautiful things are created in factories. Porsche, Honda, Apple, Prada and Boeing (to name a few) all use factories to create amazingly sophisticated products; most for a fraction of the cost of the average architect designed building. If architectural models should reflect both the finished architecture and its mode of production they will need to employ automated processes such as digital modelling, laser cutting, CNC milling and rapid prototyping. However, this elective isn’t dogmatic; several hand-made processes will also be employed (hot-wire cutting blue foam, casting, sheet metal folding). In this elective students will be trained to use and have direct access to all of these machines. In this elective students will select 3 from the number of techniques on offer to fabricate components that have precedents in architecture relating to the students design studio. Following online courses students will be expected to enroll in practical sessions. Successfully completing these courses will be mandatory. Further assessment will be based on the physical models themselves, representations of them and critical reflection on the process and outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Students will develop their understanding of Architectural theory, more completely comprehend form and advance their project management skills.
Students will be able to recognize, synthesize and apply sophisticated methods in assembly.
Students will have developed advanced skills in thinking through modelling.
Students will be able to recognize and demonstrate safe working practices (for both the Built Environment Design Lab and Fab Lab).
Students will be able to critically document a design process following an analysis and appraisal of their own work in the context of architectural precedents.
Students will be able to demonstrate care and precision in fabrication.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Bioinformatics
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course surveys the major areas of bioinformatics, exploring the history of bioinformatics in relation to advances in computing hardware and software; the biological problems currently being addressed using bioinformatics; and future applications of bioinformatics. Major topics include genomics; genome sequencing projects; proteomics; structural genomics; systems biology; phylogeny; medical informatics; and commercial applications of bioinformatics. The general nature of the data, computational problems and the approaches employed will be discussed in each case. Bioinformatics will be discussed both as a scientific discipline and as an engineering discipline. The course will also explore the role of bioinformatics in the biotechnology and pharmaceutical industries and ethical issues associated with biological data. Lectures are supplemented by practical exposure to public and commercial bioinformatics web sites and to commonly used bioinformatics software.
learning_outcomes: Describe some common application areas of bioinformatics and the techniques used therein (genome annotation, rational drug design, medical genomics etc) and describe and explain some common bioinformatics algorithms and common data types used in these applications

Apply common bioinformatics procedures using commonly available software and websites, including: retrieving relevant sequences and structures from databases; identifying ORFs in a DNA sequence; identifying the function of an unknown sequence by similarity searching; identifying the function of an unknown sequence by pattern searches or based on physicochemical properties; creating a multiple sequence alignment and a phylogenetic tree;
Construct simple shell scripts in UNIX to perform file management tasks and launch programs.
Discuss some common challenges in the engineering of computer systems for bioinformatics
Use R to visualise complex data and analyse transcriptomics data
Explain the impact of bioinformatics on modern biology and relevant ethical and social issues
Define bioinformatics and provide examples of common uses in analysing genome, protein and expression data, and in modelling biological systems
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BABS1201 OR DPST1051

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Renewal
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Urban Renewal explores key concepts concerned with urban spatial dynamics and the drivers and processes of urban spatial restructuring. You will learn about the evolution of official thinking on renewing Australia’s cities and the changing goals and implementation of these processes. You will also learn about the range of stakeholders with interests in urban renewal and their contrasting roles and perspectives. While the course has a particular focus on Sydney, examples of urban processes and policy approaches from other Australian and international cities will also be considered.
learning_outcomes: Explain different urban renewal financing and governance models.
Identify the links between economic and social change and urban restructuring.
Evaluate the real world outcomes of urban renewal processes.
Critically analyse the history and evolution of urban renewal policy.
Analyse market-driven urban renewal processes and the potential roles for government in shaping these processes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Bioinformatics
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Dive into the dynamic world of Applied Bioinformatics, a course designed to bridge the gap between computational technology and biological discovery. This course will give you the opportunity to apply computational strategies in tackling pressing challenges in biology, focusing on the practical aspects of managing, analysing, and interpreting complex biological data. Through a blend of theoretical foundations and hands-on practice, you will become proficient in utilizing cutting-edge bioinformatics tools and techniques. This includes the analysis of DNA, RNA, and protein data, as well as the exploration of molecular structure and function. Structured to mirror real-life bioinformatics inquiries, this course emphasizes the application of bioinformatics in understanding and solving biological problems. As you progress, you will acquire a toolkit that prepares you to contribute to the fields of genomics, proteomics, and more. This course is more than an educational journey; it is a step towards diverse career paths, from bioinformatician to wet-lab scientist seeking an introduction to essential bioinformatic tools. No prior programming experience is necessary; it will be taught in the course.
learning_outcomes: Explain the biology concepts that provide the context for bioinformatics analysis of biological data, including sequence, structure and function.
Identify the strengths and limitations of the key bioinformatics approaches used in sequence, structure and functional data.
Apply and evaluate sequence, structure and functional databases and associated tools to address biological problems.
Analyze, manage and interpret sequence, structure and functional data.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BABS2204 or BABS2264 or BIOC2201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Bioinformatics
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course explores the computational basis of bioinformatics and complements and extends understanding of bioinformatics tools and resources acquired in other courses, with a focus on the analysis of complex biological datasets and the application of mathematical and computational methods to problems in modern life science. Example domains include sequence analysis, gene expression and function, networks of interaction, and systems modelling. Specific topics include: Algorithms and representations in DNA and protein sequence analysis: string matching and alignment, tree building methods, hidden Markov models and other probabilistic representations, genome assembly and mapping. Computational representations in systems biology including Boolean and Bayesian networks. Optimisation and machine learning approaches used in bioinformatics.
learning_outcomes: Define and apply machine learning methods of clustering and classification in analysis of genome-scale data.
Express and apply key concepts from graph theory to model biological networks.
Research and present on a range of open-source software tools and techniques available to bioinformatics software developers.
Define Hidden Markov models, describe their associated algorithms, and discuss their application to biological sequence analysis.
Use and explain selected engineering approaches to the representation, execution and evaluation of models of biological processes and their application in systems biology.
Reproduce, explain and apply the major methods of pairwise and multiple sequence analysis in bioinformatics.
Define key computational and statistical concepts in bioinformatics approaches to pairwise and multiple sequence analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMP2041 AND BINF2010

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Genome Informatics Engineering Design Workshop
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Engineering software systems for managing and analysing large datasets derived from genomics experiments is a key application of bioinformatics. This course revolves around a guided team project for the design and implementation of a complex system bringing together a variety of tools and methods for analysing genomic data. Methodologies for requirement gathering, system design, project management and documentation will be applied. The project work will be complemented by lectures on algorithms for biological sequence analysis that form the basis of the project work.
learning_outcomes: Useand apply key computational and statistical concepts in bioinformatics
Employ practical design skills, particularly in software component design and integration
Communicate with stakeholders from a different background, especially domain experts in biology, through reports, oral presentations and documentation
Use project management, teamwork and communication skills
Identify suitable technologies and components for implementing a system meeting the specifications
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (COMP1531 or COMP2041) Co-requisite: BINF3010

title: Computational Biology Engineering Design Workshop
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Through a practical software project and targeted lectures this course examines various issues in the design and implementation of software systems for the analysis of large complex biological datasets and the application of mathematical and statistical methods to problems in modern life science. learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced practical design skills, particularly in software component integration and data management systems
Research, use and explain selected engineering approaches to the representation, execution and evaluation of models of biological processes and their application in systems biology
Research and present on a range of open source software tools and techniques available to bioinformatics software developers and use at least one of these in your own software development projects

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Biochemistry (Advanced)
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: BIOC2101 aims to introduce students to modern biochemistry with an emphasis on how we, as humans, convert foods to useful energy. Major topics covered include proteins and enzymes, carbohydrate catabolism/storage, bioenergetics, protein catabolism, fat metabolism/storage, and the overall integration of these processes and pathways in maintaining metabolic homeostasis. This course provides a solid context for new learning material by providing clinical, medical, and everyday applications that correspond to the central themes and topics. Practical classes are designed to complement the core biochemical concepts covered in lectures and introduce students to current laboratory techniques and biochemical assays.
learning_outcomes: Work safely and effectively in a modern biochemical laboratory to perform a range of biochemical assays, analytical techniques and related calculations.
Describe the integration of major metabolic pathways in the context of common human conditions, such as fasting, starvation, obesity and exercise.
Communicate experimental methods, outcomes and their interpretations in the format of a professional scientific report.
Explain the various mechanisms that control and regulate the simultaneous functioning of anabolic and catabolic processes in the cells of living tissues.
Describe and contrast the functions and key features of the major metabolic pathways in humans.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BABS1201 or DPST1051 and CHEM1011 or DPST1031 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1051 or CHEM1811 and CHEM1021 or DPST1032 or CHEM1041 or CHEM1061 or CHEM1821

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Molecular Biology (Advanced)
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to modern molecular biology and covers the molecular mechanisms of gene expression and fundamental aspects of recombinant DNA technology. The major topics covered include: the structure, function and properties of DNA and RNA; the replication and transcription of DNA; protein synthesis (translation); regulation of gene expression; molecular biological techniques (e.g. DNA cloning, hybridisation analysis, DNA sequencing, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and microarrays); bioinformatics; and applications of molecular biology. The practical sessions of this course have been designed to complement lecture material and introduce students to current experimental techniques in molecular biology.
learning_outcomes: Communicate experimental methods, outcomes, and their interpretations in the format of a professional scientific report.
Describe and compare the mechanisms for regulating gene expression in bacteria and eukaryotes.

Apply and explain a range of practical techniques in molecular biology that are commonly employed in the analysis of nucleic acids and follow the correct laboratory procedures for working safely and effectively.
Describe the structure, function and properties of nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) and explain the processes of DNA replication, transcription and translation.
Describe the theory and applications of bioinformatics and molecular biological techniques, including DNA cloning, DNA sequencing, the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and microarrays.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BABS1201 or DPST1051 and CHEM1011 or DPST1031 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1051 or CHEM1811 and CHEM1021 or DPST1032 or CHEM1041 or CHEM1061 or CHEM1821

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Biochemistry of Health and Disease
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course showcases some more advanced aspects of biochemistry that are particularly relevant to humans, providing students with a background of normal metabolism as well as exposure to changes that occur in selected pathological states. Components of the course address specific clinical problems, such as heart disease, obesity, diabetes, cancer, neurological conditions, as well as various inborn errors of the metabolism. There is a focus on the molecular underpinnings of metabolism and some basic understanding of molecular biology (including concepts like signalling and transcription factors) is desirable. This course offers multiple opportunities to research, critically analyse and communicate contested concepts, with included learning activities simulating a scientific conference.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively in a small group setting to, produce a scientific communication piece in verbal and/or written form for a non-expert/expert audience.
Engage in the practice of peer review, to provide constructive feedback on the quality of work reviewed.

List and explain the factors contributing to various conditions and disease states (such as fasting, exercise, heart disease, diabetes, cancer and neurological disorders) in which certain biochemical pathways are altered.

Identify, analyse and critically evaluate scientific literature and evidence relating to popular weight loss treatments, dietary supplementation, and medical breakthroughs in the field of human biochemistry.
Describe the key features that define ‘normal’ biochemical profiles in human metabolism (with a focus on lipid and carbohydrate metabolism).
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOC2101 or BIOC2181

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Biochemistry
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered why we need to eat and what happens to the food we eat once we digest it? Have you thought about what causes some people to become overweight and develop metabolic disorders and why most diets don’t work in the long term? Have you considered how long you will be able to survive without food? Or the best ways to improve your metabolism? The course aims to answer all these questions by introducing you to modern biochemistry. The course covers fundamental aspects of the structure-function relationships of proteins and enzymes; metabolic working of cells, tissues, and organs; the interrelationships between pathways of carbohydrate, lipid, and amino acid metabolism; the vital roles of enzymes and hormones in catalysis and metabolic regulation; the energy trapping mechanisms of animals and plants; interesting variations on the central metabolic pathways in various life forms. The lecture material will be supplemented by practical classes where you will conduct experiments to diagnose metabolic conditions. You will be expected to collaborate with other students throughout the Term in the practical class. Both lecture and practical class material will be reinforced and assessed during the revision sessions. This course covers essentially the same material as in BIOC2101 Principles of Biochemistry (Advanced), but in less detail and with more emphasis on the function of organisms and less emphasis on some of the underlying chemical mechanisms.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret data from biochemistry experiments to diagnose medical conditions.
Compare and contrast the major metabolic pathways in humans and discuss how these pathways are controlled and regulated in humans.
Collaborate with peers to evaluate how theory and practical components of biochemistry are linked.
Discuss the changes that occur in metabolic pathways under different metabolic scenarios.
Apply current biochemical methods and analytical techniques to design experiments, perform a range of assays and calculations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BABS1201 or DPST1051 and CHEM1011 or DPST1031 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1831 or CHEM1832

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Molecular Biology of Proteins
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the concepts of protein structure and function that were introduced in the two pre-requisite courses, BIOC2101 and BIOC2201, to provide a comprehensive introduction to modern protein science. The lecture series covers fundamental aspects of protein structure and function, with an emphasis on the latest analytical tools and processes employed in protein characterisation. Other topics covered include protein-protein interactions, protein folding, and protein engineering, with a strong focus on proteomics, which is the large-scale study of proteins inside the cell. BIOC3111 is core to the Molecular and Cell Biology Major and a highly valuable elective in other related discipline areas such as biotechnology, bioinformatics, and biochemistry. BIOC3111 is designed to provide an authentic experience in the inquiry process underlying scientific research and discovery. In particular, the practical component is an extended 10-week project that engages students with the process of experimental design and provides extensive hands-on laboratory experience. The course integrates focused training in scientific communication that is embedded directly within laboratory activities and assessments. These communication tasks are explicitly linked to the experimental work undertaken in class, simulating authentic real‑world scientific data reporting and interpretation, with ongoing, thorough feedback to support student development.
learning_outcomes: Competently perform laboratory techniques in protein purification and analysis.
Communicate experimental results in the form of written scientific reports.
Identify and critically evaluate relevant scientific literature.
Design scientific experiments, troubleshoot arising problems, and interpret experimental data.
Explain the main research areas of modern protein science and their relevance to biology.
Explain the fundamental concepts of modern techniques in protein analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BIOC2101 or LIFE2101, BIOC2201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Molecular Cell Biology 2
school: School of Biotechnology and Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: The discipline of Molecular Cell Biology investigates how cells develop, operate, communicate, construct multicellular organisms, control their activities, and (on occasion) go awry. To study the properties of the molecules that contribute to all these activities, modern researchers employ concepts and experimental techniques drawn from biochemistry, molecular biology, genetics and cell biology. The course will present an overview of our current understanding of the molecular mechanisms that control cellular processes in health and disease and the techniques that are used to arrive at that understanding. Lectures presented in the course will cover molecular mechanisms of the recognition and interactions between cells, cell growth, intracellular signaling, genome and transcriptome regulation, plasma membrane and cytoskeleton organization, protein and lipid transport, and cellular stress. In addition, lectures on molecular mechanisms of conditions caused by dysregulation of these mechanisms, including growth disorders, cancer, obesity, atherosclerosis, and neurodegenerative disorders will be given. The course will include laboratory classes providing a high level of hands-on experience in experiment planning, laboratory techniques used in the fields of cell biology and biomedical research, and data analysis. A structured environment and a high level of peer interactions make these classes ideal for students with and without previous experience. This course is run in parallel with an advanced version, BIOC3671, which includes a research project. The advanced course is designed for students who plan to pursue research careers in molecular cell biology or related disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret experimental results using knowledge of theory and practical methods in cell biology.
Prepare an experimental research plan for a novel experiment by locating and evaluating literature on relevant experimental techniques.
Describe the complexity of eukaryotic cells and cellular processes in healthy and diseased cells.
Communicate and discuss current strategies in scholarly literature for solving cell biological problems in written and oral formats.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOC2101, BIOC2201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering in Medicine and Biology
syllabus_overview: Embark on a transformative journey at the intersection of engineering and healthcare with our dynamic course in biomedical engineering. You will explore the fundamental principles of engineering as applied to medicine and biology, delving into captivating topics such as artificial organs, medical imaging, and tissue engineering. Gain insights into the innovative technologies revolutionizing healthcare, from the development of artificial respirators to surgical robots. Through a blend of theoretical exploration and practical applications, you will discover how engineering concepts drive groundbreaking solutions to complex challenges in the biomedical field.
learning_outcomes: Describe several applications of engineering and technology to medicine/biology.
Evaluate specific applications of technology to medicine/biology.
Apply basic mathematics, physics, and engineering methods to solve biomedical problems.

Develop a concise and professional report detailing a specific application of technology in medicine/biology using the languages of engineering and medicine/biology, and present this information orally.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Bioelectronics and Physiological Measurement
syllabus_overview: The human body is a fascinating network of electrical impulses, enabling us to perform everyday functions such as seeing, hearing, and reacting to stimuli. Understanding these electrical currents is crucial, as any disruption can lead to health issues. This course introduces you to the world of bioelectronics and physiological measurement, focusing on the essential knowledge required for bio-electrodes, the interfaces used to measure or control electrical signals within the human body. The course covers the basics of electric circuit theory and the biological mechanisms underlying electrical signals. It also includes a practical component with laboratory exercises that introduce you to the field of bioelectronics, basic programming, and bio-signal analytics and classification. By the end of this course, you will have a foundational understanding of how to use various instruments, such as oscilloscopes and signal generators, for biomedical electronics. You will also gain skills in using software tools like LabChart, PowerLab, and Matlab for programming, bio-signal acquisition, bio-signal/data analysis, and modelling techniques in simulating biological systems. Moreover, you will develop an understanding of the mechanisms responsible for bioelectric signals that are measured or elicited in medical and clinical settings. This course serves as a stepping stone for those interested in further studies or a career in bioelectronics and physiological measurement. It provides a solid foundation for understanding the complex electrical systems within the human body and how they can be measured and analysed for health and medical purposes.
learning_outcomes: Collect, process and analyse complex recordings of biological data using contemporary techniques.
Describe the electrophysiology underlying biological signals.
Analyse the utility of instrumentation in measuring time-varying signals in biological applications.
Discuss the ethical considerations of collecting physiological data.
Interpret electrical and software models of biological signals.
Integrate findings from scholarly literature and compose a report to communicate findings to a professional standard.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: PHSL2121 and ELEC1111

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Musculoskeletal Biomechanics
syllabus_overview: Musculoskeletal biomechanics is an exciting and vital field that plays a key role in improving the quality of life for millions of people. At its heart, this discipline involves understanding how bones, muscles, and joints work together to support movement and withstand forces. This course introduces you to the fundamental mechanics of the musculoskeletal system, focusing on how bones, muscles, tendons, and ligaments collaborate to support movement and withstand forces. You will explore the statics and dynamics of human movement, learning how engineering concepts can be applied to understand joint mechanics, muscle function, and load distribution across the body. A strong emphasis is placed on real-world applications, particularly in the movement and control of the upper limb. This foundational course offers students a comprehensive understanding of the critical role biomechanics plays in restoring mobility, reducing pain, and improving overall well-being. By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the knowledge to further explore and innovate in the field of biomedical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional communication skills, both written and oral, incorporating mathematical, graphical, and diagrammatic elements.
Describe musculoskeletal anatomy, including body position, orientation, planes, and joint movements.
Perform and interpret simple experiments to investigate the dynamics of human movement.
Develop reflective practice skills by engaging in self-assessment and peer feedback.
Describe the ethical considerations related to human experimentation in biomedical engineering.
Apply principles of engineering mechanics to analyse the dynamics of human movement.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PHYS1121 or PHYS1131

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomaterials and Cell Technologies
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered how cochlear implants use platinum to restore hearing in profoundly deaf people, or how prosthetic hips made of titanium can replace bone and restore movement? Or how injured nerves have been treated with nerve grafts fabricated from artificial or natural polymers? This course will take you on a journey into the fascinating world of biomedical engineering, where you’ll discover the crucial role of materials in innovative medical technologies. This course offers a blend of theory and practice. Through engaging lectures and interactive workshops, you’ll explore the diverse properties of materials vital for medical applications, covering biology, mechanics, chemistry, and electricity. You’ll also learn how biological cells and cutting-edge tests can assist in screening and validating material selection for medical applications. The curriculum is designed to provide a comprehensive understanding of material science, mechanical testing, and cellular biology. It will equip you with the skills needed to navigate the complexities of biomaterials and cellular methodologies. Whether you’re investigating the biocompatibility of new materials or interpreting cellular responses to medical devices, this interdisciplinary course will sharpen your skills and prepare you for a career in biomedical engineering. This course serves as the foundation for more specialised courses aimed at understanding, designing and evaluating the biological and mechanical performance of materials used in medical devices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the role of emerging biomaterials in biomedical technologies using current research findings.
Apply cellular methodologies to assess material performance.
Select and justify biomaterials for biomedical applications.
Reflect on learning by engaging in self-assessment and peer feedback.
Collaborate with peers to conduct mechanical testing procedures on biomaterials in laboratory settings.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM1500 and MATS1101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomedical Instrumentation
syllabus_overview: This course provides an in-depth exploration of biomedical instrumentation, focusing on the physiological measurement of bioelectric phenomena and neurostimulation. It is designed to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of the physical principles that govern the conversion of biological variables into electrical signals through transducers. Throughout the course, students will gain hands-on experience with various measurement devices and approaches, exploring the underlying biological processes that generate the quantities to be measured or controlled. Real-world examples of biomedical instrumentation, such as heart rate monitors, blood oxygen monitors, and electrocardiography, will be examined to provide practical context. A significant portion of the course is dedicated to bioelectric phenomena, bioelectrodes, and medical electronics. Students will also revisit DC and AC circuit theory to solidify their understanding of these concepts. The course includes hands-on practice in the use and testing of medical transducers and electromedical equipment commonly used in clinical and research laboratories. By the end of the course, you will have a robust understanding of biomedical instrumentation, preparing you for future roles in biomedical engineering and related fields. This course serves as a stepping stone for those interested in the intersection of biology, medicine, and electronics, and how these fields can be leveraged to improve healthcare outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate ethical considerations and implications in the development and use of biomedical instrumentation.
Explain the principles of general transduction and biosensing.
Describe the scope and applications of biomedical instrumentation.
Evaluate the safety and effectiveness of biomedical instrumentation technologies.
Review current research findings to effectively communicate emerging biosensing and transduction technologies to diverse audiences.
Apply electrical engineering concepts to solve biomedical instrumentation problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM2600

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomedical Data Analysis
syllabus_overview: Join us in Biomedical Data Analysis, an exciting course designed to equip you with the skills to navigate the vast ocean of medical and biological data. This course is a gateway to understanding the critical role of data in the biomedical field, from predicitive analytics and AI in medicine to the intricate world of bionformatics. The importance of data in health cannot be overstated. For instance, consider the role of data in predicting disease outbreaks. By analysing patterns in patient sumptoms and their geographical locations, we can forecast potential epidemics, allowing healthcare systems to prepare and respond effectively. Similarly, in the domain of personalised medicine, data analysis helps tailor treatments to individual patients, improving outcomes and reducing side effects. In the growing field of genomics, data analysis enables us to undestand the complex interplay of genes, leading to breakthroughs in disease treatment and prevention. These real-world examples underscore the critical role of data in health and the immense potential of biomedical data analysis. Designed to immerse students in the dynamic fields of medicine, biology, and data analytics, this course provides practical experience in predictive analytics, AI applications, bioinformatics, and health data science. The course is tailored to introduce a strong foundation, enabling you to navigate, interpret, and innovate within a data-rich landscape. Your learning journey will cover a wide range of topics, beginning with predictive analytics, classification, and clustering. After consolidating your learning, you will explore health data visualisation, biomedical signal processing, and medical image analytics. The exploration continues with wearables, IoT, biomechanics, and mechatronics in digital health, emphasising interdisciplinary collaboration. Striking a balance between theory and practical application, the course involves tutorials with real-world problems and datasets, providing invaluable hands-on experience that strengthens your skills and professional appeal. Whether you aim to propel your career in industry or academia, this course is designed to equip you with the skills and knowledge to make a significant impact in the healthcare industry. Your journey towards becoming a part of the next generation of data-driven healthcare professionals begins here.
learning_outcomes: Analyse medical and biological datasets to identify patterns and communicate insights to technical and non-technical audiences.
Use reflective learning practices to critically assess learning and evaluate quality of work.
Describe core concepts, methods and foundational techniques in digital medicine, digital biology and data analytics.
Evaluate the utility, effectiveness, and ethical implications of data analytics techniques and AI applications in specific healthcare scenarios.
Design digital health solutions, visualisations, or data-driven prototypes that address real-world problems in digital medicine and digital biology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ENGG1811 and (MATH2018 or MATH2019) and MATH2089

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Technology Innovation
syllabus_overview: Experience an exciting learning adventure with our comprehensive course on Health Technology Innovation, designed to bridge the gap between healthcare and technological advancement. This course emphasises the creation of practical solutions to address real-world challenges in the healthcare sector. Our flipped learning approach ensures that you not only grasp theoretical concepts but also apply them effectively. Class time is dedicated to enhancing your understanding through in-depth case studies, problem-solving exercises, and dynamic discussions with peers. You'll engage directly with clinicians to uncover real issues and identify the unmet needs of key stakeholders, gaining invaluable insights from firsthand interactions. Throughout the course, you'll develop expertise in physiology, anatomy, and therapeutics, while mastering the art of conducting systematic literature reviews, evaluating existing solutions, and performing comprehensive stakeholder and market analyses. The curriculum is designed to tackle complex clinical problems, integrating diverse perspectives to formulate actionable solutions. Beyond theory, you will actively design and critically assess innovative solutions, with a strong focus on regulatory compliance, quality management, patient safety, and privacy. You'll have the chance to apply your knowledge to real-world scenarios and create a detailed project brief that demonstrates your ability to consolidate and communicate key clinical issues. Join us on this learning adventure and take the next step towards a rewarding career in health technology and healthcare innovation!
learning_outcomes: Examine the ethical issues regarding health techologies and apply relevant approaches to prevent and mitigate ethical risks.
Identify a problem in the healthcare context using scholarly and clinical sources and discuss any assumptions or biases in its determination.
Evaluate healthcare solutions using industry-relevant methodologies and technologies.
Create and evaluate a healthcare solution that adheres to industry standards and quality management systems.
Collaborate with group members to develop self-leadership skills and/or achieve team objectives effectively.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DESN2000, BIOM3300, BIOM3500 and BIOM3600

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mechanics of Biomaterials
syllabus_overview: Biomaterials are the unsung heroes of modern medicine, silently revolutionising healthcare and improving countless lives. This course is designed to bring these heroes into the spotlight for you. This course offers an in-depth exploration of the mechanical properties of various materials and their critical roles in biomedical applications. You will engage with real-world examples such as the use of titanium in joint replacements, the application of hydrogels in drug delivery systems, and the role of biodegradable polymers in sutures. These examples will not only illustrate the practical applications of biomaterials but also highlight the underlying mechanical principles that guide their use. In addition to theoretical knowledge, the course provides hands-on experience with computational techniques used for assessing the mechanical properties of biomedical devices. This practical exposure ensures that you stay up to date with the current practices in the field. Upon completion of this course, you will be well-equipped with the knowledge and skills to innovate in the field of biomedical engineering. The understanding of biomaterial mechanics can open doors to various career paths such as biomedical device design, pharmaceutical research, and tissue engineering. Whether you choose to pursue further studies or step into the professional world, this course will serve as a solid foundation for your future endeavours in the realm of biomaterials. The potential to make a significant impact in healthcare is immense, and this course is your stepping stone towards that goal.
learning_outcomes: Use principles explaining the mechanical properties of various materials to solve problems in biomedical applications ensuring compliance with international standards.
Collaborate with team members to accomplish shared goals and evaluate the journey and results.
Identify the fundamental relationships between mechanical properties of biomaterials and their usage in different biomedical applications.
Evaluate the selection process of materials for biomedical applications by studying multiple practical examples and identifying the underlying principles.
Employ mechanical assessments of biomedical devices using state-of-the-art computational techniques, adhering to current international standards.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM2300

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biocompatibility
syllabus_overview: Biocompatibility is a fascinating field that explores the interaction between biomaterials, medical devices, and living tissues. In this course, you’ll explore medical devices, biomaterials, and tissue engineering, learning the essentials of designing biocompatible medical devices. Through a blend of lectures, hands-on activities, and self-guided tasks, you’ll navigate the landscape of biomaterials and anticipate their behaviour in biological systems. You’ll gain knowledge about the application of biomaterials in various medical devices such as breast implants, vascular stents, hernia meshes and hip implants. The core principles of tissue engineering will be discussed, empowering you to apply these concepts in creating innovative medical device designs. The course will shed light on how the processing, sterilisation, and handling of materials can influence the functionality of medical devices. You’ll gain insights into the assessment of biocompatibility for regulatory approval of medical devices, a crucial process that ensures a medical device does not produce an unacceptable adverse biological response, such as toxicity, skin irritation, or systemic effects like cancer or developmental anomalies. The course will also guide you through the body’s responses to biomaterials, enabling you to predict reactions to new device designs and critically evaluate current biocompatibility testing protocols. Engaging you with real-world case studies, this course will foster problem-solving skills and creativity in the field of biocompatibility. By the end of this journey, you’ll have gained a solid foundation of knowledge, practical skills, and a growing interest in the dynamic field of biomedical engineering. This course will empower you to apply these learnings to real-world challenges, contributing to the development of safer and more effective medical devices.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with others to achieve team outcomes.
Predict how specific materials can be affected by physiological conditions based on their biomaterial classes and general properties.
Interpret feedback and incorporate it into project work.
Propose a testing regime for a novel medical device using biocompatibility and pre-clinical biological performance testing considering relevant standards and ethical guidelines.
Examine medical device designs and discuss their effectiveness and safety considerations using principles of tissue engineering.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM2300

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mechanics of the Human Body
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered how athletes can use advanced tools to analyse their movements to improve performance? How Lord of the Rings or Avatar were created? Or how advances in wearable technology, phone apps and smart garments can be used to detect, analyse and predict injuries and health outcomes? And even be used to help people with Parkinson's disease walk with confidence? If these questions intrigue you, then this course is for you. This course introduces you to the methods used in the analysis of human movement across various fields such as sports, medicine, health, and entertainment. It includes applications in sport biomechanics and musculoskeletal modelling, providing a comprehensive understanding of how the human body moves and functions. You will be introduced to methods and software to analyse body segment and joint kinematics, joint kinetics, work and power, muscle forces and the associated energy cost. Through this course, you will gain a deep understanding of the mechanical principles that govern human movement and learn how to apply this knowledge in real-world contexts. Whether you’re interested in improving athletic performance, creating lifelike animations, developing health-focused wearable technology, or advancing medical treatments, this course will equip you with the knowledge and skills you need. Join us in exploring the fascinating world of the human body’s mechanics and discover how you can make a difference in sports, health, entertainment, and more.
learning_outcomes: Compare different types of wearable technologies used for analysing human movement.
Employ self-learning practices and team collaboration to solve problems in biomechanics.
Examine human movement science and its interdisciplinary applications across medicine, health and sports.
Evaluate human movement through the design and implementation of experiments and communicate those findings to a professional standard.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM1500

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biosensors
syllabus_overview: From designing wearable glucose monitors for diabetes management to developing lab-on-a-chip technologies for personalised medicine, biosensors are revolutionising the field of physiological measurement and clinical diagnostics. This course focuses on the design, development, and application of sensors for measuring physiological variables. It covers a wide range of biosensing technologies, including electrical, mechanical, chemical, and biological sensors, while emphasising their practical use in real-world scenarios. You will explore the principles and mechanisms governing the acquisition and processing of physiological signals, both in vivo and in vitro , through hands-on labs, design projects, and case studies. You will learn to develop and implement measurement devices and approaches, ensuring compliance with safety standards. By the end of the course, you will have a comprehensive understanding of the biosensor landscape, from the underlying science to the practical applications, and be equipped with the skills to contribute to this rapidly evolving field. Whether you aspire to innovate in the medical technology industry, conduct research in biomedical engineering, or simply gain a deeper understanding of biosensors, this course will provide you with the knowledge and skills necessary to achieve your goals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the principles and mechanisms governing the acquisition and processing of physiological signals, both in vivo and in vitro.
Use various biosensors to measure physiological variables.
Integrate scholarly works in the field of biosensing into current applications and methodologies.
Develop and implement measurement devices and approaches that capture and process physiological signals, ensuring compliance with electrical safety standards.
Integrate knowledge of biosensors to innovate and improve physiological measurement techniques in biomedical engineering.
Participate in teamwork to meet a joint objective and conduct a thorough review of the process and its conclusions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BIOM2300, BIOM2601 and BIOM2700

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Thesis A
syllabus_overview: Seen as the highlight of study at UNSW, Biomedical Engineering Thesis Projects provide a unique opportunity for you to bring together the engineering principles learned over your previous years of study and apply these principles to develop innovative solutions to unsolved engineering problems related to human health. This could include the development of a specific design prototype, process and/or the investigation of a scientific hypothesis. Thesis projects are complex, open-ended problems that allow room for your creativity, and the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of results. There will be multiple possible solutions or conclusions at the outset and sufficient complexity to require a degree of project planning. Thesis Projects are completed over three terms under the course codes BIOM4951, BIOM4952 and BIOM4953. While the project may develop as you explore new gaps in the scientific and engineering knowledge the overarching research themes and supervisor are retained across terms. In Week 7 of each term eligible students should receive an email inviting them to view the Biomedical Engineering Projects database and select their project preferences. You should then identify potential projects and discuss these projects with potential supervisors prior to commencing this course. If you have not received a communication by Week 8 about project selection, then please reach out to the course coordinator for access to the Biomedical Engineering Projects database. BIOM4951 is the first step of this exciting capstone project opportunity and potentially your future career in research and development.
learning_outcomes: Analyse data objectively using quantitative and mathematical methods.
Critically reflect on a specialist body of knowledge related to their thesis topic.
Demonstrate oral and written communication in professional and lay domains.
Develop a design or a process or investigate a hypothesis following industry and professional engineering standards.
Solve a biomedical engineering problem by applying CLOs 1-5.
Apply scientific and engineering methods to solve an engineering problem.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomaterials and Cell Technologies
syllabus_overview: Medical devices can help people hear again, feel again, walk again. Do you want to participate in the process of finding the materials that are used to make medical devices? Hearing implants use platinum to return hearing sensation in profoundly deaf people, prosthetic hips made of titanium can replace bone and restore movement, and severed nerves can be restored with nerve grafts fabricated from artificial or natural polymers. How were these biomaterials considered for these medical applications? Engineering novel biomaterials is the essence behind the success of medical devices, yet not understanding the importance of biomaterials can result in health complication, even death. This requires evaluating biological, chemical, mechanical, and electrical properties of materials and their role in the performance of medical devices? Embark on an exploration into the realm of biomedical engineering with this course, where theory meets hands-on application. Discover the intricate role of materials in groundbreaking medical technologies. You will engage in experiential learning, bridging theory with practice. Through lectures and workshops, you will delve into the multifaceted properties of materials essential for medical applications, spanning biology, mechanics, chemistry, and electricity. In addition, the exploration of material performance relies on biological cells to better evaluate these properties. So, roll up your sleeves for hands-on experiences. Through laboratory experiments, you will learn how biological cells and front-line tests can help screen and validate material selection for medical applications. The curriculum is crafted to integrate material science, mechanical testing, and cellular biology. It will equip you with the necessary skills to navigate the complexities of biomaterials and cellular methodologies. Whether you are exploring the biocompatibility of new materials or deciphering cellular responses to medical devices, this interdisciplinary journey will hone your abilities and prepare you for the forefront of biomedical engineering. This course is highly recommended for students without a background in materials science or cell biology. Students from these disciplines will gain first-hand experience in evaluating biomaterials for medical applications and interpreting cellular responses to medical devices. Conversely, students with backgrounds in materials science or cell biology will deepen their expertise through advanced discussions and practical applications tailored to biomedical contexts. Overall, this course caters to a diverse cohort of engineering students, ensuring that all participants emerge equipped with skills to contribute meaningfully to the interdisciplinary field of biomedical engineering. This course serves as a gateway to more specialised courses aimed at understanding, designing and evaluating the biological and mechanical performance of materials used in medical devices.
learning_outcomes: Utilise cellular methodologies to assess material performance.
Evaluate the selection criteria for biomaterials in medical applications.
Evaluate the role of emerging biomaterials in biomedical technologies.
Execute mechanical testing procedures on biomaterials in laboratory settings.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 72 UOC

This requires evaluating biological, chemical, mechanical, and electrical properties of materials and their role in the performance of medical devices? Embark on an exploration into the realm of biomedical engineering with this course, where theory meets hands-on application. Discover the intricate role of materials in groundbreaking medical technologies. You will engage in experiential learning, bridging theory with practice. Through lectures and workshops, you will delve into the multifaceted properties of materials essential for medical applications, spanning biology, mechanics, chemistry, and electricity. In addition, the exploration of material performance relies on biological cells to better evaluate these properties. So, roll up your sleeves for hands-on experiences. Through laboratory experiments, you will learn how biological cells and front-line tests can help screen and validate material selection for medical applications. The curriculum is crafted to integrate material science, mechanical testing, and cellular biology. It will equip you with the necessary skills to navigate the complexities of biomaterials and cellular methodologies. Whether you are exploring the biocompatibility of new materials or deciphering cellular responses to medical devices, this interdisciplinary journey will hone your abilities and prepare you for the forefront of biomedical engineering. This course is highly recommended for students without a background in materials science or cell biology. Students from these disciplines will gain first-hand experience in evaluating biomaterials for medical applications and interpreting cellular responses to medical devices. Conversely, students with backgrounds in materials science or cell biology will deepen their expertise through advanced discussions and practical applications tailored to biomedical contexts. Overall, this course caters to a diverse cohort of engineering students, ensuring that all participants emerge equipped with skills to contribute meaningfully to the interdisciplinary field of biomedical engineering. This course serves as a gateway to more specialised courses aimed at understanding, designing and evaluating the biological and mechanical performance of materials used in medical devices.
learning_outcomes: Utilise cellular methodologies to assess material performance.
Evaluate the selection criteria for biomaterials in medical applications.
Evaluate the role of emerging biomaterials in biomedical technologies.
Execute mechanical testing procedures on biomaterials in laboratory settings.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mass Transfer in Medicine
syllabus_overview: Mass transfer refers to the transportation of molecules from one location to another. In the human body, such transfer occurs mainly via diffusion and convection, and a thorough understanding of these mechanisms is fundamental to many applications in medicine and biology. In this course, you will be introduced to mass transfer in medicine and biology and learn how to apply these processes in a range of medical devices and physiological systems. Topics to be covered include the transfer of solutes across capillaries, mass transfer in haemodialysis, gas exchange in the lungs and membrane oxygenators, transfer of drugs and toxins across the skin, slow release of drugs from implants, as well as mass transfer considerations in biosensors and in tissue engineering.
learning_outcomes: Solve biomedical problems in mass transport.
Explain the principles of diffusion and diffusive mass transport across synthetic and biological membranes.
Explain the concepts of flow limitation and membrane limitation, distinguishing whether one or the other, or neither, is limiting in a particular medical application.
Analyse the relative importance of convection and diffusion in a given system.
Formulate and use models of mass transfer in medical applications such as haemodialysis, drug release and biosensors.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biocompatibility
syllabus_overview: Biocompatibility involves understanding how materials and medical devices interact with living tissues and biological systems without causing harm. In this course, you will delve into the world of medical devices, biomaterials, and tissue engineering, gaining insights into designing biocompatible medical devices. Through a combination of lectures, activities, and independent tasks, you will explore biomaterials, predicting their reactions in biological systems. You will understand tissue engineering principles and apply them to innovate medical device design. We'll delve into how material processing, sterilisation, and handling impact medical device functionality, and examine host responses to biomaterials, predicting reactions to novel device designs. Finally, you will learn to propose testing regimes for new medical devices. The course will challenge you with practical case studies, encouraging problem-solving and innovation in the biocompatibility field. By the end, you will be equipped with essential knowledge, practical skills, and a lifelong interest in contributing to the dynamic field of biomedical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Describe biomaterial classes, their general properties, and predict how specific materials may be affected by physiological conditions
Explain the principles of tissue engineering and apply these to novel medical device designs
Explain how material processing, sterilisation and handling may affect medical device function
Describe host responses to biomaterials and predict host responses to novel medical device designs
Describe biocompatibility and pre-clinical biological performance testing regimes, and propose a testing regime for a novel medical device

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cellular and Tissue Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course outlines the concepts of cell-based products for the pharmaceutical and medical device industries. This course will cover the basis of how biologics (eg protein and carbohydrate drugs and antibodies) are produced by cells; recombinant technologies to produce biologics from bacterial and mammalian systems; process design and optimisation for the production of biologics; case studies of commercial biologics; cell therapies; the principles of tissue engineering and regenerative medicine, including biomaterials, cells and growth factors, and the clinical application of these principles in various tissues.

Describe the principles of cellular and tissue engineering/regenerative medicine.
Communicate effectively in a professional environment through technical reports and presentations
Synthesise, compare and evaluate scientific literature, technical reports and presentations.
