institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Project in Chemistry
syllabus_overview: This research project course introduces postgraduate students to research. They acquire skills of being a research focused laboratory working on cutting edge science and learning the parameters that a researcher faces. It also provides hands on training in an academic laboratory and the use of various methodologies and equipment depending on the research project. The intention is to provide a whole research experience with a dedicated project. Students will learn aspects such as project planning, literature review, project development, oral and written and reporting. Please note this course is designed specifically for students who take the Professional Masters of Science. The course may be used for coursework for other postgraduate programmes (at the discretion of the programme authority).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the application of chemical principles in the research setting, including following appropriate health and safety procedures and protocols.
Communicate chemical knowledge in a variety of modes for a variety of audiences.
Investigate and solve qualitative and quantitative problems in chemical sciences
Practice ethically and socially responsible scientific research.
Understand scientific approaches by recognising the creative endeavour in acquiring knowledge and the testable and contestable nature of the principles of chemistry.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Reaction Engineering
syllabus_overview: This elective course builds on students' core knowledge of reaction engineering and is designed to give an advanced insight into the design, optimisation and operation of reaction vessels used in chemical, biological, as well as material processing industries. Topics covered include the analysis of complex industrial reaction kinetics, effect of micromixing on reactive systems, non-isothermal reactor design, nonlinear analysis in reaction systems, catalytic processes, multiphase (gas-liquid-solid) reactors for single and multiple reactions, strategies for reactor optimisation and case studies in industrial process reactor design and operation. This elective course is geared towards senior undergraduate students with interests in the design and optimisation of reaction vessels and the underlying theoretical concepts. The course is also suitable for Master and PhD research students with interests in chemical, environmental and biological reaction engineering.
learning_outcomes: Assess and communicate gained knowledge and in-depth understanding of innovative engineering concepts via multiple forms of professional communication.
Apply advanced kinetic and thermodynamic principles to simulate the progress of chemical reactions various reactor designs.
Categorize various complex reactions patterns like autocatalytic reactions, parallel and multiple reactions.
Reflect and judge on the broader impact of advanced engineering concepts to society, economy and environment
Explain the underlying principles of (bio)catalytic processes
Contextualize reaction engineering problems and approach them outside the immediate boundaries of the core course content
Interpret and asses non-ideal and non-isothermal reactor designs, as well as the concepts of recycle reactors
Analyse engineering innovations and plan (depending on their level of development) how they can be put in industrial practice
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CEIC2005 AND (CEIC3004 OR CHEM2021)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Particle Systems Engineering
syllabus_overview: The ability to create and control the properties and functions of particles has transformed our world and continues to disrupt industry with new innovations and advances. Particles occur in many processes and products, across a wide range of industries, from food and pharmaceuticals to energy and water to mining and manufacturing. Everything from basic goods like flour and cement, to the most advanced technologies like electric cars, computers and solar panels contain particles or are produced from particulate products. In fact, 80% of all products synthesized or chemically produced go through a particle phase. Therefore, an understanding of this field will be incredibly helpful in preparing for the future of chemical and chemical product engineering. In this advanced course you will further learn about the fascinating nature of particles, colloid and interface science, and its applications, techniques, and processes, with a particular focus on: Biotechnology and Pharmaceutical Food Environmental Energy Building on your existing knowledge of particle and fluid mechanics, you will be introduced to the theory and principles of colloid and interface science, and then explore advanced particle size and surface characterization techniques, as well as nanotechnology and advanced particle synthesis. You will deepen and extend your knowledge of some areas through case studies and group activities.
learning_outcomes: Work in a group to communicate your knowledge of one or two specific topics in particle technology in an understandable, clear, and precise manner.
Explain the relationship between colloid phenomena, their properties, and applications.
Identify organic and inorganic particles, and their physical and chemical material properties, such as surface charge, morphology, and crystallinity.
Describe an array of particle synthesis techniques and principles.
Investigate and critically evaluate the relative advantages and limitations of advanced particle processes for a wide range of applications.
Describe advances in the application of nanoparticles.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 120 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Transport Phenomena
syllabus_overview: This course presents a unified and advanced approach to the study of transport phenomena, which unifies the topics of mass, momentum and heat transport. Fundamental concepts and methods will include: methods for prediction of transport properties (viscosity, thermal conductivity and diffusivities); equations of change in 3-D for isothermal fluid flow, heat conduction, diffusivity, and finally the general case of simultaneous transport; dimensional analysis of the equations of transport and its use in scale up. Applications of the basic equations to the study of forced and free convection, laminar flow, turbulent flow, heat conduction, diffusion and multi-component systems will be presented. Case studies will include: viscometers, transpiration cooling, free convection heat transfer, simultaneous heat and mass transfer, evaporative cooling, drying, mass transfer with chemical reaction, etc. Multidimensional and transient problems will be covered, as will those involving compressible flows, non-newtonian flows and turbulence modelling. Most analysis nowadays involves the use of numerical software. Therefore, an introduction to the numerical solution of partial differential equations will be given, followed by the use of commercial numerical software such as COMSOL to solve practical problems. Textbooks: Bird, Stewart and Lightfoot, Transport Phenomena, 2nd Edition. John Wiley & Sons, New York 2002
learning_outcomes: Understanding of the basic physical laws and equations governing transport phenomena (heat and mass transfer and fluid flow). Students should be able to answer questions on the meaning of the several terms of the momentum, heat and mass transfer equations, vector and tensor notation, formulate differential models to explain different phenomena and perform calculation using those equations.
Be able to make quantitative predictions about the physical behaviour of systems involving transport phenomena
Be able to analyse transport phenomena problems and identify major factors
Be able to use software effectively to model reasonably complex transport phenomena problems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Risks and Impacts of a Changing Climate
school: School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences
syllabus_overview: As global temperatures near 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels and track towards 2°C, broad sectors across government, non-government and industry must consider and plan for climate change impacts. This course will present the essentials of understanding and managing climate risk. Material will be presented in a manner that is accessible to students from all backgrounds and disciplines, demonstrating how climate risk may manifest as a challenge in a wide range of sectors (e.g., built environment, engineering, business, health, law, economics and policy). We aim to provide a fundamental understanding that will inform students within their own speciality and to engage them in an emerging issue that will be critical to their long-term employability in business, industry or government. The course material is presented entirely online giving you flexibility in when to engage with the course (noting deadlines for assessment tasks). There are also online practicals which provide experience dealing with climate projection data to answer questions about future risk.
learning_outcomes: Communicate sustainable approaches and methods to manage climate change and its risks in both local and global contexts.
Select and apply an appropriate method to identify and assess climate risk for a specific group of stakeholders.
Examine key climate change processes and related contemporary phenomena in the context of climate science and analyse related data.
Suggest actions for adaptation and mitigation in response to climate change risks at various political levels.
Explore future projections of climate change and their risks and impacts on various aspects of physical, natural, socio-economic and political environments.
Evaluate climate change risk utilizing the current international climate framework and its resources.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Climate Change
school: School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences
syllabus_overview: Why do people disagree so much about climate change? How can they tell fact from fiction in the debate? How do they know climate change is happening and what are the causes? Climate change is now an issue confronting many disciplines, from architecture, engineering and business through to environmental science, public health, law and economics. This online course will draw on a broad collection of UNSW experts to cover the basics of climate change science, as well as a selection of key related areas from psychology, law, politics, economics, energy supply, ethics and health. A range of perspectives on the nature of these challenges will be treated with a critical analysis approach, as well as hands-on engagement with the peer review process, highlighting its role in the scientific process. This course is an online-only offering and therefore there are no physical attendance requirements. There are no pre-requisites and so this course suits students at any stage of their degree. Lectures are asynchronous. However, the course requires regular and consistent online participation including online group work with other students. Students are expected to familiarise themselves with the course documentation and spend around 6 hours per week on the course. This includes going through lesson content in a timely manner, participating in group work activities, contributing to online discussion forums, and submitting assessments. Take a look at our short introduction video
learning_outcomes: Work effectively in a team to solve problems in a digital environment.
Outline the key drivers of the climate system, interactions between climate system components and the mechanisms involved in anthropogenic climate change.
Evaluate climate change mitigation strategies and describe how these affect climate change impacts.
Describe the scientific method, understand the peer review process, and explain how these are embodied in Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change best practices.
Critically analyze relevant material from a range of scientific and public information sources.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Atmospheric Science
school: School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course covers the basic physical principles and processes which govern our atmosphere and its climate. Firstly, students are provided with an overview of our the Earth’s atmosphere, the main physical principles that govern its behaviour, and how to apply them to important questions about weather and climate. This overview draws on foundational theoretical and applied concepts in physics and chemistry (including calculus); shows students an important application of basic physics (and a bit of chemistry); and for Oceanography, Meteorology and Climate students, in preparation for future courses in their Programs, this provides a foundation upon which later courses will build. As part of their learning, students will be introduced to concepts including the ozone hole, the greenhouse effect, how to use charts to determine the likelihood of storms developing, why deserts occur at certain latitudes, and how to forecast the weather. Students will then have the opportunity to consider these concepts in an applied context and practise their skills through activities that integrate real-world problems and situations. This skill will add value to the work that students have already invested in learning those principles and will be relevant no matter what later path in life they take. Furthermore, both mid-term and final exams will be organised as oral exams, supporting students to learn and gain confidence in communicating within interview-style situations; an essential life skill for the rest of their careers.
learning_outcomes: Explain weather and climatic phenomena, for example why the temperature decreases with height, why low pressure systems are linked to bad weather and how the ozone hole forms.
Describe the main processes that govern atmospheric processes and patterns.

Recall and apply physical and mathematical concepts as tools to explain atmospheric phenomena, such as the rotation around high and low pressure systems, the existence of jet streams, the formation of convective storms, or the greenhouse effect.
Describe the main phenomena which determine the climate on Earth, and how it has changed over the planet’s history.
prerequisites: PHYS1111 or PHYS1121 or PHYS1131 or DPST1023 or PHYS1141 or PHYS1211 and MATH1011 or MATH1031 or MATH1131 or DPST1013 or MATH1141 or MATH1151

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Climate Systems Science
syllabus_overview: This course provides a thorough overview of the climate system and its scientific study. In lectures and hands-on lab sessions, the different components of the climate system – including the atmosphere, ocean, biosphere, and cryosphere – are introduced, and their complex interactions are discussed. These interactions include feedbacks between the Earth's carbon cycle, hydrological cycle, biosphere and key chemical species. The course covers the scientific study of the climate system, including observational approaches and uncertainties; statistical methods used to detect and understand environmental changes; and modelling techniques including idealised models, process models and comprehensive state-of-the-art climate and Earth system models. Students receive hands-on experience in running and interpreting results from a climate model to interrogate changes and interactions in the climate system.
learning_outcomes: Confidently use environmental/climate data and recognise their limitations, uncertainties, and representativeness.
Clearly communicate climate change concepts and results of simulation experiments, tailoring the communication to suit the audience.
Perform calculations of indices of climate phenomena such as El Nino using scripts, with the ability to both adapt existing and create new scripts.
Design experiments with, run, and interpret the output of a numerical climate model to study climatic changes, and show the results in the form of a scientific article.
Understand and explain in detail a range of climate phenomena and their interactions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Computing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Design Computing introduces you to the exploration and visualisation of complex data. Using a synthesis of technical and theoretical knowledge of design computing, you will apply skills in a text-based programming language to inform your own design projects and professional work. You will participate in weekly activities to experiment with and develop your technical knowledge. You will also develop your verbal and digital communication skills to present explorations and results.
learning_outcomes: Communicate complex design computing data through scripts and digital images.
Synthesise computing theory and technical knowledge for design.
Apply design computing in your own design projects and professional work.
Apply programming skills in a text-based language.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design: Technologies, Concepts and Cases
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course addresses architecture’s digital turn and introduces you to historical and contemporary discourses. It explores theoretical concepts and ideas through architectural projects that have engaged digital technologies and computational design thinking from the late twentieth century onwards. You will develop skills in verbal, visual, and written modes of analysis. You will critically evaluate discourses and architectural projects relating to digital and computational design technologies. You will also develop your verbal and digital communication skills to present computational knowledge and analysis.
learning_outcomes: Assess the ethical use of digital and computational technologies in an architectural context
Demonstrate knowledge of history and theory of computational design thinking and methods in an architectural context
Explain the use of computational thinking and methods in architectural projects
Communicate computational design concepts through text, image and media based platforms

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Future Cities: Technologies, People and Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores how digital and computing technologies have been central to visions of future cities since the mid-twentieth century, as well as the ways they are now integral to people’s everyday experiences. You will investigate how networked technologies mediate people’s movements, actions, interactions, and understandings in urban environments. By collecting data, using computational tools, and drawing on scholarly thinking, you will critically analyse contemporary human-technology-environment relations and evaluate their ethical implications.
learning_outcomes: Assess the ethical practice of digital technologies in and for the design of the built environment.
Critically analyse and evaluate computational technologies in and for the design of the built environment.
Investigate and explain historic and contemporary approaches to the design of the built environment in relation to digital culture and computing technologies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Computing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to urban computing, critique, and discourses through case examples of data and data collection. You will apply computational thinking and methods to analyse urban and spatial conditions. In addition, this course will support the creation of design projects that adopt principles of physical computing, interaction design, human-machine interaction, and data collection. The course culminates in the creation, construction, and presentation of data collection proposals and working prototypes that engage sensing and actuating technologies.
learning_outcomes: Research and analyse urban conditions using computational thinking and methods.
Apply principles of physical computing, interaction design and human-machine interaction to your design projects.
Construct interaction-design working prototypes that engage sensing and actuating technologies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design 4 (System)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Computational Design 4 investigates the application of computational thinking and methods to data, formats, and modelling to create optimisation and decision-support workflows and systems for design processes. You will apply advanced skills in visual programming and text-based programming to solve design technology interoperability problems and create systems that can address UN Sustainable Development Goals.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced programming skills to address design technology interoperability problems.
Analyse case studies of computational thinking and methods used to create optimisation and design decision-support tools and systems
Apply computational thinking and methods to data, formats, and modelling to create decision-support systems for built and urban environment design processes
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE2132

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design 1 (Building)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will develop and apply fundamental skills in visual programming languages to critically analyse complex environmental conditions while synthesising computational design thinking knowledge and methods for solving building challenges. Theoretical knowledge will cover morphology, algorithmic form, emergence, and systems. You will participate in weekly laboratory-based activities to experiment with and develop architectural forms (buildings). You will also develop your verbal and digital communication skills to demonstrate computational design ideas and results.
learning_outcomes: Communicate computational design ideas through scripts, environmental analysis and digital images.
Synthesise computational design thinking knowledge and methods for building challenges.
Apply fundamental visual programming skills to analyse complex environmental conditions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BENV1012

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design 2 (Structure)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Computational Design 2 (Structure) is the second of five computational design courses that introduce you to parametric design. You will investigate, develop, and apply computational thinking and methods in the context of the engineering discipline and practice to generate, analyse, and evaluate a structurally sound design. You will participate in weekly activities to research, design, model, simulate, analyse and evaluate the performance of structural systems.
learning_outcomes: Create and evaluate structural and civil engineering outcomes using computational design thinking and methods.
Apply advanced skills in a visual programming language interfaces and intermediate skills in a text based programming language.
Apply relevant verbal and multimedia communication skills.
Demonstrate theoretical knowledge of computational structural and civil engineering.
Evaluate and critique case studies of computational structural and civil engineering.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: BENV1012 and CODE1240

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Building Information Modelling
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to Building Information Modelling (BIM) concepts, standards and methods applicable to the built environment. You will apply Building Information Modelling (BIM) skills for the design, documentation and visualisation of buildings. You will collaborate in multi-disciplinary teams to achieve optimal design solutions.
learning_outcomes: Apply Building Information Modelling (BIM) skills for the design, documentation and visualisation of buildings.
Explain Building Information Modelling (BIM) concepts, standards and methods applicable to the built environment.
Collaborate in multi-disciplinary teams employing Building Information Modelling (BIM) skills to achieve optimal design solutions
Generate high-performance building design through Building Information Modelling (BIM) analysis.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design 3 (Urban)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Computational Design 3 (Urban) develops intermediate skills in a visual programming language interface and a text-based programming language to create algorithmic processes for data driven urban design. You will iteratively and collaboratively generate, analyse, and evaluate spatial massing and urban design layouts. You will use a dynamic game engine environment to explore and communicate design proposals.
learning_outcomes: Apply iterative design processes to generate, test, and refine urban design proposals.
Analyse and evaluate algorithms for data driven urban design.
Apply intermediate visual and text-based programming skills to the design of buildings and spaces that respond to their urban context.
Communicate design proposals using dynamic visualisation processes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE2121

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Robotic Computing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The course introduces and critiques innovative research studies on robotic fabrication techniques and technologies. In this course, you will be provided with the conceptual understanding, technical skills and working methods required to fabricate architectural elements and apply principles of robotics and digital fabrication to your design work. You will use programming languages to optimise both the design and fabrication process to improve the performance and function of the elements.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant verbal and multimedia communication skills in a professional context.
Critique case studies and developments in robotic fabrication.
Apply computational thinking and methods to robotic fabrication.
Create design projects that apply principles of robotic and digital fabrication.
Create and construct digitally fabricated working prototypes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE1161

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Information Management
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will analyse and explain design information modelling (DIM) concepts, standards, and methods applicable to the design and delivery of built environment projects. You will apply DIM skills and methods to collaborate in a shared 3D modelling environment and create real-time analysis and evaluations of project schedules and budgets.
learning_outcomes: Explain design information modelling concepts, standards and methods applicable to a design project.
Apply collaborative skills in teamwork to ensure productivity and shared responsibility.
Apply design information modelling skills to create documentation, schedules, and budgets for a design project.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Collaboration
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Digital Collaboration explores the development of design technology concepts and workflows to foster ways of designing in the architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) industry that align to the UN Sustainable Development Goals. You will research design processes and production practices in the AEC industry and identify problems and innovation opportunities that can be addressed by leveraging computational design methods and circular design principles. The course culminates in the creation of computational design workflows that integrate fabrication strategies and assembly logic to test and realise material outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Investigate opportunities for innovation and entrepreneurship in the application of computational design technologies to design and production processes.
Collaborate to ensure productivity and shared responsibility across digital platforms.
Apply skills of research and inquiry to a practice-based computational design project.
Present a computational design research project using advanced verbal, visual and digital methods.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 72 UOC overall, including CODE2120 and enrolment in an undergraduate Computational Design specialisation or program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graduation Project Research
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course is the culmination of the Computational Design specialisation in the Bachelor of Design degree. You will research and write a thesis informed by computational design theory and underpinned by your project/practice work in CODE3202 Graduation Project: Practice. The course activities focus on developing your knowledge of theoretical concepts and research skills in relation to practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate rigorous research and inquiry skills within the context of practice-based computational design project.
Demonstrate the ethical application of digital technologies in a professional context using conceptual and theoretical understanding.
Author a scholarly thesis that communicates a computational design research project.
Synthesise interdisciplinary knowledge using computational design thinking and methods.
Formulate innovative and entrepreneurial solutions by applying computational design knowledge and technologies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE3100
Corequisite: CODE3202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Design 5 (Data)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Computational Design 5 (Data) you will apply advanced skills in a visual programming language interface and a text-based programming language of designing parts that operate as part of a system. You will participate to weekly laboratory-based activities to simulate, analyse, evaluate and design parts (building, roads, functions, etc) that assembles a system like a city. You will also develop your verbal and digital communication skills, particularly with game engines, to present computational design ideas and results.
learning_outcomes: Create digital tools and workflows for the management of urban data.
Critique discourse, policies, case studies of regional and global computational urbanism
Apply computational thinking and methods including a wide range of geospatial data, formats, and modelling to analyse urban sites.
Apply proficient skills in programming to address interoperability challenges for urban data management.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE2120

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graduation Project: Practice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The Graduation Project is the culmination of the Computational Design specialisation in the Bachelor of Design degree and is delivered across two parallel and complementary courses, CODE3201 Graduation Project: Research and CODE3202 Graduation Project: Practice. The courses are structured to guide you from critical inquiry to applied action design research. You will apply your advanced computational design skills to solve real-world challenges, and learn methods to effectively communicate your research, design process, and final outcomes to diverse audiences, including industry.
learning_outcomes: Construct a physical and / or digital prototype to communicate a computational design research project.
Apply rigorous research and inquiry skills within the context of practice-based computational design project.
Communicate effectively to diverse audiences and stakeholders using advanced verbal, visual, written and digital methods.
Synthesise interdisciplinary knowledge using computational design thinking and methods.
Create innovative and entrepreneurial solutions by applying computational design knowledge and technologies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CODE3100. Corequisite: CODE3201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Critical Review of the Literature
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course is a major research-based investigation into a subject related to the student’s area of specialisation. It can be seen as a building block for ARCH 1482 and CODE4200, but it is a standalone project and yields its own outcome – a critical review of the computational design literature. This leads to a culmination of a well-informed understanding of the chosen research topic. It is expected that the critical review of the literature will offer a critical interpretation of the existing knowledge and literature. The length of the final as submitted literature review, should not exceed 8,000 words.
learning_outcomes: apply cognitive and technical skills to demonstrate a broad understanding of a body of knowledge, theoretical concepts in the field of computational design.
classify practice and critical thinking and judgement in the field of computational design.
identify technical skills to design and use research in a project to present a clear and coherent exposition of knowledge and ideas to a variety of audiences.
review, analyse, consolidate and synthesise knowledge to identify and provide solutions to complex problems with intellectual independence in the field of computational design.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Honours Thesis
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will author a written thesis that communicates your independently-led computational design honours research project. The thesis will follow the generally accepted structure of a research thesis and will include an introduction, literature review, methodology, case study, discussion, and conclusion section. Your thesis will demonstrate the application of relevant research methods, concepts, and computational design processes and technologies that you have engaged to answer your research question and to meet your research aims.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate research methods and technologies to a significant research project in the field of computational design
Demonstrate initiative and judgement in professional practice and/or scholarship in the field of computational design
Undertake a significant research project with some independence in the field of computational design
Prepare an evidence-based argument to support the relevance of your research project to the field of computational design

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: NGOs, Civil Society and Development
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will critically examine the complex role of civil society and NGOs in development activities and processes, with an emphasis on global development. In this course you will cover theoretical and practical insights concerning the role of civil society and NGOs and will learn about different types of organisations (such as humanitarian and development; faith-based; campaigning vs. service delivery) and their strategies, activities and approaches. You will explore the interfaces of these organisations and institutions with culture, gender, human rights, Indigenous rights, and dominant ideologies. You will also explore the links between civil society, NGOs and other development actors, as well as their relationship to the sustainable development goals (SDGs) and key global challenges. You will be required to engage actively online, in class, independently and in a group. You will come from any of a range of disciplinary backgrounds and will want to learn how to make a difference in social justice, development and humanitarian settings.
learning_outcomes: Document and critique the challenges and responses affecting civil society and NGO roles in both “developed” and “developing” societies
Based on research, design and communicate a set of strategies and accountabilities that reflect good practice in global development and humanitarian action

Analyse the social, economic and contextual changes, and evaluate the theories, that help to explain the emergence, growth and changing roles of civil society, not-for-profit and social purpose organisations
Develop the ability to provide advice, drawing upon theory, evidence, and experience, concerning effective activities and roles that civil society and NGOs can play in a range of development settings

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Development, Human Rights and Global Health
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will analyse the interface of three important global topics: global development, human rights, and global health. Included within this analysis will be the present status of international human rights and international humanitarian law as they apply to global health practice in relation to low and middle income countries. The course seeks to engage students, scholars, human rights practitioners, health professionals, advocates, development professionals and members of civil society in a dialogue about the reciprocal interaction between global development, human rights, and global health. It will offer tools that stakeholders can use to incorporate a human rights framework into their development and global health practice.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate how international mechanisms and procedures can be applied to development, human rights and global health and how they can be accessed
Define underlying principles and approaches to each of the fields of development, human rights and global health
Identify key actions and research that will facilitate understanding and depth of analysis of the synergy between development, human rights and global health.
Describe the relationships and interactions between development, human rights and global health

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: myBCom Blueprint
syllabus_overview: COMM0999 is a 0 Unit of Credit course that is required to be completed in the first term of the Bachelor of Commerce degree. The course introduces students to the Bachelor of Commerce program and the myBCom framework. COMM0999 provides structured onboarding to university study and the UNSW Business School community, supporting students to build confidence, connections, and early career awareness. Students explore their motivations, values, and goals, and develop a personalised myRoadmap to guide their first year. Students participate in on-campus and online activities designed to foster belonging, academic readiness, and goal setting. They identify short- and long-term development goals aligned with the Business School Program Learning Outcomes (PLOs) and plan activities to build myBCom points for future courses. Students are required to complete activities on the myBCom platform: https://mybcom.unsw.edu.au/
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise professional pathways and set career-ready goals using resources and opportunities provided within the Bachelor of Commerce.
Plan curricular and co-curricular experiences within the Bachelor of Commerce to develop a personalised action plan that reflects emerging workplace expectations.
Identify personal values, motivations, and strengths aligned with the Business School’s Program Learning Outcomes (PLOs).
prerequisites: Only available to students completing a Bachelor of Commerce as part of a single or double degree

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Climate Change Adaptation & Development
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered how climate change affects the lives and livelihoods of the poorest people in developing countries? This course exposes you to key themes in the climate change adaptation and international development debate and will enable you to critically understand the climate change and development issues affecting the capacity and well-being of local communities in Australia and developing countries. The course examines how local level responses to climate change are shaped by multi-level climate governance processes, exposes inequities in adaptation responses to climate change impacts, and explores how these adaptations can better respond to the needs of poor and disadvantaged communities.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the range of concepts, policies and practice of climate change adaptation in relation to development studies
Critically analyse climate change adaptation policy and practices in different contexts using case studies
Undertake critical social science research and analysis, independently and in a team environment, and further develop research, interpersonal, communication and teamwork skills
Propose pathways and options for reducing community vulnerability and enhancing resilience

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurship in the 21st century is rapidly evolving. Disruptive changes in technology, manufacturing, supply chains, talent, communication, and capital markets have led to the rise of global startup ecosystems. Governments, corporates and universities are recognising the potential for the next wave of economic growth to emerge from disruptive startup enterprises, and are working together to nurture them via grants, tax incentives, direct funding, subsidised space, education, competitions, purchasing policies, mentoring and partnerships. This course provides exposure to the fundamentals of global entrepreneurship ecosystems and the practical aspects of identifying, evaluating, and moving business ideas forward in them. The course inspires students to critically think about how entrepreneurs identify opportunities, understand customer needs, harness resources, create innovative business models, attract capital and solve real-world challenges. The course addresses key contemporary topics in entrepreneurship ecosystems and their application in any field—from business and design to healthcare and product development. The course aims to provide foundational knowledge of entrepreneurship ecosystems, lean startup and design thinking methodologies applied in startups. Different offerings of the course will allow students to: 1. explore the rise of Sydney as one of the world’s emerging entrepreneurial cities through experiential learning, employing the latest in VR and AR technologies, or 2. undertake a study tour of an international entrepreneurial ecosystem which will include online workshops on startup best practice overseas, and a two week intensive startup ecosystem experience. This course also provides a pathway into the UNSW Founders Program. For more information visit: https://founders.unsw.edu.au For Business School students, this course can be counted as one of your Business School electives.
learning_outcomes: Adopt a global perspective when assessing startup ecosystems.
Apply research skills to the analysis of emerging startups/social enterprise opportunities.
Identify cultural and communication characteristics critical for startup ecosystems.
Critically reflect on your own practise as an emerging entrepreneur.
Apply lean startup and design thinking methodologies to existing businesses.
Describe the interdependencies, opportunities and challenges of startups within ecosystems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Students must be in Good Academic Standing

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Decision Making
syllabus_overview: This is the first course in the Integrated First Year of the Bachelor of Commerce, which introduces you to business decision making. You will learn about economic, corporate responsibility and legal principles to understand what organisational actors need to consider and what actions they might take. Fundamental economic principles inform decision makers to ask and answer questions about how the economy works, and how these principles influence the decisions that individuals and organisations make. Core legal principles guide decision makers to protect value for owners and other stakeholders and protect both managers and organisations from public and private legal actions arising from their decisions. Corporate responsibility principles direct decision makers to meet the organisation’s responsibilities to a range of stakeholders
learning_outcomes: Identify legal issues that arise in commercial situations and analyse how they influence business decisions
Apply appropriate search strategies to research and summarise relevant and valid information from a range of suitable sources
Explain the interplay of economic, legal, and corporate responsibility principles in business decisions
Identify the key features of corporate (social, environmental) responsibility, and how the business world can contribute to the greater good
Identify appropriate economic models and analyse how they are used in business decisions
prerequisites: Only single and double degree Business School students or 6115 UNSW Preparation Program 17-19 are permitted to enrol in Term 1. Business School and non-Business School students are permitted to enrol in Terms 2 and 3. Students enrolled in Actuarial Studies or Economics programs (in single or double degree mode) are not permitted to enrol.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evidence-Based Problem Solving
syllabus_overview: Effective problem solving is a core capability of a successful business professional, and UNSW Commerce students need to demonstrate problem solving initiative and confidence in their studies and professional careers. Evidence-based Problem Solving introduces students to the fundamentals of a deliberate and structured approach to problem solving, balancing analysis and judgement, to avoid the common pitfalls of problem solving in organisations. The importance and power of evidence, and familiarity with the different sources of evidence, are critical for identifying, solving and communicating a problem. Starting from business problems that organisations are confronted with, students will develop their ethical judgement, reasoning and analysis skills, and work with both quantitative and qualitative data as a preparation for critical interpretation of data. In addition to developing an analytical mindset and new ways of working with data, students are also introduced to the basic statistical skills required for working with small data sets. This prepares students for working with big data sets and mastering common analytics tools in COMM1190 Data, Insights and Decisions. This course is a fully problem-based learning course that starts with a multi-faceted problem.
learning_outcomes: Use information from qualitative and quantitative data to identify and interpret solutions to complex real-life problems
Independently use Excel’s graphical and statistical capabilities.
Collaboratively solve problems in teams, incorporating diverse perspectives.

Draw on evidence to frame and apply logical reasoning, and distinguish relevant information from irrelevant information when providing original solutions to real life problem-solving for organisations.
Explain basic statistical methods and know when to apply appropriate methods in practical scenarios
Recognise various ethical frameworks that can apply to a situation and apply these frameworks to resolve a simple ethical dilemma.
prerequisites: Students enrolled in 3764 (Eng/Comm), Actuarial Studies or Economics programs (in both single and double degree mode) are not permitted to enrol. Only single and double degree Business School students are permitted to enrol in Term 1. Business School and non-Business School students are permitted to enrol in Terms 2 and 3.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Collaboration and Innovation in Business
syllabus_overview: “Imagination is more important than knowledge. For while knowledge defines all we currently know and understand, imagination points to all we might yet discover and create.”(Albert Einstein). This course will introduce students to innovation processes and creative thinking tools to generate, develop, and evaluate innovative ideas and solutions for complex business challenges. Across every business function, collaboration and innovation are central to solving complex problems, exploring new strategies, and working effectively within an organisation. We implement a process that follows a divergent phase of problem exploration, convergent problem definition, divergent solution development, and convergent solution delivery, all delivered within a structured and scaffolded collaborative context. The course takes a hands-on and applied project-based approach, focusing on the big picture challenges facing businesses in the 21st century. We explore how through a business lens, students can work through these complex practical challenges in diverse teams. This gives students ample opportunity to develop their creative mindset, identify and test different ideas, and learn how to present their content in an engaging and persuasive way to influence others.
learning_outcomes: Examine the causes of a societal problem through divergent and convergent collaborative approach. [PLO2; PLO3; PLO4]
Create an innovative solution that addresses a societal and business problem. [PLO2; PLO6]
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner that demonstrates differing perspectives in persuasive communication practices [PLO3]
Evaluate personal development of learning through reflection on the contributions of self and peers within the teamwork process. [PLO4; PLO7]
Recognise diverse perspectives and worldviews of others to inform innovative and collaborative processes. [PLO6]
Apply effective collaborative and project management skills to complete team project. [PLO2; PLO3; PLO4; PLO7]
prerequisites: Only single and double degree Business School students or 6115 UNSW Preparation Program 17-19 are permitted to enrol in Term 1. Business School and non-Business School students are permitted to enrol in Terms 2 and 3.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Management
syllabus_overview: COMM1140 introduces students to key concepts of accounting, finance, and taxation, with a focus on developing financial literacy skills for business contexts. The course emphasises how financial information is used to assess a company’s performance and position, and how these insights support effective business decision-making. Students will explore the link between financial information and capital markets, gaining insights into how these connections shape a company's valuation. Additionally, students will develop an awareness of how sustainability considerations are impacting business management and reporting, giving a well-rounded introduction to what it takes to understand and run a successful business.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the connections between financial reporting, corporate performance, and capital markets.
Explain the value of emerging sustainability reporting frameworks for managers seeking to manage and run a responsible business.
Assess the effectiveness of companies in controlling and managing important assets through the concepts of audit and internal control.
Identify and explain how foundational financial literacy concepts inform the preparation of various forms of financial reports used by managers.
Complete basic transaction analysis and comprehend its relevance for informed and effective decision making.
Collaborate to apply techniques and frameworks to evaluate a company's financial position and performance through interpretation of financial statements.
prerequisites: Only single and double degree Business School students are permitted to enrol in Term 1. Business School and non-Business School students are permitted to enrol in Terms 2 and 3. Students enrolled in both single and double Actuarial Studies degrees (programs 3586, 3587, 3589, 3155, 3674, 3588, 3671, 4737, 3154) are not permitted to enrol.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Business Environments
syllabus_overview: This course is integral to the Integrated First Year of your degree and builds on what you have already learned. COMM1100 explored the fundamental decisions managers need to make to keep the organisation running successfully and did so from the perspective of a structured environment. However, businesses do not operate in isolation: an organisation and the decisions their managers make exist in broader, often complex and dynamic environments. COMM1150 now introduces the interplay of organizations with their environmental contexts to achieve both commercial and societal value. It prompts students to investigate global business environments with economic, legal, political, socio-cultural, and sustainability lenses to sense disruptions and opportunities. This aim includes understanding the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and UNSW’s commitment to them.
learning_outcomes: Explain the complexity and diversity of an organisation’s global business environment.
Analyse how key features of the business environment are determined by individuals, organisations, and governments interacting within interrelated systems.
Develop a global mindset for analysing local processes and phenomena.
Apply various lenses (e.g., economic, political, sociocultural, and sustainability) and their associated concepts to understand specific business scenarios in a global environment.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM1100 and excludes MGMT1101. Students enrolled in Actuarial Studies or Economics programs (in single or double degree mode) are not permitted to enrol.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Organisational Resources
syllabus_overview: Organisations are constantly in transition. They grow, restructure, merge, digitalise, respond to crises, and attempt renewal. These transitions are not single events; they are extended periods of uncertainty in which existing routines break down and organisations must reconfigure how they use their resources. This course focuses on understanding how organisational transitions unfold over time, and how they are resourced and managed internally in more and less effective ways. Students learn to analyse organisational change as a process in which human, strategic, and financial considerations are tightly interdependent.
learning_outcomes: Analyse organisational transitions through the application of financial tools and techniques.
Identify organisational practices and processes for leadership development.
Identify different types of organisational resources and processes to guide organisational change.
Examine suitability and efficacy of an organisation's approach to resource management.
Develop novel solutions and assess their feasibility to support successful organisational transitions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM1140 or COMM1240

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Value Creation
syllabus_overview: COMM1180 explores how organisations create value through the decisions they make. From choosing which customers to target, to evaluating investments, setting prices, and measuring performance, each decision shapes the outcomes delivered to stakeholders. In this course, students engage with real business problems using a problem-based learning (PBL) approach that integrates finance, accounting, and marketing. Each week, students analyse decisions from different perspectives, considering opportunities, trade-offs, risk, and their impact on outcomes. As the term progresses, students develop core skills in evaluating investments, understanding customers, designing value propositions, setting prices, and assessing performance using both financial and non‑financial measures. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyse business situations, evaluate alternatives, and make informed decisions that influence how value is created and sustained.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively in small groups to address business problems, incorporating diverse perspectives and providing constructive feedback.
Apply methods to value financial assets and evaluate the value created or destroyed by financial decisions.
Apply critical thinking and ethical decision making, to define and measure value from different perspectives to know when value is (and is not) created.
Analyse how organisations create and capture stakeholder value through pricing and production volume decisions, plus performance measurement techniques (including potential dysfunctional effects).
Compare basic strategies to create value for and from customers, and a recognition that such value can be financial and non-financial.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM1140 or COMM1240

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data, Insights and Decisions
syllabus_overview: COMM1190 teaches students the fundamental analytical and statistical tools an organisation uses to gain insights about customers, markets, competitors and itself. In this course students apply statistics and data analysis skills to real large data sets with a focus on applications, rather than methods. They will learn how to describe, collect/source and analyse business data from a variety of business domains such as finance, marketing, management, risk analysis, etc. Effectively communicating data insights and recommendations to a non-technical audience, including data visualisation and simple dashboards, rounds off this highly applied and hands-on course.
learning_outcomes: Explain how an organisation uses analytical and statistical tools to gain valuable insights.
Work effectively in teams to communicate cohesive data insights and recommendations to a range of stakeholders.
Apply statistics and data analysis skills to real data sets from a variety of organisations and domains to generate insights in order to make informed decisions.
Critically evaluate the suitability of data and data sources to identify and analyse business problems.
Evaluate ethical implications of organisational use of big data and analytics on stakeholders and society.
Visualise and analyse data to support arguments that increase stakeholder comprehension of information and business insights.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM1110 or ECON1203 or MATH1041 or MATH1231 or MATH1241 or MATH1251 or PSYC1111.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Management for Actuarial Studies
school: School of Risk and Actuarial Studies
syllabus_overview: Are you pursuing actuarial studies and looking to build a strong foundation in financial management? Do you want to develop the skills to interpret financial statements, evaluate corporate investments, and understand how businesses raise and manage capital? Then COMM1240 – Financial Management for Actuarial Studies is the perfect course for you! COMM1240 provides actuarial students with a comprehensive understanding of corporate finance, financial reporting, and business taxation. You will learn how companies finance their operations, manage financial risk, and make investment decisions. The course also explores capital markets, corporate valuation, and governance, ensuring you develop the essential financial literacy required for actuarial practice. Additionally, you will develop an awareness of how issues of sustainability are impacting business management and financial reporting, equipping you with a well-rounded understanding of what it takes to run a successful and responsible business. This course aligns with the CB1 – Business Finance accreditation of the Australian Actuaries Institute, offering a tailored approach for actuarial students.
learning_outcomes: Examine how businesses raise capital and manage financial risk, with an emphasis on actuarial applications in insurance, investments, and financial markets
Apply techniques and frameworks to evaluate a company’s financial position and performance, including the analysis of financial statements, capital structure, and corporate governance.
Recognise the connections between financial reporting, corporate performance, and capital markets.
Explain the value of emerging sustainability reporting frameworks for managers seeking to run a responsible and sustainable business.
Identify and explain foundational financial literacy concepts and their role in the preparation and interpretation of financial reports, with a focus on actuarial and corporate finance applications.
Perform basic transaction analysis and assess its relevance for informed and effective decision-making.
prerequisites: Only students taking Actuarial Studies single and double degrees (programs 3586, 3587, 3589, 3155, 3674, 3588, 3671, 4737, 3154) are permitted to enrol.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Development Policy
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Are you interested to understand why there is a rich world and there is a poor world? What type of socio-economic and environmental policies can be identified and implemented to address some of these development challenges? In this course, you will critically engage with several of the 'big issues' concerning international development policy and highlights the link between ideas, policy and the reality of development with an emphasis on the challenges facing local communities in developing countries. The course blends theories of development with the rapidly expanding discipline of public policy to enable you to examine and explain the rate, form and patterns of socio-economic and environmental development challenges and opportunities. You will explore the influences upon this patterning and the response by local communities, state organisations and other institutions. The course will also include engagement with several sectoral policy issues on sustainable development such as participation, urban poverty, food security, equity, climate change and disasters.
learning_outcomes: Explain key concepts, approaches, issues and achievements of development theories applied as development policy in developing countries

Undertake critical social science research, independently and in a team environment, and develop the knowledge and communication skills necessary to engage in international development policy analysis and practice
Develop a critical perspective of development policies implemented to address key aspects of uneven development, focusing on major implications for the local communities

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Organisations in Their Environment
syllabus_overview: COMM1900 explores how external forces shape the key decisions managers make to guide organisations in an increasingly complex global environment. Taking the perspective of a manager, students develop the skills to analyse and evaluate the dynamic interplay of political, economic, socio-cultural, legal, technological, and sustainability forces and their implications for business decision-making. By viewing the environment as a complex dynamic system that presents managers with a range of wicked problems and tensions, students learn to identify emerging challenges and opportunities facing organisations and to make more informed and responsible decisions in a rapidly changing world.
learning_outcomes: Analyse complex and dynamic 'wicked problems' using rational, critical, and reflective thinking in a global business context.
Analyse the dynamic interplay of political, economic, socio-cultural, legal, technological and sustainability forces in a global business context.
Critically evaluate competing perspectives on corporate responsibility to explain the tensions in strategic business decision-making.
Apply systems thinking to evaluate how environmental dynamics influence organisational decision-making in a global context.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON1101 and ECON1102) or (DPBS1101 and DPBS1102)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

Students curate evidence of learning from their first year and evaluate their development against the first-year standard of the BCom Program Learning Outcomes (PLOs). Evidence of these outcomes include problem solving, communication, teamwork, responsible business practice, global and cultural competence and leadership and align to the UNSW Graduate Attributes. COMM1999 learning design promotes the knowledge, understanding, and skills that promote success across the BCom via a skills dashboard and curated learning portfolio that serves as supplementary documentation for potential employers or further academic study. Students need to obtain at minimum 25 points per PLO (course and experience) on the myBCom platform ( https://mybcom.unsw.edu.au/ ) by the end of term as a component to passing the course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Creating Social Change: From Innovation to Impact
syllabus_overview: Do you want to lead change and implement social innovations? Would you like to find ways to address complex social problems? This course is for aspiring change agents across all sectors, including business, not-for-profit and government. You will develop practical skills to lead complex systems to create better social outcomes. We explore the issues that policymakers, industry leaders and social service providers grapple with every day, such as inequality, place-based disadvantage, mental health, homelessness, and human rights. We will introduce models for systems change, and social innovation. The course will equip you with a broad understanding of social systems and the keys to initiating and sustaining positive social change. Through a range of local and global case studies, you will acquire the skills to identify and analyse stakeholders and structural elements in the social challenges that shape society. Join us to become a catalyst for change and make a tangible impact on society!
learning_outcomes: Justify complex social impact ideas logically and persuasively based on relevant evidence.
Compare and contrast approaches to social change in different cultural contexts.
Explain how a systems thinking approach supports positive social impact.
Design a social change process integrating ethical, environmental and sustainability concepts and practices.
Discuss the drivers of, and barriers, to positive social change.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industry Experience Program
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for you to apply and develop your academic knowledge and professional skills in a real working environment. You will develop your problem solving, time management and communication skills and increase your understanding of your organsation and how it contributes to the broader business landscape. You will be required to attend academic workshops throughout the term and spend a minimum of 120 hours working with your partner company on a placement or project basis. Enrolment in the course is restricted and only Business School students studying a single or dual degree who meet the requirements of the selection process will be admitted. For enquiries please contact Career Accelerator
learning_outcomes: Reflect on your experiences and assumptions and link key learnings to intended future practice
Identify and analyse an organisations’ purpose and the competitive landscape in which they operate
Display professionalism and effectiveness in a real-world business environment
Demonstrate self leadership and responsibility in a complex organisational setting

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industry Consulting Project
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for Business School students to apply their academic knowledge and other professional skills to solve real world problems as part of consulting team. Partnering with Industry, students will work with a company mentor and have the opportunity to pitch their solution to a panel of industry experts. This course is at the UNSW Kensington Campus and consists of pre-workshop modules, online discussion boards and three industry partner meetings. Each experience will be different depending on the organisations we partner with. For enquiries please contact Career Accelerator
learning_outcomes: Display self-awareness and life-long learning skills through critical reflective practice.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Future of Work Project
syllabus_overview: COMM2244 is a project based practicum aimed at developing and applying students’ skills, capabilities and knowledge of future workplaces. You will learn and practice the skills required to be successful as an individual - curiosity, creativity, empathy, and courage. You will examine how these factors underpin future career success in a rapidly changing global landscape, taking into account emerging technologies, artificial intelligence and other globalisation factors. Guided by your lecturer and as part of a small team, you will apply these skills and capabilities to a real-life business challenge for an industry partner. Your client will present a problem related to their future workforce and, in project teams, students will investigate this challenge, workshop solutions, and provide a recommended way forward. Each experience will be different depending on the organisations we partner with. For enquiries please contact the Career Accelerator team.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively, collaboratively and respectfully in diverse workplace and team situations
Identify the impact of economic, environmental and social sustainability on the Future of Work
Reflect on and apply academic knowledge, skills and capabilities to forecast capability and competency requirements for the future
Develop ability to reflect and critically think about your current and future professional goals in relation to the Future of Work
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC Business courses including DPBS equivalent courses completed and (COMM1999 for BCom students or Career Accelerator Essentials for non-BCom students).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Visualisation and Communication
school: School of Risk and Actuarial Studies
syllabus_overview: How can data help you tell a story? How can you use data storytelling to then tackle some of the big challenges we are facing around the world? Data visualisation and communication are critical skills in many professions. The creation of targeted, easily digestible visuals allows us to make sense of complex information in an accessible and easily understandable way. The ability to employ visuals will enhance almost any presentation to better engage our audience, make our messages more memorable, and facilitate more effective decision-making. In this course, we will give you the tools to create your own data story addressing a pressing and current global challenge as identified by the UN SDGs. You will learn how to design your story for your chosen audience, how to criticise misrepresentations of data (especially the intentional ones), and drive action to address your chosen challenge. So, how will you leave the world a better place?
learning_outcomes: Compose analytics-informed narratives for actionable business recommendations and communicate them convincingly to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Participate in experiential activities that will aid in evaluating career aspirations and marketing your skills to prospective employers.
Critically examine misrepresentations of data and apply relevant approaches to prevent and mitigate ethical risks.
Develop a strategy in a culturally diverse context to address a global issue
Examine stakeholder interests and devise strategies to implement innovations that consider business trends and opportunities.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON1203 or COMM1190 or MATH1151 or MATH1141 or MATH1131) and (COMM1822/COMM2822 or ACTL1101 or COMP3311)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Databases for Business Analytics
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Note: This course was previously identified as COMM1822. Students who have completed COMM1822 cannot enrol in COMM2822. This is a fundamental Business Analytics course. You will learn the concepts, techniques, and technologies relevant for creating and managing business databases, and principles and characteristics of Big Data. You will learn the Structured Query Language (SQL) language and how to use it to access data stored in relational database system, including fetch, delete, insert, and modify data.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with peers as a team to solve problems and achieve outcomes.
Discuss database ethical issues and elaborate on the privacy and security implications of Big Data and business analytics.
Access and manipulate a relational database using Structured Query Language.
Create and apply conceptual and relational database modelling methods.
Design, implement and evaluate database systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evidence-based Intervention Design and Evaluation
syllabus_overview: ​Evidence-based decision-making requires the ability to define problems, use data, design interventions and evaluate outcomes. This course is a fully problem-based learning experience in which you work individually and in teams as management consultants or advisors. You will use insights from data analysis to address one of three types of problems: motivating and designing an intervention, identifying and managing risks related to interventions, or evaluating the effectiveness and efficiency of interventions. The course is relevant to evidence-based decision-making in business, government and not-for-profit organisations. As a synthesis course, it requires you to apply and integrate knowledge and skills from across your degree, complete professional reports, and communicate findings clearly.​
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on your professional skills and behaviours, including identified gaps, and how you will adapt to a changing work environment.

Make informed decisions about how to address the research problem including what are the relevant theoretical and ethical frameworks to provide context and what are the sources of appropriate qualitative and quantitative data.
Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Identify, apply and adapt business skills and knowledge acquired across your program to critically analyse a contemporary business challenge.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Leading Change for Sustainability and Social Impact
syllabus_overview: Leading Change for Sustainability and Social Impact is a course designed for future leaders who are passionate about creating positive social and environmental change. Your ideas and passion for sustainability and social impact are just the first step to professional success. You need skills in leadership, creativity, systems thinking, communication and models for cultural change so that you can influence key decision-makers, build networks and make your idea a reality. The challenges of sustainability and social impact are driving change in many organisation, from large foundations to social enterprises, not-for-profits working with government to provide services, and small to large businesses. This course explores how to create and implement sustainability and social impact strategies for different organisational types. We take a broad view of sustainability based on the Sustainable Development Goals, acknowledging the human, social, economic and environmental elements of positive cultural change. We examine complex aspects of sustainability and social impact leadership faced by leaders from business, government and civil society.
learning_outcomes: Develop leadership skills and strategies necessary for initiating, managing, and sustaining change processes aimed at promoting sustainability and fostering positive social impact

Understand ethical awareness and responsible decision-making in leading change efforts, considering the long-term implications for the environment, society, and future generations, while navigating potential conflicts and trade-offs
Analyse and assess the interconnectedness between environmental, social, and economic factors in driving sustainable change
Collaborate in teams to leverage collective strengths, foster inclusive decision-making processes, and navigate challenges
Communicate ideas in a clear, succinct and professional manner.
Demonstrate the ability to apply systems thinking and stakeholder management techniques to address complex challenges

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Business Practicum
syllabus_overview: COMM3020 is an experiential and intensive for-credit course. It provides students the unique opportunity to gain international understanding, exposure and workplace skills through studying and working in a specified location overseas. The central component of the course is the opportunity to work in a small cross-disciplinary student consulting team on a genuine business issue of a client organisation, such as local branches of international financial, marketing and technology corporations. In addition, students will also attend master classes by local industry leaders, government officials and academic experts, and learn about the local culture through field trips to important cultural landmarks and sights.
learning_outcomes: Develop the capacity for self-leadership and self-directed learning from reflection on working in a business, working in another country, cultural understanding and yourself
Identify, analyse and apply global business knowledge and practices to a real-world business issue

Develop recommendations with a variety of stakeholders to address the business issue within an appropriate cultural context
