institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Risk Management and Business Analytics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Construction Risk Management and Business Analytics explores concepts, key elements and applications of risk management and data-driven risk assessment. The course investigates standards, best industry practices and business analytics and their application to risk management in real-world situations in engineering and construction projects. Project risk management is an iterative process and assists organisations in setting strategy, achieving objectives and informing decision-making during the project lifecycle. The course focuses on commercial risks in delivering complex construction projects. You will learn about key risk categories such as work health and safety, environment, quality and other common risks which occur throughout the project lifecycle. You will also learn how to use industry risk assessment tools and business analytics to achieve smarter engineering and construction risk reduction decisions.
learning_outcomes: Justify a research-based project Risk Management Plan, including a critical analysis and a data-driven solution plan.
Analyse and evaluate complex risks and contingencies applicable to construction projects, including environmental risks.
Apply tools and theoretical frameworks to assess risks and contingencies for construction projects.
Explain business analytics in driving smarter engineering and construction decisions.
Identify complex risks and uncertainties in relation to stakeholders’ objectives within the process of risk management.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Planning and Control
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Construction Planning and Control covers the time aspects of project management in the context of available resources and budget. Building upon basic project planning tools, including Bar Chart and Critical Path Method, this course teaches you a range of high-level construction planning and control techniques, as well as project control and risk estimation. The course requires you to create construction schedule plans for a complex construction project and produce a set of comprehensive planning documents using a similar approach used in industry practice.
learning_outcomes: Select and apply appropriate scheduling techniques for construction projects.
Develop construction planning documents covering a schedule, scope of works, contingency and risk plan.
Discuss probability scheduling for practical applications.
Calculate schedule networks through a manual approach and with appropriate software.
Develop time and resource scheduling plans based on resource and budget constraints.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Cost and Value Management
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Construction Cost and Value Management covers the forecasting, analysing, planning control and accounting of construction costs and the practice of value management in the construction industry. You will be introduced to construction cost information, databases practices, including total cost control and value management for construction projects.
learning_outcomes: Discuss value for money considerations in construction costing and value management processes.
Apply technical skills for cost and value management of construction projects using appropriate tools.
Appraise the decision-making processes in construction cost and value management.
Discuss the key aspects and processes of pre and post contract cost management.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Management Theory and Practice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will create a Construction Project Management Plan (CPMP) for a large-scale construction project. In the process you will refine your practical skills in planning, executing, monitoring, and controlling complex projects. You will learn how to incorporate various sub-plans, including scope, schedule, cost, risk, quality, health, safety, security, environmental, sustainability, procurement, stakeholder, communication, and change management plans into the larger CPMP.
learning_outcomes: Apply the theory of project management to construction projects.
Demonstrate leadership and interpersonal skills through collaboration in managing complex construction projects.
Prepare a complex and comprehensive Construction Project Management Plan inclusive of subsidiary management plans.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Infrastructure Planning, Procurement and Finance
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Infrastructure Planning, Procurement and Finance covers domestic and international infrastructure markets and challenges; understanding the transformative role of new infrastructure design and delivery to growth, urban consolidation and renewal; the role of government in infrastructure planning and provision; project service definition; business case/ feasibility; financing structures; procurement options and processes; tendering processes; public sector comparator and other ways of assessing value; delivery; commercial principles; risk management and; contract management. Increasing Australia's global competitiveness will depend critically on the efficient procurement, finance, delivery and management of effective and high quality social and economic infrastructure. Experts from industry, government and academia will work with you to critically explore best practice from around the world in social and economic infrastructure planning, procurement and finance.
learning_outcomes: Explain infrastructure provision as related to urban planning activity.
Describe the effect of infrastructure provision on the use, development, management and value of land.
Evaluate the interdependent roles and responsibilities of the many contributors to successful infrastructure projects over its entire life cycle.
Assess and manage the risks and opportunities at each stage of the infrastructure life-cycle in order to optimise project outcomes.
Contrast and critique current approaches to infrastructure procurement and finance around the world.
Analyse and develop innovative ways to procure and finance new infrastructure projects using best practice knowledge from around the world.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Contract Administration
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The course introduces you to procurement methods and the practice of construction contract management. You will learn about: (a) different options for project delivery and the options for contract price; (b) the common matters covered in the general conditions of a major construction contract, including (but not limited to) practical completion, extension of time, liquidated damages, latent conditions, delay costs, bonus and variation clauses, insurances; (c) the relevance of legal concepts, including unjust enrichment, frustration, waiver, estoppel, frustration and repudiation to contract administration; (d) alternative dispute resolution methods; (e) the purpose and application of the Security of Payments legislation for construction; and (f) the relevance of the Australian Consumer law.
learning_outcomes: Apply dispute resolution mechanisms in contract administration
Understand how to formulate contracts at different stages in a project
Evaluate payments in accordance with variations submitted
Apply contract administration and legal principles to the practice of project management

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminology: An Introduction
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Introduces the key concepts and current debates in criminology. Covers basic issues such as the definition, measurement and explanations of crime, societal reactions to crime, criminological theories, the role of research and the influence of criminology on public policy.
learning_outcomes: Identify key players, themes and debates about crime
Analyse crime problems using basic criminological perspectives
Demonstrate an understanding of key criminological theories and concepts through critical engagement with literature, news and other media
Think critically about crime and its causes
Understand and use basic terminology common to the criminological field
Outline the scope, aims and practices of Criminology as a discipline;
Describe a variety of ways to define, measure and explain crime

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Criminal Justice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be introduced to the institutions and practices of the criminal justice system. As well as considering the operation of various components of the criminal justice system - including the police, courts, and corrections - we will also address new and emerging developments in criminal justice practice, crime prevention, and responses to crime. As such, the course will provide you with a critically reflective and thought-provoking introduction to the criminal justice system, accompanied by a discussion of the key issues that arise in relation to its operation (effectiveness and non-discrimination in practice, and alignment with underlying philosophies of justice) and impact on different individuals and groups in society.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impact of criminal justice practices on individuals and groups in society
Investigate issues and debates about the criminal justice system
Assess contemporary developments in criminal justice practice and policy
Identify and describe the key components of the criminal justice system
Interrogate different interpretations and understandings of justice

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Issues in Policing
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: CRIM2014 charts the historical development of policing as a set of social and legal practices and challenges you to consider the factors which continue to shape this development. The course will provide you with a critical understanding of the key practices, processes and institutional structures which shape policing in liberal democracies. It will also challenge preconceptions about policing being merely a response to crime, and get you to think critically about how and why policing is a fundamental aspect of the criminal justice process.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and critique the 'policing' function.
Distinguish policing as a process from particular 'police' organisations.
Critically analyse concepts from the international policing literature and relate them to local developments in NSW and across Australia.
Synthesise research and theory from criminological and socio-legal sources to develop an inter-disciplinary understanding of the changing nature of policing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminal Law and Justice 1
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Subject Area: Criminology CRIM2020 introduces you to fundamental aspects of criminal justice and process. Woven through the course is a critical examination of the interaction between the criminal justice system and the criminal law: specifically, that application of the law is shaped by and dependent on decisions made by criminal justice actors including police, prosecutors and judicial officers. Specific areas of focus include: why some activities are criminalised and others not; the use and misuse of discretion; the impact of the reliance on summary justice; the significance of pre-trial processes such as arrest and bail; and the over-representation of Indigenous people and other vulnerable groups.
learning_outcomes: Debate key legal concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner
Effectively incorporate a range of legal and interdisciplinary research sources in written communication with appropriate referencing
Engage in reflective practice regarding the criminal law’s role in serving society and promoting justice
Navigate and explain the basic doctrines, principles and rules relating to pre-trial procedure in criminal litigation
Articulate legal concepts clearly, persuasively and appropriately
Use statutory interpretation principles to identify the constituent elements of criminal offences and apply to hypothetical fact scenarios
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 and CRIM1011; Excluded: Students in all Bachelor of Laws double-degree programs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Crime, Politics and the Media
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Crime and justice issues dominate politics, the media and popular culture. This course looks critically at the development and nature of 'law and order politics' and the media's fascination with crime, both of which govern popular understandings of crime risks and threats, and what may be considered appropriate policy responses to them. You will reflect on how and why crime and criminality have become a source of public fascination as well as a policy area on which elections may be won or lost. You will also examine how crime news is constructed and the implications of these constructions for those who are criminalised, victim-survivors, and the public. In exploring these issues, you will engage with numerous examples and case studies from contemporary politics, news and entertainment media, and popular culture.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the construction and portrayal of crime in news, entertainment media and popular culture
Describe and apply theoretical understandings of media and crime
Critically evaluate the relationships between law and order politics, crime and the media
Investigate and critique the relationship(s) between the media and criminal justice institutions
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Perspective in Criminal Justice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course traces the use of the criminal justice system in Australia to control Aboriginal people, from the period of colonial dispossession to contemporary times. Looking at crime and criminal justice through a post-colonial lens, we will hear from Aboriginal voices about experiences of crime and criminal justice, identify emerging trends in Indigenous justice from Australia and elsewhere, and consider the possible role of self determination and reconciliation in the 'decolonisation' of criminal justice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate culturally appropriate, historically informed strategies for mitigating crime and addressing social issues in Indigenous communities. (PLOs 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7)
Evaluate current criminal justice practices critically and from a historically informed standpoint. (PLOs 1, 2, 3, 5, 7)
Describe the significance of human rights protection, self-determination, and decolonization in reducing Indigenous crime and criminalisation. (PLOs 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7)
Explain historical applications of law and criminal justice in dispossessing, segregating, and controlling Aboriginal people. (PLOs 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminal Law and Justice 2
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Subject Area: Criminology Criminal Law and Justice 2 (CRIM2021) builds on the themes introduced in Criminal Law and Justice 1 (CRIM2020). In this course you will examine selected crimes, their legal definition and the policy contexts in which they operate. The legal definition of crime happens formally through the pronouncements of legislatures and courts: but it also happens through the operation of the criminal justice process. In CRIM2021 you will focus on the processes by which police, prosecutors and courts deal with crime. In addition, you will consider further how legal definitions, criminal justice practice and competing policy priorities are interconnected. In particular, you will scrutinize the ways in which laws are applied, and also change over time, in relation to issues such as illicit drugs and assault.
learning_outcomes: Effectively navigate and apply the substantive criminal law, both common law and statutory
Synthesize a range of legal and interdisciplinary research sources in written communication with appropriate referencing
Critically debate legal concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner
Critically evaluate key legal concepts clearly
Identify the key processes and ethical issues involved in criminalisation by engaging in policy analysis
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CRIM2020, not available to students in Bachelor of Laws double-degree programs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Prison and Punishment: Introduction to Penology
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Subject Area: Criminology This course provides an introduction to penology. It begins by considering the growing use of prisons across the developed world and is then constructed around three main themes: theorising the prison; perspectives for reform; and contemporary issues in Australian penal policy. The elective is designed to give students some insight into the frameworks used by social theorists to analyse imprisonment, with a view to examining contemporary issues such as ‘supermax’ prisons, deaths in custody, immigration detention, the civil rights of prisoners and prison privatisation. The experience of the New South Wales prison system following the 1978 Royal Commission into New South Wales prisons provides an immediate context for studying such issues and an opportunity to examine the complexities and limitations of prison reform. The course intends to focus on the wider sociological implications of imprisonment and to introduce students to the various perspectives on punishment and the prison system offered by social theorists. It is designed to encourage both a basic understanding of the core literature and the ability to apply different penological perspectives to original research. A student who has successfully completed this course should be able to: understand some of the main themes within penology; understand the relationship of penology to criminology; appreciate the wider instrumental role of the prison in the criminal justice process; and contribute to more informed policy debate about prisons and punishment.
learning_outcomes: Engage in reflective practice regarding the role of punishment in society, and the differential effects of punishment including upon marginalised groups
Identify and discuss the main themes within penology
Critically analyse contentious areas of public policy with regards to relevant theoretical frameworks and policy approaches
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminal Networks and Organised Crime
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course examines organised crime and criminal networks across a number of contexts including drug trafficking, terrorism, and the trade in illicit commodities. During the course we examine critical issues in the field including the debate about whether criminal groups are marked by structure/hierarchy or by flexibility/loose connections. We will also examine the use of Social Network Analysis by law enforcement agencies and researchers to better understand and respond to criminal networks. We will explore the utility of a "networked" perspective within criminology more generally (e.g., to explain trends in neighbourhood crime rates, gang crime). During the course, you will have the opportunity to conduct a case study on a criminal network.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the structure/function of organised crime and criminal networks, and criminal justice responses, through scholarly discussion, debate, and written analysis of case study material.
Locate network theory within the broader sociological and criminological literature.
Use Social Network Analysis to describe the structure and function of organised crime groups and criminal networks.
Identify strengths and weaknesses in contemporary scholarly discourse with respect to the structure and function of criminal networks and organised crime.
Identify and evaluate criminal justice responses to organised crime and criminal networks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Young People and Juvenile Justice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will develop a critical understanding of the juvenile law system, including legal principles, policing practice, courts, sentencing and imprisonment of young people. The course asks you to reflect on why we criminalise children and the impact this has on the communities they are part of. It takes an interdisciplinary approach to the analysis of crime policies that target young people, and asks you to think critically about how these impact marginalised youth in particular. It examines the origins of the juvenile system, current dynamics and emerging influences by drawing on key case studies related to drug use, Indigenous justice, and gender and racial politics.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on key elements of the criminal and juvenile law system, crime and social policy, and their impact on the lives of young people.
Develop analytical skills of evaluation and argumentation, and apply them in the context of contemporary debates/arguments around juvenile justice.
Demonstrate the ability to communicate research, evidence and conceptual arguments about the juvenile law system to professional audiences.
Understand the role of colonisation in the establishment of the juvenile law system and its ongoing impacts on young people.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Disability in the Criminal Justice System
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course explores current theoretical, policy and practice-oriented debates about how and why people with disability are overrepresented in all stages of criminal justice systems across western societies. The course will put these current debates in context by exploring interdisciplinary materials and approaches - including critical criminology, penal abolition, decoloniality, disability justice and critical disability studies - that provide important insights about the role of historical, social- structural and cultural factors, as well as forms of state violence, abuse and neglect in the increasing criminalisation and imprisonment of people with disability. We will hear from criminalised people with disability, as well as leading advocates and practitioners working in the field. A key aim of the course is to develop a nuanced understanding of how disability as a key analytic category and identity (alongside class, race and gender/sexuality) is central to developing a deeper understanding of the functions, purpose and consequences of criminal justice systems. A related aim is to explore how this knowledge contributes to the development of alternatives to criminal justice that are rooted in the principles of social, restorative and transformative justice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate creativity and innovation through consideration of alternatives to criminalisation and punishment

Identify and explain the role of historical, social-structural and cultural factors, as well forms of state violence, abuse and neglect in the current overrepresentation of people with disability in criminal justice systems
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the complex intersections between disability and criminal justice systems
Articulate how a critical and reflexive interdisciplinary theoretical analysis of disability assists in understanding the purpose, functions and consequences of criminal justice systems
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Explaining Punishment
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be introduced to a theoretical and policy-oriented consideration of how and why we punish criminal offending, particularly through the use of imprisonment. You will take an inter-disciplinary approach utilising law, history, sociology, and criminology. You will consider various theoretical contributions that have shaped our understanding of punishment including the work of Durkheim, Foucault, Weber, Marxist approaches, and David Garland. Finally, you will also examine contemporary law and public policy issues, including juvenile detention, women in prison, the imprisonment of ethnic and racial minorities, inequality and imprisonment, privatisation, torture, deaths in custody, the death penalty, and the impact of law and order policies on punishment.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the relationship between race, gender and class and the administration of punishment
Outline various theoretical contributions to the concept of punishment
Interrogate the relationship between sentencing and punishment
Explain punishment and penalty in modern society
Analyse the relationship between punishment and social structure, and the significance of punishment for socio-political order
Investigate contemporary issues in punishment and the related public policy dilemmas
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1 including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Crime and Punishment in Historical Perspective
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course examines the history of criminal justice systems from the eighteenth to the twentieth century. Using case studies drawn from America, Europe, Australia and elsewhere, this course examines the development of the major institutions of criminal justice, including police, courts, and prison systems, and scholarly and historical debates about the approaches of the state in dealing with crime. It examines system changes such as the origins of the police force, the introduction of the adversarial criminal trial, the decline of capital punishment, and the increasing influence of the psychological sciences. The course asks you to reflect on the different outcomes of these global developments for diverse populations and in different national contexts.
learning_outcomes: Locate and analyse historical evidence derived from criminal justice records.
Identify and analyse important turning points, people, ideas and developments in historical criminal justice systems.
Construct coherent, evidence-based arguments about the history of criminal justice.
Reflect on how modern criminal justice institutions and procedures are informed by long-term historical changes and continuities.
Evaluate and compare historical case studies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Explaining Crime
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course presents a range of theoretical frameworks through which to view, explain and understand crime. Students are introduced to traditional and contemporary theories of crime to demonstrate its changing meanings. Viewing ‘crime’ through a range of theoretical lenses allows students to see it is a shifting terrain, with its meaning depending on historical and political contexts rather than being fixed and static. Students will consider how criminological theory interacts with the criminal justice system and crime policy in the present day. Students are invited to deepen their understanding of crime by learning about the origins of criminology as a discipline, its evolution, and contemporary debates within the field.
learning_outcomes: Map the shifts in criminological theory from the late 19th century to current day (PLOs: 2, 3, 7)
Evaluate criminological theory and responses to crime through scholarly discussion, debate and written or oral analysis (PLOs: 2, 3, 5, 6, 7)
Analyse contemporary debates within the discipline of criminology (PLOs: 2, 3, 5, 7)
Identify the contexts in which criminological theories, past and present, are informing contemporary responses to crime (PLOs: 2, 3, 7)
Apply criminological theory to understand and tackle contemporary crime issues (PLOs: 2, 7)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit overall, including CRIM1010 or CRIM1011, and enrolment in a single or double degree Criminology and Criminal Justice program, or Criminology specialisation. Equivalent: CRIM3001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminology in Practice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This capstone course draws together key concepts, themes and debates in criminology and encourages the application of these to current issues. By the end of the course you will have a portfolio of knowledge concerning eight current themes within criminology, and a specific knowledge base of one particular topic of interest. Presentation skills will be strengthened and the ability to synthesis and critically review research will be tested. Through focusing on the identification of current issues, as well as mapping the scope, strengths and critique of crime and justice problems, you will gain an understanding of the work of criminologists in the real world.
learning_outcomes: Show creativity and innovation in work through the production of assessment items for the course.
Identify the links between the discipline and other related disciplines, and explain underlying theoretical assumptions of various approaches.
Demonstrate in-depth understanding of the concepts, practices and challenges of the discipline of Criminology.
Articulate challenges in researching crime and justice topics, including practical, political and ethical hurdles.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 72 units of credit overall, and enrolment in a Criminology major or a Criminology & Criminology Justice single or dual program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Crime Prevention Policy
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will map the evolution and adoption of crime prevention policy both within Australia and internationally in the context of broader social policy and shifting political landscapes. You will gain critical insight into the theory that underpins social and situational crime prevention as well as criminal justice interventions. You will also explore the challenges and benefits of crime prevention through application of theory in real world scenarios. Throughout the course consideration is given to the limited impact of crime prevention policy on complex criminal and social justice priorities such as Aboriginal over-representation in the criminal justice system and violence against women.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the influence of key crime prevention theory on criminal justice and social policy in Australia and internationally
Evaluate the relationship between design and crime and the application of Crime Prevention Through Environmental Design theory in practice

Analyse theory that underpins criminal justice policy and broader social policy to address complex social issues including domestic and family violence, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander over-representation and the relationship between alcohol and other drugs and crime
Apply evidence in crime problem analysis, the development of crime prevention strategies and evaluation
Evaluate the evolution of key concepts and theories that underpin crime prevention policy, including developmental, social and situational crime prevention
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 uoc and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cybercrime and Technology-Facilitated Harms
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will examine how the online world has borne new crimes and facilitated the commission of existing crimes. As well as exploring definitions and categories of cybercrime, you will be invited to consider technology-facilitated harm and violence, engaging with cutting edge criminological scholarship that recgonises the integration of online and offline worlds when it comes to crime, justice and victimisation. In doing so, you will examine contemporary and emerging challenges that digital and communications technologies have presented for criminologists, policymakers, and law enforcement officials in attempting to understand and respond to crime in a digital society. Topic explored may include fraud, hacking, and cyberbullying, as well as emergent issues such as image-based abuse, technology-facilitated domestic and family violence, digilantism, and cyberterrorism. In examining these topics you will consider the socio-cultural, socio-political, and social inequalities that are at play.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess formal and informal justice responses to cybercrime and technology-facilitated threats.
Identify and analyse contemporary and emerging challenges related to digital and communications technologies and technology-facilitated harms.
Understand the socio-cultural, socio-political, and social inequalities that underpin crime and justice in a digital society.
Articulate and critically evaluate concepts, typologies, and categories of cybercrime
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 UOC and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Violence and Victimisation
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will critically analyse crime prevention strategies and criminal justice responses to violent crime. You will take account of policy and legislative issues nationally and internationally, and address wider issues of risk assessment, offender treatment and victim support in dealing with violent crime. You will question the relationship between crime prevention, risk assessment strategies and treatment for violent offenders and evaluate support services and criminal justice responses towards victims of crime. To do so you will draw on case studies about serious violent crime including homicide, sexual offences, domestic violence and war crimes, and take a multi-disciplinary approach to understanding the diverse needs and challenges in preventing and responding to violence.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse how violent offenders are assessed in relation to risk posed
Critically evaluate theoretical and criminal justice policy-based frameworks for responding to victimisation
Evaluate treatment and management strategies for violent offenders
Critically evaluate scholarly debates in studies of violence and victimisation
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 uoc and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Victims' Rights
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will examine victims' rights and victimology as emerging areas of criminological theory and practice. Victimology, as a distinct discipline of criminology focused on the subjectivity and agency of the victim of crime, will phrase an inquiry into the various means by which victims are now accorded some role within the criminal justice system. The emerging significance of the victim will be assessed through the various programs now calling for the participation of the victim as relevant subjects of law and justice. These include frameworks of victims' rights, victims' compensation and the inclusion of victims in sentencing.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate policy debates about the appropriate role of victims, offenders and the state in criminal justice processes
Explain the agency of the victim in the criminal justice system
Analyse contentious areas of public policy, drawing on a variety of primary and secondary sources, and opposing theoretical frameworks and policy approaches
Evaluate the relationship between victimology, victims' rights and criminology
Critically assess the historical development and key themes of victimology
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 uoc and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: State Crime and Human Rights
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course examines issues of state crime and state violence through a critical criminological lens. It introduces you to the human rights abuses committed by states as well the challenges associated with the establishment of an international system of criminal justice. Through this course you will develop a critical understanding of different forms of state violence as well as how states may, and may not, be held accountable for the harms they produce and the crimes they perpetrate. The course considers topics such as war crimes and genocide, immigration detention, torture and rendition, natural disaster, resistance to violence and state accountability.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the challenges associated with attempts to create an international system of criminal justice.
Consider how state crime and state violence can be identified, understood and responded to across a diverse range of contemporary social harms
Critically evaluate criminological concepts of state crime and state violence
Articulate the distinctions between criminological concepts of state crime and state violence and those based more formally on international law
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CRIM2021 or LAWS1022

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Public Health and Corrections
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course invites you to explore the intersection of public health and criminal justice, focusing on the unique challenges faced by people in prison and youth detention, detainees and those supervised in the community. You'll examine how incarceration and justice involvement impacts mental health, substance use, sexual health, infectious diseases, and broader social determinants of health. Through real-world case studies, lived experiences perspectives and critical discussion, you’ll engage with pressing issues like harm reduction in prisons, ethical dilemmas in research with people who are incarcerated and the delivery of health services in correctional settings. Discover how public health can play a transformative role in rehabilitation, policy and justice reform.
learning_outcomes: Describe ethical and human rights considerations in research and practice within correctional settings.
Communicate effectively about public health and criminal justice issues with diverse audiences.
Evaluate public health responses, policies and interventions aimed at justice-involved populations.
Explain major public health issues affecting justice-involved populations, including underlying risk behaviours and their impact on health and offending.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 uoc and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law. Or 48UOC overall, including 6UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in International Public Health (3880).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminology Work Integrated Learning Placement
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the unique opportunity to gain practical experience and deeper understanding of criminal justice and related agencies. Aligned with UNSW’s emphasis on work-integrated learning, this course is a structured and supported work placement designed to give students practical experience in tackling criminal justice challenges through working with a criminal justice related government or non-government organisation. This will be a one-of a kind experience that helps students understand how criminal justice works in practice. This course is only available to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Criminology and Criminal Justice Program (BCCJ) and students enrolled in the Criminology Major in selected programs. Enrolment is by course authority and is subject to a selection process involving a written submission and interview. Placements are undertaken at external host organisations, typically one day per week, with associated coursework delivered through small online seminars and asynchronous learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Devise and implement strategies for professional learning including goal setting, accountability and self-reflection (PLO 6)
Apply relevant theories, concepts and frameworks to issues and situations observed within an organisational setting (PLOs 5, 7)
Critically reflect on the role, functions, and sectoral context of an organisation, including professional roles, interpersonal relationships and organisational practices (PLOs 5, 7)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 78UOC including CRIM1010, CRIM1011 and CRIM2042, WAM 70, and enrolled in a Criminology major or Criminology & Criminal Justice single or double degree. Students in program 4034 are not eligible to enrol. Enrolment consent required.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Criminal Trial
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: The Criminal Trial forms a public stage upon which criminal justice is performed. But, what is ‘justice’, and is it really being done? In this course, we place the common law criminal trial on trial to critically explore the dynamics and features that characterise the trial, and the values that underpin it. You will examine the criminal trial from a range of perspectives to gain an understanding of the trial process in Australia. You will then cross-examine the trial using a comparative approach that introduces you to alternative trial systems around the world. Through a close interrogation of the roles, rights and powers of trial participants in different systems, and the varying objectives of criminal trials, you will deliberate and pass judgment on the successes and failures of our criminal trial and consider possibilities for reform.
learning_outcomes: Compare the criminal trial processes of the Australian adversarial tradition with at least one other legal tradition (PLO2)
Evaluate the criminal trial as a mechanism for achieving 'justice' (PLO4)
Examine approaches to reforming criminal trial practices and related criminal justice policies (PLO5)
Analyse the relationship between socio-legal factors and criminal trial principles, structures and practices (PLO5, 7)
Construct scholarly arguments incorporating critical reflection (PLO1, 6)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 UOC and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Issues in Drug Policy
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course examines the way drug policy is made in Australia and internationally and the impact this policy has in the community, including on people who use drugs. The course draws on research from critical policy studies, critical drug scholarship and critical criminology to explore the often complex politics that rest behind the formation, implementation and enforcement of drug policy, and the differential impacts these politics can have in society. It will ask you to critically appraise the role of evidence in policy, and interrogate ideas around addiction, race, class and reform as they relate to drugs, drug use, and drug policy. The course will draw on a series of contemporary case studies, ranging from treatment and service delivery, event safety, overdose prevention, violence in the drug market, stigma and more.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the development of drug policy in Australia and internationally
Demonstrate oral and written communication skills suitable for academic and professional audiences
Evaluate the impact of drug policy and its implementation on different communities
Utilise a range of interdisciplinary sources to consider the key processes and ethical issues in the development of drug policy.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 UOC and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Restorative Justice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Explores the theory and practice of restorative justice; that is, conflict resolution that involve victims, offenders and communities in a joint decision-making process rather than traditional legal and court-based responses. Assesses the strengths and limitations of restorative justice, and examines its application in a variety of settings from youth justice conferencing to in-prison restorative programs, to indigenous circle sentencing, to school and workplace bullying and to the global arena.
learning_outcomes: Appraise current evaluation literature on recidivism, satisfaction and other measures of success following restorative processes
Outline many of the applications of restorative theory in practice, highlighting strengths and weaknesses in terms of best practice
Appreciate common critiques of the restorative movement and the practical challenges of implementation particularly concerning appropriate responses to complex and sensitive conflict scenarios

Outline the theoretical approaches, principles and definitions underlying restorative justice philosophy and reflect on differences to other models of criminal justice and conflict resolution processes
Chart the emergence of the restorative justice movement locally and internationally
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology. Or 84 uoc and enrolled in 4787 Social Work (Honours)/Law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Imagining a More Just Future
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: How can we reimagine justice in an unjust world? In this course you will critically examine persistent and emerging criminology and criminal justice scholarship that imagines just futures and learn how to develop innovative, creative and informed solutions to contemporary justice concerns. You will engage with current and emerging debates in criminology and criminal justice and learn how to navigate tensions between reformist and abolitionist approaches to conceptualising and responding to ‘crime’ problems. In doing so you will undertake targeted, creative assessments to develop skills in analysis, advocacy and problem-solving. This course will equip you with the skills to navigate changing policy and advocacy environments and to develop the intellectual resources to imagine and promote a more just future.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate cutting edge criminological theories and concepts relevant to contemporary criminal justice debates (PLO 7)
Demonstrate innovation and imagination in addressing persistent or emerging criminology and criminal justice concepts (PLO 4, 6, 7)
Understand and articulate processes of social change in criminology and criminal justice (PLO 2, 4)
Identify and interrogate the complexities associated with criminology and criminal justice issues in policy and law, including diverse stakeholders’ perspectives and competing interests (PLO 2, 3, 5)
prerequisites: 72 UOC overall, and enrolment in a Criminology & Criminal Justice single or double program or a Criminology major/minor.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminological Aspects of Cyber Security
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: How do digital crimes shape our understanding of traditional criminological theories? This innovative offering aims to introduce criminology and criminal justice students to the multifaceted realm of cybersecurity, exploring its core elements within the context of criminological, legal, policy, and regulatory frameworks. By joining this course, you will not only gain insights into the evolving landscape of cyber threats but also have the unique opportunity to collaborate with law and engineering students, addressing interdisciplinary problems and policy challenges at the forefront of cybersecurity. Investigate the complexities of cybercrime and its implications for society while honing your analytical skills in this compelling and collaborative learning environment. From understanding cyber offending to evaluating the efficacy of cyber laws and regulations, this course equips you with the knowledge and tools necessary to navigate the intricate nexus of technology, crime, and justice. It is a transformative journey to unravel the criminological dimensions of cybersecurity and chart pathways towards effective prevention and intervention strategies in an increasingly digital world.
learning_outcomes: Examine the criminological, legal, and policy landscape surrounding cyber threats, determining their impact on criminal justice practices and societal responses.
Interpret the criminological implications of cybersecurity issues, utilising theoretical frameworks to understand the dynamics of digital crime.
Review current trends and case studies in cybercrime research, discerning their relevance to contemporary criminal justice policies and practices.
Explain the interdisciplinary nature of cybercrime challenges, integrating perspectives from criminology, law, and technology to inform effective solutions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC overall, including 6 UOC at level 1 and 6 UOC at level 2 in Criminology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminology, Climate Change and the Environment
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be introduced to criminological thinking and practice in the context of climate change and the environment. It provides a critical and theoretical understanding of the criminal justice system and its interaction with the environment, including drivers and contexts of environmental and climate crimes, impacts on different human and non-human victims (e.g. ecosystems and animals) at local and global levels and the challenges of balancing environmental, social and economic justice. The course examines four mediating relationships between criminology, the environment and climate change that cover interactions between temporal and geographic scales, the economy, non-human victims and human rights and culture.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the interactions between environmental harm, environmental crime and the criminal justice system (PLO 1, 2, 3)

Using oral and written communication, analyse the impact of criminal justice practices relating to the environment and climate change on humans and non humans, present and future generations, Indigenous peoples, and local and global groups in society (PLO 3, 5, 6, 7)

Synthesise research and theory from criminological and socio-legal sources to develop an inter-disciplinary understanding of the changing nature environmental and climate harms and responses from criminal justice and regulatory systems (PLO 5, 6, 7)
Interrogate different interpretations and understandings of justice in the context of environmental and climate change harms (PLO 2, 3, 4)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 48 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Civil and Environmental Engineering Computations
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: An introduction to the application of advanced analytical, statistical and numerical techniques to the solution of engineering problems relevant to civil and environmental engineers and surveyors. Review of analytical techniques. Addressing issues of variability and uncertainty in engineering. Descriptive statistics. Foundations of Probability. Random variables. Special distributions (discrete and continuous). Normal distribution, sampling distributions. Confidence Intervals. Hypothesis testing. Inferences for proportions, variances and means. Regression. ANOVA. Numerical solution of linear and non-linear equations; numerical differentiation and integration, finite differences; differential equations, boundary value problems, initial value problems and partial differential equations.
learning_outcomes: Utilize the MATLAB environment and programming for calculating solutions to numerical problems, graphical and statistical analyses, including assignment problems in subsequent courses.
Apply various graphical and data analysis methods for summarising and understanding data.
Describe the various ways in which random variation arises in engineering contexts.

Calculate numerical (as opposed to analytical) solutions to problems in linear and non-linear equations; numerical differentiation and integration, finite differences; differential equations, boundary value problems, initial value problems and partial differential equations.
Apply various statistical models and methods for drawing conclusions and making decisions under uncertainty in engineering contexts.
Apply numerical methods and statistics to problems in the fields of Civil and Environmental Engineering and Surveying.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH1231 OR DPST1014 OR MATH1241

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Construction
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: An introduction to construction systems and processes. General Systems Theory. Engineering problem solving. Characteristics, selection and usage of plant and equipment, temporary works and specialist construction techniques. Issues relating to the design, planning and management of construction operations. Topics selected from: earthmoving, blasting and explosives, quarrying, dredging, drilling, dewatering, ground anchors, grouting, temporary works including scaffolds and formwork, concrete production, building construction using steel, concrete and masonry, compressed air and fluid power systems, cranes; construction site layout, organisation of personnel, materials procurement and handling, suppliers, subcontractors, equipment management, maintenance, estimating, work physiology and ergonomics, recycling, waste and environmental issues, sustainable construction.
learning_outcomes: Apply quantitative methods in planning and managing the processes and equipment
Explain various construction processes and equipment
Examine and evaluate sustainability and safety in construction
Analyse the production and economics of different equipment
Produce engineering reports

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Climate Change and Environmental Sustainability
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Climate change is the biggest challenge of our era and engineers play an important role in mitigating and adapting to climate impacts. You will explore the causes and impacts of climate change, the key challenges and opportunities associated with global change as well as a range of techniques to quantify environmental impacts of corporations and economies. Conceptual frameworks such as sustainability, circular economy and planetary boundaries are introduced. You will work with sustainability assessment methods and tools in detail, including carbon and environmental footprint accounting, material flow analysis and life cycle assessment.
learning_outcomes: Assess environment related problems and apply appropriate quantitative methods.
Evaluate and analyse simple environment-related systems by adopting environmental footprints, life cycle assessment and material flow analysis.
Demonstrate how information from the application of these methods and tools can be applied in solution development and make recommendations towards more sustainable decision making processes.
Investigate and discuss the implications of climate change on human and natural systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Structural Analysis and Modelling
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: From designing earthquake-resistant buildings to optimising bridges for sustainable construction, structural analysis is at the heart of civil and structural engineering. This course equips you with the core tools to understand, model, and evaluate the behaviour of real-world structures, laying the groundwork for safe, efficient, and innovative design. You’ll learn to analyse beams, frames, and trusses under a range of loading conditions and apply structural theory using industry-relevant computational tools. Through hands-on exercises and open-ended design challenges, you’ll bridge the gap between scientific principles and engineering practice. Topics include internal force diagrams, the conjugate beam method, energy principles, virtual work, the force (flexibility) method, the stiffness method, and moment distribution for continuous beams. By the end of the course, you’ll be able to interpret and evaluate structural responses using both manual and computer-based methods, essential skills for professional structural design.
learning_outcomes: Produce a professional-standard design record that clearly communicates engineering solutions to both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Calculate displacements and internal actions of statically indeterminate structures using advanced methods
Use principles of work and energy to analyse simple structures.
Evaluate structural designs using computer-based methods and propose modifications to improve structural performance.
Incorporate feedback from peers during the design process to inform the development of an individually produced engineering solution.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: (ENGG1300 AND ENGG2400) OR (CVEN1300 AND CVEN2301)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Transport and Highway Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course is presented as 2 strands. The first strand is concerned with transport planning concepts and fundamentals of traffic theory. The transport planning component dwells on technical applications related to interactions among transport, land use and the environment. Topics include: introduction to four step transport planning process, transport network principles and their applications, transport demand models and sustainable transport strategies. The traffic theory component introduces basics of traffic engineering relationships, performance characteristics of roads, traffic management and delay computations in relation to unsignalised intersections and roundabouts. This strand which is allocated approximately 2/3 of teaching content is common for both Civil and Environmental Engineering students. The second strand is specifically for Civil Engineering students. This strand relates to development of technical skills required to prepare geometric design of highways. It introduces the design and computation process of rural roads and intersections, including horizontal and vertical alignment of highways, cross-sections and earthworks.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate transport system design scenarios
Describe basics of transport modeling concepts
Calculate methods related to each step of the four step planning process
Develop horizontal and vertical alignments for simple rural road sections on different types of terrain
Present and document a road design in a standard format
Perform computational evaluations of network traffic management methods
Design cross-sections appropriate for various types of roads
Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Engineering and Environmental Sustainability
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course is presented as 2 strands. The first strand is concerned with transport planning concepts and fundamentals of traffic theory. The transport planning component dwells on technical applications related to interactions between transport, land use and the environment. Topics include: introduction to four step transport planning process, transport network principles and their applications, transport demand models and sustainable transport strategies. The traffic theory component introduces basics of traffic engineering relationships, performance characteristics of roads, traffic management and delay computations in relation to unsignalised intersections and roundabouts. This strand is allocated approximately 2/3 of teaching content and is common for both Civil and Environmental Engineering students. The second strand is specifically for Environmental students. This strand focuses on the environmental impacts of transport and sustainable development. Topics include: assessment of environmental and community impacts from traffic noise, vehicle emissions and air pollution. It also includes EIA of major transport projects, concepts of transport policy, international trends and sustainable transport.
learning_outcomes: Describe basics of transport modeling concepts
Describe the relationships between land use, transport and the environment.
Work within the generalized cost framework to optimise transport strategies
Learn calculation methods related to each step of the four step planning process
Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters
Perform computational evaluations of network traffic management methods
Estimate emissions and energy consumption under different planning scenarios and quantitatively compare prominent vehicle and fuel technologies.
Predict traffic noise levels from traffic and environmental parameters and assess the seriousness of transport noise exposure and identify control measures to reduce the exposure.
Perform life-cycle based computational evaluations of projects and policies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Water and Atmospheric Chemistry
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide an introduction to water and atmospheric chemistry as a foundation for comprehending chemical processes in both natural and engineered systems. It will build on the basic chemical concepts covered in CHEM1011/1031 and will develop additional concepts required to describe the chemical processes occurring in rivers, lakes, groundwater, marine and atmospheric environments.
learning_outcomes: Explain and solve complex, real world water and atmospheric chemistry problems
Predict the behaviour and/or estimate the concentrations of various environmentally important chemicals in aquatic and atmospheric systems.

Explain the basic concepts in water and atmospheric chemistry. including chemical equilibrium and thermodynamics, chemical reaction kinetics, acids and bases, alkalinity, solid dissolution and precipitation, complexation reactions, redox reactions and reactions on solid surfaces
Describe the various chemical processes that occur in rivers, lakes, groundwater, marine and atmospheric environments.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM1011 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1811

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Soil Mechanics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: An introductory course to fundamentals of soil mechanics. Topics include: description of soil, basic phase relationships, clay mineralogy, confined and unconfined seepage, principle of effective stress, consolidation theory, compaction, stress distribution and settlement, Mohr circle, failure criterion, strength of soils, soil testing, stress-strain behaviour of soils and slope stability.
learning_outcomes: Describe the fundamentals of soil behaviour as an engineering material
Solve a range of soil related problems especially those involving water flow, soil settlement and soil strength
Identify those aspects of soil behaviour that have a significant environmental impact
Apply soil mechanics principles to a range of geotechnical engineering problems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Operations and Control
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction to the general principles of the organisation and control of engineering operations. The course covers project management and organisation, project scheduling and control, engineering economics, procurement and contract management, cost estimation, construction safety and quality management, and engineering ethics and risk.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the elements of economics and financial management and risk management
Analyse practical considerations when managing construction projects
Characterise the key aspects of project management including time, cost, safety and quality
Articulate the role of ethics in engineering professionalism
Define engineering and management work
Apply project management tools such as: Gantt chart and CPM charts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Civil and Environmental Engineering Practice
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course is about the doing of engineering design. It will help students develop their engineersmanship. The course will make students appreciate there is more to design than analysis and following codes, and that it is a creative and innovative process. Many parts of the civil and environmental engineering curriculums involve students learning mechanistic and law-like solutions to problems, guided by text books and design standards. This type of problem solving is important. But it is just as important for students to be creative and innovative in their problem solving. Rapid urbanisation around the world means problems are becoming more complex and unexpected requiring solutions for which text books and design standards are of limited use.
learning_outcomes: Give students a respect for ethical practice and social responsibility
Provide students with the freedom to engage in independent and reflective learning
Help students become entrepreneurial leaders capable of initiating and embracing innovation, as well as engaging and enabling others
Provide an environment in which students can develop their project management ski
Enhance students’ researching/data gathering skills
Enhance students’ communication skills
Provide students with opportunities for collaborative group work
Provide student’s with experiences typical of what a graduate engineers may encounter;
Develop students' capabilities to challenge the status quo and lead innovation
Allow students to utilise capacity for analytical and critical thinking and problem solving skills
Develop students capabilities to be independent and collaborative enquirers, and to be able to innovate by applying their knowledge and skills to the solution of novel problems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Geotechnics and Engineering Geology
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course covers two important areas of geotechnical engineering: geology and applied geotechnics. The geology section covers the earth and it's formation, rock types; their behaviour and properties and subsurface mapping. The topics in the applied geotechnics include: theoretical and presumptive bearing capacity of shallow foundations, allowable settlement and foundations on sand and clay, lateral earth pressures, retaining wall design, single axially and laterally loaded piles and pile groups, excavation and dewatering.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate with engineering geologists on geologically complex sites.
Apply fundamental geological and geotechnical scientific concepts in the geotechnical design process.
Interpret the basic principles related to geotechnical theories that apply to the design and analysis of shallow foundations, deep foundations and retaining walls.
Identify geological materials
Formulate preliminary geotechnical models that can be used as the basis for engineering design by identifying the geological history of a site
prerequisites: Prerequisite:CVEN2201 or CVEN3202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Concrete Structures
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Designing safe reinforced concrete structures starts with understanding how concrete structures really behave. In this course, you will explore the fundamentals of concrete materials, including cements, aggregates, admixtures, and the properties of hardened concrete. You will also examine the mechanical behaviour of concrete and reinforcement, gaining insight into how these materials work together in structural systems. Building on this foundation, the course guides you through the analysis and design of reinforced concrete elements subjected to bending, shear, and combined bending with axial compression. You will learn how reinforced concrete components perform under both service and ultimate loads. Key topics include ultimate strength analysis and design of cross-sections in flexure (singly and doubly reinforced and ductility); serviceability analysis and design of beams (cracked section analysis, deflection and crack control); ultimate strength in shear; simple and continuous beams and one-way slabs; short and slender concrete columns (interaction diagrams). By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the skills to analyse and design reinforced concrete members that meet both safety and serviceability requirements. This knowledge is essential for civil and structural engineers involved in the design and assessment of real-world infrastructure.
learning_outcomes: Describe the properties and behaviour of concrete materials
Explain the design principles and concepts for ultimate strength design, and serviceability design
Design structural members for given conditions (bending moment, shear force, and axial force) in compliance with Australian Standards.
Use concepts of reinforced concrete (RC) to simplify reinforced concrete structure, including idealized structural members, and to identify the related load paths.
Apply the fundamentals in concrete materials to real engineering problems in large scale concrete
Conduct structural analysis to understand the behaviour of structural members
prerequisites: Prerequisites: (ENGG1300 AND ENGG2400) OR (CVEN1300 AND CVEN2301) (Pre-requisite only applicable to UG cohort taking this course).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Steel Structures
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Steel structures form the critical building blocks of our nation's infrastructure. Structural steel elements form the backbone of building structures, bridges and major infrastructure. Structural steel is one of the most sustainable building materials available as it is 100% recyclable and is being increasingly reused. It is therefore increasingly becoming one of the most important materials to assist in the reduction of embodied carbon in the built environment. Civil/structural engineers play a key role in being able to conceive, design and construct these structures in an efficient and safe manner. This course will introduce these design concepts and will focus on the design of structural elements subject to bending, shear and combined bending and axial compression. Topics include: introduction to limit states design and codes of practice (design objectives; strength and serviceability limit states); loads and load combinations (permanent/dead, imposed/live and wind loads); design of structural steel tension members; Euler column buckling; design of stocky and slender compression members; design of laterally supported steel beams, laterally unsupported steel beams (lateral-torsional buckling in bending and shear strength); steel beam-columns (in-plane and out-of-plane failure); steel members subjected to biaxial bending; design of steel frames, steel connections and detailing (force and moment connections).
learning_outcomes: Interpret the requirements of a design brief and identify the potential design problems presented by the objectives of the brief.
Practically employ design concepts of structural steel members such as tension members, compression members, flexural members and beam columns and connections in practice.
Design structural steel members, connections, and braced and unbraced framed systems, under combined actions using AS4100.
Describe steel design principles with respect to advanced theory of stability and solid mechanics.
Communicate design in written and graphical form.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport and Highway Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This is the first introductory course in the discipline of transport engineering as part of the broad field of civil and environmental engineering. An outline of the field of transport engineering and its relationships with other engineering and non-engineering disciplines is provided within the course. The course comprises two strands. - Strand one focuses on analysing, designing, and evaluating traffic and transport systems. It includes traffic flow theory and the "4-step transport modeling" method to determine travel demands, which are essential for infrastructure feasibility assessments and ensuring smooth operations. - The second strand provides a brief overview of the geometric design of Rural Highways and Roads. Topics include an introduction to road design, route location process, and design practice of urban and rural roads.
learning_outcomes: Present and document the road design in a standard format
Describe basic concepts of four-step travel demand modelling and apply computational methods related to each step
Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters
Develop and evaluate horizontal and vertical alignments according to various design criteria
Design cross-sections appropriate for various types of roads
Perform computational evaluations of network traffic management methods

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Engineering and Environmental Sustainability
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This is the first introductory course into the discipline of transport engineering as part of the broad field of civil and environmental engineering. An outline of the field of transport engineering and its relationships with other engineering and non-engineering disciplines is provided within the course. The basic concepts and terminology of the discipline is introduced. The course comprises of two strands. The first strand of the course covers the first 5 weeks of the session. This section of the course is concerned with the analysis, design, and evaluation of traffic and network systems, including the basics of traffic flow theory and the steps of the regional transport planning process. The lectures and workshops will provide an opportunity to learn the engineering properties of traffic streams along with relevant measurement and network analysis techniques. The second strand of the course covers analysis methods required for sustainable transport engineering. This includes technical skills required for the evaluation and management of environmental impacts from transport projects, including estimation of vehicle air pollutant emissions, energy consumption, and travel demand management. The course covers the application of planning concepts in the development of economically sustainable transport systems including lifecycle and cost-benefit analyses. Additionally, estimation of noise levels and engineering solutions to control noise is covered in the context of transport noise generators such as road traffic.
learning_outcomes: Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters;
Explain the economics of transport enviornmental externalities and mitigating policies and strategies
Describe the environmental impacts of transport systems
Explain basic concepts of four-step travel demand modelling and demonstrate calculation methods related to each step
Perform computational evaluations of network traffic management methods
Evaluate emerging sustainable fuels and transport fleet transition to reduce enviornmental externalities
Estimate and quantify the transport externalities (air pollution, climate change impacts and noise pollution)
