institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Water Resources Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The objective of CVEN3501 is to introduce engineering hydrology and its application in water resources management and flood estimation. Topics discussed include hydrological cycle, climatology, atmospheric circulation, meteorological measurements, precipitation, streamflow measurement, runoff components, hydrograph analysis, loss rates, IFD and design storm hyetographs, flood frequency analysis, unit hydrographs concepts and linear reservoir method, groundwater, hydraulic conductivity, Darcy's law, intrinsic permeability, water potential, hydraulic head, unsaturated zone, aquifers, aquicludes, aquitards, steady state flow, transient flow, effective stress, transmissitivity, storativity, pump test interpretation.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a hydrological assessment of a catchment.
Describe the hydrologic cycle and energy fluxes to calculate evaporation.
Assess groundwater resources, including estimating flows, storage and surface water interactions.
Quantify the size of design floods and risk of exceedance.
Collaborate as a team to prepare a report, implementing organisational and interpersonal tools effectively.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Water and Wastewater Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course introduces students to the principles of water and wastewater engineering, including water supply and wastewater disposal systems, water and wastewater treatment, water quality and indicators, open channel flow, pump selection and placement and pipe networks. Open channel flow topics include uniform flows, rapidly varied flows in channel transitions and hydraulic jumps as well as gradually varied flows and flow control. Topics covered in water and wastewater treatment include water quality parameters, unit operations in treatment of water and wastewater, sewage collection systems, pumping stations and rising mains, sludge treatment and management, and water management concepts and effluent reuse.
learning_outcomes: Describe the important characteristics of commonly applied water and wastewater treatment processes.
Solve calculations around water quality and water treatment process design characteristics.
Solve basic calculations around open channel flow hydraulics, and pumps and turbines in pipe networks.
Describe the important characteristics of open channel flow hydraulics, and the application of pumps and turbines in pipe networks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ENGG2500 OR CVEN2501

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Waste Management
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides a thorough understanding of waste and resource management. It explores the environmental, social, and economic impacts of waste, and how to reduce these effects by implementing sustainable waste management practices. The course covers solid and hazardous waste management systems from generation to disposal, including waste characterisation, minimisation, cleaner production, transfer stations, recycling facilities, off-site treatment facilities, and landfill design. Additionally, it examines the options for resource recovery, recycling, composting, energy recovery, and the opportunities presented by a circular economy. The course also addresses the pertinent legislation and policy frameworks that govern waste management in Australia. In summary, this course equips students with the knowledge and skills to manage waste and resources effectively and sustainably.
learning_outcomes: Communicate outcomes in written and spoken formats.
Describe the basic principles underpinning the management of solid wastes and hazardous wastes, including generation, minimisation, transport, treatment, recovery and residue disposal.
Design waste management and resource recovery facilities.
Characterise waste generation in a town / city / region and forecast future waste quantities and composition

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Frameworks, Law and Economics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the introduction to EISs to provide details of EIS methods, and the ISO14001 Environmental Management System framework. It then provides an introduction to engineers on environmental law in Australia and NSW, focusing on planning law, and pollution laws. Environmental economics methods to account for environmental impacts in monetary terms, and the use of market mechanisms to achieve preferred environmental outcomes is covered at a level suitable for engineers.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with an environmental economist in a multidisciplinary team to develop and prepare EIS, EMS and sustainability reports by for a range of projects, corporations and regions
Interpret the laws that apply to environmental impacts of projects in NSW and Australia, and interpret their use in EIS, EMS and sustainability reports.
Explain and demonstrate the typical structure and format of Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) and Environmental Management Systems (EMS).
Explain economic analytical methods and evaluate their application in EIS, EMS and sustainability reports.
Apply environmental analytical tools to examine and develop an EIS, EMS and sustainability report for a typical project, organisation or region.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Frameworks, Law and Economics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the introduction to EISs to provide details of EIS methods, and the ISO14001 Environmental Management System framework. It then provides an introduction to engineers on environmental law in Australia and NSW, focusing on planning law, and pollution laws. Environmental economics methods to account for environmental impacts in monetary terms, and the use of market mechanisms to achieve preferred environmental outcomes is covered at a level suitable for engineers.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with an environmental economist in a multidisciplinary team to develop and prepare EIS, EMS and sustainability reports by for a range of projects, corporations and regions
Interpret the laws that apply to environmental impacts of projects in NSW and Australia, and interpret their use in EIS, EMS and sustainability reports.
Explain and demonstrate the typical structure and format of Environmental Impact Statements (EIS) and Environmental Management Systems (EMS).
Explain economic analytical methods and evaluate their application in EIS, EMS and sustainability reports.
Apply environmental analytical tools to examine and develop an EIS, EMS and sustainability report for a typical project, organisation or region.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Thesis A
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course is the first of two parts and is undertaken prior to CVEN4041 Research Thesis B. Successful completion of Parts A and B are required to obtain the equivalent of 12 UOC. Students must complete an Honours Research Thesis application form before the start of the term. The Honours Research Thesis may describe directed research work on an approved subject and will be completed under the guidance and supervision of a member of the academic staff. The research may involve a directed laboratory or field investigation, analytical or numerical modelling, a detailed design, literature review or such other individual research project approved by the Head of School. Research Thesis Part A involves the satisfactory formulation of the literature review, the definition of the research problem, completion of a significant part of the research and the development of a thesis outline.
learning_outcomes: Be in a position to undertake research in the workforce and for higher degree studies
Satisfaction of intellectual curiosity and contribution of original ideas and higher level research
Conduct a thorough literature review
Produce a self-contained higher level research thesis
Development of transferable skills in the process of developing and crafting a feasible research project
Undertake and execute a higher level research project
prerequisites: Minimum WAM of 70 and completion of 132UOC

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Thesis B
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course is the second of two parts and is undertaken after the completion of CVEN4050 Thesis A. The Thesis involves formulating the designs for and solution to open-ended civil and/or environmental engineering problems. The problems will be drawn from industry and will be multi-disciplinary involving application of material learnt throughout the undergraduate program and will require creative thought. The course will include the preparation of relevant professional documents. Part B involves the satisfactory preparation and submission of an individual thesis addressing the project plan defined in Thesis A.

Conduct a literature review to determine the range of acceptable solutions and/or limitations of those acceptable solutions for a research project

Demonstrate professional level written communication skills and presentation skills
Execute a research project within an assigned theme

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Operations and Projects
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Most engineering work fits within what is broadly referred to as operations and projects. For example an earthmoving operation may involve trucks cycling between an excavator and some dump point; an engineering project may involve the design, construction and commissioning of infrastructure. Operations tend to be ongoing but can be time limited, while projects have a defined time frame. The course will cover issues to do with resources (materials, equipment, people), cost and time in engineering operations and on engineering projects. Examples will be chosen to highlight efficient practices and methods adopted in engineering operations and on engineering projects.
learning_outcomes: Select a suitable method for constructing underground tunnels.
Work independently on the design a permanent or temporary structure
Work effectively in teams for group assignments.
Explain the process of construction operations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Contracts
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The majority of engineering work is procured through contracts, within an array of delivery methods. The course examines the relationship between tenders and contracts and the various popular forms of delivery methods. The course covers the formation and documentation involved in contracts, the commercial aspects of contractual agreements including payment types and conditions of contract, the contractual and administrative connections of project delivery, and dispute avoidance and resolution. The contract law that will be covered is applicable to a common law system.
learning_outcomes: Review and summarise legal case studies and determine how they will impact future directions in the industry
Evaluate the elements within contract documents and how they apply to specific circumstances
Assess the engineering profession, its scope, and the role of Civil and Environmental Engineers within it.
Analyse tender documentation and contribute in the preparation of a tender
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN3101.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainability in Construction
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will provide fundamental knowledge and hands-on experience for practising sustainability in construction. The aim is teaching the environmental, social and economic impacts of buildings and built environment and demonstrating how sustainable construction design can avoid global warming and resource depletion issues. The contents of this course are designed to provide hands-on experience in analytical thinking and decision making with regards to the application of sustainability in construction projects. This course explains history and drivers of sustainability in construction and review sustainability policies, programs, and incentives in Australia. Principles of life cycle assessment (LCA) and life cycle costs (LCC) will be explained, and hands-on experience of evaluating LCA and LCC will be offered in the workshop classes and group assignment. This course also provides an overview of the current green rating systems for buildings and built environment in Australia. Additionally, examples of sustainable construction design, materials and energy resources, as well as case studies of best sustainable practices and future trends of sustainable construction will be demonstrated. A number of alternative strategies available in design, procurement, construction, operation and end-of-life phases to reduce the overall environmental impact of a construction project are discussed. Students are expected to learn how the available strategies, standards and guidelines can be applied to analyse and improve sustainability in practice.
learning_outcomes: Summarise the history and drivers of sustainability in construction, as well as sustainability policies, programs, and incentives in Australia
Demonstrate hands-on skills in evaluating life cycle assessment and life cycle cost assessment in a construction-related activity
Distinguish sustainable construction design, materials and energy resources used in case studies of best sustainable practices and future trends in sustainable construction
Explain how green rating schemes work in Australia

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Construction Practicum
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: How does an infrastructure or building project actually get delivered? In this course you will follow a real project through its full lifecycle, from initial concept and feasibility through approvals, procurement, contracts and delivery. Working individually on a realistic development scenario, you will apply the engineering, financial and management knowledge from earlier courses to make and defend real project decisions. You will work with authentic industry documents including feasibility models, development approvals and construction contracts, and you will build awareness of the digital tools reshaping construction practice. The course is designed as a bridge between the classroom and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a construction project brief under incomplete information to identify the factors driving delivery decisions across the project lifecycle.
Evaluate delivery and procurement options and justify a recommendation against competing constraints.
Create and deliver a professional project proposal in written and verbal form.
Apply the tools and methods of construction practice, with awareness of emerging technologies across the project lifecycle.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN2101 & CVEN3101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Rock and Slope Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Description of rock mass and discontinuities; rock strength and failure criteria. Core logging; field data collection, mapping and fracture surveys; data presentation; hemispherical projections; introductory rock slope stability; foundations on rock; excavation on rock; in-situ stress; stresses about underground openings; classification systems and tunnel support requirements; site investigations for landslides and slope stabilisation techniques; use of slope stability analysis programs. The course includes a compulsory field trip.
learning_outcomes: Perform basic design in rock engineering including foundation, slope stability and tunnel designs
Utilise software to assess the stability of a slope and various remediation measures
Describe the basic principles related to the theory and design of rock and soil slopes
Work effectively in a team
Illustrate the methods of site investigation, soil and rock slope analysis and different methods of slope stabilisation
Describe the basic principles related to the theory and design of rock engineering including methods for describing, recording and presenting features of rock masses
prerequisites: Prerequisite/s: CVEN2201 OR CVEN3202 & CVEN3201 OR CVEN3203

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Topics in Geotechnical Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will be delivered in two parts. Part one is focused on ground energy and ground source heat pump systems, common design parameters and approaches and available analytical solutions to understand the concept of geothermal systems. To better understand the physics and governing equations involved in ground energy systems the interactions between the systems and the surrounding ground, the educational finite element software COMSOL will be used to computationally model different cases of ground energy systems. The second part of the course covers the basic principles of critical state soil mechanics and soil plasticity, and the use of elastic-plastic constitutive models to simulate soil stress-strain behaviour. Students will learn to use elastic-plastic soil models to solve geotechnical engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept and applications of ground energy systems. Design and evaluate of these systems via hand calculations and computational modelling.
Explain the basic principles of critical state soil mechanics and soil plasticity, and use elastic-plastic constitutive models to simulate soil stress-strain behaviour.
Use finite element method to solve geo-energy problems, including geothermal energy systems and their interaction with the ground.
prerequisites: Prerequisite/s: CVEN2201 OR CVEN3202 & CVEN3201 OR CVEN3203

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ground Improvement and Monitoring Techniques
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Assessment of the suitability and design of stabilisation techniques for difficult foundation soils including instrumentation and application of observational techniques to geotechnical engineering. Topics covered will include: principles of the observational method, instrumentation, braced excavations, dewatering, grouting, underpinning, stone columns, vertical and horizontal drains, vacuum pumping, deep compaction, vibrofloatation, lime stabilisation, reinforced earth and soil nailing.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the performance of ground improvement designs.
Explain the problems of soft soils and the methods of improving their strength and serviceability.
Describe the types and functions of instrumentation used in geotechnical engineering and their advantages.
Identify suitable ground improvement methods and their critical parameters and control measures for a range of problematic soils.
Design and analyse reinforced earth structures
prerequisites: Prerequisite/s: CVEN2201 OR CVEN3202 & CVEN3201 OR CVEN3203

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Structures Practicum
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: A practical course that involves both advanced analysis and design of an engineered structure to solve a given problem. The course deals with behaviour of fundamental aspects of structural design, including advanced modelling. Students will work in groups to solve a specific problem; they will design and build their structure and then will then test it to destruction in the Heavy Structures and Materials Laboratories. Problems will be selected from concrete, steel, timber or other structural materials. The course is designed to enhance student capabilities in researching of design concepts, in further developing their problem solving skills and in determining design solutions to a client's problem.
learning_outcomes: Teamwork skills as applied to the planning, construction and testing of structural members.
Ability to research new (core) technical skills in materials and structures engineering and use them to solve problems.
Ability to reflect on the final solution in performance and improvement.
Planning of activities and projects; ability to convert a project brief to a set of integrated activities to project delivery
High level communication skills (written and oral)
Problem solving and ability to apply key structural and materials concepts to design problems
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: 2303, 3303 & 3304

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Concrete Structures
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: A course on the advanced analysis and design of concrete structures for students looking towards a career in Structural Engineering. The course deals with the design and behaviour of the following fundamental aspects for reinforced concrete member design: one-way and two-way concrete slabs (including the direct design, equivalent frame and simplified strip methods); retaining walls, strip, pad and pile footings; and the detailing of steel reinforcement in concrete members.
learning_outcomes: Analyse short and long-term deflection effects of RC structures and deflection control
Explain the limit state design concepts, specifically recognising the difference between strength and serviceability limit states
Describe and apply RC design principles to the design of members subjected to ultimate limit states of flexure, shear, and punching shear.
Design Reinforced Concrete (RC) structures with two-way actions utilizing AS 3600 and AS 1170
Interpret structural design requirements, specifications, documents, and drawings and utilize them appropriately in design
prerequisites: Prerequisite/s: CVEN3301 OR CVEN2303 AND CVEN3302 OR CVEN3304.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Timber Structures
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Structural and Construction Engineers may be responsible for the design and construction of timber structures; from timber frame housing to high rise engineered timber structures. This course provides an introduction to the design of timber structures using a range of timber products and the relevant Australian and European Standards.
learning_outcomes: Explain the unique characteristics of timber and the diverse range of engineered wood products.
Apply knowledge of mass timber construction to real-world design problems.
Evaluate the capacity of timber members and connections by interpreting and applying relevant Australian and European Standards.
Demonstrate communication skills and apply professional judgement that contributes to sustainable practice of Civil Engineering.
Design timber structures from engineered wood products and analyse components by applying relevant Standards and Guidelines.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN2303 and ENGG2400

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Structural Dynamics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Structural engineers need to understand how structures behave when subjected to dynamic loads such as wind and earthquakes. In this course, you will develop an understanding of the fundamental principles of structural dynamics, including free and forced vibration of single- and multi-degree-of-freedom systems, numerical methods and modal analysis. You will learn how to apply these principles to analyse the dynamic response of civil engineering structures and develop a foundation for assessing structures subjected to dynamic loading.
learning_outcomes: Apply the fundamental concepts of system dynamics with specific focus and application to civil/structural engineering
Apply the laws of dynamics to establish simple and realistic mathematical models of engineering structures
Identify and specify various types of dynamic loading for structural analysis
Apply dynamic analysis methods to practical problems in structural engineering and other disciplines
Analyse the dynamic response to a dynamic load and other important parameters for structural design
Evaluate the dynamic susceptibility of structures and the limitations of modelling techniques

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Traffic Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Traffic engineering professionals are tasked with the responsibility of ensuring the safe and efficient movement of people and goods through the provision and maintenance of transportation systems. The effectiveness of the transport system impacts the economic development and quality of life for the entire community. The course will cover the broad topics of traffic flow theory and modelling, traffic control device design and implementation and traffic management practices. The fundamentals of traffic flow theory and the tools necessary to assess capacity and level of service for road segments and intersections are discussed in detail during the first half of the course. The second half of the course covers the application of the theory and use of the tools to conduct traffic studies and manage and control traffic related issues. Students will have the opportunity to analyse real traffic data, develop traffic management plans and design traffic control devices using industry prevalent modelling software, such as "SIDRA Intersection", which will provide students with the necessary practical skills to be a traffic engineer.
learning_outcomes: Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters
Apply basic concepts, methods, and techniques in urban traffic management studies.
Solve complex existing and potential traffic management problems
Critically analyse field survey methodologies and traffic data
Identify and apply current technologies in traffic management and control

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Factors in Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Human factors is the discipline concerned with the understanding of interactions between humans and elements of a system. The discipline applies theory, principles, data and methods to the design process to optimise human well-being and overall system performance. This course, will rely on the field of engineering psychology, will equip students with the fundamental knowledge and skills necessary for human-centred design across many engineering disciplines, to optimise system performance and make it safe, efficient and satisfying to use. Students will also gain an appreciation of the human considerations that are critical in the successful design, operation and evaluation of Civil Infrastructure Systems.
learning_outcomes: Utilize Human Factors research methods to provide evidence when designing and evaluating engineering systems.
Apply and Integrate Human Factors principles, methods and data into the design of Engineering Systems.
Explain the Fundamental Principles of Human Factors that can be used by Engineers to Facilitate User-Centred Design.
Apply ethical principles to assess and inform human-centred engineering design.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Networks
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course covers strategic transport network planning aspects related to urban transport systems, including network-based analysis, modelling and optimisation techniques. Network representation of transport systems and traffic route choice modelling including user equilibrium and system optimal are the two main broad topics that will be discussed in this subject. Knowledge about different types of transport network solutions and when and where to apply them are important for transport modelling professionals. The subject material focuses on network theory in some depth, and a reasonable mathematical competency, as well as the ability to perform computational work, will be required to follow this subject. Computer literacy will be helpful but is not essential.
learning_outcomes: Apply network user equilibrium solution methods
Describe the fundamentals of transport network analysis
Apply transport network planning techniques
Apply route choice analysis techniques
Justify and describe the importance of transport network concepts for analysis and design

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Groundwater Resource Investigation
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Groundwater is one of Australia's most critical natural resources, yet the nation faces a persistent shortage of engineers with the skills to understand and manage it sustainably. This course equips you with theoretical, numerical and field skills to address this challenge. You will learn how to measure groundwater resources, understand groundwater recharge, its interaction with rivers and what drives movement of groundwater. You will also look at the impact of extraction on our groundwater resources. A highlight of the course is a 5-day field trip to UNSW's Wellington Field Research Station. During this trip, you'll have a chance to learn from experts in groundwater and geophysics and utilise state-of-the-art equipment. In teams, you will conduct a variety of groundwater, geochemical and geophysical surveys on site. This site features a network of boreholes through a landscape of clay and river deposits into weathered basalt overlying tight basement rocks and limestone formations, a geological setting that presents real questions about groundwater as a resource, its movement, interaction with streams and recharge. You will collect your own data, interpret it and build a synthesised site analysis interpretation with your team. Through this course, you will develop skills directly relevant to professional practice, including conducting field investigations and groundwater assessments, developing and interpreting conceptual and analytical groundwater models, analysing geological, hydrogeological and geophysical data and preparing high quality technical reports.
learning_outcomes: Develop and use conceptual and analytical models to assess groundwater flow and the potential impacts of groundwater use.
Work effectively in teams during field and analytical activities, demonstrating professional collaboration, safe fieldwork conduct, responsibility, and shared problem-solving.
Communicate technical findings clearly and professionally supported by appropriate data, analysis, and engineering reasoning.
Interpret field and experimental data to understand groundwater behaviour and aquifer properties.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN3501

title: Traffic Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Traffic engineering professionals are tasked with the responsibility of ensuring the safe and efficient movement of people and goods through the provision and maintenance of transportation systems. The effectiveness of the transport system impacts the economic development and quality of life for the entire community. The course will cover the broad topics of traffic flow theory and modelling, traffic control device design and implementation and traffic management practices. The fundamentals of traffic flow theory and the tools necessary to assess capacity and level of service for road segments and intersections are discussed in detail during the first half of the course. The second half of the course covers the application of the theory and use of the tools to conduct traffic studies and manage and control traffic related issues. Students will have the opportunity to analyse real traffic data, develop traffic management plans and design traffic control devices using industry prevalent modelling software, such as "SIDRA Intersection", which will provide students with the necessary practical skills to be a traffic engineer.
learning_outcomes: Explain relationships between fundamental traffic flow parameters
Apply basic concepts, methods, and techniques in urban traffic management studies.
Solve complex existing and potential traffic management problems
Critically analyse field survey methodologies and traffic data
Identify and apply current technologies in traffic management and control
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN2401 or CVEN3401 or CVEN2402 or CVEN3402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Structural Dynamics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Structural engineers need to understand how structures behave when subjected to dynamic loads such as wind and earthquakes. In this course, you will develop an understanding of the fundamental principles of structural dynamics, including free and forced vibration of single- and multi-degree-of-freedom systems, numerical methods and modal analysis. You will learn how to apply these principles to analyse the dynamic response of civil engineering structures and develop a foundation for assessing structures subjected to dynamic loading.
learning_outcomes: Apply the fundamental concepts of system dynamics with specific focus and application to civil/structural engineering
Apply the laws of dynamics to establish simple and realistic mathematical models of engineering structures
Identify and specify various types of dynamic loading for structural analysis
Apply dynamic analysis methods to practical problems in structural engineering and other disciplines
Analyse the dynamic response to a dynamic load and other important parameters for structural design
Evaluate the dynamic susceptibility of structures and the limitations of modelling techniques
prerequisites: Prerequisites: CVEN3301 OR CVEN2303 and CVEN2002 (or equivalent).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Wastewater Technology and Industrial Application
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip students with comprehensive knowledge and engineering skills necessary for designing water and wastewater treatment and resource recovery in a water industry context. It covers both classical engineering design practices and next-generation technologies for the management of sewer, water, wastewater, and resource recovery processes, alongside greenhouse gas emission control, an integrated management approach and emerging issues in urban water systems. These components represent specialised technical areas within the fields of water and wastewater treatment, engineering design and resource and environmental management.
learning_outcomes: Critically review the relevant material from scientific literature, industry reports, and other public sources.
Communicate technical information effectively in written and spoken formats.
Discuss the challenges faced by urban water and wastewater management, including drinking water treatment plants, sewer networks, and wastewater treatment plants.
Apply engineering calculations to evaluate current practices and technologies used in the water industry, including system performance and process optimisation.
Describe key water processing units.
Design innovative technologies or strategic solutions for future water and wastewater management, and assess their potential environmental impacts.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Groundwater Resource Investigation
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Groundwater is one of Australia's most critical natural resources, yet the nation faces a persistent shortage of engineers with the skills to understand and manage it sustainably. This course equips you with theoretical, numerical and field skills to address this challenge. You will learn how to measure groundwater resources, understand groundwater recharge, its interaction with rivers and what drives movement of groundwater. You will also look at the impact of extraction on our groundwater resources. A highlight of the course is a 5-day field trip to UNSW's Wellington Field Research Station. During this trip, you'll have a chance to learn from experts in groundwater and geophysics and utilise state-of-the-art equipment. In teams, you will conduct a variety of groundwater, geochemical and geophysical surveys on site. This site features a network of boreholes through a landscape of clay and river deposits into weathered basalt overlying tight basement rocks and limestone formations, a geological setting that presents real questions about groundwater as a resource, its movement, interaction with streams and recharge. You will collect your own data, interpret it and build a synthesised site analysis interpretation with your team. Through this course, you will develop skills directly relevant to professional practice, including conducting field investigations and groundwater assessments, developing and interpreting conceptual and analytical groundwater models, analysing geological, hydrogeological and geophysical data and preparing high quality technical reports.
learning_outcomes: Develop and use conceptual and analytical models to assess groundwater flow and the potential impacts of groundwater use.
Work effectively in teams during field and analytical activities, demonstrating professional collaboration, safe fieldwork conduct, responsibility, and shared problem-solving.
Communicate technical findings clearly and professionally supported by appropriate data, analysis, and engineering reasoning.
Interpret field and experimental data to understand groundwater behaviour and aquifer properties.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Water Quality Principles
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Fundamental aspects of the chemistry and biology of aquatic environments are reviewed and extended enabling analysis and interpretation of processes occurring in surface and ground waters, as well as water and wastewater treatment systems. Consideration is given to recent developments in water and wastewater technologies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate knowledge and technologies from published literature and effectively disseminate findings through written reports and seminar presentations.
Recognize the challenges that exist in maintaining acceptable water quality and the knowledge gaps that remain with regard to understanding and mitigating particular water quality problems.
Identify key biogeochemical processes that operate within natural and engineered aquatic systems, and examine how these processes influence water quality.
Apply knowledge of both conventional and advanced methods for treating water and wastewater to achieve desired water quality standard.
Demonstrate interpersonal and process management skills in real-world dynamic team-work environments.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN3502

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Planning Sustainable Infrastructure
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course builds on introductory knowledge from Stages 1 to 3 in water, transport, waste and engineering operations and enables students to design infrastructure systems that include social and cultural context, as well as having regard to sustainability principles in the planning of urban and regional precincts. The design brief will direct the conceptual planning of the infrastructure and allow students to be familiar with sustainability in terms of water and waste management, transport services, energy supply and distribution. This capstone course will encourage teamwork as well as independent and reflective learning through the delivery of individual and group assessment tasks that allow for critical thinking and the development of creative and appropriate sustainable outcomes in urban and regional communities.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess infrastructure sustainability at varying scales and contexts.
Formulate and address urban and regional infrastructure problems using sustainability principles.
Demonstrate creativity by developing solutions, including those that may be considered unconventional.
Work independently and as part of a team to carry out literature reviews and effectively communicate findings.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 126 UOC and 3rd year core

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Quality and Pollution
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Introduction to fundamental understanding of the causes and effects of air pollution, including engineering science behind the behaviour and modelling of air pollutants. The course covers the principles of air quality and air pollutants and describes how pollutants are assessed through analysis, modelling, monitoring and emission inventories.
learning_outcomes: evaluate various policy options in terms of their impacts on emission, air quality and health
disseminate emission and air quality results to a wider audience
estimate health impact of changes in air pollution
estimate air pollution concentrations as a function of emission, meteorology, topography and the built environment for a combination of road and industrial source
estimate emissions from industrial, manufacturing and road transport sources

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Resilient Flood Design
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on advanced topics in flood engineering for resilient water infrastructure design. The course builds from third year hydrology and hydraulics to introduce you to estimation of large and extreme floods, the analysis and design of common hydraulic structures, including flow conveyance structures, energy dissipators and culverts and other advanced topics in hydrology and hydraulics.
learning_outcomes: Apply sustainability concepts to the design of hydraulic structures.
Design common hydraulic structures by performing relevant calculations.
Apply hydrologic models appropriately to a design problem.
Calculate peak flows from large and extreme floods.
Describe the important characteristics of hydraulic structures.
Describe the sources of uncertainty in hydrologic calculations, including the effects of climate change.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Sustainability - Methods, Tools, Management
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course offers a practical and critical exploration of sustainable engineering in civil and environmental contexts. Students will engage with real-world case studies and apply tools - such as Life Cycle Assessment, Materials Flow Analysis, and Environmental Footprinting - to evaluate sustainability across products, organisations, and regions. Through lectures and interactive workshops, students will develop the ability to assess, critique, and communicate current sustainability frameworks such as circular economy, and explore diverse practices in planning, reporting, and managing sustainability within engineering projects and corporate settings.
learning_outcomes: State and explain various definitions of sustainability, Ecologically Sustainable Development (ESD) and emerging themes such as Circular Economy (CE), apply these principles to different examples and effectively communicate progress and context.
Apply sustainability accounting methods such as material flow analysis, environmental lifecycle assessment and footprint accounting methods for various case studies.

Critically assess environment-related problems and the application of appropriate tools, describing the suitability of different approaches, for different outcomes and at different scales (households, corporations, regions).
Critically evaluate sources of information concerning sustainability dimensions, including uncertainty, both individually and collaboratively.
prerequisites: Exclusion: CVEN9888

title: Satellite Remote Sensing and Applications
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the concepts, principles and techniques used for satellite remote sensing to civil and environmental engineering students. Topics include: Electromagnetic radiation Principles of satellite remote sensing Multispectral remote sensing Hyperspectral remote sensing Thermal remote sensing LiDAR remote sensing Radar remote sensing Remote sensing applications in civil engineering structural deformation urban expansion Remote sensing applications in geotechnical engineering ground settlement slope stability mine subsidence earthquakes Remote sensing applications in environmental engineering coastal erosion bathymetry water pollution vegetation monitoring groundwater extraction oil spill flood bushfire Remote sensing applications in transport road traffic conditions ship detection underground tunnelling

Be competent in processing satellite imagery including choice of sensors, satellite tasking, pre-processing, classification, and visualisation.
Be familiar with the challenges and techniques of satellite remote sensing.
Understand the strengths and weaknesses, and characteristics of several different remote sensing techniques.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Thesis A
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The thesis provides an opportunity for you to bring together engineering principles learned over your previous years of study and apply these principles to innovatively solve problems such as the development of a specific design, process and/or the investigation of a hypothesis. Thesis projects are complex, open-ended problems that allow room for your creativity, and the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of results. There are multiple possible solutions or conclusions at the outset and sufficient complexity to require a degree of project planning. The thesis requires you to formulate problems in scientific or engineering terms, manage an technical project and find solutions by applying scientific and engineering methods. You will also develop their ability to work in a research and development environment. You must identify a supervisor and project prior to enrolling in this course. This is the first course of the 3 course thesis structure.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on a specialist body of knowledge related to their thesis topic.
Demonstrate oral and written communication in professional and lay domains.
Analyse data objectively using quantitative and mathematical methods.
Develop a design or a process or investigate a hypothesis following industry and professional engineering standards.
Apply scientific and engineering methods to solve an engineering problem.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: completion of 126 UOC and 70WAM and completion of 3rd year core

syllabus_overview: This course is a core research enquiry course for students in 8621 Master of Engineering and 8338 Master of Engineering Science programs. This is the first part of the coursework project, with CVEN9051 Masters Practice Project B, following this course in a later term. This course enhances the student’s skills for undertaking scholarly enquiry by attempting to achieve a specific topic objective within a defined period of time. A significant component of the course relates to the review of literature, which promotes independent and reflective learning as well as increases students’ capacity to develop information literacy. The project work is expected to reinforce the student’s ability and confidence in the written communication of technical information.The intention with this course is to bring into focus the skills needed to investigate real life projects. The Masters Practice Project A topic is presented to the student as it would be in industry and each student is required to prepare an individual submission by way of an Engineering Report that contains all of the elements required within the Assessment Overview. Topics are related to industry projects selected from contemporary practice. The work involves industry based investigations and design applications.

title: Civil and Environmental Engineering Design Practice
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course involves undertaking and completing a series of design tasks in either civil or environmental engineering depending on whether students are undertaking the civil or environmental stream. The design tasks are chosen in one of the following areas: structural engineering, construction materials, geotechnical engineering, project management, transport, environmental and/or water engineering. Each design task in the series may be independent of each other, or may be a sequence of related sub-tasks as part of a larger goal. Assessment of each task requires the construction of working system to solve a specified problem.

Critically self-review their performance to improve themselves and their groups
Critically analyse Civil and Environmental Engineering problems.
Apply conceptual design ideas to real-world Civil and Environmental Engineering problems.
Independently solve engineering design problems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Planning Practice
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Transport planning is essential to modern society. Government investment is typically decided using transport planning models. This includes deciding how to prioritise upgrades to the transport network. A well functioning transport network enables the economy to function smoothly and reduces impacts on the environment (e.g. emissions) and improves human health. This course introduces key analytical techniques used in contemporary urban land-use and transport planning. Students will explore the components of strategic travel demand modelling, including trip generation, distribution, mode choice, and traffic assignment, with a focus on real-world application and evaluation methods. The course also covers land use forecasting methods, behavioural model calibration and validation, and the integration of mathematical programming approaches. Emphasis is placed on practical problem-solving, with case studies addressing both private and public transport planning challenges in an urban context.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate transport system equilibrium with simple examples of the interactions between land use and transport.
Evaluate transport projects through a variety of economic analysis methodologies (e.g. cost-benefit analysis, multi-criteria analysis).
Describe the relationships between Land Use, Transport and the Environment.
Explain basic concepts of four-step travel demand modelling and apply computational methods related to each step.
Evaluate transport system conditions (including public transport system) based on demand forecasts and plan for the future.

school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: CVEN9051 forms the second part of the Coursework Thesis program, and is completed in the semester after the completion of CVEN9050 Thesis A. In preparing your thesis topic in Thesis B for CVEN9051 you are able to select and nominate a Civil and/or Environmental Engineering topic that is of significant interest to you. Your topic may be associated with core elements such as Structural Design, Water and Hydraulics, Geotechnical Engineering, Transportation, Construction or Sustainability. Within Thesis B there are also project management elements that engineering professionals would be required to address and these elements will be incorporated as part of the Thesis B submission. This will enable all students to develop understanding of how their work impacts upon others and will allow them to identify the key communication pathways that are required to be addressed in the development of engineering solutions being offered. Consider the utility of your thesis topic in terms of your future career, either by re-inforcing and presenting your skills in a chosen field, or by experiencing and developing capabilities in a new area. Your thesis is a requirement for your degree, however it also presents an opportunity to explore areas of interest and demonstrate expertise when advancing in your profession As the course will involve several submissions throughout the semester, Thesis B will be completed incrementally with guidance provided at each stage.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective written and/or verbal communication skills in professional and lay domains.
Apply principles of ethical practice and social responsibility to the chosen engineering design problem
Undertake and execute a research project
Assess relevant disciplinary knowledge and acknowledge its interdisciplinary context within a literature review and/or project
Engage in independent and reflective learning when solving the chosen engineering design problem
Demonstrate a capacity for high level analytical and critical thinking to create a novel solution considering related technical, social, political, environmental and economic issues

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Operations
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course offers students an advanced understanding of the field of traffic engineering and congestion management, with a focus on transport system performance, reliability, and the analytical approached used to address congestion and delay. The course covers topics related to the analysis, design and evaluation of transport operations and congestion management systems, including data collection and analysis methods, simulation techniques and stochastic process techniques used for transport operations. Key topics include an introduction to traffic operations models, their application to traffic flow and multi-modal transport systems. Additionally, the course covers the operational characteristics of vehicles in multi-modal transport systems, including public transport, and the statistical, computational, and AI-enabled tools required to manage and analyze large volumes of real-world data. The focus of the course is on applying traffic operation models and real-world data to evaluate operational strategies and support informed transport planning and operational decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Apply and integrate transport operations models with real-world operational data using statistical, computational, and AI-enabled methods.
Critically interpret analytical and data‑based results to support transport planning and operational decision‑making for professional contexts.
Design and conduct data-driven transport operations studies to evaluate operational strategies and policy interventions.
Critically evaluate transport operation models and frameworks for analysing congestion, reliability and performance in transport systems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN2401 or CVEN3401 or CVEN2402 or CVEN3402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Demand Modelling
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course develops the foundation of transport analysis and modelling, preparing students with the advanced techniques they need in practice and research. The course offer an interactive approach to learn modelling transportation demand and safety; a broad range of econometric modelling techniques and its application to transportation systems will be considered; specific emphasis will be placed on estimation of these models and their use for forecasting and interpretation of results; transportation data, analysis and modelling including considerations of data sources, errors, time series analysis, stochastic models and extensions to simulation and optimisation in transportation systems.
learning_outcomes: Infer statistical conclusions from real world large data.
Apply basic statistics and econometrics in transport modelling.
Conduct analysis and interpretation of a comprehensive statistical method on large scale transport data using statistical packages.
Identify the properties of random variables in large scale transport data.

Describe the relationships between Land Use, Transport and the Environment.
Explain basic concepts of four-step travel demand modelling and apply computational methods related to each step.
Evaluate transport system conditions (including public transport system) based on demand forecasts and plan for the future.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CVEN2401 or CVEN3401 or CVEN2402 or CVEN3402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Logistics Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will cover the basics of logistics data analytics, simulation, optimisation and operation research models, which are critical tools to solve complex decision-making problems arising in the field of freight transport and logistics. These advanced methods will be then used to create engineering solutions to manage existing logistical systems as well as answer questions on freight transport infrastructure needs. Throughout the course, these techniques will be illustrated on challenging transport and logistics problems such as port operations, resilient supply chain network design, facility location, vehicle routing, demand prediction as well as emerging information management systems in logistics and supply chains such as blockchain. After completing this course, students will have been exposed to efficient methods and their application to solve transport and logistics decision-making problems. The course will use real data for a course project as well as invite leading practitioners to present their expertise on selected topics.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse transport logistics systems
Apply basic concepts, methods and techniques to transport logistics problems
Model real world transport logistics problems
Describe current state-of-the-art technologies and methods being used in transport logistics engineering
Solve complex and large scale transport logistics problems using optimisation and data analysis techniques

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Operations
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course offers students an advanced understanding of the field of traffic engineering and congestion management, with a focus on transport system performance, reliability, and the analytical approached used to address congestion and delay. The course covers topics related to the analysis, design and evaluation of transport operations and congestion management systems, including data collection and analysis methods, simulation techniques and stochastic process techniques used for transport operations. Key topics include an introduction to traffic operations models, their application to traffic flow and multi-modal transport systems. Additionally, the course covers the operational characteristics of vehicles in multi-modal transport systems, including public transport, and the statistical, computational, and AI-enabled tools required to manage and analyze large volumes of real-world data. The focus of the course is on applying traffic operation models and real-world data to evaluate operational strategies and support informed transport planning and operational decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Apply and integrate transport operations models with real-world operational data using statistical, computational, and AI-enabled methods.
Critically interpret analytical and data‑based results to support transport planning and operational decision‑making for professional contexts.
Design and conduct data-driven transport operations studies to evaluate operational strategies and policy interventions.
Critically evaluate transport operation models and frameworks for analysing congestion, reliability and performance in transport systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Traffic Flow Theory and Simulation
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Traffic engineering professionals are tasked with ensuring the safe and efficient movement of people and goods through the provision and maintenance of transportation systems. The effectiveness of the transport system defines the economic development and quality of life for the entire community. This course offers students an advanced understanding of traffic flow theory fundamentals and simulation modeling approaches. The course covers topics including fundamental traffic flow characteristics and variables, including their definitions and empirical relations. Other topics include queuing theory and shockwave theory and analysis. The course introduces students to both macroscopic and microscopic traffic flow models. Design and operations of unsignalised and signalised intersections, as well as network traffic flow and pedestrian traffic flow characteristics and modelling, are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Analyse traffic data for performance assessment of traffic systems
Apply concepts, methods and techniques in traffic flow modelling
Describe and apply traffic simulation methods
Design and assess various traffic management and control strategies using simulation and mathematical models
Formulate and solve existing and potential traffic systems problems
Describe the relationship between fundamental traffic flow variables

Master projects are complex, open-ended problems that allow room for your creativity, and the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of results. There are multiple possible solutions or conclusions at the outset and sufficient complexity to require a degree of project planning. The project requires you to formulate problems in scientific or engineering terms, manage an technical project and find solutions by applying scientific and engineering methods. You will also develop the ability to work in a research and development environment. You must identify a supervisor and project prior to enrolling in this course. This is the first course of the 3 course project structure.

Demonstrate oral and written communication in professional and lay domains.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Geological Environments, Geomorphology and Geohazards
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course presents the different geological environments and settings in which engineering occurs. The course covers the following main elements: Key geological issues and typical geotechnical questions associated with different geological and geomorphological environments Global tectonics and structural geology Surficial materials including different types of soils and duricrusts Surface processes and environmental effects such as sea-level change and in-situ stress features Engineering Geomorphology Hydrogeology Geohazards and their risk assessment. The course will provide a sound basis to make meaningful geological interpretations to solve geotechnical and geohazard problems.

Develop engineering geological models incorporating global tectonics, geomorphology, structural geology and hydrogeology
Make meaningful geological interpretations to solve geotechnical and geohazard problems in different geological and geomorphological environments
Explain the main surface processes and associated materials and how they impact engineering in near-surface settings

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geomechanics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Fundamentals of the effective stress concept, seepage analysis and Laplace Equation, basic and advanced theories of consolidation, nonlinearity and Biots theorem, soil liquefaction, seismic analysis of embankment dams, critical state soil mechanics, fundamentals of continuum mechanics, theory of elasticity, constitutive relationships and failure criteria for real soils, soil plasticity and Cam-clay model, fundamentals of unsaturated soils mechanics
learning_outcomes: Perform regional and site-specific liquefaction analyses
Describe the principles of soil mechanics and perform complex deformation, and stability analyses.
Perform shear strength and deformation calculations including wetting induced collapse
Perform earthquake-induced deformation and post liquefaction stability analyses
Perform soil plasticity analysis using the Cam-Clay Model
Apply basic principle of critical state soil mechanics and apply it to engineering problems
Use advanced theories of consolidation, elasticity and constitutive relationships to perform regional and site-specific liquefaction analyses.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Slope Instability and Stabilisation
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Slope stability analysis, design of stabilisation measures and assessment of risk are important roles for geotechnical engineers, engineering geologists and mining engineers. This course will build on knowledge of soil mechanics and geotechnical engineering, and analysis skills, in these areas. The course will cover the following topics: Landslide classification and recognition: relation to topography and geology. Site investigations, instrumentation and laboratory testing. Analysis of stability: selection of shear strengths, shear strength of fissured clays, review of limit equilibrium analysis, back-analysis. Pre-failure deformations of soil slopes. Slope stabilisation techniques including geometry change, control of piezometric pressures, anchoring, retaining walls, reinforced soil. Stability analysis involving unsaturated soils. Quantitative risk analysis (QRA) including assessment of the probability of failure, travel distance, risk estimation and risk acceptance criteria.
learning_outcomes: Assess the stability of slopes to determine if failures are possible, or to ascertain what soil properties were active in the lead up to previous failures.
Apply quantitative risk assessment to slope stability problems and assess the acceptability of risk.
Generate designs of stable slopes and slope stabilisation regimes to reduce risk.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Foundation Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: The course covers analysis and design of shallow foundations and limitations of methods, advanced analysis methods of single piles and pile groups under both static and dynamic loading conditions, and analysis and design methods of anchored walls and cast in-situ piles. It will cover the basics of geotechnical earthquake engineering, design of industrial machine foundations, and seismic/liquefaction analysis of soil-foundation systems. Also, issues relevant to the design of shallow foundations when interacting with unsaturated soils will be addressed. The course will require students to carry out analysis and design through project-based learning.
learning_outcomes: Perform advanced analysis of single piles and pile groups.
Explain the critical geotechnical earthquake engineering concepts related to seismic site response analysis.
Evaluate the liquefaction potential of a given site by applying soil mechanics principles and geotechnical earthquake engineering.
Explain the strength and serviceability design aspects for shallow foundations.
Analyse and design industrial machine foundations to satisfy performance criteria under operational vibration and impact loading.
Evaluate static and dynamic designs of soil-foundation systems for strength and serviceability aspects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Rock Engineering
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Introduction to rock engineering including the engineering description of rocks, discontinuities and rock mass; the strength of rock substance, defects and rock mass; laboratory testing of rock, defect surveys, data presentation and hemispherical projections; in-situ stress and its measurement; stresses about underground openings; classification systems and introductory tunnel support requirements. Investigation, design and construction of tunnels and other underground structures, rock and rock mass strength and deformability; In-situ stresses; stresses about underground openings by elastic and numerical methods; classification systems for prediction of support requirements, including NATM; design of support elements including bolts, dowels, mesh and anchors. Measurement of in-situ stresses; instrumentation and monitoring; squeezing and swelling ground. Tunnel excavation methods and their applicability, including drill and blast, heading and bench, tunnel boring machine, road headers.
learning_outcomes: Describe the basic principles related to the theory and design of rock engineering including methods for describing, recording and presenting features of rock masses
Perform a geotechnical design of slopes and foundations and support systems for underground structures.
Apply software to assess stresses and displacements for tunnel design
Determine appropriate geotechnical properties for rock masses

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geotechnical Models and Site Investigation
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course teaches the concept of Engineering Geological Models as a knowledge framework and thought system for geotechnical design and geohazard assessments. The course highlights the cognitive science behind development of a model, presents the processes and approaches that have proven successful and discusses the processes that do not work effectively. Different types of models are explained, the model building process is outlined, and the components of models are discussed for different types of engineering projects. The concept of Total Geology is explained including how it fits into the overall modeling development process as part of the desk study. The use of desk studies is highlighted as an essential method to plan efficient site investigations. The main field investigation techniques are explained including mapping and sub-surface methods such as drilling and trenching. In-situ testing of soil is covered including SPT, CPT and piezocone. Laboratory testing of soil and rock is introduced including UCS, triaxial, direct shear and ring shear. Field instrumentation for pore pressure and displacement is outlined. Data acquisition and modelling tools are introduced including engineering description systems, data bias, remote sensing, GIS, photogrammetry, borehole imaging, presentation of maps, plans and sections, 3D modelling, DFN’s.
learning_outcomes: Develop effective engineering geological models for geotechnical and geohazard applications
Apply field mapping skills to geotechnical engineering projects
Work effectively in a team in workshop and field settings.
Describe the fundamental science behind engineering geology
Select appropriate site investigation techniques for projects in different geological and geotechnical environments.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geotechnical Engineering of Dams
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course explores the geotechnical aspect of dam engineering. There has been a recent resurgence in dam upgrades and new dams in Australia and abroad, driven largely by influences of a changing climate, changes in population, and the growth of renewable energy requirements through hydroelectricity and pumped hydro. This course will establish the foundations for dam engineers and geotechnical engineers to design and assess new and existing dams. The course is structured by consideration of various geotechnical failure mechanisms for dams, in much the same way that would be considered in a failure modes workshop in industry. The key fundamental elements of the failure modes will be discussed, in addition to practical considerations for these failure modes. Focus will also be drawn to the challenges and uncertainties associated these failure modes. The key geotechnical failure modes covered are hydraulic/seepage, sliding and overturning instability, internal erosion, and liquefaction response of soils. While the course predominantly focuses on water retaining dams, breadth sessions will be also be provided to show application of these concepts to tailings dam. In particular, current best practices for assessing strength and deformation of tailings dam will be discussed, along with consideration of unsaturated tailings.
learning_outcomes: Explain the factors affecting the stability of dams throughout the complex timeline of hydraulic and mechanical loading on dams.
Examine the susceptibility of materials to internal erosion and design filters to mitigate internal erosion failure.
Evaluate existing design criteria and analysis methods in dam engineering and identify limitations and scope for improvements to existing concepts.
Describe the liquefaction behaviour of soil and its influence on post-liquefaction behaviour
Analyse seepage through embankment dams of various configurations and the control of seepage through the foundation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Geomechanics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: Fundamentals of Geomechanics is for geologists and other professionals who wish to work in geotechnical engineering, engineering geology, and environmental engineering. It covers the most important topics in soil mechanics including the basic classification of soil, phase relationships, the principle of effective stress and its importance in soil mechanics and geotechnical engineering, how water flows through soil and the equations governing the one-dimensional and two-dimensional flow of water in soils. It also covers the behaviour of soil under imposed loads, in particular the time-dependent behaviour of clay, the shearing strength of soil, and the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion.
learning_outcomes: Identify the major physical properties of soils, and classify soils based on different standards.
Explain the concepts of soil shear strength, including drained and undrained conditions.
Solve a range of soil related problems particularly those involving water flow, soil settlement and soil strength.
Predict the amount of soil settlement
Estimate effective in-situ stresses due to layers of soil, pore water pressure and surcharges.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Earthquake Engineering and Foundation Dynamics
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This is an advanced course in geotechnical earthquake engineering and engineering seismology. It covers a wide range of topics to provide a background to most aspects of geotechnical earthquake engineering, allowing students to understand the theory and practice that underlie seismic design. Engineering seismology, including earthquake generation and characterisation, wave propagation, strong ground motion and local site effects, is introduced as the basis of understanding earthquakes and their effects. The theory of deterministic and probabilistic seismic hazard assessments (SHAs) is then explained and the earthquake seismic hazard in Australia is discussed together with the Australian earthquake loading code AS1170.4. . Soil dynamics is introduced, explaining the theory of site response, soil liquefaction and ground vibrations. From this, ground motion characteristics such as response spectra and topographic amplification, can be understood. Discussion is also provided on associated site investigation and laboratory testing methods. The engineering seismology and soil dynamics components of the course allow the understanding of how earthquake resistant engineering works can be developed. The third part of the course goes into detail on the engineering design for projects including foundations, slopes, retaining walls and soil-structure interaction. This includes details on the theory, design codes and standards, as well as undertaking designs in practice. Extensive case histories are used throughout the course to help explain the theory and show its relevance.
learning_outcomes: Explain the approach to undertake a seismic hazard assessment
Understand the theory of soil dynamics and the practical implications of its use for engineering designs
Communicate and work effectively with a multidisciplinary team of geotechnical engineers, engineering geologists, structural engineers and engineering seismologists in workshop and field settings.
Describe the fundamental science behind engineering seismology
Apply earthquake engineering to develop designs for slopes and foundations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Stormwater Management
school: School of Civil and Environmental Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course explores urban water management, emphasizing urban hydrology and best practices in stormwater management. Students gain skills in hydrological modeling, traditional stormwater conveyance infrastructure design, and various green technologies under the concept of Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD) or Nature-Based Solutions (NBS). Practical assignments and fieldwork equip students to develop effective, sustainable management plans for water quality and stormwater control in diverse urban catchments.
learning_outcomes: Select and design treatment trains that ensure acceptable stormwater flows and quality for receiving water.
Characterise and design traditional stormwater conveyance infrastructure in urban drainage systems.
Work both independently and collaboratively on diverse urban stormwater challenges.
Develop sustainable urban drainage designs that employ Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD) principles.
Quantify flows from urban catchments and develop stormwater management plans.
Describe urban hydrology and the impact of anthropogenic influences on stormwater quality and quantity in urban catchments.
