syllabus_overview: This advanced course within the Graphics disciplinary studio will extend the skills you have developed in the introductory and intermediate courses into three-dimensional places and spaces, with an emphasis on research and critical thinking. You will develop interpretive narratives through graphic interventions, alongside strategies for the installation of your responses. Expressed through a design proposition and subsequent development of a graphic design project, we will continue our established disciplinary focus on typographic skills alongside a broad range of image making techniques. By the end of the course, you will have a strong portfolio piece that reflects your emerging graphic design voice.
learning_outcomes: Formulate, iterate and communicate self-directed and advanced graphic design concepts informed by theory, technical knowledge and responsible practice
Implement a self-directed graphic design narrative and associated wayfinding into a three-dimensional space using advanced typography and image making skills
Conduct rigorous design research using a range of methodologies, and communicate through a design proposition and presentation
Evidence strategy, criticality, research, experimentation, evaluation and sophisticated reflection through comprehensive and considered documentation
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES2140

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graphics 2: Identity and Form
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course within the Graphics disciplinary studio will introduce you to research-based responses to developing a visual identity in the context of a broader understanding of brand design. You will build on the typography and image fundamentals acquired in the introductory course, and develop an understanding of how to apply strategic thinking to your design process when developing visual identities and sophisticated graphic systems across a range of media. Your approaches will be framed by theory, as well as a consideration of end-users, naming and tone of voice, and practical issues such as copyright. Your knowledge of visual identity will be further advanced by applying graphic solutions to three-dimensional forms, as well as developing an understanding of issues such as materiality, life-cycle analysis, and responsible practices such as sustainability and ethics in the context of graphic design.
learning_outcomes: Apply visual identity solutions to a range of media and contexts, and evidence consideration of responsible practice
Evidence strategy, research and experimentation and their relevance to graphic design solutions through comprehensive and considered documentation
Create packaging prototypes that evidence consideration of brand design, materiality, and responsible practice
Generate, iterate and communicate sophisticated design concepts informed by graphic design theory and practice in response to a brief
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1140

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interaction 3: Emerging Applications
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This advanced Interaction Design course blends emerging technologies with systems thinking, critical design, and speculative futures. Rather than focusing on isolated products, this course asks you to understand how interactions unfold across networks of people, artefacts, infrastructures, and data. Through explorations in future-focused technologies such as AI, natural and robotic interfaces, and mixed reality environments you will examine how human physical, cognitive, and social capacities shape interactions within broader socio-technical systems. Through an in-depth project, you will interrogate current technological trajectories and propose future-oriented design prototypes. Drawing on skills from Interaction 1 and 2, this course integrates rigorous research, critical reflection, and imaginative speculation to envision responsible and human-centered technological futures.
learning_outcomes: Formulate speculative and critical design concepts that respond to future-oriented scenarios
Apply systems-thinking methods to investigate complex interaction design challenges
Produce professional documentation of design process which clearly communicates individual and group insights and informs a final interactive solution
Develop and prototype design solutions that demonstrate ethical, contextual, and responsible engagement with technologies
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES2150

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interaction 2: Design Methodologies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course within the Interaction Design disciplinary specialisation focuses on contextual awareness and inclusive inquiry through user experience research methods and rapid prototyping. Building on foundational principles introduced in Interaction 1, you will examine real-world contexts to understand how social, cultural, technological, and environmental factors influence our interactions with technology. Emphasising accessibility and inclusive practice, the course introduces methods such as contextual inquiry, observation, and advanced iterative prototyping to explore how design can address diverse user needs. Through reflective, hands-on engagement, you will design and evaluate interactive systems that demonstrate a sensitivity to context, inclusion, and adaptability in contemporary interaction design practice.
learning_outcomes: Document and reflect on the design process, demonstrating critical thinking and professional communication
Plan and execute an interaction design project using iterative, evaluative and refined prototypes
Communicate design concepts and solutions effectively through individual or co-design practices
Demonstrate the application of a range of methods for evidence-based contextual inquiry and apply inclusive design principles to interaction design challenges
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1150

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Textiles 2: Experimental Textiles
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course within the Textiles disciplinary studio involves experimentation, research and design development for innovative and experimental applications of textile designs. Experimentation and investigation are central to creating original, innovative and contemporary textile designs, and this course allows you to develop your own experimental approach to your textile design practice. By building on textile fundamentals acquired in the introductory course, you will also develop digital textile design and diverse making techniques, underpinned by more advanced design development processes. Working with industry standard briefs will allow you to take into consideration the requirements of designing for a commercial organisation. In addition, the course traces the ways in which designs can be translated into sustainable outcomes for production by hand, machine or digitally. This commitment to sustainability and social engagement in the course enables you to analyse contemporary issues, understand a designer’s responsibility, and know how to respond to professional design briefs responsibly, ethically and with cultural acknowledgement.
learning_outcomes: Plan, manage and realise a studio-based project in response to a professional design brief
Evidence an understanding of responsible practice through the application of materials and processes appropriate to experimental textile design and production methods
Conduct and critically analyse relevant textile research and curate through comprehensive and considered documentation
Demonstrate and apply experimental and innovative creative practices to the design and development of textile outcomes
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1160

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Textiles 3: Future Textiles
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This advanced course within the Textiles disciplinary studio will encourage you to actively engage with textile materials, processes and technologies to create novel responses to global and/or local issues or developments. Building on the skills already acquired in the introductory and intermediate courses, you will now identify a problem, issue or opportunity to contextualise your development of textiles. Working through an iterative design process, you will produce innovative design solutions that demonstrate a strong emphasis on personal expression and experimentation both in the use of design stimulus, materials and techniques. Studio sessions will encourage you to expand your aesthetic awareness and take unconventional approaches to textiles practice for fashion, interior, exterior or product contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain a global / local problem, issue or opportunity and analyse it within the context of textile design
Apply research findings to inform possible design solutions and evaluate their relevance and success
Investigate and communicate an effective synthesis of concepts, ideas, materials, techniques and processes through the design and development of textile outcomes
Explore the design, fabrication and presentation of textile samples or prototypes through the experimentation of materials, techniques and processes
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES2160

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fashion 2: Making Fashion
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course introduces you to the knowledge and skills essential to interpreting fashion design drawings into a three-dimensional prototype. To do this, designers need to build an understanding of the physical human form and its relationship with the industrial methods used to manufacture garments. You will develop understanding of fashion materials, flat pattern making techniques and the construction finishes that are essential to create fashion prototypes to industrial standards. Moreover, in this course you will continue to examine fashion for sustainability and the circular economy through an exploration of the methods used to reduce textile waste during fashion production.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant skills and knowledge in determining the appropriate materials, construction methods, and finishes required to generate prototypes to industry standards
Conduct and critically analyse relevant research and effectively communicate outcomes in comprehensive and considered documentation
Evidence an understanding of responsible practice through the application of materials and processes appropriate to fashion making
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles of flat pattern making in relation to the body to express innovative ideas
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1170

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design History and Theory 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The course code for this course was previously DDES1201. In this course, you will investigate the central question, “what is design?” and consider key theories that will explore this question from a number of different historical and contemporary perspectives. Using the knowledge and research and analysis skills developed in the introductory Design History and Theory course, you will further investigate these theories in relation to key contexts in design such as globalisation, sustainability, ethics and innovation. Through a series of lectures and tutorials, you will develop and implement the tools required to critically reflect upon and communicate your practice in nuanced and effective ways. At the conclusion of this course, you will understand the relevance and purpose of design theory to your own design practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically analyse various design contexts through the application of appropriate theories of design.
Apply academic research literacy through effective sourcing, attribution and critical analysis of research material.
Demonstrate refined oral and written communication skills through theoretical investigation and analysis of design case studies.
Understand and discuss key theories and concepts that are relevant to design practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1200

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fashion 3: Forming Fashion
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This advanced course explores the fashion design process from initial design to prototype through a critique of the social, political, and cultural expression of clothes. To do this, you will examine fashion semiotics and the clothing user, and activist movements that use fashion as a medium for change. During the course you will engage in a research-based approach to design to create an innovative fashion prototype for an identified clothing user. Moreover, you will explore the methods used to visually present fashion products to different audiences. In building on previous knowledge gained in fashion for sustainability and the circular economy, the course also examines the relationship between aesthetics and the lifespan of clothes.
learning_outcomes: Conduct and critically analyse relevant research and effectively communicate outcomes in comprehensive and considered documentation
Apply an understanding of the social, political, and cultural expression of clothes to create innovative design ideas
Demonstrate relevant skills and knowledge in the process of fashion creation from design to prototype
Evidence an innovative approach to responsible fashion practice through considered aesthetic, material and production decisions
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES2170

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Studio 5: Graduation Project A
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course asks you to develop a rigorous, detailed and theoretically-based design project proposal, and to then generate concept designs that respond to your design problem. You will go on to further develop and complete your project in DDES3101: Graduation Project B. Applied research, investigation and reflection on the nature of contemporary design practice will inform your self-directed project. You will work collaboratively in studio with peers, tutors and broader communities of practice, to gain further experience in the interdisciplinary nature of design.
learning_outcomes: Develop a sophisticated research proposal and brief for a real-life problem.
Effectively communicate a project proposal using sophisticated, innovative and professional methods.
Professionally manage a complex research program and project.
Evidence rigorous research and analysis into the role of contemporary design in addressing complex cultural, social and environmental issues.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Either DDES2100 or DDES2104, and one of the following DDES2101 or FADA2020 or DDES2103

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Studio 6: Graduation Project B
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This culminating capstone studio project will extend research and development undertaken in DDES3100 through to the translation of research findings and design concepts into realised design solutions in the form of a Graduation Project. The completed project will demonstrate the synthesis of previously learned disciplinary specialisations, theory, research, and practice studies with reference to more than one disciplinary specialisation in the finished project. You will be required to develop a rigorous and legible design process and demonstrate design management of the project. You will show leadership in the social, ethical and environmental impact of your design solution and apply your skills to clear documentation and presentation of an integrated design outcome.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design outcomes using sophisticated, innovative and professional methods.
Demonstrate effective design management of the project, including leadership in the social, ethical and environmental impact of a design solution.
Critically evaluate, reflect and locate the role of an emerging designer in contemporary practice.
Demonstrate sophisticated synthesis of previously learned disciplinary specialisations, theory, research, and practice.
Demonstrate critical application of research findings into a major design project.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES3100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mapping and Design Laboratory (mad.lab)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Mapping and Design is an interdisciplinary elective course run in international or local fieldwork locations and open to art, design, media and architecture students. The course immerses students in an intensive three-week program where they (1) work with local and international industry professionals on real-world briefs developed with project stakeholders from industry and government; (2) collaborate with peers from local academic institutions; and (3) engage directly with citizens and the distinct culture of the host location. The course includes lectures, peer and industry critique, field trips, collaborations and meetings across the art and design, architecture, and urban development sectors, as well as engagement with cultural institutions, local communities and the public. The course culminates in an exhibition where students pitch their project outcomes to local industry and government representatives.
learning_outcomes: Use culturally appropriate mapping and design processes in studio and fieldwork environments.
Develop strategies and tactics for site-specific urban design research.
Reflect on and evaluate interdisciplinary, transcultural design research and collaborative studio
Prototype experimental, responsive designs using analogue and digital production technologies.
Apply interdisciplinary design processes and technologies to develop design concepts in response to a brief provided by industry stakeholders.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design History and Theory 4
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This is the fourth and final course in the Design History and Theory core of the Bachelor of Design program. In this course, you will apply the knowledge and skills you have gained in Design History & Theory 1, 2 and 3 across national design histories, global design contexts, design positionality and broader contemporary social and cultural challenges to situate your practice within the expanded field of creative and cultural industries. This course will introduce you to the diverse views, ideas and practices of contemporary design stakeholders who contribute to making and thinking design in an expanded field including journalists, curators, managers, policy makers, researchers, educators, heritage and conservation specialists. The course will help you better understand how design cultures have evolved and critically evaluate a broad spectrum of positions that design stakeholders have occupied in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. At the successful completion of this course, you will be able to identify diverse and alternative career pathways to engage with and through design and effectively communicate your design position, values and philosophy to the wider world.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an advanced understanding of professional career contexts and pathways in the expanded field of design
Adapt independent and collaborative skills through work with internal and external stakeholders in professional communities
Identify and critically evaluate contemporary design practices in the expanded design field through investigative research methods
Consolidate refined and effective communication skills to engagement with diverse design cultures and discourses
prerequisites: Must have completed DDES2200

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design History and Theory 3
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The course code for this course was previously DDES2200. This course is the third course within the Design History and Theory curriculum. It builds on the knowledge and skills that you have acquired during the preceding courses. During the course you will explore the ideas of positions in design and in order to do so will examine issues of personal and professional identities through the lens of race, gender and positionalities. Through a series of engaging lectures and tutorials, you will discuss how the modes of designing have changed through time and ask the question “what does it mean to be a designer?” By engaging with contemporary design theories and the histories that have informed them, you will analyse the notion of design agency in the evolution of social, economic, technological and political contexts, both past and present. This course will enable you to further develop your vocabulary and skills in order to interpret and critically engage with contemporary design debates. Upon successful completion of this course, you will be able to position yourself and situate your design practice in broader socio-political and cultural contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify and situate contemporary design debates in broader cultural and social contexts
Demonstrate refined academic literacy skills through research, analysis and reflection on theories and their relevance for situating design practice
Interpret and discuss design theories and concepts through research, planning and active participation in class debates
Develop and argue for individual positions in design through critical engagement with theories and the histories that informed them
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DDES1201 or DDES2201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Honours Studio Research Project 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Design Honours Research Project 1 is the first in a sequence of two Honours research courses designed to support you in developing your Honours research project. In this course, you will plan and critically develop a theoretical and practice-led research project that is directly related to the concepts, materials and processes and ideas emerging from your design practice. You will experiment and prototype design propositions and develop a written dissertation that will be further developed in DDES4102 Design Honours Research project 2. This course is taught in a studio context, emphasising contemporary design practice as a key mode of investigation and discovery. The studio also operates as a collegiate and peer-oriented environment, fostering a supportive and rigorous culture of creative practice, critical discussion, and exchange.
learning_outcomes: Critically situate, frame and articulate emerging design practice engaging with historical, contemporary and social discourses
Generate and communicate design responses to complex local and/or global scenarios
Evaluate and generate methodologies for your research on, in and through design, demonstrating an awareness of ethical issues
Develop and formulate conceptual frameworks and research questions to inform design research
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in Design (Honours) program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Honours Studio Research Project 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Design Honours Research Project 2 is the final of two Honours research courses designed to support you in developing and delivering your self-guided Honours research project. In this course, you will continue to critically develop your theoretical and/or practice-led research project realised in DDES4101 Design Honours Research Project 1, in relation to both your design practice, and your scholarly research framework and written dissertation. You will then resolve your research project into a sophisticated, professional design outcome supported by a written thesis. This course is taught in a studio context, emphasising contemporary design practice as a key mode of investigation and discovery and alignment to industry. The studio also operates as a collegiate and peer-oriented environment, run over two consecutive terms, so as to allow time for experimentation, development and exploration ahead of the final outcomes that constitute the majority of your Honours grade. The studio course fosters a supportive and rigorous culture of creative practice, critical discussion, and exchange.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a capacity to deliver sustained, highly developed, refined and resolved design outcomes
Generate, develop and articulate critical, practice-led research on, in and through design
Synthesise advanced scholarly knowledge through the production of practice-based design outcomes that critically investigate questions relevant to contemporary design practice
Critically speculate through multiple modes of experimentation, materialities, technologies and practice
Synthesise theory and practice through research, writing and a distinctive approach to the discipline of design
Situate and reflect on individual design practice within the context of emerging professional networks, industries and wider global concerns
prerequisites: Must have completed DDES4101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Honours Studio Research Project 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Design Honours Research Project 2 is the final of two Honours research courses designed to support you in developing and delivering your self-guided Honours research project. In this course, you will continue to critically develop your theoretical and/or practice-led research project realised in DDES4101 Design Honours Research Project 1, in relation to both your design practice, and your scholarly research framework and written dissertation. You will then resolve your research project into a sophisticated, professional design outcome supported by a written thesis. This course is taught in a studio context, emphasising contemporary design practice as a key mode of investigation and discovery and alignment to industry. The studio also operates as a collegiate and peer-oriented environment, run over two consecutive terms, so as to allow time for experimentation, development and exploration ahead of the final outcomes that constitute the majority of your Honours grade. The studio course fosters a supportive and rigorous culture of creative practice, critical discussion, and exchange.
learning_outcomes: Critically speculate through multiple modes of experimentation, materialities, technologies and practice
Sythesise theory and practice through research, writing and a distinctive approach to the discipline of design
Situate and reflect on individual design practice within the context of emerging professional networks, industries and wider global concerns
Demonstrate a capacity to deliver sustained, highly developed, refined and resolved design outcomes
Synthesise advanced scholarly knowledge through the production of practice-based design outcomes that critically investigate questions relevant to contemporary design practice
Generate, develop and articulate critical, practice-led research on, in and through design

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Research Methods and Theory
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to a range of philosophical, conceptual and theoretical methods and frameworks to help students develop their research skills and locate their design practice that critically reflects on contemporary design contexts. It is designed to help students concurrently undertake a substantial honours level research project.
learning_outcomes: Interrogate and articulate philosophical and theoretical frameworks that critique historical and contemporary situated design discourse and practice.
Critically situate design practice as a distinctive method of research from humanities and scientific research.
Evaluate, integrate and position an understanding of the engagement and impact of design discourse, thinking and practice on responsible global political, ethical and sustainability issues.
Generate, apply and effectively communicate theoretical frameworks and methods to contemporary design discourse and practices.
prerequisites: Honours Co-requisite

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Concepts and Communication
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course is the foundation core studio in the Master of Design where you will develop an understanding of the relevance of design and its implications in social, experiential, and environmental contexts. This course introduces an integrated approach to design practice that will be further developed in subsequent core studios. Engaging in creative strategies, you will learn how to extend your abilities to develop insights to inform design solutions. You will critically analyse your design process to develop your awareness of the significance and impact of design in responding to contextual issues, placing design as a critical practice in a broader context.
learning_outcomes: Justify your application of design fundamentals to the design process.
Deploy fundamental methods of research and analysis to develop insights that inform design concepts, processes and solutions.
Reflect on the potential for design to impact change in social, experiential and environmental contexts.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Histories and Theories for Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces a number of historical and theoretical lenses to help position your design thinking and practice. You will unpack key debates in the discipline of design by exploring a range of historical and cultural contexts and practices, with particular reference to Australia and the Asia-Pacific. You will be introduced to diverse case studies that form the basis of your research essay to position yourself relative to the history and theory of the design discipline. By the end of the course, you will be able to better situate your interests and practice relative to histories and theories informing design’s past and present.
learning_outcomes: Identify, critically analyse and synthesise theories of design and their application to design contexts
Demonstrate refined communication skills through theoretical investigation and analysis of design case studies
Apply advanced academic research skills through effective sourcing, attribution, critical analysis and interpretation of research materials
Evaluate, articulate and discuss the key theories relevant to design practice

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Critical Approaches to Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon your knowledge of design as a practice for addressing social and environmental issues. You will build knowledge and understanding of design problems through evaluation and analysis of an existing real-world scenario, and produce a critical design response. You will engage with a range of human-centred research methodologies that will aid in your selection and analysis of a design problem. You will use human-centred design methodologies to develop innovative, informed and often unexpected design solutions that challenge conventions and assumptions. This course fosters the development of a peer mentoring culture through collaborative research, iteration, interdisciplinary collaboration and critique.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate creativity and critical thinking in the resolution of a design problem.
Interpret and apply human-centred research methodologies to the analysis of a design problem.
Effectively communicate design research, processes and outcomes through a variety of formats.
Document research methods and design processes to professional standards.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: SDES9204 or DDES9010

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Creativity and Entrepreneurship
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides an understanding of the various definitions of entrepreneurship, innovation and creativity and how they intersect, influence and are shaped by designers. Creativity tools and different models of thinking are examined from a theoretical and real world perspective, to provide you with knowledge and practical techniques to help develop your careers. Entrepreneurship takes many forms in different organisations and industries, and this course demonstrates the interconnectedness between new creative ideas, innovations, design thinking methods, and the various components needed to become an entrepreneur. Personal traits, different working environments, and various creative processes combine to enhance innovative idea development, and this is critically explored in the course content. Through lectures, tutorials, case studies and active learning in assessed coursework, you will engage with examples of entrepreneurial innovation, and develop your own creative capacity.
learning_outcomes: Communicate their observations regarding opportunities to enhance entrepreneurship, innovation and creativity through the use of applied design strategies, in well- designed presentations.

Critically analyse and discuss the influence that personal traits, different environments and various processes have on successfully developed, innovative ideas in relation to successful entrepreneurs.
Identify opportunities to develop design knowledge and apply skills in researching selected themes, tools, methods and aspects of entrepreneurship, innovation and creativity

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Designing in Context
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course investigates and critically analyses a range of design contexts, particularly cultural, social, behavioural, ethical, environmental, and sustainability issues within local and global frameworks. You will analyse existing design responses using tools such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) to identify and evaluate diverse stakeholder perspectives, to determine the validity of the design responses and associated processes. Building on this research, you will synthesise and apply your knowledge to a prescribed design challenge, and develop, articulate, and justify your design response. Throughout the course you will reflect upon your own practice and identify, test, and demonstrate your emerging values as a holistic and responsible global design practitioner.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and synthesise a range of design considerations in various contexts.
Demonstrate a range of diverse and appropriate outcomes that respond to a clearly defined and justified design problem.
Develop and articulate a considered identity as a responsible global design practitioner through their design decisions, perspectives and outcomes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: SDES9204 or DDES9010

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Imperatives for a Sustainable Future
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Imperatives for a Sustainable Future provides you with a critical understanding of the theoretical and practical implications of design as a professional activity. It presents design’s impacts on society, economics and the environment. It aims to develop an understanding of how to deal with wicked problems, colonial legacies and human waste issues, by using a design-thinking sustainability framework informed by ethics, systems thinking, Indigenous knowledge and non-human worlds. You will use foresight tools for developing sustainable strategies as well as methods for measuring and monitoring successful design conception and implementation. Key themes will include the four pillars of sustainability applied to products, services and systems; aesthetics of care; non-human models; the Anthropocene; responsibility in leadership; and cross disciplinary collaboration.
learning_outcomes: Identify and build cross-disciplinary teams to collaborate on solving complex problems with sustainable outcomes
Communicate and act on key sustainability issues
Identify opportunities for sustainable design within local, regional and global contexts.
Develop design based strategies to address wicked problems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio Project 1: Proposal
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Drawing on the knowledge and experience gained in studio-specialisations, this advanced-level course gives you the opportunity to apply design thinking, research and problem-framing skills to the development of a detailed and thoroughly researched design brief and presentation that respond to the complex issues and sustainability challenges facing contemporary society. Your design brief will articulate the design context, the methodologies and methods you have explored, and the criteria for guiding and evaluating the design work that you will undertake in Design Studio Project 2. You will undertake rigorous and systematic research into end-users, potential clients, and stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and synthesise complex information to articulate research questions relevant to design practice and how they relate to contemporary global issues and grand challenges.
Demonstrate autonomy, expert judgement, adaptability and responsibility in design practice.
Produce, interpret and communicate interdisciplinary and multifaceted project briefs for original design propositions related to research questions.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: SDES9204, SDES9210 and SDES9211 or DDES9010, DDES9012 and DDES9013

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio Project 2: Final Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will develop an understanding of design practice through the critical application of theories, concepts and methods explored in Design Studio Project 1. Working individually, and as part of multidisciplinary teams, you will experience the opportunity to complete and professionally present a major design project. Using an iterative process, you will experiment with materials and methods for prototyping, testing and evaluating designs that build on the knowledge and skills acquired throughout the Master of Design program.
learning_outcomes: Develop and deliver critical, persuasive and professional design presentations that communicate design research, processes and outcomes at an advanced level to specialist and non-specialist audiences, through prototyping, project pitches and exhibiting.
Demonstrate autonomy, critical judgement, speculative abilities, adaptability and responsibility, working independently as a design practitioner, and effectively as part of interdisciplinary teams.

Critically analyse, synthesise and apply complex information including conceptual frameworks, design methodologies and processes, material knowledge, and professional practice relevant to a significant research-based design project.

Creatively develop and resolve an interdisciplinary and multifaceted design project with critical, rigorous and sophisticated responses to your individual Design Project Brief produced in DDES9016 Design Studio Project 1: Proposal.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: SDES9213 or DDES9016

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Textiles: Contemporary Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9746. This course introduces contemporary textile practice in art and design applications for students involved in creative work for the first time. It introduces the context for designing and making; the narrative role textiles play in reflecting and documenting contemporary society; and the social, sustainable, re-use and environmental issues associated with this industry. The course introduces textile techniques and processes; material properties and characteristics of fibres, fabrics, and associated materials; current textile design issues and new technologies; the technical aspect of designing for a 2D surface and a 3D constructed textile; and the application of textiles across the design spectrum. It covers a variety of techniques for surface design, printing, colouring, and constructing cloth, giving students the knowledge and skills necessary to undertake contemporary textile design projects for various applications.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on and evaluate an aesthetic approach to design concepts and realised projects.
Analyse the creative possibilities of textile processes.
Interpret the role textiles can play in society and assess the impact industry has on contemporary social and environmental issues.
Experiment with the techniques introduced to investigate how to apply these to various textile processes in the design context.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Jewellery: Contemporary Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9748. This course introduces you to the fundamentals of jewellery design and aims to develop your conceptual and practical skills in the design and making of contemporary jewellery for both art and design practice. You will explore a range of traditional and new materials and processes to create diverse design outcomes from one-off objects to small-scale studio production. Practical work is contextualised by consideration of material, cultural, theoretical and historical issues relating to contemporary jewellery practice.
learning_outcomes: Create and professionally present finished contemporary jewellery solutions employing jewellery making processes, techniques and materials.
Interpret jewellery design problems by applying fundamental jewellery studio skills.
Interpret current scholarly research, historical context and practice-based research to inform and argue current perceptions of contemporary jewellery.
Analyse the field of contemporary jewellery to support the realisation of studio projects demonstrated through research, drawings and experimentation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Furniture and Lighting: Contemporary Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9747. This course focuses on the knowledge, skills and processes used in the design, fabrication and presentation of contemporary furniture and lighting. You will learn about the history of furniture and lighting design and the ways in which these foundations shape contemporary practice, with specific attention given to contemporary theories, methods and evaluation processes of sustainable design and making practices. Throughout the term you will learn the processes necessary to design and fabricate a piece of sustainable furniture or lighting - from contextual, conceptual and material research, to design development, material testing, modelling, making and prototyping.
learning_outcomes: Create a furniture or lighting design using workshop machinery and technical skills.
Understand the theory, method and evaluation processes associated with sustainable design and apply them to a design project.
Develop a design idea through various stages of research, drawing, modelling, material testing, making and prototyping.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Hybrid Crafting: New Technologies, Traditional Techniques
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously ADAD9211. Hybrid Crafting: New Technologies, Traditional Techniques introduces art and design practice at the intersection of analogue and digital design and fabrication methods. This course takes a gradual approach, guiding students through an introduction to digital design and fabrication processes available at the Art & Design Makerspaces, including 3D modelling, 3D scanning, 3D printing, and laser cutting as well as analogue making processes available in the UNSW Art & Design Workshops, including making with ceramics, wood, metal, textiles and plastics. Students will move from analogue to digital modes of design and fabrication exploring the potential for innovative form generation and fabrication methods at the intersection of these two paradigms of art and design production.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate conceptual and practical understandings of analogue and digital design and fabrication methods by engaging in practical studio activities

Conceive, realise and present a body of three-dimensional creative work that communicates expressive characteristics of digital design and fabrication processes arising from reflective studio practice
Develop and communicate professional art or design presentations

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Material Thinking
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Material Thinking provides you with a practice-based platform for understanding relationships between materials and creative practice in art and design. Lecture content, studio exercises and projects will cover a range of ways to define, categorise, interpret, and re-interpret natural, engineered, smart and virtual materials, using analogue and digital methods of manipulation. In your project work, you will expand on these ideas, developing your own material experiments to inform the creation of a self-directed art or design work.
learning_outcomes: Initiate, iterate, and fully resolve art or design projects
Identify a range of experimental procedures to explore material interpretations, properties, qualities, methods for manipulation and applications
Develop and communicate professional art or design presentations
Research and critically analyse analogue and digital material developments, properties, qualities, methods for manipulation and applications

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transforming the Everyday: Domestic Futures
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Transforming the Everyday: Domestic Futures is designed to challenge the way in which you think about and create the spaces we inhabit everyday. The philosophy behind the approach to this studio is to extend the process of design as an acquired skill through serious play, and for you to explore, examine and demonstrate your conceptual understandings. This course will provide you with the opportunity to explore in both theoretical and practical terms the future of domestic life and domestic environments. You will explore the domestic environment and how we will live our domestic lives in the future. What the domestic environment will look like, what part technology will play and what impact our growing energy use will have on our environment and our lifestyles. You will collaborate to create studio outcomes that are informed by various disciplines to develop projects that are grounded in defensible concepts. You will develop creative strategies to explore conventions used in design thinking, visualisation, prototyping, documentation and presentation. Building upon your foundations in theory and the practice of design, you will develop your skills and understandings so that you can better integrate strategies employed in the design process, thereby enhancing the realisation of design outcomes within particular contexts.
learning_outcomes: Examine complex design issues from a broader perspective and in a holistic way.
Apply fundamental research methods to inform responses to a design brief, formulate appropriate design process and facilitate potential solutions.
Generate design outcomes by investigating ideas and positions around domestic life external to the immediate problems, and conduct more pro-active approaches for new design solutions.
Apply interdisciplinary and collaborative processes in design projects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Participatory Design for Commercial Contexts
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Participatory Design is also known as cooperative design, social design or co-design, and encompasses innovative design practices which actively involve all stakeholders to ensure the designed outcomes meets the clients needs, is fit for purpose and usable. This way of design is particularly valued in the development of commercial products and services. In this course you will learn how to develop a model of practice that is interdisciplinary, collaborative and critically focussed on the ideas of 'designing with’ and social inclusion. You will be supported by relevant theory and will use an action learning approach to undertake a series of projects to develop your ability to identify commercial stakeholders, their needs and methods.
learning_outcomes: Plan and apply participatory strategies to use with clients in a design context.
Identify a design opportunity and investigate research tools to explore the opportunity with stakeholders.
Identify and address commercial design constraints.
Design a product, service or experience that addresses the needs of the identified stakeholders.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Intervention: People, Places and Cultural Contexts
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9350. Urban Intervention: People, Places and Cultural Contexts focuses on critical investigations into contemporary urban contexts and the intersections of public and private space. Working collaboratively, you will develop designs for urban Interventions to rethink the nature of public spaces and architecture in cities.
learning_outcomes: Identify design solutions by investigating ideas and positions situated in urban life.
Demonstrate design as an interdisciplinary and collaborative process.
Construct clear theoretical and conceptual frameworks to support projects.
Apply research methods to inform a response to set design briefs.
Develop and communicate professional design presentations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Typographic Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: This code for this course was previously SDES9761. Contemporary graphic design is in a constant state of flux. As a result, the ways in which we develop, consider and use typefaces is more diverse than ever. This course will explore methods by which you can generate and formalise a typeface using originality in research techniques. The course will help you understand how that typeface can then be integrated into contemporary print and screen applications. This course also gives you the opportunity to reconsider issues of legibility and readability in historical and contemporary typographic practices.
learning_outcomes: Employ principles of practice-based research relevant to the contextual and conceptual approach to a project.
Recognise historical and contemporary principles and skills in typography through practice -based research.
Create typeface and typographic publication designs to professional standards.
Apply research knowledge to contextual and conceptual design projects.
Demonstrate critical engagement through collaborative practice

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graphic Design Foundations
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9760. This course explores the principles of visual communication through a range of brand design projects. By observing the branded identities of people, places, and services as well as products and organisations, you will develop and present designed identities for print, screen, and outdoor application. Reflection on the contextual factors that impact the interpretation and use of the identity will inform its development.
learning_outcomes: Evidence practice-based research methods in a curated visual journal.
Develop the elements of graphic identity by experimenting with mark making, image making and typography.
Generate brand identity concepts through the application of research outcomes.
Present design projects using effective visual and verbal communication.
Implement design concepts across a range of print and screen-based applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graphic Design for User Interfaces
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9762. This course will take you through processes of researching, planning and designing the architecture of a user interface. You will learn how the visual design of interfaces directly relates to the way users interact and experience them, ultimately determining their effectiveness and functionality. Assessment tasks require you to plan and apply your existing visual communication skills to the graphic design of interfaces. By the end of the course you will have completed the graphic design of an user interface, and have the conceptual and practical skills, and confidence, to develop further interface designs. Knowledge and skills in graphic design processes are required before enrolling in this course. You will need at least a basic understanding of Adobe Photoshop or equivalent.
learning_outcomes: Design information architecture that relates to the perceived needs of the users of a proposed interface.
Develop appropriate concepts based on analysis and experimentation for interface design.
Demonstrate an appropriate level of detailing and design skills in the development of user interfaces.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graphic Design and Society
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously ADAD0901. This course introduces issues in graphic design and its significance in society, including communicating identities, designing for national and global audiences, graphics as strategic communication between the client and the public, and design as social policy. As a social activity, the graphic communication of image and text engages critical reflection in the production and consumption of knowledge, for example meaning making in national iconography, product advertising and editorial design. This course comprises a series of integrated lectures, learning activities and assessment tasks that inform your ability to analyse and synthesise printed and screen-based graphic designs. You will apply this knowledge in the creation of your graphic design responses to the design brief.
learning_outcomes: Articulate and develop a process that demonstrates interrogation, iterations, and critical evaluation through design decisions, perspectives and outcomes.
Critically analyse and synthesis a range of graphic design considerations from a range of contemporary and historical contexts
Develop a range of diverse and appropriate design outcomes in response to a clearly defined and rationalised design brief

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interaction Design Foundations
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9311. This course provides you with an introduction to the field of Interaction Design by exploring fundamental concepts in real-world contexts. You will develop technical, theoretical and creative skills through the generation of interactive systems, with a focus on physical objects and experiences. Interaction Design research, ideation and rapid-prototyping methods are used to determine and understand real-world problems, situations and opportunities for the implementation of innovative interactive designs.
learning_outcomes: Undertake research into relevant user activities, requirements and contexts, guided by interaction design and UX principals and methods.

Develop design proposals that describe the technical, conceptual and experiential aspects of an interactive product through visual and written communication methods, including sketches, storyboards, and prototypes.
Apply theories of user-centred design to the analysis and evaluation of interactive systems and technologies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human-Centred User Experience Methods
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9312. Building upon interaction design foundations, this course introduces advanced interaction design techniques used for the development and evaluation of human-centred interactive products and services. You will research a real-world problem, develop an understanding of users, the activities they are engaging in, and the context of use, to identify themes, issues and opportunities for interactive designs. The course culminates in the presentation of a novel interactive design proposal, developed using insights and analysis from in-depth user testing, and realised through User Experience methods and tools to communicate your ideas.
learning_outcomes: Present design-concepts using a combination of written, verbal and visual communication methods.
Apply human-centred research methods to identify design requirements for an interactive design intervention.
Employ advanced prototyping and user-testing processes to produce and evaluate interactive designs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Tangible Interfaces and Interactive Displays
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores the intersection of User Experience (UX) design and public policy, providing students with a unique opportunity to apply UX research methods to complex societal challenges. Throughout the course, students will engage with real-world social policy documents and analyse them through a human-centred design lens. By conducting stakeholder interviews, synthesising research insights, and developing actionable solutions, students will learn how UX principles can inform policy improvements that better serve diverse communities. A key focus of this course is exposing future UX designers to the evolving role of design in shaping society. As the scope of UX expands, it is crucial for designers to anticipate future directions for the field, including its application in the public sector. By working on complex, high-stakes issues such as healthcare, education, and housing policies, students will hone their research and design skills while also grappling with ethical and societal considerations. Through hands-on research, prototyping, and iterative design processes, students will not only develop practical UX skills but also deepen their understanding of the broader impact of design on public life. This course aims to equip future UX professionals with the tools to create meaningful, human-centred solutions that address the pressing challenges of tomorrow. Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9315.
learning_outcomes: Apply inclusive UX research methods to analyse social policy challenges and opportunities by conducting human-centred research, defining stakeholders, user needs and values.

Critically evaluate and reflect on the role of UX in shaping effective social policy outcomes, considering ethical implications and the needs of diverse stakeholder groups throughout the research and design process.
Synthesise research insights into clear, actionable problem statements and apply ideation and prototyping techniques to propose innovative and accessible solutions to social policy challenges.
prerequisites: Students must have completed SDES9311 and SDES9312 or DDES9151 and DDES9152 before enrolling in this course

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Wearable and Bio-Sensing Interactions
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously SDES9316. This course focuses on the design, development and evaluation of wearable and biometric (body-sensing) interactions for artistic, wellness, rehabilitation, or educational applications. Students extend their knowledge of interaction design and apply this to the development of a prototype design that analyses and responds intelligently to data collected via analogue and digital biosensors.
learning_outcomes: Develop and refine an interactive prototype, service or environment through an iterative process of research, development, testing and evaluation.
Combine wearables and bio-sensing to build a resolved, functioning, body-sensing interactive artefact, service or environment.
Describe and apply key theories, issues and frameworks from the field of human-computer interaction and media arts, to the evaluation of body-focused interactive designs
prerequisites: Prerequisite: SDES9311 or DDES9151

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Vision, Strategy and Design Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the necessary knowledge and skills required for creative leadership roles, such as design studio directors, creative directors, artistic directors, and program managers in creative and cultural institutions. This course will specifically focus on the design and leadership of an institutional vision and strategy for the purposes of producing an innovation ecosystem, including the process of design, consultation, and management required to create and lead such an ecosystem. The course will explore definitions, theories and models of creative leadership and explore notions of entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship.
learning_outcomes: Professionally manage and collaborate on a team design project
Effectively communicate understanding of the key concepts using context appropriate language along with sophisticated and professional documentation methods
Demonstrate sophisticated engagement with an industry leader
Demonstrate rigorous research and analysis into creative leadership definitions, theories, and models

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Leadership and Interdisciplinary Teams
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the many opportunities for leadership through design-led theory and practice within interdisciplinary team contexts. Through a series of theoretical and practical explorations, you are asked to analyse and reflect upon the nature of interdisciplinary teams including team structures, project phases and management, and collaboration methodologies. The coursework places a specific focus on the power of design leadership in interdisciplinary projects in fields and disciplines outside of design. You will then be asked to implement your knowledge in team contexts, where you will collaborate to solve a prescribed brief. You will experience multiple roles within the project team structure, and will be asked to test, analyse, and reflect upon different team dynamics, management strategies, and collaboration strategies through a design-led lens.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate rigorous research and analysis into the role of design as a leadership model in interdisciplinary team contexts
Effectively communicate understanding of key concepts using context appropriate language along with sophisticated and professional documentation methods
Professionally manage and collaborate on a team design project
Demonstrate the use of observation and reflective practice as methods for developing personal leadership skills

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Designing and Experiencing Immersion
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Virtual experiences and immersive environments are an integrated aspect of contemporary work, study, and entertainment. In response to this evolving landscape, this course offers a rigorous inquiry into the principles and practices that shape meaningful virtual and immersive experiences. You will explore how, when, and why immersive technologies can be incorporated into design solutions, considering neuroscientific perspectives on perception, historical uses across the creative arts and sciences, and current industry examples. Emphasis is placed on immersion as a form of embodied cognition that connects mind and body. A central feature of the course is the chance to engage first-hand with a curated selection of immersive works through VR headsets. These direct encounters give you the opportunity to analyse, reflect on, and contextualise the principles explored in class. Building on this experience, you will then develop a proposal for an original immersive concept that demonstrates your understanding of immersion’s possibilities and applications. Note: It is a requirement for students who are unable to physically attend class on campus to have their own high-end VR headset (Quest 3 or equivalent) and VR capable PC to meet assessment requirements.
learning_outcomes: Conceptualise and propose an original immersive experience that demonstrates understanding of foundational principles of immersion and embodied cognition
Assess and justify why, how, when, and where different immersive design techniques and technologies should be applied
Critically test, analyse, and evaluate immersive experiences through hands-on engagement, with a focus on how humans perceive and experience immersion

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Dimensions in Immersive Environments
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As digital and automated systems increasingly shape our daily interactions, it is essential to understand not only their potential but also their impact on human experience. This course focuses on how and why humans engage with immersive environments, examining the cognitive, behavioural, and ergonomic factors that influence performance and well-being. Through first-hand experiences with VR headsets and your own independent research, you will investigate how humans respond to stimuli within synthetic, virtual, mixed, and live immersive contexts. Particular attention will be given to ergonomics, comfort, safety, and usability. You will also explore complex aspects of cognition and perception, the evolving dynamics of human–machine interaction, and broader considerations such as accessibility and the impact of emerging technologies, including next-generation AI. By the end of this course, you will have both a theoretical and practical understanding of how to design effective interactions in immersive contexts, distinct from traditional screen-based paradigms. You will learn to apply immersive design principles to improve existing practices and to conceptualise and implement novel forms of interaction that leverage the unique affordances of immersive technologies. Note: It is a requirement for students who are unable to physically attend class on campus to have their own high-end VR headset (Quest 3 or equivalent) and VR capable PC to meet assessment requirements.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the ethical, accessibility, and human-centred implications of immersive and interactive design
Plan, prototype, test, and iterate an immersive design project that demonstrates effective application of ergonomic, safety, and cognitive principles
Apply immersive design principles to analyse and select interaction strategies appropriate to specific real-world or industry contexts
Evaluate the physiological, cognitive, and behavioural impacts of human interaction in immersive environments using established industry ergonomic and usability frameworks

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Narrative and Sensemaking in Immersive Environments
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Story and narrative have always been central to how humans communicate and make meaning. With the rise of immersive and virtual systems, new modes of narrative design are emerging that extend beyond linear storytelling to create dynamic, embodied experiences. This course focuses on narrative design in immersive environments, building on the foundations of perceptual psychology (DDES9901) and human interaction and ergonomics (DDES9902). You will examine a spectrum of narrative modalities - from visual and cinematic to aural and performative - drawing on industry examples in simulation, gaming, 360 cinema, VR, and installation art. Through the lens of multimodal sensemaking and embodied cognition, you will explore how agency, interactivity, situational awareness, and navigation transform narrative into lived experience. Key concepts such as spatial navigation and embodied action will be demonstrated and critically analysed to understand how composition and multimodality shape meaning. Your learning will culminate in the design and prototyping of an immersive narrative experience, demonstrating your ability to integrate narrative principles with the psychological and human-centred foundations established in earlier courses. Note: It is a requirement for students who are unable to physically attend class on campus to have their own high-end VR headset (Quest 3 or equivalent) and VR capable PC to meet assessment requirements.
learning_outcomes: Integrate multimodal approaches - including situation awareness, sensemaking, and embodied cognition - into the design of immersive narrative experiences
Critically analyse the role and transformation of narrative modalities across traditional and immersive forms
Design, implement, and refine immersive narrative experiences using contemporary industry standards, demonstrating the integration of narrative design principles with technical execution
Apply principles of agency, interactivity, and navigation to conceptualise and prototype immersive narrative experiences

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Models, Systems and Solution Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Models form the basis for how we represent the world and design solutions. While they are used differently across domains to analyse, test hypotheses, inform decisions and make predictions, model and systems thinking offers an important perspective to help us understand and shape our environment. Answering the question ‘what is a model?’, this course will give you a holistic perspective of models and systems examining how, why and when it is appropriate to model. You will consider how models can be used to help problem-solve and design solutions in environmental, humanitarian, and creative and creative contexts. Different modelling and systems paradigms will also be examined with a specific focus on their application in visualisation, simulation and immersive design.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate modelling paradigms and their fitness for purpose in visualisation, simulation and immersive design.
Integrate social, technical, and human perspectives into modelling and simulation design using a systems approach.
Conceptualise the use of modelling by examining techniques used in different industries.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Future Immersive Learning Methodologies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Simulation and immersive environments are enabling a range of experiential and practice-based learning approaches, propelling the development of a new learning science. This course will help you understand how the properties of immersive environments impact learning and instructional strategies. You will analyse why, how and when to incorporate immersive learning modalities together with how to design, implement and evaluate learning programs for these contexts.
learning_outcomes: Design immersive learning scenarios to meet industry needs
Assess and evaluate the effectiveness of an immersive learning experience
Analyse instructional design strategies for immersive environments

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Immersive Design, Complexity and Wicked Problems
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Visualisation, simulation, and immersive design offer new ways of engaging with the complex problems and challenges facing today’s society. In this course you will use constructive design and design thinking processes to analyse ‘wicked’ problems and consider how they might be addressed using visualisation, simulation and immersive design. You will be asked to embrace complexity, ambiguity and the interdependencies of diverse stakeholder and discipline world views in relation to real-world challenges. You will learn how to work collaboratively to examine conflicting value systems and to experiment with novel approaches to problem solving using design processes.
learning_outcomes: Use visualisation, simulation and immersive practices to sketch and rapidly prototype design solutions to complex and wicked problems.
Negotiate, facilitate and lead collaborative problem-solving processes using constructive design and design thinking.
Recognise complexity and analyse wicked problems facing industry and society.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Designing Immersion with Game Engines
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Game engines are powerful platforms for building interactive experiences across entertainment, education, training, cultural heritage, and simulation. In this course, you will learn how to use Unity 3D and C# programming to create interactive prototypes for immersive and extended reality (XR) environments. You will explore the workflows of working with digital assets, coding interactions, and deploying applications across devices, with a focus on mixed reality headsets. By the end of the course, you will have the skills to design, code, and prototype interactive XR systems that demonstrate both technical viability and design intent. Note: It is a requirement for students who are unable to physically attend class on campus to have their own high-end VR headset (Quest 3 or equivalent) and VR capable PC to meet assessment requirements.
learning_outcomes: Apply core programming concepts - variables, arrays, loops, functions, conditionals, and logical operators - within working XR prototypes
Implement basic programming principles to enable interactive user experiences in XR contexts
Identify, analyse, and apply appropriate technological affordances to specific immersive and XR design intentions
Integrate and evaluate the potential and limitations of 3D environments and digital assets in the design and implementation of interactive immersive XR experiences

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing Immersive Projects
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As immersive practices and technologies become embedded in our workplace environments, business leaders and managers are required to make critical decisions regarding their design, acquisition and operation. Management of the technology life cycle will impact the successful deployment of immersive technologies in any enterprise. In this course you will learn how to make the business case for the effective use and procurement of an immersive system. This includes undertaking a needs analysis, assessing relative benefits, value and scalability of immersive systems and simulation environments.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate a business case for the procurement of an immersive technology or system
Analyse consumer and business needs in relation to immersive technologies and simulation environments
Assess the relative benefits and values of immersive technologies and simulation environments for different levels of scalability
Critically scope project requirements to understand management implications in the effective use and procurement of an immersive system.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Visualisation, Simulation, and Immersive Design Capstone
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides you with a practical capstone work or project experience that will help synthesise the learnings and experiential insights you have accumulated across the simulation and immersive technologies program and challenge you to test that knowledge in a practical way in real world industry projects or domains. To inform your capstone choices you will be presented with and asked to investigate a cross section of industry projects and engage with leading edge industry partners and mentors. Supported by your course convenor, the capstone placement will be largely self-directed, and requires you to define your priorities and then seek out and negotiate a suitable professional placement. To this end the capstone experience also aims to hone your professional communication and will ask you to develop a professional capability statement. The capstone is multimodal and you are strongly advised to discuss your ideas and interests with your course convenor before embarking on your capstone journey.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal experience and apply program learnings to a practice-based, industry-driven research project
Engage, communicate, and negotiate with stakeholders as required in relation to the organisational and problem solving aspects of the project.
Synthesise relevant immersive practices and practically apply these in response to the industry need.
Coordinate, manage and sustain a self-directed, discipline-specific project.
prerequisites: Required Prerequisites DDES9901, DDES9902, DDES9903, DDES9904

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Information Architecture for Immersive Aesthetics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines the principles of information architecture design as they apply to the context content and users of immersive visualisations and simulations. You will learn about systems for data classification and metadata labelling, search methodologies and user navigation, and how these may be translated into interactive systems for embodied environments.
