Value different types of securities (bonds, equities, and preference shares).
Understand and solve problems involving financial mathematics.
Explain the link between corporate decision making and financial markets.
Analyse capital budgeting projects and use the net present value decision rule to decide if a firm should pursue a project.
Engage with others in culturally and ethnically diverse tutorial groups.
Communicate finance related ideas in a theoretically and applicably sound manner.
Compute the discounted value of a series of cash flows.
Understand and apply the set of tools need for sound and innovative investment and corporate decisions.
Understand the relation between risk and return, and be able to estimate the cost of capital.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 6 UOC of any DPGE, DPST, DPBS and enrolled in a UNSW Diploma program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business and the Law
syllabus_overview: Business and the Law is a foundation course in law. There are no pre-requisites for this course. This course focuses on the Australian legal system. In particular, the course considers the different sources of law and the different systems of law; the Commonwealth Constitution and Commonwealth/State relations; the role of Parliament in making statute law; the Australian court system and the role of the judiciary in making “case law”; and the role of the executive (government). Areas of substantive law relevant to commerce and business dealings that are examined in detail include contract law, tort law (with particular reference to negligence), property law, consumer law and competition law. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Teamwork. Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Oral communication. Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.

Critical thinking and problem solving. Analyse legal issues in a logical and structured way, including by identifying problems, researching relevant sources, proposing an outcome and identifying possible challenges to the proposed outcome.
Knowledge. Identify legal issues that arise in commercial situations
Ethical, social and environmental responsibility. Identify and assess ethical, environmental and sustainability considerations in legal problems.
Written communication. Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented.
Social and cultural awareness. Identify and assess social and cultural considerations in legal problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 6 UOC of any DPGE, DPST, DPBS and enrolled in a UNSW Diploma program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Practical Design Studio 1
syllabus_overview: Practical Design Studio 1 sets the foundation for the practice of design thinking in the built environment with particular emphasis on research-led design inquiry as well as pursuing expansive exploration of ideas through iterative and reflective design techniques. The design brief at the basis of the course introduces you to the key phases, processes, materials and elements of the built environment from the macro scale of landscape and architecture through to the micro scales of interiors and industrial design and the digital potential of computational design. The course will encourage a design response that is critical, curious and inquisitive leading to design proposals that speculate on the future relationships between people and the built environment. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Respond to a given design brief by assembling and utilizing a material response.
Demonstrate elementary skills in architectural communication with an emphasis on hand sketching, model making and digital fabrication in the representation of design research, process and proposal.
Explain the purpose of a design brief at a fundamental level.
Gather and interpret research to inform critical design perspectives and design strategies.
Respond to a given brief using design processes and actions.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design History and Theory
syllabus_overview: In this course we will explore connections between the disciplines of architecture, interior architecture, landscape architecture, industrial design and computation design. We will investigate sites, ideas, concepts and technologies of historic and present-day significance and the way in which their principles have survived and evolved over a long period of time. The history of design thinking offers insight into a human being, who feels an affinity with a city at all scales from landscape, street, building, room, as well as the fundamental elements of a column, door, window, ornament, chair, door handle and right down to product and object. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Describe a range of significant historical design ideas, practices and sites within their social, cultural, environmental and technological contexts.
Apply reasoned enquiry and discovery through research, analysis, critique and reflection.
Communicate effectively and persuasively in varied modes, including textual and visual.
Identify relationships between historical design approaches and contemporary design challenges.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Communication in the Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course will give you the tools and techniques to communicate your designs, ideas and concepts. You are introduced to methods of communicating from conceptual design through to design resolution. The course exposes you to a wide range of styles and mediums for communication ranging from the technical to the experimental. Through a series of projects you are encouraged to explore this range of communication styles and to embed your own personal style within the work. This course teaches both analogue and digital skills, encouraging you to oscillate between them to explore different ways of designing and communicating. Upon completion, you will have been exposed to drawing, modelling and presentation skills that form the foundation of how you will communicate your ideas, process and designs throughout your degree and into practice. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Curate exemplars of work produced throughout the course and methods of representation that best communicate the process and intent of production.
Construct digital and analogue 3D models to explore form and convey design intent.
Apply the principles of orthographic drawings across a range of scales, projects and applications.
Use appropriate visual media and language to communicate design process, proposals and technical information.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Architectural Composition and Modelling
syllabus_overview: This course builds on capabilities and skills from DPDE1002 - Communication in the Built Environment to develop a further range of communication skills specific to Design, Architecture and Computational Design. You will explore intermediate analogue and intermediate-advanced digital representation techniques in a suite of software with a digital and physical output. Emphasis will be placed on an iterative, theoretical and practical approach to making as a means of spatial exploration, research and articulation of design environments. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design proposal persuasively.
Create a design proposal using analogue making techniques and 3D digital software.
Apply design theory to the design process.
Translate verbal and written ideas into visual design work.
Formulate design drawing set using 3D software applying technical drawing conventions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DPDE1002
Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Practical Design Studio 2
syllabus_overview: “When I’m working on a problem, I never think about its beauty, I just think about how to solve the problem, but when I finish it, if the solution is not beautiful, I know it’s wrong.” - Buckminster Fuller cited in Darling, David J. (2004). The Universal Book of Mathematics . John Wiley and Sons, Page 34. The Built Environment is made up of a range of disciplines, each of which has a particular focus. However, it is common to work across or to collaborate with multiple disciplines. This studio asks you to design a range of interventions, beginning with an object, then a building and finally designing a landscape response. You are encouraged to think creatively about how you integrate your interventions with the existing site and the surrounding context. Each intervention should address challenges and opportunities identified through a thorough site analysis to create a design response that is functional, beautiful and enhances the site. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Communicate ideas, process and understanding through a range of 2D and 3D representational techniques and persuasive oral presentation.
Analyse the spatial, historical, political, environmental, material, and contextual forces that influence the site and brief.
Interrogate design methods using appropriate precedent, program and systems studies.
Develop interventions through an iterative design process that engages with context, site, and user experience.
Explain material selection, fabrication techniques, and processes.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: DPDE1001 and DPDE1005
Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Building Environments and Technics 1
syllabus_overview: Building Environments and Technics 1 is an introduction to the structural, constructional and physical principles of the built environment. The course will investigate the significance of building materials and the perception of spaces in relation to their use along with the construction of primary building elements including foundations, floors, walls, openings, roofs and stairs and their application to the built environment. The interface between architecture and interior will be explored through the principles of structure, substrate and skin with a particular emphasis on the role of materiality in construction and fabrication technologies. You will learn to read and produce documentation and models of a technical level of execution and accuracy in line with industry standards. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Identify the fundamental construction technologies and primary building components of the built environment and the interface with the human scale.
Communicate construction, structure and material application through technical drawings, specification sheets and model making.
Evaluate the importance of sustainable practice through construction and fabrication methods, material selection, environmental performance and human interaction with the built environment.
Apply fundamental construction, structural and material principles to a simple design brief.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Architectural Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the design strategies and scientific understanding needed to minimize buildings’ impact on natural resources and the environment. It includes life-cycle thinking in architectural design, a history of environmental design concepts in architecture, understanding and responding to climate, design innovation, solar architecture, building fabric performance and wind, ventilation, and cooling. In completing the course, you will master the basic techniques to reduce building-related carbon emissions and enhance human comfort through climate-sensitive design. In addition, you will gain the ability to analyze climatic and geomorphological context to optimize building design for sun, temperature, wind, human metabolism, and perception. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Design architecture that integrates relevant environmental design strategies, systems and technologies considering climate, thermal comfort, materials, and energy use.
Explain current scientific view of how nature works and relate this to building.
Analyse the characteristics of climate and demonstrate how a building may be planned and constructed to take advantage of that climate to assure the comfort of its occupants.
Explain the basic regulations and standards that govern environmental performance in buildings in Australia.
Evaluate the lifecycle environmental performance of domestic architecture in the Australian context.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives builds on your foundational study in DPDE1003 Design History and Theory 1. The course focuses on interior space as a site of dwelling and introduces you to historical, cultural and theoretical perspectives on the concept of dwelling and its material constructions. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Describe various concepts of dwelling within historical and cultural contexts.
Apply the principles of scholarly enquiry in the form of an independent research task.
Evaluate the ways in which research can inform interior architecture practice.
Communicate the outcomes of research through a combination of verbal, visual and the written form.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.
Prerequisite: DPDE1003

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio
syllabus_overview: In this course you will explore the creative processes that are specific to the design of products in Industrial Design and prepare for entry into the Industrial Design program. In this studio-based course, you will build upon your previous studies of 2D and 3D design, hand sketching, hand modelling and computer aided drawing and modelling. You will develop new skills as you embark upon product design projects. These projects guide you through the generation and expression of original product ideas in response to a design brief and present these using visual communication and model making techniques. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Develop and communicate an original idea using two-dimensional drawing and three-dimensional model making techniques for Industrial Design.
Demonstrate competency and fluency in the Industrial Design processes of research, iteration, reflection and refinement.
Use effectively materials and fabrication techniques in product design.
Select and apply elements and principles of design in two and three dimensions.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.
Prerequisite: DPDE1001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Landscape Architecture and Analysis
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the concept of landscapes as inter-related processes and systems. It focusses on the human, biotic and abiotic characteristics of landscapes in urban and non-urban settings. You will focus on plants and their role in ecology and landscape architecture through a design and botanical classification. You develop a vocabulary of planting elements and an ability to design with plants to achieve specific spatial qualities. By analyzing small-scale planting designs and developing a personal herbarium, you lay down the foundation of horticultural knowledge and develop skills in planting design and design communication. This course includes two field trips within the Sydney Region. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate your observations, analysis and proposals using a range of representational techniques.
Classify plant species according to their botanical and design features and their role in ecological communities.
Formulate and develop design strategies using plant material in evocative and ethically appropriate ways.
Interpret the key attributes and inter-relationships of landscape systems.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Technologies and Computational Design
syllabus_overview: Digital Technologies develops your abilities for applying technical and theoretical skills through computational design workflows and processes. You will develop and apply skills in text and visual programming languages to critically analyze complex conditions, while synthesizing computational design thinking knowledge and methods for solving built environment challenges. Theoretical knowledge will be introduced falling under the following categories: Morphology, Algorithmic Form, Emergence, and Systems. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain computational design thinking knowledge and methods for the built environment challenges.
Apply skills in a text-based programming language.
Critically analyse built environmental conditions through visual programming language interfaces.
Apply advanced skills in a visual programming language interface.
Demonstrate relevant verbal and multimedia communication skills.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7006 UNSW Diploma in Architecture Program.
Prerequisite: DPDE1001 and DPDE1005.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Communication and Academic Literacy 1
syllabus_overview: This course is the FIRST in a series of three skills-based Communication and Academic Literacy courses available over three terms in Diploma programs 7001 and 7002: DPGE1001 - Communication and Academic Literacy 1 (4UOC) DPGE1002 - Communication and Academic Literacy 2 (1UOC) DPGE1003 - Communication and Academic Literacy 3 (1UOC) This series is designed to equip learners with the academic literacy and communication skills they require to succeed in their tertiary studies. It is intended for undergraduate students who have met IELTS requirements (or equivalent) and have been admitted to a UNSW Diploma Program. Course materials are based on topics and issues which reflect the variety of disciplines students will go on to pursue as part of their future courses of study. Authentic tertiary input and resources are used where appropriate to ensure that learning activities are relevant and meaningful. The themes selected as the context for the learning activities reflect broad topics which may be studied from a variety of disciplinary perspectives. The focus includes macro-language skills in combination with essential academic sub-skills such as information literacy, information synthesis, and discourse management. Learners are engaged in practical task-oriented activities and assessment tasks. They are encouraged to analyse ideas, evaluate claims, and search for answers to self-generated questions. institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Public Relations and Advertising Foundations
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to Public Relations and Advertising Principles in an Australian and international context. You will examine the history, growth, and contemporary influence of both disciplines. The foundations of PR and advertising are studied, as are their influence within and outside organisations, and the linkages both disciplines have in the “communications mix”. You will be able to understand the similarity and difference between PR and advertising in relation to communication strategy, research, media relations, industry, and professional pathways. You will also gain an appreciation of the ethical dimensions and issues in allied communication disciplines. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Determine what makes for an effective communications plan.
Analyse local and international PR/Advertising campaigns.
Recognize and contrast the fundamental natures of PR and advertising, including theories, contemporary practice in a wide variety of arenas, and emerging trends.
Apply key concepts of publics/audiences, relationships and promotion.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Journalistic Voices and Values
syllabus_overview: Journalism is facing challenges on multiple fronts. Even prestigious outlets are accused of disseminating ‘fake news’ and grossly biased coverage, as the very notion of ‘factual’ reporting is questioned. Individuals implicated in alleged scandals turn to the courts to prevent exposure or to win large payouts for defamation. Journalism in the public interest risks being overwhelmed by ‘click-bait’ and the sensationalist coverage of celebrity lives. In this course you will track, analyse, and produce your own journalism about such issues and controversies. You will deal with debates around the laws applying to news coverage, journalistic ethical values and journalism’s social role, rights, and responsibilities. In the multimedia journalistic pieces you produce, you will have the opportunity to explore issues around diversity in who is given a voice in news coverage, whose issues, concerns and experiences are deemed worthy of attention, and whose views and perspectives journalists choose to report. Through a deeper understanding of voices and values, you will also learn how ‘accountable’ journalism has been meeting these types of challenges and how journalism as a 'public good' may thrive into the future. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Situate current journalistic practices in relevant social, institutional, and ethical settings.
Demonstrate knowledge of current media law and debates around journalistic ethics, principles, and practices.
Effectively apply theories around journalistic principles and practices, via the production of journalistic pieces which analyse and critically assess current wider media reporting.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: News Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: This course develops skills in the practice of news reporting as it operates widely across different domains of journalism. You will develop skills not only in the reporting of current-affairs and sports news as traditionally undertaken by newspapers and broadcast news departments, but also in the reporting of news in, for example, music, arts, travel, fashion and motoring journalism. The course will focus on skills associated with all stages of the news reporting process, and you will develop your knowledge of how potential news items are selected, how journalists manage relationships with “contacts” and how they conduct interviews. Obviously, there will also be a focus on news writing itself – the verbal styles and structures employed in news reporting of different types, and the skills required to distil sometimes complex material into a form which will attract and hold the attention of casual readers. Basic photojournalistic skills will also be covered. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Enact the social relationships and interactions involved in the news gathering and filtering process
Critically evaluate journalistic news reporting practices and the communicative functionality of news reporting texts
Apply skills in conceiving, researching and producing news reports across a range of different journalistic contexts
Understand and apply industry requirements for journalistic skills and attributes
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Film Studies
syllabus_overview: In this course you will learn essential techniques and vocabulary for analyzing, explaining and interpreting fictional and documentary films. These skills may also be applied to other audio-visual media. You will learn to recognize and apply specialized film studies terminology by closely studying films drawn from a range of contexts and historical periods. The content and design of this course has been developed to allow you to gain a broad appreciation of a variety of methodological approaches to studying film as a specific discipline. Films and reading material have been selected to provide you with a sense of the historical and cultural variability of film as an expressive medium and to expose you to different ways of watching, thinking and writing about film. The films you watch will convey the richness and diversity of cinema as a form of both popular entertainment and art. They have been carefully selected to challenge, entertain and, in some cases, deliberately frustrate your expectations regarding ‘good cinema’. After completing the course, you will possess a greater appreciation of film as a medium and a better understanding of how film style shapes meaning and the viewer experience. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and apply specialised film terminology to analyse and evaluate film texts.
Demonstrate effective application of relevant communication practices to convey the value of film as a medium of expression.
Analyse, describe and interpret films via practices of close viewing and taking into account the specificities of the film medium.
Explain how elements of film style work together with contextual factors to shape meaning and create an experience for the viewer.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Screen Production 1
syllabus_overview: In today's media rich world, we find a vast array of storytelling practices. From Facebook timelines to viral videos, news stories and advertisements, a complex range of narrative strategies are used to organize fragmentary images, sounds and memories into meaningful content. In this course you will be introduced to fundamental concepts and techniques of narrative style and structure appropriate to a range of media production environments. The course emphasizes the development of hands-on production skills and you will gain proficiency in the use of audio-visual equipment and editing software in preparation for more advanced study in screen and sound production. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Identify and implement the fundamental elements and techniques of storytelling in media rich environments.
Work collaboratively in a manner that is ethical, safe, and mindful of industry standards of best practice.
Link creative production with theoretical and critical knowledge.
Plan, shoot and produce short audio-visual stories.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Entrepreneurship
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurship is a central component of economic activity and this has never been truer than in the current industrial climate of ongoing change and disruption. In this course, you will work hands-on to develop your own original idea for a start-up to develop the drive, initiative, knowledge, and skills required of contemporary media entrepreneurship. Working independently, in teams, much of this course will focus on developing your own entrepreneurial projects to solve a campus-based problem for a niche market made up of students. We will explore and apply the principles of lean start-up and the design thinking process to develop and pitch a start-up idea. You will learn and experience essential media and communication skills involved with entrepreneurialism, including web site building, explainer video production, interviewing, pitching, as well as how to transform failure into success through iterative processes. Needless to say, these are critical skills for success for all types of careers in the media sector, which has also been profoundly affected by continuous change and digital disruption. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students .
learning_outcomes: Explain the central role played by entrepreneurship in an era of rapid and ongoing industry change and digital disruption.
Devise, launch, test, and iterate an original idea for a new start-up.
Critically examine and apply approaches from lean start-up and design thinking.
Apply critical entrepreneurial skills including pitch deck design, website building, explainer video production, user/customer/stakeholder interviewing, assumption-testing, and pitching.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Media, Society and Politics
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the complex relationship between media, society and politics by examining the ways in which information is mediated between social, cultural and political institutions. It develops a conceptual framework from which to analyse the dynamic technological and regulatory environment in which the media operates and to investigate the consequences of changes in these areas for media practitioners, politicians and ordinary citizens. Topics covered include but are not limited to media ownership and regulation; the media and society; the media and politics; the media and social movements; the politics of spin; censorship, freedom of speech/press; new media and democracy; global media and global politics. Australian cases and their comparison with other national/global material will be used throughout. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capacity to develop competencies and skills in communication, creative use of digital tools, and critical thinking and research - which are essential transferable skills required in the media/communications sector.
Apply Media Studies approaches and concepts to real world contexts to gain productive insights on the relationship between media, society and politics.
Identify the different dynamics, tensions and dimensions of various Media Studies frameworks to form a foundational map of different conceptual approaches in the field.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data in our World
syllabus_overview: Data and its rhetoric are all around us. The ways in which we imagine data as well as the data objects themselves have a profound impact on the ways in which the world is organised, how resources are distributed, how we understand recent events and what we come to know as “fact” versus mere “opinion”. In this course you will learn to both produce and critically analyse data objects. In addition to practicing data extraction, analysis and visualisation, you will learn how to evaluate the multiple examples of data that you encounter “in the wild” – data that are used by the media, by governments and civil society to explain and organise the world around you. By the end of the course, you will have gained a solid introduction to the processes involved in working with data and an ability to reflect on current debates about the impact of data on society. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Situate data in relation to settler colonialism and engage with First Nations approaches to data and justice.
Identify, analyse, and communicate data critically, creatively, and ethically.
Contextualise and evaluate current debates regarding the impact of data on society, politics, and identity.
Evaluate data and data processes in relation to social, political, material, and theoretical contexts.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 7005 UNSW Diploma in Media and Communication Program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematics 1A
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with a good working knowledge of Calculus and Linear Algebra, and will show you how these topics can be applied in interdisciplinary contexts. You will see analytical thinking and problem solving demonstrated in lectures, and you will have an opportunity to develop your own analytical thinking and problem solving skills in tutorial classes. This course will enhance your ability to solve problems using logical arguments and techniques, which are generic skills that can be applied in multidisciplinary work. The course will also engage you in independent and reflective learning through your homework problems and the Maple computing package. You are encouraged to develop your communication skills through active participation in tutorials, and by writing clear, logical arguments when solving problems. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain how a theorem relates to specific examples (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Use mathematical and other terminology appropriately to communicate information and understanding (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
State and prove appropriate theorems (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Prove specific and general results given specified assumptions (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Apply the concepts and techniques of the syllabus to solve appropriate problems (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
State definitions as specified in the syllabus (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematics 1B
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with a good working knowledge of Calculus and Linear Algebra, and it will show you how these topics can be applied in interdisciplinary contexts. The illustrative examples used in lectures and the problem based tutorial classes will help you to further develop and improve your analytical thinking and problem solving skills. Based on logical arguments and specific techniques, these problem solving skills are generic and can be applied in multidisciplinary work. The course will also encourage you to develop your communication skills through active participation in tutorials, and by writing clear, logical arguments when solving problems. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain how a theorem relates to specific examples (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Use mathematical and other terminology appropriately to communicate information and understanding (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
State definitions as specified in the syllabus (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Apply the concepts and techniques of the syllabus to solve appropriate problems (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
Prove specific and general results given specified assumptions (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
State and prove appropriate theorems (and use symbolic computing package Maple, where appropriate).
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) and prerequisite DPST1013

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Mathematics B
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with a basic working knowledge of Calculus and will show you how these topics can be applied in interdisciplinary contexts. You will see analytical thinking and problem solving demonstrated in lectures, and you will have an opportunity to develop your own analytical thinking and problem solving skills in tutorial classes. This course will enhance your ability to solve problems using logical arguments and techniques, which are generic skills that can be applied in multidisciplinary work. The course will also engage you in independent and reflective learning through your homework problems. You are encouraged to develop your communication skills through active participation in tutorials, and by writing clear, logical arguments when solving problems. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Use mathematical and other terminology appropriately to communicate information and understanding.
Recall and apply basic definitions.
Use appropriate results and theorems.
Apply the concepts and methods of the course to solve a variety of problems.
Explain how certain results relate to specific examples.
Verify specific and general results given specified assumptions.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Physics 1A
syllabus_overview: This course builds on an elementary knowledge of physics (Year 12 physics and Mathematics Extension 1, or equivalent). Students will develop their ability to use mathematics and fundamental physical concepts to solve problems related to the world around them. It is a calculus based course where concepts and principles are learned in context, by example, and then developed through problem solving. Throughout the course, the skills of problem solving are refined by knowing when and how to apply the principles of physics, mathematics and other relevant tools. This course is examined at two levels, with Physics 1A being the lower level. There are no pre-requisites but there is assumed knowledge of Year 12 Physics (or equivalent) and Mathematics Extension1 (or equivalent) and a co-requisite mathematics course has to be taken, which can be either Mathematics 1A (DPST1013) OR Fundamentals of Mathematics B (DPST1012). Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Write down and solve equations describing wave motion, and use these equations to explain physical phenomena such as (but not limited to) standing waves and interference.
Analyse problems involving friction and the forces and deformations described by Hooke's law.
Recognise that physics is an experimental science, plan and conduct experiments and analyse the outcomes, and include reliable estimates of uncertainties in measurements.
Analyse motion in two dimensions using vectors. Apply Newton’s laws of motion to objects undergoing uniform translational or rotational acceleration.

Recognise and solve problems relating to different thermodynamic processes, including adiabatic, isothermal, isobaric and isovolumetric processes. For cyclic processes, calculate changes in internal energy, work done and heat transferred in cycles.
Explain how energy conservation is related to the first law of thermodynamics. Apply the first law to solve problems.
Apply the conservation laws of momentum and energy to solve mechanics problems, including problems involving collisions, extended objects and their centres of mass.
Apply the law of universal gravitation and Kepler’s laws in combination with other laws covered in this course to describe, predict and explain the motion of satellites, planets, stars and galaxies.
Identify physical systems that can be understood using models of simple harmonic oscillation and write down equations to describe this motion.
Describe different heat transfer mechanisms and calculate the amount of heat transferred in different processes.
Explain the difference between kinetic and potential energy and use the law of conservation of energy and the work-energy theorem to solve mechanics problems.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) and corequisite DPST1013 or DPST1012

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Higher Physics 1A
syllabus_overview: This course builds on an elementary knowledge of physics (Year 12 physics or equivalent). Students will develop their ability to use mathematics and fundamental physical concepts to solve problems related to the world around them. It is a calculus based course where concepts and principles are learned in context, by example, and then developed through practice solving problems. Throughout the course, the skills of problem solving are refined by knowing when and how to apply the principles of physics, mathematics and other relevant tools. There are no pre-requisites but there is assumed knowledge of Year 12 Physics (or equivalent) and Mathematics Extension1 (or equivalent) and a co-requisite mathematics course has to be taken, which can be either Mathematics 1A (DPST1013) OR Fundamentals of Mathematics B (DPST1012). Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Interpret problems involving areas of physics from syllabus.
Analyse and quantify problems, invoking appropriate principles and interpret the solutions.
Conduct experimental investigations and record accurate measurements.
Analyse experimental results, test hypotheses and discuss their implications.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) and corequisite DPST1013 or DPST1012

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Higher Physics 1B
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the physics learnt in the prerequisite course DPST1023 to further develop an understanding of the mathematical description of the laws of nature and use that understanding to solve problems. It is a calculus based course where concepts and principles are learned in context, by example, and then by development. Throughout the course, the skills of problem solving are refined by knowing when and how to apply the principles of physics, mathematics and other relevant tools. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Analyse experimental results, test hypotheses and discuss their implications.
Interpret problems involving areas of physics from syllabus.
Design and plan an experimental investigations and record accurate measurements.
Analyse and quantify problems, invoking appropriate principles and interpret the solutions.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) prerequisite DPST1023 OR a credit (≥65%) in DPST1021 and corequisite DPST1014

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Physics 1B
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the physics learnt in the prerequisite course DPST1021 to further develop an understanding of the mathematical description of the laws of nature and use that understanding to solve problems. It is a calculus based course where concepts and principles are learned in context, by example, and then developed through problem solving. Throughout the course, the skills of problem solving are refined by knowing when and how to apply the principles of physics, mathematics and other relevant tools. This course is examined at two levels, with Physics 1B being the lower level. Students must pass the course DPST1021 or DPST1023 to be eligible for this course. Students must also enrol in DPST1014 which is a co-requisite or have previously completed the course. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Use equations to describe and explain properties of electromagnetic waves (such as wavelength, frequency, intensity, power and radiation pressure) and relate these to electric and magnetic fields and the speed of light.
Describe and explain the physics relating modern devices and technologies including semiconductors, transistors, LEDs and solar cells.
Discuss and explain (qualitatively and quantitatively) the key observations and events that led to the development of quantum mechanics.
Be able to state the definition of capacitance and use this definition with equations for electric field and voltages to calculate the capacitance of different geometries.

Calculate the electrostatic and magnetic fields produced by moving charges in a variety of configurations using the Laws of Biot-Savart and Ampère. Relate electric and magnetic fields using Faraday’s law; use this to calculate induced currents and voltages.
Be able to state the Schrödinger equation and use it to calculate energy levels in the simple case for a particle in a box.

Recognise that physics is an experimental science, have skills to plan and conduct experiments and analyse the outcomes and present the results in a variety of formats, include reliable estimates of the uncertainty in measurements.

Relate emission and absorption spectra to the energy change of electrons between states in an atom, calculate the energy levels of electrons in Hydrogen like atoms, relate this to quantum mechanical laws.
Use equations and diagrams to solve advanced problems about electromagnetic waves related to polarisation, interference and diffraction.

Use Coloumb’s law and Gauss’s law to calculate electric fields for configurations of charges, use these electric fields to calculate electric potentials. Compare and contrast electric fields to gravitational fields covered in Physics 1A.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004), prerequisite DPST1021 OR DPST1023 and corequisite DPST1014

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Chemistry B: Elements, Compounds and Life
syllabus_overview: DPST1032 deals with a range of fundamental concepts that can be used to explain various phenomena in chemistry, biology and material science. It enables students to further develop their knowledge of Chemistry and examines a diverse range of molecules and their reactions, focusing on applications such as drug development, functional materials, environmental chemistry, and renewable energies. A key part of chemistry is to study the speed of chemical reactions providing a strong foundation for material covered later in the course. The course introduces modern structure determination methods and the concepts of stereochemistry, which are important in understanding the shape and structure of chemicals. The next section of the course provides an introduction to modern inorganic chemistry and use of the Periodic Table as a powerful predictive tool. Important foci are the chemistries of main-group and transition metals. Transition metal compounds, d-element electron configuration and the reaction mechanisms exhibited by transition metal chemistry are discussed. The final section of the course introduces the chemistry of carbon-containing compounds and provides an introduction to the field by emphasising the reaction mechanisms that provide insight into how reactions of these molecules proceed. Students are introduced to a range of chemical reactions that enable the preparation of new molecules starting from readily available materials. The course concludes with a summary of how these concepts are applicable to the chemistry of amino acids, peptides and proteins. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Predict the stereochemistry of molecular structures and analyse spectral data to determine molecular structure.
Apply theory and laws to predict properties and behaviour of chemical substances.
Gather, analyse, and interpret data from first-hand scientific investigations to draw valid conclusions.
Demonstrate proficiency in defined core chemistry laboratory skills by safely investigating chemical reactions in first-hand scientific investigations.
Apply your knowledge of organic functional groups to predict the products of chemical reactions of carbon compounds.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) and DPST1031

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Chemistry A: Atoms, Molecules, and Energy
syllabus_overview: This course builds on an elementary knowledge of chemistry (high school chemistry or equivalent) to explore the quantum mechanical structure of atoms leading to an understanding of the periodic trends in the properties of the elements. This knowledge is applied to understanding chemical bonding and intermolecular forces which together are responsible for determining the properties of materials. General principles of chemical equilibrium are developed and applied to chemical reactions involving acids and bases. The applications of the laws of Thermodynamics to chemical processes are described and ultimately linked to chemical equilibrium. The course concludes with an overview of chemical reactions involving electron transfer, including their applications in biology, corrosion and energy storage for portable electronic devices. Note: Assumed knowledge equivalent to year 12 chemistry.
learning_outcomes: Apply the language of chemistry to the naming and formulae of chemical substances and to chemical equations.
Gather, analyse, and interpret data from first-hand scientific investigations to draw valid conclusions.
Apply theory and laws to predict properties and behaviour of chemical substances.
Demonstrate proficiency in defined core chemistry laboratory skills by safely investigating chemical reactions in first-hand scientific investigations.
Perform calculations to quantify substances relating to chemical reactions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evolutionary and Functional Biology
syllabus_overview: This course examines the evolutionary history of life on Earth from origins to humans and the relationship between environment, adaptation and function. Animal (particularly human) and plant physiology are covered with an emphasis placed on adaptation in the Australian context. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept of evolution and the evolutionary processes responsible for the past and present diversity of life on Earth using evidence from the fossil record and living world.
Identify and classify living organisms into higher order evolutionary groupings.
Gather, analyse and interpret data from first-hand scientific investigations to draw valid conclusions.
Relate plant and animal anatomy, physiology and reproduction to function, adaptation and environment.

Demonstrate proficiency in fundamental biological laboratory skills (such as microscopy, biological drawing, dissection, tissue sectioning and staining, and microscope slide preparation) through first-hand scientific investigations.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Molecules, Cells and Genes
syllabus_overview: This course is concerned with the basic characteristics of all life. The chemistry of life is examined, with emphasis on the ways in which living things construct and break down macromolecules. The way in which the genetic code controls these processes depends to a great extent on the structure and function of cell components, and cell biology is a major component of the course. The final topic is genetics - the way in which the genetic code is inherited and the ways in which it can be modified. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Outline the key concepts of metabolism, the consumption and generation of energy by living cells.
Practise the skills of scientific thinking, including how to decide what is true or plausible, and how scientists communicate.
Describe the principle types of living cells, the key components of cell structure, their functions, and how they relate to each other.

Outline the key concepts of modern genetics, including what genes are, how they are regulated, how genetic information is transmitted and how modern molecular biology can use genetics to understand biology.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Biomolecular Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the application of molecular and cellular biology to the fields of medicine, plant and animal science, food science, as well as marine and environmental sciences. It draws comparisons between contemporary and conventional technologies through the introduction of traditional and recombinant genetics, microbiology, biochemistry and fermentation engineering in the context of their contribution to the industrial application of biological systems. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Communicate scientific ideas and discoveries in biomolecular sciences, to the industrial, scientific and the general communities, using the written and spoken word as well as electronic media.

Identify inconsistencies in scientific thought and writing through an understanding of the relevant literature and the correct use of references to support arguments and hypotheses. Further, you will demonstrate an awareness of the ethical issues and an understanding of the issues surrounding plagiarism.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the interdisciplinary and rapidly changing nature of biomolecular sciences.
Demonstrate good laboratory skills, such as the ability to work safely and effectively in a laboratory, utilising relevant equipment, making use of protocols, manuals and safe operating procedures.
Pose questions, design experiments and interpret the resultant experimental data with respect to the literature.
Demonstrate a good understanding of the fundamental and key principles of modern molecular biology.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design in Application of Materials in Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: The design and selection of materials for applications in industry and society requires an in-depth knowledge of the structures, properties and availability of materials. This course will introduce students to the microstructures and structure-property relationships of the main types of engineering materials (metals, ceramics, polymers and composites), micromechanisms of elastic and plastic deformation, fracture mechanisms for ductile, brittle, creep and fatigue modes of failure in service, phase equilibria of alloys, and the properties and applications to commercial engineering materials. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain the different types of deformation that can occur in materials under applied loads and relate the deformation to the atomic structure.
Explain different ways that materials may fail under applied loads and the circumstances in which each failure mechanism is most likely.
Understand the context of materials science and engineering in design and applications within society.
Communicate the above using a range of media.
Describe basic property-structure relationships in materials.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Engineering Design and Innovation
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will experience first-hand one of the major things that engineers do: designing and building creative solutions to problems. They will learn to think the way that engineers think, coming up with good solutions to problems despite being limited by budget, time and resources, the requirement to also meet environmental and social objectives and of course the limitations of the laws of physics. This will help them to appreciate the central ideas of engineering design as an on-time, on-budget and fit for purpose solution to a poorly specified, open-ended problem. They will be assigned to a team to work over a ten week period to solve a practical problem. The project on offer will change from year to year. In doing all this they will start to build key skills for engineers that will be called upon repeatedly in their academic and professional lives, including concept development, critical thinking and evaluation skills, clear communication, research and information literacy skills and the skills involved in successfully functioning within a team environment to complete a given task. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the process of engineering design and the use of design methods for: Defining an open-ended design problem; Generating alternative and innovative conceptual solutions; and Evaluating these solutions.

Familiarity with the tangible elements of design within a specific engineering discipline: Demonstrate the effective use of the tools, equipment, and materials of the specific discipline; and Recognise some basic engineering materials, devices and mechanisms which form the “building blocks” of much of the world’s machinery, circuitry, and engineering systems in general.
Understand the basic elements of project management and be able to plan and schedule work activities in accordance with standard practice, including organising, conducting and recording meetings.
Understand the dynamics of collaborative teams and how to work effectively within a team to accomplish tasks within given deadlines.
Convey your thoughts and ideas effectively in an engineering design report.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the roles and responsibilities of a professional engineer, particularly as they relate to quality, safety, diversity and equal opportunity.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Mechanics 1
syllabus_overview: This is your first course in Engineering Mechanics, which is the study of the interaction of matter and forces in engineering contexts. It is evident that all objects in the world around us are composed of matter, and they are all subject to forces. As such, Engineering Mechanics is the foundational tool for engineers, and forms the underlying basis for understanding more advanced fields such as Solid Mechanics, Fluid Dynamics, Rigid Body Dynamics, Aerodynamics, Structures, Control and many aspects of Advanced Design. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to communicate clearly and precisely about technical matters related to Engineering Mechanics.
Accomplish hands on tasks that require the application of knowledge of Engineering Mechanics.
Discern the relevant principles that must be applied to describe the equilibrium or motion of engineering systems and discriminate between relevant and irrelevant information in the context.

Explain, describe and apply principles and components of Engineering Mechanics. Principles and components include: vectors, forces, torques, mass and inertia, particles and rigid bodies in two dimensions, equilibrium conditions, linear momentum and impact, kinetic and potential energy and internal forces and bending moments in beams.

Define engineering systems in a mechanically useful way and describe their equilibrium or motion in mathematical and graphical fashion and be able to relate this description to the principles of engineering mechanics.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004), DPST1013 and DPST1021 OR DPST1023

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Electrical Circuit Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to science and engineering electrical circuits. Examples of electrical and electronic devices, circuits, analogue and digital systems, and fundamental tools for their analysis. Analogue circuit analysis. Digital electronics and combinatorial logic. Analysis of DC, AC and first-order transient circuits and signals. Introductions to ideal transformer and operational amplifier behaviour. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Solve simple first order transient circuits.
Reflect a basic understanding of transformer operation, through analysis of transformer circuits.
Apply simple steady state sinusoidal analysis to circuits, and demonstrate a basic understanding of phasors and phasor diagrams for AC circuit analysis.
Demonstrate basic proficiency in building basic electrical circuits and operating fundamental electrical engineering equipment.
Analyse ideal operational amplifier application circuits.
Use Kirchhoff’s laws, node voltage and mesh current methodologies and circuit theorems to solve simple DC as well as AC circuits.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Programming
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the basics of programming. Topics covered include fundamental programming concepts, the C programming language and use of a C compiler, programming style, programming design and organisation concepts, as well as programming testing and debugging. The course does not assume any previous programming experience. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Use Linux and Unix-like operating systems to develop and test software.
Given a problem, solve it by proficiently constructing (designing, testing, debugging) a secure, reliable reliable and correct C program.
Understand the core syntax and semantics of the C programming language including types I/O, arrays, functions, pointers, structs, file manipulation and dynamic memory allocation.
Understand and employ fundamental data structures, including stacks, queues, linked lists and binary trees.
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computer Systems Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: This course provides a programmer's view on how a computer system executes programs, manipulates data and communicates. It enables students to become effective programmers in dealing with issues of performance, portability, and robustness. The course assumes that students have completed the first course in programming in the C programming language, course DPST1091. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Explain how the major components of a CPU work together, including how data (including instructions) is represented in a computer
Explain how input/output operations are implemented, and describe some basic I/O devices
Implement simple programs involving inter-process communication and concurrency
Design, implement and analyse small programs at the assembly/machine level

Describe the relationship between high-level procedural languages (e.g., C) and assembly/machine language in the conventional machine layer, including how a compiled program is executed in a classical von Neumann machine
Describe the components comprising and the services offered by an operating system
Describe the layers of architectures in modern computer systems from hardware device levels upwards
Describe the principles of memory management and explain the workings of a system with virtual memory management
prerequisites: UNSW Diplomas only (7001, 7002, 7003, 7004) and DPST1091

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Software Engineering Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: This course teaches students about software engineering principles via exposure to the important practice of building correct products in effectively functioning teams. Students will be exposed to agile software practices, team collaboration and effective communication through implementing a group project based on agile software methodologies that requires them to analyse, design, build and deploy a web-based application. This course is typically taken soon after completing DPST1091 but could be delayed and taken later. DPST1093 provides essential background for the teamwork and project management required in many later courses. Course outline information is accessible via Moodle for enrolled students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how to use version control, continuous integration, and deployment tooling to sustainably integrate code from multiple parties.
Understand key characteristics of a functioning team in terms of understanding professional expectations, maintaining healthy relationships, and managing conflict.
Demonstrate effective use of static testing, dynamic testing, and user testing to validate and verify software systems.

Understand the software engineering life cycle in the context of modern and iterative software development practices in order to elicit requirements, design systems thoughtfully, and implement software correctly.
Demonstrate an ability to analyse complex software systems in terms of their data model, state model, and more.
Demonstrate effective use of applying software development to build full-stack end-user applications.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: DPST1091

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconomics 1
syllabus_overview: Economics is about shaping a better world. It examines how people, businesses, and governments make decisions with limited resources, and how those choices affect society. In this course, you’ll learn to “think like an economist” and apply economic reasoning to real-world challenges like climate change, inequality, poverty, and access to healthcare and education. You’ll gain tools to evaluate policies, understand who benefits (and who doesn’t), and design solutions that create positive impact. We’ll explore questions such as: How can growth and sustainability be balanced? What policies reduce inequality and improve welfare? When do markets fail, and what can governments do? By the end of the course, you’ll not only master core concepts but also know how to use them to tackle pressing issues. Whether your path is business, policy, or global development, economics offers powerful insights for building a fairer future.
learning_outcomes: Articulate how individuals and society as a whole benefit or are harmed by economic markets.
Evaluate the costs and benefits of government policies that affect economic incentives and behaviour.
Explain the assumptions that underlie standard microeconomic models of individual and collective decision-making and behaviour in a world with limited resources.
Use basic mathematical tools to demonstrate the properties and predictions of economic models and calculate the effect of changes in economic variables.

Identify appropriate economic models (e.g., models of perfectly competitive markets and various market imperfections) and apply them to analyse and predict the behaviour of individuals and firms interacting in markets.
prerequisites: Excluded: Students in BCom single or double-degree programs, except for 3155 Actl/Comm and 3521 Comm/Econ, are not allowed to enrol in this course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconomics 1
syllabus_overview: Macroeconomics examines the behaviour and performance of the economy as a whole. This course explores how economists use models to understand the behaviour of key variables—output, employment, inflation, interest rates, and exchange rates—and how these models are evaluated with evidence. It also considers how governments, central banks, and international institutions in shaping outcomes through fiscal and monetary policy. By the end of the course, students will have a clear framework for understanding how households, businesses, and governments interact, and will be able to apply macroeconomic reasoning to real issues such as recessions, growth and sustainability, building the foundation for further study in economics and related fields.
learning_outcomes: Explain the main macroeconomic concepts.
Identify and interpret macroeconomic data.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Analyse macroeconomic models and use these models to explain the behaviour of key macroeconomic variables.
Identify current economic issues and debates and apply macroeconomic models to evaluate relevant policy issues.
prerequisites: Enrolment excluded for BCom single or dual-degree programs, except students in double 3155 Actl/Comm and double 3521 Comm/Econ programs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Elements of Environmental Economics
syllabus_overview: ​​How can economic policy address climate and environmental pressures without ignoring other vital societal goals? This course introduces environmental economics through the lenses of markets and market failure, showing why environmental problems arise and how economists evaluate solutions. You will examine policy tools such as regulation, taxes, subsidies, and pollution permit trading, and learn methods for valuing the benefits and costs of environmental protection. The course also develops foundations in microeconomic thinking for environmental decision-making and highlights the trade-offs involved in real policy choices. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to evaluate environmental policy instruments and explain their welfare and distributional implications using economic reasoning. You will gain an appreciation for the fact that the solutions to environmental problems are rarely simple and an ability to consider other perspectives and the complexities and trade-offs inherent in environmental policy decisions.​
learning_outcomes: Discuss and analyse the theoretical basis upon which the sub-discipline of environmental economics has been built.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Apply economic techniques to analyse environmental issues and relate environmental concerns to broader policy goals.
Recognise situations in which markets are likely to be inefficient and prescribe intervention tools to correct inefficiency.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Quantitative Analysis for Business and Economics
syllabus_overview: In today’s data-driven world, quantitative skills are essential for tackling real economic and business problems. From evaluating financial decisions to forecasting markets and assessing policy, this course is designed to give you these skills early, ensuring you can approach future studies and professional challenges with confidence. This course will equip you with a working knowledge of the most common analytical tools and techniques in economics and business, providing the basis for further studies. Topics include the mathematics of finance, matrix algebra, probability, calculus and optimisation. Special emphasis is put on the application of concepts and techniques to typical problems in business and economics. By the end of the course, you will know how to translate quantitative techniques into practical insights, interpret data effectively, and provide evidence-based solutions that prepare you for advanced coursework and professional applications.
learning_outcomes: Apply probability tools to solve risk and uncertainty scenarios.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Apply basic principles of financial mathematics to real-life problems.
Use matrix algebra to represent and solve systems of equations.
Formulate and solve business and economics optimisation problems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business and Economic Statistics
syllabus_overview: In today’s data-driven world, the ability to analyse and interpret information is a core skill for economists, business leaders, and decision-makers. This course provides the essential statistical toolkit for analysing data in economics, finance, accounting, marketing, and business. It emphasises practical application, using Excel to turn data into insights and support evidence-based decisions. Students will learn to summarise data, understand uncertainty, and test ideas with confidence. Topics include descriptive statistics, probability distributions, parameter estimation, hypothesis testing, and regression models. By the end of the course, students will be confident in using statistical methods to support evidence-based conclusions, a skill that is highly valued in economics, finance, accounting, marketing, and the broader field of business.
learning_outcomes: Formulate economics and business problems in analytical terms, and select and apply appropriate statistical methods to solve them.
Interpret and evaluate empirical results to draw evidence-based conclusions about economic and business phenomena.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Employ statistical tools and skills to interpret characteristics of data relevant to problems in economics and business.
Demonstrate ethical practice in data use, analysis, and reporting, including transparency and reproducibility.
prerequisites: Excluded: MATH2841, MATH2801, MATH2901, MATH2099, ACTL2002 & ACTL2131. Also, must not be enrolled in a BCom single or double degree (except 3155 Actl/Comm or 3521 Comm/Econ), or program 3715 or 3764

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Perspectives
syllabus_overview: ​​Understanding the big picture is the first step to making informed decisions. This course will empower students with economic principles and ideas that enable them to understand and debate how best to address pressing socioeconomic and political challenges. You will participate in active reflection and debate about the discipline’s approaches, objectives, and limitations, about the history of economic development, and about how economics can contribute to framing and solving current challenges. Topics include economic growth and development in the long run, the relationships between political regimes and economic growth, the economics of conflict, the origin and persistence of social and economic inequalities, the exploitation of natural resources and climate change. By the end of the course, you will be able to critically evaluate economic arguments, understand how to address real-world problems through different lenses, and apply these perspectives to contemporary policy debates and everyday decision-making.​
learning_outcomes: Describe the historical development of economics as a science.
Compare a range of different disciplinary paradigms (e.g., economic, psychological, and legal) and their relative usefulness when analysing different social problems.
Articulate the relevance of historical conceptions of economics to current socioeconomic problems and subfields of economic research.
Chart the present subfields of economic research and the main frontiers of economic understanding.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconomics 2
syllabus_overview: Decision-making by consumers, producers, and governments lies at the heart of economic analysis. It determines how scarce resources are allocated, how markets function, and how welfare is distributed across society. The first half of this microeconomics course is devoted to the study of decision-making and the modelling of associated market behaviour. We then study how individual economic decisions interact in markets with varying degrees of competition, paying substantial attention to the comparative welfare outcomes produced by different market forms. Additional topics include externalities, game theory and its applications, and asymmetric information. There is an emphasis on the use of analytical and mathematical models, which underpin much of current research in microeconomics. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply core microeconomic models to analyse decision-making and market outcomes, critically evaluate efficiency and welfare implications across market structures, and use formal tools to address issues such as externalities, strategic interaction, and information asymmetries.
learning_outcomes: Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Use appropriate mathematical techniques to construct and solve economic models; apply economic models to analyse choice problems and markets.
Construct economic arguments by appropriately selecting and applying economic concepts.
Use game theoretic tools to draw conclusions about environmental and sustainability problems arising from non-cooperative decision making among agents such as firms or countries.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconomics 2
syllabus_overview: The macroeconomy of a country is a complex network consisting of millions of interacting agents such as consumers, firms, banks, and government institutions. This course introduces students to some of the key models economists employ to understand how these entities interact to generate economic growth, the business cycle, and inflation. This course covers models of aggregate income determination in open economies; theories of aggregate economic behaviour with respect to consumption, investment, and financial transactions; balance of payments and exchange rate analysis; theories of inflation and unemployment; introductory dynamic analysis, and theories of growth and business cycles. The models will be applied to the data and used to analyse the observed growth patterns across the world. By the end of the course, you will have developed the tools, skills and knowledge base necessary to operate as a practicing macroeconomist.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Use standard models of the macroeconomy to interpret and analyse real world economic issues.
Explain the assumptions of standard models in macroeconomics.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Identify issues related to fairness and inequality in an economic context.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON1102 or COMM1150) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business and Government
syllabus_overview: ​​How do governments shape the business environment and influence the decisions of the businesses and individuals that interact in a market economy?
