This course examines the role of government intervention in the economy, including why markets left alone can fail, when intervention can be justified, and how policy choices affect societal outcomes. You ​will examine practical policy issues such as income redistribution, government-private sector interactions, and the evaluation of government programs. ​By the end of this course, you will have a firm foundation in government and policy analysis and be able to apply rigorous economic reasoning to analyse strategic interaction, policy design, and institutional choices. You will be equipped to contribute with precision and confidence to real-world policy debates.
learning_outcomes: Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Apply basic models and theory to explain the justifications for government interventions and to determine their possible effects.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Describe and explain the characteristics of various policies related to government interventions in markets.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modern Labour Markets: Theory and Policy
syllabus_overview: Labour markets shape income, employment, inequality and the way people experience economic change. This course gives you theoretical and practical tools for understanding how labour markets work and how policy affects workers, firms and broader economic outcomes. You will study labour supply and demand, wage determination, wage structures and wage differentials, labour productivity, labour mobility, discrimination, and the role of government and unions. The course also examines macro-institutional outcomes, including labour force participation and the evolution of labour markets. Drawing on international research and trends, it places particular emphasis on Australian labour market institutions, data and examples. By the end of the course, you will be able to use microeconomic models, empirical evidence and labour market data to analyse current debates in Australia and overseas.​
learning_outcomes: Analyse the structure of labour markets and frictions.
Apply econometric tools to analyse processes related to labour markets and develop a practical understanding of statistical inference issues.
Evaluate the interactions between aggregate economic forces and identify the role of firms, workers and government in the economy.
Consider the integral concepts of labour issues (e.g., unemployment, taxation, educational choice, wage differentials, discrimination) and interpret related data outputs.
Analyse labour market issues using current data.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1203 or COMM1190 or MATH1041 or MATH2801 or MATH2841 or MATH2901)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Economic Development
syllabus_overview: ​​Extreme poverty remains one of the central challenges in economic development. This course explores the causes and correlates of global poverty and investigates policies designed to improve welfare in developing countries. The course takes a microeconomic approach, focusing on individual and household behaviour and on market failures that can lead to sub-optimal choices. You will study the measurement of poverty and inequality, the roles of health and education, credit, savings and insurance constraints, migration, environmental degradation, and child labour. You will also consider how economists assess whether development interventions are likely to improve outcomes for their target populations. The course does not cover macroeconomic topics such as institutions, geography, growth, trade or liberalisation in depth. Students interested in those areas are encouraged to consider ECON3110 Development Economics, ECON3109 Economic Growth, Technology, and Structural Change, ECON3116 International Trade, and ECON3104 International Macroeconomics.​
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Examine and assess the economic incentives underlying selected cultural phenomena in developing countries.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Evaluate the causes of underdevelopment and the effectiveness of policies designed to address it.
Identify and assess the economic incentives that shape the adoption of sustainable practices in developing countries.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Game Theory and Business Strategy
syllabus_overview: Game theory is a structured way to think about strategic interactions and it is fundamental to the understanding of modern business strategy. In this course, you will be introduced to the basic tools of Game Theory and its applications to business choices. We will cover normal form and extensive form games, games of perfect and imperfect/incomplete information, and will introduce equilibrium concepts such as Nash Equilibrium, Subgame-Perfect Equilibrium and Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium. We will also look at repeated games and the theory of reputation. By the end of the course, you will not only be equipped with an understanding of the basic principles of strategic analysis but will also easily navigate the issues related to integrating ethical and sustainable considerations into the application of abstract theory to specific real-world business challenges.
learning_outcomes: Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Compute pure and mixed strategy Nash equilibria in normal form games, as well as pure and mixed subgame perfect equilibria in extensive form games.
Apply abstract theory to concrete problems demonstrating an understanding of the basic principles of strategic analysis including solution concepts.
Analyse problems and formulate strategic solutions with a focus on ethical and sustainable outcomes, utilising tools provided by the course materials.
Solve perfect information games using backwards induction.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON1101 or COMM1100) and (ECON1202, MATH1031, MATH1131, MATH1141 or MATH1151)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Experimental and Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: How do you do economics experiments "right" and why is it that "the way one does an experiment is unbelievably important", as a famous behavioural economist once noted? In this course, we will talk about the experimental method in economics—and how it differs from methods in other social sciences—and will do so by reading widely cited articles. We shall discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the experimental method relative to other empirical social science methods such as analysis of administrative data, and we will document how it can be used to explore the robustness of the "homo economicus" assumption of a rational, selfish decision-maker used in many economic models. By the end of the course, we will find that economic theory does a good job in many applications but that there are also important behavioural deviations from the model of “homo economicus”.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the appropriateness of the experimental method to study certain research questions.
Analyse ethical considerations and the influence of culture and socialisation on experimental results.
Discuss the key features of experimental design and implementation.
Describe and analyse the advantages and disadvantages of the experimental method.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1101 or COMM1100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introductory Econometrics
syllabus_overview: What can the data tell us and how can we tell apart correlation and causality? This course introduces the use of econometrics to explore and estimate economic relationships. Emphasis will be placed on cross-sectional data, and on understanding the conditions required for inferring causal relationships. We will tackle linear regression models, and give particular attention time series and panel data models, highlighting their relevance for economic analysis. Next, we will also consider extensions that address common data analysis complications, including heteroskedasticity, proxy variables, and other limitations. Practical computer-based exercises are integrated throughout, enabling students to gain hands-on experience with econometric software. By the end of the course, you will have the skills to critically interpret empirical relationships and a foundation for more advanced courses in econometrics.
learning_outcomes: Explain the assumptions underlying regression models.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Apply appropriate statistical software to analyse data and present regression analysis results.
Apply econometric models and methods to interpret and analyse real data in economics, finance and other social sciences.
Identify and assess environmental and sustainability considerations in problems in economics and business.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1203 or COMM1110 or ECON2403 or MATH1041 or MATH1231 or MATH1241 or MATH1251. It is highly recommended that students who complete COMM1110 also complete COMM1190 before enrolling in this course.

assessment_tasks.task_name: In-person - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly) - Term 1
Multimodal - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly) - Term 1
In-person - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly) - Term 3
Multimodal - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly) - Term 3

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Forecasting
syllabus_overview: In an uncertain and data-rich business environment, making accurate predictions is both essential and challenging. This course addresses how to transform data into reliable forecasts that support effective decision-making and strategic planning. It covers the practical use of econometric and statistical techniques applied in the business world. Building and evaluating forecasting models using time series data will be the focus of this course. By the end of the course, students will be able to formulate and use reliable forecasting models based on sound economic principles.
learning_outcomes: Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Explain the principles of time series analysis and forecasting.
Apply standard techniques to analyse real data and construct forecasting models.
Evaluate and interpret forecasting results.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON1203 or COMM1110 or MATH1041 or MATH1231 or MATH1241 or MATH1251. It is highly recommended that students who complete COMM1110 also complete COMM1190 before enrolling in this course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Methods
syllabus_overview: How can we critically assess the quality and evaluate the findings of research studies in social science? This course will provide an introduction to the most common empirical methods used in scholarship across the social sciences. Each topic will use a research article to illustrate different empirical methods, and also the range of topics that these methods are useful for analysing. Substantive topics will include: poverty, economic growth, public health, democracy, wage determination, and education. By the end of the course, students will be well equipped to become sophisticated consumers of empirical social science research, rather than necessarily becoming producers of that work.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Apply causal-inference tools and propose/justify an identification strategy for policy questions.
Explain and apply core statistical concepts underpinning empirical work in the social sciences.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Critically evaluate academic papers to assess their efficacy in identifying a causal effect.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: PPEC1001 AND ECON1202 AND in program 3478 or 4797

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Markets and Frictions
syllabus_overview: ​​Collusion and bargaining reveal how strategic behaviour can shape economic outcomes over time. This course provides an advanced exploration of the theoretical foundations of dynamic games and the mechanisms that drive these outcomes. Building on foundational knowledge in microeconomics and game theory, you will examine dynamic games, with a particular focus on collusion and bargaining. The course develops the analytical tools needed to understand how strategic incentives affect cooperation, negotiation and efficiency. By the end of the course, you will have a stronger foundation for analysing dynamic strategic interaction and for evaluating the economic mechanisms that sustain cooperation and determine bargaining outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Explain how markets work and gain an understanding of the impact of information on market organisation.
Critically appraise the relation between market outcomes and outcomes of non-market allocation mechanisms.
Construct logical and substantiated statements, proofs and analytical propositions​.
Analyse and critically evaluate the conceptual basis of economic efficiency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Macroeconomics
syllabus_overview: In today’s global economy, national policies and outcomes are deeply interconnected. This course introduces the core concepts and analytical tools of open-economy macroeconomics, providing a structured framework for examining how countries interact through trade, capital flows, and policy choices. It covers exchange rate determination, balance of payments, current account imbalances, international asset markets, and the role of fiscal and monetary policy in open economies. It also considers the functioning of different exchange rate regimes, the challenges of monetary unions, and the causes and consequences of international financial crises. Emphasis is placed on applying theory to contemporary issues and policy debates, enabling students to better interpret real-world events and understand the constraints and trade-offs faced by policymakers. By the end of the course, students will appreciate how global forces shape national economic outcomes and long-term growth prospects.
learning_outcomes: Discuss important policy issues and explain the role of key institutions in the international economy to evaluate policy implications.
Propose a clear and concise set of recommendations to a managerial audience.
Interpret and analyse real problems in international macroeconomics using the relevant standard models and their corresponding assumptions.
Assess the institutional implications of incorporating social, cultural, and ethical considerations of macroeconomic policy within and across countries.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Politics and Economics
syllabus_overview: When so many economic decisions are taken by political actors, understanding the economy also means understanding the interactions between politics and economics. This course covers theory, evidence and current issues at the intersection between economics and political science. Topics considered include economic theories of the state, regime changes and revolutions, voting theory, interest group politics, corruption, the democratic peace, and electoral competition. By the end of the course, you will have the skills relevant in understanding the delicate interplay between economics and politics.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate voting systems and democratic methods, critically assessing their advantages and contradictions.
Describe and analyse the effects of institutions on collective choice problems.
Explain major ideas regarding causes and effects of political corruption.
Identify and evaluate causes of collective action failure and the institutions that promote efficient outcomes.
Discuss the economic origins of dictatorship and democracy.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economics of Finance
syllabus_overview: ​​Insurance is the oldest and most widespread form of financial risk management. Life insurers and annuity providers play a central role in modern financial markets by pooling longevity, mortality, and investment risks. The economic analysis of insurance markets draws on, and enriches, core theories of asset pricing, corporate finance, industrial organisation, and public economics. This course uses the insurance sector—in particular life insurance and annuities—as a lens through which to understand financial economics. We begin with the institutional architecture of the insurance industry: products, balance sheets, data sources, and regulation. We then study how insurers price contracts. Next, we develop supply-and-demand models to analyse market outcomes in the variable annuity and life insurance markets and investigate how reinsurance and off-balance-sheet vehicles reshape risk. We conclude by examining insurers’ portfolio-choice decisions and their implications for asset prices and systemic risk.​
learning_outcomes: Explain the economic role of financial institutions, such as insurers, and the institutional structure of modern financial markets.
Analyse how financial frictions, regulatory constraints, and market power shape risk management, product pricing, and contract design.
Produce clear, professional work that synthesises economic theory and evidence.
Use empirical methods and programming tools to analyse data.
Apply financial economics and asset-pricing methods to value and interpret financial contracts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Development Economics
syllabus_overview: ​​Why do some countries grow and prosper while others remain trapped in poverty? Poverty and underdevelopment remain central global economic challenges. This course provides an in-depth exploration of competing explanations of underdevelopment and current strategies for promoting development. You will examine the roles of institutions, institutional change, markets, and policy in shaping development outcomes, with close attention to both domestic and international contexts. A key focus is the interaction between theory and evidence, including how to assess whether specific interventions are likely to improve welfare. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse major drivers of underdevelopment, assess development policies with theory and evidence, and identify credible pathways for improving outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Identify and assess institutional conditions necessary to sustain equitable development.
Analyse the economic underpinning of cultural phenomena in developing countries.
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented.
Evaluate interplay between markets, institutions and income distribution in causing and perpetuating underdevelopment and the effectiveness of various policies meant to address it.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101 and (ECON1102 or COMM1150)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Trade Theory and Policy
syllabus_overview: ​​What determines who gains and who loses in global trade and how governments should respond? International trade shapes economic growth, wages, inequality, and the success or failure of businesses. This course provides a rigorous analysis of trade theory and trade policy, supported by empirical evidence. You will study comparative advantage, technology differences, factor endowments, and economies of scale, and how these forces influence trade patterns and income distribution. And you will evaluate the effects of key policy tools and develop practical problem-solving skills for trade analysis. By the end of this course, you will be able to use trade models and empirical evidence to evaluate policy choices and their implications for key societal outcomes.​
learning_outcomes: Describe and interpret how institutions and policy affect international trade.
Describe and interpret the assumptions and structure of standard models of international trade theory and policy.
Use standard models of international trade to interpret and analyse real problems and issues in international economics.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Organisational Economics
syllabus_overview: Organisations face recurring economic problems: how to design incentives, allocate decision rights, resolve conflict and decide what to produce internally or outsource. This course studies the internal organisation of firms and other organisations using tools from game theory, information economics and contract theory. You will be introduced to foundational theories and then apply them to real-world managerial problems. The course examines why organisations arise in market economies, how organisational structures affect behaviour, and how economic models can help analyse incentives and conflict within organisations. By the end of the course, you will be able to use game-theoretic models to interpret organisational problems and evaluate alternative approaches to incentives and management.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and explain concepts related to organisational economics.
Solve game-theoretic models of organisational issues, and apply them to interpret and analyse real-world organisational problems.
Evaluate the effectiveness of different incentive schemes and organisational structures in motivating performance and resolving conflicts of interest within organisations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or ECON2112

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Organisation
syllabus_overview: What drives the behaviour of firms and industry dynamics in the modern economic landscape? This course studies the behaviour of firms and industry sectors, with a focus on competition outcomes and market dynamics. Through an exploration of market structures (including perfect competition, monopoly, and oligopoly), dynamic strategic interaction, price discrimination, product differentiation, advertising, entry and predation, it connects theoretical concepts with real-world relevance. By the end of the course, you will develop a deep understanding of the economic forces at play in real-world markets and how they come together to drive economic policy.
learning_outcomes: Identify economic problems faced by managers to assess trade-offs in decision-making.
Critically analyse model assumptions and real-world relevance.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Solve relevant theoretical models to address these problems.
Apply models to real-world issues, justifying proposed solutions with evidence and policy implications.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: ​​Standard economic theory assumes that people have correct beliefs based on correct statistical reasoning, that they are narrowly self-interested, and that they manage to maximise their utility. Decades of experimental evidence suggest a more complicated picture. People systematically misperceive probabilities, cooperate with strangers in ways that sacrifice their own material payoffs, and make choices that they themselves deem suboptimal. Explaining these empirical regularities requires new theory. In this course, students will study the core findings of behavioural economics, learn the formal theoretical frameworks developed to explain it, and build the empirical reasoning skills needed to critically evaluate competing accounts. Topics include reference-dependent preferences and prospect theory, intertemporal choice, risk preferences, bounded rationality, social preferences, behavioural game theory, and behavioural public policy. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to formulate behavioural hypotheses precisely, evaluate them using appropriate theoretical tools, and critically assess the evidence used to support or challenge them.​
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of behavioural economics and how it compares with neoclassical economics.
Critically question claims made by behavioural economists and use the tools learned in class to explain real-world phenomena.
Describe and interpret findings from behavioural economics research and how they apply to public policy.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or ECON2112

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economics of Health and Human Capital
syllabus_overview: ​​Health and human capital are central to individual well-being and economic growth. This course explores how natural, social, economic and political environments affect the accumulation and stock of health and human capital, and how health and human capital interact with one another. You will examine inequalities in health and human capital across society and consider how policy may help reduce them. The course is largely empirical. It moves beyond documenting correlations, such as relationships between in-utero pollution exposure and birth weight or class size and academic achievement, to ask how researchers can identify causal relationships. By the end of the course, you will understand key methods of causal inference in empirical research and be able to assess evidence on health, human capital and related policy questions.​
learning_outcomes: Recognise how the natural, social, economic, and political environments affect the accumulation and stock of health and human capital and the ways in which health and human capital interact with one another.
Consider ways in which policy may help reduce the considerable inequality in health and human capital across society.
Identify strengths and weaknesses and assess the overall validity of empirical studies in health, human capital, and beyond.
Articulate the importance of health and human capital to individual well-being and economic growth.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: ECON2101 and ECON2206

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Economics
syllabus_overview: ​Environmental problems are among the most important and contested policy issues. This course provides an economic perspective on those problems and on the policy tools used to address them. You will examine why environmental problems arise, why unregulated markets may fail in environmental contexts, and how economic instruments such as regulations, taxes, subsidies and pollution permit trading schemes can respond to these failures. The course also covers methods for determining the benefits and costs of environmental preservation. By the end of the course, you will be able to take part in environmental policy debates using economic reasoning and evidence.​
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the rationale of current environmental initiatives including climate change and water reform.
Analyse the theoretical basis upon which the sub-discipline has been built.
Critically review how economists attempt to measure environmental benefits, including the issue of time and discount rates in project analysis.
Recognise situations in which markets are likely to be inefficient and be able to prescribe a variety of intervention tools to correct the inefficiency.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Econometric Theory and Machine Learning
syllabus_overview: ​Modern econometric work increasingly draws on econometrics, data science, statistics and machine learning. This course introduces these methods through the lens of econometric theory and applications. You will study the links between theory, computational methods and the application of models to real examples. The course develops an intermediate-level understanding of modern econometric, statistical and machine learning methods, including the theoretical justifications for their use and the practical skills needed to apply them in Python. By the end of the course, you will be able to select and apply suitable methods to econometric modelling tasks, interpret programming output, and communicate evidence-based results for economics and business problems.​
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Communicate the results of an econometric analysis in a manner that lays out the problem to be solved, a description of the data, the methodology used and the proposed results.
Display sufficient facility with the theoretical underpinning of econometric models to develop an intuition for the generalisability of the models and associated methods.
Demonstrate proficiency at writing code and interpreting programming output, in order to fit and adjust models.
Select and apply suitable econometric and computational methods for tackling an array of econometric problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON3209 or MATH2801 or MATH2901 or Enrolment in FINSBH Finance Co-Op Honours or Enrolment in FINSD1 Finance Co-Op

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematical Economics
syllabus_overview: Mathematics provides the formal language of modern economics, enabling us to rigorously analyse models, clarify assumptions, and derive precise insights into how economic systems function and respond to change. This course provides a working knowledge of basic analysis, topology, and static and dynamic optimisation techniques applied in economics. Topics include logic and set theory, topological principles in Euclidean spaces, properties of real-valued functions (continuity, concavity, quasi-concavity), differentiation in multi-dimensional Euclidean spaces, classical optimisation with and without constraints, comparative statics, and envelope theorems. By the end of the course, you will become familiar with a wide range of mathematical techniques as illustrated within mainstream theoretical applications such as consumer theory and game theory.
learning_outcomes: Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Acquire mathematical concepts and methods used in economic analysis.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Apply mathematical techniques to solve and interpret economic problems.
Express economic ideas using mathematical language and analyse economic models with formal methods.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2101 or MATH1231 or MATH1241

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Econometrics
syllabus_overview: ​Financial decisions often depend on understanding how financial data behave over time. This course provides a framework for modelling financial time series data, including commodity and asset prices, interest rates and exchange rates. You will learn the key characteristics of financial data, concepts of volatility and risk, methods for modelling time-varying volatility, approaches to risk management, and relationships among financial series. The course also develops forecasting skills for financial assets and the ability to evaluate competing forecasts. By the end of the course, you will be able to use econometric and programming tools to model, estimate, make inferences about and forecast financial data.​
learning_outcomes: Apply econometric and programming tools to the modelling, estimation, inference and forecasting of financial data.
Explain various assumptions, concepts, principles, and methodologies underlying time series models for financial data.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Critically evaluate empirical econometric work.
Work collaboratively to complete a task.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2209

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Econometric Methods
syllabus_overview: Applied econometrics provides the tools to transform raw data into meaningful economic insight. It bridges theory and evidence, allowing us to rigorously test hypotheses, identify causal relationships, and inform real-world policy and business decisions. This course extends econometric modelling using linear regression to cover nonlinear models such as logit and probit, regression methods for forecasting, and an introduction to the treatment of endogeneity (e.g. instrumental variable estimation). Special emphasis will be placed on the process and potential pitfalls of conducting and evaluating applied econometric research. By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the necessary knowledge to be able to conduct your own econometric research using standard real-world economic and business data.
learning_outcomes: Apply econometric models and tools for discrete dependent variables, addressing challenges such as omitted-variable bias and endogeneity.
Apply regression models for forecasting.
Evaluate and critique the relevance of theoretical models in conducting applied work.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Apply Stata for econometric modelling.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2206 OR (In Data Sciences and Decisions AND (MATH2831 or MATH2931))

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Statistics for Econometrics
syllabus_overview: Understanding the statistical backbone of modern econometric analysis is fundamental. It underpins how economists draw reliable conclusions from data, and critically evaluate the tools used in empirical research. This course provides the foundations for modern econometric methods including probability theory, mathematical statistics, asymptotic theory, frequentist and Bayesian inference, underlying mathematical methods and an introduction to statistical computing. Mastering this course will give students a deeper understanding of the formal mathematical and statistical underpinnings of methods and knowledge commonly used in econometrics. Throughout the course, material will be presented in the context of simple models to concentrate on the concepts. By the end of the course, you will have a rigorous grasp of the statistical principles that support econometric methods, providing the foundation needed for advanced data-driven economic analysis.
learning_outcomes: Apply probability and distribution theory to inference, estimation, and hypothesis testing.
Perform computer-based calculations and simulations of statistical and econometric models.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates econometric ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Solve problems analytically using mathematical and statistical methods.
Explain the relationship between theoretical statistics and econometric techniques used in empirical analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON2206

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Big Data Econometrics
syllabus_overview: ​​How do economists turn complex data into credible evidence for decisions? The explosion of the amount, scope and availability of data has transformed how organisations make decisions. This course examines econometric and machine learning methods suited to data-rich environments, including regression, model selection and regularisation, regression trees, cross-validation, and natural experiments. You will compare how these methods perform across description, prediction, and counterfactual analysis tasks and how the key distinction between experimental and observational data must inform your analysis. You may also be introduced to newer data types such as textual, spatial, and network data. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods suited to a data-rich environment, critically assess identification and model choices, and communicate evidence with precision.​
learning_outcomes: Explain the distinction between the modelling tasks of description, prediction, and counterfactual prediction.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Use appropriate software, econometric models, and machine learning methods to analyse real data of various types and structures.

Make informed decisions about research design and the model-building process, including considerations related to big data, the relevance of theoretical models, and the environmental, sustainability, and ethical implications of applied work.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: ECON2206 or ECON2209

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Microeconomic Analysis
syllabus_overview: Understanding how individuals and firms make optimal decisions and how their interactions shape market outcomes is paramount. It underpins much of modern economics, helping explain and predict behaviour under different market structures and information conditions. This course deals with individual optimal decision making and equilibrium. Fundamental topics covered include rational choice, utility maximisation, expenditure minimisation, production theory, and decision making under uncertainty. Partial equilibrium, game theory and non-competitive environments will also be covered. The course also explores economic environments with asymmetric information, including auctions and screening. By the end of the course, you will be able to formally analyse strategic and non-strategic interactions in economic settings using microeconomic theory.
learning_outcomes: Understand formal mathematical models of economic phenomena.
Analyse formal mathematical models of economic phenomena.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Methods for Causal Inference
syllabus_overview: How can we measure the impact of economic interventions? Why do some policies succeed while others fail? This course provides the powerful tools of causal inference that can answer such questions. It covers foundational methods for identifying causal effects—including randomised controlled trials, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity designs—to equip students with the skills to critically evaluate empirical research and conduct their own rigorous analyses. By the end of the course, you will be able to evaluate and apply causal inference methods to real data to measure the effects of a wide range of policies and programs. Whether you are interested in public policy, labour markets, health, development, or finance, mastering causal inference will enhance their ability to make informed data-driven decisions and produce credible economic analysis.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the advantages and limitations of policy evaluation methods (e.g., RCTs, DiD, IV, RDD, Event Studies).
Identify and explain the distinction between correlation and causation in research applications.
Critically evaluate the empirical implementation of policy evaluation methods, assessing their appropriateness and limitations in applied contexts.
Apply appropriate designs and techniques to achieve causal identification in policy settings.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Macroeconomic Analysis
syllabus_overview: ​​This is an advanced course in macroeconomic theory. The first part of the course will briefly review business cycle facts, real business cycle models, and useful tools and technique. The second part of the course will cover the New Keynesian approach to macroeconomics, covering topics such as monetary policy and inflation, the real effects of monetary policy, the advantages of credible policy commitments and monetary-fiscal interactions. By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse macroeconomic dynamics with formal models and evaluate fiscal and monetary policy in a wide range of environments.​
learning_outcomes: Explain the assumptions underlying macroeconomic models.
Use appropriate tools to simulate models and data for statistical analysis.
Use standard macroeconomic models and empirical evidence to explain and interpret real-world problems.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

syllabus_overview: This course is part of the thesis component of the Business Economics specialisation in the BCom(Hons) program. Weekly honours seminars will be scheduled as part of this course to provide a forum in which students may present and discuss their research and obtain feedback from the other students and the seminar coordinator. The course is one of three thesis courses to be completed across the three terms in the BCom(Hons) program to achieve 24 UOC.

Write a literature review and place one’s work in the literature.

title: Macroeconometrics
syllabus_overview: ​​This course will provide you with an introduction to econometrics as it is applied in macroeconomics. Emphasis is on hands-on implementation of the methods covered in the course. Topics include macroeconomic data, linear and nonlinear time series models, practical issues with likelihood-based inference for these models, forecast evaluation, structural identification and use of micro data in empirical macroeconomics. By the end of this course, you will be able to implement core macroeconometric methods, evaluate model assumptions, and draw defensible conclusions from aggregate data in order to undertake modern macroeconomic research.​
learning_outcomes: Solve problems associated with identification using macroeconomic data.
Determine what constitutes good applied econometric practice.
Assess and analyse common pitfalls, problems, and solutions that arise in applied econometric work.
Critically evaluate applied econometric research and use statistical software effectively to conduct econometric analysis.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Econometric Theory and Methods
syllabus_overview: This course covers a selection of advanced econometric methods such as maximum likelihood, generalised methods of moments, simulated maximum likelihood, simulated methods of moments, Bayesian inference, and bootstrap methods. Irrespective of the particular topics taught in any year, the course will emphasise the theoretical foundations of methods and their application to substantive economic problems in areas such as financial econometrics, micro-econometrics and macroeconometrics. This course is designed for you to acquire a higher level of knowledge in the area of econometrics beyond that expected of a good applied economist.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise empirical studies from the viewpoint of modern econometrics.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

You will study recent developments in widely used causal research designs, along with complementary approaches for policy and program evaluation. Applications are drawn from labour, development, political economy, education, and health. The course prepares you both to conduct research using state-of-the-art microeconometric methods and to critically evaluate empirical studies. By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods, assess identification and model choices critically, and communicate evidence with precision.​

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Organisation
syllabus_overview: ​Industrial organisation studies how firms behave, how markets are structured, and how regulation affects market outcomes. This course gives you tools and knowledge for critically reading recent research papers and beginning to conduct original research in industrial organisation. You will investigate how firms exercise market power in different settings and how governments may limit negative effects through regulation. The course develops rigorous theoretical models while maintaining close connections to real-world implications. Topics include market and industry structure, firms' pricing and non-price strategies, productivity, demand, markups, supplier networks, multi-product firms, industrial policy, and contemporary policy debates. By the end of the course, you will understand how theoretical models of strategic behaviour support the analysis of firms, industries and regulation.​
learning_outcomes: Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Explain the determinants of industry structure.
Evaluate the welfare implications of strategic behaviour.
Describe and analyse the determinants of strategic behaviour in oligopolistic markets.
Model the behavior of monopolists in different circumstances.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Economics
syllabus_overview: This course provides a theoretical analysis of international trade topics with references to empirical evidence. The course discusses a range of international trade models such as comparative advantage and monopolistic competition models, showing how technological differences, differences in resource endowments, and economies of scale determine trade patterns and income distribution. How these models perform in empirical tests will also be explored by discussing relevant empirical papers and using real data to analyse the models. The second part of the course will primarily focus on state-of-the-art heterogeneous firm models of trade and on developing empirical tools to analyse firm-level micro data and product-level trade data. The effects of various trade policy instruments on welfare will also be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Identify, interpret and solve partial equilibrium and simple general equilibrium models of international trade and policy.
Use appropriate software to analyse data of various types and structures.
Analyse the effects of changing trade barriers on factor returns, composition of consumption and production, and welfare.
Use the standard models of international trade to interpret and analyse problems and issues in international economics.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Labour Economics
syllabus_overview: The course teaches core topics in the field of labour economics as well as introduces empirical methods for applied microeconomic analysis. The aim of this course is to encourage development of independent research interests in labour economics and related fields. Topics include wage and employment determination, formation of human capital, labour market discrimination, immigration, unemployment, wage differentials, wage structure, and institutions in the labour market. There will be particular emphasis on the interaction between theoretical and empirical modelling.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced econometric tools to analyse labour market related processes and develop practical understanding of statistical inference issues.
Critically analyse research in labour economics and understand underlying assumptions.
Model and analyse the structure of labour markets and their frictions.
Collect data and analyse the integral concepts of labour market issues (such as unemployment, taxation, educational choice, wage differentials, discrimination, etc.).
Analyse the interactions between aggregate economic forces and identify the role of firms, workers and government in the economy.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Economics
syllabus_overview: The course provides an economic approach to the analysis of health and medical care markets. Topics covered include the production of health, the production and consumption of medical care, the role of health as human capital, the relation between health and wealth, health insurance and the problems of adverse selection and moral hazard, the health workforce and the training of health professionals. Throughout the course reference is made to current government health policy.
learning_outcomes: Compare and contrast the different market environments in which health and health policy decisions must be made.
Describe market failures in the provision of health care and the justifications for government policy.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Explain and analyse the underlying economic frameworks appropriate for studying health and health care.
Apply a rational approach in the evaluation of government intervention and programs in health.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Measurement
syllabus_overview: ​Economic measurement shapes how economists understand data, evaluate policy and interpret economic performance. This course covers the theory and practice of measuring key economic indicators, including the Consumer Price Index, Gross Domestic Product and productivity growth. You will examine approaches used by international statistical agencies and consider how policy implications can depend on measurement techniques. The course is technically rigorous, drawing on microeconomic theory, econometric analysis and recent international research developments. By the end of the course, you will have a stronger foundation for understanding data sources, uses and reliability, and for applying rigorous reasoning to economic measurement problems.​

Identify and explain a global outlook, through awareness of similarities and differences across borders.
Demonstrate and apply up-to-date bodies of knowledge, through research-led teaching.
Participate in and demonstrate skilled, responsible, imaginative, ethical, and flexible professional practice.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Admission to Economics Honours (program 4502 or stream ECONFH4501) or Actuarial Honours (program 4520)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Topics in Economics
syllabus_overview: This course introduces advanced tools and topics in behavioural economics with emphasis on markets, game theory, and individual decision making. The course is intended both for students who wish to develop a solid background in behavioural economics to pursue research in applied fields, and for students who seek to specialise in economic theory. The course covers a broad array of topics analysed through the lens of behavioural economics. Most time will be spent on developing new tools, but economic applications will also be covered.

Build simple microeconomic models from first principles.
Independently analyse standard models in microeconomics.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Experimental and Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: This course is meant to deepen students’ understanding of the experimental method of investigation in economics and business research. It is being offered at the Honours/MEc/PhD level. In the course we will review questions of experimental design and implementation such as appropriate procedures of subject recruitment, programming tools, statistical and econometric analysis of experimental data, and other methodological issues in experimental economics. Importantly, students will develop their own experimental pilot project, from design over programming and the actual implementation to the analysis and write-up of a research paper. Grading will rely on two class presentations (design presentation 10% and results presentation 20%) and a research paper (70%).

evaluate the appropriateness of this method to study certain research questions
be familiar with all aspects of design and implementation of experiments, such as recruiting, ethics, programming, and the conduct of experimental sessions

develop a basic experimental design to test an appropriate research question

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconomics
syllabus_overview: Decision-making by consumers, producers, and governments lies at the heart of economic analysis. It determines how scarce resources are allocated, how markets function, and how welfare is distributed across society. The first half of this microeconomics course is devoted to the study of decision-making and the modelling of associated market behaviour. We then study how individual economic decisions interact in markets with varying degrees of competition, paying substantial attention to the comparative welfare outcomes produced by different market forms. Additional topics include externalities, game theory and its applications, and asymmetric information. There is an emphasis on the use of analytical tools and mathematical models, which underpin much of current research in microeconomics. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply core microeconomic models to analyse decision-making and market outcomes, critically evaluate efficiency and welfare implications across market structures, and use formal tools to address issues such as externalities, strategic interaction, and information asymmetries.
learning_outcomes: Develop and present arguments to demonstrate an understanding of key concepts of microeconomics and their appropriate usage.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Analyse choice problems and markets by identifying and applying appropriate mathematical techniques to design and solve economic models.
Evaluate environmental and sustainability problems arising from non-cooperative decision making among agents/ firms/countries.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconomics
syllabus_overview: The macroeconomy of a country is a complex network consisting of millions of interacting agents, including consumers, ﬁrms, banks and government institutions. This course introduces you to some of the models employed by economists to understand how these agents interact and contribute to economic growth, the business cycle and other macroeconomic variables. The course covers a range of topics, including ﬁscal and monetary policies, the business cycle, inflation and unemployment and economic growth models. Models developed in the unit are applied to real-world data and are used to analyse observed developments across different economies. By the end of the course, you will develop the tools, skills and knowledge necessary for you to operate as a practicing macroeconomist.

Synthesise theory and evidence to assess macroeconomic outcomes related to fairness and inequality in an economic context.
Employ advanced analytical methods to apply macroeconomic models to interpret and analyse real-world economic issues.

syllabus_overview: How do markets operate, how do firms and consumers respond to incentives, and how do government policies affect business strategy and performance? This course introduces key economic principles and their application to business decision making in a dynamic and uncertain environment. Students will develop a foundational understanding of economic principles and receive practical training in decision making, within the economic contexts which influence business activities. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply economic reasoning to strategic and operational decisions, assess policy impacts on business outcomes, and think critically about the broader economic forces shaping modern organisations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economics of Finance
syllabus_overview: The valuation of financial assets is a cornerstone of real-world financial markets. The economic theory of financial markets provides a logical foundation for modern asset pricing and portfolio choice theories. This course provides economic insights into finance and financial markets. We study equilibrium valuation and pricing through the lenses of economic concepts. Major financial instruments such as bonds, stocks, futures, and options are introduced under economic equilibrium context, and we discuss techniques to value these diverse financial assets. We then turn to the "utility-based" approach, wherein a well-defined utility structure is established as a model primitive. Maximising expected utility, we derive optimal consumption, equilibrium trades and prices. In turn, we discuss how trade is beneficial for all the participants in the market. We conclude the course with an introduction to modern portfolio theory.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and critically analyse the principles underlying the pricing of financial assets whose payoffs are contingent on certain outcomes.
Evaluate and critically analyse standard asset pricing models, including their underlying assumptions, limitations, and usefulness in financial decision making.

Employ programming tools and apply the principles of asset pricing to evaluate derivative instruments, assess the factors relevant for valuing contingent-payoff assets, and demonstrate the appropriate application of portfolio formation principles.
Synthesize ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.

This course introduces the core tools of game theory and applies them to competition, contracting, auctions, bargaining, and related strategic settings. You will study simultaneous and sequential games, imperfect information, and repeated interaction, and apply these tools across mean cases and contexts. The result is a practical framework for analysing strategic behaviour. By the end of this course, you will be able apply core game theoretic concepts to analyse strategic behaviour, market structure, and policy design with precision and confidence.​

syllabus_overview: What can we learn from data, and how can we separate correlation and causality? This course introduces the use of econometrics to explore and estimate economic relationships using linear regression models. Emphasis will be placed on cross-sectional data and on understanding the conditions required for inferring causal relationships. We will also consider extensions that address common data analysis complications, including heteroskedasticity, proxy variables, and other data limitations. And we will consider regression models for time series and panel data, highlighting their relevance for economic analysis. Practical computer-based exercises are integrated throughout, enabling students to gain hands-on experience working with real-world data and econometric software. By the end of the course, you will have the skills to critically interpret empirical relationships and a foundation for more advanced courses in econometrics.

syllabus_overview: ​Financial decisions often depend on understanding how financial data behave over time. This course provides a framework for modelling financial time series data, including commodity and asset prices, interest rates and exchange rates. You will learn the key characteristics of financial data, concepts of volatility and risk, methods for modelling time-varying volatility, approaches to risk management, and relationships among financial series. The course develops the computer-based skills needed to model financial data in practice. By the end of the course, you will be able to use financial econometric and programming tools to model, estimate, make inferences about and forecast financial data.​

Communication skills are built through this collaborative work and direct stakeholder engagement. By the end of the course, students will be able to independently design and execute applied economic research, evaluate complex policy issues using data-driven methods, and communicate analytical insights effectively to both technical and non-technical stakeholders

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introductory Economics and Data Analysis for Business Professionals
syllabus_overview: Successful business leadership depends on understanding both the economic forces that shape markets and the data that inform strategic choices. This course equips students with the ability to interpret economic trends, apply decision-making frameworks, and use data-driven insights to guide policy and business strategy. It covers the policy and strategic aspects of business management and also provides a practical and analytical approach to economic policy issues. It is structured into two parts. The first part (Economics) provides you with the tools to use economic principles in decision-making and an understanding of the broader economic environment in which business decisions must be made. The second part (Data Analysis) introduces the basic statistical tools and quantitative methods useful in understanding the types of data encountered in business. By the end of the course, students will be able to analyse economic and business data, evaluate policy implications, and make informed, evidence-based decisions in complex business environments.

This course looks at the use of econometric and statistical techniques relevant to forecasting in a business environment and computer implementation of the methods: Both short-term forecasting with simple time series models, and longer-term forecasting that include seasonal and trend terms are considered. Applied work using a statistical software package is emphasised in this non-specialist course. By the end of the course, students will be able to design, implement, and critically assess forecasting models that support strategic decision-making in dynamic market environments. Through hands-on exercises and data-driven analysis, they will gain the ability to translate quantitative results into meaningful business insights.

Building on prior study in microeconomics and game theory, you will examine dynamic games, with a particular focus on collusion and bargaining. The course develops the analytical tools needed to understand how strategic incentives affect cooperation, negotiation and efficiency. By the end of the course, you will have a stronger foundation for analysing dynamic strategic interaction and for evaluating the economic mechanisms that sustain cooperation and determine bargaining outcomes.

syllabus_overview: ​​In today’s global economy, national policies and outcomes are deeply interconnected. ​This course introduces the core concepts and analytical tools of open-economy macroeconomics, providing a structured framework for examining how countries interact through trade, capital flows, and policy choices. It covers exchange rate determination, balance of payments, current account imbalances, international asset markets, and the role of fiscal and monetary policy in open economies. It also considers the functioning of different exchange rate regimes, the challenges of monetary unions, and the causes and consequences of international financial crises. Emphasis is placed on applying theory to contemporary issues and policy debates, enabling students to better interpret real-world events and understand the constraints and trade-offs faced by policymakers. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse macroeconomic dynamics with formal models and evaluate fiscal and monetary policy in domestic and international settings.​

A key focus is the interaction between theory and evidence, including how to assess whether specific interventions are likely to improve welfare. By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse major drivers of underdevelopment, design innovative ways to assess development policies with theory and evidence, and identify credible pathways for improving outcomes.​

syllabus_overview: How can we measure the impact of economic interventions? Why do some policies succeed while others fail? Whether you are interested in public policy, labour markets, health, development, or finance, mastering causal inference will enhance their ability to make informed data-driven decisions and produce credible economic analysis.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the empirical implementation of policy evaluation methods, assessing their appropriateness and limitations in applied contexts.
Evaluate the advantages and limitations of policy evaluation methods (e.g., RCTs, DiD, IV, RDD, Event Studies).
Identify and implement appropriate research designs to achieve causal identification in complex policy contexts.
Characterise the distinction between correlation and causation and its implications for research design.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: ​​Standard economic theory assumes that people have correct beliefs based on correct statistical reasoning, that they are narrowly self-interested, and that they manage to maximise their utility. Decades of experimental evidence suggest a more complicated picture. People systematically misperceive probabilities, cooperate with strangers in ways that sacrifice their own material payoffs, and make choices that they themselves deem suboptimal. Explaining these empirical regularities requires new theory. ​In this course, students will study the core findings of behavioural economics, learn the formal theoretical frameworks developed to explain it, and build the empirical reasoning skills needed to critically evaluate competing accounts. Topics include reference-dependent preferences and prospect theory, intertemporal choice, risk preferences, bounded rationality, social preferences, behavioural game theory, and behavioural public policy. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to formulate behavioural hypotheses precisely, evaluate them using appropriate theoretical tools, and critically assess the evidence used to support or challenge them.​
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate claims made by behavioural economists and critically apply the tools learned in class to explain real-world phenomena.
Identify what behavioural economics is and acquire the material covered in the course.
Analyse and interpret findings from behavioural economics research and evaluate their applications to public policy.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON5103

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Economics
syllabus_overview: ​Environmental problems are among the most important and contested policy issues. This course provides an economic perspective on those problems and on the policy tools used to address them. You will examine why environmental problems arise, why unregulated markets may fail in environmental contexts, and how economic instruments such as regulations, taxes, subsidies and pollution permit trading schemes can respond to these failures. The course also covers methods for determining the benefits and costs of environmental preservation. By the end of the course, you will be able to analyse environmental policy debates using economic reasoning and evidence.​
learning_outcomes: Critically examine how economists attempt to measure environmental benefits.
Evaluate the theoretical basis upon which the sub-discipline has been built.
Appraise the rationale of current environmental initiatives including climate change and water reform.
Assess the economic treatment of natural resources such as water, fossil fuels and renewable resources such as fisheries.
Analyse situations in which markets are likely to be inefficient and evaluate the intervention tools that correct for it.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON5101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Econometric Theory and Machine Learning
syllabus_overview: ​Modern econometric work increasingly draws on econometrics, data science, statistics and machine learning. This course develops these methods through the lens of econometric theory and applications. You will study the links between theory, computational methods and the application of models to real examples. The course develops an understanding of modern econometric, statistical and machine learning methods, including the theoretical justifications for their use and the practical skills needed to apply them in Python. By the end of the course, you will be able to employ econometric and computational methods for a range of modelling tasks, assess their suitability, interpret programming output, and communicate evidence-based results for economics and business problems.​

Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Construct writtten code, demonstrating proficient and effective interpretation of programming output, to fit and adjust models.

Employ econometric and computational methods to tackle an array of econometric problems, critically assessing their suitability and rectifying inadequacies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Econometric Methods
syllabus_overview: Applied econometrics provides the tools to transform raw data into meaningful economic insight. It bridges theory and evidence, allowing us to rigorously test hypotheses, identify causal relationships, and inform real-world policy and business decisions. This course builds from preliminary investigations of linear regression models to introduce more advanced econometric techniques. Topics include limited-dependent variable models, treatment of endogeneity, time series econometrics and panel data. Special emphasis will be placed on the process and potential pitfalls of conducting and evaluating applied econometric research. By the end of the course, you will be equipped with the necessary knowledge to be able to conduct your own econometric research using standard real-world economic and business data.
learning_outcomes: Model and interpret economic data, addressing challenges such as omitted variables, endogeneity, and forecasting.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

Apply advanced econometric models and tools, including those for discrete dependent variables, to analyse data.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Economics
syllabus_overview: The course provides an economic approach to the analysis of health and medical care markets. Topics covered include the production of health, the production and consumption of medical care, the relationship between health and wealth, health insurance and the problems of adverse selection and moral hazard, the health workforce and the training of health professionals. Throughout the course reference is made to current government health policy.
learning_outcomes: Develop well-structured, succinct, and professional written work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Analyse market failures in health care and assess the main justifications for government policy.
Apply a rational approach in evaluating government intervention and programs in health and apply evidence from applied health economics studies.
Explain and analyse the underlying economic frameworks appropriate for studying health and health care.
Analyse and compare different market environments in which health and health policy decisions must be made.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON5103 AND ECON5205 or MATH5905) AND WAM of at least 85.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Measurement
syllabus_overview: This course covers the theory and practice of economic measurement, including the measurement of key economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index, Gross Domestic Product and productivity growth. Approaches employed by international statistical agencies will be highlighted, along with the possibility that policy implications are often reliant on the choice of measurement techniques. The course will be technically rigorous, particularly in the use of microeconomic theory and econometric analysis, and will draw on the latest international research developments.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and synthesize up-to-date bodies of knowledge, through research-led teaching.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicate ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Implement and demonstrate skilled, responsible, imaginative, ethical, and flexible professional practice.
Develop and integrate a global outlook, through awareness of similarities and differences across borders.
Work collaboratively to complete a task.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Public Economics and Regulation
syllabus_overview: ​Government intervention affects markets, private behaviour and social welfare. This course investigates the role of the public sector in the economy: where intervention may be needed, why it may be justified, how it shapes private-sector behaviour, and what welfare effects it creates. You will study welfare economics, optimal taxation, market failure, economic regulation, industrial policy and political economy. The course also uses a political economy lens to examine how public-sector behaviour is shaped by political processes as well as economic concerns. Additional video lectures introduce topics such as collusion, financial stability and shadow banks, giving a broader view of government policy. By the end of the course, you will be able to analyse the rationale, design and consequences of government intervention using economic reasoning.​
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain, using verbal, mathematical, and graphical tools, the primary economic reasons for government intervention in a market.
Evaluate and compare the economic efficiency and likely impacts of government policies on the market.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicate ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Compare and contrast different types of taxation mechanisms in the dimensions of equity and efficiency.
Identify the different groups likely to experience costs and benefits from the introduction of a new regulation or tax/subsidy.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON5101 OR ECON5111 OR MNGT5201 OR approval of the PG Coordinator

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Policy Applications of Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: ​Behavioural economics can help explain why real-world decisions sometimes differ from the predictions of mainstream economic theory. This course examines how behavioural insights can be applied thoughtfully to incentives and policy design in a variety of real-world settings. You will first consider gaps in mainstream economic theory and the ways behavioural economics has developed to address them. The course then uses frontier behavioural economics theory and case studies of policy interventions in Australia and abroad to examine the design and consequences of behavioural policies. By the end of the course, you will understand how theoretically grounded behavioural insights can enhance traditional economic analysis and inform the stewardship of modern economies.​
learning_outcomes: Articulate the policy relevance of behavioural economics, including designing policy solutions based on it.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicate ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Reflect on the future of behavioural economics and its integration into mainstream applied economics.
Apply insights from behavioural economics in understanding modern real-world policy problems.
Recognise the gaps in mainstream economic theory that behavioural economists have sought to fill
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON5103 OR MNGT5201 OR enrolment in program 8412 OR approval of the PG Coordinator

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Development in China
syllabus_overview: This course studies the process of China’s economic development, in particular the economic reforms since 1978, with a focus on Chinese institutions. Topics to be examined through the lens of standard economic theory and then applied to the case of China include trade policy, agricultural policy, population policy, industrial policy, and political economy. Through this course students will gain insight into the application of economic theory and econometric methods to understand specific issues related to the past and future economic development of China.
learning_outcomes: Describe the trajectory of economic development in China, and key features of China’s economic transition since 1949.
Evaluate the impact of the post-1978 economic reforms on different Chinese economic sectors.
Identify and explain the differences between the government’s stewardship of the economy in China versus in a democratic Western country like Australia, using economic logic and case studies.

Nominate the most significant economic reforms made in China since 1978, and explain their predicted and actual effects on the Chinese economy as a whole, using verbal, mathematical, and graphical tools.
Propose and justify the main headwinds to the further economic development and growth of China.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Topics in Economics
syllabus_overview: This course introduces advanced tools and topics in behavioural economics with emphasis on markets, game theory, and individual decision making. The course is intended both for students who wish to develop a solid background in behavioural economics to pursue research in applied fields, and for students who seek to specialise in economic theory. The course covers a broad array of topics analysed through the lens of behavioural economics. Most time will be spent on developing new tools, but economic applications will also be covered.

Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Construct simple microeconomic models from first principles.

Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
