institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconomic Theory I
syllabus_overview: Understanding how individuals and firms make optimal decisions and how their interactions shape market outcomes is paramount. It underpins much of modern economics, helping explain and predict behaviour under different market structures and information conditions. This course deals with individual optimal decision making and equilibrium. Fundamental topics covered include rational choice, utility maximisation, expenditure minimisation, production theory, and decision making under uncertainty. Partial equilibrium, game theory and non-competitive environments will also be covered. The course also explores economic environments with asymmetric information, including auctions and screening. By the end of the course, you will be able to formally analyse strategic and non-strategic interactions in economic settings using microeconomic theory.
learning_outcomes: Employ advanced mathematical methods to analyse and assess economic models and their implications.
Critically evaluate and interpret formal mathematical models of economic phenomena.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON7004 AND Enrolment in program 1540, 1561 or 8635) or Approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconomic Theory I
syllabus_overview: ​​This is an advanced course in macroeconomic theory. The first part of the course will briefly review business cycle facts, real business cycle models, and useful tools and technique. The second part of the course will cover the New Keynesian approach to macroeconomics, covering topics such as monetary policy and inflation, the real effects of monetary policy, the advantages of credible policy commitments and monetary-fiscal interactions. By the end of this course, you will be able to analyse macroeconomic dynamics with formal models and evaluate fiscal and monetary policy in a wide range of environments.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and critically assess numerical tools used to solve rational expectations models and analyse their quantitative predictions.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Analyse and explain the assumptions and structure of standard macroeconomic models.
Critically manipulate these macroeconomic models and assess the implications of their structure.
Apply macroeconomic models to interpret and analyse problems in macroeconomics.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON7004 and Enrolment in program 1540, 1561 or 8635) or Approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Econometric Theory and Methods
syllabus_overview: This course covers a selection of advanced econometric methods such as maximum likelihood, generalised methods of moments, simulated maximum likelihood, simulated methods of moments, Bayesian inference, and bootstrap methods. Irrespective of the particular topics taught in any year, the course will emphasise the theoretical foundations of methods and their application to substantive economic problems in areas such as financial econometrics, micro-econometrics and macroeconometrics. This course is designed for you to acquire a higher level of knowledge in the area of econometrics beyond that expected of a good applied economist.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and appraise empirical studies from the viewpoint of modern econometrics.
Apply learned econometric methods and implement them to solve practical problems.
Analyse and evaluate the main features of the econometric methods presented, and their statistical properties.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Conduct and evaluate the outcomes of econometric modelling.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematical Economics
syllabus_overview: Mathematical economics is essential because it provides the formal tools to express economic ideas, uncover relations not easily observed through intuition alone, and engage confidently with modern economic research and policy analysis. This course offers a rigorous introduction to mathematical economics. It equips students with the tools to analyse optimisation and equilibrium in diverse economic settings. Building on core concepts such as sets, functions, normed spaces, linear algebra, and calculus, students will apply mathematical techniques including advanced optimisation, fixed point theory, and comparative statics to analyse a range of economic problems. Emphasis is placed on both mathematical formalism and the intuition needed to apply these results in economics. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to engage deeply with analytical economic models and have a rigorous foundation for advanced economic analysis.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and communicate complex economic ideas using mathematical language.
Employ formal mathematical methods to construct, analyse, and assess economic models and their theoretical implications.
Critically evaluate and extend advanced mathematical concepts and methods central to economic analysis.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 1540 or 1561 or 8635 or Approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconomic Theory II
syllabus_overview: ​Modern macroeconomic analysis often requires solving, parameterising and interpreting formal models. This course introduces techniques for solving and analysing macroeconomic models and applying them to economic policy questions. The course begins with linearisation techniques and perturbation before moving to non-linear approximations of model solutions. You will also learn how to parameterise macroeconomic models, including calibration and basics of estimation such as the Kalman filter and maximum likelihood estimation. The course concludes with an introduction to models with heterogeneous agents. Throughout the course, you will consider how macroeconomic models can be used for economic and policy analysis.​
learning_outcomes: Analyse and explain the assumptions and structure of standard macroeconomic models.
Select and apply numerical tools to solve rational expectations models and analyse their quantitative predictions.
Analyse and critically manipulate standard macroeconomic models.
Apply macroeconomic models to interpret and analyse problems in macroeconomics and construct sophisticated arguments based on these concepts.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ECON7002 and Enrolment in program 1540, 1561 or 8635) or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Methods for Causal Inference
syllabus_overview: How can we measure the impact of economic interventions? Why do some policies succeed while others fail? This course provides the powerful tools of causal inference that can answer such questions. It covers foundational methods for identifying causal effects—including randomised controlled trials, difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, and regression discontinuity designs—to equip students with the skills to critically evaluate empirical research and conduct their own rigorous analyses. By the end of the course, you will be able to evaluate and apply causal inference methods to real data to measure the effects of a wide range of policies and programs. Whether you are interested in public policy, labour markets, health, development, or finance, mastering causal inference will enhance their ability to make informed data-driven decisions and produce credible economic analysis.
learning_outcomes: Design and apply advanced techniques to achieve robust causal identification in challenging policy settings.
Critically evaluate the advanced advantages and limitations of policy evaluation methods (e.g., RCTs, DiD, IV, RDD, Event Studies) across diverse empirical contexts.
Critically assess and synthesize the empirical implementation of policy evaluation methods, providing nuanced evaluations of their appropriateness and limitations in applied research.
Identify and explain in depth the distinction between correlation and causation in complex research applications.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM8102 or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Macroeconometrics
syllabus_overview: ​​This course will provide you with an introduction to econometrics as it is applied in macroeconomics. Emphasis is on hands-on implementation of the methods covered in the course. Topics include macroeconomic data, linear and nonlinear time series models, practical issues with likelihood-based inference for these models, forecast evaluation, structural identification and use of micro data in empirical macroeconomics. By the end of this course, you will be able to implement core macroeconometric methods, evaluate model assumptions, and draw defensible conclusions from aggregate data in order to undertake modern macroeconomic research.​
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate applied econometric research and use statistical software proficiently to conduct econometric analysis.
Solve cases associated with identification using macroeconomic data.
Analyse what constitutes good applied econometric practice.
Assess and analyse common pitfalls, problems, and solutions that arise in applied econometric work.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconometrics
syllabus_overview: ​​This course covers advanced econometric methods for empirical research in applied microeconomics and related fields. You will study recent developments in widely used causal research designs, along with complementary approaches for policy and program evaluation. Applications are drawn from labour, development, political economy, education, and health. The course prepares you both to conduct research using state-of-the-art microeconometric methods and to critically evaluate empirical studies. ​By the end of this course, you will be able to apply modern empirical methods, assess identification and model choices critically, and communicate evidence with precision.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate applied microeconomics research using various empirical research designs.
Analyse the advantages and drawbacks of different empirical research designs such as difference-in-differences, instrumental variables, regression discontinuity, and randomised evaluations.
Identify and analyse issues that arise in applying empirical research designs and approaches to address them.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Organisation
syllabus_overview: ​Industrial organisation studies how firms behave, how markets are structured, and how regulation affects market outcomes. This course gives you tools and knowledge for critically reading recent research papers and conducting original research in industrial organisation. You will investigate how firms exercise market power in different settings and how governments may limit negative effects through regulation. The course develops rigorous theoretical models while maintaining close connections to real-world implications. Topics include market and industry structure, firms' pricing and non-price strategies, productivity, demand, markups, supplier networks, multi-product firms, industrial policy, and contemporary policy debates. By the end of the course, you will be able to use theoretical and empirical perspectives to analyse firms, industries, regulation and industrial policy at a research-oriented level.​
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the welfare implications of strategic behaviour.
Model the behaviour of monopolists in different circumstances.
Critically evaluate the approaches to complexities and challenges in real-world data on firm and industry dynamics.
Solve game theory problems related to the industry structure and the determinants of strategic behaviour in oligopolistic markets.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON7001 and ECON7004 or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Economics
syllabus_overview: This course provides a theoretical analysis of international trade topics with references to empirical evidence. The course discusses a range of international trade models such as comparative advantage and monopolistic competition models, showing how technological differences, differences in resource endowments, and economies of scale determine trade patterns and income distribution. How these models perform in empirical tests will also be explored by discussing relevant empirical papers and using real data to analyse the models. The second part of the course will primarily focus on state-of-the-art heterogeneous firm models of trade and on developing empirical tools to analyse firm-level micro data and product-level trade data. The effects of various trade policy instruments on welfare will also be analysed.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and solve partial equilibrium and simple general equilibrium models of international trade and policy.
Develop succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Analyse the effects of changing trade barriers on factor returns, composition of consumption and production, and welfare.
Use the standard models of international trade to interpret and analyse problems and issues in international economics.
Evaluate the incentives and welfare consequences of offshoring.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON7001 and ECON7004 or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Labour Economics
syllabus_overview: The course teaches core topics in the field of labour economics as well as introduces empirical methods for applied microeconomic analysis. The aim of this course is to encourage development of independent research interests in labour economics and related fields. Topics include wage and employment determination, formation of human capital, labour market discrimination, immigration, unemployment, wage differentials, wage structure, and institutions in the labour market. There will be particular emphasis on the interaction between theoretical and empirical modelling.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the interactions between aggregate economic forces and identify the role of firms, workers and government in the economy.
Collect data and analyse the integral concepts of labour market issues (such as unemployment, taxation, educational choice, wage differentials, discrimination, etc.).
Critically analyse research in labour economics and understand underlying assumptions.
Model and analyse the structure of labour markets and their frictions.
Apply advanced econometric tools to analyse labour market related processes and develop practical understanding of statistical inference issues.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: ECON7001 and COMM8102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Economics
syllabus_overview: The course provides an economic approach to the analysis of health and medical care markets. Topics covered include the production of health, the production and consumption of medical care, the role of health as human capital, the relation between health and wealth, health insurance and the problems of adverse selection and moral hazard, the health workforce and the training of health professionals. Throughout the course reference is made to current government health policy.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the different market environments in which health and health policy decisions must be made.
Apply a rational approach in evaluating government intervention and programs in health, and critically evaluate health economics research papers.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
Explain and analyse the underlying economic frameworks appropriate for studying health and health care.
Analyse market failures in the provision of health care and evaluate the justifications for government policy.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON7001 and ECON7004 or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Measurement
syllabus_overview: ​Economic measurement shapes how economists understand data, evaluate policy and interpret economic performance. This course covers the theory and practice of measuring key economic indicators, including the Consumer Price Index, Gross Domestic Product and productivity growth. You will examine approaches used by international statistical agencies and consider how policy implications can depend on measurement techniques. The course is technically rigorous, drawing on microeconomic theory, econometric analysis and recent international research developments. By the end of the course, you will have a stronger foundation for understanding data sources, uses and reliability, and for applying rigorous reasoning to economic measurement problems at an advanced research level.​

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microeconomic Theory II
syllabus_overview: ​Market design uses microeconomic theory to analyse and improve the rules that govern allocation and exchange. This course introduces advanced tools and topics in microeconomic theory, with a particular focus on market design. The course is intended for graduate students who want a strong background in microeconomics for research in applied fields, as well as students seeking to specialise in economic theory. You will study a broad range of topics through the lens of auction theory and mechanism design. Most of the course focuses on economic applications, with some sections devoted to developing new tools needed for those applications. By the end of the course, you will be better prepared to understand recent research and to develop analytical models for future independent research.​
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the limitations of standard economic paradigms, such as the assumptions underlying homo economicus or efficient markets.
Evaluate alternative modern approaches to the design of better economic institutions.
Work collaboratively to complete tasks.
Analyse technical contributions to the microeconomic literature, including the construction of original models as part of thesis work.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Learning and Teaching: Language, Literacy and Numeracy
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST2003 This course will engage in substantive exploration of key concepts, issues, and debates in language, literacy, and numeracy education, with particular reference to the language, literacy, and numeracy demands of the school curriculum and pedagogy. It draws on current research to identify likely areas of difficulty in language, literacy, and numeracy learning and discusses effective teaching strategies for learners, including English as an additional language/dialect learners.
learning_outcomes: Integrate theoretical perspectives about language, literacy and numeracy with subject area knowledge and teaching practice and apply these understandings to reflect on and improve teaching practice
Identify the constraints and opportunities shaping language, literacy and numeracy teaching and learning in classrooms
Analyze the English language, literacy and numeracy demands of schooling and identify equity implications and issues for diverse students’ access to and achievement in the academic curriculum
Apply this knowledge to designing a range of language, literacy, and numeracy-developing tasks as well as develop effective teaching strategies with EAL/D students in the mainstream.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Experimental and Behavioural Economics
syllabus_overview: This course is meant to deepen students’ understanding of the experimental method of investigation in economics and business research. It is being offered at the Honours/MEc/PhD level. In the course we will review questions of experimental design and implementation such as appropriate procedures of subject recruitment, programming tools, statistical and econometric analysis of experimental data, and other methodological issues in experimental economics. Importantly, students will develop their own experimental pilot project, from design over programming and the actual implementation to the analysis and write-up of a research paper. Grading will rely on two class presentations (design presentation 10% and results presentation 20%) and a research paper (70%).
learning_outcomes: be able to present an experimental design, its implementation, and experimental results to a professional audience
demonstrate an understanding of the experimental method
be familiar with all aspects of design and implementation of experiments, such as recruiting, ethics, programming, and the conduct of experimental sessions
understand the advantages and disadvantages of the method
develop a basic experimental design to test an appropriate research question
evaluate the appropriateness of this method to study certain research questions

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Development and Political Economics
syllabus_overview: This course covers theory, evidence and current issues at the intersection between development economics and political science. We will focus on selected topics, aimed to provide an integrated understanding of some critical aspects of the political and institutional circumstances around economic development and the tools used by economists to analyse the roots of economic and political development. At the end of this course, students will have an in-depth understanding of the distinction between some of the functional causes of economic (under)development and be able to assess the potential effectiveness of proposed policies. Furthermore, students will have the tools necessary to carry out independent critical analyses of institutions and their effects on economic development.
learning_outcomes: Describe and critically analyse the interplay between markets and institutions in causing and perpetuating economic (under)development.
Critically assess the potential effectiveness of various policies that aim to promote economic development.
Identify causes of collective action failure and appreciate institutions that favour efficient collective action.

The course covers a broad array of topics analysed through the lens of behavioural economics. Most time will be spent on developing new tools, but economic applications will also be covered.

Construct simple microeconomic models from first principles.
Synthesise ideas through succinct and clear work that communicates ideas in a logical, professional manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ECON7001 and ECON7004 or approval from PG coordinators of Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Educational Psychology
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: An introduction to the study of Educational Psychology which examines some aspects of development and of learning and instruction. Topics include: cognitive development, development of memory, the role of knowledge, problem solving and thinking, an introduction to instructional methods.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of knowledge base in the development of expertise and differences between experts and novices
Explain the significance of work by prominent educational psychologists
Apply knowledge of the human memory system to evaluating teaching and learning procedures
Explain the basic concepts of a cognitive perspective in Educational Psychology
Explain how knowledge is constructed and its relationship with the memory system
Explain the main characteristics of major structural components of human memory

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Social Perspectives in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Do schools reduce or reinforce inequalities based on social, cultural, economic, and gender differences? What makes schools effective? Is education a public good or a private commodity? And what is the role of teachers, given that most research shows that schools only play a small role in explaining differences in how children do in school? By the end of this course, you should be able to discuss these four key questions. To do so, the course uses equity and social justice as key themes, and current research in educational sociology as evidence. You should complete the course with a critical understanding of how education, teachers and teaching interact with society.
learning_outcomes: Examine, discuss and evaluate education policies such as those relating to low-SES, race, and multiculturalism.
Describe, discuss and analyse the relationships between educational outcomes of school students and the differences between schools and within schools.
Identify and explain the relationships between family background factors such as SES, race and gender and the educational outcomes of school students.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Literacy in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher this course provides you with knowledge about language and children’s language and literacy development. It will introduce you to the socio-functional theory of language; how children learn to mean nonverbally and verbally in early childhood; and how they perceive and create meanings orally, in written language and multimodally in primary school years. You will also explore differences and diversity in language and literacy development among bilingual children and children with language development delay. This course develops your synthesis and analytical skills to gather and evaluate research information about diverse children’s language and literacy development and analyse their needs.
learning_outcomes: Reflect school practice against the content knowledge obtained in the course
Identify and label language functions and expressions
Analyse children’s language and literacy work samples for types and expressions of meanings (e.g. phonological, lexio-grammatical and nonverbal)
Evaluate children’s language and literacy work samples for their needs
Synthesise and critique research information about diverse children’s English language and literacy development and needs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of History and Geography in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to develop content knowledge that underpins the teaching of Human Society and its Environment. As a pre-service teacher you will engage with the necessary knowledge of Australian history and geography from a personal, local, national and global perspective; as well as engaging with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander history and culture. You will develop content knowledge on the complex factors that have shaped Australia as a nation including British colonisation and Indigenous peoples, the development of democracy, and migration. You will investigate Australia’s identity through geographical concepts including place, environment, sustainability and change. You will also develop an understanding of geography as an interaction of people, places and environments across a range of scales. In this course you will develop knowledge of the skills required to acquire, process and communicate geographical information so as to better understand your role as responsibly informed global citizens. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing the skill of inquiry learning; being able to evaluate sources of data (both primary and secondary) as being reliable; identify bias and different perspectives; critically analyse findings; and draw and present conclusions using the appropriate contextual language in a range of communication forms.
learning_outcomes: Engage with issues at a personal, local, national and global level as active and responsible global citizens
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and understanding of Australia’s identity through geographical concepts including place, environment, sustainability and change
Understand primary-school aged children’s knowledge and skills development in learning about Australian history and geography

Evaluate data and information for reliability and bias; represent data and information in appropriate forms; interpret data and information gathered; analyse findings and results; draw conclusions; analyse and use sources
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and appreciation of the complex factors that have shaped and continue to shape Australia as a nation historically

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Science in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a preservice teacher, this introductory course provides you with a foundation to primary school scientific subjects and content. You will study concepts from the earth, space, biological, and physical sciences as they relate to the NSW Science K-6 Syllabus. This course also aims at developing your skills in communicating scientific findings and using technology for teaching.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how to apply the scientific method to conduct scientific investigations within the primary school classroom
Identify how various technologies can be applied across a range of activities
Demonstrate an understanding of the content within primary school science
Communicate science to a range of audiences

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of the Arts in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with fundamental knowledge of The Arts in education. You will examine the basis on which learning in the visual and performing arts is grounded and the nature of students’ learning progression in the primary years of schooling. As a means for exploring and researching the disciplines of Visual Arts (including Media Arts), Music, Dance and Drama this course introduces you to a conceptual framework comprising the core and essential concepts of arts practitioner, artwork, audience and subject matter. You will learn to apply this framework in your own research of instances of arts practice and draw links to ways arts practices can be explained and interpreted. Through this research you will examine the different artforms in each discipline, how artists make artworks, how works are consumed and valued by different audiences on personal, community, symbolic and critical levels, and what artworks represent about our local, national and global societies, including Australian, Indigenous Aboriginal, Asian and international artists from historical and contemporary contexts. This course also develops your skills in critical interpretation when examining and interpreting different forms of art.
learning_outcomes: Research, interpret and explain the relationships between artists/practitioners, audiences, artforms and subject matter in the representation of meaning in each Arts discipline
Conceptualise, synthesise, evaluate and develop a range of resources, including digital resources, to demonstrate understanding of practice in the Arts
Demonstrate a broad knowledge and understanding of the concepts, substance and structure of the Arts as distinct disciplines in local, national, global and Indigenous contexts
Analyse research on how children learn conceptually and practically in Arts disciplines

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides preservice teachers with fundamental knowledge about engagement with, and discussions about, mathematical concepts which have been shown to be relatively challenging for students to understand. Concepts, aligning with the NSW syllabus include: proportional reasoning that underpins understanding of fractions, decimals, percentage, scale, similarity, and probability; variation and uncertainty; and generalisation. These concepts are relevant across the number and algebra, measurement and space, and statistics and probability curriculum strands. Preservice teachers will deepen their procedural knowledge and conceptual understanding of these mathematical concepts with an emphasis on building their confidence, and appreciation of the interconnected nature of mathematical content and the role of mathematics as a critical tool to address problems of global significance as well as personal relevance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and analyse mathematical resources
Solve a variety of problems requiring a varying degree of mathematical thinking
Demonstrate knowledge, skills and attitudes appropriate to mathematics and the teaching of mathematics
Meet the equivalent of HSC Band 4 level competence in mathematics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Professional Engagement
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Subject Area: Education This course provides an opportunity for students to understand the structure and practice of education in NSW and appreciate the cognitive and societal factors that shape students' experiences and educational outcomes. Through a university-based seminar and 15 days of school-based fieldwork, the course enables students to observe and interact with a diverse range of students and professional educators and to actively reflect on the teaching and learning that is taking place in an educational institution. Note: In order to undertake professional experience placements, you must: meet eligibility criteria; understand the policies and procedures that apply to professional experience placement; and provide satisfactory evidence of the NSW Mandatory Compliance Documentation (via InPlace).
learning_outcomes: Follow the key principles described in codes of ethics and conduct for the teaching profession, and the relevant legislative, administrative and organisational policies and processes required for teachers according to school stage.
Identify and describe the learning strengths and needs of students from diverse linguistic, cultural, religious and socioeconomic backgrounds and the implications for teaching.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 72 UOC overall, including EDST1108 or EDST2009. Students must have passed LANTITE.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Motivation in Learning and Teaching
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Drawing on a range of contemporary motivational theories, this course considers their implications in the school context, with a focus on learning and teaching. These seminal theories serve as a foundation to an extensive empirical research base that enables students to learn about the nature of motivation in their own lives, with an emphasis on learning and educational settings. It also supports teachers to apply a range of practical strategies and techniques in their own pedagogy.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of contemporary perspectives on motivation
Apply motivational theories to learning and teaching situations
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Critical Issues in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course critically examines issues and innovations of contemporary relevance in state, national and global curricula. You will learn about the history and significance of curriculum innovations including learning progressions, general capabilities, and the integration of curriculum perspectives across disciplines and how these developments shape the role of the teacher, students, subject content and the broader purposes of schooling. Using social, philosophical and ethical frameworks you will evaluate the impact of these developments on education, discipline content, learning and teaching in the 21st century context.
learning_outcomes: Acquire and/or improve, through philosophical examination, the use of the critically reflective skills of explanation, evaluation, analysis and argumentation
Critically reflect on the conceptions of, purposes for, and goals of education, and how these relate to the student, the teacher, discipline content and schools
Critically examine contemporary curriculum developments and their impact on learning, curriculum construction, classroom pedagogy and assessment
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Communication Skills for Teachers
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will improve your reading, writing and oral communication, and enhance your ability to communicate effectively with students, parents and other key stakeholders using a variety of skills and strategies. The course has a particular focus on intercultural understanding and language and literacy development for teachers new to Australian educational contexts.
learning_outcomes: Assess their own language and literacy skills and those of their students
Generate and implement strategies for ongoing improvement
Communicate effectively with students, parents and other key stakeholders in a range of different modes and contexts
Demonstrate the required language and literacy skills to gain teacher accreditation
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1, and enrolment in an Education program. Please contact the School of Education for enrolment

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Perspectives in Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The course code for this course was previously EDST1108. Teachers hold significant responsibilities to support, implement, respect, and learn from Indigenous perspectives in the classroom and in educational communities. In this course, you will learn how to enact this responsibility in classroom teaching, schooling, educational policy, and other professional practices. First, you will reflect on and locate yourself, your beliefs, and your perspectives as a future teacher in relation to land, language, culture, time, place, and relationships. You will then learn how this positionality impacts and informs your responsibility as a teacher, and helps you understand your students and their learning needs. Finally, you will engage with a range of Indigenous perspectives, research, theory, policy, and evidence to critically evaluate teaching resources and scenarios. This course will shape your professional practice in teaching in Australia or in other places that have their own histories of occupation, colonisation, or custodianship.
learning_outcomes: Identify, evaluate and justify curriculum and pedagogical practices in relation to Indigenous education
Explain what the professional, political and personal responsibilities of an educator are in relation to Indigenous education
Develop suitable skills and strategies to work effectively as a teacher with diverse Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders peoples, perspectives, and histories
Respect and value Indigenous sovereignties and the ability to genuinely promote Reconciliation through education
prerequisites: Prerequisites: 24 UOC overall, including EDST1101 and EDST1104, and either EDST1003 or EDST2003.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced TESOL Methodology
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you gain new or updated skills in the specialist TESOL field. You engage with (advanced) language teaching methodology and its practical applications through a program of seminars and online interactions. Topics cover different approaches to English language learning and teaching, including effective teaching strategies and techniques for teaching reading, writing, listening and speaking, materials development, and the planning and evaluation of individual lessons and units of work. The role of ICT and the internet is addressed as an integral part of the whole course.
learning_outcomes: Integrate key theoretical and practical issues and debates around contemporary TESOL teaching methods and techniques in lesson plans
Evaluate and adapt teaching and learning materials to suit students' own teaching context, based on their understanding of the relevant research literature
Identify, describe and critique the underlying principles of TESOL methodology
Critically analyse the strengths and weaknesses of different methodological approaches to TESOL and the implications for students' own teaching situation
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST3200 and enrolment in program 4072 Education (Primary)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Early Learning of Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with wide knowledge of mathematics content and mathematical applications. Special emphasis is put on your confidence, enthusiasm and finding meaning to learn, apply and teach mathematics. The course introduces you to the key mathematical concepts in the Australian curriculum, focusing on a few key understandings including reinforcing concepts considered earlier in the program (proportional reasoning, uncertainty and variation, and generalisation). You will also learn how the foundational mathematics skills can be scaffolded to move learners forward from early stages of learning towards increasingly sophisticated ideas. During the course you will become familiar with literature and learn to reflectively develop as a teaching professional.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the diversity of mathematics content, its applications and what working mathematically means
Reflectively develop as a mathematics teaching professional, understanding the value of the subject and demonstrating enthusiasm to teach the subject
Demonstrate understanding of educational research and the goals of curriculum documents related to mathematics content
Apply evidence of early learners’ mathematical development of mathematics to design learning activities
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1311

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Culture, Identity and Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines various theorizations of identity and culture, investigating how different conceptualizations of identity and culture constrain and/or enable particular educational responses to a range of sociopolitical and socioeconomic issues, at the societal, institutional, classroom and individual level.
learning_outcomes: Develop a critical understanding of key concepts, issues and debates in relation to the notions of culture and identity
Develop a critical understanding of the intersection of issues of culture and identity with education; and how particular views of culture and identity differentiate students
Develop the critical capacity to evaluate different views of diversity in relation to the future of education and schooling in Australia within the wider context of globalization and cosmopolitanism
Identify the role of language and discourse in sustaining and/or challenging particular power relations among cultures and identities
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit at Level 1

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Creative Arts (K-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be provided with knowledge and skills in the field of Creative Arts in education. Experiences in the areas of Visual Arts, Music, Dance and Drama will develop your pedagogical knowledge and understanding of the distinctive nature of each discipline. You will develop a critical appreciation of the unique contributions the arts make to society and how these contributions can be engaged with, and interpreted in, the primary school classroom. Pedagogical principles, theoretical components and practice within Music, Visual Arts, Drama and Dance are examined and applied in the design and implementation of classroom practices in school settings. Students should have completed EDST1244 before undertaking this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply an understanding of diversity within and across the arts in educational settings.
Plan and implement developmentally appropriate creative arts learning experiences for a diversity of primary learners.
Employ a broad knowledge and understanding of the creative arts as distinct forms of representation, skill and knowledge.
Integrate understandings of content, concepts and pedagogy across all strands of the creative arts.
Develop an appropriate range of resources which involve the integration of the creative arts and ICT.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1244 and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Problem Solving in Mathematics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with knowledge, confidence and interest to understand and use mathematical problem solving in your teaching of mathematics and to build the problem solving capacities of your students. The course introduces you to three types of mathematical problems: 1) abstract riddles that have historically entertained people and assisted the development of the thinking skills of humankind, 2) modelling problems requiring the application of mathematical theories into real life situations, and 3) interdisciplinary challenges people are facing in the future that require out of the box thinking. You will consolidate your foundational mathematics skills and become confident users of mathematical ideas. During the course you will become familiar with the intertwined development of mathematics and humankind.
learning_outcomes: Identify the role of mathematics in life challenges in general
Solve a variety of problems requiring a varying degree of mathematical thinking
Demonstrate competence in using mathematical problems as affordances in teaching
Gradually develop an identity as a mathematics teaching professional responding to the educational goals but also wider challenges of the future of a mankind
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST3380 or EDST6780, and enrolment in program 4072 Education (Primary)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematics 1 (K-2)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will be introduced to the continuum of mathematics learning K-6, with reference to the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. There will be a focus on evaluating and teaching number concepts, taking into account the range of developmental understanding and student ability prior to school entry. The emphasis will be on the pedagogical approaches and teaching strategies suitable for Early Stage 1 and Stage 1 which will develop your understanding of the three strands in the NSW Syllabus - Number & Algebra, Measurement & Geometry, and Statistics & Probability. There will also be a focus on the formative and summative assessment strategies needed to evaluate student progress in the early years. Students should be enrolled in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program and have completed EDST2112 before undertaking this course.
learning_outcomes: Select, design and apply relevant digital tools to support mathematical understanding and learning.
Implement a broad and critical understanding of the NSW Mathematics K-10 syllabus. Select appropriate concepts, sequence and connect lessons, and map progress.
Evaluate and appropriately use teaching resources such as calculators, games, hands-on materials, and puzzles.
Identify and communicate mathematical concepts underpinning the development of mathematical knowledge, skills and understanding, using appropriate terminology.
Identify and describe a range of home and community numeracy practices, including the impact of parental/carer attitudes and different cultural systems including Australian Indigenous communities.
Identify and apply a range of assessment and pedagogical strategies suitable for different developmental stages and levels of understanding in mathematics.
Identify and apply engaging teaching activities and materials to accommodate diverse student abilities (including gifted students).
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST2112, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Early Reading Instruction
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will learn how to teach children how to read. Among the range of approaches to early reading instruction, evidence best supports reading instruction that is explicit, systematic, and sequenced. Such instruction includes the components of phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, and oral language development. You will learn what these skills are, how to teach them, how to assess them, and how to respond with evidence-based interventions to develop early reading skills. Students should have completed EDST1120 before undertaking this course. Students should not be enrolled in EDST3221 and EDST3200 before completing EDST3182.
learning_outcomes: Assess children's reading in relation to phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, comprehension, and oral language.
Teach children how to read.
Describe a range of approaches to teaching reading and identify those supported by evidence.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1120, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Teaching Reading and Viewing in the Years 3-6 Syllabus
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course prepares you for teaching 21st century literacy with focus on the teaching of reading and viewing of written and multimodal texts in printed and digital platforms that students from years 3-6 encounter in the English and other subject areas. For the English subject, you will be introduced to a range of children’s literary genres by Australian, Indigenous Aboriginal, Asian and international authors in conventional and contemporary media including novel, picture book, graphic novel, and film. You will also learn about key English textual concepts as well as language and multimodal resources for constructing these concepts. For other subject areas, you explore a range of factual texts and their distinctive language and visual features. Building on the subject content knowledge, you will develop your understanding of curriculum documents relating to Reading/Viewing and content pedagogical knowledge at macro (programming), meso (lesson planning) and micro (teaching delivery) levels. The course also introduces you to technological applications that can be used for teaching Reading and Viewing and pedagogies to differentiate instructions for diverse learners.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and select appropriate literature and factual texts to be used as teaching resources

Create a program for teaching Reading/Viewing in the English and other curriculum areas including a teaching and learning sequence, detailed lesson plans, assessment and differentiation activities for diverse learners
Analyse and evaluate written and multimodal texts for prominent textual features to develop a scope and sequence of teaching content
Use technology to develop teaching resources for teaching Reading/Viewing and deliver the teaching of multimodal digital texts
Report on students’ Reading/Viewing learning progression
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1120, and either EDST3182 or EDST6782, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Curriculum, Pedagogy and Assessment - Teaching Writing (K-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course prepares you with curriculum, content and pedagogical knowledge for teaching composition of oral, written and multimodal texts in the K-6 English syllabus. You will learn about children’s writing development processes from oral language, to letter, word and text composition. You will also learn about contemporary text creating practices required in the 21st century curriculum including drafting, composing and publishing. The course also introduces you to pedagogies to assist primary school students develop their creating competence including computer assisted pedagogies. In this course, you will learn to compose model texts to be used as teaching resources, analyse and evaluate teaching resources, and develop a program for teaching and assessing writing/creating with detailed lesson plans and activities to cater for learner diversity.
learning_outcomes: Use digital technologies to assist with developing teaching resources for teaching Writing/Creating and deliver the teaching of written and multimodal texts composition
Apply an understanding of the Writing/Creating process and various pedagogies to assist students throughout the process

Create a program for teaching Writing/Creating in the English and other curriculum areas including a teaching and learning sequence, detailed lesson plans, assessment and differentiation activities for diverse learners
Demonstrate an understanding of children’s writing development including the role of oral language in learning to write and the whole-body approach to learning to write in young children
Analyse and evaluate model texts and students’ writing samples
Report on students’ Writing/Creating learning progression.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1120, and either EDST3182 or EDST6782, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Society and its Environment (K-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment strategies, classroom management and development/selection of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of human society and its environment in the primary school classroom. Students will engage in the selection/development/evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of key concepts in human society and its environment.
learning_outcomes: Integrate HSIE learning to other KLAs.
Incorporate different types of learning experiences: project-based; strategies for local inquiry; using HSIE artefacts, sources and resources as the basis for research.
Articulate and demonstrate an understanding of why HSIE is taught in primary classrooms.
Include Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander histories and cultures in the curriculum in a respectful manner.
Plan and sequence learning programs and develop resources suitable for Stages across K-6.
Design successful learning experiences for primary students in HSIE.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1143, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Primary School Personal Development, Health and Physical Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a preservice teacher, this course provides you with essential knowledge of Physical Education skill learning and primary school Health content for teaching PDHPE in the Australian classroom. Through a practical approach, the course introduces you to the 12 Fundamental Movement Skills (FMS). You will learn the theoretical underpinnings of key elements of Health and Personal Development, with a focus on sensitive topics. This course also develops your understanding of how each of the focus areas of PDHPE (Movement Skill and Physical Activity; Respectful Relationships and Safety; Identity, Health and Wellbeing; and Self-Management and Interpersonal Skills) are interrelated and how they combine to create a holistic approach to teaching PDHPE.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how to differentiate movement skill learning for children of different physical and mental abilities
Demonstrate an understanding of the interrelatedness of the focus areas of PDHPE and the relationship between health promotion and health education
Identify and describe the topics which may be deemed “sensitive” within Health and Personal Development, within the context of the primary school classroom
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the movement skills relevant to a primary-school aged child, and how children learn these skills

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (K-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will focus on teaching the NSW PDHPE syllabus which covers physical, social, emotional, cognitive and moral development of students across K-6. You will explore key researchers and current findings in child and adolescent development, especially in relation to pedagogical issues and strategies for this age group. Integration of aspects of PDHPE in the other KLAs will be explored, along with the literacy and numeracy demands of the PDHPE syllabus. Students should have completed EDST4002 before undertaking this course. This course is complemented by a minimum of 5 days of supervised professional experience.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse theories and research in child and adolescent development and apply to classroom practice and behavioural management.
Design action plans and programs to foster personal responsibility, effective communication and interpersonal skills, resilience, goal setting and lifelong physical activity.
Identify and critically examine factors currently affecting the health, safety and well-being of young Australians.
Compare differences between skills of stability, loco motor and manipulative control of objects and how these contribute to success in sport.
Communicate effectively with community advocates and understand their role in educational settings.
Justify the inclusion of the interrelationship of strands within PDHPE in the school curriculum.
Identify physical, social, emotional, cognitive and moral development across K-6.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST4002, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Education: Inclusive Strategies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the field of special and inclusive education. It surveys the characteristics, training, and educational needs of students with a disability. The course emphasizes accommodating students with a disability in inclusive settings, including legal mandates and regulations; characteristics and educational needs of students with a disability; and evidence-based practices which can be used with these students in the general education classroom. By the end of the course, students will have a broad overview of the field and its key concepts, issues, and the relevant Department of Education policies. They will be conversant with the main categories of students with a disability and know some ways of accommodating for these students in the inclusive classroom.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to apply research-based decision making to select appropriate programming options for students with diverse needs.
Develop strategies to implement NESA syllabus documents including Life Skills outcomes and content, and additional literacy and numeracy support.
Understanding of differentiated instruction and layered curricula
Demonstrate proficiency in the knowledge of the current issues and attitudes affecting policymaking, identification of needs, and educational provision for diverse students in NSW.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 78 units of credit overall, including EDST2002, and enrolment in an Education Secondary program OR Enrolment in Bachelor of Education Primary (Honours) or Bachelor of Education Primary.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mathematics 2 (3-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will build on the knowledge, skills and understanding developed in EDST3179 Mathematics 1. The focus is on Stages 2 and 3 in the NSW K-10 Mathematics syllabus. You will engage in findings from contemporary research to explore pedagogical strategies suitable for developing student understanding of numeracy; and how this understanding supports mathematical understanding across Stages 2 and 3. Formative and summative assessment strategies suitable for this age group are included, along with skills needed to identify and analyse a range of data about students’ progress. You will also consider how to support learners as they transition to Stage 4 in Mathematics. Students should have completed EDST1311, EDST2112, and EDST3179 before undertaking this course. The course is complemented by a minimum of 5 days supervised professional experience.
learning_outcomes: Design and evaluate differentiated programs of work to engage and accommodate the diversity of student abilities (including gifted students).

Design and evaluate a range of pedagogical and formative and summative assessment strategies suitable for the full range of developmental stages and levels of understanding in the middle and primary years. Analyse quantitative and qualitative data to enhance the development of mathematics.
Apply a deep understanding of the NSW Mathematics K-10 Syllabus to select concepts, write programs, and map student progress across stages.
Evaluate and construct original and creative teaching resources to support differentiation.

Apply knowledge of how home and community experiences affect numeracy experiences and development. This includes the impact of parental/carer attitudes and different cultural systems, including Australian Indigenous communities.

Identify and explain how student development can differ for mathematics and numeracy; and demonstrate how both aspects are applied in student’s lives to meet a range of diverse social and cultural needs.
Design, evaluate, and apply relevant ICT tools to support mathematical understanding and learning, and develop numeracy skills.
Apply the mathematical concepts underpinning the development of mathematical knowledge, skills, and understanding using appropriate terminology to real-world situations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST3179 or EDST6779, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Science and Technology (K-6)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines the syllabus, curriculum planning, assessment and classroom management strategies relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary school classroom. You will engage in the selection, development, and evaluation of activities and resources relevant to the teaching of science and technology in the primary (K-6) classroom. The course aims to enable you to harness children’s natural curiosities to develop interest, enthusiasm, and knowledge for science and technology. Students should have completed EDST1200 before undertaking this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of how the skills, knowledge and understanding of the Science and Technology syllabus documents relate across strands and sub-strands for all Stages.
Apply knowledge of the nature of science, as well as knowledge of areas of scientific and technological content.
Identify and apply appropriate ways to harness children’s natural curiosities to develop interest and enthusiasm for science and technology.
Critically examine and evaluate relevant research and pedagogies to enable primary- aged students to engage and learn the skills and concepts of science and technology effectively.
Develop a unit of work which incorporates skill development embedded in effective learning experiences.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST1200, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Responding to Gifted and Talented Students
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the field of gifted education, delving into talent development and best practices for identifying and responding to the needs of gifted and talent students. Students will explore (a) models of giftedness, (b) domain-specific and general characteristics of gifted learners, (c) underachievement, (d) teacher responsibilities, and (e) differentiated instruction and curriculum design for all learners.
learning_outcomes: Describe current issues in the education of gifted students
Apply research-based decision-making to link identified characteristics with appropriate differentiated curriculum, teaching and learning.
Justify the need for multiple-criteria identification processes and procedures, and relevant provisions to meet the academic, social and emotional needs of gifted students
Match research on the cognitive and affective characteristics of gifted students to practical teaching strategies and individual learning needs
Differentiate teaching and learning for gifted students
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 78 UOC overall, including EDST6760, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program or 4072 Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing the Classroom Environment
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Classroom management and student engagement is the number one concern of all new teachers. This course provides students with both the theoretical and practical applications of classroom management principles necessary for new teachers to make professional decisions with respect to classroom management concerns. The focus of this course is on creating an engaging classroom environment and on positive behaviour interventions and support, including the evidence-based practices crucial to effective classroom management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to engage students effectively in the learning process.
Plan, manage and deliver productive lessons
Use strategies and tools to address the diverse learning needs of students and maintain learning engagement
Manage difficult behaviours and create a safe and productive learning environment
Develop and maintain a positive learning environment in the classroom
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 78 UOC overall, including EDST2002, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Secondary) program. Or 42 UOC overall, and enrolment in an undergraduate Education (Primary) program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Multiliteracies Education for the Multimodal Digital World
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As the world is facing a digital technology booming era, you will need to be well-prepared in terms of knowledge and skills to confidently participate in the 4.0 society. The aim of this course is to prepare you, as a pre-service teacher, for this compelling mission. You will be equipped with knowledges to integrate the learning outcomes from other curriculum areas such as Arts, Science, Technology and the Australian curriculum (v9)’s general capabilities in teaching the K-6 English curriculum. At the heart of this course is the teaching of multimodal digital literature adaptation for critical comprehension and creative composition. You will learn about key literary concepts and language and multimodal resources for realising these concepts. You will also learn to apply and critique technology assisted pedagogies for teaching critical comprehension and creative composition of literature and non-literature multimodal digital texts. The knowledge and skills gained in this course will also help you to design differentiated literacy instructions for struggling, high performing and EAL/D students by using multimodal texts for differentiated content, process and learning environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of multimodal digital literacy practices and texts in the present world
Use digital technologies to assist with developing teaching resources for teaching critical comprehension and creative composition of multimodal digital texts
Apply knowledge about literary concepts and multimodality to evaluate and analyse multimodal literary texts for relevant teaching content
Apply knowledge gained in this course to solve other traditional literacy education issues such as differentiated instructions for teaching reading/writing to struggling and high achieving students
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST3200 and enrolment in 4072 Education (Primary)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Honours Research Methodology
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an overview of the philosophical, practical, and ethical issues involved in designing and conducting research in education. Students will be introduced to the need to conceptualize research at multiple levels, including epistemology, theory, approach, and strategy. The course will also focus on data collection and analysis, and the interpretation of data.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate the ability to identify and implement an appropriate research design in response to a particular research issue.
demonstrate knowledge, understanding, and practical skills needed to analyze, explain, and critique qualitative research reports
demonstrate a theoretical understanding of and skills needed to design, conduct, and evaluate research studies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Honours Seminar 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: A seminar course for honours students in the School of Education preparing students for the writing of an honours thesis. Topics include using library resources for honours students including research consultation and access to databases; structuring and writing a thesis, gaining ethics approval for collecting data; constructing a conceptual framework for a thesis; researching and writing literature reviews; the role of theory in research and the use of theory in framing and conducting a research project in Education; planning and managing a research project; formal requirements for the thesis structure and presentation.
learning_outcomes: Begin to incorporate theory into a research project at a sophisticated level.
Gain an understanding of the requirements of academic research in consultation with an academic supervisor.
Understand and be able to satisfy the ethical requirements and responsibilities of researchers.
Write a thesis proposal and outline designed to embody the results of independent research.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Honours Seminar 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: A seminar course for honours students in the School of Education preparing students for the writing of an honours thesis. Topics include structuring and writing a thesis, research design; researching and writing thesis chapters; planning and managing a research project; thesis presentation.
learning_outcomes: Write a thesis designed to embody the results of independent research.
Demonstrate knowledge of ethical requirements and responsibilities of researchers by conducting an honours research project.
Incorporate educational theory into a research project at a sophisticated honours level.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in the Education honours program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reimagining Mathematics Education
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: As a pre-service teacher, this course provides you with opportunity to consider and engage with current issues in mathematics teaching. You will consider from a research perspective such things as: the evidence for and against particular pedagogical approaches to mathematics teaching that are recommended across a range of Australian educational jurisdictions; the role of technology, including AI, in teaching and learning mathematics; and the role of data, including data generated from standardised tests such as NAPLAN, school based tests, and teachers’ informal records, in informing mathematics teaching. In this course, you will gain experience in evaluating the quality of research evidence, arriving at justifiable positions on controversial issues, and articulating the research evidence for mathematics teaching practices that you intend to implement in your classroom.
learning_outcomes: Understand the role of research in informing mathematics education policy and guiding mathematics teaching practice.
Evaluate and critique research relevant to mathematics teaching and learning
Articulate and justify with reference to research, a personal position on at least one issue
Understand and articulate research based arguments for and against a range of topical issues in mathematics teaching and learning
prerequisites: Prerequisite: EDST3380 or EDST6780, and enrolment in 4072 Education (Primary)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Methods 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this course is to introduce you to the different research approaches, research methodologies and methods used in education research. This course will help you to formulate a research question, choose an appropriate research approach and methodology, including a rationale for methods for a research investigation in education. Note: This course is only available to EdPrDoc students.
learning_outcomes: Explain the relationship between different types of research questions, theory and methodology.
Formulate a research question consistent with an underlying research methodology for a high-quality research project in education.
Select and document an appropriate research approach and methodology, including a rationale for a high-quality research project in education.
Articulate a research plan for a high-quality research project in education.
prerequisites: Currently enrolled in program 1975 Education.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Methods 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course follows on from EDST5031. It builds on your understanding of different research approaches, research methodologies and methods used in educational research. It will prepare you to conduct a small research project, and includes instruction on the selection and application of appropriate methods for sampling, data collection and analysis. Note: This course is only available to EdPrDoc students.
learning_outcomes: Identify different qualitative and quantitative research methods and discuss issues related to data quality when conducting research in education
Develop data collection instruments consistent with an underlying research methodology for a small research project in education
Identify different qualitative and quantitative data analysis strategies and select appropriate strategies for a small research project in education

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Current Issues in Education 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides you with an understanding of the purpose of the literature review and conducting a quality literature review in education. The course will be conducted seminar style and is designed to help you to analyse, synthesise and evaluate literature to provide a theoretical or conceptual framework for a small research project in education. Note: This course is available only to EdPrDoc students.
learning_outcomes: Articulate key findings from a comprehensive review of theory and research from literature related to a research topic in education.
Analyse and evaluate theory and research in the academic literature related to a research topic in education.
Identify gaps in theory and research in the academic literature related to a research topic in education.
Synthesise related theory and research in the academic literature to support a theoretical or conceptual framework to guide a small research project in education.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Effective Communication in Education Contexts
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Strong communication skills are essential for success in learning and crucial for effective teaching. In this course you will be equipped with effective communication skills for interacting with a range of stakeholders in education contexts, including peers, colleagues, students and university staff. You will also learn how to effectively employ different text types and modes of communication. The course has a particular focus on developing capabilities in reading and writing texts common in education contexts. The course also focuses on increasing your confidence and effectiveness in a range of oral communication activities, including class discussions, online interactions, collaborative group activities and class presentations.
