institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Personal Financial Planning
syllabus_overview: This course equips you with the essential knowledge and practical skills to effectively build, manage, invest, and protect your personal finances throughout your life. Tailored for university graduates, it delves into critical financial topics, including assessing your current financial situation, setting long-term goals aligned with your values and ethics, and creating a roadmap to achieve financial independence. You will explore key areas such as career planning, home ownership and debt management, tax planning, risk identification and management, and selecting the right investments to reach your financial goals. This course provides a comprehensive foundation to help you take control of your financial future with confidence and the foundational knowledge to determine whether you are interested in pursuing a career in the wealth management industry.
learning_outcomes: Create personalised financial planning and investment strategies to achieve long-term financial goals, ensuring alignment with personal values, ethical considerations and evolving financial landscapes.
Explain the role of professional financial planners and the structured financial planning process they use to provide advice to their clients.
Analyse and critically assess financial and investment concepts.

Demonstrate key personal financial planning and investment strategies, including effective household budgeting, property acquisition, debt management, retirement savings, tax planning, risk management and building a diversified investment portfolio.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Corporate Finance
syllabus_overview: This course is an introductory course in financial management. It stresses the modern fundamentals of corporate financial decision making with special reference to investment, financing and payout decisions. While building upon introductory courses in accounting, economics and quantitative analysis, the course develops distinctive conceptual frameworks and specialised tools for solving real world financial problems at both the project and corporate level. The course is a blend of theory and practice. While diligent practice will make you competent in financial techniques, a good grasp of theory will help you think systematically about ways to solve a problem for which no existing technique is suitable or available.
learning_outcomes: Analyse individually and in teams the investment recommendations and evaluate their worth.
Construct financial models to value investment proposals.
Analyse using investment decision rules the financial value of corporate securities and projects.
Collaborate in teams and positively influence team members to solve complex problems and pitch investment recommendations.
Evaluate the fundamental value drivers of corporate securities and projects in terms of business nature, risk and return trade-offs, capital structure, cost of capital, and payout policies.
prerequisites: Corequisite: ACCT5930 and (ECON5103 or ECON5258)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Markets and Institutions
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will explore the key financial markets, institutions, and participants that shape the Banking and Finance industry. Whether you are planning your own financial future or preparing for a career in business or finance, this subject builds essential financial literacy to support confident decision-making and set you up for more advanced finance study. You will systematically examine major financial markets, the roles of participants, and the range of financial instruments they offer. This is an ideal starting point if you are interested in roles such as financial analyst, planner, CFO, or investment banker.
learning_outcomes: Explain the roles and interactions of financial institutions and market participants, including investors and intermediaries.
Simplify and convey complex financial concepts to a specific audience to influence their behaviour.
Apply principles of ethics to evaluate business practices and their impacts in the banking and finance industry.
Analyse the structure and function of key financial markets (debt, equity, foreign exchange, and derivatives), including the instruments traded and the role of major institutions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Investments and Portfolio Selection
syllabus_overview: This course develops a basic conceptual framework to understand modern investments. Students will develop a more complete understanding of the risk-return tradeoff and the effects of diversification. Using this knowledge, students will learn how to price assets, build investment portfolios, and evaluate alternative investment strategies in securities markets, including equities and fixed income. By completing a real-world portfolio optimisation task, students will learn how to apply the theory in practical settings.
learning_outcomes: Explain the limitations of the models in certain situations and the resulting implications for designing investment strategies.
Apply the standard models of asset pricing to measure, price and manage risk; value securities; and solve real problems in investments.
Analyse the operation of financial markets and common financial products.
Create an optimal investment portfolio by applying portfolio theory.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (COMM5005 or ECON5248 or COMM5011 or COMM5000 or COMM5501) OR (ACTL5101 AND ACTL5102) OR enrolment in program (5273 or 7273 or 8413 or 9273 or 8161 or 8750 or 8719) OR (REST0001 AND enrolment in program 8127 or 8318) OR (ECON5257 AND enrolment in program 8415 or 8409)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Corporate Finance
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with essential knowledge for managing exchange rate risk in multinational firms and financial institutions. It covers practical applications of currency forecasting, speculation, and hedging to inform international investment and financing decisions. The course offers a solid theoretical foundation in international finance, paired with hands-on experience through data analysis and scenario-based exercises. Students begin by examining international monetary policy and foreign exchange markets from a macroeconomic perspective before studying the determinants of exchange rates. The focus then shifts to the development of hedging strategies for mitigating the risks associated with exchange rate fluctuations. With a comprehensive understanding of hedging instruments established, the course progresses to firm-level applications, exploring how multinational corporations can strategically invest and secure financing in global markets while managing associated risks. By the end of the course, students will have a thorough grasp of the key principles and tools essential for effective global financial management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the international macroeconomic and political environments relevant to multinational firms.
Identify exchange rate risks and develop hedging strategies to address them.
Understand and evaluate multinationals' exposure to exchange rates.
Assess the different exchange rate systems across countries and identify the determinants of foreign exchange rates.
Demonstrate ability to effectively perform quantitative analyses as a team in the context of international finance.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or Corequisite: (FINS5513 or FINS5514) OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Portfolio Management and Modelling
syllabus_overview: Provides a foundation for analysis of portfolios: the dynamic selection of securities and management of funds. The course covers a wide range of financial models in the areas of investment analysis, portfolio theory, portfolio risk management, and investment style analysis.
learning_outcomes: Construct written work that is logically and professionally presented.
Explain the assumptions of standard models of portfolio management.
Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Build and analyse investment portfolios.
Use the standard models of finance theory to interpret and analyse real problems in portfolio management.
Gain an understanding of the effects of different portfolio management strategies over time.
Implement dynamic portfolio insurance trading strategies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or Corequisite: FINS5513 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Capital Budgeting and Financial Decisions
syllabus_overview: Capital Budgeting and Financial Decisions explores the critical financial choices that shape a firm's success. These decisions - where to invest, how to finance growth, whether to distribute profits, and when to restructure - are at the heart of corporate strategy. In this course, you will explore key financial theories and examine real-world data and case studies to understand how businesses navigate complex financial landscapes. By applying these concepts to practical finance problems, you will develop the analytical skills needed to make sound financial decisions in professional settings.
learning_outcomes: Apply current knowledge of corporate finance theories to local or global businesses.
Infer and interpret the basic theories of corporate finance decision making.
Work collaboratively to analyse and communicate corporate finance concepts effectively in a structured and professional manner.
Use the standard models of capital budgeting, capital structure, dividend policy, and restructuring to identify, interpret, and analyse real problems in corporate finance.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (COMM5005 or COMM5011 or COMM5000 or COMM5501 or ECON5248 or FINS5511 or FINS5513) OR enrolment in program (8411 or 8413 or 8416)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Asia-Pacific Financial Markets
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory course on Asia-Pacific emerging markets. It provides an overview of issues that are relevant for an understanding and analysis of these markets. Topics include interactions of local institutions and finance, financial markets and instruments, corporate governance, financial crises, globalization, family business models, global fund management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective written and oral communication skills.
Examine and suggest solution to resolve issues in Asia-Pacific emerging markets.
Understand and analyse the financial issues involved in an Asia-Pacific emerging market.
Demonstrate the ability to recognize the benefits of teamwork; the ability to recognize social/ethical/cultural responsibility and awareness.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or co-requisite:(FINS5512 and FINS5513) OR (FINS5512 and FINS5514) OR enrolment in Program 8406 OR granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for 8476 program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Alternative Asset Classes
syllabus_overview: This course covers alternative asset classes, which can be understood as non-conventional asset classes not previously examined in mainstream finance courses. The course focuses on venture capital and private equity investments, as these are the most prominent types of alternative assets. Topics to be discussed include, but are not limited to, i) the venture capital industry in Australia (and other countries), and other sources of funds for financing new ventures (including angel investors, banks and other institutions), ii) venture fundraising and characteristics of venture capital firms, iii) characteristics of entrepreneurial ventures at different stages of development including: (a) Seed, Start-up, (b) Expansion, Mezzanine,(c) Buyout, Turnaround, iv) the characteristics of financial contracts in venture capital including the staging and syndication of deals, forms of finance (debt, convertible debt, preferred equity, convertible preferred equity, common equity, warrants, and combinations of these instruments), board representation, restrictive covenants and confidentiality agreements, v) exiting an investment through (a) initial public offerings,(b) mergers and strategic acquisitions and (c) secondary sales, buybacks, write-offs, vi) various entrepreneurial firm valuation techniques, vii) buyouts and going-private transactions including (a) buyout industry in Australia, (b) special features of buyout transactions and (c) Valuation of buyout deals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the business strategy of various entrepreneurial ventures and provide suggestions as to how they can raise financing for expansion.
Understand why the need for venture capital arises and its role in financing innovation

Use your knowledge of contracting problems in start up financing to predict likely conflicts of interest that arise in a venture capital setting and suggest methods and instruments that can be used to overcome them.
Explain how the structure of entrepreneurial financing arrangements alleviates some of the difficulties in funding new firms.
Understand the different methods for valuing a start-up and apply these methods to obtain a valuation for a real life start-up firm.
Construct written work which is presented in a logical, profession and convincing manner, with the aim of persuading a venture capitalist to provide funding.
Understand the nature of Alternative Asset Classes how venture capital and private equity investments compare to other alternative assets.
Understand the broader private equity market, with a focus on buyouts transactions including their negotiations and other key buyout deal characteristics
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (FINS5513 or FINS5514) OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Corporate Governance: Accounting and Finance Perspectives
syllabus_overview: Not available to students who have completed FINS3626 in the last three years. Aims to provide students with a practical and in-depth understanding of the way corporations are monitored, governed and controlled. Examines relationships and conflicts between key stakeholders (e.g. shareholders, managers, directors, employees, banks, regulatory bodies, etc.). Both internal aspects (e.g. performance evaluation, board structure, audit process, executive compensation, ownership structure, etc.) and external environments of corporate governance (legal protection of shareholders, hostile takeovers, proxy contests, bank monitoring, competition, etc.) are discussed in detail. The scope of coverage extends beyond Anglo-Saxon countries to examine issues in alternative governance systems adopted in Continental Europe, Asia and Latin America.
learning_outcomes: Consider the impact of corporate governance on financial reporting practices and the audit process, and on financing practices;
Critically evaluate and assess the strengths and weaknesses of different internal governance mechanisms;
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented;
Assess different external pressures on corporate governance and apply your knowledge to analyse real corporate examples and cases;
Understand the role and responsibilities of directors of public corporations;
Understand the principles of corporate governance and how they are applied in Australia and overseas;
Evaluate the impact of social and cultural differences on corporate governance mechanisms.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner during class discussions;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (ACCT5930 or ACCT5906) and (FINS5511 or FINS5513 or FINS5514) or enrolment in program 8426

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Personal Risk, Insurance, and Superannuation for Financial Advisers
syllabus_overview: This course covers insurance, personal risk management, and superannuation from a personal perspective for financial planning for individuals, families, and businesses. The course focuses on providing financial advice concerning the relevant areas through performing needs analysis and analysing the clients’ goals and objectives to provide appropriate advice and personal strategies to assist the clients in meeting their goals and objectives. The course covers the provision of compliant scaled financial product advice relating to the relevant area in the form of a Statement of Advice (SOA).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the Australian superannuation and social security systems, rules, and their taxation implications for providing personal advice to clients.

Demonstrate an understanding of the advisers’ responsibilities in providing insurance advice to clients, including the communication of client contractual rights, responsibilities, and the claims process for a range of insurance policies.
Develop strategies and communicate risk, insurance, and superannuation recommendations for personal advice, including constructing a statement of advice to the best interest duty standard.
Determine retirement planning needs in specific client situations and evaluate the appropriateness of various superannuation structures and products.
Demonstrate and apply an understanding of the critical elements of an insurance contract in the provision of personal insurance advice.
Demonstrate and apply risk management strategies to determine a client’s insurance coverage needs to the best interest duty standard.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Institution Management
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to the management of financial institutions, focusing on commercial banks. Your learning will focus on the importance of applying state-of-the-art risk management techniques to manage the varied types of risk that arise in bank operations. You will be first introduced to the important roles of financial institutions. Through a combination of basic and applied knowledge, students examine the principles of the theory and practice of defining and measuring various types of risk these institutions can be exposed to, and effective policies and strategies for successful risk management. You will also be introduced to international regulations and standards of banking practice and how they impact the functioning of domestic and multinational institutions.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and work effectively in teams and as individuals in solving financial institution problems.
Identify the strategic implications of evolving market and societal issues on financial institutions.
Apply relevant techniques for measuring, managing and monitoring financial institutions’ exposures.
Articulate the sources and management of risks faced by financial institutions.
Explain the importance of financial institutions in the economy.
Analyse the regulatory framework and its effects on financial institution capital.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or Corequisite: (FINS5513 or FINS5514) OR (enrolment in program 8406) or (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Real Estate Finance and Investment
syllabus_overview: This course exposes students to concepts, theories and the latest industry practice in commercial real estate finance investments. The course material presented is technical yet will strike a balance between theory and practice. This will help students acquire knowledge and develop the analytical skills for analysing commercial real estate finance investments. It also introduces valuation and appraisal methods used for real estate finance and investment decision making. These skills are of particular use to students who are interested in seeking employment as analysts in sales, leasing, construction and development management, research, consulting and investment banking.
learning_outcomes: Identify and assess environmental and sustainability considerations in problems in Real Estate.
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented.
Work collaboratively to complete a task.
Understand and apply generally recognised investment valuation techniques to real estate.
Distinguish between the different valuation approaches in real estate.
Conduct real estate investment analysis and make investment recommendations.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or Corequisite: (FINS5513 or FINS5561) OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Derivatives and Risk Management Techniques
syllabus_overview: An intermediate course on options, futures and techniques for managing asset risk. Topics covered include an overview of derivative securities, forward and futures contracts (on stock indices, investment and consumptive assets), options (on stocks, stock indices and futures), hedging positions in options and other derivative securities, binomial option pricing, risk-neutral valuation, the stochastic process followed by stocks, numerical techniques in option pricing, options on non-traded assets, exotic options and pricing biases.
learning_outcomes: Understand how to extend the binomial model to price American options on futures, indices, and currencies, as well as calculating the Greek letters for American options using binomial trees.
Understand the Black-Scholes option pricing model, including some of the mathematics behind the model (such as Wiener processes and Ito’s lemma).
Understand futures and forward contracts, using them for hedging, defining an optimal hedge ratio, and pricing them using no-arbitrage arguments.
Understand currency swap contracts, the comparative advantage argument, and their pricing.
Understand how to price call and put options using binomial trees, based on delta-hedging (no-arbitrage) arguments, and risk-neutral pricing.

Understand how to price options on futures, options on stocks paying dividends and dividend yields, and options on currencies. We also discuss the early exercise of American call options on these assets.

Understand and use the options Greek letters, which explain the price sensitivity of options to changes in underlying variables, such as the stock price, time, the risk-free rate, and volatility. Also, understand how the Greek letters help with hedging.

Understand options payoffs, using those payoffs to find (i) bounds on options, (ii) the put call parity relationship, and (iii) interesting combinations of options, while understanding the motivation for investing in them.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (FINS5513 or RISK5002 or RISK5003 or RISK5009) OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fixed Income Securities and Interest Rate Derivatives
syllabus_overview: Studies pricing, hedging and risk management of fixed income securities and interest rate derivatives. Includes: term structure dynamics (including bond price lattices, spot and forward rate models), analytical and numerical techniques, duration measures, interest rate derivative securities (including options, futures and swaps), the interaction between interest rate risk and credit risk, mortgage-backed securities and value-at-risk, the concepts of general collateral, an accessible treatment of the arbitrage-free models of the term structure, including the concept of state prices and no-arbitrage.
learning_outcomes: Understand interest rate futures and forward contracts and their market conventions, using them for hedging, defining an optimal hedge ratio, and pricing them using no-arbitrage arguments.

Understand how to price options on bonds using binomial trees, as well as Black’s formula, with volatility depending on the bond’s duration. Also, understand how to price caps, floors, collars, swaptions, and other related securities.
Understand interest rate swaps, including the comparative advantage argument, the pricing of floating rate debt, and the valuation of swaps.

Understand how to price mortgage-backed securities, including the timing risk due to the prepayment option. Understand some derivatives on mortgage-backed securities, such as interest-only and principle-only strips, and collateralised mortgage obligations (CMOs).

Understand the term structure of interest rates—that is, the relationship between a bond’s yield and its maturity—as well as the term structure of volatilities, and the relationship between a bond’s volatility and its duration.
Understand how to price options on zero coupon bonds and coupon bonds using the Hull-White model, which is similar to Black-Scholes, but with mean-reversion in the risk-free interest rate.
Understand the basics of bond pricing, duration and convexity, as well as duration-based portfolio management.

Understand features of corporate bonds, such as callability, convertibility, sinking fund provisions. Also, understand the Merton model of risky debt, the dilution effect caused by convertible debt and warrants, and the key features of CDSs and CDOs as well as the role they played in the global financial crisis.
Understand the definition of Value-at-Risk and apply it to bonds and options.
Understand how to model interest rates and bonds using binomial trees, based on delta-hedging (no-arbitrage) arguments, and risk-neutral pricing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5513 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Planning Advice and Ethics
syllabus_overview: This is a capstone course in the financial planning curriculum to provide students with a practical understanding of the provision of financial product advice and managing clients’ relationships. It consolidates and completes student knowledge and skills required for pursuing employment in the financial planning industry. The course a study of important aspects of ethics, professional standards and Chapter 7 of the Corporation Act to the standards set by the Financial Adviser Standards and Ethics Authority. The course also covers the different elements of financial planning advice including understanding the client's situation and needs, conducting analysis and research, formulating appropriate financial planning strategies, choosing suitable products, preparing a fully compliant financial plan, implementing the financial plan and providing ongoing review and services to the client. The course also covers the knowledge and skills required for providing personal life insurance and general insurance advice. It is a required course for professional recognition in financial planning.
learning_outcomes: Preparation and presentation of a comprehensive statement of advice
Demonstrate a working knowledge of the operations of the financial planning industry.
Demonstrate practical understanding of client relationships and practice management
Describe the main pieces of legislation governing the financial planning industry.
Explain the financial planning process and how to create a fully compliant financial plan.
Be able to discuss and write about the links between financial planning techniques and compliance and ethical issues.
Application of ethics and professional standards to the service of providing professional financial advice to clients
Critique practitioner’s perspectives on how to offer financial services.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 42 UOC and (FINS5561 or FINS5510)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Takeovers, Restructuring and Corporate Governance
syllabus_overview: This course comprises a complete, yet concise synthesis of the recent available literature and professional practices in the areas of takeovers, restructurings and corporate governance within a logical, analytical framework. Topics covered include the strategic rationale for business combinations; legal and commercial aspects of takeovers in Australia and the US; transaction structuring and financing; takeover tactics and defence; valuation and pricing of targets; and other forms of corporate restructuring, including private equity, LBOs and divestitures.
learning_outcomes: Develop critical and analytical skills, and be able to articulate research results in report format and oral presentation. Apply valuation models, particularly industry standard methods, including DCF and comparable companies analysis.
Work in teams to dissect information in cases, industry reports, financial statements and market-based data in order to evaluate M&A transactions.

Construct written work that is logically and professionally presented. Summarise your analyses and key findings in a highly succinct but effective sales pitch. Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
Demonstrate creative and innovative forward thinking to solve problems while working in a team environment.

Understand the takeover process, specifically the commercial, legal, tax and financial issues, in Australia and overseas markets. Appreciate the key principles of corporate governance and control strategies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (FINS5513 or FINS5514) OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Estate, Retirement Planning and Asset Protection
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with key estate planning knowledge and skills to provide clients a holistic financial and estate planning service. The course deal with the practical application of how an adviser deals with other professionals including lawyers, accountants, tax advisers, etc to help manage the clients’ estate planning needs, including issues related to succession planning and asset protection. The course consists of a theoretical element and a practical case study element addressing issues facing clients and practitioners in the advice space. It is a required course for professional accreditation.
learning_outcomes: Ability to identify possible estate and retirement planning strategy options.
Ability to define and determine requirement for retirement planning issues related to certain clients and the role of Superannuation/ SMSFs.
Preparation and presentation of a comprehensive statement of advice.
Ability to address key issues related to wills and appointment of power of attorneys.
Ability to define and determine key asset protection and succession planning issues related to certain clients.
Demonstrate a working and practical knowledge of estate and retirement planning relevant to the financial planning industry.
Demonstrate practical understanding of client relationships and practice management.
Dealing with complexity related to marriage breakdown, administering and estate, and asset transfer including superannuation and in particular SMSFs.

Critique practitioner’s perspectives on how to offer estate planning service to financial planning clients include dealing with other professionals (accountants, lawyers, etc) and managing the process.
Be able to understand and analyse client overall estate and retirement planning needs.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: FINS5510

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Finance
syllabus_overview: Sustainable finance is a rapidly expanding global industry that integrates long-term financial performance with positive environmental and societal outcomes. This course examines how finance and investment professionals influence sustainable economic activity by identifying risks, opportunities, and impacts arising from social, environmental, and governance considerations. Students will critically evaluate ethical frameworks, investment approaches, and regulatory developments shaping this dynamic sector. Through real-world case studies, rigorous data analysis, and academic research, students will design innovative investment strategies and products aligned with sustainability objectives and responsible business practices. This course equips students with the practical knowledge and analytical skills needed to lead and thrive in the evolving world of sustainable finance.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical decision-making frameworks to investment processes.
Identify and assess environmental, social responsibility and corporate governance issues and risks in investment decision making.
Propose and assess the impact of a socially responsible investment product and strategy.
Assess the state and practices in the socially responsible investing sector.
Articulate the roles and impact of finance and investment professionals in directing economic activities.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5513 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476) OR (18 UOC in postgraduate courses)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Investment and Advanced Funds Management
syllabus_overview: This course covers advanced topics in investments and active funds management. Namely : 1) equity valuation; 2) alternative investment classes; and 3) portfolio performance measurement and risk management. These topics are currently highly relevant to industry practice and widely adopted. The equity valuation part covers security analysis based on discounted cash flow analysis and relative valuation. The alternative investment part includes hedge fund strategies and factor-based investing. Commonly utilised methods in practice for portfolio performance measurement and risk management are also studied and applied. In addition to applications with real financial data, students are also exposed to relevant research.
learning_outcomes: Know how to apply the main methods of security analysis.
Solve real investment problems as valuing a stock or measuring the performance of a portfolio.
Understand alternative investment classes, the respective instruments and economic drivers.
Discuss merits and limitations of current methods of portfolio management.
Become familiar and discuss recent relevant research on financial investments.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5513 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cryptocurrency and Decentralised Finance
syllabus_overview: This course will give you an introduction to cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin and Ethereum and decentralised finance (DeFi). The course begins with a brief history of money before outlining the underlying cryptocurrency principles of blockchains. Ethereum and smart contracts are introduced, which form the basis of DeFi applications such as automated market makers, decentralised borrowing and lending markets, stablecoins, on-chain derivatives, DAOs and insurance. The course will also give a brief overview of blockchain scalability (layer 2 solutions), the evolution of fundraising, regulation and implications and applications in traditional finance. The course will involve practical activities with cryptocurrencies, trading on a DEX and creating your own cryptocurrency (ERC20 token).
learning_outcomes: Interpret the ethical implications of decentralised finance systems and applications in the global business context.
Appraise the purpose and value of decentralised finance systems relative to traditional finance based on existing research.
Explain key components of decentralised finance systems and make transactions using smart contracts.
Critically evaluate a Decentralised Finance protocol, addressing any technical and institutional limitations and planned proposals to address these.
Collaborate with peers in a virtual environment and apply problem-solving techniques to achieve goals efficiently and effectively.
Examine key developments of decentralised finance systems and their impact on the global business environment and communicate your findings clearly to non-technical stakeholders.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5512 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Toolkit for Financial Market Decisions
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to some of the computational tools and techniques necessary to navigate through recent technological advances in the financial services industry. Using a hands-on approach, you will learn how to write simple Python codes to solve a number of practical problems. Potential projects covered in the course include the collection of Internet-based financial data, real-time analysis of arbitrage opportunities, implementation of event studies, and asset pricing, along with related analytical methods. The concepts learned in this course will help you develop a Python toolkit, which can be extended to tackle more complex problems in both traditional Finance and FinTech.
learning_outcomes: Develop a kit of common tools used in the financial markets that can be applied in a variety of real-world settings.
Translate abstract financial theories into usable tools for competing in the finance workplace.
Implement alternative ways to collect, manipulate, and analyse data to answer questions related to market efficiency.
Evaluate implications of technological advances on the current and future states of the financial services industry.
Collaborate in teams to find solutions to real-world problems in the finance sector.
Apply state-of-the-art code-sharing techniques and version control systems to navigate a real-world team project.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: FINS5512 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Market Data Literacy
syllabus_overview: Financial market data literacy requires an understanding and appreciation of the connections between banking, finance and technology. This course builds the foundation and functional knowledge about financial market data by exposing various data handling, analytics and computational methodologies in applied form. In this course, you will develop skills in data handling in the context of banking and finance, gain exposure to state-of-the-art data modelling and analytics, and become proficient in the Financial Data Professional (FDP) Charter. This will involve drawing on real-world data problems and practical implications, and using the latest industry algorithmic solutions and Python programming scripts. Concepts are honed using a workshop-style approach in which students will interact with data in the virtual iLab.
learning_outcomes: Critically review and examine various data handling, analytics and computational methodologies.
Effectively apply algorithmic solutions and programming scripts to address real-world financial data problems.
Design, deliver and justify innovative data-driven solutions for the banking and finance sector.
Analyse, organise and interact with large sets of both structured and unstructured financial data.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5546 or (ECON5103 and enrolment in program 8959).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Funds Management
syllabus_overview: This is a laboratory and theoretical based course that develops fundamental concepts of asset valuation in a world with time varying risk, in order to construct and manage an investment portfolio. The course focuses on the recent advances in quantitative finance including risk modelling, forecasting, portfolio construction and evaluation. The aim is to provide students with a practitioner-orientated view of asset management where concern is based on generating superior returns. Topics focus primarily on empirical and practical tools required to actively manage an investment over time.
learning_outcomes: Explain standard approaches to quantitative analysis in investments.
Communicate time varying risk and portfolio management ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
Use quantitative methods in investment with computing skills in matrix programming and statistical software.
Construct written work in time varying risk and portfolio management which is logically and professionally presented.
Evaluate methods of quantitative analysis.
Work collaboratively to complete a group assignment.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: FINS5513 OR (enrolment in program 8406) OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Technology
syllabus_overview: This course examines the transformative landscape of technological advancements and their fast-evolving impact on the banking and finance industry across personal, institutional, and regulatory dimensions (collectively referred to as "FinTech"). It delves into innovative thought processes and frameworks designed to navigate complexity, foster new business opportunities, and manage risks effectively. Students will analyze the evolution of FinTech, exploring how these technologies are reshaping financial services, enhancing customer experiences, and creating new market opportunities. Topics include the evaluation of regulatory frameworks, strategic solutions for AI and blockchain integration, and the design of innovative financial products driven by data analytics. Through critical analysis on real-world use cases and collaborative projects, students will develop advanced competencies in assessing business models and formulating strategic solutions for modern financial challenges. The course culminates in a final group project, where students will propose a new FinTech startup idea that leverages the latest technological innovations, demonstrating their comprehensive understanding of the course material.
learning_outcomes: Analyze the transformative roles of FinTech solutions across various banking and finance domains, and evaluate the effectiveness of tools and methodologies in delivering ethical, responsible, and business-savvy solutions.
Examine the evolution of FinTech across global banking and finance ecosystems, the challenges and opportunities presented by technological innovations, and their impact on the financial industry.

Build knowledge in designing, building, and scaling FinTech platforms amidst rapid technological evolution, while also identifying essential building blocks for successful AI-powered FinTech innovations.

Collaborate with peers, applying a framework to develop and pitch an innovative FinTech solution that addresses specific market demands (or creating new ones), reflecting the transformation of banking and finance in the digital economy.

Assess the historical and current regulatory frameworks in FinTech, evaluating their effectiveness in addressing challenges posed by technological advancements such as AI, and identifying the necessary guardrails.
Analyze business models of real-world FinTech platforms, assessing their abilities to adapt and sustain themselves amidst the increasingly dynamic technological landscape shaped by AI advancements.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5546 or (ECON5103 and enrolment in program 8959).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Behavioural Approaches in Finance
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the concept of behavioural finance and its impact on financial markets and decision-making. We will introduce and investigate behavioural traits, including over confidence, confirmation bias and loss aversion and discuss how these traits can function as obstacles to the use of traditional finance tools as studied in other courses. We will also consider how best to avoid the pitfalls inherent in financial decision-making. At the end of this course, students will understand the nature and impact these psychological factors have on important business decisions.
learning_outcomes: Understand how cognitive biases predictably and consistently affect our decisions, and how our intuitions on how the mind works are faulty.
Apply this understanding to help promote more efficient financial decisions for different categories of actors (e.g., individual investors, professional traders).
Explain new concepts to fellow students, bring new ideas and convince the audience of their relevance, produce remarkable oral presentations.

Use knowledge learnt from this course to share with others novel insights on fundamental social questions such as: Why do some people gamble? Why do the elderly take excessive risks? Why do people save too little?
Understand how these biases affect the decisions of finance practitioners.
Prepare a group discussion in collaboration and teamwork.
Analyze the root cause of corporate malfeasance and suggest institutional innovations to improve modern business environments.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FINS5513 OR enrolment in program 8406 OR granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for 8476 program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: From Startup to Wall Street: Financing Innovation and Strategic Exits
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with the advanced tools and frameworks necessary to finance, scale, and strategically exit high-growth ventures. Moving beyond early-stage ideation, it delves into later-stage entrepreneurial financing, covering growth equity, venture debt, IPO preparation, mergers & acquisitions, and private equity buyouts. Students will learn to model venture cash flows under uncertainty, design optimal capital structures, manage investor relations, and evaluate exit pathways from both entrepreneurial and investor perspectives. The course combines rigorous financial analysis with practical strategy, preparing students to make high-stakes decisions as founders, CFOs, venture partners, or strategic consultants. No prior advanced finance required as we build your capability step by step.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate in teams to structure, model, and pitch optimal capital and exit strategies with strong financial justification.
Apply advanced financial strategies to evaluate later-stage funding instruments and make informed decisions on capital structure, growth financing, and risk under uncertainty.
Communicate financial strategies and exit plans clearly to diverse professional and investor audiences.
Design robust funding, valuation, and exit plans using advanced financial models and scenario analyses.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 42 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied AI for Finance
syllabus_overview: This course explores how AI is making transformative impact in the global financial sector and equips students with the knowledge and skills needed to succeed at the intersection of AI and finance. Topics of interests include, but not limited to AI in banking automation, predictive analytics for market intelligence, risk management and fraud detection, corporate finance, algorithmic trading, as well as asset and wealth management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the role of AI in the global financial sector and explain how banks and financial service providers shape and respond to its implementation.
Apply AI methodologies and coding skills to generate strategic solutions in banking and finance case studies, demonstrating awareness of key technological drivers.
Describe theoretical, conceptual and mathematical foundations of various recent AI techniques and methodologies and analyse application of these new techniques within finance and banking environment.
Use industry-level AI platforms to implement finance applications and critically assess the capabilities and limitations of AI systems.
Evaluate AI solutions in finance, incorporating principles of AI ethics and responsible use, and respond constructively to feedback in collaborative settings.
Explain the banking and finance ecosystem and evaluate its response to emerging AI methodologies within evolving regulatory frameworks.
Communicate AI-driven solutions effectively to professional industry audiences through structured presentations and pitches.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (FINS5512 or MFIN0001) AND (FINS5546 or COMM5007)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Capstone - Portfolio Management Process
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to develop and evaluate investment strategies using the analytical approaches employed by portfolio managers and investment professionals. Students will learn how to generate investment ideas, support them with financial and market data, assess risk, and communicate their recommendations in a professional investment pitch. Throughout the course, students will apply financial analysis, portfolio construction, and evidence-based decision-making to real-world investment opportunities. Emphasis is placed on developing practical skills in security analysis, data interpretation, risk assessment, and investment strategy design. These skills are relevant to careers in investment management, financial analysis, asset management, and related fields, while also providing a strong foundation for students with a personal interest in investing and portfolio management. By the end of the course, students will have gained experience in developing, evaluating, and presenting investment strategies that integrate financial theory with practical application in contemporary financial markets.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate investment opportunities using financial data, risk analysis, and market research.
Design portfolio strategies that align with defined investment objectives and risk profiles.
Communicate and justify investment recommendations using evidence-based investment analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 42 UOC and (FINS5513 or enrolment in program 8476)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Trading in Financial Securities
syllabus_overview: The course provides a practical insight into quantitative trading. It provides students with a comprehensive understanding of quantitative analysis in financial markets, emphasizing risk management and the development of effective trading strategies. Through theoretical concepts, practical exercises, and real-world applications, students gain knowledge in statistical analysis, algorithmic trading, market microstructure, risk management, and back testing. By the end of the course, students will have acquired the skills to analyse financial data, assess market dynamics, manage risks, and evaluate the performance of trading strategies through back testing.
learning_outcomes: Skills: Students will develop practical skills in back testing and performance evaluation, including the ability to design, conduct, and interpret back tests to assess the performance of trading strategies. They will also learn how to evaluate and optimize trading strategies based on the results obtained.
Application: Students will be able to apply statistical analysis and modeling techniques to derive insights from financial data, enabling them to develop and evaluate trading strategies.
Knowledge: Students will demonstrate a solid understanding of quantitative analysis in financial markets, including the different trading strategies employed and the importance of risk management.

Critical Thinking: Students will develop critical thinking skills in assessing market microstructure, analyzing order book dynamics, and understanding the impact of market liquidity on trading strategies.
prerequisites: Prerequisite FINS5512 OR (granted MFIN0001 48 Units of Credit in Admission Block Credit for program 8476) Corequisite: FINS5546 OR COMM5007

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Asset Pricing
syllabus_overview: This course provides critical understandings of the concepts and empirical approaches in asset pricing. Main topics include model testing, financial market anomalies, market efficiency, and asset management. This course exposes students to both conventional views and recent evidence on selected topics.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply basic empirical methods in asset pricing tests.
Critically assess and interpret papers in the field of empirical asset pricing.
Develop collaborative teamwork and research skills via completing a research paper.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner in written and oral communication.
Analyse data, develop and logically support hypotheses, and conduct empirical tests.
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented.
Synthesise and interpret major empirical findings in asset pricing literature.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 8161 or 8719 or 8759 or (FINSOS Banking & Finance Postgraduate Specialisation of the 8635 Program)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Asset Pricing Theory
syllabus_overview: This course is offered as part of and is required for the PhD, MPhil, Pre-Doctoral Studies Master, and Finance Honors programs. The course constructs the main theoretical foundations of asset pricing. A large emphasis is devoted to fostering our understanding of financial markets and, especially, of the role of investor preferences as a fundamental driver in the pricing of securities and investment decisions. The course covers the latest research focusing on the empirical determination and the theoretical explanation of various risk premia, such as those present in the equity, bond, and derivative markets.
learning_outcomes: Students will define and address finance problems, and propose effective evidence-based solutions, through the application of rigorous analysis and critical thinking and problem solving.

Students will interact and collaborate effectively with others to achieve a common business purpose, fulfil assignment, and the presentation project, and will reflect critically on the process and the outcomes.

Students will harness, manage and communicate finance information effectively using multiple forms of communication across different channels. Students will communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.

Understand financial markets, asset returns and risk, decisions under uncertainty, role of investor preferences, term structure of interest rates, incomplete/asymmetric information, derivative assets, default risk, and equilibrium asset pricing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Corporate Finance
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to prepare Honours and Ph.D. students to do research in Empirical Corporate Finance. The course is organised around published and working papers in the field with an emphasis on econometric methods and the publication process. Rather than providing an exhaustive overview of the field, the course focuses in depth on selected topics to illustrate different empirical approaches. Using papers from various sub-fields of corporate finance, the course will attempt to expose students to issues of identification, endogeneity, and instruments. The course will also attempt to strengthen your ability to digest and critique academic research. Finally, it will help improve your presentation skills through constructive feedback.
learning_outcomes: Develop effective oral communication skills to communicate research ideas and issues in a clear and logical manner.
Demonstrate and apply leadership skills through initiation of a research project.
Demonstrate and relate the understanding of the appropriateness of empirical research techniques in various contexts.
Apply the principles of good empirical work to complete a data exercise (mini-research).
Analyse and synthesise written work which is logically and professionally presented.
Review global research.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Methods in Finance 2
syllabus_overview: Research Methods in Finance 2 is an advanced course on empirical research in finance. Course topics encompass (i) econometric theory and methods, (ii) data collection and management, and (iii) programming. The course establishes a unified framework for analysing three econometric methods (least squares regression, maximum likelihood, and generalised method of moments). These econometric methods are applied to topics in corporate finance and asset pricing. The data section of the course covers appropriate use of database management systems, such as SAS and SQL. Programming is taught using general-purpose languages so that students learn how to write structured, modular program design. Programming examples are geared towards solving common problems in Financial research. Throughout the course, specific topics are selected to reflect student's interests
learning_outcomes: Analyse empirical questions to identify and discuss characteristics that make econometric identification challenging.
Critique research papers in the field, evaluating key assumptions in the work and conclude any potential violations therein.
Write programs using a general-purpose programming language to solve basic problems found in research.
Execute empirical techniques used in finance by applying OLS, MLE, and GMM to real problems.
Combine financial datasets and solve data-related issues commonly encountered by researchers.

Evaluate and illustrate common features of and key differences between Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE), and Generalised Method of Moments (GMM) from a theoretical perspective.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Empirical Corporate Governance
syllabus_overview: This course explores a number of empirical questions and statistical techniques from corporate finance, with application to topics in corporate governance. Topics covered include applications of agency theory and optimal contracting theory, an overview of internal and external corporate control mechanisms, and a survey of major methodological approaches used in this research area including their strengths and weaknesses. The primary topics to be covered are corporate boards of directors, executive incentives, and manifestations of poor governance. We will also discuss some of the major databases used for this type of research. The topics to be covered are all in the lecturer’s area of expertise. The course assumes a sound knowledge of the economic theory relating to the foundations of finance, including basic agency theory and financial contract theory. The course will emphasize both the major economic questions concerning the needs for and the effectiveness of these critical corporate governance mechanisms and to help researchers to create effective research designs necessary to produce compelling evidence of causal relationships.
learning_outcomes: Construct written work which is logically and professionally organized and articulated. Summarise your analysis and key findings in a highly succinct, but compelling fashion.
Explain and evaluate major empirical approaches used in undertaking research in corporate governance.
Understand major corporate governance mechanisms.
The class will function as a team to understand the strengths and weakness of each piece of research covered in class.
Develop critical economic perspectives and analytical skills, and be able to articulate your own research results through written reports and oral presentation.
Explain major theories and evidence concerning major corporate governance mechanisms.
Understanding how governance mechanisms are used to monitor and discipline corporate managers and directors and what are common methods of extracting private benefits of control.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner and be able to defend your economic analysis and statistical approaches in Q&A.
Highlight how effective corporate governance mechanisms are across countries and how they can be supported or undercut by government decisions.
Analyze data and test hypotheses and familiarity with the major databases in this research area.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Corporate Finance Theory
syllabus_overview: The course introduces contract theories, which have formed the fundamental framework for corporation finance research, and reviews their applications in corporate finance. The course consists of four main parts: (i) optimal contracts under moral hazard problems; (ii) mechanism design under asymmetric information problems; (iii) incomplete contract and firm theory; and (iv) topics in corporate finance.
learning_outcomes: Review the state of art corporate finance theories, and develop either empirical or theoretical research idea for thesis.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
Understand the working knowledge of basic contract theories.
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented
Understand comparative statics, and be able to develop testable hypothesis.
Analyse central issues in corporate finance using the framework of contract theories
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Finance Research in Practice
syllabus_overview: The goal of this course is to help Finance PhD students develop their research ideas and to better prepare them for successful academic careers. This will include advice on selecting research topics, working on their presentations skills, developing strategies for effective student-faculty interactions, and preparing them for the job market. During our meetings students will have an opportunity to discuss research ideas in an collaborative, non-judgmental environment. The discussion will be centered on topics considered relevant to the Finance research community (e.g., issues being discussed in top Finance journals). There is an emphasis on developing the students’ presentation and communication skills as well as some insights on how to sidestep common pitfalls during their transition from students to academic researchers.
learning_outcomes: Identify and avoid mistakes commonly made by graduate students in their transition to academic researchers.
Develop critical economic perspectives and analytical skills, and be able to articulate key research results through written reports and oral presentation.
Understand trends in research topics, rising econometric and analytical standards and what makes for a significant contribution to the literature.
Formulate a research topic relevant to the Finance research community.
Demonstrate the ability to critically reflect on your own work and research ideas as well as providing constructive feedback on the research of others.
Identify and develop the knowledge and skills necessary for effective preparation and delivery of academic presentations. Increase confidence in communicating your research.
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner and be able to defend your economic analysis and statistical approaches in Q&A. Understand how to respond to critiques of your research.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Microstructure of Markets
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course critically evaluates models of financial markets (market microstructure) and examines how asset prices are established in actual markets such as the stock exchange based on actual trades. It differs from asset pricing theory in which prices are assumed to be set such that supply and demand are equated via some costless auction-type frictionless mechanism that remains an undisclosed ‘black box’. Actual markets require actual rules and these rules affect the way in which prices are established, the way in which information possessed by traders is incorporated into asset prices, why some markets and stocks are liquid and why some markets are more fragile and costly than others. While this course is based on a relatively-new excellent text by three leading lights in the field, it is supplemented by a number of state-of-the-art studies that significantly advance our understanding of the role of different types of risk-volatility and illiquidity-in determining asset prices and the equity premium, for example, why it is that households can outperform professional investors?, how information contained in the stock price enables boards and CEOs to be monitored, and the role of counterparty transparency in improving market efficiency. Many of these papers are written by or with former students in the course. It first presents the basic modelling and tools used in the market microstructure field which analyses how prices are established in securities markets and whether or not markets are liquid. The course then analyses components of market design such as transparency and fragmentation (maker-taker fee structures and inverted markets, how investor heterogeneity leads to the (false?) rejection of asset pricing models, and how market design affects asset prices and corporate performance. This market microstructure course helps to address many of these fundamental issues, as well as equip students to read, understand and apply the rapidly developing market microstructure field in areas such as merchant banking. The goal of the course is to establish perspectives, approaches, tools and methods of independent thinking, analysis, and problem solving. Topics include exchange design rules, transparency and opacity, asymmetric information, private information, liquidity provision and pricing, volatility, transaction costs, strategic and noise trading, algorithmic trading, information and trading profits, dark pools, liquidity and returns. Three groups of traders are considered: domestic and foreign institutions and households. Households can be clients of either ‘full-service’ brokers or ‘discount’ brokers. This course complements courses in asset pricing that students may have done or be doing. Analysis of microstructure is becoming increasingly relevant for research in corporate finance, as well, for example, FINS5576 and FINS5577: Advanced Topics in Asset Pricing and Advanced Topics in Corporate Finance.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective written business communication skills, conveying ideas about market microstructure research in a succinct and clear manner.
Appraise the role played by informed traders and other participants such as liquidity providers and “noise traders” in the functioning of security markets.
Evaluate and justify why some security trading venues globally are more successful than others and why.
Develop and hone your critical thinking and collaborative teamwork skills through completion of your own market microstructure research project within a team.
Explain how the design features of trading venues affects price discovery and the matching of buyers and sellers for financial instruments and the well-being of different participants.
Demonstrate effective oral business communication skills, verbally communicating ideas about market microstructure research in a succinct and clear manner.

Explain and interpret the links between market microstructure and related areas such as asset pricing, investment, role of illiquidity in asset pricing, corporate finance, corporate governance and contract design.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Continuous-Time Finance
syllabus_overview: The course consists of two major parts. The first one is a more technical prerequisite of the second, but it delivers its own insights into the modelling of financial problems. It deals with Stochastic Calculus as a basis to model the stochastic development of asset prices, interest rates or latent variables. At the end of this part students should be familiar with Ito's Lemma and stochastic differential equations. This part asks for a positive attitude of students towards a more formal reasoning. It will take up about 30% of the lectures. The second part deals with a number of classical continuous-time applications in Finance. First, three problems which are based local on a no-arbitrage condition will be discussed: option pricing, structural models of credit risk, and the trade - off theory of the optimal capital structure. Second, portfolio theory and the characterization of expected asset returns in equilibrium will be analysed. These two problems were the first applications of the continuous-time finance approach. For the last topics, we have some flexibility: we can choose between several models that can be useful in a variety of settings, such as models with mean reversion, stochastic volatility, jumps, or regime switching. Alternatively, we could look at more sophisticated derivatives, such as term structure models, or models of credit default swaps.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and appraise applications of the Black-Scholes PDE, such as the models of risky debt due to Merton and Leland, barrier options, the Black-Cox model of risky debt, and the Brennan-Schwartz approach to real options.

Explain how changing probability measures (e.g., producing the risk-neutral probability measure) can help with option pricing, and employ the derivation of the Black-Scholes partial differential equation (PDE).
Identify and apply definitions of Markov processes and martingales, as well as Wiener processes, integration with respect to a Wiener process, and Ito’s lemma.

Explain and apply portfolio optimisation in continuous-time – including the derivation of the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation and its first order conditions, how the first order conditions can lead to the Intertemporal CAPM model (ICAPM), and the approach due to Karatzas and others that can help with constrained optimisation.
Discuss more advanced models, such as models with stochastic volatility, jumps, or regime-changes, OR, more advanced option pricing models, such as term structure models or credit risk models.
Discuss the basics of conditional expectation with respect to a filtration, including its relation to OLS regressions.
Analyse and demonstrate the benefits and uses of models with mean reversion.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in program 1561 or specialisation FINSCR2585 or FINSOS8635.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Full-Time Masters Research Thesis Banking and Finance
syllabus_overview: The Master of Philosophy (MPhil) consists of: An average of four coursework courses totalling 24 units of credit usually undertaken in the first year of candidature. A thesis not exceeding more than 40,000 words on an approved topic to the value of 48 units of credit. Prior to the thesis stage students must have the following skills: A good and thorough knowledge of advanced finance and the mathematics of modern finance. This knowledge is necessary to understand and appraise publications in high quality finance journals as well as working papers, and it forms the base on which the thesis is built through the use of mathematical modelling techniques. A solid understanding of: (i) the breadth and depth of econometric and statistical analyses; and (ii) the structure of financial institutions and markets A diverse and comprehensive knowledge of major areas of banking, finance, insurance and risk management. The capacity for analytical and critical thinking. Students must display originality in approaching research questions and issues. Excellent written and oral skills.

communicate complex issues and impart scholarly knowledge, both orally and in writing, to peers and the faculty

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Workshop in Finance 2
syllabus_overview: This course provides an up-to-date survey of contemporary research issues and topics in all areas of finance. It will be delivered by experts in their field of interests. The topics planned include but may not be confined to: financial intermediation, corporate finance, asset pricing, and mathematical finance.
learning_outcomes: Explore and develop new research ideas and topics that advance the literature
Identify, learn and apply new empirical methodologies used in latest research
Identify areas in the literature that require further research and/or specific research questions that remain unaddressed

Effectively communicate critiques of existing papers and new research ideas to peers

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Part-Time Masters Research Thesis Banking and Finance
syllabus_overview: The Master of Philosophy (MPhil) is designed to provide an opportunity for students to develop research competence in a limited timeframe. The program duration is 1.5 years full-time or 3 years part-time. Depending on the area of study selected, Banking and Finance provides training for a wide range of vocations including: multinational financial managers, multinational bank and insurance managers, multinational funds managers, venture capital and private equity specialists, corporate financial managers or treasurers, portfolio managers for trust funds, superannuation funds and insurance companies, investment analysts and financial researchers in stockbroking firms, merchant banks, trading banks and government departments, management consultants and takeover specialists in corporate advisory divisions of merchant banks, public accounting firms, and management consulting firms. Within the Australian School of Business, the highest international standards in both fundamental and applied research are maintained and, through that research the advancement, development and practical application of scientific research of relevance to industry and commerce is supported. This standard is maintained in several ways including the publishing of research findings, the organisation of a series of research seminars, sponsorship of the Australasian Finance and Banking Conference and by supporting the acquisition of Australian and International databases utilised by researchers in the School.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Food Science, Society and Sustainability
syllabus_overview: These days everyone has an opinion on food - its health effects, its quality and taste, its environmental impact. In this course you will examine the development, the science, and the place of food in society so you can engage in these contemporary debates about the future of food. Society’s attitudes and understanding of the role that food plays in our health has been rapidly changing in the last decade. Existing food hierarchies have been overturned and diet orthodoxies disrupted. We are learning more and more how changes to diet can promote or discourage chronic disease like diabetes, osteoporosis, and Alzheimer’s. At the same time, we are increasingly aware of the way that food production, packaging, and distribution is impacting the environment and contributing to climate change. This leads many to consider the ethics of food creation and consumption. This course will give you insights into the breadth and depth of food science - a rapidly evolving discipline. The course will introduce you to some of the common scientific principles, practices, and challenges related to our food systems. You will examine the interactions between the food industry and consumer ethics, health, and behaviour. Finally, you will consider the arguments around food packaging and the role of innovation in food product development, food waste and sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Formulate scholarly and reflective perspectives through written and oral communication
Apply systems thinking to current and future challenges in the supplying the world with sufficient, sustainable, and nutritious food.
Critically analyse relevant material from a range of scientific and public information sources.
Explain the contributions that people, professions, and food science disciplines can make to addressing current and future food challenges.
Discuss how food science contributes to individual, societal, planetary, and economic health.
Define introductory concepts in food science, including the components, properties, and functions of foods.
