institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introductory Exercise Science
syllabus_overview: This course presents an overview of the vocational activities within the allied health profession of Exercise Physiology. The sub-disciplines of exercise science (exercise physiology, biomechanics, motor control and exercise psychology), and related biomedical sciences, are introduced through examining how the body responds to physical activity. This course includes a clinical practicum component in the University's Lifestyle Clinic. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively and concisely through written reports of scientific experiments or clinical experiences
Explain the role and responsibilities of exercise physiologists in the provision of health care.
Describe the different sub-disciplines of exercise science and an appreciation of the interdisciplinary nature of exercise physiology.
Apply basic principles of movement analysis
Describe the processes involved in patient care, from initial patient referral through to exercise programming and delivery.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 3871 program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Exercise Programs and Behaviour
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the literature examining the effects of physical activity on health and the principles of exercise programming for apparently health populations. Practical training in this course will encompass: fitness assessments, basic pre-screening and interview techniques, and exercise technique and prescription. Psychological aspects of exercise, in particular motivation, adherence and addiction, will also be addressed. These skills will be put into practice with students developing and delivering a supervised exercise program for a healthy adult. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Apply screening tools to determine an individual’s suitability for exercise
Develop motivational interviewing skills to help facilitate individual behaviour change
Design and implement an exercise program for a group of healthy individuals
Create, implement and evaluate a holistic lifestyle change program for an indiviudual healthy adult
Conduct basic health and fitness assessments to assess an individual’s health status
prerequisites: Pre req: HESC1501 and PSYC1001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomechanics
syllabus_overview: You will study the basic principles of biomechanics and apply these to the analysis of human movement and the musculoskeletal system. Basic mechanics (statics, kinematics and dynamics) will be studied in two dimensions. The biomechanics of many common movements will be studied. Your understanding of mechanics, coupled with your knowledge of functional anatomy will be applied to study normal gait dynamics, musculoskeletal function, work and power. The mechanics of tissues in the musculoskeletal system will be introduced. Methods for assessing movement, quantitative and qualitative, will be covered.
learning_outcomes: Describe how biomechanics fits within the interdisciplinary context of movement science and can inform health and exercise science practice.
Explain how basic physical principles apply to human motion and the mechanical properties of musculoskeletal tissues.
Work collaboratively in a team to collect and interpret biomechanical data.
Apply problem solving and critical thinking abilities to assess human motion and the effects of load on the musculoskeletal system.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Movement Assessment and Instruction
syllabus_overview: This course will equip you with knowledge and skills for assessing and instructing clients and patients in exercises and other movements. You will integrate concepts from biomechanics, functional anatomy, motor learning and skill acquisition in the analysis of exercises, work tasks and activities of daily living. You will apply your theoretical understanding of biomechanics and functional anatomy in practical analysis of movement, using both quantitative and qualitative approaches. The course will also cover aspects of exercise instruction and approaches to movement education. You will develop practical skills in teaching new or modified exercises, work tasks or activities of daily living, giving consideration to pedagogical theory in relation to instructing clients and patients regarding movement and exercise. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Describe and demonstrate the appropriateness and effectiveness of a variety of teaching and feedback strategies for movement instruction and exercise delivery
Identify the biomechanical loads experienced by specific anatomical structures during different postures and movements and recognise when this poses a risk of injury
Demonstrate theoretical understanding and practical skills regarding the collection, graphical presentation and interpretation of quantitative motion analysis data
Demonstrate an understanding of the implications of individual differences on motor learning and skill acquisition
Effectively communicate information to clients and patients in training and rehabilitation programs
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ANAT2451 (or both ANAT3131 and ANAT3141) and HESC2451 (or BIOM2451 or SESC2451)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Exercise Science
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is on advanced understanding of exercise prescription, delivery and testing among apparently healthy and sporting populations. It covers the areas of exercise science, functional anatomy and motor learning, including strength and conditioning, agility training and skill development. This course offers a mixture of traditional and interactive/ hands-on approaches to learning and teaching. Skills and techniques performed by Accredited Exercise Scientists & Accredited Exercise Physiologists (AES & AEP’s) in the sector of apparently healthy and elite populations will be developed in this course. Students will also complete 40 hours of Exercise Science clinical practicum hours throughout this course. This practicum experience is developed under the supervision of AES’s, AEP’s or other suitably qualified health professionals. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge and evidence-based practice to prescribe physical activity and design exercise programs to maintain and promote good health and improve performance for clients across the lifespan.

Apply the principles and skill sets of exercise science, including the design and delivery of exercise programs and assessments to meet the specific needs of apparently healthy clients; and be able to adapt the delivery of an exercise prescription to respond to environmental change or change in the needs or capacities of clients.

Conduct accurate health and exercise evaluations, assess physical activity status, and perform common assessments appropriate for the specific needs of apparently-healthy clients, in accordance with best practice.

Integrate knowledge, interpret results and communicate scientific data and movement techniques to clients effectively; and act in a manner that is sensitive to client diversity and equity, and is consistent with the ESSA Code of Professional Conduct and Ethical Practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HESC1511, HESC2501 and HESC2452

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Physical Activity and Health
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is on the effects of exercise on apparently healthy populations and those with increased cardiovascular risk across the lifespan. Psychological aspects of exercise, including the application of behaviour change and self-management strategies, comprise a significant component of this course. The literature addressing the impact of physical activity on cardiovascular risk reduction and the prevention of disease will be discussed in detail through examining the mechanisms by which exercise alters metabolic, vascular, muscular and cognitive function, both chronically and acutely. Health-based screening and intervention techniques (including basic nutrition assessments) will be applied with students undertaking a supervised lifestyle change project.
learning_outcomes: Record, analyse and interpret information from assessments and convey the results, including the accuracy and limitations of the assessments or exercise program, through relevant verbal and/or written communication with the client or involved professional.

Identify risk factors associated with sedentary lifestyles and metabolic dysfunction and explain the role of sedentary behaviour and physical activity in the aetiology, prevention and management of lifestyle-related chronic diseases namely obesity, metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular disease.
Apply best-practice principles to design, implement and interpret results of a supervised lifestyle change program for individuals with different levels of cardiovascular risk
Select, develop and conduct a range of health assessments and screening tests that are safe, and effective for individuals with different levels of cardiovascular risk
Demonstrate basic knowledge of dietary assessment and a healthy food intake and use this to provide dietary recommendations to adults with different levels of cardiovascular risk
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HESC2501, HESC1511 and HESC3511

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health, Exercise and Sport Psychology
syllabus_overview: In this course you will develop an understanding of the psychological theories of human behaviour and how to apply them to work with clients leading to improved practice. It provides advanced understanding of contemporary psychological theories so that you are equipped with the knowledge and skills required to work optimally with individuals in health, exercise and sports across the lifespan. This course builds on the content covered in the early stages of the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate counselling and communication skills to develop realistic goal setting, exercise adoption and adherence, and safe participation in physical activity.
Formulate strategies for behaviour modification for acute and chronic health conditions to increase adherence to exercise and physical activity programs.
Explain the role of exercise, physical activity and sport on mental health and wellbeing. Understand group dynamics and sport.
Describe human behaviour in terms of personality, motivation and learning. Relate these influences to the behavioural aspects of health, exercise and sport.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC1001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Neuromuscular Rehabilitation
syllabus_overview: This course provides the opportunity for students to understand the potential, and limitations, of exercise as a tool for clinical rehabilitation in patients with neurological disorders. Specific information about a range of neuromuscular disorders is provided, and students are encouraged to apply their knowledge to case studies and scenarios in order to develop the scientific and clinical attributes necessary to contribute effectively to a neuromuscular rehabilitation team. This course offers a mixture of traditional and interactive/case study approaches to learning and includes a series of simulated case study learning sessions that emphasise the application of theory to clinical situations. These simulated case study learning sessions are designed as a bridge between the lifestyle change project with an apparently healthy client in HESC3504 and the year 4 clinical practicum courses in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of current and emerging neuromuscular rehabilitation approaches.
Competently administer and interpret basic functional, psychological, biomechanical or neurological tests relevant for neuromuscular rehabilitation.
Demonstrate sound clinical reasoning to inform targeted therapeutic exercise programs specific to patient presentation
Effectively prescribe appropriate and safe exercise programs for patients with neuromuscular disorders
Apply knowledge of the pathophysiology of a range of neuromuscular disorders at a level sufficient for effective communication with health care professionals and patients.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HESC2452 and NEUR3101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Exercise Prescription in Diverse Populations
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the role of engaging diverse populations in physical activity and exercise. Students are provided with the opportunity to develop an understanding of specific needs for engaging in physical activity, including specific limitations, considerations, individualisation of testing and training procedures. This course examines current literature regarding the impact of physical activity on the health status of a diverse range of populations. Target conditions covered in this course include children, corporate health, women’s health issues (menopause, pregnancy, gestational diabetes) and indigenous populations; as well as people with cancer, chronic kidney disease, mental health disorders, and sleep disorders. This course offers a mixture of traditional and interactive (case study) approaches to learning. Lectures will build on material presented in HESC3504 (Physical Activity and Health) and HESC3541 (Clinical Exercise Physiology) and in-depth knowledge on these diverse populations will be provided.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of an Exercise Physiologist in delivering multidisciplinary care across a variety of diverse populations for effective exercise-based intervention strategies
Demonstrate an understanding of individual differences in response to physical activity and exercise, and their implications
Describe the effects of regular physical activity on health outcomes in a diverse range of populations

Demonstrate foundational knowledge of diverse populations (including children, women’s health issues. different cultural backgrounds) and other conditions (including people with chronic kidney disease, mental health disorders) and their exercise needs

Demonstrate an ability to design safe, evidence-based and culturally appropriate lifestyle interventions for a range of diverse populations, including exercise interventions, treatment goals and specific needs for the target conditions
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HESC3541, HESC3504

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Exercise Physiology
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you information about the epidemiology and the pathophysiology of respiratory, metabolic, cardiovascular and immune diseases. You will gain knowledge of how to set up and implement exercise testing and programming in these special populations in order to provide symptomatic relief, as well as to manage the underlying disease. You will also learn how to manage the interaction between exercise and medications in these special populations. By the end of the semester you will be able to successfully use exercise testing and programming in individuals with these diseases to improve their health and quality of life. The teaching and learning approaches used in this course will include problem-based learning as well as more traditional evidence-based information provided during the lectures. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Collect, analyse and interpret data from exercise testing to construct individualised exercise programs
Administer pre-exercise screening and safely conduct exercise testing, including monitoring of the cardio-respiratory function at rest and during exercise and recovery
Identify exercise limitations and contraindications to exercise associated with the chronic diseases addressed in this course
Describe the physiological mechanisms responsible for the development of the chronic diseases addressed in this course, as well as the medications used to manage these diseases
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HESC2501, PHSL2502, PATH2202 or PATH2201, PHSL2501

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Workplace Assessment and Rehabilitation
syllabus_overview: In this course you will develop the knowledge and skills required for employment opportunities as an Accredited Exercise Physiologist (AEP) within the workplace assessment and rehabilitation sector. You will have the opportunity to develop competency and understanding of workers compensation systems and SIRA legislative requirements; the epidemiology of occupational injury; occupational health and safety; functional capacity assessment; workplace injury prevention and rehabilitation; exercise interventions in workplace rehabilitation; and report writing and communication with key stakeholders at a professional standard. This course offers a mixture of online and student-based learning activities (team-based learning), with the emphasise on the application of theoretical knowledge towards AEP professional practice.This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of the professional scope of practice of an Accredited Exercise Physiologist (AEP), legal boundaries within the State Insurance Regulatory Authority (SIRA) framework, legislative obligations, and responsibilities of key stakeholders, relating to workplace assessment and rehabilitation.
Effective communication and reporting of findings from assessments of the workplace and injured workers to other health professions and stakeholders
Critically evaluate the work demands of different occupations and plan and implement work specific functional capacity assessments
Develop competency with education and exercise prescription for individuals with workplace injury referred for exercise rehabilitation
Develop competency in biopsychosocial assessment of injured workers and formulation of graded return to work plans
Design, develop and implement work place injury prevention training programs
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 3831 Science (Medicine) Honours OR (Completed HESC2452 and HESC3532)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Exercise Physiology Research Seminars
syllabus_overview: This course will train you to be able to critically interpret scientific and clinical research linked to the field of exercise science and exercise physiology to enhance your clinical practice. You will learn the skills necessary to find, read, understand and communicate clinical research in the practical sessions and seminars. Assessment tasks provide experience in looking up original research articles, appraising their value and communicating this to colleagues and the general public via an oral or poster presentation. Assessment tasks will also teach you to work in a team environment.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise original research, including methodology, statistical results and ethical considerations for integration into best practice and research in exercise science and exercise physiology.
Recognise significant research advances made in the fields of exercise science and exercise physiology as well as summarise and present these in both written and oral formats.
Critically self-evaluate and reflect upon participation/effort, effectiveness and productivity in a team environment and an individual learning scenario .
Demonstrate interpersonal skills to participate effectively in a team work environment
Describe the scientific research process to facilitate critical evaluation and communication of scientific evidence for translation into clinical practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 3831 Science (Medicine) Honours program OR (Completed MATH1041, HESC2501 and 12 UOC of Level 3 HESC Courses)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project
syllabus_overview: This course will lead on from the prerequisite course, HESC4501 Exercise Physiology Research Seminars, and will give students experience in conducting a literature review on a self-selected topic related to exercise physiology. It is primarily a self-directed project that involves deciding on a research question/topic and addressing this question by a narrative review of the literature. Assessment tasks will provide experience in a range of research activities such preparation of abstracts and written reports, and oral and poster presentations. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Be able to organise, present and discuss research data
Develop an understanding of current techniques used in biomedical research
Develop skills in critically evaluating research articles and writing a literature review
Synthesize and analyse data from review of scientific literature
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH1041 and HESC4501

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Internship A
syllabus_overview: This course is the first term (10 weeks) of a 20-week supervised research internship based on an individual research project supervised by a member of academic staff. The project may encompass a systematic literature review, resource or project development, or a clinical or laboratory investigation. The project may also involve a ‘placement’, possibly outside UNSW, in research or industry, which may occur outside session. The course will develop your ability to formulate research questions, conduct in-depth studies, analyse and present data, and write reports. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and work effectively with peers, colleagues and stakeholders
Develop skills in scientific communication, including oral and written skills
Develop an understanding of current techniques used in biomedical research
Develop a research question based on review of existing scientific or clinical research
Synthesise, organise and present data from critical review of the literature
prerequisites: Prerequisites: MATH1041, HESC4501 and WAM equal or above 65

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Practicum A
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with an opportunity to consolidate and extend clinical skills through supervised placements in the workplace. A minimum of 200 hours of clinical practical experience will be completed within a clinical environment. This is done under the supervision of an accredited exercise physiologist. These practicum hours are a requirement of the accrediting professional body. Performance is monitored through workplace competencies, a VIVA exam, supervisor report and self-reflection. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Integrate your knowledge, skills and clinical experience of exercise physiology using reflective practice
Prescribe physical activity and exercise programs to maintain and promote good health for apparently-healthy and chronically-ill people
Implement motivational and lifestyle behaviour-change strategies to facilitate behaviour change and enhance self-management
Educate clients on the benefits of physical activity for prevention and management of disease, injury and disability
Communicate effectively with patients from diverse backgrounds, your clinical supervisor, and other health professionals working in a multi-disciplinary team
Independently assess lifestyle behaviours and functional capacity, and perform health-risk appraisal and exercise tests, for apparently-healthy and chronically-ill people
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Completed all Stage 3 courses

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Internship B
syllabus_overview: This course is the second term (10 weeks) of a 20-week supervised research internship based on an individual research project supervised by a member of academic staff. The project may encompass a systematic literature review, resource or project development, or a clinical or laboratory investigation. The project may also involve a ‘placement’, possibly outside UNSW, in research or industry, which may occur outside session. The course will develop your ability to formulate research questions, conduct in-depth studies, analyse and present data, and write reports. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and work effectively with peers, colleagues and stakeholders
Gain practical experience in performing techniques used in biomedical research
Evaluate the efficacy of project methods in addressing research questions
Synthesize, organise and present scientific data in the format of a scientific journal article
prerequisites: Prerequisite: HESC4561

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Practicum B
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with an opportunity to consolidate and extend clinical skills through supervised placements in the workplace. A minimum of 200 hours of clinical practical experience will be completed within a clinical environment. This is done under the supervision of an accredited exercise physiologist. These practicum hours are a requirement of the accrediting professional body. Performance is monitored through workplace competencies, case justification exam, supervisor report and self-reflection. This course is restricted to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Exercise Physiology 3871.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively with patients from diverse backgrounds, your clinical supervisor and other health professionals working in a multi-disciplinary team
Prescribe physical activity and exercise programs to maintain and promote good health for apparently-healthy and chronically-ill people
Educate clients on the benefits of physical activity for prevention and management of disease, injury and disability
Independently assess lifestyle behaviours and functional capacity, and perform health-risk appraisal and exercise tests, for apparently-healthy and chronically-ill people
Integrate your knowledge, skills and clinical experience of exercise physiology using reflective practice
Implement motivational and lifestyle behaviour-change strategies to facilitate behaviour change and enhance self-management
prerequisites: Prerequisite: HESC4611

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interprofessional Practice and Collaborative Care
syllabus_overview: In this foundations course, you will learn what it means to be a healthcare professional in Australia, including understanding the healthcare system, professionalism, and the diverse needs of individuals and communities. You will develop cultural capabilities knowledge and self-reflective skills required to deliver culturally safe healthcare to First Peoples and help address health inequities. Working in interprofessional teams, you will strengthen your ability to provide high-value, person-centred care. Professional behaviour, communication, and attire will form part of your learning and assessment throughout the course.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate health promotion, disease prevention and sustainability frameworks that aim to enhance health equity and population health outcomes.
Demonstrate understanding of the codes of conduct relevant to your profession, describe the components of ethical practice, including informed consent, confidentiality and record keeping.
Demonstrate the development of foundational self-reflection skills for lifelong professionalism in health practice for inclusive and culturally responsive care.
Explain the structure of the Australian health care system and principles of person-centred care and interprofessional collaboration, including communication strategies in health professions.
Apply ethical and professional principles for culturally capable practice with First Peoples.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 3894 Nutrition/Dietetics and Food Innovation OR 3895 Pharmaceutical Medicine/Pharmacy OR 3896 Exercise Science/Physiotherapy and Exercise Physiology OR 3897 Applied Exercise Science/Clinical Exercise Physiology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Academic Preparation for Health Studies
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will develop skills to help you to succeed in your studies to become a health practitioner. You will learn to how to: apply academic integrity to your studies, think critically, find, assess and use digital resources for learning, complete basic mathematical procedures and write and present information to a minimum academic standard. A strong understanding and application of these skills will be required in every course you complete in your program. Additionally, you will be introduced to strategies and tools that optimise wellbeing during your studies and will be built upon in future studies to ensure career resilience. This is a mandatory course for students enrolled into a health science program.
learning_outcomes: Identify situations that constitute plagiarism, student misconduct and unethical behaviour and how these can be prevented
Apply critical thinking frameworks to solve a question or problem
Demonstrate high quality academic writing and presentation skills in individual and teamwork settings
Identify the components of digital literacy and apply searching, appraising and synthesis skills to find answers to a question or problem
Explain the importance of self-care to academic success, and plan strategies to enhance wellbeing
Demonstrate mastery of basic mathematical concepts required for successful completion of health studies
Explain the importance of academic integrity in health professions training
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 3894 Nutrition/Dietetics and Food Innovation OR 3895 Pharmaceutical Medicine/Pharmacy OR 3896 Exercise Science/Physiotherapy and Exercise Physiology OR 3897 Applied Exercise Science/Clinical Exercise Physiology
Co-requisite: DIET1001 or PHRM1011 or EXPT1182

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Driving Behaviour Change 1
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to key theories and techniques used to help individuals adopt and adhere to health behaviours. You will develop important communication skills and apply these concepts to deliver person-centred behaviour change support to diverse populations.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement tailored plan using evidence-based behavioural theories for an individual to improve their adherence to key health behaviours including diet, exercise and medicine management
Demonstrate appropriate standards of care for an individual within relevant ethical and legal frameworks

Analyse and reflect on your verbal and non-verbal communication with individuals, carers, families, other healthcare professionals and relevant stakeholders to build rapport and to ensure the delivery of high-quality care
Analyse the role of different health professionals to provide care for individuals from various populations across the lifespan

Demonstrate how you would collaborate appropriately with other healthcare professionals to develop education strategies and management plans for individuals from various populations that may be at risk of adverse healthcare outcomes
Discuss the role of mental well-being and the social determinants of health and their impact on key health behaviours including diet, exercise and medicine management.
Identify indicators of physical or mental health that signal the need for referral to other healthcare professions
Provide empathetic and respectful care tailored to individual needs and circumstances, including gender, culture, beliefs, socio-economic status and personal preferences
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: HLTH1000

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research for Healthcare Practices
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will learn how evidence for healthcare practice is generated, how to assess evidence for bias, applicability and relevance, how to interpret basic statistical results and distinguish between outcomes of statistical significance and clinical relevance, how evidence is synthesised and transformed into practice guidelines, and how to apply these guidelines to patient and/or client care. For example, how and when to use tests and treatments. These skills are essential to enable you to practice in a competent, safe and effective manner. By the end of the course, you will be able to read and interpret information in a research article that is used to inform practice.
learning_outcomes: Explain how evidence is synthesized and translated into practice
Identify well-constructed questions that address an area of healthcare practice.
Describe different study designs, explain their strengths and limitations and suitability to answer different questions in healthcare.
Describe the role of evidence-based healthcare in effective, ethical and safe healthcare practice

Calculate and interpret measures of frequency, effect sizes and associations commonly used in health care research and evidence generation, and distinguish statistical significance from practical relevance.
Describe how research results may be influenced by chance, bias and confounding and how this may be minimised
Critically appraise the validity of published evidence and assess its applicability to a range of population groups
prerequisites: HLTH2000

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Driving Behaviour Change 2
syllabus_overview: This course will provide you with a foundational knowledge of common mental health conditions and how these conditions impact health behaviours relevant to your future profession. You will learn how to recognise the signs and symptoms of mental health conditions, and how to communicate and work collaboratively to deliver person-centred care.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement therapeutic interventions or education programs for individuals with mental illness to improve adherence to key health behaviours (such as diet, medicine compliance, exercise)
Analyse and reflect on your verbal and non-verbal communication with individuals who live with mental health conditions to ensure the delivery of appropriate and high-quality care
Distinguish the scope of practice of different allied health and medical professions within the field of mental health to ensure appropriate referral and collaborative care
Conduct yourself within all relevant ethical and legal frameworks to provide appropriate standards of care to people with mental health conditions
Assess the impact of mental health conditions on key health behaviours

Provide empathetic and respectful person-centred care tailored to individual needs and circumstances, including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities, gender, culture, beliefs, socio-economic status.
Collaborate with other healthcare professions and relevant stakeholders to co-manage people with mental illness over the lifespan
prerequisites: Prerequisites: HLTH2000

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Leading Change in the Health Professions
syllabus_overview: This course prepares future health professionals to lead change through reflective practice, evidence-based decision-making, advocacy, and quality improvement. You will develop leadership, negotiation, and advocacy skills to address challenges in healthcare delivery. Emphasis is placed on designing and evaluating improvements using recognised quality improvement tools and methodologies such as 'Plan-Do-Study-Act (PDSA)' and 'Design Thinking'. You will also explore how health professionals' actions can contribute to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, particularly those related to health equity, access to care, and sustainable health systems. Through interdisciplinary collaboration and real-world case studies, you will learn to advocate for clients, communities, and your profession while promoting ethical, safe, and equitable care.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of advocacy within health professions and how effective change leadership, including through advocacy and quality improvement strategies aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, can be initiated in diverse settings and populations.

Analyse workplace attitudes and behaviours that are unethical, unsafe, or non-evidence-based, and propose strategies to promote physical and cultural safety, responsiveness, and positive workplace cultures.

Design an advocacy strategy and associated products that communicate a cohesive, actionable message to enable change for individuals, communities, or the profession, incorporating recognised quality improvement methodologies.

Identify opportunities to access health and social care services, determine when additional support or resources are required, and implement strategies, underpinned by advocacy and quality improvement frameworks, to improve equity and service delivery.

Articulate the need for and demonstrate effective negotiation skills with key stakeholders in health practice, including in the context of implementing advocacy and evidence-based quality improvement initiatives.

Evaluate personal and team leadership styles and demonstrate how interdisciplinary collaboration and reflective practice contribute to effective teamwork, achievement of program learning outcomes, and UNSW graduate capabilities.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PHCM2100 or HLTH2001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Identifying and Solving Clinical Problems
syllabus_overview: You will develop advanced skills in evaluating and contributing to solving complex clinical problems with individuals and collectives across service, community, and system contexts. Using real cases, you will work individually and in groups to analyse issues, consider person, family and system contexts, and design person-centred strategies across workplace settings. For example, you may explore a case involving a person with complex health and social needs, requiring you to assess priorities, cultural safety considerations, interprofessional communication, and system barriers to care. You will focus on the practical application of skills and knowledge in complex situations across different workplace settings from an interprofessional lens, preparing you for future placement and practice. The course emphasises cultural safety, critical self-reflection, and advanced communication to support your work with diverse populations, help you manage complex interactions, and enable collaboration across professions. You will examine leadership and system-level perspectives to develop innovative, safe, and coordinated responses to evolving clinical challenges at individual, collective and, system levels.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively using advanced techniques and collaboration to develop innovative solutions to complex real-world health problems
Critiques own thinking and biases and acts to meet end user’s contexts, needs, wants and priorities considering culture, values and belief systems
Contribute to solving clinical problems (including contexts and end user needs, wants and priorities) and use critical appraisal skills to optimise person centered-care
Evaluate the theoretical underpinnings of leadership, innovation and entrepreneurship to develop solutions to evolving clinical problems
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: HLTH3001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: School of Health Sciences Honours (Part Time)
syllabus_overview: The School of Health Sciences Honours part-time program is run over six terms. It provides advanced research training in health science research, including the disciplines of Exercise Science, Exercise Physiology, Physiotherapy, Dietetics, Nutrition, and Pharmacy. You will undertake a supervised research project that places emphasis on advanced disciplinary knowledge, the use of specialised techniques relevant to your chosen research area, critical thinking and scientific communication. You will develop skills in oral presentation by presenting your work in research seminars, and skills in scientific writing via completion a research proposal and a research manuscript based on substantial independent research activity. The Program is also comprised of compulsory Research Skills educational content, School of Health Sciences (SoHS) research seminars and Departmental/Research Institute/Lab Group seminars throughout the Program.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in oral and written forms in a clear and concise manner to an informed scientific audience
Interpret and critically evaluate the research literature, ideas and practices in health science research relevant to the research project.
Apply relevant research processes and methodologies to conduct a research project.
Design and implement a feasible research question and related hypothesis where applicable.
Collect and/or analyse and interpret qualitative and/or quantitative data, and reach appropriate conclusions that are supported by evidence.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ethical implications involved in health research
prerequisites: Enrolled in HLTHAH Health Sciences specialisation

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Research Project
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will contribute to an in-depth study of a relevant health science issue. You will apply the research skills you have acquired throughout your program to: identify a specific issue that requires investigation, formulate a research question, ethically and systematically collect relevant data, analyse, interpret and discuss your findings, draw conclusions, articulate the implications of your results, and disseminate the findings to the target audience. The research project may be a negotiated student-led proposal or be a proposal offered by an academic supervisor. Projects may be in a cross-disciplinary partnership with another School or Faculty at UNSW, or with an external stakeholder. You will be expected to carry out the research project independently, with the support of academic supervisor(s). With your academic supervisor(s), you will develop a ‘contract’ which outlines the roles and expectations for each, including an agreed meeting schedule, communication methods, milestones and timeline. This activity is a hurdle task and your contract with your supervisor must be submitted at the beginning of the first of the two research terms. You will not receive feedback on this task To fulfil the research project requirements of your degree, you must enrol in this course over two terms (2 x 6UOC) to complete a 12UOC research project. The assessment tasks for your research project are spread over two terms (Term 2 and Term 3 of Year 5). You will receive an ‘EC’ (enrolment continuing) on your academic transcript at the end of your first term of HLTH5002. Once all assessment tasks have been completed and graded at the end of your second term, a numeric grade will be applied to your second term of HLTH5002. Further details on the UNSW grade definitions can be found here: https://www.student.unsw.edu.au/grade
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the research process, including formulating a research question and proposing appropriate methods to investigate the question.
Demonstrate professional skills in planning, time management, teamwork, ethical practice and reflective practice.
Manage the collection, analysis and interpretation of data throughout the research process together with a supervisor(s) and within ethical standards.
Demonstrate effective oral and written communication skills that enables information to be disseminated clearly and concisely and be of a standard acceptable to a scientific journal and conference
prerequisites: Enrolment in Program 3896 (Bachelor of Exercise Science / Master of Physiotherapy and Exercise Physiology)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Research Training
syllabus_overview: Identifying a problem, selecting the appropriate methods to investigate a problem, and testing the efficacy and effectiveness of a potential solution in partnership with the end-users are all critical skills required in health practice and in careers in non-health sectors. In this course, you will continue to develop your knowledge of the research process and learn methodologies to help you ask the right questions to understand the size, scope and complexity of a problem. You will also learn how to select the right outcomes for measurement, and select the right methods to measure those outcomes. Then, you will learn how to distribute your findings using language that is appropriate for the audience. This course introduces concepts of research co-design, de-colonising research methods and includes non-traditional ways of conducting research where you will learn how incorporating Indigenous and other methods of knowing and thinking can positively impact on your ability to understand a problem and develop ethical, sustainable and effective solutions. This course has 2 streams: General and Research Intensive. Students who are completing a research project later in the year will complete the Research Intensive stream. All other students will complete the General stream. This course includes a 2-week intensive in Weeks 0 and 1. General stream In small teams, students in the general stream will choose a research problem to investigate, and with guidance, select and apply tools and methodologies to produce a group research protocol. Pharmacy students must select a research problem related to Quality Use of Medicine (QUM) or Drug Use Evaluation (DUE). For all other students in this stream, you may organise yourselves into and select a profession-specific or interprofessional team and research problem. Research Intensive stream Students completing the Research Intensive stream will work individually on a problem that will form their research project in Terms 2 and 3. Details regarding your research project will be provided to you by your Program Authority. In this course, you will learn how to approach investigating your assigned research problem, including how to apply tools and methodologies relevant at each step, culminating in a draft research protocol at the end of the course. You will then use the research protocol to inform your research project in subsequent terms.
learning_outcomes: Formulate a defined research question that can be investigated
Describe the basic research process and why research skills in health practitioners are important for high quality and ethical practice
Describe the role of human research ethics committees and identify the relevant committee’s approval for your research task
Describe the difference between narrative and systematic literature reviews and undertake a basic narrative literature review

Explain how different methods collecting, analysing and interpreting data may be used to complement each other in order to understand and resolve a problem, and traditional and non-traditional ways of knowing and thinking

Compare and contrast commonly used data collection methodologies, including experimental studies, surveys, focus groups and key informant interviews, understand when and why each methodology should be used, and describe the process of each methodology including key considerations

Explain the importance of conducting research in partnerships in relation to ethical research and its impact on health care practices, the importance of using strengths-based approaches to data analysis and interpretation, and how co-design principles may be used to achieve this
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PHCM2100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Preparing for a Career in Health and Beyond
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will learn skills essential to your career and career progression such as interview skills and CV preparation. You will learn how to find, evaluate and secure employment positions in health and more broadly. You will develop an understanding of what is expected of new graduates and how to optimise your career progression, including planning for ongoing accreditation/registration, supervision, mentoring, and wellbeing. You will also learn the fundamentals of how to establish and manage a private practice or small health-related business, including financial and resource management, marketing, and risk management, with attention to ethical conduct, engagement with First Peoples and other priority groups, and sustainable practice aligned with relevant United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). The course also introduces current and emerging digital health tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI), and their safe, ethical and culturally responsive use.
learning_outcomes: Analyse health graduate employment opportunities and strategically address the selection criteria for a position.

Demonstrate and critically reflect on essential verbal and non-verbal communication and presentation skills required to secure employment, including culturally responsive communication with diverse communities, including First Nations peoples.

Synthesise and evaluate the accreditation or registration requirements of your profession and develop a plan for early career-growth that integrates career resilience, wellbeing, mentoring, cultural safety capability, and digital capability.

Apply and evaluate the business, management and marketing skills required for establishing and maintaining an ethical, culturally safe, and sustainable health practice or small business aligned with relevant UN SDGs.
Appraise current and emerging digital health tools that may be used in health practice.

Analyse the ethical and legal considerations, risks, and potential conflicts of interest that health professionals may face in practice, including in digital/AI contexts and when working with First Nations peoples and other priority populations.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: HLTH4000 OR Enrolment in 3897 Applied Exercise Science/Clinical Exercise Physiology or 3896 Exercise Science / Physiotherapy and Exercise Physiology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: School of Health Sciences Honours (Full Time)
syllabus_overview: The School of Health Sciences Honours full-time program is run over three terms. It provides advanced research training in health science research, including the disciplines of Exercise Science, Exercise Physiology, Physiotherapy, Dietetics, Nutrition, and Pharmacy. You will undertake a supervised research project that places emphasis on advanced disciplinary knowledge, the use of specialised techniques relevant to your chosen research area, critical thinking and scientific communication. You will develop skills in oral presentation by presenting your work in research seminars, and skills in scientific writing via completion a research proposal and a research manuscript based on substantial independent research activity. The Program is also comprised of compulsory Research Skills educational content, School of Health Sciences (SoHS) research seminars and Departmental/Research Institute/Lab Group seminars throughout the Program.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and critically evaluate the research literature, ideas and practices in health science research relevant to the research project.
Design and implement a feasible research question and related hypothesis where applicable.
Apply relevant research processes and methodologies to conduct a research project.
Communicate effectively in oral and written forms in a clear and concise manner to an informed scientific audience
Collect and/or analyse and interpret qualitative and/or quantitative data, and reach appropriate conclusions that are supported by evidence.
Demonstrate an understanding of the ethical implications involved in health research
prerequisites: Enrolled in HLTHAH Health Sciences specialisation

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Health Research Project
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will contribute to an in-depth study of a relevant health science issue. You will apply the research skills you have acquired throughout your program to: identify a specific issue that requires investigation, formulate a research question, ethically and systematically collect relevant data, analyse, interpret and discuss your findings, draw conclusions, articulate the implications of your results, and disseminate the findings to the target audience. The research project may be a negotiated student-led proposal or be a proposal offered by an academic supervisor. Projects may be in a cross-disciplinary partnership with another School or Faculty at UNSW, or with an external stakeholder. You will be expected to carry out the research project independently, with the support of academic supervisor(s). With your academic supervisor(s), you will develop a ‘contract’ which outlines the roles and expectations for each, including an agreed meeting schedule, communication methods, milestones and timeline. This activity is a hurdle task and your contract with your supervisor must be submitted at the beginning of the first of the two research terms. You will not receive feedback on this task To fulfil the research project requirements of your degree, you must enrol in this course over two terms (2 x 9UOC) to complete an 18UOC research project. The assessment tasks for your research project are spread over two terms (Year 4 Term 3 and Year 5 Term 1). You will receive an ‘EC’ (enrolment continuing) on your academic transcript at the end of your first term of HLTH5003. Once all assessment tasks have been completed and graded at the end of your second term, a numeric grade will be applied your academic transcript for your second term of HLTH5003. Further details on the UNSW grade definitions can be found here: https://www.student.unsw.edu.au/grade

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Presentation and Communication Skills
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: Find your voice and speak with confidence. Tell a story, pitch a concept, engage an audience and share ideas. In this course, you will learn how to make your mark in the world. You will develop skills in presentation and communication used by influential leaders, compelling storytellers and effective presenters. You will study storytelling by leading actors, motivational speeches by powerful communicators, and public speaking in professional practice. Practical workshops will introduce you to techniques of audience awareness, physical presence and vocal projection. By following examples and rehearsing in class, you will develop the confidence to present your ideas in an authentic voice and communicate your message with clarity and conviction.
learning_outcomes: plan, rehearse and deliver an engaging presentation for an audience
respond constructively to presentations given by others
analyze and apply presentation techniques in vocal projection, physical presence, audience awareness, and clear communication
describe and evaluate how presenters communicate in a range of genres and contexts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Personalised English Language Enhancement
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Personalised English Language Enhancement (PELE) is a self-directed learning course designed to help you enhance your communication skills in English. In this course, you will be guided to develop a personal project that meets your needs and implement it in a warm and safe environment being supported not only by the teachers but also by peer mentors. In addition, you will learn a number of important skills needed for life-long learning, including reflective thinking and time management.
learning_outcomes: Develop a personal project tailored to individual linguistic needs, utilising tools and resources for language enhancement
Communicate critical personal learning outcomes with peers
Analyse and identify specific linguistic areas that need improvement within a given context
Evaluate personal progress and cultivate reflective, critical thinking skills
Demonstrate advanced communication skills by implementing a sustainable personal project that enhances linguistic proficiency in a given context

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Fieldwork
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce you to fieldwork in an international setting. It will allow you to learn about a particular region and context and to practice fieldwork methodologies in a local community. Before leaving, you will participate in a workshop about the history, politics, economics of the area you will be studying. You will also learn about the environmental and development challenges that the community is facing. On arrival, you will receive fieldwork training on economic and social impact analysis from UNSW and local staff. Under supervision, you will then undertake fieldwork in a designated community before attending a final de-briefing workshop where you will be encouraged to reflect on your experience with your peers.
learning_outcomes: Explain key social, political, economic, and environmental events that affect the field context;
Conduct social and economic impact fieldwork including baseline surveys;
Articulate and explain methodologies that are appropriate to fieldwork and the challenges, possibilities and limitations thereof;
Articulate how historical relationships and dynamics impact the field context;
Communicate and synthesize fieldwork experiences.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit overall

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Music on My Mind: Psychology and Music
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: This course asks questions about music cognition and behaviour: How do we perceive music? Why can an instrument sound musical? How do we respond to and process the sound? What happens when we are preparing and performing music? Why can performers become debilitatingly nervous? What is the relation between music, sex and cheesecake? Can music make you smarter, and what is the Mozart Effect? Why does that tune get stuck in my head? How old must a person be before they can hear and appreciate music? You will address these and related questions through examination of the music psychology literature, and the critical evaluation of your own musical attitudes, beliefs and behaviours.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the sources and ways in which music processing is understood, and compare these with folk psychological and intuitive understandings
Identify how music psychologists investigate questions about music.
Explain how music is defined from a psychological point of view.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Experiencing the Sydney Opera House
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: The Sydney Opera House on Gadigal Land at Bennelong Point is one of the world’s most distinctive and instantly recognisable buildings. You will have seen it on postcards, tourist brochures, television shows, films, souvenirs, art works and there is even a kit that allows you to build your own version from LEGO. But what Country is it built on? What is the history of it as an idea and building? How does it fit into the local and international arts ecology? And how do we experience the site from our own cultural positions? Whether this is your first time in Sydney, or you have lived here all your life, this course gives you the opportunity to think about this iconic building from a range of perspectives to understand and appreciate it anew. This course uses experiential learning practices such as fieldwork, creative reflection, and on-site engagement to explore the Sydney Opera House as a cultural landmark. Through walking tours, critical perspectives and First Nations frameworks you will develop analytical and creative thinking skills that can be applied back into your field of study.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and engage with cultural context in relation to the built environment
Apply experiential learning as a tool for locating cultural context
Research, write and develop creative and analytical connections between your disciplinary background and cultural context

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sounds Good: Music, Pleasure and Wellbeing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: School of the Arts and Media
syllabus_overview: Why is music so enjoyable, and is it really good for us? This course addresses a range of questions concerned with the pleasure and health aspects of music. Other questions discussed include: Is it possible to hate music? Is it good for your brain? Why can music be used to treat some illnesses and reduce anxiety? Can it be bad for you? A range of approaches are considered, from mass media and personal perspectives, through to philosophical inquiry, aesthetics and psychology. The course aims to challenge and furnish you with skills in critically evaluating various views on how music preference and wellbeing programs emerge, and presents recent thinking on the topics. Tutorials focus on designing and evaluating practical applications of music in health and entertainment settings.
learning_outcomes: Undertake further research on questions concerned with music cognition and wellbeing.
Critically evaluate arguments about the acquisition of music preferences and health related outcomes through music intervention.
Apply a range of scholarly methods when investigating music and the arts.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Experiencing Sydney Crime
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Sydney has a long and well-established criminal past, documented not only in our history books, but also popular culture artefacts. Whether this is your first time in Sydney or you have lived here all your life, this course gives you the opportunity to further explore the criminal history of Sydney. Visiting sites such as the Justice and Police Museum and the Hyde Park Barracks, and locations associated with Sydney's deviant past, you will examine the city's connection with crime through a series of self-paced walking tours. In response to what you encounter, you will develop critical reflective responses to these experiences and, in the process, learn something new about yourself and your learning.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on developing knowledge acquired through experiential learning.
Describe different aspects of Sydney's crime history informed by a range of disciplinary perspectives.
Describe a personal learning strategy to apply in future learning.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indigenous Languages of Australia
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: By taking this course, you will gain an appreciation of Australia’s rich and complex Aboriginal linguistic heritage in contemporary and traditional contexts. You will delve into a curated range of topics including language and the land, kinship and social organisation, narrative and conversation, language acquisition, language contact, language and education, language maintenance and revival. Each of these topics will be discussed with reference to engaging case studies of current research and current community-based projects. Through the exploration of these topics, you will learn about the characteristic linguistic properties of Australian languages and apply analytical skills to the description of Australian language data. There will be a focus on how new ways of speaking are created, how languages are lost, and the ways in which Aboriginal speakers are teaching and reviving their traditional languages today. You will work with a selection of authentic NSW Aboriginal language material from State Library of NSW collections. In doing so, you will have hands-on experience in how to find and utilise rich archival linguistic material and the ethical practices in the management and use of Aboriginal language materials. You will take away from this course a deepened understanding of social and cultural diversity as seen through the lens of language, analytical methods and critical thinking skills, and knowledge of research ethics and intellectual integrity.
learning_outcomes: Recognise common linguistic features of Australian languages
Exhibit research ethics and archive protocols in the management of Aboriginal language material
Identify current debates and issues in the study of Australian languages
Apply principles of language analysis and description to Australian language data

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Taste of Research Project: Arts and Social Sciences
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will engage in a real-life academic research experience on a major project led by UNSW scholars in Arts & Social Sciences. You will work with a leading scholar, complete original research and write a paper about your area of research.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on your research tasks, demonstrating your understanding of your research project in light of some relevant literature
Execute assigned research tasks in a competent, professional and timely manner
Reflect on your experience of working on a research project
