institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials & Tech 1: Physical Principles
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This is the first of two courses designed to provide you with a platform to understand physical principles and manufacturing technologies encountered by Industrial Designers. In this course, you will cover the basic principles and related physical properties of materials, mechanical devices, electricity and electronic products. Such knowledge will enable you to understand and conceive of product design solutions that are informed by realistic expectations with regard to the intended product function, performance and use. In addition, the course will equip you with the foundational language necessary to discuss your design proposals with technical experts, such as manufacturing engineers and materials specialists.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate verbal and visual presentation skills appropriate for the communication of technical information in Industrial Design
Analyse and apply basic physical principles and simple mechanical devices to design solutions
Identify and describe basic electrical principles and electrical components within electrical and electronic products
Describe and analyse a design in terms of structure, mechanisms, stresses and forces, and tolerances and measurement
Describe a range of basic physical principles, properties of materials and technologies typically encountered in industrial design

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 1A
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This studio-based course introduces students to the fundamentals of two-dimensional and three-dimensional design, from an industrial design discipline perspective. Studies will include: understanding the basic elements of two and three-dimensional design, and the development of analytic and communication skills necessary for understanding 2D and 3D design. It will examine the development of the creative processes concerned with the exploration and manipulation of the elements of design
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a basic understanding of industrial design processes and methods
Demonstrate design literacy through an understanding of design principles and elements.
Communicate an idea using two dimensional and three dimensional techniques.
Demonstrate competency in basic model making techniques

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 1B
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This studio-based course enhances students' understanding of the fundamentals of two dimensional and three-dimensional design, from an Industrial Design discipline perspective. Building on their studies in Studio 1A, this course will include: enhancing the understanding of the elements of two and three-dimensional design, and the continuing development of analytic and communication skills necessary for understanding and producing 2D and 3D design. The course will examine the creative processes concerned with the exploration and manipulation of the elements of design.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competency in model making techniques of moderate complexity as a means of exploring and communicating ideas.
Demonstrate design literacy through the appropriate selection and application of design principles and elements.
Communicate and clearly articulate an idea using two-dimensional, three-dimensional, drawing and model making techniques.
Demonstrate, through examples of work, a basic understanding of industrial design processes and methods.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 1A: Product Design Fundamentals
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 1A: Product Design Fundamentals introduces you to industrial design as a human-centred and contextually situated practice focused on shaping everyday products. The course builds foundational capabilities in framing design problems, understanding context and use, generating ideas, and exploring concepts through making. Learning is structured through a sequence of guided design challenges that support the development of design thinking. You will investigate how products relate to users, use situations, and broader social, cultural, and environmental conditions, and apply this understanding to generate and refine design proposals. Studio activities emphasise sketching, physical modelling, prototyping, and reflection as integrated tools for thinking and learning. Through iterative exploration, testing, and feedback, you will progressively develop design concepts and demonstrate how decisions evolve over time. The course establishes core habits of inquiry, iteration, communication, and reflection that underpin industrial design practice and support progression into more technically and contextually complex studio work.
learning_outcomes: Identify and interpret context, including user needs, to frame product design opportunities and constraints.
Communicate design processes, decisions, and outcomes, incorporating reflective evaluation to support ongoing development and learning.
Produce models and prototypes demonstrating form, use, and basic functional intent.
Generate design directions in response to a defined brief and context using exploratory design methods.
Evaluate design proposals through iterative refinement using testing, feedback, and critical judgement.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 1C
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this studio-based course, students will build upon previous studies of two and three-dimensional Industrial Design to embark upon several Industrial Design projects that explore varied approaches to the generation and expression of high-quality ideas. You will be guided through simple product design projects to examine the creative processes used in Industrial Design and present these using visual communication and model making techniques.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate use of materials and fabrication techniques in product design.
Competently develop and communicate an idea with two dimensional, three dimensional, drawing and model making techniques.
Demonstrate competency and fluency in Industrial Design processes and methods.
Demonstrate design literacy through appropriate selection, application and evaluation of design principles and elements.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Communications 2 - Sketch Modelling
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: A combination of on line resources and practical exercises are used in this course to enable students to develop skills in a range of practical methods for making and evaluating physical models as part of an iterative design process. The skills are applicable to design projects students will undertake in Design Studio courses. Techniques and theory explored in this course include rapid methods of hand making and finisihing of models; digital fabrication; and use of sensor technologies to explore the working of products and sytems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence and safe practice in a variety of model-making techniques and materials
Make creative use of modelling techniques to communicating design ideas
Integrate the use of modelling techniques in design exploration

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 1B: Materials, Form and Meaning
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 1B: Materials, Form and Meaning develops your ability to explore and resolve product form through material behaviour and fabrication processes. You will examine colour, material, and finish (CMF) as drivers of perceptual and experiential outcomes, and consider how material selection, surface qualities, texture, and form influence function, perception, and user experience. Through studio projects, you will investigate how two-dimensional materials can be transformed into three-dimensional forms using processes such as cutting, folding, perforation and assembly. You will also explore how abstract qualities such as mood, sensation and emotion can be translated into coherent product forms that communicate meaning beyond function. Through iterative sketching, drawing, modelling and prototyping, supported by material experimentation and critical feedback, you will develop your understanding of craftsmanship, construction logic and the relationship between form, material behaviour and intended use. Through these experiences, you will build a foundation for more complex challenges in subsequent industrial design studios.
learning_outcomes: Produce resolved prototypes demonstrating appropriate material selection, fabrication techniques, and structural resolution.
Generate design concepts that explore material behaviour and formal possibilities in response to a defined brief.
Analyse existing products and precedents to understand how material properties, form, and surface qualities influence product function, perception, and meaning.
Evaluate and refine design concepts through iterative modelling, testing, and feedback.
Communicate material, form, meaning, and design intent through visual and physical representations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: IDES1311 or IDES1212

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Communications A: Analogue Visualisation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course enables you to develop a range of practical skills in the visual representation of three-dimensional forms, using a variety of media and techniques including freehand sketching, model making, and technical drawing with reference to Australian Standards AS1100. You will learn how to layout your product designs in graphic posters for maximum visual impact and gain experience in presenting to an audience of your peers and tutors. These communication tools will help you effectively develop and convey ideas, shapes, and forms, as part of an iterative design process, and will support important design practices for your further studies in the Industrial Design specialisation.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design ideas through creative use of modelling techniques.
Apply the conventions of Engineering Drawing as they relate to manufacturing specification for Industrial Design products.
Communicate design concepts using a range of visual and written techniques.
Integrate modelling techniques in design exploration.
Demonstrate competent and safe practice in a variety of model-making techniques and materials.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Communications B: Digital Visualisation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Communications B: Digital Visualisation builds your ability to create, develop, and communicate product designs using industry-standard digital tools. You will learn to model products using parametric CAD, organise components into assemblies, produce technical drawings to Australian Standard AS1100, and create rendered images that clearly communicate form, structure, and detail. Through guided exercises and applied projects, you will develop accurate and well-structured digital models based on real-world products. You will explore how digital models support design development, testing, and fabrication, and how they are used to communicate with technical and professional audiences. The course also introduces basic validation processes, where digital models are compared with physical outputs to assess accuracy, fit, and correspondence. Emphasis is placed on logical modelling workflows, precision, and clarity of communication. By the end of the course, you will be able to produce coherent digital models, drawings, and visualisations that support your studio work and prepare you for more advanced design, prototyping, and manufacturing-focused projects.
learning_outcomes: Develop accurate parametric CAD models of product components and assemblies using structured modelling workflows.
Evaluate digital models and visualisations to verify dimensional accuracy, fit, and correspondence with physical form.
Produce orthographic, sectional, and exploded technical drawings derived from digital models in accordance with Australian Standard AS1100 conventions.
Communicate product structure, assembly, and design intent through digital and physical representation methods.
Integrate CAD modelling, technical drawing, digital visualisation, and physical outputs within a coherent industrial design workflow.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials and Manufacturing for Industrial Designers 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Materials and Manufacturing for Industrial Designers 1 will introduce you to the physical principles, material properties and manufacturing concepts that underpin industrial design practice. Your learning will focus on how forces, structure, material behaviour and simple mechanisms influence product performance and feasibility. Through analysis, prototyping and testing, you will investigate how materials and structures behave under load, how simple mechanical systems transfer energy, and how components function within everyday products. You will apply this understanding in hands-on projects that involve building and testing physical artefacts, analysing performance using diagrams and measurement, and interpreting results through appropriate technical terminology. You will also undertake introductory product disassembly and analysis to identify materials, manufacturing processes, fasteners and basic electronic components. Through reports and visual documentation, you will integrate experimentation, analysis and technical communication. You will develop foundational capabilities in understanding and explaining how materials, physical principles and manufacturing processes shape product outcomes, preparing you for later industrial design studio courses.
learning_outcomes: Explain the properties and behaviour of common engineering materials, and the capabilities and constraints of manufacturing processes.
Examine how materials and manufacturing processes relate to form, function, and production requirements in existing products.
Analyse how forces, structures, material properties, and simple mechanical systems influence product performance, function, and feasibility.
Communicate material, manufacturing, and technical performance considerations using visual, written, and analytical formats.
Evaluate and justify material and manufacturing process selection based on performance requirements, constraints, and intended use.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Theory 2: Society
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: IDES2021 sensitizes industrial design students to be more mindful of their role and responsibility to human society and to the natural environment that nurtures society. It highlights how the design process can become more ethical and more responsive to social needs, and how design can empower individuals and groups to catalyse and realize positive change in the present and future of their communities. It broadens the social impact and influence of design beyond pure market orientation through the inclusion of marginalized and underrepresented user groups and through addressing significant issues affecting society such as crime, social injustice, disabilities, public safety, climate change, food security, extreme poverty, responsible consumption, equality, education access, refugees, and the developing world. Through online videos and in-class workshops, students will explore how design innovation can enrich the quality of life and wellbeing for all without sacrificing ecological sustainability or economic prosperity.
learning_outcomes: Reflect upon their personal design values as a reference for their studies and future professional work.
Articulate responses to ideas and theories through visual and verbal media
Critically assess the positive and negative impacts of design activities on the natural environment and on the broader society.
Appraise the potential influences and interdependencies of design problems to the overall system.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Theory 4 : Methods
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The course introduces a range of established Industrial Design research methods. These are methods in which students will apply some rigour to activities such as observation of user behaviours, simulation of Industrial Design alternatives, and analysis of available information. Lectures, case studies and online resources will provide a theoretical platform for students, but learning will include application, practice and reflective discussion of methods in Industrial Design challenges. The focus is on developing rigour around academic research skills and writing within the context of Industrial Design research. Students will be given a list of specific topics to choose from to start their Industrial Design research process. The term will culminate with a Industrial Design Research Report, covering problems and/or opportunities identified for the selected topic, a literature review, data gathering, synthesis and analysis of information and research results.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate current and proposed designs with research methods such as empathy, observation, simulation, co-designing, creative thinking, iterative processes, etc…
Apply and practice methods in an iterative design process supported with sketching and modelling techniques as a means of further evaluation
Reflect and report on the impact of research methods in design projects, revealing both theoretical understanding and knowledge acquired through practice.
Identify and define design problems/opportunities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Communication 3: 3D CAD Modelling
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to computer modeling, with a parametric modelling application widely used in the design industry. You will develop competency with modelling that supports exploration of design in subsequent studio courses. Learning is structured around lectures and demonstrations followed by structured learning activities. Assignment tasks engage you in designing, modelling and communicating components with a degree of complexity typical of consumer product design solutions.
learning_outcomes: Communicate details with engineering drawings derived from 3D CAD models.
Split and connect components in the virtual CAD environment to create an assembly of parts.
Produce digitally rendered visualisations of products created in a CAD application
Develop CAD models of components with the degree of complexity and form commonly expected in consumer products.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials & Tech 2: Manufacturing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course follows on from Physical Principles for Designers. It places an emphasis upon the relationship between Industrial Design practices and manufacturing processes. You will develop knowledge of engineering materials and manufacturing processes tailored for the Industrial Designer. You will learn to communicate intelligently and effectively with other manufacturing specialists. The focus will be upon plastics, metal alloys, fastening systems and component assembly processes. Other materials and manufacturing processes will also be covered, but in much less detail. Specific topics within this course include, thermoplastics and injection moulding, design for assembly (and disassembly), fit and tolerancing, design specification (AS1100) and advanced manufacturing technologies.
learning_outcomes: Detail and specify manufacturing materials and processes for design projects
Apply effective oral, written and visual communication skills to describe designs related to a range of materials and manufacturing processes, delivered to diverse audiences and contexts
Explain design considerations, properties and performance characteristics for a range of materials
Analyse products and describe a range of key manufacturing materials and manufacturing processes

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Theory 3: People
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces theory and strategies for designing for people and particularly addresses understanding of human diversity. Attention is given to access, usability, comfort and performance of the human/product system. Class activities and assignments support learning of stategies for representing and engaging users in the design process, drawing on perspectives of Ergonomics/Human Factors, User Interface (UI) design and Inclusive Design. Students are equipped to investigate human-use implications of their own current and future design practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply methods for user-testing of a proposed user interface in a given context for a product/system.
Propose and integrate a range of ergonomic evaluation strategies within a design process.
Identify and make use of appropriate guidelines, resources and strategies in designing for physical/cognitive accommodation of a range of users.
Describe the variability of needs and capabilities of people in relation to the use of a product/system.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 2A
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: IDES2221 develops competencies in designing products of intermediate complexity. Through a series of presentations and class activities students will apply knowledge from previous courses to design projects. These design projects include the design resolution and detailing of appropriate forms and assemblies when designing for manufacture. Students will advance their design communication skills for specifying form, details, assembly, fit and finish to accurately communicate their design intent with other design and manufacturing specialists.
learning_outcomes: Design and detail a product appropriate for specific materials and production techniques.
Demonstrate a developed design process and methods in a design projects of moderate complexity.
Identify and describe the materials and manufacturing process used in a variety of mass-produced components and products.
Resolve and communicate product form and function with given technical constraints.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: IDES1211, IDES1212, IDES1213

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 2C
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: IDES2223 continues to develop students' Industrial Design process and build confidence in their methods and application of knowledge. A sequence of projects will include industry collaborations and introduction of specialised knowledge of market segments and production systems. Projects will increase in complexity and in the effectiveness of communication of Industrial Design outputs with visual, written and physical models. Learning from past and concurrent Design Theory course courses will be evident in the Industrial Design outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate refinement in design thinking while resolving Industrial Design problems of increased complexity
Plan and manage an Industrial Design process, allocating appropriate time and resources to each phase
Work effectively as a member of a team, demonstrating adaptability to team-based decision-making processes and commitment to a shared outcome.
Comprehensively communicate an Industrial Design process and recommended outcomes as if to a client.
prerequisites: IDES1211, IDES1212, and IDES1213

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 2A: Production at Scale
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 2A develops and deepens your knowledge about the construction, material choices, and manufacturing considerations when designing products for manufacture. Course content will cover production processes that vary in scale as well as the technical requirements associated with these. In this studio course, you will advance your design communications skills to create persuasive and accurate design documentation that specifies form, details, assembly, fit and finish. The projects will require you to explore the opportunities and challenges associated with a prescribed range of materials and manufacturing processes in the design and development of fully resolved product proposals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the materials and manufacturing processes used in a variety of design components and products.
Critically reflect on your design process in a design project of moderate complexity.
Design and detail a product that is appropriate for specific materials and production techniques.
Communicate product form and function with given technical constraints.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FADA1010 or IDES1211, IDES1311 or IDES1212, and IDES1312 or IDES1213, and IDES1315, and IDES1316

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 2B: User-Centred Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 2B: User-Centred Design develops your ability to design products where user experience, interaction, and meaning are the primary drivers of decision-making. The course focuses on understanding user behaviours, needs, and contexts, and translating these into coherent design responses. Through studio projects, you will apply user-centred research methods to investigate how people interact with products and systems. Emphasis is placed on how physical form, interface, and interaction contribute to usability, cognitive understanding, and emotional experience. Learning is structured through research, concept generation, prototyping, and evaluation. You will develop and test design proposals that respond to user insights while maintaining consideration of material, technical, and manufacturing constraints. The course supports increasing independence in design decision-making, preparing you for more self-directed and integrated studio work in the later stages of the program.
learning_outcomes: Communicate user insights, design intent, and interaction concepts through visual, physical, and narrative formats.
Analyse user behaviours, needs, and contexts to inform product design decisions.
Generate design concepts through iterative development integrating user experience, form, aesthetics, and interface.
Apply user-centred research methods to investigate interaction, usability, and experience.
Evaluate design proposals through prototyping and testing in relation to usability, interaction, and feasibility, including material and manufacturing considerations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FADA1010 or IDES1211, IDES1311 or IDES1212, and IDES1312 or IDES1213, and IDES1315, and IDES1316

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Theory D: Society and Environment
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Theory: Society and Environment examines how industrial design shapes, and is shaped by, social, cultural, ethical and environmental systems. The course positions products not only as functional artefacts, but as material interventions with consequences for people, communities, ecosystems, production systems and patterns of consumption. You will investigate contemporary issues such as sustainability, social responsibility, circularity, equity, resource use, waste, technological change and the environmental impacts of product lifecycles. The course develops your ability to interpret complex contexts, identify relationships between product design and broader systems, and make informed judgements about responsible industrial design practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the social, cultural and environmental contexts within which industrial design operates.
Assess theoretical perspectives applying to people and environments for industrial design practice.
Communicate critical analyses and arguments using written and visual formats.
Critically evaluate case studies of design interventions addressing societal and environmental challenges.
Reflect on the responsibilities of designers operating within complex social and environmental systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 2C: Sustainable Futures
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 2C: Sustainable Futures develops your ability to respond to environmental and social challenges through product-based outcomes. The course examines how design decisions shape use, behaviour, production and broader systems. Through studio projects, you will analyse real-world contexts to identify opportunities and constraints, and develop responses that consider environmental impact, resource use and behaviour within designed systems. Learning is structured through context review, problem framing, concept generation, prototyping and evaluation, supported by iterative development and critical reflection. You will define clear problems, explore multiple directions and resolve coherent proposals appropriate to their context, while justifying decisions in relation to environmental, social and production considerations.
learning_outcomes: Produce resolved prototypes and specifications demonstrating feasible material and manufacturing strategies.
Communicate design intent, process, and outcomes through visual, written and physical formats.
Analyse social and environmental contexts, existing products, and precedents to identify opportunities and constraints for responsible product design.
Generate product design concepts that address identified challenges and opportunities.
Evaluate and refine design concepts through lifecycle thinking and consideration of material, social and environmental impacts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: FADA1010 or IDES1211, IDES1311 or IDES1212, and IDES1312 or IDES1213

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Theory A: Human Factors in Product Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Theory C: Human Factors develops your ability to understand and evaluate how people interact with products, systems, and environments, and how this informs responsible industrial design practice. The course introduces ergonomics, anthropometry, usability, and inclusive design, focusing on how human capabilities, limitations, and variability shape product use. Through observation, measurement, prototyping, and user testing, you will examine physical and cognitive interaction, analyse usability and accessibility, and interpret how design decisions affect safety, comfort, and experience. You will undertake observation-based inquiry to identify barriers in everyday activities, using first-hand evidence to interpret user needs and inform inclusive design responses. You will apply human factors principles and methods to evaluate interactions, using evidence from testing and analysis to support design reasoning. The course also develops your ability to interpret guidelines, standards, and research, and to critically reflect on ethical and inclusive implications. These capabilities support studio work by strengthening evidence-based design judgement in relation to human use and interaction.
learning_outcomes: Analyse human physical and cognitive capabilities, limitations, and variability in relation to product and system use.
Apply human factors principles and data to inform and justify industrial design decisions.
Evaluate product and interface interactions through user testing and analysis in relation to usability, safety, and inclusion.
Reflect on the ethical, social, and inclusive implications of design decisions for diverse users.
Communicate human factors analyses and findings using appropriate visual, diagrammatic, and written formats.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials and Manufacturing for Industrial Designers 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Materials and Manufacturing for Industrial Designers 2 emphasises the close relationship between industrial design practice and manufacturing technologies. You will deepen your knowledge of engineering materials and manufacturing processes, enabling you to communicate intelligently and effectively with other specialists in industrialised production. You will learn about cover plastics and metals, with specific emphasis on thermoplastics and injection moulding, sheet metal and tube, CNC machining, advanced manufacturing technologies, composites, fit and assembly, and design specifications to Australian Standards.
learning_outcomes: Analyse products and describe a range of key manufacturing materials and manufacturing processes.
Explain design considerations, properties and performance characteristics for a range of materials.
Communicate design approaches employing a range of materials and manufacturing processes using written and visual formats.
Detail and specify manufacturing materials and processes for design projects.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: IDES1311, IDES1315 and IDES1316

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Theory 5: Perspectives
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In todays world, problems are often complex, interrelated, dynamic and multifaceted. The role of design and innovation amid such complexity is crucial. Students in this course will learn from a range different perspectives, presented in lectures and readings, and a series of exercises in which they will analyse and evaluate issues and synthesise findings into new opportunities. Students will work collaboratively and iteratively using both visual representations and physical mock-ups to arrive at design propositions that they have to pitch to the class. Learning from this course therefore supports students in proposing design interventions that encompass a wide scope of issues, are enduring and ultimately more successful.
learning_outcomes: Engage critically and creatively with other disciplinary frameworks in design thinking and in relation to the generation and testing of product and system ideas.
Compare and contrast a range of disciplinary perspectives applied through small or big issues (such as the UNSW Grand Challenges).

Pitch a novel idea of moderate complexity with visual and written media to a relevant audience, revealing understanding of other disciplinary perspectives as well as the contribution of design thinking and process.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computer Aided Product Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course is structured around lecture/demonstrations and practical computer lab classes in which you will learn various aspects of computer modelling and advanced techniques for communication of design ideas. Building on CAD modelling skills already acquired, you will undertake exercises and project work based on design examples and presentation methods typical of industrial design practice. Learning from this course will support your capability in subsequent design studio courses and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Employ surfacing tools and techniques to design objects with free-formed curved surfaces.
Prepare animations from CAD models.
Communicate effectively with digital images to varied audiences and at different stages of the design process.
Make digitally rendered images with lighting and surface effects for enhanced realism.
Create realistic composite images of an object in context with rendered CAD models and photographs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design in the Asian Century
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design in the Asian Century invites you to explore the world of industrial design through the lens of the 'Asian Century', a transformative era in which Asia's vibrant growth and investment in technology and education are reshaping global design and innovation. This two-week elective, set in a host Asian country, immerses you in design practices and manufacturing processes unique to Asia. You will experience first-hand the blend of traditional and contemporary designs in everyday objects, systems, and lifestyles in that region. You will interact in design workshops with Asian industrial design students from partner universities, absorb the rich design heritage of your host country, and learn to imagine solutions that are culturally sensitive and contextually relevant. These experiences will not only expand your design worldview but also help you embrace a global design mindset and understand the power of cultural diversity in creative problem-solving. By the end of this course, you will emerge as an Asia-literate designer, ready to contribute to the globally interconnected industrial design realm that is increasingly influenced by Asian dynamics.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on your learning experiences encountered in Asia.
Identify and critically analyse the unique features of Asian industrial design.
Document diverse Asian design elements through visual means.
Demonstrate cultural preparedness for an international design context.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 3A
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on the capacity of industrial design to address complex and pressing issues in the real world and will highlight the ecological and social responsibilities you will take on as an industrial designer. You will develop design competence beyond purely commercial objectives by using industrial design as a tool for achieving certain aspects of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. With each undertaking you will be expected to demonstrate a high level of technical resolution and documentation, and a rigorous engagement with the environmental and societal issues that are seen as opportunities for design intervention.
learning_outcomes: Undertake a rigorous design process to generate, develop and communicate innovative, sound and sustainable solutions to real-world design problems
Apply and integrate your prior knowledge of design principles, modeling, drawing, manufacturing, materials, marketing and information searching to arrive at work approaching a professional standard
Reflect on the overall impacts of your design solutions, your design process, the development of your skills and abilities
prerequisites: Pre-requisites: IDES2221, IDES2222, IDES2223

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design Studio 3B
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In IDES3321 you will focus on applying and synthesising knowledge gained from previous courses to prepare you for industry practice and working on projects that consider commercial requirements and constraints. This studio course will highlight the necessity for a refined design process within a commercial framework. You will gain further experience in applying research and design methodologies to produce outcomes that address technical and manufacturing constraints while at the same time prioritising social, consumer and market needs. Each undertaking has a strong emphasis on innovation, technical resolution and high-level design documentation to a professional standard. A rigorous and responsible approach to product design is fostered by addressing real-world consumer, environmental, social, commercial, technological and manufacturing needs.
learning_outcomes: Independently manage a product design process from research to design and show coherent connections between knowledge and process
Communicate, in written and visual media, the process of design, design exploration and the rationale for choices made
Describe a proposed final design with a level of detail and specifications suitable for transfer to production
Demonstrate synthesis of socio-cultural and technical understanding in the completion of a design project of moderate complexity
prerequisites: Pre-requisites: IDES2221, IDES2222, IDES2223

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 3A: Integrated Product Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 3A prepares you for industry practice by working on projects that consider commercial requirements and constraints. The studio course highlights the necessity for an iterative but structured design process within a commercial framework. You will gain further experience in applying design research methodologies to produce outcomes that address technical and manufacturing constraints while at the same time prioritising social, consumer and market needs. You will engage in practical projects that parallel industry processes, with each undertaking having a strong emphasis on innovation, technical resolution, and high-level design documentation to a professional standard. A rigorous and responsible approach to product design is fostered by addressing real-world consumer, environmental, social, commercial, technological, and manufacturing needs.
learning_outcomes: Describe a proposed final design with a level of detail and specifications suitable for transfer to production.
Synthesise socio-cultural and technical knowledge in the completion of a design project of moderate complexity.
Communicate the process of design, design exploration and the rationale for choices made through written and visual media.
Independently manage a product design process from research to design resolution.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: IDES2321 or IDES2221, IDES2322 or IDES2222, and IDES2323 or IDES2223

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Studio 3B: Graduation Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Studio 3B: Graduation Project is the culminating studio in the Industrial Design specialisation, requiring you to independently conceive, develop, and resolve a substantial design project. Building on prior research work, you will define and pursue a self-directed design opportunity, integrating user, technical, material, and contextual considerations within a real-world framework. The course emphasises independent inquiry, critical judgement, and professional responsibility. You will develop your project through iterative prototyping, testing, and evidence-based refinement, demonstrating your ability to evaluate design decisions and resolve complex challenges. Increasing responsibility is placed on your capacity to manage project direction, justify decisions, and respond to constraints. You will produce a highly resolved design outcome supported by validated prototypes and coherent documentation demonstrating technical credibility and feasibility. Outcomes will be presented through a public exhibition and supported by portfolio-ready documentation, requiring clear and professional communication to diverse audiences. The course prepares you for professional practice and further research by consolidating independence, judgement, and accountability in industrial design.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design intent, process, and outcomes through coherent visual, verbal, and artefact-based formats for diverse audiences.
Generate an original industrial design proposal through a research-informed and iterative project development process.
Produce a highly resolved design outcome demonstrating technical feasibility, integration, and professional standards.
Analyse user, contextual, and technical considerations to frame a self-directed design opportunity.
Evaluate design proposals through testing, feedback, and evidence-based refinement.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: IDES3331 and IDES3333

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Theory C: Speculative Product Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Theory C: Speculative Product Design challenges you to transcend traditional industrial design through speculative design practices, where imagination and critical thinking converge to create visionary product concepts. You will interrogate current norms and propose innovative solutions for tomorrow's challenges. As you navigate through this course, you will critically engage with the past, present, and future of industrial design, using this rich contextual framework to ideate products that aim to transform future societies and environments. The course fosters a space where design meets prediction, encouraging you to synthesise historical design trajectories with emergent trends to create designs that both reflect and influence the ethos of the times to come.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the potential influences and interdependencies of industrial design problems to the natural environment and on the broader society.
Pitch design ideas effectively using visual and verbal formats.
Compare and contrast a range of disciplinary perspectives applicable to various industrial design issues.
Generate a novel idea of moderate complexity that addresses an industrial design issue.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Theory B: Product Design Research Methods
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Theory B introduces you to a range of established industrial design research methods, theories, and approaches to understand existing products and develop new ones. The course focuses on rigorous academic research skills and writing within the context of industrial design research, including activities such as observation, analysis and interpretation of user behaviours, simulation of design alternatives, and analysis of available information. You will deepen your understanding of design thinking and the industrial design process. Your learning will include question framing, writing a challenge statement and a research proposal, reviewing the literature, data gathering, decoding product design forms and values, information analysis and synthesis, and authoring an industrial design research report. You will develop a theoretical platform to underpin your industrial design research enquiry and deepen your understanding of users in terms of their habits, behaviours, and emotions.
learning_outcomes: Apply design research methods to the investigation of design challenges and problems to identify opportunities.
Develop a design brief through examination and formulation of essential components.
Evaluate current and proposed designs using various design research methods.
Apply an iterative design process through product design research methods.
Critically reflect on the impact of design research methods and knowledge acquired through theory and practice.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Theory E:  Past, Present, and Future
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Theory E: Past, Present and Future introduces you to the historical, cultural, and theoretical foundations of industrial design and their relevance to contemporary practice. The course examines key movements, artefacts, and ideas that have shaped the discipline, and explores how design responds to changing technological, social, and cultural conditions across global contexts. Through visual analysis, case studies, and creative project-based work, you will interpret historical precedents and examine how products reflect values, behaviours, and systems of their time. Emphasis is placed on understanding relationships between form, function, meaning, and context, and on recognising how historical knowledge can inform contemporary design thinking and future directions. The course supports the development of critical awareness and interpretive skills through designerly modes of inquiry rather than traditional essay-based approaches. You will engage with historical material through visual, material, and project-based outputs that connect analysis with application. These capabilities support your studio work by strengthening your ability to situate design decisions within broader disciplinary, cultural, and future-oriented contexts.
learning_outcomes: Communicate historical and theoretical insights through visual, material, and project-based formats.
Situate industrial design practices within broader cultural, social, and technological contexts.
Identify and interpret key historical movements, artefacts, and ideas in industrial design.
Apply historical precedents to inform contemporary and future-oriented design thinking.
Reflect on the evolving role of industrial design in shaping everyday life and future possibilities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Capstone Research
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Capstone Research focuses on design research and design research methods, in preparation for the final capstone project in the following term. You will develop research knowledge and skills, as you produce a substantive design research report based upon an agreed topic. The report, covering problem and/or opportunity identification, data gathering, synthesis and analysis of information and research results will conclude with a design brief, and proposals to guide your capstone project the following term.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique professional design practice including Intellectual Property, product standards, compliance and business cases.
Critically reflect on theoretical knowledge, ideas and design practice(s) intergrating different perspectives.
Select and apply suitable design research methods to identify and describe design problems, target market and user needs.
Plan, research, and write a professional Design Research report, to industry standard.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Advanced Studio, you will engage with a real-world design brief co-developed with an external industry partner and adopt the mindset and practices of a consultant industrial designer. The course simulates the expectations, deliverables, and pace of professional practice. You will be challenged to rapidly interpret the brief, analyse the problem space, identify stakeholder needs, and communicate your reasoning with clarity and purpose. Throughout the course, you will practise active listening, critical questioning, research, and strategic reframing to define and refine design opportunities, while developing your own iterative design process that will carry forward into your Capstone Project and future professional practice. You will develop advanced industrial design capabilities across concept exploration, research, visualisation, CAD, prototyping, and narrative-based communication. Iterative feedback from academic staff and industry partners will guide the development of your work as you progressively increase the fidelity and resolution of your design response.The assessment is a single project with presentation milestones and a final consolidated project booklet communicating design outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design intent, processes, and outcomes through advanced visual, verbal, and written design communication methods
Generate and develop creative design concepts that respond effectively to identified user needs, technical constraints, and industry expectations
Plan and execute a staged industrial design project that meets milestone requirements and progressively advances design resolution
Evaluate design processes and outcomes using critical reflection and feedback to refine, justify, and strengthen design decisions against professional standards
Analyse complex design briefs to identify key problem factors and define opportunities for innovation within contemporary industrial design contexts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Capstone Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This capstone project in the honours program is an opportunity to synthesise the skills and knowledge gained throughout the BID program. The work produced for this course will represent the culmination of studies in the program and provide an opportunity to demonstrate capabilities as an emerging design professional. This course builds directly upon the work undertaken in the previous term in IDES4100 Capstone Research. Previously learned skills and knowledge will be drawn upon and applied to a self-managed project that will 'showcase' the student's capabilities to potential employers. .
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective project planning and time management in the design process.
Resolve a design solutions to the level expected in professional practice.
Effectively communicate the purpose and details of the design outcome to a standard expected in commercial practice.
Demonstrate their readiness as an emergent professional industrial designer.
Demonstrate the capacity to address all areas of product design project from brief to completion.
prerequisites: Completion of IDES4100

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Industrial Design Capstone Project B
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Industrial Design Honours Project B is the concluding phase of the Honours capstone project. Building on the design direction established in Industrial Design Honours Project A, the course focuses on advancing the project toward a resolved design outcome suitable for professional and public presentation. You will undertake detailed development and refinement of your project through modelling, prototyping, testing, fabrication, and validation activities, integrating considerations of usability, materiality, manufacturing feasibility, functionality, aesthetics, and contextual relevance. Emphasis is placed on disciplined iteration, technical resolution, and the synthesis of research insight with professional design judgement. You will be expected to demonstrate increasing independence in project management, production planning, decision-making, and delivery while generating evidence that supports and validates design decisions. The course culminates in the delivery of a resolved Honours-level design outcome supported by technical documentation, validation evidence, and exhibition-quality communication materials. Upon completion, you will have independently resolved, validated, and communicated a substantial research-informed industrial design project demonstrating advanced technical capability, professional judgement, and readiness for professional practice or higher degree research.
learning_outcomes: Deliver an independent design project through effective planning, management, and production processes.
Demonstrate advanced material, technical, and manufacturing resolution through digital modelling, prototyping, and fabrication processes.
Advance and resolve a substantial industrial design project to an Honours-level standard.

syllabus_overview: This course takes you into the landscape to apply theory to practice and have experiential inquiry and engagement. You will encounter large-scale inclusive conservation practices that include people, culture, and the more-than-human world in the context of protected areas and learn from a range of participants who hold different orientations and perspectives. You will grapple with the challenges to conservation and protected areas through co-learning and rethinking what we do in rapidly changing socioecological contexts. title: Political Ecology: Sustainable Development & Justice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This subject takes an international perspective on ecological and social inequity and other global challenges, focusing on ongoing impacts of colonisation, the role of environmental conventions and trade rules, and the impact of global governance strategies such as the “sustainable development goals.” This course will be of particular interest if you are concerned with issues of global inequality, environmental justice, and the roles of the state and civil society. In this course, you will explore the environmental challenges that face the “Global South” and engage in a productive critique of neoliberal models of economic growth and development that underlie these challenges. The course provides you with an understanding of the historical, political, and international contexts within which issues of environment and “development” are framed, governed, and (in some cases) addressed. You will consider the social and environmental impacts and implications of global value chains and production networks, as well as efforts to undertake more ethical and sustainable approaches. You will engage in case studies and learn about applied, practical, and reflexive approaches for addressing globally interlinked issues facing the “Global South,” or “majority world.”

Apply critical thinking to core concepts relevant to emerging global environmental issues and challenges

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Corporations, Capitalism, & Transforming Environments
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the evolution of business organisations and the political economy of capitalism, focusing on the interplay among large corporations, governments, investors, consumers, and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) as they intersect with the climate, environment, and civil society. You will focus on large multi-national corporations and on emerging alternative forms of business organisation, such as social enterprises, cooperatives, and B corporations. You will examine the purpose of the contemporary corporation and issues of how society should best assess business performance and how alternative models of corporate governance offer pathways to better account for and acknowledge environmental and social concerns. You will review the main sustainability reporting frameworks and examine how effective they are in transforming corporations and other organisations into more ethical, environmentally sustainable, and socially just ways of operating. You will consider contributions of capitalism and for-profit multinational corporations to climate crisis and other environmental and social challenges and query whether the existing neoliberal paradigm is best placed to respond to and address such anthropogenic disruptions. In examining the role of state regulation, civil society, and more local democratic options, you will also consider the effectiveness of historic and more recent major political, social, and protest movements on government policy and corporate actions.

In this course, you will gain confidence in permaculture restorative frameworks and methodologies in the contexts of environmental management, leadership, and sustainability. Permaculture design seeks to reconnect people with ecological processes, inter-relationships, and interdependence of living things and to integrate these knowledges to tend to ecosystems in ways that care for the Earth, care for people, and use a fair share of resources. Permaculture has an important role to play in the rapid transition to zero carbon or net negative carbon through restorative and regenerative ecological, social, and cultural practices. The course will have a focus on implementing permaculture solutions, demonstrating how theory learned during seminars applies to real world systems.In successfully completing this course, you will develop applied skills to design and implement urban/suburban permaculture solutions. In addition, in earning an 80% or higher in the course, you will earn a Permaculture Design Certificate.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Policy and Participation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Calls for public participation in, and indeed the democratisation of, decision-making have become a hallmark of contemporary environmental politics, policy, and practice. Many contemporary environmental issues are characterised by institutional commitments to fostering public engagement and participation in decision-making together with greater transparency in the deployment of scientific and policy expertise. However, despite notable successes, such developments often fail to enhance public trust and build more socially responsive and responsible forms of environmental policy and regulation. Outside these institutionally sanctioned spaces of formal consultation, new public collectives function to create spaces of participation that are resistant to processes of political closure and public capture. These insurgent formations call into question normative commitments to institutional accountability and transparency, while also enacting novel participatory collectives situated across a multitude of socio-political sites. While an array of environmental knowledges – both progressive and reactionary – jostle for recognition and political prominence, in this course you will explore ways in which the work of assembling diverse publics capable of testifying to the violence of environmental disruption, and of crafting resilient and emancipatory futures, is indicative of the enduring compulsion toward participation in environmental issues. You will consider these issues through engagement with environmental participation theory and practice, and through direct engagement of a range of real-world examples. You will examine how the right to participate in environmental issues that affect you – codified in the Rio Declaration – raises profound questions concerning contemporary democracy, representation, expertise, and activism. You will develop your own advocacy skills and practical skills for designing and coordinating community participation and engagement initiatives.
learning_outcomes: Critically articulate both the limitations and potentials of environmental participation
Synthesise contemporary theory and practice of environmental participation
Design new models and approaches to environmental participation
Apply understandings of environmental participation to the analysis of real-world examples and case studies

You will bring course concepts and lenses to everyday and extraordinary places and situations in order to question and understand the sociocultural underpinnings of, and responses to, ecological relations. syllabus_overview: This course explores ways contemporary societies are proactively responding to fossil fuelled climate disruption and examines critical and creative ways these responses can be strengthened. Informed by theories of climate justice, the course enables you to critically analyse existing forms of climate action and provides opportunities to engage with, design, and implement arts-based, community-led, decolonising, and other creative, innovative, and novel efforts to reduce emissions and their effects. You will explore efforts at local, national, and international scales, including those of communities, governments, and businesses, and consider examples from around the world. The course includes a significant student-led component designed to increase students' capabilities as leaders for climate justice.

faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores the roles cities can and do play in driving, exacerbating, and potentially addressing a range of environmental and social challenges. With the majority of the world’s human population now living in cities, and with human urban accretion accelerating at a time of multifaceted anthropogenic ecological crises, it is essential environmental leaders have a transdisciplinary understanding of urban processes and impacts on our shared environments. Accordingly, in this course you will address both the promise and risks of urbanism through a variety of lenses and dynamics, such as sustainability, environmental resilience, socioeconomic class, environmental justice, development and new approaches to urban nature and urban futures. This course will involve required fieldwork to enable you to apply, evaluate, and adapt course concepts in a number of real-world urban sites, while developing ideas, experiences, and practices in urban environmental and social change-making.

faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Effective environmental leadership and care is dependent on accurate and responsive information about our environments – but how do we know the world? The course aims to make the familiar aspects of science strange and the strange aspects familiar, encouraging embodied experience of scientific methods as well as situating such practices within their political and cultural contexts through analysis and through meeting with experts. You will learn to become comfortable with the use of a range of scientific modes of exploring environmental questions and to challenge yourself to think about the limits, insights, and contingencies of scientific practice. This course is suitable for both scientifically and non-scientifically trained students.

syllabus_overview: Regimes of environmental law serve as a ubiquitous background to almost all environment and society relations and challenges. syllabus_overview: This 12 UoC project allows you to conduct a piece of research on an environment and society leadership topic. Each project will be individually supervised and will generally require you to conduct a literature review and develop research aims and methods. You will produce a research report of approximately 12,000–13,000 words, although you may negotiate alternative formats if you would like your research outputs to be presented in a creative project format. You may select from a range of topics as agreed with your supervisor. Likewise, the permissible use of AI based tools to be agreed with you supervisor. Theoretical, conceptual, and methodological approaches are expected to be of a high standard. An oral defense of the research project is a precondition to receiving a mark on the project. Master’s students may, with permission from your academic supervisor(s), extend your project or undertake an additional project by enrolling in more than one IEST Research course. This consent is based on staff availability to supervise the topic.
learning_outcomes: Communicate research results in article/report or alternative project format effectively.
Develop and describe appropriate research methodologies.
Plan and develop a robust research project.
Analyse and interpret data.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 UOC of IEST courses and minimum WAM 75. Consent required from the Environmental Management Program Convenor.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Transformation in Business
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This foundational (Level 1) Information Systems (IS) course introduces students to the role and implications of IS in business and society. As an overarching theme, this course examines various information technologies, their issues, impacts and management of organisational objectives and human behaviour. This course will teach students to appreciate and assess existing and emerging technologies affecting businesses, business relationships and their products and services. In taking this course, students will be provided with tasks and assignments that will aid in refining their ability to evaluate the value of IS and deploy them strategically to improve businesses. The tasks and assignments will also enhance their professional competencies, which include communication, teamwork, project management and research skills. The topics covered in this course include understanding the role of Information Systems and IS Professionals in businesses, the relationship between systems, organisations and strategy, the nature and purpose of information systems, the analysis and improvement of business processes, and the emerging trends in IS. The course will also explore contemporary technology-enabled phenomena that disrupt the business landscape. The course also touches on business analytics and artificial intelligence systems that support organisation decision-making. Students will discuss the considerations behind the acquisition and development of IS and the issues common to the management of IS projects. Lastly, the course addresses the need to manage cybersecurity and risks and the potential ethical and social problems businesses face using IS. Assessment adopts a competency-based approach that emphasises demonstrated achievement of learning outcomes through authentic tasks, reflection, collaboration, and professional communication. Students are assessed against clearly defined competency standards aligned with the course learning outcomes. Students must demonstrate competency in all assessment components to successfully complete the course.
learning_outcomes: Describe the components, functions, and nature of Information Systems, and situate them within the academic and professional discipline of Information Systems.
Explain how Information Systems enable business operations, decision-making, and strategy across organisational contexts.
Explain existing Information Systems solutions, identify their key components, and discuss their business implications.
Collaborate effectively with team member to achieve shared objectives, demonstrating professional teamwork and self-leadership skills.
Identify relevant Information Systems frameworks and explain how they relate to real-world business problems, recognising their ethical and professional implications, and outline possible solutions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Business Databases
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This is a foundational (Level 1) Information Systems (IS) course that introduces students to the concepts, techniques, and technologies relevant for creating and managing business databases. It will explain the major components of IS, which are critical to capturing, transmitting, storing, retrieving, manipulating and displaying information used in business processes. Through this course, students will be exposed to the fundamental knowledge of business databases, which are foundational for many advanced courses. Students will be given tasks and assignments to help them acquire the ability to create and manage business databases.
learning_outcomes: Apply Structured Query Language to access and update databases.
Discuss professional responsibilities and ethical issues regarding databases.
Apply conceptual and relational database modelling methods.
Carry out professional teamwork.
Design and implement database systems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Networking and Security
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This is a level 1 undergraduate course that emphasises the importance of Information Technology (IT) infrastructure and security for the smooth operation of businesses in today's digital world. As businesses increasingly rely on technology, the need for skilled IT professionals who can design, implement, and manage secure IT systems is growing. In this course, you will gain a deep understanding of IT infrastructure and security in the business environment. You will develop skills and foundational knowledge to pursue a career in cybersecurity or other related fields. You will learn the different components of IT infrastructure and security, as well as the best practices for designing, implementing, and managing secure systems. In parallel you will gain a deeper appreciation for the importance of the 'People, Processes, and Technology' components of cybersecurity. By completing this course, you will develop the prerequisite skills and knowledge required to enrol in the Level 2 intermediate IS course – INFS2701. Assessment adopts a competency-based approach that emphasises demonstrated achievement of learning outcomes through authentic tasks, reflection, collaboration, and professional communication. Students are assessed against clearly defined competency standards aligned with the course learning outcomes. Students must demonstrate competency in all assessment components to successfully complete the course.
learning_outcomes: Analyse relevant technical and managerial considerations related to the design, deployment, ethics and/or the uses of secure networking technologies within various business contexts.
Create practical solutions based on your knowledge of business data networks, frameworks and regulations and their security that demonstrate analytical and practical skills.
Explain and apply principles of networking and cybersecurity in various business contexts.
Apply knowledge of the current architecture of the Internet and the entities involved with the day-to-day running of networking technologies to solve real-world problems.
Collaborate effectively with teammates in a culturally diverse environment to achieve project goals.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Major Research Project/Thesis in Environmental Leadership
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture

Each project will be individually supervised and will generally require you to conduct a literature review and develop research aims and methods. You will produce a research report of approximately 18,000-20,000 words, although you may negotiate alternative formats if you would like your research outputs to be presented in a creative project format. You may select from a range of topics as agreed with your supervisor. Likewise, the permissible use of AI based tools to be agreed with you supervisor. Theoretical, conceptual, and methodological approaches are expected to be of a high standard. An oral defense of the research project is a precondition to receiving a mark on the project. Master’s students may, with permission from your academic supervisor(s), extend your project or undertake an additional project by enrolling in more than one IEST Research course. This consent is based on staff availability to supervise the topic.

Communicate research results in article/report or alternative project format effectively
Analyse and interpret data
Plan and develop a robust research project

This course is only available to Information Systems, UNSW Business School Co-op Scholars who are enrolled in the BIS (Co-op) (Hons) 3964 or the BCom IS (Co-op) 3554 Degree Programs. Please note INFS2101 is only available to UNSW IS Co-op Scholars and there are no options for International Fee Payment students.
