Examples include: standard relational database issues; analytical database topics; requirements imposed by the move to big data; business analytics infrastructure and tools used with big data. SAS software tools will be used for the skills components of the course: “SAS SQL 1: Essentials” and “Introduction to SAS and Hadoop”
learning_outcomes: Design and assess the value of relational and non-relational database infrastructure.
Evaluate and propose relevant and feasible database infrastructure solutions for specific business analytic problems.
Apply conceptual database modelling techniques (e.g., ER modelling) and normalisation techniques.
Analyse advanced issues in (both relational and non-relational) database design and management.
Build and utilise database solutions to support big data analytics.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Analytics Methods
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: The proliferation of digital platforms, IoT devices, and online transactions has led to an explosion of data. In today's data-driven world, organisations are increasingly leveraging advanced analytics to extract actionable insights from this ever-growing volume of information. Predictive analytics play a vital role in helping organisations anticipate outcomes, optimise decisions, and improve business performance. This course provides a structured and conceptual foundation for predictive analytics, encompassing both forecasting and prediction techniques. It begins with the principles of data-driven inquiry—how to formulate hypotheses, design analytical approaches, and evaluate evidence. Students will learn forecasting methods such as regression and time series analysis to interpret trends and project business outcomes. The course then extends to prediction methods from supervised learning, exploring how modern machine learning algorithms can enhance decision making across marketing, finance, operations, and other business domains. While technical competence is essential, the emphasis of this course is on business interpretation and strategic application—understanding what models reveal, when they are appropriate, and how their insights can guide managerial actions. The goal is not only to build accurate models, but also to translate analytical results into business value and informed decision-making. You will apply these methods using Python, a versatile programming language with extensive libraries for data wrangling, analysis, and visualisation. Through hands-on exercises and business case studies, you will develop both technical proficiency and analytical reasoning skills essential for effective predictive analytics practice in business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Predict future outcomes based on historical data through the application of analytics programming language tools.
Examine the ethical implications of data analytics and communication and their impacts on business and society.
Apply analytic techniques to solve problems and identify opportunities for growth in the business context.
Compose a narrative that illustrates and solves a business problem, and present it convincingly with the aid of visual analytics.
Collaborate with team members to achieve team objectives.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMM5007

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Social Media Analytics in Practice
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Social media and advanced Web technologies, including generative AI tools (e.g. image recognition systems, automated audio-editors, and natural language generation software) have remarkably spurred the rise of digitally empowered consumers, challenging businesses to thrive on social media. In this digital era, consumers have gained a powerful voice, taking over online conversations by generating multimodal content across social media platforms (images, videos, audio, text, and emotional icons). Businesses striving to stay ahead of the competition leverage unstructured social media data to design and implement successful social media strategies. In this course, we equip students with the necessary knowledge and competencies to collect and analyse unstructured social media data using recent technologies such as R, SAS Viya for text analytics, Social Network Analysis, Microsoft Azure AI Services and Google Vision AI. Workshops are practical and designed to engage students in extensive hands-on activities and challenging case studies to develop their critical thinking and analytical skills to address real-life business problems. Upon successful completion of the course, students are expected to demonstrate both a professional perspective as well as technological confidence in social media analytics and its implications for the business context.
learning_outcomes: Consolidate analytical and critical thinking skills to solve real-life business problems helping companies thrive on social media.
Analyse strategic issues related to social media use to solve business problems.
Develop collaborative teamwork skills for solving AI-driven business problems.

Discuss ethical implications aligned with SDGs (Sustainable Development Goals) principles/objectives when conducting social media analytics and articulate their impact on individuals, organisations and society at large.
Apply analytical techniques to analyse unstructured social media data to derive actionable insights/recommendations to address business challenges.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Information Systems Strategy and Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on advanced concepts, practices and issues in the strategic management of IT. The course covers four key themes. It begins with an exploration of the strategic value of IT, including the role of business-IT alignment in realising that value. Second, the course explores strategic IT decision processes, including planned and emergent strategy-making and IT governance. Third, the course examines strategy implementation issues, including the role of IT leadership, project and portfolio management, and sourcing decisions. The course closes with a review of the strategic role of IT-enabled innovation and current trends in strategy and IT. In this course, you will analyse and discuss academic and practitioner papers, cases and examples, and examine strategic IT issues in practice. Where appropriate, you will also be encouraged to draw from and reflect on your own industry experiences.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively and responsibly as part of a team to apply and contextualise theory to industry.
Apply IS/IT strategy development and decision making processes, and examine their alignment with the overall organisational strategy.
Investigate strategic potential and report on strategic implementation in IT management.
Critically review and explain the strategic management of IT, including key issues and challenges, capability and governance.
Using industry skills and techniques, evaluate an organisation's current state, analyse the strategic contribution of IS/IT and propose opportunities for further improvement.
Examine the value and role of IS/IT in assisting organisations to meet strategic goals.
prerequisites: Prerequsite: INFS5602 or INFS5978 or INFS5848 or INFS5885

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Systems Project
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This capstone course offers to each student the opportunity to demonstrate mastery of the theory and practice of information systems management by applying the knowledge and skills gained in the Master of Information Systems Management (MISM). Thus, this course should be completed in the last session of the MISM program. By taking this course, students develop practical research skills by independently completing a research report on an emerging information systems topic that is relevant to their personal interest and future needs. In addition, students are encouraged to develop the critical thinking and self-efficacy skills that are key to success in modern organisational settings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in writing and oral communication skills.
Appreciate the ethical, social, and environmental implications of your research.
Demonstrate your ability to research an emerging topic applying critical thinking skills.
Apply critical management skills such as: self-management, task management, time management, and quality management.
Demonstrate an in-depth knowledge of a specific area of IS management.
prerequisites: (In program 8425 OR 8435 OR 8426 OR 8446 OR Head of School approval) AND completion of 48 UOC within program.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Web3 and Blockchain Applications
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Blockchain as a technology has captured the imagination of businesses since 2009 when the Bitcoin protocol was introduced to the world. Blockchain is a distributed ledger technology that is regulated through a consensus mechanism and secured with cryptographic technology. Although functionally identical to a distributed ledger, the integrity of transactions in the Blockchain is protected through the involvement of network actors in maintaining, updating, and validating all transactions in the network through consensus. By design, a blockchain is virtually immutable and resists data modification. Despite originating as the foundational architecture for transferring cryptocurrencies in the likes of Bitcoin, the application of blockchain technology has since progress beyond its original purpose. With its potential ability to serve as the critical infrastructure of a radically new economy like the advent of the web3 environment, Blockchain applications have the potential to serve as a foundational technology for new socioeconomic systems. This innovation could usher in a new and decentralised paradigm of data governance that will support a decentralised peer-to-peer economy where value and creativity can flow freely with expensive rent-seeking behaviour of traditional intermediaries. The course aims to introduce students to the world of blockchain innovations with specific focus on those that will manifest in the web3 environment such as the metaverse, AI-enabled commerce, self-sovereignty-based governance, and decentralised autonomous organizations (DAOs).
learning_outcomes: Illustrate how organisations could use the Blockchain technology to help organisations improve their business operations and participate in the web3 environment.
Explore different characteristics of entities that will constitute a web3 social and economic environment.
Describe characteristics and components of the Blockchain technology and its use cases in society and economy.
Explain how organisations could use the Blockchain technology to aid in integrating with the web3 environment.
Evaluate the range of cultural, security, privacy and ethical issues that could be addressed through the Blockchain technology.
Differentiate centralised versus decentralised design of business processes, their benefits and limitations.
Communicate an argument effectively in oral and written form.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Information Systems Consulting
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the key concepts, practices and issues in engaging and providing Information Systems/Information Technology (IS/IT) consulting services, from both the client and the consultant perspectives. The course examines the value propositions of IS/IT consulting, how IS/IT consultants engage with organisations and key stakeholders, and how they help analyse and solve business problems. The course seeks to familiarise you with the IS/IT consulting process, common consulting frameworks and the benefits and limitations related to their use, key types of IT consulting engagements, and current trends in IT consulting related to the opportunities and challenges brought about by rapidly advancing technologies.
learning_outcomes: Develop effective writing skills to deliver logically and professionally presented consulting reports.
Select appropriate IT consulting frameworks and methods for analysing realistic business scenarios.
Discuss how risks and ethical dilemmas in IS/IT consulting engagements can be managed with ethical decision making framework.
Recommend appropriate strategy and solutions for managing cybersecurity risks for organisations.
Develop leadership project management skills in cybersecurity initiatives.
Explain the value proposition of IS/IT consulting and its alignment with organisational IT strategy.
Identify and engage internal and external stakeholders effectively using stakeholder management frameworks.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Information Systems and Technology Project Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This is a postgraduate Information Systems (IS) Course under the Digital Transformation specialisation. This course aims to equip you with both theory and practical skills in the management of projects and programmes concerning the development and implementation of business solutions in the information systems context. The course will cover both predictive and adaptive approaches of project management used in contemporary organisations and will give students an exposure on fundamental components and plans for projects. This course is suitable for students who intend to be project managers as well as those who will work as part of a project team in contemporary organisations. The course aims to further develop you as a scholar and future business professional. The course will refine your communication skills and group-work skills, improve your time management and enhance your research skills. The course assumes no prior experience in project management, but does assume that you are familiar with the systems development lifecycle and have a good understanding of the processes involved in the development of information systems. The course is delivered in a three-hour in-person seminar format.
learning_outcomes: Examine ethical and cultural implications in managing information systems projects.
Operate collaboratively with team members and build the capacity to enable others to contribute towards achieving team objectives.
Construct a workable project management plan that includes scope, tasks, schedule, communication, human resource, risk and cost components.
Explain different project management approaches/methodologies in the management of IS/IT projects.
Explain the fundamental components of effective project management.
Develop recommendations using both verbal and written communication methods.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Operations Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Operations management is one core area underlies every enterprise, which is concerned with the processes of producing and delivering goods and services. The focus is to ensure that business operations are efficient in terms of the use of resources and effective in terms of meeting customer needs. This course covers a set of well-established topics such as operations strategy, process analysis, quality management, queuing analysis and forecasting.
learning_outcomes: Propose business solutions in written and verbal forms for operations improvement and process design projects.
Identify inefficiency and ineffectiveness in business operations and propose changes or major redesigns to improve the process.
Practice team skills to organize a functioning team to analyze and improve business process.
Understand the nature of queuing phenomena and manage conditions of variability and perceived wait time.
Understand the theory and implementations of quality control activities for different industries.
Understand the importance of operations strategy to ensure strategic alignment between a company's strategy and operations activities and ability to evaluate operations strategy.
Analyze business operations using appropriate performance measures, such as flow time, throughput rate and capacity.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Service and Quality Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the key concepts in managing service organisations and their operations. The focus is on creating value and customer satisfaction. This course covers in-depth discussions of services, value creations, service strategy, and the issues related to the development of a service system. This course also addresses topics crucial to effectively and efficiently operating a service system, such as managing supply and demand, and service quality management.
learning_outcomes: Explain the strategies for managing service capacity and demand, including customer waiting.
Describe key characteristics and management principles of different types of service operations systems.
Analyse process flows of a service firm in terms of process capacity, utilisation and bottleneck.
Design a Walk-through-Audit (WtA) to evaluate the service quality of a firm from the perspective of a customer.
Explain major philosophies behind the design and development of a quality improvement program.
Interact with team members to achieve group objectives.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Supply Chains and Logistics Design
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the key concepts of supply chain management. Students will improve their ability to understand the interconnectedness of business units and organisations within the supply chain. Supply chain management deals with the management of materials, information and financial flows in a network consisting of suppliers, manufacturers, distributors, and customers. The coordination and integration of these flows within and across companies are critical in effective supply chain management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse inventory issues and recognise the role of inventory in supply chain operations.
Understand the key trade-offs between physically efficient and market responsive supply chains and how these two types of supply chains fit into varied product market requirements.
Understand the bullwhip effect of a supply chain, including its primary causes and the strategies to dampen the effect.
Analyse how cross-functional drivers, such as sourcing, pricing and information technology, may be employed to improve the performance of a supply chain.
Analyse how logistical decisions (e.g., facilities, inventory, and transportation) impact the performance of the firm as well as the entire supply chain.
Interact with team members to achieve group objectives.
Develop strategies to improve supply chain ethics and supply chain sustainability.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Programming for Data Analytics
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This is an intermediate PG Information Systems (IS) elective course that is designed for business students from a variety of disciplines. It introduces students to data processing and programming by providing a first step towards learning web programming technologies for data analytics. Course content is presented through three learning modules. These include Python syntax, business data processing, and managerial issues. In Module 1, students systematically study Python syntax. In Module 2, students learn how to analyse business data using Python. This module teaches from the basics of data analytics to exploring many different types of business data. Students learn how to prepare data for analytics, perform simple statistical analysis, create meaningful data visualisations, and predict future trends from data. In Module 3, the course introduces students to emerging technologies as well as the social, legal, and ethical issues relevant to the technologies discussed in this course. Throughout the course, students are introduced to a number of Python libraries for importing datasets, data frame manipulation, visualizing the data, and building machine learning models.
learning_outcomes: Develop ability to interpret and write reliable, well-structured, and well-documented software programs.
Develop problem-solving skills in designing and implementing programming solutions.
Examine and debug basic software programs.
Describe and apply the principles of object-oriented programming in developing software programs.
Comprehend and apply software testing methods.
Demonstrate ability to effectively use an Integrated Development Environment for conducting analytics.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: INFS5710

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business in the Digital Age
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: The course is delivered in a three-hour seminar format. Digital technologies such as business analytics, fintech, algorithms, and artificial intelligence are transforming businesses globally and becoming an inseparable element in innovating businesses. This course aims to equip students with the ability to analyse, evaluate and develop the strategies of businesses in the digital age. Taught in a 3-hour weekly seminar format, this course, will focus on the strategic, managerial, operational and technical factors in the development of an organisation's digital competencies and capabilities. We investigate current business and technology trends, including the individual, business and societal implications in the contemporary digital landscape. The course makes extensive use of current case studies and gives students the opportunity to design innovative business strategies in the digital age.
learning_outcomes: Develop appropriate and well-justified solutions in response to challenges faced by businesses in the digital age.
Design and deliver an innovative digital business strategy that seamlessly integrates the multiple aspects of organisational functions and responds to complex user needs.
Work collaboratively and effectively with peers to develop innovative ideas and produce a digital business proposal.
Critically evaluate a range of different digital business models and their potential for innovation and disruption.
Examine the impact of the digital revolution on business, and identify the opportunities and challenges it presents.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Cybersecurity for Business
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This is a Level 5 postgraduate course designed to deepen students' awareness and knowledge of IS/IT security-related issues within the dynamic realm of cyberspace. It places a specific emphasis on the imperative need for ethical viewpoints, approaches, and responsible practices from a management perspective when addressing the multifaceted challenges and solutions inherent in IS/IT-related security problems. The course explores the symbiotic relationship between human and technical influences in cybersecurity, delves into risk management and breach mitigation strategies, provides insights into data governance and management frameworks, and identifies emerging trends and influences that will shape the future of cybersecurity and data governance. Through real-world business cases and scenarios, students will analyse the implications these issues present to various stakeholders and develop the skills needed to responsibly manage cyber-related security challenges.
learning_outcomes: Explain fundamental cybersecurity and data governance concepts and processes.
Evaluate the ethical and legal implications of cybersecurity practices, with a focus on regulatory impacts related to privacy protection and data quality.
Apply best practice frameworks and tools to assess cybersecurity, identify threats, and propose protective measures.
Examine the relationships between data governance, data management, and cybersecurity practices, emphasising their collaboration in delivering quality and compliant solutions.

Collaborate effectively with team members to address cybersecurity challenges, reach consensus on actionable solutions, and communicate findings using language suitable for both technical and non-technical audiences.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Responsible Information Technology Management: AI and Beyond
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: The proliferation of information systems (IS)—such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, social media, etc.—has sparked a transformative impact, offering profound benefits to individuals, organisations, and society at large. However, with these technological advancements lie not only substantial challenges in its adoption but also a “dark side” stemming from both intentional exploitation and unintended consequences, and potential misuse by well-intended or malicious actors, posing significant harm to everyone involved. With businesses increasingly reliant on a constellation of information technologies—not just AI but also on the secure, decentralised ledgers of blockchain, the predictive power of big data, and the interconnectedness afforded by IoT—for competitiveness and growth, it is imperative for Information Systems (IS) students, the future leaders of technology management, to not only excel in the capabilities of these technologies but also possess the knowledge, skills, ethical awareness, and sustainability mindset necessary to navigate, lead, and mentor the complex digital landscape responsibly and contribute positively to both business and society. This course provides a realistic view of the constantly evolving technology landscape, exploring complex “wicked problems” associated with these advancements. It complements existing courses of any field by offering a deep examination of technological adoption and management through a synthesis of largely neglected paradigms like humanities, metaphysics, philosophy, symbolism, classical wisdom, cognitive science, and psychology. Assessments for this course will be evaluated using the rhetorical traditions, and a final exam will evaluate how much you have absorbed and your comprehension of the course material. All these components will be in-class and through the use of pen and paper. No electronics will be allowed for these components. This course is offered as an elective course for digital transformation, business analytics and cybersecurity specialisations.
learning_outcomes: Engage in critical reflection using various industry and societal perspectives to propose responsible information technology practices, aiming for sustainable and ethical practices within various cultural contexts.

Synthesise both theory and real-life practice to analyse how information technology design and management lead to challenges in organisations and societies, including legal, regulatory and governmental challenges.
Demonstrate growth mindset and leadership skills essential in professional practice, including strategic thinking, decision-making, and effective communication.
Investigate the complexities of real-world information technology management and adoption challenges in a global context using research-integrated methods.
Critique the multidimensional impacts of various information technologies and AI on individuals, organisations, and society, evidencing the dual aspects of advancements and their potential risks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (INFS5602 or INFS5700 or INFS5704 or INFS5705 or INFS5706 or INFS5917) AND minimum of 18 UOC completed at UNSW

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing Cloud and Network Security
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course provides a holistic overview on our use of digital communication technologies and examines the cyber security implications in contemporary business contexts. Students will develop knowledge and practical skills on digital communication infrastructure, models and protocols, as well as on the People, Processes, and Technology components of cyber security. This course engages students in real-world organisational cyber security scenarios and digital sandbox environments to facilitate critical evaluations of technological and cyber security decisions in organisations and develop practical solutions for organisational cyber security management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ability to effectively communicate principles and policies of digital communication and cyber security, and explain their applications in various business contexts.
Develop skills to analyse issues associated with business data networks and their security and to develop practical solutions towards their resolution.
Demonstrate ability to evaluate relevant technical, managerial, and ethical considerations related to the design, deployment and/or the uses of secure technologies within various business contexts.
Demonstrate ability to effectively communicate the current architecture of the Internet and the entities involved with the day to day running of digital communication technologies.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cybersecurity Leadership and Risk Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Businesses are navigating through challenging global uncertainties (e.g. pandemic, war, climate changes) worldwide. IS/IT is an indispensable part of all business operations today; however even the most advanced technologies still cannot avoid the risks and vulnerabilities faced by organisations. IS/IT provides means by which organisations process their transactions, the mechanisms by which business stakeholders communicate, and the performance and productivity tools in which information is created, managed and maintained in order to pursue the visions and strategies of organisations. The problem is exacerbated by cyber adversaries keeping pace with global uncertainties with many adapting to a changing target landscape. This course addresses knowledge and leadership in planning and managing IS/IT risks in organisations, in the face of the current cybersecurity landscape. This course further investigates these risks in a systematic manner and looks at the current theory, methods and best practice for their identification, assessment, analysis and mitigation.
learning_outcomes: Assess the methodology, framework and processes of IS/IT risk management applied to cybersecurity problems.
Analyse and evaluate the risk management posture of organisations, needs using modern tools and techniques.
Explain the cybersecurity problems faced by contemporary organisations in order to remain strategically competitive.
Discuss IS/IT risk management strategies, and governance decision-making in the face of cybersecurity dilemmas.
Develop and maintain IS Cybersecurity plan, including contingency plan.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Practices in Cybersecurity Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: It is impossible to predict when cybersecurity incidents happen, but managers can decide how prepared their business will be when they do. Beyond the technical aspects of cybersecurity, there are also many managerial and organisational issues that have to be addressed and carefully managed. These include internal and external communication, critical incident responses, and installing or refining a security framework with the appropriate controls to prevent future incidents. This course will cover the contemporary practices in cybersecurity management so that students are equipped with an understanding of how to manage and respond to these issues, as well as the short- to long-term implications of cybersecurity incidents. Along with becoming familiar with concepts and frameworks that are grounded in data on actual attacks launched against businesses, students will learn how to formulate and prioritise measures that (1) prevent/reduce the impact of cybersecurity attacks, (2) prepare for an array of different attacks, and (3) enable the early detection of attacks. Students will also be exposed to methods for implementing automated controls in a cost-efficient and effective manner. This course is designed to facilitate the effective management of, and response to, a wide range of cybersecurity incidents, but the principles, practices, and recommendations covered may apply more broadly to a range of critical and adverse situations such as crises and natural disasters.
learning_outcomes: Assess the effectiveness of cybersecurity incidence response frameworks.
Demonstrate skills to work as part of an incident management team.
Identify opportunities to enable cybersecurity controls through contemporary automation tools.
Demonstrate skills to communicate with a range of stakeholders.
Formulate a plan to minimise the impact of cybersecurity incidents.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cybersecurity Analytics
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course will cover the intelligence and data analysis techniques and skills that will help businesses improve their detection and response to cybersecurity attacks. These techniques can be applied before, during, and after an attack to gain actionable information that will reveal a business’ capability gaps, pain points, and requirements. Students will be exposed to the mindset, tactics, and techniques of cyber adversaries, so that they can leverage established frameworks and best practices to put forward effective countermeasures. The course will also cover the fundamentals of digital forensics, which help business managers acquire a better understanding of what is behind the devices and systems they use, and leverage this body of knowledge to improve their organisation’s incident response and threat prevention. Like police technology detectives in the 1990s, students will learn how to gather high-quality digital evidence, as well as analyse them to understand how information systems and networks can be compromised and, at the same time, how to protect them.
learning_outcomes: Review and apply modelling and intelligence techniques in response to cybersecurity threats.
Gather and document digital evidence in an effective and legally compliant manner.
Evaluate the existing digital forensics and threat intelligence capabilities of a business.
Acquire data analysis skills to better comprehend, interpret, and respond to complex cybersecurity threats.
Communicate information and findings effectively to external investigators and law enforcement agencies.
Discuss the challenges of threat intelligence and digital forensics, and the techniques and best practices for overcoming these challenges.
Collect data on cyber adversaries and leverage this data to design and execute countermeasures.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Accounting Information Systems
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Accounting Information Systems aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the development, use and management of information systems used within the realm of accounting. The course aims to develop knowledge and understanding of the role of accounting information systems in organisations, examine the information technology components of information systems and review the means by which organisations acquire and deploy accounting information systems. The course will include hands-on usage of accounting information systems and tools germane to the area. The course also includes a study of contemporary issues confronting accounting information systems such as governance, security and ethical practices related to the development and use of these systems.
learning_outcomes: Explain how Information Systems support strategic planning, internal control, and decision-making.
Propose appropriate systems development and implementation approaches for Accounting Information Systems environments.
Evaluate governance, risk management, cybersecurity, and ethical issues in Accounting Information Systems and recommend improvements.
Communicate analyses, system documentations, evaluations, and recommendations effectively in written and oral formats.
Explain the components of Accounting Information Systems and their role in supporting business processes and financial reporting.
prerequisites: Prerequisite or corequisite: ACCT5930 and enrolment in 8409 or 8415 or ACCTES8404 or ACCTES8417 or ACCTES8544 or ACCTES8339

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Theoretical Foundations of Information Systems
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: The course examines the most influential and innovative theoretical approaches and theories in the Information Systems (IS) discipline. Based on exemplary published works for each selected theory, students will examine theory’s particular focus, background and ontological assumptions, as well as its epistemological implications and contribution to knowledge. Such an examination will enable an insight into theories’ application, contribution and implications. By engaging in theoretical discourse and critically assessing selected theories students will gain deeper understanding of major theoretical developments in the IS discipline and their relevance and implications for practice. The seminar character of the course assumes active participation and contribution by the students.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend, assess and review major theoretical developments in the IS discipline.
Demonstrate skills and knowledge that enable you to participate in theoretical debates regarding IS research and its relevance to practice.
Apply a selected theory in empirical research and draw novel insights.
Construct written reports of theoretical nature that are logically and systematically presented, in a style of IS research journals.
Critically analyse and assess theoretical foundations of research papers and their contribution to knowledge.
Communicate conceptual ideas in a coherent, succinct and convincing manner, suitable to both research and practitioner audience.
prerequisites: Enrolled into one of the following Research Programs: 1521, 1545, 1561, 1535, 2585, 1540, 1525, 1550, 1605, 1532 or 1745 or 8409 or 8415 or stream ACCTYS8404

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Topic in Information Systems and Technology Management
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course involves creation and submission of a research report about an IS/IT management related topic of your choice. The report must demonstrate critical thought and exhibit a level of analysis appropriate to a Masters degree, and display a high level of professionalism and competence in presentation. Enrolment Requirements: Head of school approval
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply research skills.
To develop your management skills.
Develop and apply your writing skills.
To develop your communication skills.
Develop an in-depth knowledge into specific area of IS/IT management.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Integrated Technology and Analytics Applications
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: INFS5997 Integrated Technology and Analytics Application is a Capstone course that invites you to apply business knowledge and technical skills acquired during their MCom program to tackle real-world problems. This course takes a “living lab” approach to immerse you in a project-based experiential learning environment, where you can deeply engage with and apply multi-disciplinary frameworks to develop user-centric, evidence-based digital solutions for real-world problems. You will synthesise and apply knowledge from different key learning areas (KLAs) to identify, analyse, and frame complex business challenges, fostering a holistic approach to problem-solving. Emphasising critical thinking and innovative problem-solving, the course equips you to critically apply information systems concepts and tools to prototype effective digital solutions. These solutions aim to generate positive, impactful outcomes for stakeholders, acknowledging the vital role of responsible technology design in today's world. Ethical considerations and sustainability are at the forefront of our approach. You will apply ethics and sustainability frameworks within an SDG (Sustainable Development Goals) context to ensure the responsible development of digital solutions. Furthermore, the course emphasises the importance of lifelong learning and personal growth, encouraging you to engage in reflective learning and recognise opportunities for continual development. This practical-oriented experiential learning will equip you with essential career-ready, whole-person skills and attributes, which are pivotal for a successful transition into the workplace. Assessment adopts a competency-based approach that emphasises demonstrated achievement of learning outcomes through authentic tasks, reflection, collaboration, and professional communication. Students are assessed against clearly defined competency standards aligned with the course learning outcomes. Students must demonstrate competency in all assessment components to successfully complete the course.
learning_outcomes: Critically apply information systems concepts, and design and analytical tools to prototype effective, innovative, evidence-based, digital solutions which have positive and impactful outcomes for stakeholders.
Demonstrate reflective learning, opportunity appreciation for personal growth and life-long learning.
Apply effective and appropriate communication skills to articulate the problem-solving process, and justify the potential impact of the digitally enabled solution to a range of audiences.
Apply ethics and sustainability frameworks to the development of responsible digital solutions.
Evaluate and apply project management methodologies to effectively work in, and manage, cross-functional teams.
Synthesise and apply disciplinary knowledge to identify, analyse and frame complex, open-ended business challenges through open ended exploration.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 42 UOC and completion of INFS5602 or INFS5603 or INFS5885 or INFS5848 or INFS5700 or INFS5907

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Key Debates in International Studies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The world we live in is complex, with deeply embedded connections between local, national, international and global phenomena. Today we struggle to understand how to manage the effects of people, finance, services and ideas as they flow across borders. This course introduces you to the field of international studies as an interdisciplinary endeavour. We will explore insights gained from geography, economics, anthropology, sociology and politics to better understand the way global flows interact and how they affect countries in both the developed and developing world.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how these dynamics contribute to changes in citizenship and self-determination, the emergence of conflict and the movement of people across borders
Analyse and critically evaluate debates in international studies from an interdisciplinary perspective
Identify and elaborate on the dynamics and processes that are driving changes to international trade, culture, media, information and politics
Demonstrate familiarity with changes to the structure and form of states, cities and international organisations
Display effective research and communication skills and be able to apply them in essays, presentations and other forms of assessment

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Methods in International Studies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will equip you with a set of research method skills. The course focuses on teaching ‘how’ to undertake and analyse research methods through experiential learning and the use of contemporary and familiar case study examples of research topics relevant to international studies. We will get out of the classroom and practice what we are learning. The course will introduce both traditional methods (for example, discourse analysis, surveys and interviews) as well as innovative methods that draw on the affective turn as well as digital ethnography (for example, embodied observation, sonic movement, photo elicitation and geo-tagging). Underpinning this tuition of research methods is the rationale for generating data through research methods in the first place. All research undertaken with people in international landscapes will involve research methods to understand the interactions, mobilities, modifications, attachments and feelings to, and about those landscapes. This course will equip you with the skills to conduct research methods yourself but it will also develop your awareness of how the data you use is generated, as well as providing the contextual foundation in research ethics and researcher positionality.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise knowledge from lectures and workshops to experiential knowledge gained through fieldwork
Identify the strengths and weaknesses of different research methodologies and distinguish the most culturally, socially and politically applicable research method
Apply knowledge and skills of a broad range of social research methods in a field setting;
Analyse, use and effectively communicate primary and secondary source data in essays, presentations and research reports
Demonstrate how research methods are discussed and utilised in relation to contemporary debates in international studies;
Recognise the ethical, political, cultural and social implications of conducting research
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in an International Studies program (pre 2017). Or INST1005 and INST1006 and enrolment in an International Studies program (2017+). Or ARTS1250 and enrolment in a Geographical Studies major or minor

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Studies Advanced Seminar
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines contemporary topics and the complex interdependencies shaping global affairs, including global governance stakeholders, geopolitical tensions, and grand challenges. You will explore key areas of global interdependency such as the economy, environment, energy and resource politics, human mobility, security and territorial assertions. Through rich discussion, the course investigates how global stakeholders shape and negotiate these dynamics, and invites you to reflect on where you might position yourself within the international sphere. It also provides space for consolidating and reflecting upon learning across the degree and supports the development of professional skills relevant to a wide range of international career pathways.
learning_outcomes: Identify key dynamics and processes that are shaping interdependencies (e.g., economic, environmental, human development, political, security) in today's world
Integrate analytical skills, writing capabilities, problem solving and communication skills in the context of complex international issues and global challenges
Analyse these dynamics and processes in relation to a specific country, region or case study
Develop professional competency and relevant knowledge required for careers in international organisations, diplomacy and global governance
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 72 units of credit overall, and enrolment in an International Studies program or specialisation

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 1 sets the foundation for the thinking and practice of Interior Architecture as a distinctive idea and research-led field of design inquiry and practice. The design component introduces you to the processes, materiality and elements of Interior Architecture. Emphasis is placed on an expansive approach to spatial enquiry, underpinned by thoughtful and self-reflective research. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other Year 1 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Implement a basic schematic design-led proposition based on project specific research.
Communicate project specific research and Interior Architectural ideas through basic visual and verbal formats.
Analyse the requirements of an Interior Architecture brief at an elemental level.
Assemble and utilise a basic materials palette as part of an Interior Architecture project.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The World in Transition
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The course code for this course was previously INST1006 In this course you will study how historical dynamics have shaped the current global system. We ask "how did we get here today?", by looking at the historical relations between governments and peoples on the continents of Europe, Africa, Middle East, Latin America and Asia. Using historical, area studies, and international studies literature, we will examine how specific assumptions, social formations and territorial claims have contributed to trajectories of development and underdevelopment. Using literature from the continents concerned, we also examine how key representations of those who were colonised gave rise to resistance and movements for self-determination.
learning_outcomes: Explain how historical trajectories have created contemporary relations of dependence and inequality in at least one area of the world, such as Latin America, Asia, the Middle East or Africa.
Display effective research and communication skills and apply them in written work, podcasts, and other forms of assessment.
Demonstrate knowledge of how historical dynamics associated with colonialism and imperialism have contributed to claims for self-determination and independence.
Demonstrate a sound working knowledge of the structures and processes involved in slavery, colonialism and imperialism.
Identify and explain key concepts relevant to the historical evolution of the global system.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit overall

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Composition 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Composition 2 builds on BENV1010 to extend communication capabilities and skills specific to interior architecture. You will explore intermediate analogue and digital representations; and develop specialised model making techniques within a workshop context. Emphasis will be placed on an iterative approach to making as a means of spatial exploration, research and articulation of interior environments. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other year one BIA (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Develop competency in analogue and digital representation techniques appropriate to each phase of the design process
Construct 3D models using industry model-making conventions in a workshop environment, through a process of design interrogations
Demonstrate proficient ability in a range of technical drawing conventions and model making techniques to convey ideas
Develop idea-led design enquiry through the application of a reflective design practice utilising a range of 2D representational techniques and methods

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Composition 3
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Composition 3 extends the range of Interior Architectural communication capabilities from BENV1010, INTA1002 & BENV1012. In this course, you will engage with a further range of advanced techniques and applications for representing spatial atmosphere and effect, including analogue drawing, digital representation and layout along with advanced model making. Workshops will also provide you with verbal and visual communication tools of relevance to the practice of Interior Architecture. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other year two BIA (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced capabilities in a range of digital platforms associated with 3D modelling and fabrication as a communication and design tool
Demonstrate an advanced range of analogue and digital representation skills that are appropriate to each phase of the design process
Demonstrate a range of advanced design compositional skills and an ability to communicate complex design ideas verbally and visually, to a range of audiences
prerequisites: Prerequisites: BENV1010 or INTA1001, and INTA1002; or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 2 focuses on the articulation of design ideas through research, thinking, drawing and making, practices. The design component introduces you to languages and elements of Interior Architecture, spatial enclosure and definition, including issues of materiality, assemblage and composition, human scale and form, in relation to simple forms of Interior Architecture occupation. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other Year 1 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Generate a basic materials palette as a representation of design intent, using research-led enquiry.
Communicate design ideas through graphic and / or verbal presentations.
Analyse and interrogate an Interior Architectural brief to create an elemental design proposition.
Manipulate spatial enclosure at a fundamental level, including rudimentary environmental control and spatial organisation.
Develop proficient plans, elevations and sections, from a research-led and idea-generated position.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Technics 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Technics 1 sets the foundation for the craft and discipline of Interior Architecture. You will be introduced to the people, processes, principles, and primary building elements of Interior Architecture through lectures and weekly studio-based workshops. You will explore core considerations around the role of the interior architect, and the design, documentation, and construction processes. In addition, you will develop a basic understanding of the key aspects of design-making including aesthetics, functionality and sustainability, structural principles, and basic constructional assemblies. You will demonstrate your understanding of basic materiality, and the typical construction assemblies through industry standard documentation practices. This course is designed to be completed alongside Year 1 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses and Interior Technics courses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate basic documentation skills specific to the practice of Interior Architecture.
Demonstrate basic sustainable design concepts through research and application to Interior Architecture.
Identify the major constructional systems and primary building components used in the formation of interior space.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Technics 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Technics 2 focuses on the basic constructional assembly systems and components of interior architectural building elements. You will learn about the core considerations of structure, substrate, and skin. You will explore these basic construction assembly systems from a macro to micro scale, starting from larger elements of the interior to smaller joinery items. You will develop the technical documentation techniques required as an industry professional through lectures and studio-based workshops. You will explore the role of the builder versus the role of the interior architect and the coordination between the two. Emphasis is placed on your ability to resolve and employ basic building elements as informed by design intent, aesthetics, functionality, and sustainability thematic. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other Year 2 Interior Architecture (Hons) and Interior Technics courses.
learning_outcomes: Resolve the constructional assembly of building elements that form the interior environment.
Develop material palettes informed by design intent, aesthetics, functionality and sustainability considerations.
Demonstrate proficient documentation skills specific to industry practices in Interior Architecture.
Explain the properties and environmental impacts of the major material groups used in Interior Architecture.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Technics 4
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Technics 4 focuses on the systems of environmental controls, including lighting, acoustics, thermal comfort and building services. You will learn about interior environmental control principles, their relationship to the human experience and explore the design, documentation, and coordination process. You will explore how interior environments can be controlled through design principles, spatial geometry and material selections. You will develop an understanding of interior architectural environmental control through studio-based workshops and lectures. You will communicate your understanding through a comprehensive technical documentation set as per industry standards. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other Year 2 Interior Architecture (Hons) and Interior Technics courses.
learning_outcomes: Communicate Interior Architecture environmental controls in a comprehensive and extensive documentation package, according to industry conventions.
Identify and analyse technical principles of natural and artificial lighting, passive and automated thermal comfort, building services and acoustics specific to Interior Architecture.
Apply technical principles in an interior design scheme in a way that is mindful of environmental and social responsibility.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: INTA2001 and INTA2002, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Technics 3
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Technics 3 focuses on the material and the constructional idea of structure, substrate, and skin in a small-scale interior element. You will explore the application of materials in conventional and non-conventional details as informed by aesthetics, functionality, and environmental sustainability. You will develop core considerations of small-scale interior details, such as size, format, edges, junctions, and fixings. You will explore and resolve the constructional and compositional application of materials of a small-scale interior element. Through this process, you will develop an understanding of the role of an interior architect versus the builder/consultant and the coordination between the three. You will communicate your understanding through a detailed technical documentation set as per industry standards. This course is designed to be completed alongside all other Year 2 Interior Architecture (Hons) and Interior Technics courses.
learning_outcomes: Identify and resolve primary edge, junction, fixing, and pattern details common to Interior Architecture.
Demonstrate intermediate documentation skills specific to industry practices in Interior Architecture.
Employ ethical material and detailing strategies as informed by design intent, aesthetics, functionality and sustainability considerations.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: INTA2001 and INTA2002, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Dissertation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The dissertation is to be a written work of scholarship of between 6,000 and 8,000 words that deals with the theoretical basis of your proposed Graduation Project – or a topic of your choice. It will demonstrate your ability to thoroughly research an approved topic and present a well-reasoned argument in support of a clearly stated hypothesis. It is to be completed before the commencement of the Graduation Project.
learning_outcomes: Apply an understanding of academic conventions in research and writing.
Investigate some aspect of the graduation project in depth.
Explain a clear understanding of the relationship between theory and design practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: INTA3002, INTA3003, INTA3004, and either BENV1015 or INTA3001

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course sets the foundation for thinking about interior space within historical, cultural and theoretical contexts. Students will be introduced to methods of research, analysis, interpretation and documentation within the context of academic conventions and in relation to the development of design propositions.
learning_outcomes: Recognize the relationship between history, theory and Interior Architecture practice
Utilize academic conventions in relation to research, writing and other forms of scholarly investigation
Evaluate and identify how research can inform interior design propositions
Describe aspects of the history and theory of interior architecture and design within larger social, cultural and technological contexts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives 2 focuses on interior space as a site of dwelling and introduces you to historical, cultural and theoretical perspectives on the concept of dwelling and its material constructions. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other Year 1 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of scholarly enquiry in the form of an independent research task.
Effectively communicate the outcomes of research through a combination of verbal, visual and the written form.
Describe and evaluate the ways in which research can inform Interior Architecture practice.
Describe dwelling concepts within historical and cultural contexts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 3
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 3 focuses on the translation of Interior Architectural design research, thinking and spatial ideas through multiple and iterative design practices. The primary focus is public interior environments. You will gain a deeper understanding of design language and the elements of spatial dynamics relevant to public use by working on complex spatial and material relationships and various forms of occupation. Emphasis is placed on an expansive approach to spatial translation underpinned by creative thinking and self-reflective research. This course is designed to be completed alongside all other Year 2 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Transform and manipulate spatial enclosure at a systematic and logical level both functionally and experientially.
Prepare an Interior Architectural design proposal based on methodical analysis and interrogation of a given design brief.
Generate and propose a materials palette as an integral representation of design intent.
Communicate design proposals at various phases of the design process using relevant representation techniques.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: INTA1000 and INTA2000, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives 3
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Critical Perspective 3: Consumption focuses on interior space as a site of consumption, and analyses the diversity of tangible, social and political elements that are consumed in interior spaces. It explores the role of Interior Architecture as a strategy of communication, mediation and engagement through an historical, cultural and theoretical investigation of a range of typologies including retail and hospitality. This course is designed to be completed alongside all other Year 2 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the ways in which research can inform Interior Architecture practice.
Effectively communicate the outcomes of research verbally as well as through a combination of visual and written material.
Assess the social, cultural and historical contexts and implications of Interior Architecture typologies.
Identify and critically analyse key issues associated with a given research topic related to consumer focused architecture.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: INTA3002, and either BENV1161 or BENV1015; Or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Critical Perspectives 4
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: INTA3004 Critical Perspectives 4 builds on your previous studies and the other courses in the Critical Perspectives stream. This course focuses on interior space as a site of constructed identity. The role of interior architecture in codifying and reproducing social identities will be explored through an historical, cultural and theoretical investigation of a range of typologies including civic, community and corporate. This course also provides the foundation for independent research in your final year of study and is educationally sequenced alongside all other year two BIA (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Communicate your research processes and findings verbally and/or through a combination of visual and written material.
Apply research methods and techniques specific to the practice of Interior Architecture to an independent task.
Reflect on the ways in which research can inform interior architecture practice.
Critically analyse key issues associated with social and cultural identity as related to the practice of Interior Architecture.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: INTA3002, and either BENV1161 or BENV1015 or INTA3001; OR completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 4
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 4 focuses on the practice of Interior Architecture as informed by creativity, research and design. You will apply the language and elements of spatial organisation to complex forms and patterns of occupation including workplace and institutional typologies.
learning_outcomes: Develop design proposals informed by knowledge and appreciation of the cultural and theoretical contexts of Interior Architecture.
Verbally communicate design ideas at each phase of the design process.
Apply digital and analogue representation techniques appropriate to each phase of the design process.
Apply analytical and research methods relevant to Interior Architecture projects.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: INTA1000 and INTA2000, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Practice of Interior Architecture
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Practice of Interior Architecture presents fundamental elements of current best business practices from the profession of Interior Architecture. The profession requires the ability to work collaboratively with other design practitioners and to understand the professional framework of current business practices. This course extends your range of practical skills for entering professional life. You will develop your knowledge and proficiency in relation to legal and ethical codes of practice, networking, negotiation, and collaboration. You will develop skills in research investigation analysis and interpretation through short assignments which relate to your concurrent studio work and produce a design portfolio in response to a simulated employment advertisement.
learning_outcomes: Identify and integrate the requirements of a design enterprise in relation to the required governing body processes.
Locate and assimilate foundational professional practice skills and fundamentals within your individual studio practice.
Apply professional skills associated with Interior Architecture and related built environment professions.
Evaluate and address legal and governmental frameworks specific to the practice of Interior Architecture, including copyright, fee structures and mechanisms.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 5
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 5 focuses on the development and realisation of interior spatial narratives through research-led design practice. Emphasis is placed on the integration of design and professional practice through projects focused on complex forms and patterns of occupation in small to medium scale buildings. This course is designed to be completed alongside all other Year 3 Interior Architecture (Hons) courses.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate design ideas graphically and verbally in each phase of the design process.
Apply reflective and iterative design methodologies as a means of developing a design proposal.
Demonstrate an enquiry process which supports the development of an Interior Architectural design proposal.
Relate areas of research and enquiry in Interior Architecture practice to relevant grand challenges of the industry.
Synthesise complex space planning considerations through an evaluative design process.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 6 focuses on the development and realisation of interior spatial transformations through research-led design practice. Emphasis is placed on the integration of design and professional practice through projects focused on complex forms and patterns of occupation in medium to large scale buildings. You are introduced to fundamental elements of current business practices and the information and knowledge required to comprehend the practices, processes and procedures within the profession of interior architecture. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other year three IA (Hons) courses.

Constructively engage as part of a team dynamic involved in creative and analytical problem solving through Interior architecture projects.
Evaluate complex knowledge associated with relevant and current modes of operation critical to the practice of Interior Architecture and the current global grand challenges.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 7
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 7 focuses on the agency of the interior in the context of the urban morphologies and civic typologies of the twenty-first century city. This final year studio provides an environment that mirrors a professional design practice in which you will refine, synthesise, and communicate the knowledge and skills acquired in previous studios with proficiency. You will engage in research and translate this research into a design proposition. The research phase of the studio includes site, heritage and context analyses, which in turn will inform your development of a project brief. You will prepare the brief in the form of a Design Research Report and use this as the basis for preparing an initial design response. The outputs of this studio, the design research, design brief and design proposition, form the basis of your final design studio, Design Practice 8.

Locate and analyse the project specific knowledge relating to site, heritage and context.
Prepare a design research report to professional standards.
Apply creative and analytical problem-solving skills to the development of research and design projects.
Test and assess a range of design propositions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 8
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Interior Architecture Practice Studio 8 focuses on the second phase of detailed design and resolution of the final design project, culminating in a cohesive and comprehensive design response. This studio builds on the design propositions developed in Design Practice 7: Propose. Using the design proposition developed in the Investigation phase, you will then work on detailed design development and resolution of a number of key spaces and elements within the scheme, incorporating work from all phases in a final presentation. The outcome from this studio is a rigorous, inventive and professional design proposal which includes documentation of design research, design process and the developed design. This course is educationally sequenced alongside all other year four IA (Hons) courses.

Develop a resourcefulness with the practices, processes and procedures related to the profession of interior architecture and its regulatory environment, through the process of design enquiry.
Articulate a sophisticated and thorough interior architecture aesthetic and functionality built for an ability to integrate ‘zeitgeist’.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

Classes provide an opportunity to clarify and extend work covered in Introducing Law & Justice. Describe personal strengths, challenges and goals in relation to academic success within a law degree (PLO 9)

Examine principles and structures of the Australian legal system focusing on cases and judicial decision-making (PLO 1, 4)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Contracts: Problems of Performance, Breach and Termination
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: The course examines systematically and in-depth (to an extent not feasible in basic undergraduate Contract law courses) major principles of Australian law governing the performance, breach and termination of many commercial and conveyancing transactions. It is primarily concerned with complex applications of general contract law principles rather than the more specific rights that are sometimes conferred by statutes dealing with "consumer" contracts. As well as investigating many practical problems in applying the law, the course makes a sustained attempt to assist students to discern frequently unrecognised interrelations between legal principles, and thus to acquire a better integrated view of an area of law which (despite its practical importance) is widely regarded as amorphous and highly challenging. The course addresses a range of difficult practical, legal and evidentiary questions that have been raised in recent appellate judgements but often remain incompletely answered. Main Topics Contingent conditions precedent to performance Promissory and concurrent conditions Discharge by performance Nature of breach Entitlement to terminate for breach and repudiation Entire and severable contracts Affirmation following serious breach Nature and consequences of termination for serious breach
