title: Landscape Studio 2 - Design Process
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: You will be introduced to a range of design process methods for site planning and design generation. You will investigate the contrasting perceptions of a sites history to determine a socially and environmentally just design response.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and integrate physical, social, environmental, cultural and theoretical factors into a coherent landscape architecture design scheme.
Demonstrate an iterative design process in developing a landscape design response to a given site and brief.
Communicate conceptual and functional design intentions using drawings, models and verbal techniques.
Demonstrate the fundamental concepts and principles of landscape architecture design in response to a given site and brief.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Architecture Communication 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Architecture Communication 2 develops your personal vocabulary of landscape representation techniques and your ability to develop and communicate design ideas. The course introduces you to two and three dimensional analogue and computer-aided design processes. You will develop a range of communication techniques including 3D visualisation (perspective sketches, montages, 3D and terrain modeling), colour rendering, and the use of digital media.
learning_outcomes: Discuss design ideas in formal and informal settings and respond to feedback from peers and tutors.
Visualise design processes using analogue and digital media such as freehand sketches, diagrams, photomontages, 3D renders and orthographic drawings.
Communicate design outputs to professional landscape architecture presentation standards.
Develop digital 3D models for the testing and development of design propositions.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: LAND1141/ BENV1010

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: History of Landscape Architecture
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The History of Landscape Architecture introduces you to key works of landscape architecture and garden design. You will explore the ways in which human inspirations and technological innovations have influenced and shaped the most significant landscape transformations over the last 5,000 years. This historical perspective on the artistic achievements of landscape architecture is foundational knowledge for you as a landscape architecture student and has broad application for understanding the history of our urban environments.
learning_outcomes: Communicate characteristics and principles of designed landscapes through a range of visual forms.
Analyse cultural and social factors which have influenced approaches to designed landscapes.
Apply research skills to critically analyse historical precedent projects.
Describe the characteristic features, environmental settings, and spatial qualities of select designed landscapes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Plants and Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Plants and Design focuses on the aesthetic and functional aspects of plants in site-specific design contexts. You will be introduced to basic botanical and horticultural concepts, and criteria for plant selection including aesthetic, functional and ethical. You will develop a vocabulary of planting elements, and an ability to design with plants to achieve specific spatial qualities at a range of scales. Principles of planting design are explored through the study of historic and contemporary landscape architectural designs.
learning_outcomes: Identify plant species and describe their distinguishing characteristics using botanical terminology
Document and analyse a given planting plan for its aesthetic, cultural, and functional attributes, and communicate this analysis using effective drawings and language
Communicate horticultural and planting design concepts through writing, drawing and verbal presentations.
Prepare a conceptual planting plan for a small site addressing spatial, visual, temporal and sensory attributes and using informative and evocative diagrams and drawings.
Demonstrate working knowledge of plant species in relation to how they are used to structure planting designs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 3 Landform and Planting
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Landscape Studio 3, you will undertake landscape design with a focus on landform and planting. Landform consideration includes investigation into the relationship between topography and natural systems, constructed environments and ecological sustainability. Planting consideration requires you to apply your knowledge of local geology, vegetation and climate, alongside sustainability goals and spatial and aesthetic qualities.Your design project will embrace the manipulation of landform and knowledge of planting design to achieve a range of functional, ecological and spatial outcomes for a real site.
learning_outcomes: Generate planting design strategies which address issues of climate adaptation, mitigation and resiliency in a metropolitan context.
Communicate design concepts, principles and processes using visual, digital and verbal modes of presentation.
Modify landform elements to achieve functional and aesthetic goals.
Analyse landform types and planting structures at a range of scales.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND2152 and LAND2102 and LAND2142; or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Landscape Analysis you will analyse natural and human-made landscape spaces. You will use a range of analogue and digital technologies to describe, understand and interpret spatial and visual properties of landscape with a particular emphasis on the interrelationship between geology, climate, soils, hydrology, vegetation, fauna and humans. You will learn several mapping methods and tools that can be used to study spatial and visual characteristics including First Nation ways of knowing, doing and being. Concepts of ecology, sustainability, biodiversity, habitat fragmentation, and landscape ecology will underpin your understanding of relational and aesthetic spatial structures.
learning_outcomes: Generate spatial data to enhance the understanding of a given landscape's context and attributes.
Record and communicate field and desktop observations using a range of analogue and digital methods.
Identify the fundamental human and more than human attributes and relationships that shape a given landscape.
Assess concepts of sustainability in relation to a given landscape.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 4 Design Detail: Resolution and Representation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Studio 4 Design Detail: Resolution and Representation focuses on the relationship between design detail and site scale design. You will develop fluency in computer-aided design programs required to support the resolution and representation of detail design. Projects focus on people and place, at the scale of the urban street and/or urban plaza, and integrate the knowledge acquired in landscape construction and documentation courses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an iterative design process between analogue and digital design media.
Develop and resolve design propositions for urban streets, plazas and squares.
Communicate design processes and proposals to professional landscape architecture practice standards.
Integrate sustainability outcomes through ethical, social, cultural and environmental design decisions.
Apply intermediate knowledge of landscape architectural design principles, precedents, materials and construction technology to a given design brief.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Planting Design at the Landscape Scale
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Planting Design at the Landscape Scale, you will develop your knowledge of plants and plant communities through a focus on medium to large scale planting design and green infrastructure that supports healthy urban environments. You will examine planting design strategies and structures as integral components of urban and suburban landscape systems. You will explore the planting design strategies that have been implemented or proposed in the Sydney Region. The course is offered at the same time as the second-year design studio, LAND2201(Landform and Planting) allowing you to draw on and apply the knowledge and skills to your studio project.
learning_outcomes: Document landscape scale planting strategies to professional standards.
Analyse large scale vegetation complexes using digital datasets.
Explain the relationship of landscape vegetation structure to urban form and contemporary ecological theory.
Develop landscape scale planting strategies for green infrastructure features which address issues of adaptation, mitigation and resiliency in a metropolitan context.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND2152, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Design and Documentation 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will learn the principles of documenting sustainable landscape architecture projects for construction. Topics covered include material selection, standard construction practices, Australian Standards, grading, drainage, detail and construction design.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design ideas using a range of techniques as appropriate to professional standards.
Identify a range of elements and materials used in the construction of sustainable landscape architecture projects.
Prepare a range of typical documentation drawings for construction that convey material selection and technical resolution to industry standards.
Apply the concepts, principles and techniques of landform grading and contour manipulation to a range of circumstances.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: LAND2102 and LAND2152, or completion of the UNSW College Diploma of Architecture

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Design and Documentation 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Design and Documentation 2 focuses on interpreting and documenting the structural design and construction techniques for a range of landscape architecture elements and site problems, such as earthworks, site drainage, constructed wetlands, retaining and free-standing walls, pavements, furnishings and small roads and structures.
learning_outcomes: Produce design drawings, construction details and technical specifications relevant to detailed design phase.
Interpret design details used by landscape contractors.
Apply basic structural and site engineering principles to resolve the design of landscape architecture elements.
Assess materials and construction methods incorporating knowledge of environmental sustainability principles and best practice.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 5: Landscape Planning and Systems
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Planning and Systems covers site-planning methods and techniques for the practice of landscape architecture. Working at a range of scales, you will learn methods for systematically analysing and planning a site that prioritises landscape systems and their performance. This studio course aims to develop your skills and ability to generate and test evidence-based design responses to a range of social and ecological programmatic requirements and prioritise sustainable outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Apply specific social sustainability concepts to the landscape planning process within an Australian context.
Communicate design ideas using a range of techniques as appropriate to professional standards.
Formulate a landscape planning design response that addresses the relationships between landscape sites, landscape systems and landscape performance at a range of scales.
Analyse data related to landscape specific systems and processes, such as biodiversity, climate resilience, and social equity to support sustainable landscape performance and site planning.
prerequisites: Prequisite: must have completed 78UOC core courses (=years 1+2)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 7: Design with a Complex Program
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: You will consider and resolve multiple and complex environmental, cultural and social issues of an urban site to a program-specific level. Your project may include preparing competition entries and/or be interdisciplinary in nature. You will refine your professional skills by working collaboratively in small groups. Verbal and graphic presentation skills will be extended to a professional level, using a diverse range of computer software programs and incorporating a range of media and models. A personal design portfolio forms part of this studio, with a satisfactory mark required for successful completion of the course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate ethical, social, cultural and environmental responsibility in design decisions for the practice of landscape architecture.
Critically evaluate urban public spaces, strategic planning documents and background studies for application in a design project.
Visualise design ideas effectively using analouge, digital, verbal and written modes of communication as appropriate to audience, purpose and context.
Generate and test a range of innovative design ideas and alternative scenarios in relation to complex site and program information.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 6: Design for Landscape Performance
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Studio 6: Site Planning - Landscape Performance and Site Design extends your ability to design for landscape performance building on the knowledge of the site from Term 1. You will formulate a comprehensive design response that addresses the social and ecological programmatic requirements and priorities. You will synthesise your knowledge of spatial, social and ecological systems and apply this knowledge to the development of a landscape masterplan for the site. You will produce a design proposal that engages in site specific landscape issues and dynamics and explores how these contribute to spatial, environmental, and social transformation of the site over time.
learning_outcomes: Resolve a comprehensive design proposition to address spatial, social and ecological systems.
Critically evaluate principles and strategies at a range of scales to determine relationships between site systems and their spatial contexts.
Communicate design ideas, processes and proposals to landscape architecture practice standards.
Integrate sustainability outcomes through ethical, social, cultural and environmental design decisions.
Develop a design proposal that provides the basis for ecologically and socially sustainable development.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Landscape Design Seminar
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously LAND1322. This course introduces you to urban landscape design theory. You will revisit concepts that have informed the design of cities and extend your knowledge via a critique of the spatial, cultural, and environmental qualities that shape them. Key theories will be introduced to you through the lens of landscape architectural practice. In doing so, you will understand the role of landscape architecture as a key driver of urban form and how you can engage with the social and environmental challenges of urbanisation. Importantly, this course provides you with a conceptual foundation for years 3 and 4 design studios.
learning_outcomes: Explain how landscape architects engage with the environmental, cultural and physical processes that shape urban form
Critique urban landscape design theories and frameworks using written and visual landscape analysis techniques
Communicate urban forms and processes through written and visual landscape analysis techniques
Interpret and explain urban morphology through applying knowledge of urban landscape design theory

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 7: Design with a Complex Program
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Studio 7 focuses on multi-faceted and scalar issues of contemporary urbanism and sustainability as they relate to landscape architecture. You will investigate novel aesthetic, environmental and social approaches to the design of complex urban landscapes, and resolve critical landscape issues related to the challenges of urbanisation. The studio may include preparing competition entries and/or be interdisciplinary in nature. A personal design portfolio forms part of this studio, with a satisfactory portfolio result a requirement for successful completion.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design ideas, processes and proposals using a range of techniques appropriate to landscape architecture professional standards
Collaborate with peers on a complex urban landscape design project demonstrating shared responsibility and productivity
Generate a site-specific design proposal at multiple scales that responds to a given urban landscape design scenario and its future sustainability
Critically evaluate strategic landscape planning documents, design competition briefs, and background studies related to a complex urban landscape context.
Develop urban landscape scenarios that respond creatively to complex sites, issues and briefs.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND2312

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Performance and Management
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously LAND1351 . Landscape Performance and Management explores the performance of landscape architecture in terms of delivering social, economic and environmental benefits. You will understand how landscape performance and management are integral dimensions of the design process. You will explore frameworks and tools for managing and assessing landscape performance, and be able to apply these to develop your knowledge of contemporary approaches to landscape design.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate diverse landscape management and performance issues in contemporary designed landscapes in relation to sustainable landscape architecture practice.
Identify landscape performance and management outcomes in a range of designed landscapes.
Advocate for improved social, economic and environmental outcomes for a current landscape issue in Australia.
Formulate effective propositions to determine sustainable landscape performance outcomes of contemporary designed landscapes.
Communicate landscape performance and management through verbal and written formats.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: must have completed 78UOC core courses (=years 1+2)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 10: Graduation Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Studio 10 facilitates a rigorous, independent and highly resolved individual design investigation which is underpinned by your proposed critical theoretical approach. You will employ the knowledge, skills and understanding you have gained in previous years to explore issues and approaches in design which are of particular interest to you in your graduating design project. You will critically test and resolve your design proposal working across multiple scales.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design insights, intentions, processes, and methodologies for diverse professional audiences using appropriate formats and conventions in landscape architecture practice
Generate creative and evidence-based design propositions informed by critical theoretical frameworks and reflective inquiry
Strategically evaluate and prioritise design responses that address complex ethical, social, cultural, and environmental challenges in landscape architectural practice
Apply advanced landscape architecture concepts, processes and knowledge to the development and resolution of a design project
Advocate for ethical, social, cultural, and environmental sustainability principles in shaping responsible and context-sensitive landscape architectural practices
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND2412 and LAND2421

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 8: Urban Landscape Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Landscape Studio 8 you will investigate the interdependency of landscape and urban morphology by testing large-scale urban design propositions for a chosen site. You will respond to current government planning and policy documents and their aspirations for the site. You will undertake complex site analysis to inform the development of a landscape structure plan for the site. This course along with the concurrent course, LAND2421, generates the urban design context and theoretical framework for your graduation project and the subsequent design studios, LAND2412 Landscape Studio 9 and LAND2413 Landscape Studio 10.
learning_outcomes: Develop urban design concepts which integrate theoretical frameworks, apply sustainable development principles and respond to local, regional and global landscape issues and conditions.
Communicate design processes, outputs, and methodologies to professional landscape architectural standards.
Collaborate with peers on a complex urban landscape design project demonstrating shared responsibility and productivity.
Demonstrate an iterative design process in a response to a range of feedback inputs.
Critically analyse urban landscape form and conditions at a range of scales.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: must have completed 108 UOC core courses (=years 1+2+3)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Studio 9: Urban Public Domain
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Landscape Studio 9: Urban Public Domain develops your abilities as a creative and scholarly practitioner of landscape architecture in preparation for your graduation studio. You will extend your investigation of a chosen site by exploring human-scale design requirements and challenges of the contemporary urban public domain. You will engage in site investigations, precedent studies, and analysis of urban design theories and guidelines. Your research findings from these activities will inform and support your preparation of preliminary design concepts and performance guidelines for your Graduation Studio project.
learning_outcomes: Engage in reflective practice and iterative processes of inquiry and testing to support the design process.
Analyse and codify functional and pragmatic design aspects of the urban public domain at a range of scales.
Relate research findings from diverse sources to support the development of design proposals.
Generate novel design concepts informed by principles of sustainability and landscape performance.
Explain design insights, intentions, processes, and methodologies to a communication standard appropriate to the practice of landscape architecture.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: LAND2411 and LAND2421

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Landscape Theory and Research
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Contemporary Landscape Theory and Research, you will develop the conceptual and research framework to support your graduation studio project. You will investigate and test current theories of landscape and urban design through the critical interpretation and analysis of recent projects and scholarship. Through structured research and writing tasks you will develop the methodological and analytical skills needed to engage in research related to design.
learning_outcomes: Select and collate scholarly material relevant to the disipline of landscape architecture.
Develop a research position through an iterative process of critical review, reflection and revision.
Discuss and synthesise diverse research approaches and positions relating to the practice of landscape architecture.
Critically analyse scholarship pertaining to research and theory as related to the practice of landscape architecture.
Communicate your insights and ideas using a range of written techniques as appropriate to professional standards.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Master Landscape Studio 1: Site Planning - Landscape Performance and Site Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Master Landscape Studio 1 you will learn the importance of site-planning for the practice of landscape architecture. Working at a range of scales, you will learn methods for systematically analysing and planning a site that prioritises landscape systems and their performance. The course aims to develop your skills and ability to generate and test evidence-based responses to a range of social and ecological programmatic requirements and priorities.
learning_outcomes: Formulate a landscape planning design response that addresses the relationships between landscape sites, landscape systems and landscape performance at a range of scales
Analyse data related to landscape specific systems and processes, such as biodiversity, climate resilience, and social equity to support sustainable landscape performance and site planning
Communicate design ideas using a range of techniques as appropriate to professional standards
Apply specific social sustainability concepts to the landscape planning process within an Australian context

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Professional Practice for Landscape Architects
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously LAND1482. Professional Practice for Landscape Architects introduces you to the practice of landscape architecture, its scope and potential with a focus on current issues and practices. You will learn about professional registration, ethics and values, client relationships, project procurement and management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate collaborative skills in teamwork that ensure productivity and shared responsibility.
Apply principles of project procurement to develop a tender document derived from a hypothetical project brief.
Discuss the trajectory and scope of landscape architecture practice.
Explain current sustainability, ethical, legal, and administrative issues relevant to landscape architecture practice.
Communicate landscape principles and ideas graphically, verbally and in writing to professional industry standards

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Master Landscape Studio 2: Design for Landscape Performance
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Master Landscape Studio 2: Design for Landscape Performance extends your ability to design for landscape performance building on the knowledge of the site from Term 1. You will learn to formulate a comprehensive design response that addresses social and ecological programmatic requirements and priorities. You will synthesise your knowledge of spatial, social and ecological systems and apply this knowledge to the development of a landscape masterplan for the site. You will produce a design proposal that engages in site specific landscape issues and dynamics and explores how these contribute to spatial, environmental, and social transformation of the site over time.
learning_outcomes: Communicate complex design ideas, processes and proposals to landscape architecture practice standards.
Integrate sustainability outcomes through ethical, social, cultural and environmental design decisions.
Critically evaluate principles and strategies at a range of scales to determine relationships between site systems and their spatial contexts.
Resolve a comprehensive design proposition to address complex spatial, social and ecological systems.
Develop a design proposal that provides the basis for ecologically and socially sustainable development.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Planting Design at the Landscape Scale
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Planting Design at the Landscape Scale, you will develop your knowledge of plants and plant communities through a focus on medium to large scale planting design and green infrastructure that supports healthy urban environments. You will examine the role of plants in various situations, such as in landscape remediation and regeneration, alongside planning for climate change resilience. You will explore the planting design strategies that have been implemented or proposed in the Sydney Region.
learning_outcomes: Utilise digital datasets to analyse and interpret large scale vegetation complexes.
Develop landscape scale planting strategies for green infrastructure features which address issues of adaptation, mitigation and resiliency in a metropolitan context.
Explain the relationship of landscape vegetation structure to urban form and contemporary ecological theory.
Document landscape scale planting strategies to professional standards.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: People Place Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: People, Place, Design introduces you to environment-behaviour research and theory. This field is dedicated to understanding and conceptualising the intricate relationships people have with their environments. Our discussions revolve around the significance of this knowledge in the context of contemporary design and planning practice. We delve into the complexities of designing for diverse user groups. The course also explores various approaches that promote universal design and social inclusion. A key part of your learning journey will be understanding how planning and design can foster social and environmental sustainability within communities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate collaborative skills in teamwork that ensures productivity and shared responsibility.
Communicate using written, verbal and design techniques to professional standards.
Investigate environment-behaviour theories and concepts relevant to design and planning practice.
Critically evaluate environment-behaviour methods relevant to design and planning practice.
Apply environment-behaviour theories, concepts and methods to the design solution for a real world people-place challenge.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Ecology and Landscape Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Urban Ecology and Landscape Design examines the influence of urban ecology on the practice of landscape architecture over the last 50 years. You will explore both the theoretical and practical applications of urban ecology principles and concepts as applied to established, regenerated and new urban landscapes. You will draw on both international and local case studies to map the trajectory of key ideas, projects and designers that influenced changes in the role of ecology in relation to landscape design. Topics include succession, adaptation and resilience, novel ecosystems, landscape ecology, ecological urbanism, and landscape urbanism.
learning_outcomes: Explain principles and concepts of urban ecology in relation to designed landscapes.
Articulate and defend evidence-based perspectives on urban ecological issues through clear, critical, and professional oral communication.
Critically assess and evaluate the application of urban ecological concepts and theories to designed urban landscapes.
Communicate concepts of urban ecology through various modes of drawing, diagrams and writing to support themes and relationships of urban ecology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Analysis
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Landscape Analysis you will explore natural and human-made landscape spaces. You will use a range of analogue and digital technologies to describe, understand and interpret spatial-visual properties of landscape with a particular emphasis on the interrelationship between geology, climate, soils, hydrology, vegetation, fauna and humans. You will learn several mapping methods and tools that can be used to study spatial-visual characteristics including First Nation ways of knowing, doing and being. Concepts of ecology, sustainability, biodiversity, habitat fragmentation, and landscape ecology will underpin your understanding of relational and aesthetic spatial structures.
learning_outcomes: Assess concepts of sustainability in relation to a given landscape context.
Identify the fundamental human and more than human attributes and relationships in a given landscape.
Record and communicate field and desktop observations using advanced analogue and digital methods.
Interpret spatial data to an advanced level for diverse landscape settings.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Case Studies in Landscape Architecture
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will explore case studies as a research method in landscape architecture. The course will develop your critical skills in landscape projects analysis to inform and support your own landscape practice. The course situates key landscape architectural projects in their social, political, environmental and economic contexts and develops your capacity to apply design and planning principles to inform the practice of landscape architecture. It will draw on both historical and contemporary cases in landscape architecture.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the themes and design principles that have informed key projects in the history of landscape architecture
Apply appropriate case study research methods to the analysis of landscape architecture projects
Communicate case study findings in written, visual and verbal modes

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Master Landscape Studio 3: The Public Realm
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Master Landscape Studio 3 explores approaches to the strategic planning and the design of the urban public realm. You will develop knowledge of the spatial and functional requirements and user expectations of a range of public realm types and their relationship to each other and built form. You will learn how to integrate public realm policy, strategies into design proposals that responds to various spatial and stakeholder conditions.
learning_outcomes: Develop public realm design strategies at a specific scales to address various spatial requirements.
Generate advanced design propositions by applying knowledge of public realm types, forms and precincts to a given site.
Critically analyse the dimensions of a study site, including relevant public realm policy documents and stakeholder input.
Communicate complex landscape architectural information, concepts and propositions using analog and digital techniques as appropriate to professional standards.
Collaborate with peers demonstrating effective planning, management and monitoring processes within your design workflow.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND7102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Master Landscape Studio 4: Constructed Ecologies
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Master Landscape Studio 4: Constructed Ecologies approaches the designed landscape from an ecological perspective. Your design process will rely on ecological knowledge and principles to inform, inspire, and shape the designed landscape. You will examine different types of constructed ecologies for social, climate and habitat health and integrate your findings into your design propositions.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate concepts of landscape architecture for application to local complex environments.
Communicate complex landscape architectural information, concepts and propositions using analogue, digital and verbal techniques as appropriate to professional standards.
Generate design propositions by applying advanced knowledge of constructed ecology types, forms and precincts to a given site.
Collaborate with peers demonstrating effective planning, management and monitoring processes within your design workflow.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: LAND7201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Urban Landscape Visualisation
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Advanced Urban Landscape Visualisation introduces methods of representing complex landscape systems and dynamics, using visual scripting interfaces and technologies. You will explore design decisions by simulating and evaluating changes to environmental conditions with a focus on landform, hydrology and planting.
learning_outcomes: Visually communicate dynamic landscape conditions affected by and adapting to climate change for a range of audiences.
Analyse associations between system components, design parameters and outcomes.
Evaluate environmental conditions through technological principles and simulations.
Apply adaptive technologies to explore and test iterative design processes.
Synthesise adaptive technology outcomes to inform design outcomes that respond to climate change.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Technology 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Landscape Technology 1: Landscape Performance (Materials and Fabrication) focuses on sustainable contemporary landscape materials, construction techniques and design methods for application within a complex urban environment. You will develop the capability to investigate and apply techniques for the design of constructed ecologies for improved landscape performance. Digital modeling and construction techniques are used to increase your capacity to communicate and test design options.
learning_outcomes: Communicate contemporary landscape materials, construction techniques, and design methods to professional industry standards.
Apply design techniques to contemporary landscape materials and construction processes within a complex urban environment.
Assess the sustainable performance of landscape materials and construction techniques in relation to constructed urban ecologies.
Investigate the compositional and structural aspects of contemporary materials used in the construction of sustainable landscapes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LAND7201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Regional Landscape Outreach Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Regional Landscape Outreach Studio provides with you with a learning experience in a regional landscape context. You will draw on your knowledge and skills to engage with a challenging socio-environmental issue in a real-world landscape planning and/or design situation. You will engage in community participation processes to investigate diverse challenges faced by regional communities as they plan and design for sustainable landscapes. The studio will typically include a public exhibition and/or a publication component.
learning_outcomes: Analyse ecological, social, political and economic opportunities and challenges in a regional landscape context
Collaborate with local community, organisations and/or public agencies within the field to inform planning and/or design decisions
Communicate to public and peer audiences through contextual graphic and verbal presentation techniques
Demonstrate cultural and ecological awareness, environmental and social responsibility and respect for diversity within a regional context
Apply landscape architecture concepts, processes and knowledge to critically position a design scenario suitable for a regional context

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Theory and Research
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Advanced Landscape Theory and Research engages you in a process of scholarly exploration through investigating contemporary landscape architecture works and theories in relation to the design process and design research. The course provides a testing ground for the exploration of research issues relevant to the Capstone Studio project site. This course will assist you to define the research context and questions, for your Capstone Studios. You will develop skills in research design and methods, critical review, research by design, documentation and writing. You will prepare theoretically informed research proposal which forms the basis of the design work in the Capstone Studio sequence.
learning_outcomes: Explain the interrelationship between theoretical positions and research methods within the context of a design research proposal.
Interpret landscape architecture projects and design processess to reveal new insights.
Critically analyse theoretical approaches to landscape architecture practice and design.
Communicate research design proposals in written, visual and verbal formats, at professional standards.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Masters Landscape Studio: Capstone Part 1
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will begin your major independent design project. This course is the first of two concurrent design studios that culminate into your major independent design project. Your independent design project will consider how the most pressing environmental and social issues of the day can be addressed to support human and more than human landscape systems. Through a suite of directed design approaches, you will develop future scenarios which will guide and challenge your design thinking in terms of scale, complexity and performance.
learning_outcomes: Assess and apply design principles and strategies to enhance landscape performance benefits.
Communicate design processes and proposals using analog and digital techniques as appropriate to professional standards.
Apply advanced analysis techniques to develop complex design propositions and scenarios.
Synthesise ecological and cultural systems into innovative spatial configurations across a range of scales.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Masters Landscape Studio: Capstone Part 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Masters Landscape Studio: Capstone Part 2 builds on Capstone Part 1 by guiding the development of your design proposition and research agenda into a fully resolved detailed design proposal. The detailed design proposal is informed by consideration of broader city scale landscape systems and climate positive design outcomes.Through rigorous design investigation, you will demonstrate sophisticated knowledge of the relationship between landscape systems and urban settlements and extend your abilities to plan and design a sustainable landscape as an integrated component of city and metropolitan systems.
learning_outcomes: Develop an independent and climate positive design proposition which encompasses principles of sustainability for human and more-than-human kin.
Communicate complex landscape architectural information, concepts, and propositions clearly, concisely and effectively to advanced professional standards of presentation.
Demonstrate how detailed decisions related to topography, water, vegetation and material selection deliver improved landscape performance.
Critically evaluate and synthesise your design proposal at a range of scales to demonstrate advanced resolution and integration of landscape systems and conditions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Professional Practice for Landscape Architects
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Professional Practice for Landscape Architects introduces you to the practice of landscape architecture, its scope and potential with a focus on current issues and practices. You will learn about professional registration, ethics and values, client relationships, project procurement and management.
learning_outcomes: Communicate landscape principles and ideas graphically, verbally and in writing to professional industry standards
Demonstrate collaborative skills in teamwork that ensure productivity and shared responsibility.
Explain current sustainability, ethical, legal, and administrative issues relevant to landscape architecture practice.
Apply principles of project procurement to develop a tender document derived from a hypothetical project brief.
Discuss policies and regulatory frameworks relevant to the trajectory and scope of landscape architecture profession.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Landscape Technology 2
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Note: The code for this course was previously LAND7321 . In Landscape Technology 2 you will use innovative digital methods and responsive technologies to transform your landscape design concepts into evidence-based construction propositions that support optimal landscape performance. The course includes application of digital tools for mapping, visualisation, simulation and terrain analysis.
learning_outcomes: Explain key theoretical principles for landscape performance assessment
Communicate landscape performance assessment results verbally and visually through appropriate techniques and digital tools
Assess the performance of landscape materials and construction techniques
Evaluate landscape sites and design propositions using responsive technologies and digital tools

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Governance for Responsible AI
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: In Governance for Responsible AI, you will explore how organisations develop policies for AI development and use that reflect legal obligations, ethical guidelines, and technical standards. As AI becomes more integrated into society, understanding how to govern it responsibly is essential. This course will guide you through the challenges of ensuring fairness, transparency, and accountability in AI systems. You’ll analyse real-world examples, evaluate global frameworks, and develop strategies for addressing issues like bias and privacy. This is a core course for COMMI1 and COMMI2 AI in Business and Society.
learning_outcomes: Propose organisational policy to promote responsible and ethical AI use in diverse sectors.
Evaluate global governance models for AI and analyse potential improvements to address trustworthiness.
Apply legal and ethical frameworks including technical standards applicable to the development and use of AI.
prerequisites: Students must have completed 72UOC
Students must have completed ARTS2115 Philosophy of AI and INFS2604 AI Fluency

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Methods for Higher Degree Research in Law and Criminology
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the variety of research methods used in legal and criminological, with a focus on the methods that are most relevant to higher degree research (HDR) candidates. In relation to each method, topics covered include: The relationship of choice method to wider questions of research design; selecting and collecting data; analysing data; ethical considerations. HDR students will delve into qualitative, quantitative, and doctrinal methods, facilitating informed decision-making in choosing methods appropriate to their research projects. An emphasis is placed on understanding the relationship between research methods and broader questions of research design and project theorisation. Practical challenges associated with data gathering and interpretation are explored, alongside ethical considerations inherent to various research methodologies. Additionally, candidates will engage with norms of quality and rigor, critical for producing impactful research. By fostering critical evaluation skills, this course empowers HDR candidates to navigate diverse research landscapes effectively.
learning_outcomes: Explain the variety of research methods used in legal and criminological research and their suitability for addressing specific research questions and contexts.
Identify ethical considerations inherent in legal and criminological research methodologies, demonstrating sensitivity to ethical dilemmas and ability to develop ethically sound research practices.

Apply data analysis techniques to interpret research findings, showcasing proficiency in both qualitative and quantitative techniques of analysis relevant to law and criminology research as well awareness of critiques and limitations of different data analysis techniques.
Link questions of research method to wider debates about research design, project theorisation and research epistemology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of LAWS0007, and enrolled in a Higher Degree Research degree in the Faculty of Law & Justice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Higher Degree Research in Law and Criminology
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: This course encourages HDR candidates to reflect on the foundations of research in criminology and law. This engagement with foundational questions provides a basis for critical engagement with the diversity of ways in which scholars conduct research. This engagement, in turn, helps HDR candidates situate themselves in relation to existing research traditions and articulate and justify how their proposed approach to research differs from other possible approaches. This course also prepares HDR candidates for their research project by providing a basic understanding of the requirements of a research thesis, and relevant practical skills. The course is compulsory for all newly enrolled PhD, LLM by Research and MPhil candidates in the Faculty of Law and Justice. In the case of PhD candidates, satisfactory completion of the course will constitute a requirement for PhD confirmation. PhD candidates will still be required to satisfy all of the other conditions set for confirmation of their candidature.
learning_outcomes: Knowledge of the diversity of approaches to research in criminology and law and their appropriateness for addressing particular types of research questions.
An understanding of the requirements of your research thesis and the skills you will need to develop.
The ability to develop an appropriate and internally consistent approach to your research, to situate this approach in relation to other existing approaches and to justify your choice.
prerequisites: Enrolment in a Faculty of Law & Justice PhD, LLM by Research or MPhil program

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)
Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Criminal Laws
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: LAWS1022 is only available in T3 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Student Services for more information. This course follows from LAWS1021 / JURD7121 Crime and the Criminal Process, and applies the perspectives and themes of that course to the doctrinally central criminal offences and defences. These are examined in a contextual framework that emphasises the policy and social issues underpinning the development and application of the law. This critical approach allows students to appreciate a complex set of conflicting ideologies, principles, discretion and histories informing the criminal law. The course draws on materials from other disciplines – especially criminology, history, sociology and feminist theory, which enhance students’ appreciation of the law in context. Social issues including race, class and gender are stressed. Comparisons with jurisdictions other than NSW are undertaken where this highlights relevant policy issues, legislative alternatives, or demonstrates the contingent nature of the law in question. Throughout, detailed doctrinal analysis of the chosen offences/defences takes place and students develop the skills of legal element analysis of both statutory and common law offences and defences. Main Topics Assault (including aggravated assault and domestic violence) Sexual Assault Homicide Defences (including mental illness, automatism, self-defence, extreme provocation, substantial impairment, intoxication) Dishonest Acquisition Extending Criminal Liability (including complicity) Sentencing
learning_outcomes: Use statutory interpretation principles to identify the constituent elements of criminal offences and apply to hypothetical fact scenarios. (PLO 4)
Navigate and explain the basic doctrines, principles and rules relating to pre-trial procedure in criminal litigation. (PLO 1)
Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by discussing and debating course concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate an ability to incorporate a range of legal and interdisciplinary research sources in written communication with appropriate referencing. (PLO 5)
Demonstrate awareness of principles of criminal justice and their relationship to the broader context. (PLO 1)
Engage in reflective practice regarding the criminal law’s role in serving society and promoting justice. (PLO 3)
Demonstrate effective written communication skills by articulating legal concepts clearly, persuasively and appropriately. (PLO 7)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of LAWS1021.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Crime and the Criminal Process
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: LAWS1021 is only available in T2 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Student Services for more information. This course introduces students to fundamental aspects of criminal justice and process. Woven through the course is a critical examination of the interaction between the criminal justice system and the criminal law: specifically, that application of the law is shaped by and dependent on decisions made by criminal justice actors including police, prosecutors and judicial officers. Specific areas of focus include: why some activities are criminalised and others not; the use and misuse of discretion; the impact of the reliance on summary justice; the significance of pre-trial processes such as search, arrest and bail; and the over-representation of Indigenous people and other vulnerable groups. Crime and the Criminal Process also introduces the doctrinal building blocks of criminal law, and applies these principles to a number of key statutory offences such as public order offences and drugs offences which illustrate the process themes above. The impact of public policy and law reform is an important underlying theme. Main Topics Criminalisation, over-criminalisation and defining crime Criminal process, including police powers and pre-trial process Components of criminal offences: physical and mental elements Drugs (NSW only), including harm minimisation policies and incursions into general principles of criminal law Public order offenses
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of principles of criminal law and their relationship to the broader context. (PLO 1)
Navigate and apply the substantive criminal law, both common law and statutory. (PLO 1, 4)
Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by discussing and debating course concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate effective written communication skills by articulating legal concepts clearly, persuasively and appropriately. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate knowledge of the key processes and ethical issues involved in criminalisation by engaging in policy analysis. (PLO 1, 10)
Demonstrate an ability to incorporate a range of legal and interdisciplinary research sources in written communication with appropriate referencing. (PLO 5)
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of LAWS1052

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introducing Law and Justice
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Introducing Law and Justice is the first of the foundational level core courses for the LLB degree. This course introduces students to the history, operation and contemporary dynamics of our legal system. It provides a grounding in the core legal skills necessary for successful study and practice, including legal research and writing; case analysis and critique; and the interpretation and application of statutes. All of these skills will continue to be developed through your LLB studies. All classes in Introducing Law and Justice are small, with a focus on interactive teaching. All students enrolled in Introducing Law and Justice will also enrol in the co-requisite course, Legal Research and Writing, LAWS1055, which introduces foundational legal writing and research skills, such as legal citation, location of primary and secondary materials and various forms of legal writing and argument, including a case note and legal essay. Students will attend classes for Introducing Law and Justice as well as classes for Legal Research and Writing. The skills and knowledge taught in Legal Research and Writing are foundational to the skills and knowledge covered and assessed in Introducing Law and Justice.
learning_outcomes: Engage with Indigenous legal traditions and practices, as well as Indigenous perspectives on law, social justice, and policy in Australia. (PLO 2)
Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by scholarly, reflective and respectful discussion. (PLO 7)
Effectively articulate legal concepts and analysis in written communications that adhere to citation protocols and principles of academic integrity. (PLO 7)
Navigate and apply legislation with reference to modern approaches to statutory interpretation. (PLO 1, 4)
Explain the key elements of a case and engage in critical analysis of judicial decision-making. (PLO 4)

Critically evaluate the operation of the law in practice from a range of perspectives, with attention to principles of law and justice and the context of Australia’s settler-colonial legal system.(PLO 1, 2)
Apply knowledge of intentional torts to hypothetical fact scenarios. (PLO 1, 6)
prerequisites: This course is strictly for students undertaking Law programs only. Corequisite: LAWS1055. Students must be enrolled in LAWS1052 and LAWS1055 in the same term.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Legal Research and Writing
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: Legal Research and Writing provides students with an introduction to key legal skills necessary for successful study and practice of the law. This course introduces foundational legal writing and research skills, such as legal citation, location of primary and secondary materials and various forms of legal writing, including case notes and answering problem questions. All students enrolled in Legal Research and Writing will also enrol in the co-requisite course, LAWS1052 Introducing Law and Justice, which introduces students to the history, operation and contemporary dynamics of the Australian legal system, to the relationships between law and justice and to the core legal skills necessary for successful study and practice. Students will attend classes for Introducing Law and Justice as well as classes for Legal Research and Writing. The skills and knowledge taught in Legal Research and Writing are foundational to the skills and knowledge covered and assessed in Introducing Law and Justice and later courses.

Locate and cite relevant primary and secondary legal sources using appropriate legal research methods. (PLO 5)
Recognise responsible and appropriate use of generative AI in legal research and writing within the context of university studies and legal practice. (PLO 5, 7)
Articulate legal concepts and analysis clearly across different forms of logically structured, written communication. (PLO 1, 7)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Torts
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: LAWS1061 is only available in T1 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Student Services for more information. This course continues students’ introduction to the law of torts which began with Introducing Law and Justice where trespass to the person is covered. Other torts, notably trespass to goods and to land, and conversion, are covered in Principles of Private Law. Torts considers the part of the law of torts concerning liability to pay compensation for wrongfully caused injury, damage or loss, with an emphasis on liability caused by negligence, breach of statutory duty and nuisance. Both liability and remedies at common law and under the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW) are examined. Students are introduced to the complexities of interpreting statutory regimes, and their inter-relationship with common law precedent. The course critically examines the wider social implications of various approaches to compensating those who suffer personal injury, using some theoretical perspectives including law and economics, feminist theory and critical legal theory to do so Main Topics The role and function of tort law Nuisance Negligence – the duty of care in general Negligence – duty – personal injury Negligence – duty - pure economic loss Negligence – duty – special defendants including public authorities, medical, landlords, parents and children etc Breach of duty Causation and remoteness including eggshell skull rule and probabilistic causation Concurrent liability – vicarious liability Concurrent Liability - non-delegable duty Defences to negligence Assessment of Damages Assessing the law of negligence – does it operate as it should? Breach of Statutory Duty

Apply knowledge and understanding of the principles of tort law to hypothetical fact scenarios. (PLO 6)

Engage in critical analysis of tort law. (PLO 1, 4)
Demonstrate awareness of the place of tort law within law generally, and in a broader context. (PLO 1, 3)
Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by discussing and debating course concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner. (PLO 7)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contracts
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: LAWS1075 is only available in T3 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Student Services for more information. Contract Law is a core compulsory course, continuing the work completed in Principles of Private Law. Like tort law, contract law is one aspect of the law of obligations. Contract law is the study of legal obligations voluntarily assumed. The course focuses on understanding the nature, significance and operation of legal agreements in disparate contexts, varying from corporate to commercial practice, and from family and consumer to employment law. Particular attention is placed on the decisions of appellate courts, and on key legislation such as relate to consumer law, unfair contracts and unconscionable dealings. The course also aims to provide future lawyers with the knowledge needed to negotiate, draft and interpret contractual documents. Main Topics Terms (including implied terms) Interpretation (including the parol evidence rule and exclusion clauses) Misrepresentation and misleading or deceptive conduct (including the Competition and Consumer Act 2010) Mistake, unconscionable dealing and other vitiating factors Frustration Performance, breach and termination of contracts Damages and rescission
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by discussing and debating course concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate effective written communication skills by articulating legal concepts clearly, persuasively and appropriately in providing informed advice. (PLO 7)
Evaluate and advise upon appropriate remedies in statute, common law and equity. (PLO 4)
Evaluate the law of contract in different social contexts. (PLO 1)
Develop skills in drafting contractual documents including memoranda, contract terms and their interpretation. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate awareness of principles of performance and breach in contract law. (PLO 1)
Apply key principles of contract law to hypothetical fact scenarios. (PLO 6)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Associations
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: LAWS1091 is only available in T2 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Student Services for more information. This course examines the central legislative rules and legal principles of corporation's law. Foundational principles such as limited liability and rights attached to shares are examined together with the rights of shareholders and other stakeholders. There is a particular focus on the appointment and removal of directors and officers, and their duties and decision-making processes. Wider policy issues, including the powers and role of the regulators, are also examined. Main Topics Introduction to the corporation and incorporating under Australian law The implications of separate legal personality and limited liability The corporate constitution Decision making by the Board of Directors and General Meeting Theories of the corporation and corporate governance Corporate contracting Directors’ statutory and general law duties Shareholders' remedies Corporate insolvency Corporate groups

Communicate legal concepts clearly and persuasively through both oral and written forms, incorporating research sources with appropriate referencing when requested. (PLO 7)
Evaluate the impact of legal regulations on corporate stakeholders using relevant principles of the corporation. (PLO 1, 3)
Apply foundational principles and/or theories of business associations to analyse hypothetical corporate scenarios. (PLO 1)
Interpret and navigate legal texts, including statutory and judicial materials, to solve complex legal issues. (PLO 4, 6)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Legal System and Skills A
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: LAWS1121 – Legal System and Skills A (‘LSSA’) is a core course for Humanities Pathway Program (Law) students. The focus of LSSA is to examine the nature of law in Australian society. It teaches about the historical foundations and contemporary workings of the Australian legal system by adopting a critical and contextual approach. Students develop an understanding of law in practice through visiting courts and tribunals, which complements theoretical learning about the Australian common law. Integrated into LSSA is the development of introductory academic skills including critical analysis, oral and written communication, academic literacy, problem-solving and research. These skills and knowledge are an essential foundation for subsequent core courses for Humanities Pathway Program (Law) students in Term 2 and Term 3. Main Topics Lawyers’ work, skills and knowledge History of the Australian legal system Australian legal principles and institutions Introduction to traditional and critical jurisprudence Classification of law Sources of law The doctrine of precedent, judicial method and judge-made law Frameworks for legal thinking, reasoning and legal problem-solving Legal citation Introduction to legal research through the UNSW Library Locating and using secondary legal materials and case law

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Legal System and Skills B
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: LAWS1122 – Legal System and Skills B (‘LSSB’) is a core course for Humanities Pathway Program (Law) students. LSSB further develops the understanding of the contemporary workings of the Australian legal system gained in LAWS1121 – Legal System and Skills A by adopting a critical and contextual approach. A case study of topical Indigenous legal issues is used to critically examine the extent to which the Australian legal system achieves equality. Students develop an understanding of law in practice through visiting Parliament, which complements learning about the legislative process and statutory interpretation. Students also develop an understanding of the role of evidence and the rules of evidence in legal disputes. Integrated into LSSB is further development of introductory academic skills including basic logic, persuasive writing and plain legal English writing. These skills and knowledge are an essential foundation for subsequent core courses for Humanities Pathway Program (Law) students. Main Topics The legislative process Navigating legislation Statutory interpretation techniques Introductory logic Writing in plain legal English The nature and rules of evidence in legal disputes Equality in Australia Indigenous legal issues Locating and using primary and secondary legal materials from other common law jurisdictions Locate and using legislation and other parliamentary materials

Research, critically analyse and compare issues of inequality in Australia and other common law jurisdictions, particularly with reference to Indigenous populations. (CLOs 8-11).

Demonstrate legal research skills (CLOs 10-11).

Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by scholarly, reflective and respectful discussion. (CLOs 1-4 and 6-11).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Public Law
school: School of Global and Public Law
syllabus_overview: LAWS1141 is only available in T2 by School Consent. Contact UNSW Law Students Services for more information. This course introduces students to the study of public law, including its history, institutions, methods of reasoning and fundamental principles. Students will acquire an understanding of the introductory principles and theories of administrative and constitutional law as they apply to the essential features of the Australian system of government, and their implications for human rights and the rule of law. The course exposes students to this material through an examination of Australia’s hybrid constitutional inheritance from the United Kingdom and United States, as adapted in the creation and subsequent development of the federal Commonwealth. In doing so it also examines the implications of colonisation for Indigenous legal systems and assertions of Crown sovereignty. The role, powers and interrelationship of the three arms of government are considered in contemporary as well as historical context, as are the issues of rights protection and constitutional change. The course prepares students for their later study of the courses LAWS1160: Administrative Law and LAWS2150: Federal Constitutional Law, and also introduces students to the fundamentals of the skill of statutory interpretation in the public law context. Main Topics Constitutionalism Australia’s ‘Washminster’ Inheritance The Westminster Tradition The American Tradition The Creation of the Federated Commonwealth of Australia Colonisation, Indigenous Sovereignty and Crown Sovereignty The Colonial Laws Validity Act 1865 and the Path to Federation The Acquisition of Legal Independence and Popular Sovereignty The Legislature History and Development The Franchise and the Composition of Parliament Legislative Power Judicial Review of Legislation Statutory Interpretation State Constitutions and State Legislative Power The Executive History and Development Federal and State Executive Power Judicial Review of Executive Action Non-Judicial Forms of Executive Accountability The Judiciary History, Development and Composition A Foundation of Judicial Independence Rights Protection and Australian Constitutionalism Constitutional Change
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective written communication skills by articulating legal concepts clearly, persuasively and appropriately. (PLO 7)
Demonstrate comprehension of principles of public law and their relationship to Australian government. (PLO 1)
Develop an awareness of the principles of statutory interpretation and demonstrate a capacity to apply them in a public law setting. (PLO 1, 4, 6)
Explain the origins and later adaptations of Australian public law. (PLO 1)
Engage in critical analysis of how the principles of Australian public law operate to support and constrain the exercise of governmental power. (PLO 1)
Demonstrate effective oral communication skills by discussing and debating course concepts in a scholarly, reflective and respectful manner. (PLO 7)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Conceptual Foundations of the Legal System
school: School of Global and Public Law
syllabus_overview: LAWS1123 - Conceptual Foundations of the Legal System (‘CFLS’) is a core course for Diploma in Humanities/Enabling Program (Law Stream) students in their second and final session of study. This course is worth 6 units of credit. It complements, and is studied in the same session as, LAWS1124 - Lawyers and Society. CFLS develops students’ understanding of the functioning of the legal system and facility with foundational legal skills that students acquired in LAWS1121 – Legal System and Skills A . Students are introduced to fundamental concepts and legal paradigms in three core areas of substantive law: contract; tort and criminal law. The course focuses on students’ acquisition of legal problem-solving skills in both oral and written contexts to enhance students’ understanding of legal principles found in case and statute law in these three fields. It provides preparation for, and an introduction to, the study of Contract, Tort and Criminal Law in the LLB program. Module 1: Contract A good grounding in the basic principles of contract law is a fundamental element of any legal education. This Module is an introduction to the study of voluntarily assumed legal obligations which govern many important areas of daily life. This Module focuses on students acquiring a sound understanding of a number of basic principles of contract law, through common law method, with particular focus on the elements required for the formation of a valid contract, namely offer and acceptance; consideration; intention to create legal relations; certainty and privity. Module 2: Criminal Justice The aims of the Criminal Justice module are to introduce students to foundational elements of the criminal law, and some key issues related to criminal justice. The course will include an examination of the components of criminal offences generally, and will take two substantive offences (murder and offensive language/behaviour) to see how these elements play out in practice. Module 3: Tort This module covers the part of the law of torts which signifies, broadly speaking, the law determining liability to pay compensation for wrongfully caused injury, damage or loss through medical negligence. The prime objective is to introduce students to the core principles of negligence, including a critical understanding of the policy considerations informing the law. A second objective of this course is to examine a relatively limited number of leading cases and legislation in selected areas and thereby develop skills of analysis, synthesis and evaluation. A third objective is to encourage students to consider the way in which the law of torts operates in the context of society as a whole, and the ways in which it is influenced by such particular factors as insurance, social security, and the need (or absence of a need) to ascribe fault. Thus there is a theoretical component to the course which introduces various debates about the nature and effectiveness of tort law.
learning_outcomes: Conceptual Foundations of the Legal System is part of the Nura Gili Enabling Program. As such no CLO or PLO are included at this time. Enrolled students please refer to the Moodle page for more information.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Lawyers and Society
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: The KLC component of Lawyers and Society fits with your other law courses in that it demonstrates law in practice and the specific ways in which it impacts on disadvantaged clients. Law is a subjective, constantly changing area and this course will give you the opportunity to explore some of the ways in which law is used in the legal aid system to assist people who are disadvantaged. The Legal Ethics component of Lawyers and Society complements the KLC component of Lawyers and Society by providing some theoretical background to many of the ethical issues you could encounter as a practising lawyer. It also provides an introduction to the Bachelor of Laws core course LAWS1230 – Lawyers, Ethics and Justice. Main Topics The aims of the KLC component of Lawyers and Society are to:- encourage students to keep studying law allow students to see law in practice to make their studies relevant allow students to bond with each other allow students to see how the law affects/can help disadvantaged people develop written and oral communication skills develop knowledge of law develop ability to critically examine the law and its effects make students law studies relevant to their lives through clinical work provide additional support for students This is achieved through a combination of approaches. You will be introduced to an overview of the legal aid system through visits to: the Local court, pro bono section of a commercial law firm, Legal Aid Commission and the Public Defender’s Office. You will also be taught a concentrated course on interviewing skills as they relate to disadvantaged clients. You will interview real clients in order to improve your oral and written communication skills. You will also have the opportunity to work with later year law students learning about legal file work.
