institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Mathematics for Finance
syllabus_overview: Finance is concerned with making definite numerical recommendations that frequently can only be obtained by analysing sophisticated models using high-speed computers. This course studies the design, implementation and use of computer programs to solve practical mathematical problems of relevance to finance, insurance and risk management. It includes a review of MATLAB/Python, floating point numbers, rounding error and computational complexity, and a selection of topics from: approximation and parameter estimation, Fourier series and the FFT, finite difference approximations, partial differential equations (Black-Scholes PDE), sparse linear systems, nonlinear algebraic equations, trees, Monte Carlo methods and simulation, random numbers and variance reduction and numerical integration. The teaching activities include weekly lectures in which the theoretical background is explained and weekly practical computing laboratory classes.
learning_outcomes: Apply quantitative skills and mathematical reasoning to solve problems relevant to finance, insurance and risk management.
Apply the underlying mathematics, computational techniques and problem solving skills relevant for problems in financial mathematics.
Select appropriate computational techniques to analyse financial data and interpret the answers within a financial problem.
Determine confidence in a computed answer and the risks associated with a given computational problem.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 8411 or 8416 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Stochastic Differential Equations: Theory, Applications, and Numerical Methods
syllabus_overview: Stochastic differential equation models play a prominent role in a range of application areas, including biology, chemistry, epidemiology, mechanics, microelectronics, economics, and finance. This course covers the theory and applications of stochastic differential equations, the design and implementation on computers of numerical methods for solving these practical mathematical equations. The course will start with a background knowledge of random variables, Brownian motion, and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process. Other topics studied include: stochastic integrals, the Euler-Maruyama method, Milstein, higher order method, stability and convergence. In addition to lectures, the distinct tutorial and lab classes will give students the opportunity to work on both mathematical exercises and computing problems.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish different types of stochastic differential equations and different types of solutions (Ito vs Stratonovich, strong solution vs weak solution).
Appraise the confidence in computer solutions and predict uncertainties associated with a given computational problem.
Describe, identify the strengths and weaknesses, and explain the differences in the numerical solutions learnt (Euler-Maruyama, Milstein, high order schemes, implicit schemes).
Implement methods learnt by writing computer code or using available software.
Explain the convergence, consistency, and stability of each method.
Identify applications in modelling for each equation.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graph Theory
syllabus_overview: Graphs are fundamental objects in combinatorics, which can be used to model the relationships between the members of a network or system. They have many applications in areas such as computer science, statistical physics and computational biology. Specifically, a graph consists of a set of vertices and a set of edges, where an edge is an unordered pair of distinct vertices. This course is designed for Honours and postgraduate Mathematics students. Through a series of seminars and tutorials, students explore various aspects of graph theory, including: matchings, coverings and packings, connectivity, graph colourings, planar graphs, extremal graphs and Ramsey theory, the probabilistic method, random graphs. There is an emphasis on proof in this course. Note : Course not offered every year - contact School for more information.
learning_outcomes: Understand various combinatorial and probabilistic techniques used in graph theory.
Manipulate and apply concepts and techniques to solve simple and complex problems in graph theory.
Understand a range of concepts and definitions used in graph theory to solve problems.
prerequisites: Enrolled in program 5659 or 8750 or 8161 or 8719 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Numerical Linear Algebra
syllabus_overview: The course is intended for students from Science and Engineering programs with interests in mathematics, statistics, data science or numerical simulation. Algorithms from numerical linear algebra are ubiquitous in scientific and statistical software. The theoretical component of the course aims to impart an understanding of how these algorithms work as well as an appreciation of their potential limitations. To illustrate the applications of numerical linear algebra, a variety of examples from statistics, data science and applied mathematics are described. The course includes a substantial computing component providing practical experience with widely used software libraries.
learning_outcomes: Identify relevant structure in a matrix and select and analyse a specialised algorithm that exploits this structure for improved efficiency.
Use a suitable programming language to solve simple and complex problems in linear algebra via calls to numerical library functions.
Describe the role of numerical linear algebra in a variety of scientific and statistical applications.
Use standard matrix factorisations to construct solution procedures in numerical linear algebra.
Quantify the relative merits of direct and iterative methods for problems in linear algebra.
Estimate how the computational cost of an algorithm scales with the problem size for simple and complex problems in linear algebra.
Identify matrix properties that can compromise the accuracy and reliability of numerical computations.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Combinatorics
syllabus_overview: This is a course for graduate and advanced undergraduate students, forming an introduction to modern combinatorics. The emphasis is on theory, proof and problem solving. Topics may include extremal set theory, extremal graph theory, Ramsey theory and arithmetic combinatorics. Combinatorial methods taught in this course range from the pigeonhole principle, double counting, and the linear algebra method to possibly generating functions or the probabilistic method. Exact content depends on the lecturer-in-charge. Content is delivered in lectures and explored in tutorials.
learning_outcomes: Communicate mathematics clearly in written form using formal proofs.
Identify appropriate techniques to solve simple and complex combinatorial problems.
State and prove classical theorems of combinatorics.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Functional Analysis
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction to functional analysis. It is a proof-based course covering abstract topological vector spaces before specialising to Banach spaces (complete normed spaces). Students will prove several key results due to Banach and its school. The course also by considers Hilbert spaces and decomposing compact operators acting on them. This course is lecture based, with tutorials every week.
learning_outcomes: Construct arguments using concepts from a range of different areas of mathematics (e.g., analysis and linear algebra).
Assess the appropriate tools to solve varying problems in functional analysis.
Understand proofs and adapt them to prove other statements in functional analysis.
Use online tools to find information to solve problems in functional analysis.
Communicate ideas in functional analysis competently in written form.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Algebraic Topology
syllabus_overview: This course introduces Algebraic Topology, one of the most vibrant subjects of late nineteenth-century and twentieth-century mathematics, with important applications to physics, differential geometry, algebraic geometry and analysis, increasingly also to chemistry, biology and other sciences. You will learn and apply notions of category theory like functors and natural transformations, of homotopy theory as well as notions of homological algebra like homology studied in the particular case of complexes obtained from arbitrary topological spaces. Tutorials will discuss problems that will enhance the understanding acquired in the lectures. This course is suited to students who have successfully completed both MATH3711 (Algebra) and MATH3701 (Differential Geometry and Topology), and are looking to expand on their knowledge from these courses.
learning_outcomes: Apply mathematical theory to solve concrete and theoretical problems in topology.
Communicate mathematical problem solving to an academic audience in an effective written format with advanced competency.
Use algebra knowledge about groups, rings, group homomorphisms to reformulate topology and geometry questions.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Number Theory
syllabus_overview: Being at the intersection of two of the most beautiful and important areas of mathematics, Algebra and Number Theory, this course will build on your abstract algebra background to address number theoretic problems regarding integers or rational numbers, and their generalisation to algebraic numbers. The course will start with recalling some algebraic background, such as field extensions and basic Galois theory. We will then start developing the theory of algebraic numbers and algebraic integers, ideals in rings of integers and their factorisation, followed by ramification theory which roughly describes the decomposition of prime ideals in a given number field when lifted to finite extensions. We will continue with ideal class groups and units, and if time allows, we will discuss also valuations and several applications. These concepts will be explored through a series of lectures, along with weekly tutorial exercises, and towards the end of the course, we will also discuss some relevant research topics.
learning_outcomes: Gain a solid theoretical background in the theory of algebraic numbers. evidenced by the ability to reproduce definitions and prove basic properties and results related to number fields, as well as apply them to solve relevant problems.
Apply the concepts and techniques s to solve appropriate number theoretic problems.
Communicate mathematical ideas effectively using correct terminology and appropriate technology like LaTeX.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 5659 or 7659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modern Differential Geometry and Topology
syllabus_overview: Topology and differential geometry both deal with the study of shape: topology from a continuous and differential geometry from a differentiable viewpoint. This postgraduate course begins with a study of curves in the plane and in space focusing on how they bend. Surfaces are also introduced, studying the first and second fundamental forms introduced by Gauss, the various measures of curvature and what they mean for the external and internal appearance and properties of surfaces. The course also provides an opportunity to prove the important Gauss-Bonnet theorem and use it to examine topological properties of surfaces, such as the Euler Characteristic.
learning_outcomes: Provide a complete topological classification of a particular surface.
Compare and contrast the differences and connections between topology and differential geometry for surfaces.
Apply intrinsic and extrinsic theorems of differential geometry of manifolds to calculate the curvature of a surface and the properties of special curves on surfaces.
Solve problems of the differential geometry and topology of curves, including calculating their invariants and using them in applications.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modern Analysis
syllabus_overview: This is a Masters course aimed at students completing a mathematics major or program. It is assumed that students are familiar with single and several variable calculus as taught in first and second year mathematics courses. The central concepts of calculus are limits and continuity. These concepts can be extended to quite general situations. The simplest of these is when there is some way of measuring the distance between two objects. Some of the most important examples of these “metric spaces” occur as sets of functions, so this course looks at ways in which one might say that a sequence of functions converges. Taking these ideas one step further, we look at convergence which does not come from a generalised distance function. These are the ideas of point set topology. The course includes topics such as countability, continuity, uniform convergence and compactness, as well as normed vector spaces, which are the central object of study in functional analysis. The course consists of 4 hours of lectures per week and 1 hour of tutorial.
learning_outcomes: Apply abstract mathematical theory to concrete problems.

Describe and apply definitions, theorems, and concepts of basic mathematical analysis, including the theory of metric, topological, and Banach spaces to basic, as well as some more advanced, problems.
Construct rigorous mathematical proofs and use them to solve problems.
Communicate mathematical reasoning effectively in written and oral form.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modern Algebra
syllabus_overview: In Modern Algebra we examine some of the basic notions of modern algebra that arose in the late 19th and early 20th century. The most fundamental notion is that of a group, which is how mathematicians study symmetry. In this course, groups are studied in detail both from an abstract point of view and also to study symmetry in geometry. The other important concept studied is that of a ring. The algebra of adding and multiplying matrices has many similarities with the algebra of numbers. The notion of rings generalises both of these two examples. The course examines factorisation theory for certain rings. The course is indispensable for all further studies in pure mathematics. All Masters level students of pure mathematics who have not covered this material should complete this course. Knowledge of linear algebra is a prerequisite for this course. This is a demanding course usually with 4 hours of lectures and another hour for a tutorial each week.
learning_outcomes: Solve algebra problems using the theory of groups, rings and fields covered in lectures.
Develop defect-free proofs in algebra.
Formulate mathematical content logically so that any mathematician reading it can easily verify its veracity.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Harmonic Analysis
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course introduces students to Harmonic analysis. Harmonic Analysis studies functions and measures defined on topological groups (such as the real numbers, the integers or the unit circle). Through a series of lectures and tutorials, topics will be chosen from convergence of Fourier integrals, maximal functions. The course is not offered each year. Please contact the School for further details. .
learning_outcomes: Explain the difference between L1-inversion and almost everywhere inversion of the Fourier transform.
Define the concept of tempered distributions and use tempered distributions to find Fourier transforms of functions that are neither L1 nor L2, such as the inverse linear function.
Define the Fourier Transform in L1-setting, and explain the limitations of such a definition; explain that L1-Fourier transform is a continuous and vanishing function (the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma).
Compute the Fourier transform of the Poisson and the Gaussian kernel, and use Poisson, Gaussian and other kernels as approximate identities to invert L1-Fourier transform.
Present arguments and mathematical ideas in written and oral form.
Prove the algebraic relationship between the Fourier transform and other operators such as translation and dilation.
Extend the L1-theory to the L2-theory of the Fourier transform and prove the Parseval Identity.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolled in program 5659 Mathematics and Statistics or 8161 Financial Mathematics or 8719 Mathematics or 8750 Statistics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Galois Theory
syllabus_overview: The theory of fields holds the key to questions which frustrated mathematicians for hundreds of years, including the impossibility of squaring a circle or trisecting an angle with ruler and compass, or finding a formula for solving quintic equations. The key to their study involves the Galois group which, loosely speaking, captures the symmetry of the field. Through a series of seminars, the course addresses the following topics: fields, Eisenstein criterion, field extensions, algebraic extensions, groups of field automorphisms, normal and separable extensions, finite fields, Galois correspondence, solvable groups, solving equations by radicals, ruler and compass constructions, Kummer extensions, Artin-Schreier extensions. Note : This course is not offered every year - contact the School of Mathematics and Statistics for more information.
learning_outcomes: Report solutions and proofs using multiple modes of mathematical communication.
Analyse and solve problems in field theory using Galois groups.
Solve problems using advanced knowledge of abstract mathematical concepts and fundamentals of modern algebra.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modules and Representation Theory
syllabus_overview: Performing linear algebra over a ring of scalars instead of a field leads to the notion of a module. The theory of modules is surprisingly subtle and has many applications, not only to other parts of mathematics but also to mathematical physics. This course focuses on the theory of modules over principal ideal domains and over semisimple rings. The first has applications to linear algebra. The second has applications to group representations which is essential to the study of symmetry. Topics include modules, modules over a principal ideal domain, group representations.
learning_outcomes: Write clear, concise, and correct mathematical proofs.
Communicate mathematics effectively with peers and the instructor, both verbally and in writing.
Use fundamental concepts in modern algebra to solve concrete mathematical problems.
Typeset mathematics using the LaTeX document preparation system.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 5659 or 7659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Regression Analysis
syllabus_overview: Regression is a set of statistical techniques widely used to analyse relationships between several variables. The topics covered in this course include: linear regression; weighted least squares; generalized linear models (GLMs); fitting GLMs and examining model diagnostics; Poisson regression, binomial regression; analysis of variance; penalized regression methods; splines; penalized splines; thin plate splines; variable selection; generalized cross-validation; local likelihood; kernel smoothing; generalized additive models; multinomial logit analysis; ordinal logistic regression. Lectures will be complemented with worked examples where students will perform data analysis and statistical programming using the R software.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and discuss the mathematical and statistical results from the regression analysis in written form.
Relate the output of statistical software to the theoretical formulas presented in the lectures.
Assess the strengths and weaknesses of regression models, hypotheses and intuitions of the various approaches.
Analyse a given data set by choosing the appropriate regression technique.
Apply the appropriate R package for regression analysis and effectively apply R programming skills to the appropriate regression technique.
Describe the output of statistical software and interpret the results.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Continuous Time Financial Modelling
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course focuses on the continuous-time modelling of financial markets. The main goal of the course is a detailed study of the classical Black-Scholes options pricing model and extensions. The notion of a continuously rebalanced trading strategy is introduced, and the arbitrage-free and completeness properties of a financial market model are examined. The course also introduces and studies the concepts of historical, implied and stochastic volatilities. We study contingent claims of American, Asian, barrier style in the Black-Scholes model. In the final part of the course, alternative models to pricing contingent claims in continuous time are explored.
learning_outcomes: Draw conclusions based on the financial assumptions and financial products in continuous time.
Communicate, both verbally and written forms, mathematical information, ideas, results, discussion, conclusions and referencing of your work and others
Apply conclusions based on the appropriate results and a set of assumptions in continuous time financial modelling in both the Black-Scholes models and other financial models.
State definitions and results of continuous time financial modelling in relations to Black-Scholes modelling and other models.
Apply the appropriate theorems/results to problems in modelling, hedging, and pricing of financial products in continuous time.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH5975 or permission of course authority.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Measure, Integration and Probability
syllabus_overview: Measure Theory provides one of the key building blocks of Analysis, Probability Theory, and Ergodic Theory and is an indispensable tool in the theory of differential equations, Harmonic Analysis, Mathematical Physics and Mathematical Finance. In this course students will develop a proper understanding of measurable functions, measures and the abstract Lebesgue integral. Special attention will be paid to applications of Measure Theory in the Probability Theory such as construction of probability spaces for random variables and stochastic processes, Laws of Large Numbers, the Central Limit theorem and their applications. The Radon-Nikodym Theorem will be applied to introduce a general definition of conditional expectation. Pre-requisites: 24 units of level III mathematics or a degree in numerate discipline or permission of the Head of Department.
learning_outcomes: Communicate measure theory effectively in written form.
Apply concepts of measure theory and integration theory.
Solve concrete problems in measure theory.
Explain the connections of measure and integration to the probability theory.
Apply the standard instruments of measure theory including convergence theorems, absolute continuity and Fubini theorem.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 8271 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Statistical Methods in Epidemiology
syllabus_overview: Epidemiology is the study of factors that impact on the occurrence and outcome of diseases in human populations. The course introduces the main statistical concepts, methods and models used in the design and analysis of epidemiological studies. Extensive use of statistical computing and analysis of real datasets is an essential part of this course.
learning_outcomes: Explain the di fferent measures of disease-exposure association, the diff erences between the measures and under what circumstances each is appropriate, andcalculate these measures
Explain the idea of matching in epidemiological studies and the reasons why it is used
Interpret the coeffcients of a logistic regression model for diff erent types of studies
Use the theory of maximum likelihood estimation to derive estimators and standard errors for parameters in a logistic regression model
Explain the concepts of causality, confounding, and interaction
Use the computer language R to analyze data from epidemiological studies, and interpret R output.
Explain the key features of epidemiological studies and what distinguishes them from other types of studies
Examine whether interaction and/or confounding is present in an epidemiological study
List the di erent types of epidemiological studies, explain their key features and the distinctions between them, and the advantages and disadvantages of each type of study
Derive and use statistical techniques appropriate for matched studies
Explain how the design features of the di erent types of studies dictate the methods of analysis appropriate to each
Explain the di fferent measures of disease occurrence and calculate these measures
Solve theoretical problems related to epidemiological studies
Check the validity of a logistic regression model using residuals and influence measures
Explain generalized linear models (GLMs), and indicate how logistic regression models fit into the GLM framework
Explain the di erent types of regression models used in epidemiological studies
Implement techniques to deal with interaction and/or confounding in an epidemiological study
Assess the statistical significance of disease-exposure association by applying hypothesis tests and calculating confidence intervals for measures of disease-exposure association
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data and Machine Learning
syllabus_overview: A wide range of statistical methods and computational tools have been developed in the past few decades to gather information from data. This postgraduate course covers the key techniques in data mining and machine learning with theoretical background and applications, delivered through a series of lectures and tutorials.The topics include methods such as linear and logistic regression, neural networks, Bayesian neural networks, clustering and dimensionality reduction, ensemble learning, and an introduction to deep learning. Emerging machine learning tools and libraries are used to illustrate the methods in programming environments that include Python and R.
learning_outcomes: Develop models for solving data mining problems that include clustering, regression, and classification.
Demonstrate an applied working knowledge of the methodologies covered with practical assignments.
Select appropriate statistical and machine learning approaches to analyse data.
Build machine learning models using real-world data sets and use evaluation metrics to compare their performance.
Identify the fundamentals of machine learning and data mining through model development.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373 and complete either COMP9020 or COMP9021 as a prerequisite.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Stochastic Processes
syllabus_overview: The theory of stochastic processes deals with phenomena evolving randomly in time and/or space, such as prices on financial markets, air temperature or wind velocity, spread of diseases, number of hospital admissions in certain area, and many others. This course introduces some of the basic ideas and tools to study such phenomena. In particular, we will introduce the concept of martingale to study phenomena evolving in discrete time and the concept of Poisson process (and its generalisations) and Brownian Motion to study processes evolving continuously in time. Some applications to statistical inference will also be discussed. For students in the Master of Financial Mathematics program, the course will also provide foundational knowledge for more advanced courses.
learning_outcomes: Define the properties of various stochastic process models and related random elements.
State the most rudimentary concepts and theorems of measure-theoretic probability theory.
Apply the theory of stochastic processes to model real phenomena and answer some questions in applied sciences.
Provide logical and coherent proofs of important theoretic results.
Identify appropriate stochastic process model(s) for a given problem.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5518 or 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8518 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Experimental Design and Causal Inference
syllabus_overview: This course in statistics that covers the design and analysis of experiments and observational studies to answer causal questions. Topics include potential outcomes, causal estimands, and the importance of the design phase in both experiments and observational studies. Experimental design topics will include randomisation techniques, such as blocked and factorial experiments, and analysis methods, including both parametric and randomisation methods. Causal inference topics will include propensity scores, weighting, and matching. Students will put methods into practice using the statistical software R throughout the course. The intended audience of this course is wide-ranging, from statistics and data science students to students in the social and natural sciences (biology, psychology, economics, and others). This course is jointly taught at two levels. MATH3852 is for 3rd year undergraduates, whereas MATH5852 is for Honours & Masters students.
learning_outcomes: Apply methods in the course to the analysis of datasets using statistical software packages and interpret the results. Create meaningful conclusions based on analysis.
Identify and evaluate experimental designs for different settings.
Evaluate the key differences between experiments and observational studies
Estimate propensity scores and apply them in the design and analysis of observational studies.
Describe the potential outcomes framework and apply causal estimands.
Analyse experimental data generated from different designs.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Time Series
syllabus_overview: The course is concerned with the theory and application of appropriate statistical techniques for analysis of time series data -- data collected over time. The course will help students develop a sound understanding of stationary and non-stationary time series models and their properties in discrete time. The topics include the theory of stationary time series; methods for trend and seasonal analysis and adjustment; modelling and forecasting with autoregressive moving average processes; modelling the impact of exogenous or intervention variables on responses; models for stochastic volatility and long-term dependence; regression models for time series. Applications are primarily drawn from finance and public health and the R software environment is used to perform appropriate analyses for numerical examples.
learning_outcomes: Apply diagnostic checking for the adequacy of the fit of a model.
Generate, interpret and explain R software output appropriate for time series identification, modeling and forecasting.
Identify appropriate models for time series.
Perform linear prediction for a range of time series models.
Understand the properties of the major types of time series observed in discrete time.
Estimate the time series models using different methods.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5518 or 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 5518 or 8518 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Multivariate Analysis
syllabus_overview: The course gives a methodological background in multivariate analysis as a backbone of Applied Statistics. It introduces multivariate techniques including principal component analysis; canonical correlation analysis; cluster analysis; factor analysis and discriminant analysis. Computing and data analysis features prominently in this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply multivariate techniques and models to the analysis of datasets, interpretation of results and drawing of conclusions.
Perform different multivariate inference procedures by using the available powerful procedures in the R and/or SAS system.
Use the general terminology, notation, and concepts in the theory, methods, and applications of multivariate analysis.
Use the properties of the multivariate normal distribution to justify optimality properties of Statistical Inference procedures based on multivariate normality.
Formulate and solve inference problems that use one or a combination of different multivariate statistical procedures.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Probability and Stochastic Processes
syllabus_overview: This course covers probabilistic concepts which are necessary to study various complex phenomena arising in Engineering, Biology, Medicine and Economics. This course introduces basic concepts which are needed to analyse different phenomena. In particular, we discuss the concepts of random events, random variables, structures of dependence, computation of probabilities using the Central Limit Theorem, simple Markov chains, and Brownian motion.
learning_outcomes: Use key theoretical tools to explore properties of random variables.
Apply principles of Markov Chains and Brownian motion to practical and theoretical problems.
Derive fundamental results in the theory of probability and random variables.
Apply the principles of probability to practical and theoretical problems.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5518 or 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8518 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Statistics and Statistical Computations
syllabus_overview: This course addresses the foundational principles of statistical reasoning. In particular it introduces the most common methods for estimating unknown parameters of key statistical models in order to draw conclusions and make decisions without complete information. Practical implementations using statistical software packages are continuously presented to students. Students explore methods for estimating parameters using Maximum Likelihood and Bayesian inference, for constructing confidence intervals and performing hypothesis testing, for fitting linear and general linear models. Each week, the course includes typically 4 hour of pre-recorded lecture video and 1 hour of face-to-face tutorial during which students will have the opportunity to reinforce their learning.
learning_outcomes: Interpret results generated from statistical software output
Write and execute basic R programs to perform statistical analysis.
Apply theoretical concepts and appropriate theorems to solve problems.
Use appropriate statistical terminology and reporting conventions to effectively communicate analysis and findings to a general audience.
Define and explain key statistical terms, concepts, and theorems.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5518 or 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8518 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Bootstrap and Other Resampling Methods
syllabus_overview: The course presents the basic techniques of resampling methods useful in statistics. These have grown very popular over the last two decades as they offer reliable alternatives to traditional asymptotic approaches, mostly based on Central Limit Theorems. The flagship instance of resampling-based approaches is the so-called `bootstrap' , by now considered as a real breakthrough in statistics. A very versatile technique, the bootstrap allows easy determination of the sampling distribution of any statistic of interest (estimator or test statistic) in a variety of situations. In fact, the bootstrap bypasses heavy analytical developments by substituting appropriate simulations. In many cases, the quality of the bootstrap approximation is better than its asymptotic counterparts, while in other situations, there is no asymptotic approximation available and the bootstrap turns out to be the only possibility for statistical inference. In this course, the bootstrap and other related resampling methods are first introduced in a general framework and their theoretical properties are investigated. Then, they are illustrated through many standard problems of statistical inference and common questions in related fields.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the results and draw appropriate conclusions, when the resampling techniques are used to solve problems with real data.
Create and develop short pieces of code in an appropriate software to generate output in regard to the previous learning outcome.
Understand the underlying mechanisms for justifying the resampling approach.
Select and apply correctly the main resampling methods for statistical inference.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Statistical Machine Learning Theory
syllabus_overview: This course gives students a statistical and mathematical perspective on modern machine learning methods, with the aim of obtaining a deeper understanding of how such methods work and have been derived. This theoretical knowledge will then be used to demonstrate how to fine tune machine learning methods for complex applications. This course will focus on principles of neural networks (convolutional, recurrent, sequential methods), optimisation methods relevant for machine learning and generative AI (autoencoders, diffusion models, generative adversarial networks). This course is intended as an elective for Statistics majors & minors, Quantitative Data Science Major and Mathematics majors, both at the undergraduate and postgraduate level. Prior knowledge of basic probability is necessary, and knowledge of stochastic processes will be advantageous but is not required. This course complements MATH5191 Optimisation for data science by focusing on various neural network architectures and training methods that make use of some optimisation methods explored in MATH5191, along with probabilistic aspects governing generative modelling. Additionally, this course focuses on mathematical and statistical foundations of many machine learning methods discussed from a computational perspective in MATH5836. This course is jointly taught at two levels. MATH3881 is for 3rd year undergraduates, with MATH5881 for Honours & Masters students.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate existing methods and justify which tools are most appropriate for particular applications based on their strengths and weaknesses.
Formulate and derive basic neural network and generative modelling methods using tools from linear algebra, calculus and basic probability theory.
Construct bespoke machine learning methods for complex applications.
Explain background concepts underlying modern machine learning.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Longitudinal Data Analysis
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on modelling response profiles over time, whilst accounting for the correlation that will typically exist between measurements taken on the same individual and the variability between individual response profiles. MATH5885 brings together multivariate regression modelling, time series modelling and random effects modelling for continuous and discrete valued response measurements and aims to enhance a student’s capacity to analyze and understand large, complex data sets. The focus will be on applications to biomedical studies, but the ideas have a wider application, for example, to panel studies that arise in market research and social surveys.
learning_outcomes: Use the linear mixed effects models for analyzing continuous longitudinal data and show how this extends to generalized linear mixed effects models for analyzing non-normal longitudinal data.
Use the R software to fit the models studied, visualize patterns, and interpret the output.
Learn the key features of longitudinal data and the ability to use longitudinal data analysis techniques.
Distinguish between a "subject-specific" and "population-average" interpretation of parameters.
Derive the likelihoods for correlated data and use them to calculate maximum likelihood estimates. Also, learn to use the concept of residual maximum likelihood (REML).
Use linear models when incorporating correlated errors to analyze longitudinal data.
Explain the distinct types of correlation that can occur in longitudinal data and choose appropriate models for correlation structures in given datasets.
Use marginal models to analyze non-normal longitudinal data via generalized estimating equations.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nonparametric Statistics
syllabus_overview: This course introduces modern nonparametric techniques for statistical analysis. Nonparametric methods are often said to “let the data speak for itself”, as they do not require the analyst to make any strong assumptions about the process which generated the data. This is in contrast with classical statistical procedures which are essentially parametric: they assume that the data follows a prescribed model defined in terms of a small number of parameters. As this course gives another insight into statistical theory, it can be thought of as an interesting complement to most of the other statistics courses which the student may have taken in their program.
learning_outcomes: Apply the fundamental principles of smoothing for hypotheses testing when analysing real-world data sets.
Research scientific literature in the field and review recently published papers introducing novel nonparametric approaches for data analysis.
Use R software to answer concrete questions about real-world data sets and for intensive computing methods such as the bootstrap.
Apply the fundamental principles of smoothing for nonparametric curve estimation when analysing real-world data sets.
Explain why non-parametric techniques for data analysis are needed and useful.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Stochastic Processes
syllabus_overview: This is an advanced level postgraduate course in probability theory and stochastic processes for mathematics/statistics and data science students. Topics covered include rigorous definition of probability and random variables; convergence of random variables; Poisson and Wiener process, and Ito Calculus.
learning_outcomes: State the defining properties of various stochastic process models and related random objects.
Provide logical and coherent proofs of fundamental results in the theory of stochastic processes.
Identify appropriate stochastic process model(s) for a given research problem.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 7659 or 7546 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Statistical Inference
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course presents general inference theory based on maximum likelihood and on Bayes methods. Estimation, confidence set construction, and hypothesis testing are discussed within decision-theoretic framework. Computationally intensive methods such as bootstrap are also discussed and are compared to asymptotic approximations such as saddlepoint and empirical likelihood.
learning_outcomes: Use computer packages to generate output for common Inference procedures and for computer-intensive calculations such as bootstrapping and robust estimation.
Apply concepts of finite-sample and asymptotic efficiency of inference procedure to appropriate problems.
Explain how statistical inference arises from the first principles of probability theory.
Use parametric, nonparametric, Bayes and robust inference methods.
Apply the fundamental principles of inference: sufficiency, likelihood, ancillarity, and equivariance.
Estimate key population parameters of interest, test hypotheses about them and construct confidence regions.
Apply the parametric and non-parametric delta method, asymptotic normality, Edgeworth expansions and saddlepoint method to solve appropriate problems.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design & Analysis of Clinical Trials
syllabus_overview: This course will provide an introduction to statistical methodology used in the conduct of randomised controlled clinical trials. We will start with an introduction to the basic philosophy and history of the randomized controlled trial, and discuss design issues such as methods of randomization and sample size determination. Extensive use will be made of computer methods in analysing data sets.
learning_outcomes: Solve theoretical problems related to the design and analysis of clinical trials
Explain the key features of randomized controlled clinical trials and what distinguishes them from other types of studies
Explain the issues related to multiple comparisons and how adjustments should be made for them
Explain why and how clinical trials are monitored, and implement monitoring schemes
Perform appropriate analyses of data from clinical trials, using the computer language R , and interpret R output
Explain the issues related to subgroup analyses and perform a subgroup analysis
Explain bias and how it might a ffect clinical trials
Explain how sample sizes can be calculated for di fferent types of outcomes in clinical trials, and implement these calculations
Explain the intention-to-treat principle and why it is widely used in clinical trials

List the di fferent types of clinical trials, such as parallel group, crossover, and equivalence trials, explain their key features and the distinctions between them, and analyse data from these trials
Explain the importance of randomization and the di fferent methods of random allocation used in clinical trials, and prepare randomization schemes based on these methods
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project
syllabus_overview: This course is an opportunity to bring together the skills the students have developed during their Master program and apply them to a substantive new problem. Students will work in a small group and present results in thesis form and in a presentation. Students will be supervised by an academic staff member from the School and meet one hour per week to discuss and work on the group project. Note: Available only to students for whom it forms part of their program requirements. Students usually complete their project during the last one or two Terms of their program. Students are not eligible to start a project until they have completed at least 36 UoC (typically, 6 courses) over at least three terms.
learning_outcomes: Produce a report involving enquiry-based learning and analytical skills as they relate to mathematical and statistical sciences.
Analyse and solve advanced problems in the mathematical and statistical sciences.
Conduct independent and collaborative enquiry effectively.
Communicate a research topic effectively to a range of audiences both in written and oral forms.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must be enrolled in 8161, 8719 or 8750 and have completed 36 UOC in one of these programs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Survival Analysis
syllabus_overview: Survival analysis is the analysis of data representing the time to occurrence of a certain event or endpoint (time-to-event data). This course introduces the special features of time-to-event data and explores methods and models available to deal with them. Extensive use will be made of the computer methods in analysing real datasets.
learning_outcomes: Understand the counting process formulation for survival data to calculate residuals and influence for survival models including assessing the proportional hazards assumption.
Understand the key features of survival data including censoring, truncation, hazard, and frailty.
Solve theoretical statistical problems related to the analysis of survival data.
Understand and apply the Cox proportional hazards model to examine the effect of covariates on survival including the use of time-dependent covariates.
Understand and apply parametric and non-parametric inference techniques for the analysis of survival data.
Use common R packages and functions for the processing and analysis of survival data.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Bayesian Inference and Computation
syllabus_overview: After describing the fundamentals of Bayesian inference, this course will examine the specification of prior and posterior distributions, Bayesian decision theoretic concepts, the ideas behind Bayesian hypothesis tests, model choice and model averaging, and evaluate the capabilities of several common model types, such as hierarchical and mixture models. An important part of Bayesian inference is the requirement to numerically evaluate complex integrals on a routine basis. Accordingly this course will also introduce the ideas behind Monte Carlo integration, importance sampling, rejection sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo samplers such as the Gibbs sampler and the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm, and use of the Stan posterior simulation software. The intended audience of this course is wide-ranging, from statistics and data science students to economics, actuarial, computer science and natural science (e.g. biology, geology, physics) students. Prior knowledge of basic probability is necessary, and knowledge of stochastic processes will be advantageous but is not required. The purpose of this course is to introduce students to Bayesian statistical concepts not seen in core courses which are primarily focused on frequentist statistics. This course is jointly taught at two levels. MATH3871 is for 3rd year undergraduates, whereas MATH5960 is for Honours & Masters students.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of computational techniques that are critical for Bayesian inference.
Explain and apply the background concepts underlying Bayesian inference.
Perform Bayesian analysis on realistic data using either common model types or using newly-constructed/bespoke models for new problems.
Prove theoretic results underlying some common Bayesian models and simulation techniques.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5546 or 5659 or 5959 or 7546 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8543 or 8544 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Discrete Time Financial Modelling
syllabus_overview: The course provides an overview of the most important classes of financial contracts traded on over-the-counter exchanges between financial institutions and their clients in discrete time. The option of European and American style, futures contracts and forward contracts is also discussed. The basic ideas of arbitrage pricing are studied in the classical Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binominal model of stock price. Subsequently, the valuation and hedging of European and American options and general contingent claims are established. The proofs of the fundamental theorems of asset pricing for finite models of security markets which is central to the modern theory of derivative pricing are given.
learning_outcomes: Apply probability theory and stochastic analysis to practical problems.
Identify and apply which procedures are appropriate for a given financial problem.
Solve practical problems to understand the usefulness of probability and stochastic analysis in a professional setting.
Communicate mathematics and statistics effectively in written and oral forms.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Categorical Data Analysis
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course provides the theoretical foundation and methodological background for the analysis of categorical response data. Through a series of lectures and labs, a range of topics will be introduced including the Bernoulli trial, the analysis of contingency tables, and generalised linear models including logistic and Poisson regression. Statistical computing is an integral part of this course.
learning_outcomes: Solve theoretical statistical problems related to the analysis of categorical data.
Understand and apply the terminology, notation and concepts in the theory, methods, and application of categorical data analysis.
Write SAS code for data input, data processing, and for conducting analyses using categorical data.

Apply inference techniques for log-linear models, logistic regression, Poisson regression, logit and probit models to a rigorous standard, including model comparisons and the use of model selection strategies within a hierarchical set of models.
Use common SAS procedures for categorical data analysis such as FREQ, LOGISTIC, CATMOD and GENMOD to analyse datasets, interpret the results and draw conclusions.
prerequisites: Enrolled in program 5659 or 8750 or 8161 or 8719 or 8959 or 9372 or 9373 or 7659

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Stochastic Analysis
syllabus_overview: Modern theory of financial markets relies on advanced mathematical statistical methods that are used to model, forecast and manage risk in complex financial transactions. After the publication in 1973 of the ground-breaking paper of Black and Scholes on the arbitrage pricing of European call options, Stochastic Analysis became an indispensable tool for the theory of financial markets, derivation of prices of standard and exotic options and other derivative securities, hedging-related financial risk, as well as managing the interest rate risk. This is a postgraduate level course in which you will learn the basic concepts and techniques of Stochastic Analysis, such as Brownian motion, Ito stochastic integral, Ito's formula, changes of measures, stochastic differential equations and their relations to second-order partial differential equations, and Feynman-Kac formula.
learning_outcomes: Apply probability theory and stochastic analysis to practical problems.
Communicate mathematics, in particular stochastic analyses, effectively in a written form.
Identify which analysis procedure is appropriate for a given research problem.
Explain the usefulness of probability and stochastic analysis in a professional setting.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Term Structure Modelling
syllabus_overview: The fixed income market is an important sector of the financial market on which various interest rate sensitive instruments, such as: bonds, swaps, swapations, caps, ect. are traded. The management of interest rate risk -by which we mean the pricing and hedging of interest rate products - is an important and complex issue. It creates a demand for mathematical models capable of covering all kinds of interest rate risks.The course provides an overview of various concepts of interest rates and the most important interest-rate sensitive contracts. The crucial part of the course is the presentation of various methods of modelling of the term structure of interest rates, and the variation of interest rate derivatives within the framework of each methodology.
learning_outcomes: Provide logical and coherent proofs of important theoretical results covered in the course.
Apply the theory covered in the course to model real phenomena and answer some questions in applied sciences.
Price financial derivatives associated with a particular term structure model.
Identify appropriate term structure model(s) for a given research or applied problem.
State the defining properties of various term structure models (such as short term models of interests rates, Heath, Jarrow and Morton (HJM), etc) .
Demonstrate an understanding of the usefulness of these concepts in your career of Financial Mathematics.
prerequisites: Enrolment in program 5659 or 5959 or 7659 or 7959 or 8161 or 8411 or 8416 or 8719 or 8750 or 8959
Prerequisite: MATH5965 and MATH5975

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Biomathematics
syllabus_overview: This course introduces mathematical modelling and data analysis for biological and biomedical systems. The course is suitable for students with an interest in the real-world application of differential equation modelling. Examples of the biological systems studied in the course include: population dynamics, the spread of infectious diseases, drug delivery and metabolism, biochemical reactions, the formation of animal coat patterns, and the growth of tumours. The emphasis in this course is on the development of the governing model equations, and on the analysis and interpretation of the model solutions. Methods for computer simulation of the model equations will be demonstrated but students’ knowledge of these methods will not be assessed in the course. In addition to lectures, the course will feature tutorials and workshops. Weekly tutorials require the class to solve a series of mathematical problems that build upon the lecture material. Workshops (several during the course) further consolidate the lecture material as the class makes use of modelling, analysis and computer simulations to perform in-depth studies of particular biological applications. Assumed Knowledge: Completion of two years of an undergraduate degree in mathematics or statistics.
learning_outcomes: Communicate discipline specific information in written form with appropriate referencing.
Mathematically analyse ordinary differential equation models of biological systems by identifying steady states, their stability, and any bifurcations that occur as a parameter is varied.

Derive or explain partial differential equation models for the time-dependent dynamics of structured populations and the spatio-temporal dynamics of biological diffusion and transport, and analyse and interpret the solutions of such models.

Derive or explain ordinary differential equation models for the time-dependent dynamics of populations, epidemics, drug metabolism and chemical reactions, and analyse and interpret the solutions of such models.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5659 or 8161 or 8719 or 8750 or 7659
