institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Materials and Chemistry
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the fundamentals of Materials Science and Chemistry used in engineering. The different classes of materials used in engineering designs are introduced, and their basic structural, mechanical and functional properties are defined, and the mechanical properties are measured in laboratory activities. The relationships between a material’s underlying structure and its properties are explored. The ways in which materials fail within engineering settings are identified. The chemistry part of the course builds on an elementary knowledge of chemistry (equivalent to one year of high school chemistry, such as Year 11 chemistry, or CHEM1001 at UNSW) to explore the structure of atoms leading to an understanding of the properties of materials at an atomic and molecular level. This knowledge is applied to understanding chemical bonding and intermolecular forces which determine the engineering properties of materials. General principles of chemical equilibrium are developed and applied to chemical reactions involving acids and bases and organic molecules to understand the reaction materials can undergo. The course will consist of lectures, laboratories and tutorials split between the two disciplines: Materials Science and Engineering and Chemistry. This course is intended for engineering students to take early in their programs.
learning_outcomes: Solve numerical problems related to mechanical behaviour and explain the mechanical properties of different types of materials.
Interpret information and numerical data to explain and/or rationalise real-world phenomena by integrating multiple chemical principles.

Conduct laboratory experiments in a safe manner and manipulate apparatus, perform quantitative and qualitative materials and chemical analyses, evaluate the accuracy and precision of measurements, and interpret results and observations.
Describe relationship between a materials structure, properties and processing.
Connect chemical concepts to real-world applications through a firm foundation in the fundamentals of chemistry for materials science.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Materials for Engineering Applications
syllabus_overview: This course introduces Engineering students to the field of Materials Science and Engineering. Throughout society, different materials are chosen for various applications. How and why given materials are selected, is a key step in the Engineering process. In this course, students will learn about the different classifications of materials, how their atomic structure and processing leads to the desirable properties needed for industry. Laboratory work will be used to examine the testing techniques employed by materials engineers to determine the properties and which processes are best suited for a given material. Students will be challenged to select the correct material for a real-world problem through their understanding of mechanical, chemical and structural properties of materials. The delivery of course content is through a combination of lectures, tutorials, laboratories and project work. No prior science knowledge is required to undertake this course.
learning_outcomes: Describe the relationships between a materials multi-length-scale structure and its mechanical and functional properties.
Classify materials into general groups of metals, ceramics, polymers and composites.
Apply communication and problem solving skills to identify ideal materials for design applications.
Apply materials testing methods to investigate and quantify material properties.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This first-year (Level 1) introductory course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the structure and properties of materials, highlighting their major positive impact on society, particularly in structural, biomedical, and transport applications. The course commences with the factors influencing the microstructure of materials, and the impact of microstructure on the properties and performance of engineering materials (metals, ceramics, polymers and composites). The course then covers topics on the micromechanisms of elastic and plastic deformation, and fracture mechanisms for ductile and brittle materials. It also introduces students to phase equilibria and how temperature and composition affect the expected phases in a material, which are further understood with the use of phase diagrams. Students will gain an insight into why materials science and engineering matters via interviews with academic staff in the school about their current research, and visits to major industrial materials companies in New South Wales. Introductory materials laboratories will allow students to test and characterise materials and analyse data related to material properties. This is the introductory materials core course for students in the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. Successful completion of the course is a requirement for some Level 2 materials courses in these programs. The course content will be delivered through a series of standard and flipped lectures and tutorials. A knowledge of high-school level chemistry and physics (NSW HSC Year 11 or equivalent) will provide a strong foundation for the course.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key application areas of different materials classes and explain the reasons underlying the suitability of the material class for each application.
Perform experiments and analyse data relating to materials property structure relationships.
Describe basic property-structure relationships in materials.
Explain the mechanical behaviour of different types of materials and how it relates to their atomic and microstructure.
Communicate the application and context of materials science and engineering within industry and society using written and oral formats

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Physical Properties of Materials
syllabus_overview: This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the physical properties of materials and their application in the design and operation of functional devices. These devices include critical components found in electric vehicles, computers, televisions, mobile telephones, and more. The course begins with a discussion of the limitations of classical physics in describing physical properties. Elementary quantum and statistical mechanics are then introduced to provide a more accurate description, demonstrated firstly by explaining electronic conduction in materials and their categorisation as insulators, semiconductors, metals, and superconductors. Students will also learn about intrinsic (pure) and extrinsic (doped) semiconductors and the concept of selective doping to create p-n junctions, the essential building blocks of electronic devices. The course then focuses on magnetic materials, with particular emphasis on their ferromagnetic and ferrimagnetic properties, including the origin of spontaneous magnetisation, magnetic domains, magnetic anisotropy, and magnetic hysteresis. Thermal properties are also discussed, focusing on the roles of phonons and electrons on heat capacity, thermal expansion, thermal conductivity, and thermoelectricity. Lastly, students will learn about optical properties, and the interaction of materials with light through absorption, transmission, refraction, and reflection. Examples of technologically significant electronic, magnetic, thermal and optical devices are provided to demonstrate the application of the fundamental principles presented in the course. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, in-person laboratory classes, assignments, and tests. Previous knowledge of first year calculus, physics, and chemistry is required.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of elementary quantum and statistical mechanics to explain electronic conduction in materials, including their classification as insulators, semiconductors, and conductors (metals).
Explain the principles and importance of magnetic, thermal, and optical properties in the operation of technologically-significant devices and components.
Calculate the electrical conductivity of metals and semiconductors and utilise the concept of selective doping to explain the functioning of p-n junctions in electronic devices.
Demonstrate basic practical skills by examining and quantifying selected material properties relevant to commercially significant functional devices.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH1131 or DPST1013 or MATH1141 and MATH1231 or DPST1014 or MATH1241 and PHYS1121 or PHYS1131 or DPST1023 and CHEM1011 or CHEM1031 or DPST1031 or CHEM1811

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials Characterisation
syllabus_overview: This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the principles and applications of the main analysis techniques for characterising the structure and composition of crystalline and amorphous materials. The course covers topics on specimen preparation, crystallography, diffraction theory, and associated diffraction and scattering techniques, optical microscopy, electron microscopy, spectroscopy, image analysis, and methods for quantifying microstructural features. Laboratory classes complement the lectures to equip students with basic practical skills in specimen preparation and operation of selected characterisation instruments and related software, as well as cultivating safe working practices in the laboratory. The course will provide the intellectual framework for other core and elective courses that require knowledge of the structure-property relationships in materials. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. It is also suitable for science and engineering students who need a fundamental understanding and practical skills in the characterisation of materials. The course includes weekly lectures, self-learning online activities, and in-person laboratory classes. Previous knowledge of introductory materials science and engineering is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of operation of major equipment and instruments used for characterisation of materials.
Select the appropriate materials characterisation technique(s) to determine the composition and structure of a given material.
Quantify the composition and structure of materials at the following scales: crystal structure; nanostructure; and microstructure.
Demonstrate basic practical skills in examining and quantifying material structures.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mechanical Behaviour of Materials
syllabus_overview: This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering extends on the fundamentals of mechanical behaviour of engineering materials introduced in MATS1192 Introduction to Materials Science and Engineering. The course provides a systematic and quantitative treatment of how materials respond to stresses and strains. Key topics include stress, strain, axial and multiaxial loading, and the analysis of stresses in components under axial, torsional, bending, and transverse shear stresses. The course extends this knowledge to complex stress states in combined loading scenarios, employing numerical and graphical methods, such as Mohr’s circle leading to failure criteria (e.g. Tresca, von Mises). The course then covers the mechanical properties and behaviour of engineering materials, examining metals, polymers, ceramics, and composites, and exploring their elastic and plastic deformation mechanisms at atomic, molecular, and microscopic levels. Material failure and its prediction are covered, including crack propagation, ductile and brittle modes of failure, yield criteria, creep and fatigue. The influence of factors such as strain rate and temperature on mechanical behaviour is analysed. The course provides a solid foundation for more advanced level courses covering the structure-property-processing-performance relationships of specific classes of materials. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. Teaching methods include lectures, tutorials, and laboratory classes to provide hands-on experience with mechanical testing. Previous knowledge of first-year calculus is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Calculate and analyse the distribution of stresses in engineering component(s) subjected to different types of loading conditions.
Analyse data to determine the mechanical properties and failure modes of common engineering materials.
Explain the mechanical behaviour of materials and interpret the key differences between behaviour of various classes of materials based on their different chemical and structural characteristics.
Apply knowledge of mechanical behaviour and failure of materials to the design of engineering components, including recommending and justifying selection of materials.
Apply the principles of solid mechanics and identify states of stress and strain in engineering component(s) subjected to various loading scenarios.
Evaluate the mechanical response of materials under different loading conditions in terms of elastic and plastic deformation and failure.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS1101 or MATS1192 or DPST1061 or MATS1110

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Diffusion and Kinetics
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to reaction kinetics, including elementary and non-elementary reactions, reaction order, activation energy, Arrhenius law, irreversible and reversible reactions, degree of reaction; heterogeneous reactions, kinetics of solid state-gas (fluid) reactions, elementary steps, rate-controlling steps, intrinsic kinetics. Through a series of lectures and a laboratory class, the course also explores: diffusion and mass transfer in the gas and fluid phases, solid state diffusion, atomistics of diffusion, Fick's first and second laws; thin film solution and tracer diffusion measurements, semi-infinite and infinite diffusion couples - diffusion in a concentration gradient; temperature effects; surface, grain boundary and dislocation pipe diffusion; diffusion in ionic solids, interdiffusion and the Kirkendall effect, measurement of variable diffusion coefficients and compares thermodynamics vs. kinetics in an applied environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate, describe and/or relate the role of microstructural features such as grain boundaries, dislocations and point defects in diffusion and kinetics.
Interpret and quantify time dependent chemical kinetics and mass transfer processes which occur in materials, materials processing and synthesis operations.
Communicate scientific information relating to chemical kinetics using precise terminology relating to basic principles of diffusion and kinetics.
Derive fundamental kinetics and diffusion laws and use these to model material processes and behaviours.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Fluid Flow and Heat Transfer
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the fundamentals of fluid flow and heat transfer, and their applications in materials engineering. The fluid flow section starts with the concepts of fluids and static fluids, followed by the description of various fluid flows and their governing equations. Finally, the principle and applications of Bernoulli’s equation are discussed. The heat transfer section introduces the mechanisms, governing equations and applications of conductive heat transfer, convective heat transfer and thermal radiation. The course includes face-to-face lectures, in-class quizzes and weekly tutorials.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively to explain fluid flow and heat transfer phenomena and present solutions in written format.
Analyse fluid flow and heat transfer phenomena in materials engineering in order to generate solutions.
Explain the phenomena relating to fluid flows and heat transfer and the underlying mechanisms.
Apply governing equations to solve fluid flow and heat transfer related questions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Thermodynamics and Phase Equilibria
syllabus_overview: This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the fundamental principles of thermodynamics and their application in understanding the physical and chemical behaviour of pure substances, solutions, and multiphase systems relevant to the discipline. The course begins with an overview of essential thermodynamic concepts and the three laws of thermodynamics. Building on this foundation, students learn about thermodynamic relations, gas-solid equilibria, ideal and non-ideal solutions, colligative properties, phase stability and the molecular basis of thermodynamics. Selected topics on materials thermodynamics illustrate these principles, including the oxidation and reduction of metals and oxides, thermodynamics of polymer solutions, solubility of gases in liquids and solids, lattice defects, and interfacial phenomena. The second part of the course focuses on phase equilibria, covering the types of unary and binary phase diagrams, Gibbs phase rule, lever rule, and experimental and computational tools for constructing phase diagrams. The practical application of binary phase diagrams will be utilised for designing microstructures in technologically significant material systems. The course provides students with a solid foundation in basic thermodynamic principles and phase stability, preparing them for advanced courses requiring these essential concepts. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. Lectures, tutorials and laboratory activities are the primary modes of delivery. Previous knowledge of first-year chemistry, physics and calculus is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the three laws of thermodynamics, through both qualitative explanations and mathematical expressions, in the context of the behaviour and processing of materials.
Explain the relation between thermodynamics and phase equilibria for constructing binary phase diagrams from basic thermodynamic parameters.
Interpret binary phase diagrams in terms of specifying materials processing parameters and as a predictive tool for materials performance.
Construct technologically significant binary phase diagrams using thermodynamic software and predict the phases expected during heat treatment.
Apply thermodynamics concepts to predict the behaviour of materials, and solve thermodynamic problems associated with the processing and properties of materials.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: CHEM1011 or CHEM1031 or CHEM1811 or MATS1101 or DPST1031

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Materials Processing
syllabus_overview: This course on Sustainable Design and Environmental Impact offers a comprehensive exploration of key materials sustainability challenges, principles and practical approaches. Students will learn problem-solving methodologies and analyze the environmental footprint of processes like production, maintenance, and disposal. They will study embodied carbon and energy, pollution, life cycle analysis, energy recovery, carbon sequestration, pollution minimization, and sustainable material selection and processing technologies. Through in-person lectures and tutorials, students will gain a deep understanding of sustainable practices. The course may incorporate innovative approaches like flipped classroom sessions and field trips. This course equips students with expertise in evaluating environmental impacts and implementing sustainable solutions. It is relevant to engineering, environmental sciences, and related fields. By completing this course, students contribute to a more resilient future.
learning_outcomes: Analyse selected underlying environmental challenges and propose and justify solutions that reduce or eliminate energy consumption, wastes and greenhouse gases in materials processing, design and application.
Solve problems relating to material supply chains, sustainable material selection, and lifecycle assessment using rigorous standardised approaches and critical analysis.
Critique and compare the distinguishing features of different types of energy sources, their conversion methods and appropriate related measures in energy recovery and efficient utilisation.
Assess the energy consumption of a given operation and greenhouse gas emission using lifecycle assessment, adopting an appropriate analysis scope.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Transport Processes in Materials Engineering
syllabus_overview: This Level 2 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the processes by which heat, mass and momentum move through and between materials and systems of relevance to the materials engineering discipline. The course commences with an overview of fluid properties, including a detailed comparison between Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids, followed by a description of fluid mechanics, mechanical energy balance of flow and Bernoulli’s equation. It then covers the mechanisms of heat transfer by thermal conduction, convection, and radiation, through to the mechanisms of diffusion of atoms, ions and molecules in materials, the application of Fick’s laws of diffusion, and specific examples of diffusion in solids, including the role of crystalline defects as enhanced diffusion pathways. Students will apply these fundamental principles of transport phenomena to areas of technological importance in materials science and engineering, including fluid flow during casting, polymer processing, the design of heat-resistant barriers and heat treatment processes, oxidation of metals, and doping of semiconductors. The course provides a solid foundation for those higher-level courses requiring knowledge of transport processes. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. The course includes lectures, weekly tutorials, assignments and in-class quizzes. Previous knowledge of first-year calculus and chemistry is required.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and solve complex problems related to transport phenomena in materials engineering.
Apply governing equations to solve simple transport phenomena problems.
Explain the underlying mechanisms of phenomena relating to fluid flow, heat transfer and diffusion.
Communicate and explain effectively about fundamental transport phenomena and present solutions in written format to professionals in materials science and engineering.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATH1231 or MATH1241

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Ceramic Processing
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the interplay between processing, (micro)structure, and properties of technical and functional ceramic materials, with a focus on their responsible manufacture and use across a wide range of technological and societal applications, including building and civil construction, energy storage and conversion, computing and electronics, nuclear, and health and biomedicine. The successful use of ceramics in these applications is critically dependent on the composition-(micro)structure-property correlations of the materials which, in turn, are determined by the processes used to manufacture them. The course begins with an overview of the fundamental behaviour of ceramics, focusing on how composition and microstructure influence their mechanical, physical and chemical properties. The course then examines the main routes for fabricating ceramics through coverage of conventional key steps including raw materials, powder preparation, powder compaction and dry forming, wet forming, plastic forming, and sintering (conventional and advanced), conventional fabrication routes (slip casting, sintering, sol-gel etc). Advanced routes (hot isostatic pressing, CVD, sputtering, additive manufacturing etc.) for ceramics in both bulk and thin film forms for different applications are also examined. Students learn about the critical role of processing methods in determining ceramic microstructures, properties, and performance, and how these materials are designed and engineered for specific products and devices across diverse industries. The principles of ternary phase equilibria are introduced to support understanding of the relationships between composition, processing, and phase evolution in industrially-significant ceramic systems. A focus throughout the course is analysis of processing problems and prescribing evidence-based solutions. The course is completed as weekly lectures, self-learning online activities, assignments, and in-person laboratory classes targeted towards solving ceramic processing related problems and challenges. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. It also provides foundational, ceramics-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design. Previous knowledge of crystallography, thermodynamics, and binary phase equilibria is required.
learning_outcomes: Analyse typical problems encountered in ceramic processing and propose appropriate improvements/remedies to avoid them.
Explain the fundamental chemical and/or physical phenomena that underpin each of the main stages of ceramic processing.
Describe the main processes and related technology involved in the manufacturing of specific classes of ceramic products.
Perform calculations related to aspects of drying and firing processes used in ceramic manufacturing, and calculations related to predicting thermal/mechanical performance for applications.

Explain and predict the effect of heat treatment conditions on the high temperature reactions of specific ceramic materials, their resultant phase composition and microstructure, and their effects on performance.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2008

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Micromechanisms of Mechanical Behaviour of Metals
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts that govern the micromechanical behaviour of metals and alloys, and the principles involved in designing alloy microstructures with enhanced properties and performance. The course commences with an overview of the various types of crystalline defects in metals, with a particular focus on the structure and properties of dislocations and their response to external stimuli such as stress and temperature. This is followed by a discussion of dislocation theories of strengthening through their mutual interactions (work hardening), and their interactions with key microstructural features such as solute atoms, precipitates, dispersoids, and grain boundaries. The course then covers the effects of deformation temperature and strain rate on dislocation dynamics, microstructural evolution, and mechanical behaviour. The foregoing concepts are used to illustrate the principles involved in designing alloy microstructures for low- or high-temperature strength, creep resistance, and superplastic formability, as well as for optimising industrial metal working processes such as rolling, forging, and extrusion, with a focus on ethical and environmentally responsible production practices. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on applying these principles to explain the development and processing of key commercial ferrous and non-ferrous alloys used in structural and functional applications. The course includes lectures, tutorials, assignments, and tests, as well as interactive online tutorials where students have the opportunity to practice applying their theoretical knowledge, solve problems, deepen their comprehension of the subject matter, and receive feedback on their learning. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. It also provides foundational, metals-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design. Previous knowledge of crystallography and mechanical behaviour of materials is required.
learning_outcomes: Apply theories of dislocation behaviour to explain plasticity in metals and alloys.
Communicate information regarding the mechanical behaviour of metals in written format using precise scientific terminology.
Correlate the effect of microstructural development through alloying and heat treatment to mechanical properties.
Explain how knowledge of strengthening mechanisms can be applied to predict and optimise mechanical properties of alloy systems.
Solve problems in alloy design by consideration of the interplay between crystalline defects, material microstructures and processing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering in Process Metallurgy
syllabus_overview: This is an elective course for 3rd or 4th year undergraduate students of Materials Science & Engineering focusing on the fundamentals of process and physical metallurgy principles, some of which have been introduced in 1st year (e.g., in MATS1192 ‘Design and Application of Materials in Science and Engineering’). The first part of this course focuses on traditional and modern processes required to refine iron from ores into iron and steel. Students will also learn how to describe and evaluate recent major developments in the steel industry, and how to apply this knowledge to identify areas for improvement in terms of the sustainability of these processes. The second part focuses on the physical metallurgy of simple steels before exploring the process metallurgy of specialty alloys and non-ferrous alloys. Prior knowledge of the basic principles governing processing-microstructure-property relationships of alloys will be expanded to consider various factors affecting the final properties of semi-finished metal products such as thermo-mechanical treatments, segregation, complex heat treatments, additive processing routes, workflows during non-ferrous processing, energy consumption, and other environmental aspects. This is a face-to-face course with live lectures and tutorials.
learning_outcomes: Describe relationships between the processing route, microstructure and final properties of steels and other common engineering alloys, and devise strategies to advance these relationships to achieve superior properties.
Explain and critically analyse traditional processes used to refine iron and steels from its ores.
Evaluate recent major developments in the steel and non-ferrous metallurgy industry and apply this knowledge to identify areas for improvements in terms of the sustainability of these processes.
Communicate scientific concepts to a specialist audience in both written and oral formats.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Polymer Science and Engineering 1
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with a fundamental and practical understanding of polymer science and engineering, the importance of polymers in engineering and society, and the ethical and environmental considerations associated with their manufacture and use. The course begins with a review of polymer classification, followed by a revision of basic organic chemistry and an introduction to polymer chemistry, focusing on raw materials and polymer synthesis. Key polymerisation techniques, including free radical, ionic, and condensation methods, are presented with attention to their underlying mechanisms and kinetics. Students explore how monomer selection and polymer architecture (for example, linear, branched, or crosslinked) influence molecular structure and enable the tailoring of mechanical, physical, and chemical properties. Core aspects of polymer physics are also addressed, such as chain dimensions, thermodynamics, and solution behaviour, together with the influence of bulk morphology and multicomponent systems on functional performance. The course further integrates polymer synthesis with key manufacturing methods for producing commodity and specialty plastics, and examines issues of recyclability, degradation, and environmental impact. The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, laboratory activities and tests. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and the Materials Science Major of the BSc and BAdvSci(Hons) programs. It also provides foundational, polymer-specific knowledge essential for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design. Previous knowledge of organic chemistry, thermodynamics and chemical reaction kinetics is required.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively as a team member to analyse scientific data and implement scientific writing.
Analyse technological developments in commodity and advanced polymers using the life cycle assessment.
Identify suitable characterisation techniques based on polymer solubility and chemical structure.
Explain the synthesis of polymers using fundamental polymer chemistry.
Predict and interpret the behaviour and properties of polymers as a function of their morphology and composition.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Phase Transformations
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to the transformations that occur in metals, ceramics, and polymers, emphasising how these transformations can be exploited to control microstructure, thereby enhancing processability, properties, and overall performance. The course begins by addressing the limitations of phase equilibria and introducing key concepts of time, driving force, and interfaces to explain transformation mechanisms and kinetics. It builds on fundamental principles of thermodynamics, diffusion, and kinetics to describe phase nucleation and growth, overall transformation kinetics, microstructural development, non-equilibrium phase formation, and the origin of isothermal and continuous cooling transformation diagrams. The course then covers liquid-to-solid transformations, examining solidification mechanisms, cast structure development, microsegregation (and homogenisation), interface stability, single crystal growth, glass formation and devitrification. It then extends to diffusional and non-diffusional solid-state transformation mechanisms, with applications to the formation of precipitates, pearlite, bainite, martensite and recrystallized microstructures. Students will learn, through case studies, how transformations underpin modern materials manufacturing, from static and continuous casting of metals to polymer processing, glass manufacturing, semiconductor fabrication, materials joining, additive manufacturing, and thermal or mechanical processing, and how these processes influence the resulting material structures and properties. The case studies also demonstrate the ethical and sustainable approaches used in these industries. The course includes lectures, problem-solving sessions, assignments, and tests. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program. The foundational principles in the course underpin many of the key concepts covered in the accompanying Level 3 material-specific courses. Previous knowledge of crystallography, thermodynamics, phase equilibria, and transport phenomena is required.
learning_outcomes: Review published literature on a selected topic on solid-state transformations and critically analyse the information via a written report.
Solve quantitative problems relating to phase transformations by employing advanced critical thinking and analytical skills.
Explain the key thermodynamic and kinetic criteria required for a phase transformation to occur, and their influence on overall transformation kinetics and final microstructure.
Design simple thermal and mechanical processing routes to optimise the microstructure and properties in a diverse range of materials.
Discuss how phase transformations play an important role in the industrial processing of engineering materials.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS2003 and MATS2006 and MATS2008

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design and Application of Materials in Science and Engineering 3
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering introduces students to essential computational tools for design and modelling in technological and professional materials engineering applications, emphasising the responsible and ethical use of data and simulations. Selected computer simulation packages will be used to explore complex, real-world materials engineering phenomena. Starting with an overview of computational materials modelling methods across length scales from the atomic to the macroscopic, this course will cover several important modelling techniques. Computer-aided design (CAD) will be introduced for precise geometry creation and virtual prototyping of material structures. Finite element analysis (FEA) will be applied to study temperature distributions, stress-strain behaviour, and mechanical integrity in materials with complex geometries, with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) used to analyse transport phenomena involving fluid flow and heat and mass transfer in materials processing and performance applications. Finally, machine learning (ML) techniques, leveraging big data, will be introduced as a powerful technique for materials selection and discovery, property prediction, and the optimisation of processing conditions and performance characteristics. Together, these approaches form a foundational toolkit for more advanced studies in computational materials science and engineering. The course includes lectures and high-level hands-on lab practical activities. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program. Previous knowledge of computing, mechanical behaviour of materials and transport phenomena is required.
learning_outcomes: Apply fundamental concepts of modelling in materials engineering to manually solve simple mechanical structure and transport phenomena related problems based on the governing equations and basic numerical methods.
Solve complex problems in materials engineering involving mechanical structures and transport phenomena using commercial CAD/CFD/FEA software packages.
Critically evaluate the validity and accuracy of numerical solutions for mechanical structure and transport phenomena problems in materials engineering.
Outline and critique the key applications of machine learning in materials engineering, including the responsible and ethical use of data.
Interpret numerical results to draw meaningful engineering conclusions about mechanical structures and transport phenomena in materials.
Communicate materials engineering problems and their numerical solutions clearly and effectively in written form.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design and Engineering of Composites and Coatings
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering builds on students’ prior knowledge of metals, ceramics, and polymers to demonstrate how composites and coatings with varying compositions and characteristics can be created from these individual constituents. The course emphasises the relationship between structure (microstructure & nanostructure) and processing for generating novel, advantageous properties in these materials for advanced structural and functional applications. The course begins with an introduction to the types of composites (polymer-, ceramic-, and metal-matrix, nanocomposite, hybrid) and coatings (metal, ceramic, polymer, composite), as well as the different possible forms of the individual components in these composites (fibres, whiskers, and particulates). The course then covers the mechanical and physical properties of composites and coatings, the methods for testing these properties, and how they relate to the individual component materials and their forms, demonstrating how unique properties can emerge when individual materials are combined. The final part of the course covers fabrication routes for different types of composites and coatings, the impact of processing conditions on structure and properties, and strategies for recycling these materials for value-added applications. Case studies are integrated throughout the course to illustrate the design of optimal composites and coatings for advanced structural and functional applications, while balancing performance with environmental responsibility and ethical industry practices. The course will be delivered through lectures, assignments, laboratory activities, and tests. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program. It also provides essential knowledge across the material classes for final-year courses that incorporate materials selection and design. Previous knowledge of the structure-processing-property relationships for metals, ceramics, and polymers is required.
learning_outcomes: Explain and justify the design of composites and coatings for different applications based on consideration of processing, properties, intended application, and environmental considerations.
Assess the suitability of techniques to fabricate and characterise composites and coatings in a safe and ethical manner.
Analyse and interpret data to understand the effects of component type and form on properties and applications of composites and coatings.
Collaborate professionally and effectively in a scientific/engineering team, contributing equitably to achieve shared goals.
Communicate technical information, including experimental findings and materials selection justifications, effectively in an appropriate scientific manner.
Apply mathematical skills and techniques to solve composite and coating selection and design problems.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials Industry Management
syllabus_overview: This Level 3 core course in Materials Science and Engineering provides students with an integrated overview of key management concepts relevant to the materials engineering profession, including project management, risk management, marketing, and career development. Professional ethics is embedded throughout, with an emphasis on workplace expectations and ethical conduct. The course begins with project management, where students learn about the project lifecycle, including planning, scheduling, reporting, stakeholder engagement and team dynamics. Students also develop a project plan relevant to the materials industry to demonstrate their ability to build a sound business case while meeting ethical and professional responsibilities in execution. This is followed by the principles of risk management, where students develop a risk management plan to accompany their project management plan. Marketing is also addressed, including market analysis and product development, ensuring truthful representation and promoting sustainable business practices. Career development is an important part of a professional engineer’s journey, so the final part of the course focuses on job application strategies and résumé writing, all within the framework of ethical workplace behaviour. The course includes lectures, including those delivered by academic guests, professionals and industry representatives, and tutorial sessions covering the key concepts of course components and related assessments. This course is a core component of the BE(Hons) (Materials Science and Engineering) program and a prescribed elective in the Materials Science Major of the BAdvSci(Hons) program. It is also available as an Employability Experiences elective in the BSc program.
learning_outcomes: Apply in-depth project management skills to the development of a suitable business case for a concept implementation and planning an appropriate and detailed project management plan for its implementation.
Apply economic, accounting, marketing, and strategic business analysis principles where appropriate to real engineering situations arising within a commercial context.
Write a risk management document that would appropriately complement a project management plan, and implementing principles of process resilience engineering.
Describe key career development and professional issues for engineering graduates, and critically assess proposed solutions through the creation of a project management plan.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials Science Work Placement 1
syllabus_overview: This course enables science students studying majors in the School of Materials Science and Engineering to apply their disciplinary knowledge and transferable skills in a professional context, through a work placement experience at an organisation external to UNSW. Students will have the opportunity to develop key professional skills that align with their career goals and contextualise their field of study in a professional workplace setting. The main component of the course is a minimum 105-hour work placement related to the students field of study. The placement can be paid or unpaid. This supervised workplace experience is supported by professional development and discipline-specific modules that students can select from, in line with their individual career goals. MATS3199 will count as a science or free elective and is graded on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Work placements are not guaranteed. Students are required to either apply for a faculty-advertised placement or submit an application for a self-sourced placement to be undertaken as part of the course, subject to approval. institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Secondary Processing of Metals
syllabus_overview: This course will provide advanced knowledge in solidification, welding (emphasis on effect of welding on microstructure, HAZ etc.), fundamentals of metal working (including hot working, Zener-Hollomon parameter, dynamic recovery and recrystallization and cold working, formability, residual stresses, powder metallurgy and sintering, machining, recrystallisation phenomena. Emphasis on the effect of processing conditions on microstructure and hence properties. Common classes of magnesium alloys, copper alloys and cast irons to be taught illustrating some of the principles involved. The course will be delivered through lectures and is for students in the final years of their materials science /and engineering degrees.
learning_outcomes: Make informed decisions in recommending selection of processing methods by applying metal deformation and forming theories based on knowledge of secondary metal processing.
Conduct online research for literature review and case studies in the field of secondary metal processing.

Critically analyse the problems relating to metal deformation, deformed metal recovery and recrystallisation, solidification, welding, etc. using knowledge of metal deformation and restoration, solidification in secondary metal processing.
Communicate in the written format using correct terminology.
Collaborate with peers to solve problems relating to materials and processing method selection.
Relate the microstructure of processed materials to processing conditions and behaviour in service.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design and Advanced Ceramics
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for 3rd, 4th or final year students undertaking studies in the discipline of materials science to enhance knowledge and understanding of advanced ceramics (oxides and non-oxides) for structural, thermal, electrical, piezoelectric, magnetic, optoelectronic, chemical, nuclear, biological, and wear applications. The contents will focus on fabrication of advanced materials in bulk and thin film format for use in these applications. The design of these materials will be focused in terms of the fundamental structure-microstructure-property relationships and how these can be tailored through alteration of the processing conditions to fabricate optimal advanced ceramics while reducing chances of failure. This will be achieved through use of case studies and examples related to the design of these advanced ceramics for superior mechanical properties (strength, modulus, and toughness), electrical (dielectric, ferroelectric, piezoelectric), magnetic (ferromagnetic, ferrimagnetic), electromechanical, optoelectronic, tribological (wear resistance), thermal (expansion, conductivity, heat capacity), thermomechanical (thermal shock, refractoriness), chemical (corrosive), nuclear (radiation resistance), and biological (bioaffinity).
learning_outcomes: Design ceramic materials with optimal properties for different applications by alteration of ceramic microstructures and resultant properties through specific processing methods

Describe and evaluate the range of typical properties of advanced ceramics with the aim of utilising them in high-demand applications requiring specific mechanical, thermal, thermomechanical, chemical, and nuclear applications.

Describe and evaluate the range of typical properties of advanced ceramics with the aim of utilising them in high-demand applications requiring specific electrical, electronic, magnetic, and optoelectric properties.
Evaluate peer-reviewed literature to present a cohesive summary of advanced ceramic design and fabrication in a professional, written format.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS3002

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Process Metallurgy Advanced
syllabus_overview: Reaction rate and expressions for different reaction systems; kinetics and thermodynamics of metallurgical reactions; heat balance and mass balance of chemical reactors; batch and semibatch reactors; plug flow reactors (gas reactants in most metallurgical processes); mixed tank reactors (smelting, steel refining); catalytic reactions Heterogeneous reactions; fixed bed reactors (stack leaching processes); fluidised bed reactors (fluid bed roasting, alternative ironmaking technologies); moving bed reactors (blast furnace, Corex process). Types of metallurgical reactors, batch and continuous, plug flow and well-mixed reactors. Tracer additions. Chemical performance of a metallurgical reactor. Principles of metallurgical reactor design. Major technologies in ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy and their development.
learning_outcomes: Diagnose a metallurgical reactor
Design a metallurgical reactor
Apply metallurgical engineering to technology development
Identify constraints in metallurgical technologies
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS3003

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fracture Mechanics and Failure Analysis
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering will further develop capabilities in fracture mechanics and fractography for students with a Materials or general Engineering background. Fracture is the most common form of engineering failure, costing the global economy enormous amounts of money as well as many lives. Through a combination of lectures, tutorials, laboratories and project work, students will develop advanced knowledge fracture mechanics. Understanding methods for calculating stress distributions in real-world components, risks for fracture initiation, fatigue and lifetime analysis, and materials degradation mechanisms provides engineers with the tools for the design of components that can operate safely for known time-periods. By applying forensic fractographic analysis, students will learn how to identify the causes of fracture in real industrial-scale failures. Previous knowledge of mechanical properties of materials is required.
learning_outcomes: Analyse fracture surfaces and assess the distinguishing features of the different types of service failure.
Recommend remedial actions for the prevention of material failure in damaged structures.
Predict mechanical loading and material preparation conditions leading to the onset of failure.
Evaluate component lifetimes under cyclic loading using fatigue failure descriptions.
Communicate effectively on materials failure, fractographic and fracture mechanic analyses in written form using the correct terminology and appropriate style.
Assess various mechanisms of materials degradation leading to increased chance of failure.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Composites and Functional Materials
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for 3rd, 4th or final year students undertaking studies in the materials science discipline or combined degrees with materials science. The course aims to enhance knowledge and understanding of two important categories of advanced materials, namely functional materials and composite materials. The classes will comprise of lectures focusing on key topics in these fields, relevant laboratory activities, and design problems related to materials design in these fields. The functional materials part will focus on the fabrication of functional materials in different nanostructural forms (0D, 1D, 2D, MOFs, and composite bulk forms), including selected carbon-based materials, and the design of these materials for advanced applications in energy, catalysis, electronics, sensing, membranes, and environmental technologies. The composite materials part will focus on different types of composites (polymer, metal, and ceramic matrix composites), their fabrication routes, importance of their properties (strength, modulus, fracture etc.), failure mechanisms in the bulk and individual components, recycling methods, and designing composite materials for different applications (structural and non-structural).
learning_outcomes: Investigate and select suitable material properties (microstructural and nanostructural) for the design of functional materials used in energy and environmental applications.
Design composite materials for structural applications by investigation and selection of constituent materials based on their macro and microstructural material properties.
Evaluate the correlations of material properties with the fabrication methods in order to determine the optimal processing conditions for different applications.
Explain the properties and characteristics of functional materials and composites for high-performance applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Polymer Science and Engineering 2
syllabus_overview: The course focuses on advanced polymers, including but not limited to polymers in dielectrics, optoelectronics, solar technology, and medicine. It expands on concepts taught in MATS3004 Polymer Science and Engineering I. Students will learn about polymerization techniques used to produce polymers and copolymers with enhanced functionalities, the rubber elasticity theory that governs the behavior of elastomeric materials and networks, and the rheological property of polymer melts critical for their industrial processing. The course also covers failure mode of polymeric products while in usage. The course includes lab activities intended as a practical companion to the concepts taught in the lectures, thereby, enabling the student with a technology-enhanced learning experience.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate processing-structure-properties relationships in different classes of polymers.
Identify bulk properties of polymers and their degradation mechanisms.
Assess relevant parameters vital in design consideration of polymers for specific applications.
Execute experimental work for the synthesis and characterization of polymers.
Analyze scientific data and demonstrate scientific writing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MATS3004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineered Surfaces to Resist Corrosion and Wear
syllabus_overview: Degradation of engineering materials occurs most commonly through corrosion and wear. This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering teaches students how to minimise and control the rate at which these occur to extend the lifespan of engineering components. The course is taught through lectures and laboratories and covers three main areas: Corrosion and Control Strategies: Corrosion occurs in several ways. Students will learn the causes of each type of corrosion, and how to prevent corrosion, or reduce the rate at which corrosion occurs in established systems. Wear: Wear occurs in many engineering applications. Students will learn about the primary mechanisms by which wear occurs, and how simple models of these wear mechanisms allow the main parameters and materials properties affecting wear rates to be identified. Surface Engineering: Students will learn about the purpose of engineered surfaces to increase the lifespan of materials by increasing resistance to both corrosion and wear, with a focus on the hardening of steel and the common coating methods used in industry to protect different materials. Previous knowledge of thermodynamics, kinetics, and mechanical properties is required.
learning_outcomes: Explain the main mechanisms by which wear occurs and the key parameters and material properties that affect wear rates.
Select and justify appropriate materials, protection strategies and surface engineering methods to be used in practical scenarios where resistance to corrosion and/or wear is required.
Identify and explain the relationships between materials, microstructures and environments in relation to corrosion behaviour.

syllabus_overview: An experimental or technical investigation or design related to some aspects of materials engineering in the specific discipline (ceramic engineering, metallurgical engineering or materials engineering). Note: This course is taken twice for a total of 12UoC

Understand and apply advanced materials concepts and knowledge to analyse and solve problems in the discipline of materials science and engineering.
Effectively and professionally communicate technical/scientific information in both written and oral forms.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Materials Selection and Design
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 course in materials science and engineering will teach students to apply the factors influencing the selection of a material for a specific application. Building on the processing-structure-property relationships of materials taught in earlier class-specific materials courses, students will apply this knowledge by examining possible candidates from all material classes in conjunction with environmental, sustainability, economic, ethical, health and safety, and other societal factors for justifying selection of appropriate materials. This approach will highlight the inherent compromises in the materials selection process, balancing design requirements with available material property profiles. The course will cover a range of topics, including methodologies for materials selection, the important concept of ecological footprint in materials selection, and how a material’s life cycle contributes to this footprint. The course will introduce methods for measuring and minimising the ecological footprint, making use of advanced approaches and analysis methods to select appropriate materials and processing routes based on economic and other factors. With this knowledge and skills, students will be able to select the most suitable material(s) for a given application, taking a holistic view of the numerous factors that impact the materials selection process. The course includes lectures, tutorials, computer laboratories, site tours, group project work, presentations, assignments, and exams. Students will use commercial software packages to gain experience using life-cycle assessment and materials selection programs. Knowledge of the processing-structure-property relationships of metals, ceramics, polymers, and their composites is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Compile and compare data from existing materials-related facilities in relation to their ecological footprint and make recommendations to minimise environmental and social impacts.

Explain and justify to professionals in materials science and engineering the subjectivity and uncertainty in decision-making in the context of materials selection and the relative weighting of social, environmental and economic factors.
Determine the most appropriate material and processing method for specific applications based on rigorous materials selection methods.
Analyse and evaluate the environmental, social and economic impacts and perform life-cycle assessments of proposed and existing materials and processes.
Apply advanced approaches, analysis methods and commercial software to select appropriate materials and processing routes that minimise ecological footprint.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Structural Materials in Transportation and Infrastructure
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering introduces students to advanced manufacturing processes of structural materials used in current and future transport and infrastructure applications. The course will cover structural engineering alloys such as advanced steels, specialty alloys, and select non-ferrous alloys, state-of-the-art construction materials, and various composite materials. Specifically, students will learn about the fundamentals of processing of advanced structural materials via advanced manufacturing routes, which may include subtractive manufacturing such as sintering, strip casting, and thermomechanical processing, and additive manufacturing such as 3D printing. The course content and activities will provide the students with the skills to design innovative manufacturing processes and state-of-the-art structural materials in terms of property requirements, sustainability, cost, and ethical principles. The course content will be delivered through a series of flipped lectures based on online materials and standard lectures delivered by guest speakers from industry and academia. It also includes laboratory work focused on manufacturing of selected structural materials to achieve superior properties and a major group project on the current practices in manufacturing processes of structural materials for selected applications in either transport or infrastructure. Previous knowledge of the processing-structure-property relationships of metals, ceramics, polymers, and their composites is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Explain the specialised and technical advanced manufacturing processes of materials used in transport and structural applications.

Devise innovative and sustainable engineering solutions to complex problems in the manufacturing of advanced structural materials based on rigorous analysis of current industrial practices, research, and trends.
Design and evaluate manufacturing operations for advanced structural materials to improve structure-property relationships.

Assess and compare current practices in advanced manufacturing processes of structural materials in terms of their sustainability and ethical principles and communicate results professionally and effectively within and outside of the discipline.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Management and Communication for Materials Engineers
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 course for materials science and engineering students focuses on developing and advancing skills in data analysis, as well as writing and presenting for the materials engineering profession. Students will learn how to analyse and compress data in suitable forms for visual presentation, and give effective oral presentations. Within the data analysis component, students will learn how to handle and represent data associated with various materials engineering problems, including data pre-processing, exploratory data analysis, understanding the importance of errors and statistics, data representation and ethical considerations in data handling and reporting. In the professional communication part of the course, students will learn about the principles of scientific writing and professional communication, how to identify and adapt to different audiences, and how to write clear and concise technical documents. They will also learn how to structure an effective oral presentation, create visual aids, and maintain professionalism in communication. The course includes lectures, computer-based lab work, presentations, and written reports. Previous knowledge of numerical methods and statistics is required.
learning_outcomes: Communicate data and technical information, including their relevance and application in the context of materials science and engineering within industry and society, using both written and oral forms.
Discern the effectiveness of different types of graphs and figures for communicating and presenting data and information.
Reflect on and identify personal strengths and areas requiring further development in their written and oral communication skills.
Apply and compare a variety of data analysis and representation techniques.
Critique published data and technical text to justify what constitutes an acceptable, effective and high-quality forms of presentation.
Select, apply and justify choice of appropriate communication methods and presentation styles for different settings.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials for Renewable Energy Technologies
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering introduces students to the materials used in devices for production and storage of sustainable and renewable energy. The course is designed to equip students with the knowledge and skills to make informed decisions about selecting and using a particular material and processing route for a given energy component or device. The course focuses on the technologies and materials used in solar, wind, nuclear and hydrogen power use and storage. Students will learn the materials requirements in relation to application demands for technologies used to generate energy from sustainable sources, including batteries, supercapacitors and clean chemical fuels. Through group activities and critical thinking exercises, students will understand how to evaluate and select optimal materials and processes for specific energy applications, based on consideration of their complex property profile requirements. Real-world examples and case studies will be used to illustrate the concepts covered in the course. Additionally, guest speakers from relevant industries and research fields will be invited to provide contextual insights and perspectives. The course includes lectures, group project work and presentations, reports, quizzes and a final exam. Previous knowledge of chemistry, physics and physical properties of materials is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Explain the fundamental principles of devices for renewable energy conversion and storage, and hence the property requirements for materials to be used in these devices.
Explain the composition-structure-property relationships of materials in reference to their applications and processing in energy technologies.
Communicate effectively about materials selection and evaluation for energy production and storage, both verbally and in writing.
Combine fundamental knowledge with information from real-world case studies to contextualize materials selection and use in industry and research related to energy technologies.
Select appropriate materials and processes for renewable energy production and storage applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials and Processing of Electronic Circuits and Devices
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering introduces students to materials selection and optimisation strategies for existing and future electronic devices. The course commences with an outline of the various classes of materials, and their structure-property relationships, used in various functional devices, including semiconductors and superconductors, and magnetic, spintronic, ferroelectric, piezoelectric and two-dimensional materials. Applications of these materials in devices such as diodes, transistors, sensors, microelectromechanical systems (MEMS) and non-volatile memory is discussed. The course then covers the principal fabrication methods for electronic devices, including single crystal growth and purification, implantation, lithography and etching, and thin film growth. In addition, practical aspects of device fabrication and performance, including defect engineering, methods of device packaging, sources of failure, and methods of fault diagnosis in devices will be covered. The selection of particular materials and fabrication processes for electronic applications will be contextualised through case studies relating to applications of devices in, for example, the internet of things (IoT), computing systems, communication systems, health care and environmental monitoring. The course includes lectures, laboratory activities, a group project, and exams. Previous knowledge of chemistry, physics, and physical properties of materials developed in previous studies will be built upon in this course.
learning_outcomes: Collect and analyse data related to functional properties of materials.

Work effectively in a group and communicate effectively with group members to enhance each other’s understanding of the multidisciplinary knowledge and application of electronic materials and devices.
Justify the selection of the various types of materials for use in electronic devices, based on their typical properties.
Describe the structure-property relationships and processing of materials used in electronic devices.
Explain how the functional properties of electronic materials can be manipulated through processing in order to obtain optimal performance for different applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Materials and Processes for Biomedical Applications
syllabus_overview: This Level 4 elective course in materials science and engineering introduces students to various classes of biomaterials, including polymeric, metallic, ceramic, and composite materials for use in advanced medical technologies. The first part of the course covers the physical, chemical, and biological properties of these materials, especially in the context of material biocompatibility. These concepts are taught through topical case studies highlighting the importance of material selection for optimal performance at the tissue interface. In the second part of the course, students are introduced to material design and selection criteria in terms of biofabrication techniques that are revolutionizing the field of medical devices and therapeutics. The course also includes hands-on lab activities designed as a practical companion to the lectures, enabling the student to experience technology-enhanced learning. The course includes face-to-face lectures, laboratory classes, project work and an exam. Knowledge of the processing-structure-property relationships of metals, ceramics, polymers, and their composites is recommended.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key areas of application for different biomaterials and explain the reasons underlying the suitability of the biomaterial class for different biotechnology and medical device applications.
Critically analyse research relating to biomaterials and biofabrication methods.
Explain the different biofabrication methods appropriate for different classes of biomaterials.
Communicate the application and context of biomaterials and biofabrication within industry and society using written and oral formats.
Describe biomaterials classifications and key properties essential for medical use.
Analyse scientific data and demonstrate scientific writing.
