institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Technology Management and Innovation in Mining
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Through this course, you will gain an overview of various mining operations and the core technologies involved, explore historical and recent trends in mining technology development, and understand the dynamic management requirements associated with evolving technologies -particularly in diverse resource and economic contexts. You will also have the opportunity to identify innovative and potentially transformative technologies and mining systems. You will work both individually and in small groups to explore how your chosen innovations and/or new technologies fit within a mining industry application and then evaluate your ideas through structured technology audits, risk assessments, implementation plans, capital justification and possible commercialisation opportunities for the technology – for both the Australian and/or international mining industries.
learning_outcomes: Assess the management requirements for implementing and maintaining innovative technologies in mining operations.
Develop and appraise commercialisation strategies for identified innovative solutions, considering intellectual property and entrepreneurial opportunities.
Analyse the technology needs of mining systems within the context of overall mine performance measures, including economic, safety, and social factors.
Generate innovative solutions to significant challenges in the mining industry and society by applying creative and unconventional thinking.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 96 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mining Geomechanics
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to introduce engineers and geologists to the major geomechanics components associated with mining operations, primarily underground. The course will cover the rock mass responses to excavations in both coal and metalliferous operations. It is, therefore, ideally suited to engineers or geologists who have an understanding and experience in the mining industry but are seeking to develop more specialist skills in the geomechanics field. The course content will include but not limited to the following components: Fundamentals of rock mechanics Overview of soil mechanics Rock mass classification Coupled rock behaviour Numerical methods in mine geomechanics Rock testing Managing risks in geotechnical engineering Geotechnical design principles and design acceptance The course is structured to provide an initial overview of basic principles applied to rock mechanics and geotechnical engineering, plus the major geomechanical properties and behavioural characteristics of rock material. This then leads to the application of these principles to the practical issues of site investigation, excavation design and ground reinforcement. An important component will be an emphasis on the interdependencies between geotechnical parameters and mine design/operational decisions and requirements. The link between geological and engineering disciplines is an important component in successfully managing these dependencies. The course will be presented through a series of lectures, facilitated discussion sessions and case studies, but will also include practical tutorial sessions and laboratory exercises.
learning_outcomes: Show a good understanding of key numerical methods used in mining rock mechanics.
Describe the basic mechanical properties of rock and how these are applied to analyse problems in mining geomechanics.
Demonstrate a sound working knowledge of fundamental mechanisms and geotechnical principles within the context of practical mining applications.
Recognise the role and importance of these principles in a comprehensive range of mining applications, both from a technical perspective, and from the risk and operational management perspective.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mining Industry Research Project 1
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: The MINE8440 course is a core requirement for postgraduate Masters level students to demonstrate a substantial research project or scholarship. The research course is also available for Graduate Diploma level students, and is essential for these students who are intending to articulate to the Masters level. This course is intended to develop the capability and requisite skills of an engineer to build a foundation of knowledge related to a particular problem in mining engineering. The research should link closely with industry partners or applied research that will be of benefit to industry. This research foundation provides a basis on which to design a solution that is robust and safe, cost effective and appropriate to the end-user. It is essential that this foundation reflects not only established thinking and practices but equally important, it should account for divergent and newly developing views as well as any limitations or weaknesses that underpin current understanding. The quality of the engineering solution is therefore a function of the quality and timing to complete this investigation; an investigation that forms part of a process known as research. The research scope of MINE8440 is to significantly extend any previous industry research that has been undertaken by the student and/or others including one or more of the following categories: site or laboratory testing; related numerical modelling; comprehensive cost-benefit or geostatistical analysis; extension of constitutive theory. On completion of this course, a student should be capable of preparing: a research proposal that accounts for the current understanding of issues pertinent to a defined topic; objectives of the proposal research project and the tasks, activities and resources necessary to achieve that objective a critical review of literature encompassing a critique of the current state of knowledge as well as information on other related issues; and a research thesis including new, original data and analysis and detailed interpretation and recommendations for implementation and further research to address any limitations and uncertainty that is identified With permission from the School,and consistent with Program rules, this course can be extended as MINE8445 and/or MINE8690 with significantly more comprehensive research and thesis. Note: Permission to enrol in this course requires written evidence of industry support and/or agreement of an academic supervisor in the School. Industry support is essential for research projects that are to be extended for Masters programs that require MINE8455 and/or MINE8690, and is highly recommended for Graduate Diploma programs. Industry support is to include in-kind contributions from industry staff, access to relevant site data and/or samples and/or resources to support applied research. Industry agreement to publish results of the research is required, or an agreement to publish aggregated results that do not identify specific mine sites or confidential information. Alternatively, academic supervisors offer research projects as part of applied research programs.
learning_outcomes: Develop a project management plan that outlines objectives, definition of tasks, activities and resources needed to achieve that objective, a schedule of activities and significant milestones, and a risk assessment with appropriate management and control measures.
Construct a literature review encompassing a critique of the current state of knowledge related to the topic and other related information.
Define the major issues and benefits associated with a research topic.
Formulate a technical report that is consistent with the requirements and standards of the School of Mining Engineering and relevant professional societies.
Evaluate library search relevant to the research topic and obtain reference sources from various relevant sources.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geotechnical Data Collection and Analysis
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides an in-depth exploration of geotechnical data collection and analysis techniques essential for mining engineering. Students will learn about various rock mass classification systems, sources of ground stress, and the application of statistical methods. The course covers the fundamentals of seismic monitoring technologies, data processing, and interpretation, with a focus on real-world case studies. Key topics include: Classifying rock masses using methods such as Q, RMR, GSI, CMRR, and GSR. Understanding and managing sources of stress in the ground. Applying statistical methods to describe, model, visualise, and analyse geotechnical data. Implementing seismic monitoring technologies and interpreting seismic data for geotechnical purposes. Selecting and installing underground geotechnical monitoring systems. Measuring and interpreting data from excavations. Conducting mine hazard mapping and addressing design issues. The course emphasises the critical role of data interpretation and statistical analysis in geomechanics for effective design, study, and operational management. Practical examples and case studies will illustrate both effective and ineffective data use, highlighting the necessity of understanding data before applying it in design and numerical modelling. Assessment will consist of assignments designed to demonstrate practical competence and a deep understanding of the material. In-class tutorials will reinforce learning and provide hands-on experience, preparing students to develop and communicate effective geotechnical models and management plans.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate seismic monitoring technologies, data, applications, processing, and interpretation, while identifying potential challenges and implications, using real-world case studies.
Assess and interpret geological and geotechnical data collected through various monitoring methods.
Develop and communicate effective geotechnical models and management plans that incorporate data from various sources.

Understand and explain the significance of geotechnical data in geo-engineering, including rock mass characterisation methods, data collection techniques, and ground stress, and apply these methods in practical scenarios.
Apply and analyse statistical methods to describe, model, visualise, and analyse geotechnical data.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MINE3310

title: Mining Industry Research Project 2
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering

It is essential that this foundation reflects not only established thinking and practices but also, equally important, accounts for divergent and newly developing views as well as any limitations or weaknesses that underpin current understanding. The quality of the engineering solution is, therefore, a function of the quality and timing to complete this investigation, an investigation that forms part of a process known as research. The research scope of this course is to significantly extend any previous industry research that has been undertaken by the student and/or others, including two or more of the following categories: site or laboratory testing; related numerical modelling; comprehensive cost-benefit or geostatistical analysis; extension of constitutive theory. On completion of this course, a student should be capable of preparing: a conference paper an examiner copy of the thesis and final corrected thesis submission With permission from the School and consistent with Program rules, this course can be extended in combination with MINE8690 to produce a significantly more comprehensive research and thesis. Note: Industry support is essential for this research project. Students need to have written evidence of industry support and/or the agreement of an academic supervisor in the School in order to complete the course requirements. Please contact the School if more information is required.
learning_outcomes: Design and assemble appropriate resources necessary to support the research investigation.
Present the research results in the form of a thesis dissertation and presentation.
Collate and analyse results of investigation.
Prepare a document to the standards required for a conference hosted by Australian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy (AusIMM), or similar relevant professional body.
Formulate relevant conclusions and recommendations against the project objectives.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MINE8440 or MINE8690

syllabus_overview: This course will consist of a research investigation thesis project (no course content teaching). Students will be expected to develop a project topic, investigation objectives and project plan and submit it for approval before proceeding. The project must be focused on a topic which is predominantly of a geotechnical nature within a mining context. It must include a significant component of investigation and analysis. Assessment will include both the written report and the presentation which may be required to be presented in a face to face or distance mode.

Have the ability to undertake research into an are after appropriate theoretical training.
Have the opportunity to apply theoretical analysis to a mining operation.
To be able to present the research outcomes in a presentation and written format.

title: Management Systems - Projects, Processes, Contracts, Contractors
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Different aspects of mining operations require different management approaches. This course provides applied management theory and practices in each area of project, process, contracts and contractor management. In each case, examples and case studies are linked to mining operations. The course works through a typical mining system to identify the embedded sub-projects and processes which are inherent to the mining system and demonstrates the role and benefits of applying different management techniques. Managing contracts, including on-going contractor management both at the construction and ongoing operational stage of a mine is addressed in the course.
learning_outcomes: Analyse an organisation, identify deficiencies in the design, devise a more appropriate design for the organisation and prepare a suitable strategy to implement the new design.

Articulate the various factors that should be considered when managing modern organisations and ensuring that appropriate systems are in place that are consistent with achieving the goals of the organisation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Slope Stability
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will deal with the major topics of engineering geology and groundwater controls on surface mining slope stability in the form of discontinuities, variable materials and pore pressures; effect of excavation method and scheduling in pit stability; the fundamental basis of stability analysis; advantages and disadvantages of a range of mathematical models; remedial measures that can be taken to stabilise slopes; pit slope design in the context of overall mine planning. In addition to dealing with the underlying principles, the course may involve workshops and field inspections so that the participants gain hands-on experience of practical cases.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic mechanical properties of rock and how these are applied to analyse problems in mine slope stability.
Apply fundamental mechanisms and geotechnical principles within the context of practical surface mining applications.

Recognise the role and importance of these principles in a comprehensive range of surface mining applications, both from a technical perspective, and from the risk and operational management perspective.
Illustrate the key numerical methods used in mine slope designs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Space Resources Engineering
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: In-situ resource utilisation (ISRU) — the concept of using local materials in space to support human activity - is widely recognised as one of the most transformative ideas for the future of space exploration. It underpins the emerging field of space mining, which has so far primarily focused on overcoming engineering challenges. Many scientists agree that, in the near future, we may begin extracting resources from off-Earth bodies such as asteroids, comets, the Moon, Mars, and its moons. These celestial bodies represent some of the most distant and untapped sources of materials ever considered for human use. For humanity to establish a sustained presence in deep space, including potential colonisation, it will be essential to produce key materials and products locally - making ISRU a critical enabler of space settlement. To succeed, space mining operations will need to function autonomously or be remotely operated from orbiting stations, spacecraft, or Earth. The uncertainties and technical challenges involved are significant and will require the development of new knowledge and capabilities. As a result, mining expertise will play a central role in enabling ISRU, and engineers will need to acquire new or specialised skills to meet the demands of this frontier. In this course, students will be taken through the engineering lifecycle of new technologies and encouraged to think about how their unique skills can be applied to these projects. The course aims to provide information on space resources, develop a knowledge of technical and business risks and develop a scoping study for space mining operations. The course will be in short course format (5 days) including a series of lectures from research and industry experts, tutorials, and individual and group projects.
learning_outcomes: Analyse technical and financial risks of potential space mining operations.
Develop a scoping study level of financial and technical models for space mining operations for different commodities.
Review the current status of space resource utilisation.
Apply systems engineering principles for feasibility of potential space mining operations.
Employ team skills, and advanced written and oral communication skills.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mineral Processing
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides basic knowledge in mineral processing and extractive metallurgy and is delivered to students who have no training in this area. After completion, students are expected to be equipped with basic concepts and knowledge to work effectively with metallurgists/ mineral processing engineers in the field. The course begins with an overview of mineral processing and its associated disciplines, such as mineralogy, and hydrometallurgy, which are required for the production of metals and other products from mineral ores and wastes. Topics covered include comminution, physical separation, flotation, leaching, solvent extraction and electrowinning/refining. These unit operations are also discussed in case studies which cover base metals grinding and flotation circuits, Carbon-In-Pulp for gold processing and copper heap leaching-solvent extraction and electrowinning circuits. Videos and YouTube sites relevant to the field are collated for the course, and students are advised to go through them to see how mineral processing is performed in mining operations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate sustainability aspects in mineral processing, encompassing water usage, energy efficiency and the mine-to-mill concept.
Evaluate the fundamental principles governing physical and chemical processes used in selectively separating minerals from ore.
Evaluate the implications of mineralogical characteristics for processing requirements.
Analyse basic mass balance calculations.
Analyse commonly used mineral and hydrometallurgical processing routes in base metals and precious metals processing.
Analyse the fundamental principles of crushing and grinding in mineral processing.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Mining Excavations
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course explores the mechanics, technologies, and practical applications of rock fragmentation and excavation—critical aspects of mining and tunnelling. You will develop a deep understanding of rock breakage and fragmentation theories, rock mass properties, discontinuities, and stress states that influence excavation performance. The course covers the fundamentals of blasting mechanics, including types of explosives, initiation systems, and blast design for both underground and surface mining. It also examines blast hazard management, vibration control, and the latest advancements in blasting technologies, including alternatives to conventional blasting. Drilling methods and equipment are also explored, with a focus on production drilling techniques, drill bits, accessories, and performance considerations. In addition, you will study the principles of coal and rock cutting mechanics, cutting tool performance, and rock cuttability assessment. The course delves into advanced excavation technologies, including full-face and partial mining machines, tunnel boring machines, and modern drilling systems. This course integrates theory with real-world applications, equipping you with the knowledge and skills to tackle the challenges of rock excavation using conventional and emerging mining and tunnelling technologies.
learning_outcomes: Explain the contribution and influence of in-situ stress and stress redistribution on excavation stability and potential failure mode.
Apply fundamental principles to design safe, efficient blasting and machine mining for optimal blasts, cutterhead efficiency, and economic productivity.
Identify relevant requirements for the security, storage and handling of explosives.
Select appropriate methods of rock excavations for given in-situ rock conditions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Geology and Geophysics for Mining Operations
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course bridges the critical disciplines of geology, geophysics, and mining engineering, providing an in-depth exploration of essential techniques for mining operations. Students will gain a comprehensive understanding of fundamental geological principles, such as basic geologic concepts, minerals, rocks, tectonics, geological structures, and the tectonic stress field. The course examines geophysical investigations, covering stereographic projection, drilling and sampling methods, and quantitative analysis of geophysical logs. Students will investigate mineral exploration, learning about strategies, tools, and geophysical surveys. Airborne geophysics is also a key focus, with discussions on general considerations and survey specifications. Additionally, the course covers ore deposits and coal geology, examining processes and classifications. Mine hydrogeology is addressed, focusing on water management and groundwater monitoring. Through practical examples and case studies, students will develop the skills necessary to effectively interpret and apply geological and geophysical data in mining operations.
learning_outcomes: Explain fundamental geological principles and their relevance to mining operations.
Utilise geological and geophysical methods to estimate rock properties and assess mineral deposits.
Develop reports and presentations that integrate geological and geophysical data for mining decision-making.
Evaluate geophysical investigation methods and their applications in mining.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Design and Feasibility
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides non-mining engineers with the tools to plan, design, and conduct a feasibility study at a mine site. Topics include: Feasibility study process Mine planning methodologies and scheduling techniques Mine cost structures and cost estimation (theory and practice) Underground mine design principles and production scheduling Open pit mine design principles Pit shell optimisation Financial analysis of mining projects The course uses an active-based learning approach, offering hands-on experience in planning for real mining projects.

Apply theoretical principles and practical methodologies associated with mine design to a real feasibility project.
Develop project management capability within a self-managed team environment.
Apply project evaluation and financial analysis techniques to assess the technical and financial viability of mining projects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Management for the Mining Industry
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive and practical understanding of the impacts both positive and negative that mining may have on society and the environment. On completion of this course, students should be able to identify, analyse and apply state-of-the-art techniques in environmental management of mine sites as well as identify the major issues and management strategies associated with social/community impacts of mining in Australia and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Identify, analyse and apply state of the art techniques in environmental management of mine sites.
Describe and apply the principles of Sustainable Development.
Demonstrate a knowledge of the legal, political & ethical context of mining in Australia and overseas.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Uranium Mining Fundamentals
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Uranium Mining Fundamentals will cover all stages of mining, from exploration of ore geology to mine feasibility and design and mine operation. Global and Australian uranium potential and leading practices for mining uranium will be evaluated and critiqued. Mining methods considered for efficient and safe extraction of uranium will include open cut, underground and In Situ Recovery (ISR) leach methods. The fundamentals of mine geomechanics, including slope stability and ground support requirements, will be presented as part of mining method selection, along with consideration of grade control and ventilation for safe underground mining. Fundamentals of milling and chemical processing of uranium ore will be presented, focusing mostly on production to the yellow cake stage (uranium oxide powders). Technical aspects of mining and milling operations are complimented with consideration of health and safety, economic, community, environmental and regulatory issues associated with uranium mining, presented within a risk management framework.
learning_outcomes: Develop a plan for a hypothetical mining operation, integrating exploration, mining, processing, safety measures, adherence to regulations, and waste management strategies.
Analyse the potential risks and hazards associated with uranium mining and evaluate how legislation mitigates these risks.

Describe relevant terminologies and concepts related to uranium mining operations, covering from assessing feasibility to the operational stages, including associated exploration and milling practices.

Assess information requirements for designing a uranium mine as an open cut, underground or ISR (in situ recovery), and for safe and efficient mining and milling operations, including consideration of ground support and ventilation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Water and Waste Management
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Mine water and waste management are critical issues for safe and efficient underground and pit mining operations and to minimise environmental impacts at all stages from feasibility assessment to mine closure. Leading practices for mine site water accounting and assessment will include depressurization and dewatering, geotechnical stability, sustainable water supplies and surface diversions, discharge and pump system management. Fundamentals of hydrogeology and hydrogeochemistry for mining will include monitoring and management of groundwater storage, salinity and acid mine drainage; potential contaminant migration processes; geochemical reactive transport modelling and tracing methods. The course will focus on aqueous aspects of mine water including engineered seepage barriers, water recycling and treatment options, with an overview of waste rock and tailings management.
learning_outcomes: Apply this knowledge to critically review water and waste management practices at a mine and to creatively solve problems in a manner that is responsive to change.

Identify and assess information requirements for depressurization and pumping operatons, sustainable water yields and diversions, and the safe management of waste rock and tailings. Skills to locate, critically evaluate and use information are to be developed in an interdisciplinary context.

Undertake presentations that develop essential communications skills and collaborative team work. Team work skills are to recognise diversity and the importance of working within an international community.

Demonstrate knowledge of water and waste management practices for mining from feasibility assessment, operations to closure. This knowledge is to demonstrate ethical practice and social responsibility in an international context.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Slope Monitoring Technologies
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course covers the instrumentation and monitoring devices available to the mining industry to monitor and manage pit slope movement. Students will be able to detail the different types of slope movement typically observed in excavated, constructed and dumped slopes, as well as the various warning signs of instability. The course will discuss monitoring strategies (e.g. targeted, background monitoring), and the link to the range of monitoring instrumentation and tools available to geotechnical engineers to manage and track slope movement. Practical cases are used to demonstrate why monitoring is required in pit slope risk management and the advantages and limitations of each tool (e.g., accuracy, precision, data corrections). Practical application and deployment of available monitoring instrumentation and devices will also be demonstrated through case studies and in-class demonstration. This includes estimating time to failure from radar monitoring data and using monitoring data to reconcile numerical models. Risk management strategies are also discussed using Trigger Action Response Plans, Critical Control Registers, and Geotechnical Hazard Alerts. The intensive four-day course will include guest lectures from industry.
learning_outcomes: Design a most efficient monitoring technique for any particular surface mining application.

Determine the role and importance of these techniques in a comprehensive range of surface mining applications, both from a technical perspective, and from the risk and operational management perspective.
Describe the principles of mine slope monitoring and identify the conventional and advanced mine slope monitoring technologies that are currently in use.
Summarise and compare the appropriateness and effectiveness of different monitoring techniques.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Tailings Management
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the critical considerations in the siting, construction, stability, operation, maintenance and rehabilitation of tailings storage facilities (TSFs) for sustainable tailings management. It is divided into four modules: (1) background, characterisation and behaviour of tailings, (2) TSF siting, design and construction, (3) TSF water management, operations and monitoring, and (4) TSF closure, rehabilitation and sustainable practices.
learning_outcomes: Outline and evaluate TSF operation, governance, and practices including water management.
Evaluate tailings characterisation and behaviour, historic TSF failures, regulations and guidelines and sustainability aspects, and compare the good and bad practices.
Investigate emerging and leading practices of tailings closure, rehabilitation, and sustainable practices and develop strategies and an implementation plan for a selected mining operation.
Employ Australian and International frameworks for siting, design and construction of TSFs and evaluate how they influence TSF safety and sustainability.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mining Design Practice
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Design practice is a final year course intended to enable students to integrate material learnt in several sub-disciplines of mining engineering. The objective is to develop the students' self-directed learning, design, teamwork and managerial skills. The course involves undertaking and completing a series of design tasks in mining engineering stream. Each design task in the series may be independent of each other, or may be a sequence of related sub-tasks as part of a larger goal.
learning_outcomes: Apply technical knowledge to produce discipline-specific designs in mining engineering.
Identify, document, and improve issues related to mining engineering knowledge base.
Gain in-depth knowledge of relevant discipline and its interdisciplinary content.
Effectively explain design decisions, displaying communication, negotiation, and advocacy skills.
Develop the capacity for analytical and critical thinking and its application in discipline-specific creative problem solving.
Demonstrate an ability to work in teams and learn from peers and mentors.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Heat in Underground Mines
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course module deals with the issues of heat in underground mines. The module topics are psychrometry, heat transfer, sources of heat and heat stress management. The module provides the means to analyse a mine's ventilation circuit to determine the magnitude of heat management controls required, such as refrigeration. This course is one of the eight required courses for the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046). Ventilation Officer students are not required to take this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the requirements for heat management plans and calculatation of heat stress indices.
Explain scientific principles and calculation methods required to describe the properties of moist air and quantify heat and moisture sources in underground mines.
Demonstrate working knowledge of laws and relationships to calculate heat load arising from identified heat sources and air temperature changes.
Explain scientific principles and calculation methods required to quantify mine refrigeration requirements.

syllabus_overview: This course module deals with the occurrence, effects and control of atmospheric contaminants in underground mine environments. These include toxic and or flammable gasses and dust originating from strata, mine equipment or the mining process. The causes, effects and control of mine fires are also considered. This course is one of the required courses for the statutory appointment of Ventilation Officers in NSW and QLD and the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046).
learning_outcomes: Apply scientific principles and calculation methods required to describe the occurrence and behaviour of dust and fire in mine ventilation networks together with methods of control.

Describe the various instruments and systems available for detecting mine gases. In particular what systems are appropriate under various circumstances, their limitations and interpretation of data obtained.
Explain scientific principles and calculation methods required to describe the occurrence and behaviour of gases in mine ventilation networks.
Recognise scientific principles and calculation methods required to quantify radon sources and control requirements in underground mines.

Appraise the preferred design options with economic considerations to be made in the operation of ventilation systems
Apply the risk management approach to control hazards & review safety management plans for mine ventilation systems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ventilation and Mine Services
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course module covers laws and relationships required to describe the behavious of mine or ducted ventilation systems. These relate to fluid flow, friction losses, fans and network analysis. Use of ventilation surveys to provide design parameters or reconciliation with predictive models is also covered. This course is one of the required courses for the statutory appointment of Ventilation Officers in NSW and QLD and Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046).

Appraise the various equipment employed for monitoring and surveying of mine ventilation systems and the range of parameters that may be encountered in water, air and gas reticulation systems.
Explain scientific principles and calculation methods required to describe fluid flow in mine ventilation networks and associated gas drainage or water reticulation systems.
Demonstrate methods for analysing mine ventilation networks using both simple series and parallel airway groups and iterative (computer simulation) methods.

title: Coal Mine Hazards and Control
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course module describes hazards and controls specific to underground coal mines, such as seam gas emission, outbursts and spontaneous combustion. The module includes methods of quantifying or predicting management requirements based on the properties of the working section and adjacent seam gas reservoirs. This course is one of the required courses for the statutory appointment of Ventilation Officers in NSW and QLD and the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046).

Apply scientific principles and calculation methods required to characterise coal mine seams in terms of gas emission regimes.
Explain scientific principles and calculation methods required to describe the occurrence, detection, prevention and control of spontaneous combustion in underground coal mines

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Ventilation
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course covers basic principles of coal and metalliferous mine ventilation and underground environmental control. The emphasis is on the practical aspects of mine ventilation to ensure that learning outcomes are immediately relevant to the industry. Course topics include those common to both types of mines, such as fan performance and circuit analysis using Ventsim, occurrence and control of gases, dust and heat together with design and management of ventilation systems. Coal mine specific hazards such as spontaneous combustion, outbursts and management of seam gas emissions are also covered. It is preferred if practical course assignments be undertaken at operating mine sites however this is not a course prerequisite. The course is an online course, which is ideal for mining professionals to take at remote mine sites.
learning_outcomes: Provide competency in fundamental calculations using laws and relationships provided and decision making ability in mine ventilation design and problem solving.
Develop the knowledge of underpinning scientific and engineering principles for mine ventilation
Improve the awareness of the significance of related topics in underground mining environments
Develop essential skills in designing and managing of ventilation systems in underground mines.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Spontaneous Combustion and Reactive Ground
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Spontaneous combustion is considered one of the core risks in underground coal mines. Similarly, reactive ground provides a similar risk to underground metalliferous mines. Ventilation control forms a significant part of the management plans to control these hazards. Significant incidents have occurred in Australia and overseas that had the potential to cause loss of life. This course will address the causes, incidents and controls required to manage this hazard. Additionally, case studies and spontaneous management plans will be reviewed. This course is one of the required courses for the statutory appointment of Ventilation Officers in NSW and QLD and the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046).
learning_outcomes: Determine the risks associated with spontaneous combustion of coal and reactive ground in metal mines.
Describe and evaluate the detection and analytic processes used to determine the presence of an event happening in the mine.
Develop ventilation strategies to manage and control the risk of spontaneous combustion and reactive ground.
Describe and evaluate the detection and analytic processes used to determine the propensity to risk
Evaluate existing management plans to control spontaneous combustion and reactive ground
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5046

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Ventilation Legislation
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Explosions, disasters accidents and incidents have been an unfortunate part of working life. These events invariably led to changes in legislation. By studying past disasters participants will be better equipped to prevent their re-occurrence. Current legislation will be studied in this context rather than just studying the statutes. Also, the historical reasons for the establishment of limits will allow the participants the opportunity to explain the significance of legislative compliance. This course is one of the eight required courses for the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046). Ventilation Officer students are not required to take this course.
learning_outcomes: State and interpret the relevant legislation pertinent to mine ventilation
Describe the legislative responsibilities and duties of a ventilation practitioner
Evaluate incidents that have occurred with in the mining industry both domestic and international.
Develop strategies to assist mines in compliance with Acts, Regulations, codes and standards relevant to mine ventilation
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5046

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mine Ventilation Practices
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: Mine Ventilation Practice details the techniques and processes required to put ventilation theory to effective use in an underground mine. Examples of the world's best practices will be discussed and reviewed. Techniques used by coal mines will be explored as to their applicability to hard rock mines and vice versa. Through directed learning participants will design a ventilation system for a mine. This course is one of the eight required courses for the Graduate Diploma in Mine Ventilation (MINE5046). Ventilation Officer students are not required to take this course.
learning_outcomes: Define and describe the issues arising from the selection of various ventilation circuits
Describe and assess the factors to be considered in mine ventilation design
Evaluate the types and requirements for various ventilation control devices
Evaluate the need for and methods of pressure control and balancing
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5046

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Design and Manufacturing
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered how devices and machines are manufactured with such precision? Have you pondered over the manufacturing process involved in creating robotic movements and appendages? All of this is possible due to fundamental machining methods. Without understanding the physical construction of our designs, it is impossible to create successful prototypes and products. In this course, you will learn how to create graphical outputs such as 3D models and engineering drawings that facilitate design solutions. Additionally, you will acquire the skills necessary to take your computer-aided design (CAD) model from the virtual world and machine it on a computer numerical control (CNC) machine. By the end of the term, you will have the skills and knowledge to marvel at your own machined creation.
learning_outcomes: Interpret engineering drawings to drive manufacturing processes.
Prepare components for manufacture using CAM software.
Recognise the role Australian Standards play in engineering practice.
Operate fundamental metalworking machinery to generate components.
Identify which manufacturing processes must be used to create desired products.
Explain how manufacturing processes impact design and production.
Construct CAD models and engineering drawings from real world inputs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Mechanics 2
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides essential knowledge and skills for students to analyse the kinematics and kinetics of rigid bodies and mechanical vibrations. Topics include the following: Plane kinematics and kinetics of rigid bodies; Equations of motion, work and energy; Introduction to mechanical vibration; Free and forced responses of single degree-of-freedom spring-mass-damper systems, vibration isolation; Harmonic analysis; Linear vibrations of multi-degree-of freedom systems.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles and techniques of mechanical vibrations to solve engineering mechanics problems.
Apply the principles and techniques of kinematics and kinetics to solve engineering mechanics problems.
Analyse the principles and components of engineering mechanics in relation to practical problems.
prerequisites: Exclusion: MECH2300, MECH3300 AND Prerequisite: (CVEN1300 or MINE1300 or MMAN1300 or ENGG1300 or DPST1072) AND (MATH2019 or MATH2018 or (MATH2111 and MATH2221) or (MATH2011 and MATH2121) or (MATH2069 and MATH2121))

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fluid Mechanics
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Fluid properties. Fluids in static equilibrium. Buoyancy. Pressures in accelerating fluid systems. Steady flow energy equations. Flow measurement. Momentum analysis. Dimensional analysis and similarity. Pipe flow. Incompressible laminar and turbulent flow in pipes; friction factor. Laminar flow between parallel plates and in ducts. Elementary boundary layer flow; skin friction and drag. Pumps and turbines. Pump and pipeline system characteristics.
learning_outcomes: Be able to determine pressure drops for pipe systems and choose appropriate pumps and turbines depending on the application
Be familiar with the terminology associated with fluid mechanics
Be able to use fluid properties correctly to solve problems
Understand the principals of flow rates and velocity measurement
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (MATH1131 or DPST1013 or MATH1141) and (PHYS1121 or PHYS1131 or DPST1023 or PHYS1141)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Linear Systems and Control
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course aims to introduce students to the fundamental principles of control theory for dynamic systems. It provides an overview of modelling, feedback control, and stability analysis as the essential foundation for designing control systems for a wide variety of applications, such as stability control, fluid flow control, and temperature regulation. Throughout the course, students will learn key concepts and tools for system design and analysis, including: ordinary differential equations, linearisation techniques, Laplace transforms, transfer functions, block diagrams, transient and steady-state response of first and second-order systems, poles and zeros, the concept of system stability, root locus, Bode plots, PID control, state space models (SISO and MIMO systems), state feedback control, state observers, controllability and observability. This course is designed for students in Aerospace, Mechanical, and Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering, and incorporates a wide range of examples from various engineering disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Design controllers for linear systems.
Analyse the behaviour and stability of linear time-invariant systems.
Apply state space representation to linear systems.
Create linear mathematical models of engineering systems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ELEC1111 and MMAN2300 Exclusion: MECH3211, MTRN3212

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Thermodynamics
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the students to the terminology, principles and methods used in engineering thermodynamics. The word “thermodynamics” was coined by Lord Kelvin from Greek words for heat (therme) and power (dynamis). Given that power is the rate at which work is performed, it follows that the word thermodynamics captures two of the most important ways in which energy is transferred, i.e. through heat and work. The subject of thermodynamics is therefore about energy and its transformations. Thermodynamics has a broad application area ranging from microscopic organisms to common household appliances, transportation vehicles, power generation systems and even philosophy. The knowledge of thermodynamics gained in this course is essential to many other courses studied in mechanical engineering degree programme, such as advanced thermofluids, aerospace propulsion, internal combustion engines, refrigeration, air conditioning and solar energy. This introductory course covers basic concepts of thermodynamics: Systems, property, state, path, process; Work and heat; Properties of pure substances; Tables of properties and equations of state; First law of thermodynamics; Analysis of closed and open systems; Second law of thermodynamics; Carnot cycle; Clausius inequality, entropy, irreversibility, isentropic efficiencies; Air-standard cycles; Vapour cycles.
learning_outcomes: Carry out, on working machinery, measurements of thermodynamic and mechanical properties and identify links between theoretical analysis methods and actual performance.
Apply the 1st law of thermodynamics to solve steady-state problems on closed and open systems.
Demonstrate knowledge of key concepts of thermodynamics such as heat, work, internal energy.
Apply the 2nd law of thermodynamics to analyse the behaviour of internal combustion engines (air-standard cycles), vapour and refrigeration cycles
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (MATH1131 or DPST1013 or MATH1141) and (PHYS1121 or PHYS1131 or DPST1021 or DPST1023 or PHYS1141)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Professional Engineering and Communication
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Professional Engineering and Communication is a subject designed to expose and involve students in a wide variety of topics and tasks which will be of lasting use going into Industrial Training, the final year thesis, and beyond that, a career in engineering. This course focuses on the non-technical aspects of engineering practice that centre around communication, ethical considerations, and professional conduct. Skills relating to problem solving, research, team working, and project planning and basic management will developed to standards expected of graduates entering the workplace - students are then expected to utilise and build on these skills in their final year to provide them with high-level skills that will make them sought after in the employment market. Despite their non-technical nature, the concepts involved in this course are just as challenging as those that are involved in the technical analyses with which most engineering students are more familiar. A professional engineer can expect to find herself or himself working on several memos, reports and presentations at any given time - it is an essential part of performing effectively in industry. Therefore many tasks will be undertaken, some short and relatively simple, with others more complex and nuanced, partly reflecting the timelines and pressures of the working environment and providing an opportunity to work in different teams on different tasks. Analysis of team structures and interpersonal communication also forms part of the course, as aspects of teamwork such as leadership, conflict resolution, managing differing technical skill levels and cultural backgrounds are vital in professional practice and must be appreciated as useful skills for the engineer. The centrepiece of the course is a group research project on an area pertinent to modern engineering. This, along with guest lectures from industry professionals will be used to provide insight into the working relationships between professional engineers, clients and management in order to prepare students for the workforce.
learning_outcomes: Be able to communicate effectively, both orally and in written form across a variety of media types.
Explain and reflect on the qualities of a professional engineer
Apply project management skills to research projects
Lead and contribute to teamwork

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mechanics of Solids 2
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Membrane stresses in axisymmetric shells, simple bending, bending of composite and reinforced concrete beams, principal and cross moments of area, unsymmetrical bending, transverse shear stresses in beams, shear centre, column buckling, theory of elasticity: compatibility - equilibrium - constitutive equations - plane stress/strain, st Venant's principal, application of theory of elasticity to axisymmetric problems, torsion of prismatic bars, torsion of multiply connected thin-walled sections, deflection analysis based on the principle of virtual work, fatigue and fracture.
learning_outcomes: Analyze deflection of trusses and beams using principle of virtual work
Write reports to communicate information at a professional engineering standard
Apply acquired knowledge to conduct a systematic analysis of a real-world system
Determine stresses in axisymmetric shells/vessels, unsymmetrical bending, shear and column buckling
prerequisites: Prerequisite: (MATH2019 OR MATH2018) AND (ENGG2400 OR MMAN2400)

title: Mechanics of Solids 2
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Additive Manufacturing
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Additive manufacturing, also known as 3D printing, is an emerging advanced manufacturing technique which has enjoyed a rapid growth in recent years. This course will introduce you to the fundamental aspects of additive manufacturing. This course will focus on various additive manufacturing techniques where you will gain basic knowledge and theory about the history, development and fundamental engineering aspects of this technique. You will also cover additive manufacturing process optimization including the selection and use of materials as well as look at the current major applications where additive manufacturing is used in addition to investigating the future development of this emerging manufacturing technique
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles and develop a systematic plan for additive manufacturing process optimisation
Relate additive manufacturing to other manufacturing techniques
Plan and execute appropriate design process for additive manufacturing
Understand the fundamental basis and nature of additive manufacturing techniques

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Micro/Nanofabrication and Technology
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course offers an in-depth exploration of micro and nanofabrication technologies, leading the forefront of innovation in diverse sectors such as electronics, healthcare, aerospace, renewable energy, and bioengineering. It will provide opportunities for students to develop advanced manufacturing technologies skills and knowledge which is crucial for enhancing their competitiveness in today's job market. Targeted towards undergraduate and postgraduate students who have a foundational background in engineering, physics, materials, or a closely related discipline, the program comprehensively covers the fundamental principles, cutting-edge methodologies, and diverse applications of micro and nanofabrication techniques. Students will gain firsthand experience in fabricating micro and nanoscale devices, employing techniques such as lithography, etching, chemical vapor deposition, and nanoimprint lithography. Furthermore, the course explores the science of materials at the micro and nano levels, exploring how their properties change at these scales and how these changes can be harnessed to create innovative solutions to complex problems.
learning_outcomes: Analyze and interpret experimental data obtained from micro/nanofabrication processes, including measurements of feature sizes, surface roughness, and film thickness
Design and fabricate nanoscale devices, such as wearable sensors, transistors, and microelectromechanical systems
Describe the fundamental principles of micro/nanofabrications and explain their limitations and challenges.
Demonstrate manufacturing skills in micro/nanofabrication, including cleanroom procedures, equipment operation, and process optimization
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 120 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Management
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: Engineering Management is designed to help you to learn how to manage the operations in organizations and also to build a business or commercial case for making engineering related decisions, such as investment in plant, equipment and processes. Although the main emphasis will be on product and process, consideration will also be given to designing engineering services. The course offers a broad managerial perspective emphasizing the strategic impact of operations decisions and the interfaces between operations and the other functional areas of organizations, including of course, finance. The course presents four subject areas, considered to be critical in terms of managing and leading engineering operations. They are: Issue analysis and decision making Investment analysis and engineering economy Costing and operations analysis Quality management, including design Within each subject area the course will cover many conceptual and analytical techniques, all supporting fact- and data-based analysis and decision making with the aim of improved product and process performance, economy and sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Perform investment and feasibility analyses

Describe and analyse the role that the operations management function plays in international business and how the operations function can play a strategic role in improving the global competitiveness of the organisation
State what an organisation needs to do to remain competitive in today's environment
Determine whether a process is capable of producing a product or service to specifications
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Completion of 96 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Finite Element Methods
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course will train you to analyse real world structural mechanics problems using the finite element method. You will be introduced to the mathematical basis of finite element analysis, on which nearly all structural analysis software is built. You will learn how to apply commercially available finite element software to solve real-world engineering problems. The course will cater to the specific challenges of engineers across different mechanical disciplines. Any student wishing to extend their structural analysis skills should take this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply fundamental finite element analysis techniques to solve simple engineering problems
Perform a detailed finite element study to investigate a real world engineering problem
Plan and execute appropriate finite element analyses to solve a range of solid mechanics and other engineering problems.
Explain the underlying mathematics behind finite element analysis software solvers

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital and Artificial Intelligence Technologies for Engineering Applications
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides essential knowledge and skills for engineers in the fields of sensing, digitalisation and data analytics, especially artificial intelligence (AI), for typical engineering applications. Topics include the following: sensors and modern acquisition systems; engineering signals and their time/frequency domain representation; support vector machines and neural networks for industrial applications; explainable artificial intelligence. This is done with a hands-on approach where students actually develop a digital sensing and data-analytic solution (student project) to an application challenge. The teaching team will strive to offer application challenges that relate to multiple engineering areas such as mechanical, aerospace, mechatronics and manufacturing engineering.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop data-driven models to formulate engineering problems as classification or regression tasks
Choose and implement data driven AI solutions for select engineering problems
Create validated digital acquisition systems
Discuss key concepts and methodologies for a rational design of sensing and digital acquisition systems
prerequisites: Prerequisite: COMP1511 or COMP1911 or ENGG1811

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Thesis B
school: School of Mechanical and Manufacturing Engineering
syllabus_overview: The thesis provides an opportunity for you to bring together engineering principles learned over your previous years of study and apply these principles to innovatively solve problems such as the development of a specific design, process and/or the investigation of a hypothesis. Thesis projects are complex, open-ended problems that allow room for your creativity, and the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of results. There are multiple possible solutions or conclusions at the outset and sufficient complexity to require a degree of project planning. The thesis requires you to formulate problems in scientific or engineering terms, manage a technical project and find solutions by applying scientific and engineering methods. You will also develop their ability to work in a research and development environment. You must identify a supervisor and project prior to enrolling in this course. This is the second course of the 3 course thesis structure. MMAN4952/9452 is the second of three parts of individual thesis. All three parts must be completed in 3 consecutive terms in order to pass the course.
learning_outcomes: Apply scientific and engineering methods to solve an engineering problem.
Demonstrate oral and written communication in professional and lay domains.
Develop a design or a process or investigate a hypothesis following industry and professional engineering standards.
Analyse data objectively using quantitative and mathematical methods.
Critically reflect on a specialist body of knowledge related to their thesis topic.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: MMAN4951

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Responsible Management
syllabus_overview: This course provides the foundations on which your MBA is built. Throughout the course, you and your cohort will be introduced to foundational concepts and skills in critical areas including: High-performing Teams Cross-cultural Leadership Communicating with Influence Complex Problem-solving Ethical Leadership Self Leadership Adaptive Leadership The course culminates in Leadership Week followed by ALiCE (Adaptive Leadership in Complex Environments), an experiential week that will allow you to work in teams to review, integrate and apply all your newly acquired knowledge and skills gained throughout the Foundations course in complex and high-pressure situations.
learning_outcomes: Create and contribute to high- performing teams and enable diversity to leverage the individual differences and strengths of all team members
Apply knowledge relating to leadership, ethics and sustainability, cross-cultural leadership and complex problem solving, in the contexts of local and global business
Develop persuasive communication skills (oral and written) that help you to influence others
Understand and apply key principles and methods of leadership development and apply a variety of techniques to improve your leadership
Recognise and respect the cultural norms, beliefs and values of others, and apply this knowledge to interact, communicate and work effectively

Master projects are complex, open-ended problems that allow room for your creativity, and the acquisition, analysis and interpretation of results. There are multiple possible solutions or conclusions at the outset and sufficient complexity to require a degree of project planning. The project requires you to formulate problems in scientific or engineering terms, manage a technical project and find solutions by applying scientific and engineering methods. You will also develop the ability to work in a research and development environment. You must identify a supervisor and project prior to enrolling in this course. This is the third course of the 3 course project structure. MMAN4953/9543 is the final 3rd part of individual thesis. All three parts must be completed in 3 consecutive terms in order to pass the course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Operationalising Strategy
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is to teach you how to successfully implement strategy (i.e. 'what should managers do to align their organisation to deliver on their strategy?'). This includes: ensuring your strategy is sufficiently clear (building on from the core AGSM Strategy course) developing strategic and operational plans - the strategic planning and review cycle operating models organisation structure team, job-role design and workforce planning KPIs and performance-management culture governance and risk.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economics in Management Practice
syllabus_overview: The performance of an organisation is driven by firm-specific, industry and economic factors. Economics in Management Practice has been developed to give you a deeper understanding of all three of these factors and to provide a rigourous foundation for any further study that you pursue in the area of Strategy. Microeconomics is the focus of Units 1 to 6 of this course. It provides you with a deeper understanding of both firm-specific and industry factors that drive financial performance. These Units cover the purchase decisions of individual customers and how the features of the industry will influence company profitability. An understanding of microeconomics helps managers to better understand and predict the behaviour of customers, competitors and suppliers. These concepts are foundational to any further study in the area of strategy. Macroeconomics is the focus of Units 7 to 11 of this course. It provides you with a deeper understanding of the economic factors that drive financial performance. These Units cover that factors that drive economic growth, inflation, employment, interest rates and exchange rates. An understanding of macroeconomics helps managers to better understand and predict how changes in the economy will affect the industry in which they operate.

Understand how national, international and global economic trends affect the business environment and growth perspectives.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Entrepreneurship and Innovation
syllabus_overview: This course suits individuals looking to build their strategic abilities around entrepreneurship and the innovation associated with entrepreneurship. It provides exposure to both the fundamentals of business innovation and the practical aspects of identifying, evaluating and moving business ideas forward. The course uniquely exposes current students with current ideas and thoughts from innovators, venture capital (VC) groups, and successful startup CEOs within the Sydney ecosystem. This dynamic course pulls together many of the components already learned in the MBA Program, providing those with entrepreneurial aspirations the opportunity to realise their dreams. Two streams of entrepreneurship are covered in the course: startup creation and startup innovation. Specific methodologies covered include integrated experiences of Design Thinking and The Lean Startup. This is a hands-on opportunity to learn about venture creation, startup resourcing, strategy and management, design and innovation involving your own startup. Entrepreneurship and innovation is a hot topic today – many startups continue to raise money through angel investors and VCs, but the road is a challenging one. Understanding what makes entrepreneurship and innovation in startups work is paramount to success. We will help you develop your confidence, your products, your pitch, and your funding to help get you started on the road to your startup success.
learning_outcomes: Understand how social impact entrepreneurship has the potential to make the world a better place
Apply the Lean Startup methodology to a project
Take advantage of the local entrepreneurial ecosystem compared to international ecosystems.
Analyse ethical obligations and ethical professional practices within organisations as they apply to the startup and key stakeholders
Identify common characteristics of successful entrepreneurs and ventures - startup and corporate
Develop the entrepreneurial mindset
Understand the different forms of corporate innovation and entrepreneurship and what makes them successful
Identify a range of strategic options for growing an entrepreneurial venture and their strengths and weaknesses, including government funding and commercial funding
Understand and apply concepts such as minimal viable product, split testing, 'fast-fail', product-market fit, the Business Model Canvas and Design Thinking

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Accounting and Financial Management
syllabus_overview: The course provides a broad introduction to how accounting contributes to an organisation. You will examine how accounting can help managers measure and analyse their organisation's economic performance, to improve resource allocation, and build accountability for performance through effective governance. The users of accounting information are typically classified as either external (such as investors or lenders) or internal (such as operational managers). Different users have different information needs. This course deals with the needs of these two main user groups and how senior managers can more effectively use accounting data to connect with them. The course explores accounting techniques and terminology, to equip you with sufficient conceptual and practical skills to make you confident in your ability to understand and communicate complex financial strategies. You will also examine the design and operation of accounting systems. As a result, the course integrates ideas and concepts from accounting with a range of other disciplines and reveals how the effective use of financial information provided by such systems can improve organisational decision-making. You will also examine how firms use non-financial information such as environmental, social and governance (ESG) to communicate their performance and strategies. It is assumed that participants have little prior knowledge of accounting and financial management.

Effectively collaborate in both the construction and presentation of management information data pertaining to a reporting entity or unit.
Explain the objectives, concepts and relationships that underpin both internal and external financial reports.

Research and analyse the financial performance of organisations.

syllabus_overview: This course provides an immersive and experiential opportunity to work inside a startup or scaleup. You will be embedded as an intern within an organisation, contributing to strategic projects that deliver meaningful value to the host. The course emphasises learning through practice rather than coursework, enabling you to apply your MBA knowledge and prior professional experience in a dynamic entrepreneurial environment. Placements are arranged prior to the start of term, and you are expected to spend a minimum of one day per week (i.e. 10 days) with your host organisation. You will gain firsthand insight into entrepreneurial practices, decision-making, strategic problem-solving, business-process modelling, and AI strategy and/or implementation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Analysis and Statistical Modelling for Business
syllabus_overview: In recent years, organisations have aligned technology and business in order to adapt to a challenging and hyper-competitive market environment. In a situation where organisations in many industries offer similar products and use equivalent technologies, business processes are established as one of the last points of differentiation. In a similar way, data and algorithms have become the new stronghold upon which to leverage differentiation processes, products, services and decision-making. As a result, increasingly more companies use different analytical strategies to improve decision-making, optimise processes and create data-driven products. However, as in many other areas, technology is not sufficient to generate competitive advantage status. For example, decision-making requires actual art (based on experience and intuition) and science (based on analysis) to survive the increasing complexity of the market. Understanding how to use data, models, visuals and dashboards to create competitive advantages can be the key to the success or failure of a company in the coming years. This course aims to introduce professionals to Data Analytics and how to develop efficient strategies within organisations. The efficiency is achieved through the combination of multiple technologies (from Business Intelligence to Big Data) and the use of algorithms to generate insights and predict the future behaviour of an organisation. This course introduces managers to several techniques that are relevant for managerial decision-making, such as data preparation, data analysis, data visualisation and data storytelling. This course will help students to develop expertise in a standard set of data literature techniques, which will be useful in analysing business-related data. These techniques are widely applied in a number of areas of management, including operations, marketing, finance, and human resources.

Apply data visualisation principles to select the best visualisation analysis
Think analytically using data to increase your capability as a manager and to support your business intuition
Run one of the most relevant tools in the market for data preparation and data analysis

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Analytics and Decision-making
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide a broad strategic perspective on issues and challenges related to incorporating data analytics and AI into business decision-making for strategic gain and meaningful change. Due to the complex and multi-faceted nature of the world of analytics, leaders and managers need some basic and abstract familiarity with the technical building blocks of analytics. This enables them to speak the language of analytics with fluency. Also, since emerging tools and objects in the world of AI and analytics are underpinned by these technical building blocks, this familiarity enables leaders and managers to separate hype from reality with confidence and make better decisions when integrating analytics/AI into their organisations. We deliver this course in three phases to provide an integrated strategic–technical–execution view of data analytics. In Phase 1, we will explore the concept of data strategy and its connection to business strategy. In Phase 2, we aim to help you understand basic analytics and statistical concepts, building technical confidence to distinguish between hype and reality in analytics and AI, while learning to speak the language of analytics fluently. In Phase 3, we will address the challenges of incorporating analytics and AI into organisations and explore their potential to create business value and drive innovative changes in business processes.

Select and appropriately apply various data-analytics techniques to identify business problems, trends and patterns used to inform business decision-making.

Explain the importance of ethics and governance in order to apply relevant frameworks in data-driven organisations, and evaluate the social and ethical implications of data collection and analysis.
