Distinguish aspects of workplace learning that enable individuals, teams and organisations to obtain knowledge, skills and attitudes to solve work-related problems and improve performance. (PLO1; PLO2; PLO3; PLO4; PLO5)

Develop and evaluate their own self-management and work-management skills, including autonomy, judgement and self-directed learning by synthesising the knowledge, skills and values acquired through the practical legal training program. (PLO1; PLO2; PLO3; PLO4; PLO5)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Key Issues in Australian Foreign Policy
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Australia finds itself in a rapidly changing and uncertain international environment, presenting foreign policymakers with a number of key issues, challenges, and risks to address. In this course, you will consider some of the main themes and issues in contemporary Australian foreign policy. The course begins with an exploration of the foundations of Australia’s foreign relations, including the formulation and implementation of foreign policy, national identity, and the extent to which Australia can be described as a ‘Middle Power’. You will then look at some of the key issues in Australian foreign policy. These include Australia’s evolving relationships with traditional allies, its management of relations with rising powers, national security, immigration, and Australia’s participation in the global economy.
learning_outcomes: Assess Australia’s contemporary international environment
Outline and evaluate the foundations of Australian foreign policy
Conduct independent and scholarly research
Consider key issues and themes in contemporary Australian foreign policy

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Politics: The Globalisation of World Politics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Examines different and competing perspectives on international relations; analyses the key structures and processes of global politics and explores selected current issues. The course provides an examination of theoretical traditions in International Relations, and a survey of the historical evolution of the global system. It also examines the role of the nation-state, the nature of conflict in contemporary world politics, global governance, the global economy, the importance of identity in world politics, human rights, and globalization.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the impact of globalisation on world politics
Summarise and explain the main theoretical approaches in International Relations
Analyse the roles of major actors in global politics
Critically evaluate the key structures and processes of the global system

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Organisations and Global Politics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Examines the role of international organisations in global politics. Explores the effectiveness of security arrangements at the regional and global levels. Analyses the roles of international organisations in global economic governance. Evaluates the relevance of international organisations in providing solutions to the social and humanitarian challenges facing humanity at the beginning of the 21st century.
learning_outcomes: Locate, evaluate, prioritise and deploy appropriate information in a sophisticated and persuasive manner;
Identify and outline the diverse and contested structures of the international system;

Analyse, explain and critique basic and more advanced literatures relating to the theories and practices of international organisation, including a variety of concepts, theories and categories of analysis;
Describe and discuss a variety of debates and approaches surrounding the role and function of international organisations in global politics;
Summarise and evaluate debates, communicating your ideas with fluency and vigour, informed by an understanding of ethical issues and a self-reflexive awareness of the reasoned views of others.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The International Political Economy
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides a theoretically grounded introduction to the evolution of a global economy. It pays particular attention to examining the drivers, dimensions and dynamics of economic globalisation, and to analysing the implications of this complex process for the distribution of wealth and power in the international system. The course contributes to an enhanced understanding of the relationship between the political and economic spheres of social life, and of why this understanding is important.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between the major theoretical perspectives of IPE(including their basic assumptions and the worldviews they generate).
Compare the value of different theoretical perspectives for the analysis of specific problems of international political economy.
Evaluate analyses of IPE from a theoretically grounded point of view.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Politics of International Law
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Human rights play a crucial role in the international political system. This course challenges you to analyse that role and major interpretations of that role. The course is concerned with the development of human rights across geographical, cultural and legal boundaries, in a dialogue between international human rights institutions and domestic politics. Please note that this is an International Relations course focussing on the interaction of law and politics in the area of human rights. It is not a Law course. No prior knowledge of international law is required. Accordingly, we cover the sources, core principles and concepts of human rights in international law; distinguish political from legal interpretations of human rights; and explore the relationship between domestic policy formulation and international law. The course examines the sources of human rights, the rights of individuals, the duties of states, and mechanisms of recognition and protection. It draws on comparative material from different jurisdictions to explore questions such as discrimination on the basis of race and sex, religious freedom, economic and social rights in development, and human rights in the context of addressing terrorism.
learning_outcomes: Identify key actors in the international human rights system and assess their role in shaping the system
Understand the place of instruments such as the United Nations Charter, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and central conventions in the international legal and political system
Identify the various ways in which politics and law are related in terms of human rights at the international level, and explain how this relationship operates and why it matters
Understand some of the key concepts and principles of international human rights and some of the central controversies surrounding the development of international human rights law
Thoughtfully consider different theoretical perspectives to explain international political and legal developments in human rights
Read and analyse an international convention and appreciate the various elements that have gone into its development

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: China and Asia-Pacific Security
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: For those interested in the future of regional security in the Asia-Pacific and international relations, cultivating an understanding of China and its foreign policy is imperative. This course offers you the opportunity to study China as a global power in the making. Focusing on China’s evolving engagement with the post-Cold War regional order, you will explore how China’s 'rise' as a great power over the past three decades has profoundly impacted both regional and global security. You will be provided with the analytical and theoretical tools to critically examine Chinese foreign policy, and gain insight into policy debates on whether China is fundamentally a status quo or revisionist power.
learning_outcomes: Examine the key opportunities and challenges China faces in its domestic political transformation and 'rise' as a global and regional power.
Analyze the Chinese foreign policy-making process and, in particular, the historical and philosophical foundations of China's regional engagement strategy.
Critically apply International Relations theory to explain China's external behaviour and the implications of its growing power for regional security in the Asia-Pacific.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Between War and Peace: The World's Major Powers and Their Competing Visions of Global Order
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines the foreign and defense policies of the world’s major powers, including the United States and China, from 1945 to the present. It focuses on their competing visions of global and regional order and their strategies for achieving them. It highlights how these competing visions often resulted in disagreements, occasionally leading to wars and proxy conflicts among major powers. In this context, it discusses how these powers defined their national interests and articulated their geopolitical and security concerns. It also analyses the geopolitical, military, economic and domestic constraints under which these powers operated and the economic and military means they relied upon to achieve their visions of global and regional order. In other words, POLS5129 considers the various factors that have influenced their diplomatic and military approaches to international politics, including threat perceptions, ideological considerations, military and economic capabilities, as well as geopolitical and strategic constraints. You will examine the key political, economic and military developments that have shaped contemporary world politics from the second half of the 20th century to the first three decades of the new century. This course is specifically designed for postgraduate students interested in contemporary diplomacy, geopolitics, and statecraft, who seek to understand how the world’s major powers have pursued their national interests in a complex post-war international system.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate research and critical analysis skills.
Develop an awareness of the political, strategic and economic factors that have shaped the foreign policies of the world’s major powers.
Explain key aspects of the foreign policies of the world’s major powers.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Peace and Security
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course conceptualises and contextualises international security and peace through the lens of the academic discipline of International Relations. The goal is to equip you with the knowledge of different approaches, competing paradigms, and theoretical debates relevant to understanding the real-world security issues unfolding in the contemporary international politics. The first part of the course explores the traditional approaches to international security and examines such pivotal international issues as the rise of China and the transformation of the global power structure, Russia’s foreign policy resurgence and implications for the trans-Atlantic security, the spread of nuclear weapons and the North Korean nuclear crisis, the geopolitical dynamics surrounding the South China Sea dispute, the survival of small and middle powers amongst great power confrontation, and other issues. The second part of the course shifts the focus to the non-traditional/human security threats in the 21st century with special emphasis on ethnic and civil conflicts, terrorism, environmental degradation and climate change, cyber-security, and other issues falling under the category of non-traditional security.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the strengths and limits of the existing theoretical frameworks in explaining key issues in global and international security affairs
Analyse and appraise the international security challenges covered in the course as well as the stakes, approaches, policies, dilemmas, and behaviour patterns of the involved players
Recognise, compare, and apply different theoretical paradigms, approaches, and concepts to analyse and explain various global and regional security challenges

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Political Violence, Insurgency and Terrorism
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the key concepts, unifying themes, trends, central actors and issues (causes and strategic responses) in the study of insurgency and terrorism in the 20th and 21st Centuries, but with an emphasis on the evolution of the phenomena since the end of the Cold War. In doing so, the course reflects on some of the historical and more enduring forms of political violence—asymmetric and irregular warfare—which draw attention to the underlying and fundamental causes of rebellion/terrorism and responses to it. You will explore how non-state armed groups organise themselves, extract resources, deploy violence, attract recruits, and both fight and negotiate with states. You will also explore the nature and challenge of global terrorism across levels of analysis, focusing on the responses and strategies of both non-state and state actors. This course utilises perspectives and knowledge drawn from international relations, political science, history, terrorism and counter-insurgency studies to examine, in a holistic manner, the phenomenon of contemporary political violence.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate central actors and issues (causes of terrorism and strategic responses to terrorism) in the study of insurgency, terrorism, and political violence
Appraise key theoretical approaches to the study of insurgency, terrorism and political violence’
Critically examine key concepts and unifying themes in the tudy of insurgency, terrorism, and political violence

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Middle East, Global Politics, and the Question of Palestine
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course examines the dynamics of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict and its place in global politics and the politics of the Middle East. You will gain an appreciation of the historical context and events that have shaped the conflict, as well as knowledge of the different — and competing — theories that explain it. You will investigate topics such as Zionism and the rise of Arab and Palestinian nationalism, the Arab–Israeli wars, Israeli and Palestinian politics, and Palestinian resistance. Topics will also include the peace process, the Arab uprisings and their impact on the Israeli–Palestinian conflict, the Gaza wars, and future visions for Israel/Palestine.
learning_outcomes: Present effective briefing on various Middle Eastern issues in clear and concise oral and written contexts
Examine contemporary developments in the Middle East with an understanding of their global significance in the context of the regionâ??s complexity
Explore and contextualise the changing interpretations which have characterized historical and contemporary writing on the Middle East
Apply key international relations theories and conceptual approaches to the study of the Middle East

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Gender in Global Politics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Both within and outside the discipline of International Relations, there is today an acute awareness both of the need to take gender seriously and the importance of facilitating the transfer of knowledge between academics, practitioners and policymakers. POLS5132 explores the contributions and insights offered by feminist and gender scholars of global politics. You are asked to reflect on what it means to recognise gender in the structure, practice and theorising of global politics, exploring core subjects in the study and practice of International Relations through a gender lens. Taking this approach allows you to interrogate gendered structures of power and practice, analyse differences or similarities among masculine, feminine and fluid subjects in their experience of global politics, and critically assess the kinds of problems presented by efforts to theorise the body in global politics. Throughout, you will be encouraged to develop an informed awareness of specific issues relating to broader concerns in global politics, including race, postcolonialism, economic development, globalisation, security, conflict, peace and postconflict reconstruction. You will become familiar with the academic literature that constitutes the field of feminist International Relations and will gain insight into key debates such as those about theory and practice, scholarship and education and academia and policymaking as they relate to gender and global politics.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse key concepts, theories, and debates in the study of gender in global politics.
Communicate persuasive, evidence-based arguments about gender and global politics to diverse audiences.
Apply a range of theoretical approaches and perspectives related to gender to analyse contemporary issues in global politics.
Critically evaluate and reflect on how gender shapes global political institutions, processes, and outcomes across diverse issue areas.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Developing Countries and the International System
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: What are the legacies of colonialism in the international system? What - if any - measures can developing countries take to redress power imbalances in the contemporary political order? In this course, you will explore these and other questions related to developing countries and the ways in which they are affected by, and negotiate, issues of sovereignty, human rights, development, democracy, global trade and aid, amongst others. In doing so, you will investigate the utility of competing perspectives on understanding developing countries within the discipline of International Relations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the salience of competing views on the impact of the international system
Identify the constraints and opportunities faced by developing country policy-makers;
Analyse the impact of global forces on development choices;
Evaluate the strategies of developing countries in regional and global governance;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Philosophy and the Market
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The course will examine how political philosophers have thought about the meaning of freedom, equality and justice in market societies. You will study prominent representatives of important traditions in political philosophy, including Marxism, liberalism and republicanism. Thinkers covered may include Smith, Hegel, Marx, and Foucault. The course will introduce you to classic criticisms of commerce as corrupting of virtue and examine debates about whether economic power gives rise to domination. It will contrast these with liberal arguments that markets enhance individual freedom. It will also introduce you to contemporary critiques of neo-liberalism. Through guest lectures you will engage with researchers across several disciplines whose work explores the impacts of market dynamics on issues that may include the Green Economy, Indigenous Intellectual Property rights, and colonialism and world markets.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate key concepts of political philosophy such as freedom, democracy, equality, domination and justice, as applied to the understanding of market societies
Critically discuss the principal modern and contemporary philosophical approaches to understanding the emergence of market societies
Research complex issues and concepts and clearly present arguments and conclusions in both oral and written form
Apply key ideas of modern and contemporary political philosophy to critically analysing market societies in relation to equality and justice
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit overall, including PPEC1001, and enrolment in a Politics, Philosophy and Economics program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: PPE Capstone: Facing Contemporary Challenges
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This is the capstone course for the Bachelor of Philosophy, Politics and Economics program. In this course you will apply your accumulated understanding of PPE to the analysis of contemporary social and political problems, and examine potential solutions from the perspectives of feasibility, efficiency and ethics. The course will focus on the interactions between unfolding historical processes and established social, political and economic institutions. At the end of this course, PPE you will be ready to approach public policy questions as an independent professional.
learning_outcomes: Develop solutions to contemporary social problems using PPE principles, and examine their feasibility, efficiency and ethical implications.
Use the key foundations of philosophical, political and economic approaches to understand and interpret the world, in local and global context.
Apply the study of PPE to analyse historical and contemporary philosophical, political and economic challenges, debates and problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 72 units of credit overall, including PPEC2001, and enrolment in a Politics, Philosophy and Economics program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Politics, Philosophy and Economics
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
school: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce you to the disciplines of Philosophy, Politics and Economics, and more specifically to the synergies and tensions of their distinctive approaches to knowing the world. The major challenges facing policymakers today – from inequality to geopolitical instability – are at once political, economic and philosophical. How these challenges are understood and addressed rest on ideas and methods developed by foundational thinkers in Philosophy, Politics and Economics, especially by those whose thought traverses these disciplines. In addition, the course will introduce PPE approaches via a critical assessment of two important concepts in contemporary politics and society - democracy and development.
learning_outcomes: Identify the synergies and tensions between philosophical, political and economic approaches to and practices of knowing the world, in local and global context.
Describe the key foundations of philosophical, political and economic approaches to knowing the world, in local and global context.
Connect the study of PPE to historical and contemporary philosophical, political and economic challenges, debates and problems, in local and global context.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a Politics, Philosophy and Economics program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mental Health Assessment and Treatment
syllabus_overview: This course will review key principals underpinning mental health assessment and treatment decisions, across all the mental illness category groups and treatment settings. Key assessment approaches and skills will be explored, along with a bio-psycho-social model for treatment and management decisions. This course will review the major psychiatric disorders, with reference to the DSM-5-TR and ICD-11 diagnostic classification systems. Disorder categories will include psychotic disorders, mood disorders, anxiety disorders and eating disorders, as well as an overview of personality and substance use disorders. The course will review common psychopharmacological treatment approaches (including antidepressant and antipsychotic medications) including considerations of the benefits and side-effects of each medication category. An overview of the benefits and side-effects of each medication category will be considered. This course will also provide you with a foundational understanding of key psychological modalities used in treatment, with emphasis on cognitive behavioural therapy, brief solution focused therapy and an overview of other psychological therapies such as acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) and dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT) and others. On completion of this course, you will be able to complete a full, comprehensive mental health assessment, provide an initial diagnostic formulation and differential diagnosis, and develop a meaningful mental health treatment plan, with an understanding of the most appropriate treatment modality for each of the major mental health disorders.
learning_outcomes: Compare appropriate psychopharmacotherapy treatment(s) utilised in the treatment of mental health conditions and how these apply across differing patient groups.
Explain the key principals underlying mental health assessment to inform treatment decisions.
Evaluate the efficacy of how major mental illnesses are treated across inpatient and outpatient services nationally and internationally.
Formulate comprehensive psychiatric assessments, using clinical case studies and generate concise diagnostic impressions, utilising psychiatric diagnostic nosology.
Appraise the bio-psychosocial model and its application in the treatment of mental illnesses, including strengths and limitations of this model.
Develop well-considered comprehensive individualised treatment plans, using diagnostic nosology.
Critically evaluate appropriate psychological treatment(s) utilised across a variety of mental health conditions.
prerequisites: Enrolled in 7365 Mental Health Practice program

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamental Psychological Therapy Skills
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce psychological treatment modalities and provide a framework to select the appropriate treatment for a particular mental health disorder. The course will include various psychological therapy theories including, but not limited to, cognitive behaviour therapy (CBT), dialectical behaviour therapy (DBT), acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT), mentalisation based therapy (MBT) and transference focussed therapy (TFT) fundamentals. By the end of this course, you will understand the theoretical frameworks of these therapeutic interventions and be able to implement aspects of each in your clinical practice, providing patients with high quality psychological treatment. This course provides an opportunity for you to practice the skills you have learned throughout the course with the course convenor(s) who have expertise in the delivery of psychological therapies.
learning_outcomes: Develop a treatment modality, using a specific psychological therapy, chosen specifically to meet the patient's need, in both a group and individual therapy session.
Justify an effective treatment plan using psychological therapy treatment modalities.

Evaluate the appropriate psychological therapy approaches to treat mental health disorders, explaining their benefits and comparing how these are applied across a range of mental health disorders and differing patient needs.
Describe psychological therapy approaches and apply the underpinning key principals and theories with clients.
prerequisites: Enrolled in 7365 Mental Health Practice Program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Philosophies of Mental Health Care, Services and Systems
syllabus_overview: This course will explore the key philosophies underpinning mental health care, services and systems within an Australian and International context. Students will be provided with a comprehensive understanding of trauma-informed care, the bio-psychosocial model and working within a multidisciplinary team, focussing on delivering least restrictive care under a recovery model. Students will obtain an understanding of the way in which mental health services and systems are constructed and the reasons for service delivery design. Students will navigate services and systems, including beyond the formal mental health services, to support patients to holistically meet the needs of this patient group.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the current mental health systems, the need for more efficacious service delivery and future opportunities and explain the challenges of implementing differing approaches into current practice.
Compare the roles and accountabilities of the multidisciplinary team employed in the provision of mental health care.
Explain the key philosophies underpinning mental health care both nationally and internationally.
Demonstrate advanced understanding in the delivery of trauma-informed care to a psychiatric population.
Develop a plan of how to navigate the current mental health services and systems, including the benefits and limitations of current service offerings.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge in how mental health systems and services are constructed and how philosophies of mental health care underpin these.
prerequisites: Enrolled in 7365 Mental Health Practice program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Assessing Risk and Managing Challenging Behaviour
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the assessment and formulation of risk for violence and self-harm, its application to management approaches, and consideration of the strengths and limitations of different approaches. Students will gain practical experience in developing and utilising clinical skills in risk assessment and management, and in strategies for preventing and de-escalating risks. Acute emergency management of difficult behaviour will also be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Explain the difference between risk prediction and risk management, including the benefits and limitations of these approaches to risk assessment.

Formulate an appropriate risk assessment tool based on a mock patient, demonstrating an advanced knowledge of the tool, its benefits and limitations and explain the appropriateness of this chosen tool to a range of scenarios.
Develop a tool for de-escalating risk and managing difficult behaviours.

Apply several risk assessments, critically evaluate their individual benefits and limitations for use with a psychiatric population. Compare the benefits and limitations of utilising these tools in specific risk assessments.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of risk assessments and risk mitigation plans and how mental health services respond to risk.
prerequisites: Enrolled in 7365 Mental Health Practice program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Law and Mental Health
syllabus_overview: This course examines the interface of psychiatry and the law; unlike other subjects in the Forensic Mental Health degree, this unit of study focuses on law in the civil context rather than in forensic matters. The course provides an introduction into the history and development of the Australian legal system and psychiatry; creation of legislation; expert evidence (theory and practice). The course also provides an overview of Mental Health Legislation in Australia such as relevant sections in the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW) and the Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW); legal aspects of cognitive impairment, capacity, guardianship, and confidentiality.
learning_outcomes: Locate, read, and interpret case law and legislation.
Describe the concept of legal capacity and apply it in the context of psychiatric illness.
Detail the application and limitations of confidentiality and the privacy laws in mental health.
Describe and apply general principles of expert evidence.
Outline the system of law in Australia and describe key legal concepts such as the doctrine of precedent, separation of power, statutory interpretation, sources of law and legislation.
Analyse a range of legal issues in relation to cognitive impairment.
Describe the objects, key definitions and general structure of the Mental Health and Cognitive Impairment Forensic Provisions Act 2020 (NSW).
Briefly outline the history of Asylums, Mental Health related Inquiries, and the Mental Health Commissions in Australia.
Describe the objects, key definitions, and general structure of the Mental Health Act 2007 (NSW) and other jurisdictions, and recount the steps in the processes of civil commitment.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in either 5512, 7312 or 9012 Forensic Mental Health Programs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychiatry and Criminal Law
syllabus_overview: This course explores the interface of psychiatry and the law in terms of the current literature, as well as from legal and clinical perspectives of how these disciplines interact in courtroom settings. It will become evident that medical and legal perspectives on mental illness do not always coincide; yet mental health professionals and legal professionals have to work together to produce outcomes that are in the best interests of the accused, and society at large. This course will provide you with an understanding of introductory and conceptual issues; criminal responsibility; punishment; criminology; complete and partial defences; insanity; automatism; preventative detention; fitness to stand trial; personality disorders in forensic mental health; and sentencing.
learning_outcomes: Explain the conceptual basis of the diseased mind and liability for offending behaviour.
Discuss key components of core mental health legislation.
Discuss the core concepts in forensic mental health.
Select appropriate psychological and legal approaches in order to facilitate constructive clinical outcomes.
Discuss the ethical issues surrounding medical and legal approaches to managing mentally ill offenders.
Integrate legal and psychiatric constructs to communicate meaningfully in clinical and legal settings.
Critically appraise contradictions between medical and legal understandings of mental illness.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 5512 or 7312 or 9012 (Forensic Mental Health) programs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Forensic Mental Health Systems
syllabus_overview: The course explores the wide range of forensic mental health systems that exist, and the institutions that receive input from forensic mental health services. Course content will examine the different models of care underpinning these systems, as well as the essential components and roles which are involved in planning a comprehensive mental health service. It aims to provide a detailed understanding of the complex network that is involved in the care of mentally ill people who are in contact with the criminal justice system, including the important role of clinical corporate governance and responsibilities of staff, and human rights in forensic mental health care. Topics covered during the course include the functioning and roles of: the State Parole Authority (NSW); the Serious Offenders Review Council (NSW); Mental Health Review Tribunal; the Health Care Complaints Commission; Australian and NZ Royal College of Psychiatrists; and the Medical Board. Also covered are: Corrections and the Prison Medical Service; Forensic Mental Health Hospitals and secure facilities; and the forensic aspects of psychiatry in the armed forces.
learning_outcomes: Plan and contribute effectively to a comprehensive mental health service for an area, indicating essential components and roles.
Discuss the ethical and human rights issues surrounding medical and legal approaches to managing mentally ill offenders.
Discuss the detailed functions of the institutions and services covered by forensic mental health services and how they interact.
Define the role of clinical corporate governance within forensic mental health services.
Describe the range of demands made on forensic mental health services and the models of care underpinning them.
Define the role of the staff in the various institutions and services, relate the various responsibilities of a range of staff, including moral distress in forensic mental health settings.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Violence
syllabus_overview: The predominant focus of criminal forensic psychiatry is violent behaviour. In order to practise in the criminal forensic psychiatric arena, practitioners need to understand the various types of violence and the epidemiological distribution of violence. The course will provide a broad overview of specific violent behaviours and equip students with a basis upon which to build a more in-depth understanding of the topics. Topics covered in this course will include: the relationship between mental illness and violence, risk assessment of mentally disordered offenders: risk assessments, statistical issues and using the HCR-20 risk assessment tool, violence risk formulation and management, theories of aggression, psychopathy and personality disorder, homicide, domestic violence and other types of offending such as fire-setting, stalkers, extremism, and sexual violence.
learning_outcomes: Use a sound knowledge of the causes and nature of aggressive and violent behaviour when working in forensic mental health professional contexts.
Explain trends in violent crime in Australia and internationally.
Discuss the relationship between mental illness and violence and the limits of knowledge as it pertains to that relationship.
Explain the nature of stalking, arson, homicide, sexual assault and suicide, and apply that knowledge in your practice.
Manage the risk of violence posed by mentally disordered offenders.
Assess and formulate the risk of violence in mentally disordered offenders.
Discuss the epidemiology of violence.
Discuss the consequences of violence for victims and their families, the families of the perpetrators, mental health workers and society in general.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mental Disorders, Personality Disorders & Crime
syllabus_overview: Why do the courts care about mental disorders? Why are psychiatric experts called to give evidence in courts? Why do we not just lock up mentally ill offenders as they pose an unacceptable risk to the community? What are the differences between a mental illness and a personality disorder? Mental illnesses affect around 20% of the population. For some people, these illnesses lead to, or contribute to, a person committing a criminal offence. Mainstream media adds to the stigma and controversy surrounding offending and mental illness, often only reporting on high-profile cases with fatal or catastrophic outcomes and neglecting to report on positive outcomes where intervention has succeeded. To help provide assessment and treatment to this group, society requires a skilled and empathetic workforce who are able to provide a service to this often-maligned group. By dispelling myths and providing factual information we can enhance the services offered to mentally ill offenders and provide better outcomes for them and the community in which we live. This course is delivered fully online. This course is designed to give you a foundational understanding of mental disorders and personality disorders and how these are related to crime. You will be able to describe major mental disorders/illnesses, identify signs and symptoms of these disorders/illnesses and understand the available treatment modalities. With this knowledge and understanding you will be able to make meaningful and feasible recommendations and solutions to courts and decision makers, aligned with your discipline, to reduce the burden of mental disorders on the community and criminal justice system. To assist with consolidating your learning, this course uses real, deidentified cases to highlight common mental disorders and personality disorders, discussing the crimes committed by the individuals and providing insights into treatments available both within the criminal justice system, and in the community for those diverted from full-time custodial sentences.
learning_outcomes: Explain forensic mental health concepts, legal terms and diversion schemes
Critically analyse the theories underpinning forensic mental health assessment and treatment and how these relate to those involved in a criminal justice system
Write a comprehensive assessment and management plan for a justice involved person suffering from a mental disorder or personality disorder
Classify major mental disorders and personality disorders and explain how these can lead to a person being involved in a criminal justice system
Critically appraise how a criminal justice system responds to forensic mental health issues by designing an improved approach based on best practice
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 3831 Science (Medicine) Honours

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Substance Use Problems and Offending
syllabus_overview: The course is an overview of substance use problems and the associations between substance use problems and a range of criminal behaviours and violence, and the interface with the forensic system. We will review the management of people with substance use problems in the forensic system and discuss projects such as the compulsory drug treatment program. Finally, we will look at the ethics of drug policy and harm minimisation principles. Some of the newer addictions will be mentioned. This course will cover the following material: Understanding the nature of substances including alcohol, amphetamines and methamphetamine, cannabis, opioids and other special groups. Understanding the bio-psycho-social model of drug use. The psychiatry of substance abuse. Treatment and control of substance abuse. Association between addictive behaviours, substance use and a range of criminal behaviours and violence. Explore the interface between substance use and the Criminal Justice System including NSW Drug Court and therapeutic jurisprudence. Ethics of drug policy and harm minimisation principles. Substance use among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. Dual Diagnosis treatment strategies and models of care.
learning_outcomes: Explain the treatment options and models of care available for the treatment of substance use disorders and dual diagnosis.
Explain the association between addictive behaviours, substance use and a range of criminal behaviours and violence.
Critically analyse the ethics of current substance use policies and harm minimisation strategies.
Analyse the interface between substance use and criminal justice system such as the NSW Drug Court and therapeutic jurisprudence.
Identify the main classifications of substance use disorders and the main categories of substances of abuse
Explain the biological, psychological and social factors associated with substance use and abuse

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Disordered and Criminal Sexual Behaviour
syllabus_overview: Forensic sexology and, in particular, sexually disordered behaviour, are topical, interesting and exciting areas of study. This course covers a body of research over the past 150 years, and the explosion of a broad range of studies on sexually disordered and sexual offending from the 1980s onwards. Topics studied during this course detail the definitions, epidemiology, aetiology, presentations, diagnosis, assessment issues, treatment and management, recidivism, and risk assessment of the paraphilic disorders. This includes the clinical assessment and comprehensive understanding of the paraphilic disorders including exhibitionism, sexual sadism, paedophilia, zoophilia, necrophilia, voyeurism, frotteurism; those paraphilic disorders or criminal sexual behaviours involving activities which would bring these individuals to the attention of authorities such as transvestism or cybersex; incest; rape; biological and psychosocial sex offender treatments; risk assessment and risk management of these offending behaviours or paraphilic disorders.
learning_outcomes: Use specialist knowledge about assessment, treatment and management in case involving exhibitionism, sexual sadism, child molestation, fetishism, rape, voyeurism, frotteurism and sexual masochism, amongst other sub-categories.
Discuss the forensic, legal, social, psychological implications for sex offenders.

Deploy a sound knowledge of the possible aetiology and clinical presentation of disordered and criminal sexual behaviour when working in forensic, social, legal, welfare, psychological, mental health and other professional contexts.
Assess the risk of sexual, violent and criminal re-offending of general sex offenders and different types of sex offenders.
Explain the varying definitions, terms and diagnostic criteria of various paraphilic disorders, their sub-categories and types of criminal sexual behaviours.
Evaluate a range of sex offender treatments, modalities and management interventions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 3831 Science (Medicine) Honours

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Families, Children, and Adolescent Forensic Psychiatry
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of how children, adolescents and their families’ interact with the civil and criminal legal systems. Practitioners in the field commonly encounter complex cases, and this course provides an overview of the mental health, social and legal aspects of working with young people, with offending and forensic behaviours, and their families. Topics covered include: the law relating to children and adolescents; children in care: civil aspects; adoption and fostering; non-delinquent conduct disorders; young offenders; child custody in relation to offending; Juvenile Justice in NSW; approaches to treatment and facilities available; children and adolescents: reports to court; law and treatment: the Australian Family Law.
learning_outcomes: Describe the normal development of behaviour and emotion in children and the processes of attachment to their carers.
Appraise the range of contributors to the development of offending behaviour in youth and apply that knowledge in your practice.
Explain trends in adolescent offending and recidivism and describe the mental health and substance use patterns of young offenders (behavioural health), both in Australia and internationally.
Apply the evidence base for interventions available to young offenders, with special consideration to young people with complex mental health presentations.
Integrate your knowledge to evaluate the outcomes for children where development is disrupted, such as those with parents who are mentally ill or who fail to provide adequate care and protection.
Examine the role of the Child and Adolescent Forensic professional in civil, family and criminal court matters.
Assess the risk of violence and other forensic behaviours in young offenders and mentally disordered young offenders.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 5512 or 7312 or 9012 (Forensic Mental Health) programs or 9201 Law program

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Civil Law in Relation to Psychiatry
syllabus_overview: This course examines the links between psychiatric and psychological disorders and the various civil law jurisdictions. Course content will provide perspectives on legal theories underpinning relevant legislation and law, as well as insight into the clinical application of these in courtroom and tribunal settings. It integrates legal and psychiatric constructs, appraises contradictions between medical and legal understandings of mental illness, and discusses ethical issues surrounding medical and legal approaches to people with mental disorders involved in the civil law jurisdictions. Topics covered during the course include: introduction to forensic civil psychiatry; principles of torts; medical negligence; the Coroners Court; mental harm; malingering; occupational psychiatry; assessing capacity; and assessing testamentary capacity.

Explain the basic legal concepts of torts law.

Understand common clinical conditions encountered in the context of psychiatric injuries.
Discuss the ethical issues surrounding medical and legal approaches to people with mental disorders involved in the civil law jurisdictions.
Explain the role of the expert witness in civil law proceedings.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Unusual Forensic Behaviours and Special Groups
syllabus_overview: This course is an overview of less common but important forensic mental health topics relating to the unusual behaviours and special groups that can confound health and justice systems. The course will enable students to apply diverse theoretical models to unusual behaviours in order to understand the psychopathology and motivations behind the behaviours. The course will cover a diverse range of rarer psychiatric presentations and special groups such as intellectual disability, deception, property crime, arson, kidnapping, feigned illness, and extremism as well as miscellaneous approaches such as psychological autopsy and understanding the limits of eye witness testimony.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology 1A
syllabus_overview: This course introduces some of the key concepts, theories and methods which underpin psychology as a science. It begins by reviewing historical and scientific foundations for the study of human behaviour. Lectures and tutorials then cover a series of key research topics in psychology, including development, social, emotional, and cultural influences on behaviour, theories of personality and application of psychology to health and wellbeing. Through interactive tutorials, research participation and written assessments, the course aims to train students in psychological research including communicating research findings, developing research questions, and critically evaluating research. There is no assumed knowledge, and the course is suitable for any UNSW undergraduates with an interest in contemporary psychology, behavioral science research methods and the important role of psychological science in modern society.
learning_outcomes: Recognise diverse but complementary theoretical and experimental approaches to major topics in psychology.
Apply psychological research, theories, and principles to everyday life.
Evaluate psychological research in terms of the scientific method and research ethics;
Formulate psychological research questions and propose ways to scientifically and ethically test these questions.
Carry out effective targeted information searches;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology 1B
syllabus_overview: This course introduces psychology as a biological science. The emphasis is on understanding the links between the neurobiology of the brain, sensory organs and nervous system and human behaviour. The lecturers on this course will provide students with diverse perspectives on psychology from various experimental traditions and levels of analysis – behavioural, cognitive and neurophysiological. Topics covered in lectures and tutorials on this course include cognitive psychology, animal learning, psychobiology, perception, and abnormal psychology. Through interactive tutorials, group presentations, research participation and a written essay, the aim of the course is to develop fundamental skills in finding, evaluating, generating, and integrating psychological research evidence. There is no assumed knowledge, and the course is suitable for any UNSW undergraduate with an interest in experimental psychology, cognitive science, clinical psychology and neuroscience.
learning_outcomes: Work in groups and individually to effectively communicate concepts and ideas related to psychology.
Link psychological research, theories and principles to concrete examples of their application in everyday life.
Recognise diverse but complementary theoretical and experimental approaches to major psychological issues.
Locate reliable and relevant information using online research database searches to support scholarly activities.
Evaluate psychological research in terms of the scientific method and research ethics.
prerequisites: None

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Psychological Applications
syllabus_overview: This course offers an introduction to psychology as a scientific discipline and as a profession, with special emphasis on initiating the academic and professional development of students in the Bachelor of Psychology programme. The content of this course is structured around the graduate attributes associated with the scientist-practitioner model, the basis for the training of psychologists in Australia and internationally. You will be introduced to diverse areas of professional psychology practice, and a major focus of the course will be research training within a group setting. This course also provides a first step in your development of psychological literacy, that is, the capacity to intentionally utilise your psychological knowledge, skills and attitudes to achieve personal, professional, and societal goals. In preparing students to “think like a psychologist”, this course will cover topics including critical and creative thinking and fundamentals of research design, as well as providing students with career-relevant perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Individually and collaboratively apply skills of analytical, critical and creative thinking.
Apply career literacy skills e.g. writing an effective curriculum vitae.
Apply psychological knowledge in undertaking research, identifying and developing career pathways, and evaluating scientific literature.
Demonstrate knowledge of ethical issues regarding psychological research.
Apply the key features of undertaking research in psychology: that is, be able to design, conduct, and communicate scientifically meaningful research.
Effectively work in a team, including applying written and oral communication and presentation skills.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 3632 - Psychology (Honours) OR corresponding Double Degrees (3798 or 4721, 4756).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Psychology of Addiction
syllabus_overview: Have you ever wondered why some people become addicted to drugs or alcohol while others do not? Is addiction nature or nurture? Has the War on Drugs been effective at reducing illicit drug use? Is substance use a modern cultural phenomenon? Will using drugs really fry your brain? These questions and more will be explored in The Psychology of Addiction. PSYC1022 is a first-year introductory course with no prior knowledge of Psychology required. The course content is accessible to both science students and those in non-science programs. PSYC1022 provides foundational understanding of biopsychosocial issues relevant to licit and illicit drug use, the development and maintenance of addiction, and the treatments and systems in place to counteract the impact of substance use. The content begins with exploring sociocultural perspectives and historic origins of drugs. We then address psychological and biomedical harms, neuropharmacology, and the effects that drugs of abuse have on learning, motivation, cognition and behaviour. We conclude the course by covering behavioural and pharmacological interventions, preventative education programs and prohibition, and the role of scientific evidence in government policy. Learning activities and assessments are fully online with no face-to-face attendance required. Activities are designed to facilitate active and collaborative learning in small online study groups to enhance your learning experience and foster a supportive online community. Emphasis is placed on students developing Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) strategies, which are particularly beneficial to those who are transitioning into university. PSYC1022 is delivered to a diverse university-wide cohort, giving students the opportunity to meet students outside their own discipline who share similar intellectual interests, whilst benefiting from diverse perspectives and approaches to studying and learning.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective scientific writing skills for the purpose of informing and arguing.
Describe and evaluate research methods used in the field of addiction and interpret numerical data in relation to theoretical issues.
Integrate and evaluate transdisciplinary evidence in order to understand biopsychsocial factors relevant to the development, maintenance, and treatment of addiction.
Discuss major transdisciplinary concepts, theories, research findings, and trends in the field of drug and alcohol addiction.
Apply Self-Regulated Learning strategies to study course content for the purpose of developing effective learning and academic skills.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Abnormal Psychology
syllabus_overview: This course provides a contemporary overview of human mental disorders. It will address questions such as How is “abnormal” defined? What causes mental illnesses and how are they treated? Each week students will explore a different mental disorder (e.g. depression, anxiety, bipolar, OCD, substance use disorder) and discuss the symptoms, causes and treatments. Students will also learn about the scientific models that link factors as well as breakthroughs in scientific understanding and treatment of mental disorders. This course is appropriate for students with and without a background in science and is taught entirely online through Moodle. N.B. This course is not a treatment program for mental health disorders and should not be viewed as a substitute for professional intervention.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend and apply knowledge of major concepts of abnormal psychology with regard to: risk factors, classification, aetiology and treatments of common mental disorders.
Analyse and critique theory and research in the discipline of psychology and communicate these in a written format.
Apply critical thinking skills in order to intellectually engage with literature, differentiate quality empirical evidence from speculation, develop an argument and critique those of others.
Comprehend and apply knowledge of the scientific method in order to understand how these principles are applied in abnormal psychology research and clinical settings.
Demonstrate an understanding of the historical context, ethical principles and values in the area of abnormal psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Perspectives on Anxiety, Mood and Stress
syllabus_overview: This course will provide a comprehensive overview of emotions research, how this produces feelings of stress and how these concepts relate to some of the most common mental disorders - depression and anxiety disorders. Students will learn about psychology as a science and how psychological research is performed (including animal and human studies). Throughout the course we will examine how the findings from this research informs the clinical description of disorders and the treatment of anxiety, stress and low mood. This course is not a treatment program for mental health disorders and should not be viewed as a substitute for professional intervention.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology of Work
syllabus_overview: How can knowledge of psychology help you to be a better manager, employee or employer? This course will examine the ways that industrial and organisational psychology is applied in the workplace. The course will examine research methods used to improve employee well-being and organisational productivity in areas such as recruitment and selection, personality and preferences at work, workplace emotions and assessment, motivation at work, team roles and dynamics, conflict resolution, leadership and organisational culture and change. Effectively communicate in written and verbal formats to convey your own skills and abilities in the context of recruitment, selection and professional development.
Demonstrate effective self-management, interpersonal, and teamwork skills for the purpose of professional and academic development.
