institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology 4A
syllabus_overview: This course complements PSYC4103 Psychology 4B as part of the compulsory coursework requirement of the Honours Program in Psychology. PSYC4093 is split into a core component and an elective component. The core component is taken by all students and comprises a weekly 2-hour lecture (Weeks 1-10) and 1 hour tutorial (Weeks 1-10). The core component covers (i) ethical issues for psychologists, and (ii) history and systems of psychology. The ethics section of the course deals with the principles of ethical conduct by psychologists and places emphasis on ethical issues in professional practice. It provides students with an understanding and familiarity with the regulatory and legislative framework pertaining to the practice of professional psychology. Some attention will be given to ethical issues in research. The history and systems section of the course provides ahistorical introduction to some of the enduring conceptual issues in psychology. Its aim is to clarify contemporary treatments of these issues by considering their past. The elective component is delivered in a seminar mode with students split into smaller groups. Each elective stream engages students with a contemporary research topic and consists of a weekly 2-hour seminar in Weeks 1-10.
learning_outcomes: Analyse contemporary research and practices in psychology with respect to their historical origins and cultural contexts using advanced knowledge of the history and evolution of psychology as a scientific discipline.

Evaluate and resolve ethical issues related to professional and research practice in psychology in a culturally-appropriate way using advanced knowledge of the APS Code of Ethics, legislation, and legal obligations relevant to the field of psychology.

Lead discussion, debate issues, and formulate arguments about the application of contemporary theory and research in psychology to real-world problems by applying advanced oral and written communication skills.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: Enrolled in PSYCAH stream

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology 4B
syllabus_overview: This course complements PSYC4093 Psychology 4A as part of the compulsory coursework requirement of the Honours Program in Psychology. PSYC4103 is split into a core component and an elective component. The core component is taken by all students and comprises a weekly 2-hour lecture (Weeks 1-9) and 1 hour tutorial (Weeks 1-9. The core component takes a scientist-practitioner approach, linking real world problems faced by organisational, forensic and clinical psychologists with empirically-supported interventions. It develops deep understanding of psychological testing, including the theoretical and empirical bases underpinning the construction, implementation, and interpretation of some of the more widely used cognitive and personality assessments. The course also develops foundational skills in the ethical use of psychological tests and foundational knowledge and skills in interviewing and counseling. The elective component is delivered in a seminar mode with students split into smaller groups. Each elective stream engages students with a contemporary topic and consists of a weekly 2-hour seminar (Weeks 1-9 or 2-10).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate strategies for ensuring and improving ethical use of psychological testing by applying advanced understanding of the foundations of psychological assessment and testing techniques widely used in cognitive and personality assessments.
Evaluate evidence-based approaches to psychological intervention in order to solve problems and make recommendations in the context of culturally-responsive professional practice in psychology.

Lead discussion, debate issues, and formulate arguments about the application of contemporary theory and research in psychology to real-world problems using advanced oral and written communication skills.

Conduct a culturally-responsive interview by applying interpersonal skills (active listening, clarifying and reflecting, effective questioning, summarising and paraphrasing, developing rapport, and empathic responding).
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: Enrolled in PSYCAH stream

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evaluating Evidence
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419), providing students with knowledge about the characteristics of the scientific method in general, with a particular focus on experimental methodology, experimental design , and data analysis in the behavioural sciences. It provides a comprehensive foundation in critical thinking, enabling students to understand and critically evaluate published research, and discriminate between evidence-based information and pseudoscience. This includes a background in the design and execution of empirical studies, a basic understanding of statistics and its function in scientific research, the interpretation of experimental findings, and the ability to evaluate conclusions and extrapolate their implications in broader contexts. Students will explore different methodological approaches and data collection and analytic techniques via online lectures and discussion, as well as gaining practical experience in experimental design and the critical evaluation of research. This course is appropriate for students with and without a background in science and is taught entirely online via lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate sources of information and the quality of evidence they provide by assessing the research methodologies and statistical practices applied, and discriminating science from pseudoscience.
Extrapolate from research findings to infer the practical and theoretical implications applicable in broader real-world contexts.
Acknowledge and discuss issues pertaining to experimental and professional ethics in the context of psychological research and its dissemination.
Communicate effectively in written formats to clearly and coherently review the outcomes of empirical research for a broad audience.

Identify and describe characteristics of the scientific method and psychology as a scientific discipline, including theoretical aspects of research methodology, design, data analysis and interpretation in the behavioural sciences.
Design an experiment, interpret results, and draw appropriate evidence-based conclusions, by applying knowledge of research methodology and statistics in the behavioural sciences.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Psychology
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419). It introduces the principles and methods of psychology as a basic science, with specific reference to fundamental topics that will prove relevant to the study of child development. Students will explore the social and biological bases of behaviour in introductory topics including: Human Development, Attention and Memory, Learning and Cognition, Personality and Social Psychology, Abnormal Psychology, and Health Psychology. In addition, students will be trained in the methods of psychological inquiry and the critical evaluation of research. This course is appropriate for students with and without a background in science and is taught entirely online, using a variety of lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Communicate scientific information and arguments effectively in written formats.
Incorporate diverse perspectives and employ a culturally sensitive approach to discussions of psychological constructs, research, and practice.

Apply foundational academic literacy skills in conducting a literature search for peer-reviewed papers, summarising relevant literature, and employing appropriate citation and referencing conventions.

Identify and describe a diverse range of fundamental psychological constructs, including normal and abnormal psychological development, mechanisms of attention, memory, learning, and cognition, social influences on behaviour, and the psychology of health.
Review and discuss evidence-based practice and professional ethics in psychology.
Evaluate competing theoretical and empirical perspectives and effectively select and apply relevant information to support psychological arguments.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Child Development
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419). This course will address topics relating to the development and interaction of biological, cognitive, emotional, and social processes across the stages of early life, including prenatal, infancy, childhood, and adolescence. Course content will review the research methodology, findings, and contemporary theories relating to the normal development of perception, cognition, social interaction, and emotion. Students will gain experience in the design and evaluation of empirical research in the area of developmental psychology, and the application of this research in broader societal contexts. This course is taught entirely online via lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and discuss current theoretical and empirical evidence relating to the biological, cognitive, emotional and social mechanisms that underpin normal developmental change.
Solve everyday problems by applying knowledge of human development and relevant psychological concepts, theories, and research findings to real-world applications.
Apply interpersonal skills to collaborate effectively with peers in a group setting and provide constructive feedback in order to complete projects in a timely, sensitive, and ethical manner.
Evaluate the research design, methodology, and findings of empirical studies of human developmental psychology.

Identify and describe the research and professional ethics and values pertaining specifically to developmental psychology, with the ability to promote evidence-based approaches to understanding and explaining changes in human thought and behaviour across early life.
Critically engage with problems and construct arguments relating to the development of human behaviour and mental processes using the scientific method.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5111 and PSYC5112

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Learning and Cognition
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419). This course will address advanced-level topics relating to learning and cognition. These include models of associative learning, the biological and physiological basis of learning, decision-making (choice, control, and judgement), models of attention and memory, and thinking and reasoning. In addition, this course will discuss the ways in which theories and models of learning and cognition can be applied in child development and education. Course content will review the research methodology, findings, and contemporary theories relating to fundamental learning and cognitive processes. Students will gain experience in conducting empirical research, scientific writing, and the application of theoretical and empirical research to real-world situations. This course is taught entirely online, using a variety of lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Discuss research and professional ethics and values as they apply to the psychology of learning and cognition, with a focus on the evidence-based application of psychological knowledge, interventions, and tools in the context of child development.
Employ sophisticated written and oral discussion skills in the context of psychological science to communicate information in an effective manner, including providing feedback to peers.

Identify and apply advanced knowledge of the major concepts, theories, and empirical findings pertaining to models of learning and memory, their physiological and biological basis, and the higher-order processes of thinking, reasoning, and decision-making.
Evaluate the psychological and biological factors that influence the way children learn, think, and behave, in a manner that is sensitive to cultural and individual diversity.

Apply research methods in the field of learning and cognition at an advanced level, with the ability to evaluate research design and methodology, interpret research findings, draw appropriate conclusions, and discuss their implications.
Critically engage with research and theory in the domain of learning and cognition and apply key principles to discuss child behaviour and development across broader contexts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5111 and PSYC5112

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Developmental Psychopathology
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419). This course will provide an in-depth examination of the most common developmental disorders affecting children and adolescents, including attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), conduct disorder (CD), oppositional defiance disorder (ODD) and eating disorders (ED), anxiety and autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Course content will address contemporary research findings and theories relating to the aetiology and treatment of these conditions, as well as discussion around what is and is not a disorder in the context of official diagnostic criteria and individual variation in developmental milestones and capabilities. Students will gain experience in the design and implementation of empirical research into developmental disorders, as well as the application of psychological tools and interventions in clinical settings. This course is taught entirely online, using a variety of lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe current research and theory pertaining to the nature, aetiology, and treatment of common developmental disorders.
Design and evaluate novel experimental studies in the domain of developmental psychopathology by applying advanced skills in critical thinking and research methodology.

Discuss the importance of codes of conduct when dealing with clinical populations, and the implementation of evidence-based diagnostic tools, interventions, and treatment strategies in clinical practice.

Synthesise knowledge of developmental psychopathology in order to solve problems and formulate suggestions for improving policy and practice in broader societal contexts (e.g. education, health, and legal systems).
Employ sophisticated skills in scientific writing to effectively and concisely convey details of novel research and findings in the format of an academic research article.
Discuss contemporary issues pertaining to research in the domain of developmental psychopathology, and in translating this research to inform clinical practice and policies in broader contexts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5113 and PSYC5114

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Wellbeing and Resilience
syllabus_overview: This course forms part of the Graduate Certificate in Child Development (7419), and will address advanced-level topics relating to the development and maintenance of wellbeing and resilience in children and adolescents. These include self-esteem, self-efficacy, coping, risk-taking, and responsibility. Course content will involve a critical review of current research findings and contemporary theories pertaining to development within these topic areas, as well as a discussion of factors that can interact with and obstruct this development. Students will develop skills in the creation of novel research questions, translating empirical data to real-world contexts with practical applications, and disseminating scientific ideas in a variety of formats for different purposes. This course is taught entirely online via lectures, tutorials (synchronous and asynchronous options), self-paced learning modules, readings and revision exercises.
learning_outcomes: Review and interpret an advanced body of knowledge about the core factors that contribute to the development and maintenance of wellbeing and resilience in early life, including related empirical research and theory.
Design empirical investigations into childhood/adolescent wellbeing, including an evaluation of where current evidence is lacking, and the derivation of novel research questions for testing.
Write effectively in a variety of formats, in a manner that is sensitive to the values and beliefs of others and is considerate of different perspectives.
Innovate evidence-based solutions to applied problems in the domain of psychological wellbeing by integrating empirical and theoretical information about key constructs and their interrelationship.
Recognise and apply the values and ethics of psychology, specifically with respect to the accurate and unbiased translation of scientific research into the public domain.

Apply effective interpersonal communication skills to engage in productive and respectful discussion with peers around the interpretation and application of psychological research, including the provision of critical, actionable feedback.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5113 and PSYC5114

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: History and Professional Ethics in Psychology
syllabus_overview: This is a core course that forms part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program. The course covers the history and systems of psychology and the ethical issues for psychologists. The history and systems section of the course provides an historical overview to some of the enduring conceptual issues in psychology. It aims is to clarify contemporary treatments of these issues by considering their past. The ethics section of the course deals with the principles of ethical conduct by psychologists and places emphasis on ethical issues in professional practice. It provides students with an understanding and familiarity with the regulatory and legislative framework pertaining to the practice of professional psychology. The course will cover ethical issues in psychological research, including animal research. Students will gain advanced knowledge in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Articulate advanced disciplinary knowledge, clearly and effectively through written information.
Discuss the APS code of Ethics, legislation, and legal obligations relevant to the practice of professional psychology.
Manage ethical issues by using advanced knowledge of ethical frameworks.
Evaluate the key theoretical concepts of the history and evolution of psychology as a discipline.
Identify and solve ethical issues presented in the context of case studies from the discipline of psychological practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Research Methods and Statistics
syllabus_overview: This course is one of the core units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology program. This course provides students with advanced skills in the application of statistical methodology for the analysis and interpretation of empirical data in the behavioural sciences. It builds upon an established foundation in critical thinking and the evaluation of scientific evidence, equipping students with the capability to design and execute empirical investigations, collect and collate data, apply appropriate analytic techniques, and correctly interpret experimental findings. Students will gain practical experience in a range of methodological approaches to data collection and analysis via online lectures, activities, and live Q & A discussion sessions. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Integrate the values and ethics of psychology, including sensitivity to cultural and individual diversity, when developing and reporting on empirical research studies.
Present the outcomes, conclusions, and broader implications of statistical analyses through clear and coherent written communication.
Evaluate the implementation and interpretation of different psychological test measures.
Apply advanced methodologies and statistical approaches to design, analyse, and interpret a research study in the psychological sciences.
Review empirical literature and synthesise key concepts, theories, and evidence relating to a particular research domain.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Application of Psychological Practice
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with an understanding of the theoretical and empirical bases underpinning evidence‐based approaches to psychological intervention. Students will develop foundational knowledge and skills in interviewing and counselling, and advanced disciplinary knowledge. The course will explore a range of topics covering Clinical, Forensic and Organisational psychology. Students will focus on key aspects of professional practice within the relevant legal frameworks. Students will gain advanced knowledge of major psychological assessment tools, including evidence based critical evaluation of these tools, via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Use empathetic and responsive communication in a manner that is culturally appropriate and sensitive to the diversity of individuals in the context of interviewing and counselling.
Evaluate the theoretical and empirical bases that underpin the construction, implementation and interpretation of widely used psychological assessment tools.
Analyse the theoretical and empirical findings that underpin the specialised advanced knowledge required in some key areas in the practice of psychology.
Present a clear and coherent exposition of knowledge and ideas to a variety of audiences with high-level written and verbal communication skills.
Synthesise the evidence-based research for a range of psychological interventions regarding major psychological disorders within the relevant legal framework.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Behavioural Neuroscience
syllabus_overview: This course provides an advanced examination of the processes of learning and memory and the neurobiological mechanism that underpin them. These include learning about relations between events (Pavlovian conditioning), learning about relations between one’s behaviour and events (Instrumental conditioning), and how these forms of learning control behaviours. Emphasis is placed on contemporary theories and approaches including the role of interactions between environmental events, synapses and genes. Topics include: appetitive and aversive motivation in learning, behaviour and psychopathology; Pavlovian conditioning; instrumental conditioning; the neural mechanisms that underpin memory. Students will gain advanced knowledge in Behavioural Neuroscience, via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced skills in critical thinking in order to analyse the current peer-reviewed research across a range of topics in the field of behavioural neuroscience.
Relate advanced knowledge in the field of behavioural neuroscience to a wider community context, with a focus on the translation of current research to psychological interventions.
Present current research and theory in the field of behavioural neuroscience in a clear and effective manner, in both oral and written formats.
Evaluate key concepts in the field of behavioural neuroscience with an advanced understanding of the theoretical perspectives and empirical findings that underpin these.
Demonstrate empathetic communication skills that are sensitive to the diversity of others.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mental Health and Illness
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with advanced disciplinary knowledge in the area of Clinical Psychology. The course will involve the evidence-based practice for the diagnosis and treatment of a range of mental health disorders. The course will provide students with an advanced understanding of the theoretical background, diagnosis and treatment of a range of mental health issues, including depression, anxiety, schizophrenia and substance abuse. The course focuses on the current research in this area and provides students with the tools to critically evaluate this evidence to develop best practice in the field of Psychology. Students will gain advanced knowledge in some the key areas of Clinical Psychology, via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced skills in critical thinking in order to analyse the current peer-reviewed research across a range of topics in the field of clinical psychology.
Demonstrate empathetic communication skills that are sensitive to the diversity of others.
Evaluate key concepts in the field of clinical psychology with an advanced understanding of the theoretical perspectives and empirical findings that underpin these.
Relate advanced knowledge in the field of clinical psychology to a wider community context, with a focus on the translation of current research to psychological interventions.
Present current research and theory in the field of clinical psychology in a clear and effective manner, in both oral and written formats.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cognitive Science
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with advanced disciplinary knowledge in the field of cognitive psychology, examining the theoretical basis of how we think. The course will cover key concepts including, attention, memory, judgement and decision making. The course will provide students with an advanced understanding of the theories and models used in this area. The course will focus on contemporary issues such as misinformation, climate change and decision making in the modern world. Students will develop the skills required to critically evaluate the theories and models used to explain the behaviour associated with these areas of cognition. Students will learn to apply this knowledge to a wider community context. Students will gain advanced knowledge in cognitive psychology, via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Relate advanced knowledge in the field of cognitive science to a wider community context, with a focus on the translation of current research to psychological interventions.
Evaluate key concepts in the field of cognitive science with an advanced understanding of the theoretical perspectives and empirical findings that underpin these.
Present current research and theory in the field of cognitive science in a clear and effective manner, in both oral and written formats.
Demonstrate empathetic communication skills that are sensitive to the diversity of others.
Apply advanced skills in critical thinking in order to analyse the current peer-reviewed research across a range of topics in the field of cognitive science.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Graduate Diploma in Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Social Psychology
syllabus_overview: This course provides an advanced examination of the current research that addresses the nature of the individual and their interaction with the social environment. This course will focus on topics relating to self-identity, culture and social dynamics and constructs. Topics will include the formation of identity, cross-cultural psychology, indigenous psychology, biological mechanisms underpinning social learning and attribution, as well as social disorders. The course will cover the theoretical and experimental evidence for a range of social phenomena. The course will explore the importance of understanding the self and society within a broad and diverse context. Students will gain advanced knowledge in social psychology, via a combination of online instructional videos and activities and small-group seminars. This course is taught entirely online.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project: Introduction Part 1
syllabus_overview: This course is the first in the series of research units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program. In this course students are guided in the processes of identifying a research question, conducting a literature search, and outlining a research design for the purposes of writing the introduction chapter of the thesis. This course will draw upon and enhance students’ existing body of psychological knowledge and established skills in information synthesis and problem-solving. Students will gain knowledge and practical experience in the stage 1 implementation of a research project in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities, small-group seminars, and one-on-one academic supervision. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Incorporate the values and ethics of psychology when developing a research focus for empirical study, such that the design accommodates cultural and individual diversity.
Apply advanced research skills to generate novel research questions for investigation that show an appreciation for methodological constraints of research in psychology.
Collate literature covering a range of theoretical perspectives and empirical findings to provide a comprehensive overview of a particular domain of psychological inquiry.
Apply advanced psychological knowledge to assess the current state of the evidence in a particular psychological domain and identify avenues for further investigation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in program 5332 Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project: Introduction Part 2
syllabus_overview: This course is the second in the series of research units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program, and follows on directly from PSYC5208 Research Project Introduction Part 1. In this course students are guided in the processes of constructing a research proposal, and conducting a literature review for the purposes of writing the introduction chapter of the thesis. This course will draw upon and enhance established skills in the critical evaluation of empirical evidence, applied research methodology and problem-solving, and coherent written communication. Students will gain knowledge and practical experience in the stage 1 implementation of a research project in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities, small-group seminars, and one-on-one academic supervision. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe psychological test instruments suitable for application in specific psychological research contexts.
Apply advanced research and problem-solving skills to produce a sensible research proposal for an experimental study
Articulate advanced psychological knowledge via effective written communications suitable for a broad audience.

Synthesise a range of theoretical perspectives and empirical findings in a particular domain of psychological inquiry to produce a rationale for empirical investigation that furthers that line of inquiry.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5208 and enrolment in program 5332 Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project: Methods
syllabus_overview: This course is the third in the series of research units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program. In this course students are guided in the processes of identifying and operationalising research variables, evaluating psychological tools of measurement and assessment, and constructing a reliable and valid research design, which will culminate in writing the methodology chapter of the thesis. This course will draw upon and enhance established knowledge of research methodology in the behavioural sciences and develop a contextually grounded appreciation for the respectful and ethical execution of psychological assessment. Students will gain knowledge and practical experience in the stage 2 implementation of a research project in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities, small-group seminars, and one-on-one academic supervision. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate a range of psychological assessment tools, including a consideration of their applicability, reliability, and validity under different conditions.

Communicate scientific knowledge through the clear and coherent articulation of methodological information, with a degree of detail sufficient for other researchers to accurately replicate the method.
Formulate an effective, appropriate, and feasible procedural design for an empirical research project.
Draw upon both practical and theoretical knowledge of psychology to tailor methodological approaches according to specific characteristics of the research context.
Discuss ethical considerations relevant to the undertaking of research and assessment in psychology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5208 and PSYC5209 and enrolment in program 5332 Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project: Results Part 1
syllabus_overview: This course is the fourth in the series of research units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program. In this course students are guided in the collection, organisation, and summarising of empirical data, which will be applied in writing the results chapter of the thesis. This course will draw upon and enhance existing knowledge pertaining to the rationale underpinning different statistical approaches, as well as skills in data description and presentation. Students will gain knowledge and practical experience in the stage 3 implementation of a research project in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities, small-group seminars, and one-on-one academic supervision. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Use graphical representations to present empirical findings in a manner readily interpretable by a broad audience.
Apply knowledge of statistical principles to identify suitable methods of analysing specific datasets
Record and appropriately interpret the outcomes of various psychological assessment measures.
Collate and summarise complex datasets independently, identifying and extracting key information.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5210 and enrolment in program 5332 Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project: Thesis
syllabus_overview: This course is the sixth and last in the series of research units that form part of the Graduate Diploma in Psychology (Advanced) program. In this course students will be guided in the discussion of research findings in relation to the empirical literature and broader societal contexts, a consideration of methodological limitations of psychological research, and the dissemination of research findings to a broad audience. This will be applied in writing the discussion chapter of the thesis, and subsequently collating the full thesis for submission. Students will gain knowledge and experience in the final stage 4 implementation of a research project in psychology via a combination of online instructional videos and activities, small-group seminars, and one-on-one academic supervision. This course is taught entirely online.
learning_outcomes: Produce a dissertation that synthesises advanced knowledge of psychology both broadly and in a specific research domain.
Identify and discuss opportunities for the application of empirical findings in psychology across diverse, real-world contexts.
Disseminate theoretical and empirical information to a broad audience through clear and coherent written and oral communication.

Identify and describe strengths and limitations of research methodology in the psychological sciences and apply critical thinking and problem-solving skills to formulate novel ideas and suggestions for future research opportunities.
Incorporate the values and ethics of psychology when engaging in psychological discourse.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: PSYC5211 and PSYC5212 and enrolment in program 5332 Advanced Psychology.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychological Assessment
syllabus_overview: Psychological Assessment teaches students how to use, administer and interpret major psychological tests, including the Wechsler Intelligence scales and other tests used routinely to assess memory and cognition. It also addresses issues in determining real and unusual differences in test scores, the influence of cultural factors on norms and test interpretation as well as the communication of assessment findings. It is assumed that candidates will have covered topics to do with test validity and reliability in prior courses. This course entails theoretical and practical components presented in a series of 1 hour lectures and 2 hour practicals. The course covers fundamental issues for students training to become Clinical Psychologists. Case examples throughout the course are provided to ensure relevance is clear. Teaching strategies of PSYC7001 encourage candidates to think and act as professional interns. Material covering important theoretical and practical knowledge, general principles in assessment and particular methodological issues to do with test instruments will be covered in lectures. Specific skills in tests and assessment procedures will be taught in practical tutorials. Test interpretation and report writing will be taught via programmed assignment work or other activities in the tutorials. Candidates are encouraged to work both independently and in small groups to learn test administration and test interpretation. While tutorial time will focus upon teaching skills in targeted assessment procedures, it is expected that candidates will practice these techniques outside formal teaching hours in order to reach a criterion level of competency. Candidates should also make use of the Test Library, to acquaint themselves with different kinds of tests available for assessment that are not necessarily covered in the course.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the importance of qualitative and convergent information, and the limitations surrounding test measurement.
Explain the impact of cultural and cohort effects on normative data as well as how individual characteristics such as personality and motivation can influence test performance.
Competently and accurately write a report that represents test scores, conveys meaningful information, and is suitable for a range of readers.
Relate the constructs measured by different tests and interpret differences between scores.
Administer and score psychometric tests associated with intelligence, memory, academic performance and other areas including language and executive function.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 1400 Psychology or 1404 Psychology (Clinical)/Psychology or 8256 Psychology (Clinical)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Neuropsychology
syllabus_overview: This course introduces clinical psychologists to the principles of neuropsychology. The course commences with an overview of the neuroanatomy of the brain, followed by discussion of major areas of cognitive function that can be disrupted by focal brain lesions. Some common neurological disorders will then be described including characteristic presentations on cognitive testing. The course will finish with a focus on rehabilitation of brain injury and evidence-based practice for interventions to address neuropsychological disorders. This course is designed to equip Clinical Psychologists to safely interact with, assess and treat adults with acquired brain damage. It is expected that candidates who have completed PSYC7210 will be confidently able to undertake basic neuropsychological assessment and prepare reports for real clients, under the supervision of a professional psychologist. They should also be able to interpret neuropsychological reports written by others, appreciate the importance and influence of cultural context on the manifestation and impact of neuropsychological impairment, devise therapy programs that take into account cognitive deficits and appreciate how a psychologist operates within a multidisciplinary team. The course entails 2 x two hour lectures each week, which will include case discussions. It is expected that students will spend an additional 6 hours per week reading and researching each topic discussed in class.
learning_outcomes: Explain how cultural context influences test performance, family function and rehabilitation goals.
Integrate evidence-based approaches to remediation and rehabilitation, and the role of other disciplines in patient care and rehabilitation.
Accurately identify major lobes of the brain, subcortical structures, connections, and blood supplies.
Relate basic features and theoretical perspectives of major neuropsychological disorders and major neurological conditions.
Explain the patterns of test performance that characterise neuropsychological disorders along with the importance of qualitative information and observed behaviours.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Restricted to programs 1400, 1404 and 8256

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Adult and Child Clinical Psychology 2
syllabus_overview: Consistent with PSYC7212, this course provides theoretical knowledge and practical skills in child and adult clinical psychology for candidates undertaking postgraduate training in clinical psychology. The focus is on aetiology, assessment, diagnosis, case conceptualisation, and empirically-supported treatment of clinical disorders across the lifespan. These problems will be considered within the individual client’s relevant sociocultural context, with consideration given to providing culturally-responsive approaches to clinical care and collaboration with other professionals if indicated. The course is guided by a scientist-practitioner approach and covers best practice guidelines, with particular emphasis on consideration of our professional obligation to conduct safe and ethical practice and to protect the public while delivering evidence-based clinical services. The teaching activities include lectures, interactive activities (e.g., group discussions, role-plays), and self-guided online modules. Individual lecturers may assign readings that should be completed prior to the lecture.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced psychological knowledge, including theories of psychological disorders, models of health, and international taxonomies, to their practice in clinical psychology as it relates to common psychological disorders.

Apply advanced psychological knowledge to culturally-responsive interventions in clinical psychology, including selection of interventions, appreciation of contextual issues and collaboration with other professionals, as it relates to common psychological disorders.

Apply advanced psychological knowledge to culturally-responsive assessment in clinical psychology, including use of assessment processes, development of case formulation and evaluation of client processes, as it relates to common psychological disorders.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Restricted to programs 1400, 1404 and 8256

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychology of Health and Illness
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the applications of psychological principles, derived from human and animal research, to human health and rehabilitation including health promotion, risk factor reduction, psychological assessment, management and remediation of medical and neurological disorders, with a special focus on chronic illnesses. It forms part of postgraduate level training in Clinical Psychology and develops the knowledge and skills of candidates in working in health-related clinical settings.
learning_outcomes: Describe the diagnosis, assessment and treatment issues relevant to common psychology-related health problems.
Develop behaviour change and health promotion strategies in the context of psychology-related health problems.
Compare and contrast prevalent theories of health behaviours through the critical review of health and psychology literature.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evidence Based Clinical Psychology
syllabus_overview: A continuation of the problem-oriented approach begun in PSYC7212, this course examines the theoretical basis of models of psychopathology, assessment and intervention, and related professional issues. This course covers a range of topics which include psychopharmacology, and evidence-based practice for a range of conditions. The course entails 2 x two-hour face-to-face workshops each week, delivered by UNSW School of Psychology academics as well as discipline-expert guest speakers. There is an emphasis on the development of critical evaluation of the evidence base for psychological therapies; hence, in the final weeks, candidates work in groups to develop their own workshops on an evidence-based psychological therapy to deliver to the class.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how common psychotropics interact with psychological treatments and describe the resultant implications for inter-professional practice.
Compare and contrast psychopharmacological therapies used in the treatment of psychological disorders, and identify the advantages and disadvantages of each.
Identify and evaluate issues associated with ethical research and safe practice of clinical psychology.
Compare and contrast empirically-supported treatments of psychological disorders.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Topics in Clinical Psychology
syllabus_overview: This is an advanced course within the Master of Psychology (Clinical) program comprising a workshop series that explores complex clinical issues, including working with severe client presentations and specific client populations. Candidates will be encouraged to take an evidence-based approach, linking research evidence, clinical judgment and diversity factors. This course introduces the theory and practice of more severe psychological conditions, including defining features and characteristics; diagnostic and assessment issues; evidence-based intervention strategies; and procedures for evaluating outcome of interventions. This course emphasises the importance of individual and cultural diversity factors in the practice of clinical psychology when working with clients from diverse backgrounds. The course also focuses on developing the understanding of candidates in inter-professional learning and practice, including consultation and collaboration with other professionals particularly in the context of complex client presentations.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced psychological knowledge to interventions in clinical psychology, including selection of interventions and appreciation of contextual issues, as it relates to severe and complex mental health issues.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Neuropsychology 1: Disruptions
syllabus_overview: This course orientates clinical psychologists to the principles of neuropsychology and how neuropsychological processes can be disrupted. It builds on assumed knowledge (basic neuropsychology, psychopharmacology, neuroanatomy, test administration) that form part of the core competencies of registered psychologists that have previously completed Level 3 and 4 post-graduate training. The course commences with refreshers concerning the assessment of major neuropsychological systems, including memory, executive function, behaviour, social cognition, language and perception and the assessment of premorbid abilities and performance validity. The course then focuses on neuropsychological disorders that affect older adults, considering genetic, medical and psychosocial precursors to dementia, use of biomarkers and cognitive and behavioural assessments to facilitate differential diagnosis. Issues with respect to assessing the older adult and managing cognitive decline will be addressed. In addition, the course will focus on the major categories of neuropsychiatric disorders, including mood disorders, trauma and psychosis as well as comorbidities. The course will conclude with a focus on building mental health and resilience in these populations. This course is the first course you must enrol in, along with PSYC7237. The course combines asynchronous lectures (1 – 2 hours), two-hour practical tutorials, and workshops. The focus will be on specific cases using problem-based learning approaches, for example, when discussing a case of Alzheimer’s Disease, the neuroanatomy, common neuropsychological profile (e.g. amnesia and aphasia), recent neuroscientific theories (e.g. of memory and language), psychopharmacological interventions, assessment approaches, cultural considerations, communication with other relevant professionals, report writing and remediation implications will be considered. Students will be expected to take an active role in preparing for, presenting and discussing cases to foster opportunities for peer-to-peer learning. While lectures will focus upon the basic elements of neuropsychology, the topic is a broad one and the study guide and reference lists provide the opportunity for in-depth study. It is expected that students will independently read on each topic discussed in class. In addition, students are encouraged to prepare for case tutorials in small groups, in order to hone skills in test interpretation and critical consideration of treatment approaches. All the tests discussed are available in the Test Library and students are encouraged to familiarise themselves with these as they come up in class. This is a unique opportunity to develop this knowledge base, because few professional settings will offer as expansive a resource in tests as does the UNSW Test Library. Finally, the material presented in this course will be of direct relevance when conducting neuropsychological assessments on placement. Lecture notes and references should be utilised heavily when taking on such clients.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Neuropsychology 2: Lifespan
syllabus_overview: This course builds on Neuropsychology 1: Disruptions by providing an in-depth understanding of how neuropsychological function and disorders manifest across the life span. The course focuses on normal and abnormal development of the central nervous system, a range of developmental, acquired and genetic disorders that can disrupt neural and cognitive development in childhood and the impact of these disorders when acquired in adulthood. Students will participate in active problem solving of common issues that arise with respect to assessment and interventions in children and adults, as well as methods for working within the broader context of families, schools and support providers. Major categories of brain disruption will be covered including damage arising from head trauma, stroke, epilepsy, neurological disease (Multiple Sclerosis, Huntington’s Disease), neurosurgery, oncology, and substance use. It is expected that students who have completed PSYC7241 will be confidently able to interview clients of all ages, including children and their families, undertake a comprehensive medical and psychosocial history, select appropriate assessment instruments, interpret neuropsychological test data and qualitative information to diagnose a disorder, appreciate the importance and influence of cultural context on the manifestation and impact of neuropsychological impairment, and understand how to work with the family and other organisations and professionals to support the child with cognitive and/or behavioural difficulties. The course combines asynchronous lectures (1 – 2 hours) with two-hour practical tutorials or occasional full day workshops. The content is designed to focus on specific cases using problem-based learning approaches. Thus, for example, when discussing a case of foetal alcohol syndrome, the neuroanatomy, common neuropsychological profile, assessment approaches, cultural considerations, communication with other relevant professionals, report writing and remediation implications will be considered. Students will be expected to take an active role in preparing for, presenting and discussing cases to foster opportunities for peer-to-peer learning. Students will be provided with preliminary readings and case material in order to prepare for the tutorials. Case discussions will provide class members the opportunity to practice integrating lecture-based information in order to plan the assessment, diagnosis and management of individuals with neuropsychological disorders and consider the broader assessment context (cultural factors, roles of other professionals, additional neuro-clinical tests, co-morbidities). While lectures will focus upon the basic elements of neuropsychology, the topic is a broad one and the study guide and reference lists provide the opportunity for in-depth study. It is expected that students will independently read on each topic discussed in class. In addition, students are encouraged to prepare for case studies in small groups, in order to hone skills in test interpretation and critical consideration of treatment approaches. All the tests discussed are available in the Test Library and students are encouraged to familiarise themselves with these as they come up in class. This is a unique opportunity to develop this knowledge base, because few professional settings will offer as expansive a resource in tests as does the UNSW Test Library. Finally, the material presented in this course will be of direct relevance when conducting neuropsychological assessments on placement. Lecture notes and references should be utilised heavily when taking on such clients.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Neuropsychology 3: Interventions
syllabus_overview: This course builds on Neuropsychology 1 & 2 (PSYC7240 and PSYC7241) by focusing on interventions for children, adults and older adults who have neuropsychological disorders. The course is based around workshops that address major tenets in neuropsychological interventions, (1) clinical psychological approaches in people with neuropsychological disorders (2) cognitive remediation of neuropsychological disorders (3) behaviour management and carer support. Throughout this course, the scientist practitioner model is emphasised, specifically trainees will be trained to understand the importance of evidence-based practice, procedures in how to evaluate evidence and how and when to use practice guidelines (information that is additionally covered in NPEP 1). As a result of the teaching and learning strategies outlined in this course, it is expected that students who have completed PSYC7242 will be confidently able to research, evaluate and select appropriate interventions to address neuropsychological disorders from childhood through to adulthood, to adapt these to take into account the cultural, familial and community context and appreciate how a neuropsychologist operates within a multidisciplinary team. Specifically, trainees will learn to consider how cognitive behavioural and counselling approaches they are already familiar with can be adapted to facilitate functioning in people with neuropsychological disorders. They will also be introduced to how cognitive rehabilitation based on brain plasticity has been applied to a range of neuropsychological disorders (e.g. social cognition, spatial neglect, self-awareness). In addition, they will learn about behavioural approaches to improving interpersonal function and strategies for carer support. They will also appreciate how these approaches can be combined for maximum effect. The course combines day workshops with asynchronous lectures and tutorials. The content is designed to focus on specific cases using problem-based learning approaches. Thus, for example, when discussing a case of an adult with traumatic brain injury, the common neuropsychological and behavioural difficulties will be discussed and strategies for intervention canvassed and compared in the context of cultural considerations and the role of other relevant professionals. Students will be expected to take an active role in preparing for, presenting and discussing cases. Many treatment manuals discussed are available in the Test Library and students are encouraged to familiarise themselves with these as they come up in class. This is a unique opportunity to develop this knowledge base, because few professional settings will offer as expansive a resource in intervention manuals as does the UNSW Test Library. Finally, the material presented in this course will be of direct relevance when conducting neuropsychological assessments and implementing interventions on placement. Lecture notes and references should be utilised heavily when taking on such clients.

syllabus_overview: This course involves an in-depth study of selected topics from the field of Psychology and law that have been subjected to rigorous experimental study. The course particularly focuses on the design of research in Psychology-law, on the relationship between research and policy and on attempts to use research to inform changes to public policy and law. Example topics include Eyewitness identification evidence, Traumatic Brain Injury and offending, Decision making in forensic science and Risk assessment. The sessions are delivered in a tutorial format where students present and discuss selected readings. This course is designed for students in the Master of Psychology (Forensic) program.

syllabus_overview: This course provides continued training in psychological assessment, treatment skills and ethical practices as required in the professional context. This course is associated with external placements as part of the requirements for competency attainment. Presented through lectures and workshops, material is balanced between lectures, case presentations and hands on experiential learning leading to in vivo experience in placements.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate skill development through reflective and reflexive tasks, and feedback from others.
Communicate effectively (orally and in writing) and respectfully in a variety of formats and contexts in multidisciplinary forensic psychology environments.
Apply critical thinking skills to ethical decision making, client assessments, and intervention techniques.
Apply knowledge of Forensic Psychological practice in order to utilise a culturally respectful, evidence-based approach to understand and change behaviour and attitudes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in (1405 Psychology (Forensic)/Psychology OR 8257 Psychology (Forensic)) AND PSYC7419

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Assessment in Forensic Psychology
syllabus_overview: This course presents a framework of standardised tests and procedures used by psychologists to evaluate intellectual, cognitive and adaptive functioning, as well as tests used to evaluate general psychological functioning. Students are presented with technical, administrative, scoring and interpretation of a sampling of standardised tests with an emphasis on tests typically used by forensic psychologists in forensic contexts, especially within the court system.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the validity of test results and individual test profiles.
Apply knowledge of psychological testing in order to evaluate the utility of individual tests and their use in the forensic context at an individual and group level.
Evaluate the limitations of psychological test measurement and how limitations are communicated and integrated in the context of a forensic assessment.
Competently administer and score Wechsler Scales and other cognitive and psychological tests with adequate standardization.
Communicate effectively and accurately in a written report the results of test scores for a forensic audience.
Communicate concepts around the framework of psychometric principles and theories underlying standardised psychological testing methodology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 1405 Psychology (Forensic)/Psychology OR 8257 Psychology (Forensic)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Forensic Interventions 1
syllabus_overview: This course takes a scientist-practitioner approach, connecting a framework of how psychological intervention works. A strong emphasis will be placed on links between research and clinical practice and how one informs the other. Teaching activities include lectures and interactive learning activities.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of the common factors involved in therapeutic engagement with forensic clients including reflective practice as part of culturally sensitive professional and ethical practice.
Effectively utilize ROM (Routine Outcome Measurements) techniques to measure and evaluate treatment outcomes.
Conduct a culturally responsive case formulation leading to an effective treatment plan utilizing forensic and clinical skillsets.
Conduct preliminary differential diagnosis of psychological and forensic psychological disorders and risk using dominant diagnostic frameworks and considering systemic and cultural issues.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 1405 Psychology (Forensic)/Psychology OR 8257 Psychology (Forensic)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Forensic Interventions 2
syllabus_overview: The course provides theoretical knowledge and practical skills for working with various vulnerable forensic populations, with consideration to the relevant social and cultural context, including ethical and systemic issues that confront these specific populations. Course content is delivered through a flipped classroom environment, where students prepare through readings and a guest expert comes in to discuss topics related to particular vulnerable populations, such as people across the lifespan who have experienced neglect or abuse, interpersonal violence, mental health or cognitive challenges, or displacement.
learning_outcomes: Create culturally appropriate and responsive case formulations by applying major theoretical frameworks to case specific information.
Critique the diversity of systemic approaches to working with vulnerable populations.
Formulate an ethical framework for working with various vulnerable forensic populations.
Evaluate the theoretical and practical aspects of specialised assessment and treatment for specific vulnerable forensic populations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 1405 Psychology (Forensic)/Psychology OR 8257 Psychology (Forensic)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Thesis (Forensic) 2
syllabus_overview: This course is for students enrolled in the postgraduate MPsychol(Forensic) Program. Students are required to complete an empirical research project under the supervision of a member of academic staff in the School of Psychology which is written up as a thesis in the form of a journal article. Research projects may be carried out on any topic that is relevant to forensic psychology. The thesis and research project are assessed across three courses – Thesis 1, Thesis 2 and Thesis 3 – in which students would normally be expected to enrol for terms 1 to 3 respectively.
learning_outcomes: Apply a high level of critical thinking and technical skill in research design and communication.
Independently undertake research activities in an ethical manner.
Critically review literature associated with a research-based project.
Present a clear and coherent synthesis of forensically relevant, ethical research, and its significance to a variety of audiences.
Plan and execute a research-based project that is applicable to the field of forensic psychology.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 8257 Psychology (Forensic)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Professional Psychological Practice
syllabus_overview: This course provides continued training in psychological competencies, including assessment, intervention and ethical practices as required in the professional psychology context. Activities undertaken during placement typically include client work, supervision, placement administrative responsibilities, client preparations, and professional development activities that support clinical practice. Additional hours may also be required to demonstrate sufficient professional competencies. This course is associated with placements at internal UNSW-based training clinics and external field placement sites, as per psychology accreditation requirements. This is a Workplace Integrated Learning (WIL) course.
learning_outcomes: Be professional and accountable in all areas of professional activities including concern for welfare of others, responsiveness to supervision and timely approach to clinical work, and, apply ethical and professional codes, standards and guidelines in professional work, demonstrating a clear commitment to their application and an overarching obligation to protect the public.
Work with the client, carers and relevant professionals to actively integrate individual perspectives and cultural considerations into all aspects of client care.

Apply knowledge of psychological theories of cognition, behaviour, and emotion in clinical assessments, case conceptualisation and diagnosis, and apply critical thinking skills in the selection of evidence-based interventions according to individual needs across the lifespan.

Communicate effectively and respectively (orally and in writing) in a variety of formats and contexts in multidisciplinary environments and to a range of audiences including consultation with other professionals and sensitively communicating with individuals of all ages and cognitive abilities
Demonstrate skilful delivery of counselling skills and evidence-based interventions, taking a collaborative and responsive approach

Assess cognitive, behavioural, affective, and psychosocial function using psychometrically sound tools that are appropriate and sensitive, including application of knowledge regarding performance validity and premorbid ability.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 1404 Psychology (Clinical)/Psychology; OR 8256 Psychology (Clinical); OR 1405 Psychology (Forensic)/Psychology; OR 8257 Psychology (Forensic); OR 8266 Clinical Neuropsychology

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Practices in the Petroleum Industry
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of communication skills and business practices within the petroleum industry. Students will learn professional communication techniques, including interview preparation, meeting skills, written report and resume creation, oral presentation skills, and ethical considerations specific to the industry. The course also delves into key business practices, such as understanding Joint Ventures, production sharing contracts, gas contracts, and company structures. It covers strategies for acreage and reserves acquisition, farming/farmouts, and the analysis of company reports. Additionally, it explores reserves reporting and the dynamics of relationships with governments and partners. This course equips students with the essential skills and knowledge for a successful career in the petroleum industry.
learning_outcomes: Present themselves and an argument in a professional and effective manner, in person, orally and in writing using simple business English
Recognise business terminology and practices of the oil & gas industry
Identify the elements of petroleum law, oil and gas accounting and reserves estimation
Identify the basics of environmental protection and the challenges and opportunities presented by shale gas and coal seam gas

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reservoir Engineering A
school: School of Minerals & Energy Resources Engineering
syllabus_overview: This fundamental course provides students with a comprehensive understanding of the principles, concepts, and techniques used to quantify subsurface reservoirs. It will cover basic concepts of origin, accumulation and recovery of hydrocarbon fluids, reservoir description, recovery mechanisms, porous media properties and core analysis procedures, volumetric methods, hydrostatics, PVT behaviour and fluid properties, material balance equations for different subsurface reservoirs, fluid flow in porous media for linear and radial systems, steady-state, pseudo-steady-state and unsteady flows, wellbore productivity, wellbore damage and skin factor.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding and apply fundamental theories and concepts to solve reservoir engineering problems, e.g. initial hydrocarbon in place, basic rock and fluid properties, hydrostatic pressure distribution, water influx and single-phase fluid flow
Analyse the underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and arguments concerning fluid flow under different reservoir conditions
Analyse drive mechanisms and calculate general material balance equation for subsurface reservoirs

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
