institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Generative AI for Risk Management
school: School of Risk and Actuarial Studies
syllabus_overview: This course positions generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a transformative tool for identifying, assessing and mitigating risks across financial services and related sectors. Through research-infused seminars, hands-on labs and real-world case studies, students will learn to: integrate GenAI into enterprise risk management frameworks; apply stochastic and simulation techniques to quantify uncertainty in model outputs; generate synthetic risk scenarios for stress-testing and capital planning; and design responsible prompt-engineering workflows. Ethical, governance and regulatory considerations—including transparency, bias mitigation and auditability—are embedded throughout. Graduates will be equipped to lead the responsible adoption of GenAI in high-stakes risk management environments.
learning_outcomes: Develop responsible prompt-engineering pipelines tailored to risk-management use cases, balancing model performance with compliance requirements.
Critically assess emerging research and tools in generative AI for risk applications, synthesising findings to inform best practices.
Evaluate and mitigate ethical, governance, and regulatory risks in GenAI workflows, ensuring transparency, bias control, and auditability.
Design and execute stochastic simulations and synthetic scenario generators to quantify tail risks and stress-test exposures.
Integrate generative AI techniques into end-to-end enterprise risk-management frameworks, from risk identification to monitoring
Communicate complex GenAI-driven risk analyses effectively in professional reports and executive presentations for both technical and non-technical audiences.
prerequisites: Prereqs: ACTL5110

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: World Biennales: Field Trip
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course offers first-hand experience of biennales in various parts of the world. As part of this course, you will visit two to three biennale (or triennale) exhibitions over a two-week intensive. The exhibitions and their content will be examined from the point of view of various disciplines, such as curatorial, art history and theory. The course provides you with an understanding of contemporary, innovative approaches to art and exhibition-making. In addition to introductory seminars prior to departure as well as on-site discussions led by lecturers, you will hear from curatorial and/or education staff at the biennales, and, where possible, participating artists. Each course is unique, depending on which biennales are on in any given year. Generally, the course will cover European biennales one year (e.g. Venice, Istanbul, Lyon) and Asian biennales in the next year (e.g. Gwangju, Shanghai, Singapore, Sharjah). Note: You are responsible for your own travel arrangements and associated costs. An additional up-front fee is also required by the university to cover the cost of delivering a course overseas (specific details are confirmed each year).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the conceptual, collaborative, and practical approaches to exhibition-making in local and global contexts
Critically analyse the impact of different geographical and cultural contexts on art and curatorial practice
Engage a range of theoretical frameworks to critically analyse contemporary art exhibitions in relation to local and global contexts
Use research methods and scholarly analysis to develop informed arguments about innovative art and curatorial approaches
prerequisites: Must have completed at least 12 UOC in 9318 Master of Curating and Cultural Leadership with a WAM of 70+

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Australian Arts Ecology
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Understanding the complex and dynamic Australian arts sector is a key foundation for successful professional engagement in the cultural and creative field. This course maps the Australian arts ecology and situates it within broader local, regional, national, and international contexts and the social and political forces that shape them. By bringing a critical lens to the sector, it aims to develop understandings of the arts as an interrelated network of histories, discourses, institutions, policies, events, and individuals. It also enables you to share and locate your cultural experiences and knowledge within curatorial and cultural practices in Australia so that you may deepen your own sense of agency and potential in this multi-layered and ever-changing environment.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge of the contemporary arts ecology to analyse roles, projects and relationships in the sector.
Analyse the historical and contemporary network of relationships between organisations and actors that form the Australian Arts Ecology.
Apply a variety of research methodologies to investigate curatorial and cultural topics.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Art Writing and Publishing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Critical writing is a key part of the contemporary art ecology and is changing rapidly alongside new digital technologies and networked practices. This course will introduce you to creative, critical, and professional art writing and publishing. You will engage with different modes of writing and publishing in relation to contemporary art and design. The role of writing and publishing in an increasingly interdisciplinary and digital context will be considered: this will include engagement with catalogue essays, curatorial statements, journal papers and online articles. The course focuses on the practice of writing (voice, register, style, structure and editing) and art and design communication strategies in the creative and cultural industries. You will engage with leading Australian arts publications to gain experience and knowledge in the field. You will also work individually and collaboratively to develop advanced critical reading, writing and editing skills.
learning_outcomes: Work individually and collaboratively to develop texts appropriate for publication in arts and cultural contexts.
Write informed and critical texts for a variety of professional arts and cultural contexts
Apply professional reading, writing and editing skills to prepare texts for the arts and cultural sector.
Critically analyse different kinds of contemporary art writing and publishing.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cultural Heritage, Ethics & the Law
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Accountability and responsibility are two of the key issues at the heart of every cultural transaction and exchange. Therefore a strong professional understanding of ethics and the law are essential for graduates aspiring to curatorial roles and cultural leadership. This course is designed to examine the ethical and legal implications of interactions between artists, curators, exhibiting spaces and the public. It will enable the development of a broad critical perspective on the cultural, legal, political and moral contexts of mainstream and alternate cultural spaces. Issues discussed include theft and illegal export of cultural heritage items, curatorial conflicts, contracts, copyright, moral rights, art in public spaces, and censorship.
learning_outcomes: Analyse ethical and legal principles in a curatorial context and their impact on cultural practices.
Appraise legal resources and support available to cultural practitioners.
Communicate ethical ideas and information relevant to cultural property and legal issues.
Develop and support arguments on current legal and ethical issues relating to curatorial contexts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Curating: Theories and Practices
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Contemporary curating is a dynamic profession that responds to and initiates cultural change. It is a practice that is continually being re-examined and reinvented. At the same time it has a long and rich history that intersects with the histories of art production, material culture, aesthetic experience, collection, display and the institutions of museums and galleries. This course investigates contemporary curatorial practices and the theories that inform them. It examines current debates in light of the historical evolution of the profession, including issues such as globalization, technological change, shifting notions of the public, spatial politics, new theories of objecthood, reconsiderations of art institutions, alternative views of time and history and interdisciplinary collaborations. The course pays special attention to experimental and innovative forms of curating and the particular kinds of new knowledge produced through curatorial practice. Through a close examination of the work of a diverse range of curators it builds an understanding of the individuality of curatorial practice as well as the shared languages, concerns and skills that define the field. The course is delivered in collaboration with Galleries UNSW and other industry partners to offer guest lectures and seminars by outstanding Australian and international curators.
learning_outcomes: Apply a variety of research methodologies to support curatorial and cultural enquiry
Integrate contemporary curatorial theories to situate curatorial and cultural practices in a diverse range of social, political, and historical contexts.
Analyse and critique the work of individual curators through close examination of their practices.
prerequisites: Must have completed at least 36 UOC in 9318 Master of Curating and Cultural Leadership.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Capstone Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course offers opportunities to integrate your previous studies, consolidate your skills, and address meaningful challenges relevant to your career in curating and cultural leadership. The course is designed to be undertaken in the last study period prior to graduation and focuses on developing a bespoke cultural project that will assist you in taking the next steps in your professional journey. Independent critical reflection and collaborative models of cultural practice are equally central to the course. You will be supported throughout the course through a variety of workshops, group discussions and consultations, all aimed at giving you the feedback to advance your chosen pathways in curatorial practice and cultural leadership.
learning_outcomes: Research and evaluate a variety of professional pathways relevant to your goals in the creative and cultural sector
Work independently to develop and deliver a significant project that integrates ethical and social responsibilities in curatorial and cultural leadership
Critically reflect on and contextualise key theoretical concepts and practical skills gained in the program
Demonstrate highly effective writing and oral communication skills appropriate for professional contexts in the creative and cultural sector
prerequisites: Must have completed at least 60 UOC in 9318 Master of Curating and Cultural Leadership

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Audience Engagement
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Many cultural institutions today consider audiences to be at the centre of their operations. This new focus on audiences, has also seen education as core business of cultural institutions. Such shifts in thinking are evidenced in a variety of ways including for example, the increasing importance of 'pedagogy' within curatorial practice. New ways of conceptualising and understanding the public are being developed to better accommodate the varied needs of those who visit museums and galleries. At the same time, professionals within public programs departments are developing a wide range of programs and events that promise to engage, educate and entertain visitors at almost every stage of their life. To gain a competitive edge arts professionals are also striving to attract and maintain the interests of their virtual visitors through social and locative media and new digital platforms. The rapid rise of affordable internet access enables many people to engage interactively with the museum professionals who make key decisions about what is presented and why. This course is designed to assist future professionals to understand current models of interpretation and to use this knowledge to create new ways of enhancing visitors' engagement with art. The content covered includes a critical analysis of key historic and contemporary interpretive strategies as well as associated learning theories that underpin these strategies. Using real world examples, the connection between audience engagement and the evolving practices of exhibition-making, installation and display will be highlighted. This course equips you to make context-based assessments about the professional requirements of audience engagement, and helps you understand how to design and implement appropriate projects and programs while achieving key organisational goals.
learning_outcomes: Develop a set of innovative interpretive strategies appropriate to facilitating visitor engagement in a cultural setting.
Identify and communicate an understanding of the connection between audience engagement modes and the evolving contemporary practices of exhibition making, installation and display.
Critically assess a variety of theoretical approaches to audience engagement.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cultural Management and Policy
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to some of the key skills and knowledge required to work in the cultural sector, including: establishing organisations, organisational governance and business planning, as well as policy and funding frameworks. It reviews the development of cultural policy and implementation in Australia, as a key context for cultural sector organisations. This course will consider the development of national and regional cultural infrastructure and the factors determining the allocation of public funding. A variety of organisational forms will be considered and comparisons with international models considered.
learning_outcomes: Design organisational structures and cultural policies appropriate to achieve identified objectives
Analyse organisational and policy issues and contexts in order to enhance the development and deployment of resources
Identify and evaluate the strategies and structures of arts organisations in relation to broader cultural contexts

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Visual and Museum Cultures of the Asia Pacific
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces a comparative study of contemporary visual art and museum cultures in the Asia Pacific. As arts professionals - curators, administrators, writers, etc - develop relationships with colleagues through the region, an understanding, not only of the visual arts but also of the museum sector, is becoming essential. Case studies of international exhibitions, and related arts programs, will be examined.
learning_outcomes: Investigate artistic, cultural and theoretical frameworks that are emerging in the Asia Pacific region to challenge dominant Western narratives
Research and discuss artistic and cultural knowledges and practices associated with the Asia Pacific region
Develop ethical, respectful and sustainable approaches and practices relevant for professional contexts in the Asia Pacific region

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Visual Cultures
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores contemporary histories of visuality, from early ethnography to avant-garde cinema verité to post-documentary experiments with the truth. Set within a broad and emergent field of global visual studies, this course examines critical moments in the social, political and historical role of film, art and media activism to explore how vision has been shaped and transformed by technologies of the camera. Beginning with the invention of photography, the course tracks theories of representation and cultural production across a range of visual practices and platforms, including video, satellite television, digital and the phone-made, AI, VR, immersive new media, Tubesites/the blogosphere/vlogosphere, as well as short and long form documentary and feature films. With a focus on Australian practices in relation to transnational histories and contexts, the course introduces theoretical frameworks and interdisciplinary techniques of critical ethnography, documentary and decolonial analytics to advance your skills in visual literacy and art analysis.
learning_outcomes: Articulate complex concepts and themes relevant to global and transnational histories of visuality.
Identify and apply independent research skills, analytic techniques, and critical frameworks to examine and evaluate advanced concepts, practices, and histories of visual technologies.
Critically analyse and contextualise diverse global visual practices and technologies in relation to social, cultural, and political contexts of production and reception.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Contemporary Art
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to global contemporary art; art that critically reflects, responds to and intervenes in the key forces shaping the present condition. Globalisation, border politics and decolonisation are the key socio-historical contexts for this course, as you examine art’s relationship with, and response to, economic, historical, ecological, and political contexts. To navigate the breadth and complexity of global contemporary art, you will engage with a series of key concepts such as ‘contemporaneity’ and ‘global art’, drawing from a range of contemporary writers and artists. By doing so, you will develop a vocabulary and tool kit, grounded in theory and practice, through which to critically engage with the intersections of art, culture, and the processes and politics of making and re-making worlds today.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how artists, thinkers and curators engage with pressing political, social, economic and ecological issues to critically engage with the global present
Apply independent, scholarly research skills to analyse art of the twenty-first century
Articulate complex concepts relevant to global contemporary art practice and discourse

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Conservation, Registration and Handling
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The collection, preservation and conservation of objects and artworks is a central role of the cultural sector. The way we understand objects and their relations to collections are changing. Likewise, new art practices and non-object based projects provide challenges to organisations whose mission is to display and preserve contemporary culture. Professionals working with diverse collections need to be able to identify and comply with various and sometimes competing frameworks of significance and value when working with material culture. As well as examining the recording of collections and exhibitions, you will consider issues relevant to material preservation and conservation addressing debates of cultural sensitivity and significance in order to understand how collection policies determine what gets preserved in contemporary institutions. An understanding of these issues and adoption of these skills will ensure best practice when handling objects in both exhibition and collection management settings. This course will help you develop knowledge of the professional procedures required of galleries, museums and custodians of cultural heritage. The content will engage with leading arts organisations so that you will understand how these procedures operate within diverse gallery and institutional contexts.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategies to mitigate risk in the conservation, preservation, display, and transit of artworks and cultural materials.
Identify and apply relevant industry standard processes for assessing the significance and meaning of artworks and cultural materials.
Document issues affecting the condition and preservation of artworks and cultural materials using industry standard principles and practices.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Histories of Contemporary Art
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course introduces you to recent histories and contexts that inform the major themes of contemporary art. The course locates art practices within wider social, cultural, political, and philosophical contexts, and introduces the histories of postmodernism, feminism, globalisation, decolonisation and other major frameworks that continue to shape contemporary art. The course focuses on art practices since the 1960s and examines how the rise of installation, performance and conceptual art have influenced the breakdown of traditional discipline boundaries. You will develop critical visual analysis skills through discursive tutorial activities, academic reading, writing and research tasks. You will be encouraged to work collaboratively to develop and share your analytic and reflective skills. This course will provide you with the background knowledge required to undertake independent creative enquiry in your chosen field.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic research skills to select and integrate high quality scholarly sources.
Examine and evaluate the impact of historical themes, movements and events relevant to contemporary art.
Critically analyse art practices in relation to complex contemporary questions, problems and contexts.
Construct a persuasive and supported argument in relation to art using appropriate essay structure.

title: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Art

Focused through a series of specific artist case studies, the course aims to facilitate rigorous discussion and analysis of contemporary First Nations art in Australia as well as its intersections with complex and diverse social, cultural, political, and artistic contexts. By privileging First Nations voices and perspectives and by enabling close analysis and detailed discussions, the course will deepen your engagement and appreciation of the diversity of Indigenous artistic and cultural practices.

Identify and articulate complex ideas that inform contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander art practice and discourse.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Curatorial Studio: Social Space
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Contemporary curatorial practice is increasingly preoccupied with notions of public engagement. Changing cultural perspectives and a sharpened focus on the relationship between art and social change are informing new imperatives for art in the public domain. This studio aims to equip students with a critical understanding of some of the key theoretical and practical issues confronting curators working in “social space”. The studio is aimed at those wishing to extend the curatorial field beyond existing audiences of the “white cube” to reach variegated, specific and diverse publics both within and without gallery spaces. Through this studio students will critically evaluate notions of “community”, “participation”, “collaboration” and “public” to develop their own ideas on how to construct an encounter between “audience”, “social praxis” and “art”. The course will provide real life situations in which students can develop their own independent approaches to curating in social situations within the public domain. By the end of the course students will have chosen a specific artwork or community with which to work, developed a curatorial premise and produced a project text. Students will develop skills in determining who is their intended audience, strategies for working with that audience, and evaluating how successfully their proposed project operates within the defined social space. The studio will equally weight research, collaborative, curatorial and textual components, encouraging students to engage with the complexity of how curatorial knowledge is produced and activated.
learning_outcomes: Integrate knowledge of key curatorial theories to develop and extend curatorial approaches engaging with social spaces, relations, and discourses
Document and reflect on curatorial experiences in relation to social space to identify sustainable methodologies for professional practice
Initiate, plan, and deliver a cultural project engaging with social space using collaborative, speculative and experimental curatorial approaches
Draw on contemporary curatorial discourse to critically evaluate curatorial practice in relation to social spaces, relations, and discourses

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Exhibiting Cultures
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides a critical introduction to the histories and theories of art institutions and exhibitions. The focus will be on the transformations in our public collections and museums and their role in our collective futures. You will be introduced to major frameworks and contexts through which museums and exhibitions have been understood. This will include institutional and exhibitionary analysis, approaches to objects and collections as well as key models of museum communication. Exhibitions are important sites for private reflection, the contestation of power as well as participation in public meaning making, this course will provide you with the foundation for involvement in these important cultural fields. You will also consider the impact of alternative approaches to curatorial practices in global networked culture. This course is designed to provide you with core knowledge of the discipline from which to develop your own critically reflective approach to professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse museological practices, institutional forms and issues in relation to diverse contexts locally and globally.
Research and analyse the history, purpose and strategies of institutions in the creative and cultural industries.

It provides opportunities to analyse real-world public art projects and to extend and apply this knowledge as you develop your own curatorial project outside of conventional exhibition spaces. The course focuses on historical debates and contemporary theories that frame curatorial practices in public space. It connects you with emerging ideas about site specificity, performance and temporary events, social engagement, modes of spectatorship and participation, as well as strategies of intervention, collaboration, and appropriation. From this informed position, you will be supported to develop collaborative, speculative and experimental curatorial approaches that incorporate project planning and delivery strategies for working in non-traditional scenarios.

faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: The history of curatorial practice is entangled with the human desire to collect, organise, and display objects. This curatorial studio explores the reconfiguration, reinterpretation, and re-imagination of culturally significant collections and archives in contemporary curatorial practice. It explores the relationships between cultural objects (including artworks), exhibitions, and audiences with reference to key theoretical and historical frameworks informing contemporary curatorial and artistic interventions into cultural collections and archives. Through a series of case studies, field trips, guest presentations and structured learning activities, you will develop practical skills and knowledge relevant to professional contexts, as well as conceptual and analytical skills to critically engage with this multifaceted field of practice. In doing so, this curatorial studio enables you to develop critically informed and innovative approaches, leading to collaborative curatorial projects that engage directly with real-world collections and archives.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Science and the Cinema
syllabus_overview: Can you imagine Dennis Quaid, Uma Thurman, Sam Neill or Kate Winslet as scientists? Well, Hollywood has, in a series of movies which use real scientific concepts as an integral part of the plot. Often the script writers stretch these concepts beyond the realms of reality to make the movies even more exciting. In this general education elective that is delivered completely asynchronously via pre-recorded material, you will view a series of movies which deal with a range of scientific issues with accompanying lectures to help you understand the concepts. Movies you will watch include Gattaca (starring Ethan Hawke, Jude Law and Uma Thurman), Jurassic Park (Sam Neill, Jeff Goldblum and Laura Dern), The Day After Tomorrow (Dennis Quaid, Jake Gyllenhaal and Emmy Rossum) and more. So enroll, see some movies and you might learn enough science to create your own genetically modified organism, alternative source of energy, deep space exploration vehicle or help save the world from a cataclysmic disaster. This course is delivered purely online! There is no prior knowledge required, anyone can take this course no matter their scientific background.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyze and discuss the suitability of the scientific content/theories in a film in terms of how they are used to create a narrative (a plot/plot device).
Recognize and describe the scientific content that is contained in a film and how a narrative (a plot/plot device) is constructed around this.
Create an original piece of work that applies the knowledge on Science and Cinema acquired from the course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Improving Communication Skills for STEMM
school: School of Biological, Earth and Environmental Sciences
syllabus_overview: Good communication skills are required in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, medicine, aviation, and many other STEMM disciplines. Communication is paramount for ensuring safety and efficiency in key areas such as aviation and medicine, whether written, verbal or visual. Students must be able to craft their messages into different shapes for different audiences, whether they are writing a lecture, report, research paper, or presenting to peers or public audiences. These skills are not only helpful for learning at university but are also essential for a successful career. This course combines theoretical and practical learning. Self-paced weekly lessons are designed to teach foundational knowledge and include activities for students to reflect on their understanding of key concepts. Weekly live, online classes and interactive, consolidating concepts learnt in the lessons and encouraging students to practise communication skills by interacting with peers and disciplinary experts. Students begin the first half of the course by learning how to learn in the first week. This includes exploring techniques and strategies for effectively receiving, retaining and recalling information, understanding how to actively learn, and the concept of deep learning versus surface learning. Through understanding these foundational skills, students are set up for success, not only in this course but their future careers. Students then apply these base skills to a more communications-specific context, including writing succinctly in the narrative, using descriptive and academic styles, listening actively and reading critically and reflectively. They also learn the anatomy of a compelling presentation tailored to different audiences. The second half of the course builds on these skills, with students developing an evidence-based article in The Conversation style. Students begin with a topic in which they can balance expert consensus with public opinion. They learn to develop a research question for their article, search primary literature and secondary sources, analyse and evaluate the information, and apply lessons on separating fact from fiction. They then outline the article, create several drafts, and edit it into a well-balanced, coherent, cohesive, and referenced final product.
learning_outcomes: Apply the people-oriented dramatic story arc technique to convey and communicate ideas related to STEMM for impact, influence and engagement.
Evaluate and synthesise a range of perspectives on a STEMM topic, using critical thinking skills and the most appropriate approach for collecting evidence.
Explain how various modes of written and verbal communication can be adapted to respond to the needs of different audiences.
Clearly and effectively communicate for different purposes and audiences, in both verbal and written form.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Level 2 Research Skills
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will discover the university research environment by collaborating with peers and UNSW researchers on an authentic research project. Students can choose a disciplinary-focused or interdisciplinary project, across a broad range of fields in the Faculty of Science. Students will then be placed into a project group based on their preferences and availability. Students will work independently and with their project group throughout the term and receive guidance and mentorship from active researchers with expertise in the project area. To support skill development and peer connection across research groups, students will complete a self-paced online module and participate in a 1-hour interactive workshop each week. These activities provide guidance on how to complete the project milestones and assessments (e.g., literature review, video presentation), as well as introduce key skills and activities in academic research (e.g., ethics, data analysis and communicating results). By completing this course, students will gain important research and transferable graduate skills that are highly valued across a range of graduate pathways and will prepare them for further research opportunities in their program.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graduation Portfolio
syllabus_overview: You've spent years developing scientific knowledge and skills—but can you confidently explain your unique value to potential employers? Do you know how your science degree translates to career opportunities beyond the lab? Can you articulate what makes you stand out in a competitive job market? These questions and more will be addressed in SCIF3010 Graduation Portfolio, your final step in the Bachelor of Science or Bachelor of Advanced Science programs. SCIF3010 is a compulsory capstone course that must be completed in the final term of your enrolment . Through three focused fully online modules delivered via Moodle and the SciConnect platform, you'll explore target industries and career pathways, assess your program learning outcomes and transferable skills, and develop a compelling digital portfolio that showcases your capabilities. The course requires approximately 15 hours of engagement and uses a Satisfactory/Unsatisfactory grading basis. By completion, you'll have transformed your academic achievements into a powerful professional narrative, equipped with the tools and confidence needed to successfully transition from university student to science professional. An overall Satisfactory grade is required to progress to graduation from your Bachelor of Science or Bachelor of Advanced Science program.
learning_outcomes: Research the landscape of a target industry and the professional skills used in a chosen field.
Identify, evidence, and articulate Program Learning Outcomes, UNSW Graduate Attributes, and transferable skills through digital portfolio development.
Use written communication skills to convey unique value as a graduate through professional branding and effective presentation of career readiness to potential employers.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Science Industry Project
syllabus_overview: SCIF3000 is a project work-integrated-learning course aimed at integrating and applying students' disciplinary knowledge and transferable skills to real-world scientific work. You will work with a partner organisation from industry, government, or the not-for-profit sector on a project that affects their organisation. You will use science to design work tasks and develop evidence-based recommendations for your partner organisation. You will reflect on your experiences and use those reflections to inform your professional identity and paths forward in your career(s). Guided by academic and workplace mentors, you will work in multidisciplinary teams to learn and apply employability skills like teamwork, project management, problem solving, and communication as you deliver an outcome for your partner organisation. By engaging with experiential learning and authentic, meaningful work, you will consider and commence the transition from studying at University to working within your chosen career(s). Your project will be unique based on partner requirements and expectations. The course is available to domestic and international students, and can be considered as part of the requirements to fulfil the Bachelor of Science Employability Experiences Units of Credit. This course also applies research skills learned in the Bachelor of Advanced Science (Honours) to real-world work.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Tourism in Regional Australia
syllabus_overview: This course offers an introduction to concepts and tools necessary for understanding the challenges of sustainable development in the transport-environment-tourism nexus. Students will develop skills in comprehending and assessing the environmental, social and economic sustainability of societal decisions in the context of tourism. A field excursion to Lady Elliott Island located in the Southern tip of the Great Barrier Reef will be undertaken with the objective of allowing students to develop an understanding of these societal trade-offs. The field-based learning will emphasise teamwork, as well as independent observational and enquiry skills using remote eco-resort as a context. Topics will include issues at the interface of transport and tourism management and sustainable development principles. Students will engage in preparatory learning leading up to the excursion, as well as reflective learning through assignments during and post-trip. Around 24 hours of class, including education tours, fieldwork and presentations, are delivered on the island during the field excursion. This is a summer intensive course. Students should be aware that additional costs associated with the field trip will be incurred including return airfare to Lady Elliott Island (LEI), accommodation and food. This course is also available as AVIA3900.
learning_outcomes: Explain the layers of complexity involved in the sustainable management of transport and tourism

Recall and appropriately apply principles, techniques and methods learnt for assessing sustainable development using transport operations or/and ecotourism in the Great Barrier Reef as an illustrative context.
Effectively communicate the interdisciplinary challenges of the aviation-tourism-environment nexus to various audiences.
Appraise and convey the impact of aviation on sustainable development in a local and global context.
Critique the trade-offs between economic, social and environmental considerations in relation to sustainable tourism in regional Australia.
Discuss the sustainable management challenges of a reef eco-tourism resort.
Identify and extract relevant and contextual information, both in the field and in desktop research, for addressing challenges relating to sustainable tourism.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Science HDR First Year Onboarding
syllabus_overview: This course provides all commencing higher degree research (HDR) candidates in the Faculty of Science a comprehensive and integrated induction as they begin their research training degree. The course is designed to introduce HDR candidates to the core principles of scientific research, to develop their science communication skills and provide them with essential skills for a smooth progression to the second year of their research program. Students will engage in several intensive days across the Term. Through a series of lectures, workshops, and online training modules, students will have the opportunity to engage with peers and relevant research support teams within the Science Faculty and UNSW Sydney. Successful completion of this course is also dependent on completion of any/all local (School-based) inductions relevant to their project or discipline. Note: This course is specifically developed for candidates undertaking Higher Degree Research (HDR) in the Science Faculty at UNSW.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the responsibilities as a research scientist, including the importance of upholding research integrity.
Demonstrate the interpersonal skills required for effective project management and contributing to an inclusive and respectful research culture.
Formulate a research question that addresses an important knowledge gap or problem and describe the methodological approaches required to address the question.
Locate and critically evaluate scientific literature.
Effectively communicate research principles and research training impact in both written and verbal formats.
Locate relevant resources available to support HDR training, professional skills and career development.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Object Design Dialogues: Concept to Fabrication
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This specialist course covers foundation studio knowledge, skills and professional methodologies for object design. In particular, you will learn to engage in a design practice, which integrates technical knowledge and skills with material, form and contextual issues in contemporary object design. You will explore the relationship between an object's meaning (both social/cultural) and its material properties, structural qualities, construction methods, finishes, fittings and connections. Projects will address the conceptual, material and sculptural understandings of 3D object design. You will develop an understanding of scale models, drawing conventions and their presentation, in particular working to scale, using notations, dimensions and the use of drawings for 3D computer modelling, digital visualisation, prototyping and presentation. Through a series of lectures and demonstrations you will be informed of the different skills, knowledge and abilities a designer requires in order to create a three dimensional object. You will work on one project throughout the course and have three sequential assessment tasks covering; research and concepts, design development and final design synthesis and presentation. You will work between the design studio, object design fabrication space and computer lab at different stages in order to realise the project. SDES2410 Object Design Dialogues is an introductory 2000 level studio course. It is one of a suite of two interrelated core courses in Year 2 that contribute to a four-course specialist object 'stream' in the BDes(Hons) programs completed over Years 2 and 3.
learning_outcomes: Experiment with a range of materials and processes relevant to the design, fabrication and presentation of contemporary object design.
Identify and evaluate conceptual frameworks for idea generation used in the national and international practice of object design.
Employ modelling and drawing conventions for visualisation and prototyping of studio projects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ceramics: Space, Structure and Surface
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores the personal and public contexts for ceramics, from the intimate character of domestic objects to the richness of pattern and scale in architecture. Lectures and studio workshops will introduce slip casting and press moulding processes, printed surface treatment, glazing and firing technologies to support your imaginative practice in the medium. You will undertake assessable studio research tasks, workshop activities and practical projects to create singular and serial objects that connect the material and psychological aspects of space, applying a knowledge of digital technologies to augment traditional methods relevant to the studio and industry. The course encourages cross disciplinary thinking and activity, situating ceramics within Art, Design and Media studies. It is one of two interrelated Year 2 core courses that contribute to a four-course specialist Ceramics 'stream'. It may also be taken as an elective if spaces are available.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and communicate a synthesis of concepts, designs and processes in response to a design brief.
Analyse and critique art and design practice, processes and precedents in the context of contemporary ceramics practice.
Explore and apply design elements and principles using analogue and digital technologies in the serial production of ceramic objects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course enables undergraduate students to undertake an approved 'Special Project' as part of their academic program. SDES 3801 'Special Project' courses are proposed by the School of Design Studies, COFA and are available to undergraduate students as an elective or general education course. A 'Special Project' involves specific, one off opportunities that may arise, which will benefit an individual student or groups of students, including participation in scheduled industry, professional community or other design related activities. This includes supervised international experiences (such as a study tour; exhibition participation or attendance; specific workshops or courses with leading designers etc) or special projects such as professional practice in the context of specific events (eg National or International Biennales, Design conferences, festivals, events or competitions etc) or the opportunity to undertake an individual project in conjunction with an academic within the University, for example. Course content, focus and outcomes of specific projects may be individually negotiated or may be established and repeated periodically, depending on the nature of the 'Special Project' and the interest and availability of groups of students at a particular time. A generic Course Outline for SDES 3801 is available from the UNSW Online Handbook. Specific course outlines will be written and distributed for each 'Special Project' offered. These will detail the academic content, objectives, assessment criteria, modes of teaching and learning, expectations and requirements of student participation appropriate for the event or proposal.
learning_outcomes: Aquire specific experience from engagement in an one off opportunty that is presentated locally, nationally or internationally.
Articulate how selected or nominated projects broaden individual educational experience in relation to professional Design practice, communication or scholarship.
Undertake a specific design research project.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ceramics: Form and Context
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course situates ceramics in the built environment and reconsiders its meaning and value within the complexity of urban infrastructure. Extending the dialogue that explores ceramics in an expanded field of art and design, you are encouraged to develop an imaginative, contextualised practice through innovative approaches to the medium applied in different professional settings.Topics include tableware and home ware design, architectural ceramics and public art. Projects explore the expression of ideas through public awards and exhibitions that engage themes linking consumer psychology, social and environmental sustainability in the context of architecture, food, the gallery and the home. They facilitate the acquisition of higher level research, presentation and communications skills developed through visualisation, prototyping, documentation and specialised fabrication for ceramics and associated media. This course extends a foundation in ceramic studio practice acquired in 2000 level Ceramics courses. Emphasising cross disciplinary thinking and activity the course connects specialist areas of ceramics practice across the fields of design, media arts and fine arts. It supports students who wish to pursue ceramics as either an integrated or specialist area of study. Assessment in this course includes practical studio projects, exercises, presentation and written reports.
learning_outcomes: Communicate resolved ceramic design prototypes that synthesise ideas and processes in response to a design scenario.
Critically respond to a design brief using scholarly and applied research to develop integrated design solutions addressing a contextual cultural issue.
Work collaboratively to organise and present work in the public sphere.
Combine analogue and digital ceramic processes to develop design solutions for different industry contexts.
prerequisites: L2 Ceramics Prerequisite

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course enables postgraduate students to undertake an approved 'Special Project' as part of their academic program. SDES 9758 'Special Project' courses are available as electives to postgraduate (coursework) students.
