The increasing importance of digital advocacy and activism for policy change, and the opportunity for higher order cognitive engagement - beyond desk based research and analysis – that technology now offers makes this course a timely contribution to the professional development of those working in policy and advocacy as well as informing those in related areas as to its role in policy change.
learning_outcomes: Use policy and advocacy frameworks and concepts to map, analyse, and strategize stakeholder and interest group positions, their role in the policy process and outcomes, and the forums – physical and virtual – in which they are most likely to be active or engage.
Apply theory to a real world social policy issue by creating a basic digital campaign strategy (paper design or prototype).
Critically evaluate civil society policy advocacy campaigns in the digital online/arena through the lens of advocacy and social change theory and use of different online strategies.
Articulate the relationship between advocacy, policy practice and policy change.
Do in depth analysis of and define a social problem and frame the issue in policy terms.

Demonstrate a strong awareness of the complex and dynamic nature of advocacy work (negotiation, facilitation, collaboration, and campaign execution) through collaborative campaign development, including online strategy, and reflective classroom engagement.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Social Sciences Internship
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this work integrated learning experience, you will apply and extend your theoretical knowledge and practical research, communication and collaboration skills in a professional environment. You will be placed with a research institute, an international organisation, a non-government organisation, or a government agency in a part-time capacity. During this time, you will complete a research project negotiated with your workplace supervisor. Successful completion of the internship is dependent on the fulfilment of a contract that will be jointly negotiated between the internship director, workplace supervisor and you, the student. Your work placement will be supplemented with workshops at UNSW that offer you an opportunity to reflect on your professional placement and the institutional practices, policies, and processes you encounter.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate applied independent problem solving ability in the workplace through the successful completion of the internship and the research project(s) required by your agency.
Articulate an awareness of career options and possibilities
Deploy theoretical insights from the discipline to reflect critically on policymaking and/or organisational processes.
Communicate clearly and effectively in both written and oral form.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: 24 units of credit, WAM of at least 70, and enrolled in a Master of International Relations, Master of Public Policy and Governance or Master of Development Studies. Consent required.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Methods and Project Design
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the process of conducting research and will present contemporary social research methods of relevance to the study of policy, development and international relations. In the course, you will explore the processes involved in locating and making sense of information and in generating new information through research. Covering both qualitative and quantitative research methods, the course reviews survey design, in-depth interviews and focus groups, observational research and textual analysis. You will learn the concepts and challenges associated with conducting research. You will also acquire skills in research design, data collection, data analysis and report-writing.
learning_outcomes: Explain a range of basic social science research methods including survey design; interviews; and observational research.
Recognise key issues in research planning and design.
Select appropriate methods for addressing particular research problems.
Understand the elements of a literature review.
Understand the whole research process: from conceptualisation and designing a research project, to methods and techniques of gathering information, to data analysis, ethics, and report-writing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a Master of Development Studies, International Relations, or Public Policy and Governance

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research in the Real World
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores how social science research can drive positive, real-world change. Guided by the principles of knowledge translation, you will learn how to generate and use social science evidence to shape how real-world problems are understood and responded to by decision makers and communities. You will learn from both academic and non-academic practitioners with experience translating social science research into policy and practice. You will explore these processes through a multidisciplinary approach that provides practical knowledge and skills suitable for use in a wide range of real-world settings.
learning_outcomes: Identify and synthesise high quality social science evidence to shape understandings of, and practical responses to, real-world problems
Demonstrate skills associated with scholarly inquiry including critical analysis, argument and written expression.
Explain the core principles of knowledge translation and research impact as they apply to social science research
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in Stream A of the Master or Development Studies or International Relations. Or SRAP5101 and enrolment in Stream B or C of the Master of Development Studies, International Relations, or Public Policy and Governance

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Report
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will have the opportunity to undertake a piece of directed original research with the support of an academic advisor. You will complete a number of formative tasks, building up to the submission of a single research report detailing the design, conduct and findings of your research. 8939 Master of Development Studies, 8225 Master of Arts (International Relations) and 8248 Master of Policy Studies must seek approval from the Program Convenor to enrol in the course.
learning_outcomes: Critically engage with current scholarship in their field of study to inform research and contribute to knowledge in this field; and
Design, develop and report on research activities and questions, showing awareness of research ethics and selecting appropriate research methods related to their research topics;
Demonstrate resourcefulness, creativity and flexibility in the application of knowledge and skills to solve problems related to research.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit overall, including SRAP5101, and enrolment in Master of Development Studies, International Relations, or Public Policy and Governance.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Academic Writing in the Social Sciences
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be taught the academic skills you need to succeed at the masters level. This course will be particularly useful for students who have not studied at an Australian university or who are returning to university after a period in the work force. You will learn the key stages in the research and writing process, how to construct compelling paragraphs, including introductions and conclusions, how to engage convincingly with others’ work, how to read and write critically, and how to make effective use of theory. To give you an opportunity to practice these skills, your assessments will enable you to apply these skills in a range of formats, focusing on particular themes that are addressed by international policy frameworks.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply effective research strategies.
Recognise and evaluate conflicting perspectives in academic research and international policy documents related to the course themes.
Present a persuasive and well-substantiated argument
Engage appropriately with others' work, including using an academic referencing system.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in a Master of Development Studies, International Relations, or Public Policy and Governance

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This is a 12 UOC Research Project course. You will enrol in a 6 uoc course in each of two successive terms with a result reported by a single grade at the end of the second 6 uoc course. It provides you with the opportunity to complete an individual research project. As a research course, it is designed to allow you to apply the knowledge you have gained throughout your period of study and, if completed successfully, to improve your prospect of acceptance into research degree programs at UNSW and other universities. Students in programs 8939 Master of Development Studies, 8225 Master of Arts (International Relations) and 8248 Master of Policy Studies must seek approval from the Program Convenor to enrol in the course.
learning_outcomes: Design, develop and report on research activities and questions, showing awareness of research ethics and selecting appropriate research methods related to their research topics;
Critically review current scholarship in their chosen field of study to inform research and contribute to knowledge in this field; and
Demonstrate resourcefulness, creativity and flexibility in the application of knowledge and skills to solve problems related to research.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 18 units of credit overall, including SRAP5101, minimum WAM 75 and enrolment in Master of Development Studies, International Relations, or Public Policy and Governance. Consent required.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Independent research - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Development and the Urban Environment
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Sustainable Development and the Urban Environment offers a comprehensive exploration of how cities can be shaped to be environmentally responsible, socially equitable, and economically resilient. The course examines contemporary planning, design, and governance strategies that support the transition toward more sustainable and adaptive urban systems. Particular emphasis is placed on improving air and water quality, restoring biodiversity, strengthening social cohesion, and enhancing overall urban liveability. Through concepts such as resource and energy flows, climate adaptation and resilience, and emerging circular urban models, you will engage with the dynamics that underpin sustainable urban development. The course draws on real-world case studies and practical approaches used in planning and design practice. By the end of the course, you will understand the challenges and opportunities inherent in advancing urban sustainability. You will be equipped with practical, transferable knowledge applicable to urban planning, design, public policy, community engagement, and broader sustainability initiatives.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate in interdisciplinary teams to address challenges of sustainable urban development and produce holistic, forward-looking solutions
Discuss and assess how environmental, social, and economic dimensions interact within urban systems and drive their development and performance
Critically analyse the significance of the interdependence between urban form and function for achieving sustainable urban development
Analyse the application of sustainability principles across the built and natural environments, considering their interactions, impacts, and long-term resilience outcomes
Critically examine how sustainability is embedded in urban development decisions, growth trajectories, and strategies in order to transform cities over time

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Building Ecology and Life Cycle Thinking
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Building Ecology and Life Cycle Thinking introduces a whole-of-life approach to built environment sustainability. This course discusses design approaches in the changing environmental/climate context. You will learn about the life cycle of built form from the availability and acquisition of natural resources and raw materials, through processing and manufacture to on-site construction and use, maintenance and refurbishment, and eventual demolition and reuse/recycling or disposal. This course introduces various environmental assessment methods adopted in the built environment sector to minimise initial and recurrent embodied carbon, waste generation and operational carbon throughout the life of buildings.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate tools used in building assessment such as life cycle assessment (LCA) and environmental rating systems.
Analyse and justify the selection of construction materials and products based on their environmental implications.
Apply statutory controls associated with building design and materials selection to reduce carbon emissions.
Explain building ecology/life cycle thinking drawing on an environmental sustainability perspective.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Energy and the Built Environment
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will gain comprehensive knowledge of energy related issues in the built environment. Material covered in this course includes energy demand and supply, technologies and infrastructure, greenhouse gas/ carbon emissions, energy related interactions with other aspects of sustainable development and aspects of energy efficient cities, precinct and buildings. You will also learn about tools for assessing energy performance, related policies, planning, design, management and technological strategies applied at different scales and stages in the built environment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and justify energy efficient approaches to reducing carbon and greenhouse gas emissions in the built environment sector.
Evaluate mandatory and voluntary energy efficiency standards and tools to achieve zero carbon or carbon positive developments.
Explain the fundamental issues and challenges of sustainable energy generation and consumption in the built environment sector.
Critically review energy modelling assumptions, climate data sets and default values to inform design decisions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainability and Habitability
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Habitability relates to liveability and quality of life, and is an important indicator of sustainable development. Material and activities in this course examine the potential for policy, planning, design and management interventions to influence habitability, inclusive of health, safety and security, comfort and amenity, equity and community engagement, as a dimension of sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Assess the human impact on the built environment in relation to habitability and quality of life as a key dimension of sustainability.
Evaluate a place (building, park, neighbourhood) in terms of its performance as a human habitat.
Demonstrate collaborative skills in teamwork that ensure productivity and shared responsibility.
Discuss policy, planning, design and management interventions to facilitate sustanability in the built environment.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Integrated Design Studio
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In Australia and globally, the challenge of climate change is driving growing interest in the design and construction of high performance buildings which are climate appropriate, energy efficient and generate energy from renewable sources. This studio course provides the opportunity for BE Masters students to work together in teams with colleagues from the Faculty of Engineering on real world, industry-linked projects focused on the integrated design of sustainable, high performance buildings. The studio will be structured around cross-disciplinary collaboration and integration of low energy, passive design strategies from project conception, and will include opportunities for interaction with experienced industry professionals. Lectures in advanced topics of ESD design and evidence based methods and tools, including evaluation and prediction of building thermal, energy and daylighting performance, will complement and inform students' studio work.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to communicate a design concept for a high performance, energy efficient and low environmental impact building.
Demonstrate the ability to pursue a sustained, multi-disciplinary integrated design process from concept to developed design.
Apply building performance prediction and post-construction performance evaluation techniques to inform the design process and facilitate reflective practice.

Understand and apply the fundamental principles, constraints, technologies and tools of sustainable design to the creation of a new high performance building from concept stage to design development, including consideration of: • triple bottom line and life cycle thinking • site analysis – climate, context and landscape • passive and active energy efficient design • building materials – long life, loose fit, low impact • human comfort, health and wellbeing • Water and waste cycles

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental Auditing
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Environmental Auditing integrates scientific/engineering principles, technical and environmental aspects of facility operations, knowledge of management systems, regulatory frameworks and audit techniques to evaluate the environmental impacts of an organisation's activities and to manage potential environmental liabilities, risks and hazards. The course provides students with the necessary knowledge to undertake environmental audits of facilities and operations with the objective of minimising environmental risk and improving environmental performance. Topics include environmental risk assessment; material accounting, pollution prevention and cleaner production tools; legislative requirements; environmental indicators and reporting; management systems auditing; and specialist audit types (energy, waste, contaminated sites). UNSW is Exemplar Global Certified TPECS Provider for the Competency Units EG - AU Management systems auditing and EG - EM Environmental management systems.
learning_outcomes: Plan and conduct an effective environmental audit
Understand the principles, procedures and techniques of the different types of environmental audit
Apply effective material accounting and risk assessment methods to identify and evaluate the significance of the environmental aspects and impacts of an organisationâ??s activities
Assess the effectiveness of methodologies (management and technological) to control environmental hazards and facilitate cleaner production of products/services
Demonstrate ethics and professionalism in the practice of environmental auditing
Determine the adequacy and effectiveness of an organisationâ??s environmental management system
Understand the Australian environment legal and regulatory context and the role of organisation-specific policies and procedures in environmental management

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing the Sustainable Built Environment
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: Managing the Sustainable Built Environment focuses on sustainable management of the built environment. It covers strategic asset management from a sustainability/life cycle perspective and integration of sustainability criteria into project procurement, supply chain management, space planning / utilisation and the operational management and maintenance of buildings, facilities and infrastructure. You will critically examine a range of frameworks and tools to assess, report on and manage energy, water and waste, facilitate stakeholder engagement and address emerging greenhouse and energy compliance requirements.
learning_outcomes: Apply space planning principles to improve sustainability performance.
Develop a business case for a facility sustainability project.
Develop a sustainability management plan for a facility which addresses elements of the UN's Sustainable Development Goals.
Develop and integrate sustainability criteria into a facility management project brief and contract.
Evaluate tender submissions on facility management contracts against sustainability criteria.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Sustainable Infrastructure
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course provides foundation knowledge for planning and managing sustainable infrastructure and public services. By infrastructure we mean built facilities and networks – either above or below ground – that support health, safety, and welfare. This is a broad take that traditionally has included publicly- and privately-owned providers of systems such as: Utilities – gas and electricity, water supply and sewerage, waste collection and disposal Public Works – roads and bridges, dams and canals, ports and airports, railways Community Facilities – prisons, schools, parks, recreation, hospitals, libraries Telecommunications - telephony, internet, television, satellites, cable, broadband, etc. Public services in this context refers to public or social programs designed to benefit a class or classes of citizens, including health care, housing, workfare, education etc.This course prepares students to be proficient in a life-cycle method of infrastructure planning and management, which starts with a needs assessment, and encompasses programming, planning, design, costing, budgeting, financing, operations, maintenance, rehabilitation, replacement/redesign, and evaluation. We will also cover selected infrastructure and service systems, to be selected by the professor in consultation with the students, in order to best meet their interests. These typically include transport, public health, water, sewage treatment, energy, and telecoms. This course provides professionals and researchers with the theory and the tools needed to perform basic infrastructure planning and research. This course is designed to provide a basis for life-long inquiry into infrastructure. It is for students of urban planning, urban design, landscape architecture, architecture, property development, civil and environmental engineering, public health, and public administration.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate collaborative skills in teamwork that ensure productivity and shared responsibility.
Demonstrate an understanding of life cycle thinking in planning sustainable infrastructure.
Evaluate the role of sustainable infrastructure in the planning and urban development process.
Analyse the roles of government, private sector, and other agents in infrastructure development processes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Graduate Research Project
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course comprises a supervised research project pertinent to the broad domain of sustainable development in the built environment. Students may propose their own research project, or organise a topic in consultation with the course convener. A research topic may extend to areas of interest in closely related disciplines if suitable arrangements can be made for supervision. The objectives, research questions and methodology should be well resolved prior to proceeding with the other aspects of the research. The outcomes should demonstrate advanced understanding of the selected topic and highly developed communication skills. Students should also consider the practical application and potential impact of their research project
learning_outcomes: To be able to initiate, develop and implement a professional quality research or design project pertinent to sustainable development of the built environment
To have achieved an advanced understanding of a particular aspect of sustainable development relevant to their personal and professional development.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reproductive Anatomy and Physiology
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course aims to provide you with an in-depth understanding of the anatomy and physiology of the reproductive systems of both males and females, essential for clinical practice in reproductive medicine and women’s health. In this course you will develop comprehensive knowledge of the reproductive system development, function, and dysfunction across the human lifespan, with emphasis on clinical applications and evidence-based practice. This is a core course of the Masters of Reproductive Medicine and Masters in Women’s Health Medicine. Students are recommended to enrol in this course early in their program.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the physical, emotional and hormonal changes occurring during puberty, pregnancy, and menopause, and evaluate their clinical implications for reproductive health.
Analyse the mechanisms of sexual determination, differentiation, and the developmental stages required to achieve reproductive competence.
Critically evaluate the physiological processes which underpin fertility and infertility in context of clinical relevance
Integrate the anatomical, physiological and psychosocial processes that influence sexual function and dysfunction in males and females.
Explain the anatomy and physiology of the male and female reproductive systems and identify the hormonal mechanisms that regulate their functions
prerequisites: Must be enrolled in either 9014 or 7014 (Women's Health Medicine) or 9065, 7379 or 5508 (Reproductive Medicine)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Basic Reproductive Physiology
syllabus_overview: This course begins in the areas of genetics and molecular biology, then explores the reproductive, and other related hormonal systems, and their effect on reproduction. The male reproductive function and spermatogenesis are also reviewed. The mechanism of sexual determination, differentiation and development towards reproductive competence are examined.
learning_outcomes: Explain the mechanism of sexual determination, differentiation and the developmental stages to achieve reproductive competence.
Describe the stages of the ovarian and menstrual cycle.
Outline the basic principles of genetics and molecular biology in relation to reproductive physiology
Discuss the various reproductive hormones, their type, production, storage, transport and mechanism of action.
Outline the process of spermatogenesis and discuss the use of semen analysis to diagnose male infertility.
prerequisites: Reproductive Med program only

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reproductive Anatomy and Physiology
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course aims to provide you with an in-depth understanding of the anatomy and physiology of the reproductive systems of both males and females, essential for clinical practice in reproductive medicine and women’s health. In this course you will develop comprehensive knowledge of the reproductive system development, function, and dysfunction across the human lifespan, with emphasis on clinical applications and evidence-based practice. This is a core course of the Masters of Reproductive Medicine and Masters in Women’s Health Medicine. Students are recommended to enrol in this course early in their program.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the physical, emotional and hormonal changes occurring during puberty, pregnancy, and menopause, and evaluate their clinical implications for reproductive health.
Analyse the mechanisms of sexual determination, differentiation, and the developmental stages required to achieve reproductive competence.
Critically evaluate the physiological processes which underpin fertility and infertility in context of clinical relevance
Integrate the anatomical, physiological and psychosocial processes that influence sexual function and dysfunction in males and females.
Explain the anatomy and physiology of the male and female reproductive systems and identify the hormonal mechanisms that regulate their functions
prerequisites: Enrolment in 3831 Science (Medicine) Honours

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contraception
syllabus_overview: This course examines the clinical, social, epidemiological and ethical aspects of contraception and family planning. Students critically consider the various methods of contraception, sterilisation and pregnancy termination. Through case-based and evidence-informed learning, the course develops student’s capacity to provide nuanced, person-centred contraceptive counselling across diverse clinical, social, and demographic contexts.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the mechanisms of action of contemporary and emerging contraceptive methods, and apply to individual patient needs.
Critically analyse global contraceptive needs and evaluate how social, cultural, economic and policy factors shape equitable access to contraceptives across diverse populations.
Evaluate and compare the various methods of contraception in terms of efficacy, benefits, risks and side-effects to support clinical decision-making.
Develop and justify evidence-based contraceptive advice tailored to a range of clinical scenarios and individual patient/client’s needs.

Integrate medical, psychosocial, cultural, and ethical considerations to determine the suitability of contraceptive options for individuals across a range of clinical needs, life stages, and reproductive goals
Describe and justify the recommended management of complications or side effects associated with various methods of contraception.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Reproductive Endocrinology
syllabus_overview: This course explores the range of endocrine disorders associated with menstrual irregularities and infertility and the laboratory methodologies of the major reproductive hormone assays used in the clinic for the diagnosis, prognosis and monitoring of endocrine disorders. The course also explores the current best practice in the clinical management of common reproductive endocrine disorders.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of evidence-based counselling to a range of clinical scenarios
Critically interpret reproductive hormone assays and apply the results to clinical scenarios in infertility and reproductive endocrinology
Apply clinical and biochemical information in the diagnosis and management of common reproductive endocrine disorders
prerequisites: For student currently enrolled in Reproductive Medicine programs (7379, 5508, 9065)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fertility Treatments
syllabus_overview: This course explores different treatment options available to patients in their treatment of infertility. This encompasses surgical, medical and assisted reproductive techniques. The principles of various ART techniques will be covered in depth.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based principles when preparing advice to patients &/or other professionals on assisted reproductive technologies to a range of patient scenarios
Evaluate the treatment options, monitoring and risks of controlled ovarian hyperstimulation, including the clinical use of GnRH agonists and antagonists, and their suitability for the patient
Assess the short- and long-term risks of Assisted Reproductive Technologies (ART) to different patient scenarios
Critically evaluate Preimplantation Genetic Testing (PGT) techniques and their application, benefits and considerations to a range of clinical scenarios
Describe the principles, roles, benefits and analyse the patient-specific risks of endoscopic surgery, including laparoscopy and hysteroscopy and their role in fertility care
Compare and contrast different pharmacological properties of medications used in infertility treatments
prerequisites: For student currently enrolled in Reproductive Medicine programs (7379, 5508, 9065)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Laboratory Aspects of ART
syllabus_overview: This course deals solely with the laboratory aspects of Assisted Reproductive Treatment, from oocyte collection, gamete preparation and embryo culture up to and including methods of presenting results. It introduces the use of Quality Systems and risk management in human embryo culture, and the rationales for choosing various laboratory techniques and their potential complications. This course will provide a better understanding of the complexities of the laboratory and culture technique requirements currently in use. It has five main modules. The first two introduce the basic aspects of setting up an ART laboratory and highlight the importance of quality management systems including Benchmarking and evaluation of Performance Indicators to support meaningful self-assessment of laboratory outcomes. The third covers sperm preparation for ART, and in the fourth, we look at the biological processes that can affect laboratory outcomes, and briefly cover the oocyte retrieval process. The final module covers the practical aspects of an ART laboratory, such as insemination methods, fertilisation, embryo culture, embryo transfer, and cryopreservation. Assessments in this course are a formative MCQs, two summative essays and finished with a summative MCQs.
learning_outcomes: Identify common risks in ART laboratories, devise methods to control these risks and evaluate their effectiveness
Identify the biological events that determine the overall outcome of an IVF cycle and discuss how they can be supported by the laboratory systems
Outline the systems needed to create a functional ART Laboratory
Evaluate the scientific principles, process management and risk minimisation methodologies necessary to maintain a functional ART laboratory
prerequisites: Currently enrolled in RepMed program

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Female Fertility
syllabus_overview: This course is predominantly an introduction to female infertility with areas of study including epidemiology, preliminary and advanced investigation and diagnostic techniques. Although not focusing on technique the role of ultrasound, endoscopic and radiological procedures will be explored. By the end of this course students are expected to confidently obtain medical history, examine and manage patients presented with fertility issues explored in this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply evidence-based principles when preparing advice to patients &/or other professionals regarding aetiology, investigation and management of disorders of female fertility
Examine the aetiology of conditions that may affect female fertility and apply this to the design of relevant investigative approaches in the clinical setting
Critically evaluate evidence-based management options and apply these to the development of management plans for a range of clinical scenarios
Analyse the female reproductive system with respect to points of damage that result in infertility including, pelvic inflammatory disease, ectopic pregnancy and endometriosis
prerequisites: For student currently enrolled in Reproductive Medicine programs (7379, 5508, 9065)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Menopause
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will examine the historical context and epidemiological patterns of menopause and its management. You will gain an enhanced understanding of the physiological processes and pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the menopausal transition. Through an evidence‑based framework, the course will equip you with the clinical knowledge required to competently assess and advise on the management of menopausal symptoms, therapeutic options, and potential long‑term health consequences.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the physiological transitions and pathophysiological developments characteristic of menopause and its sequelae
Analyse the historical contexts and demonstrate understanding of the epidemiological evidence shaping current conceptualisations of menopause
Design an appropriate investigative strategy to evaluate menopausal symptoms and their related clinical consequences.
Apply current evidence to develop management strategies for menopausal symptoms, and their related health consequences

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethics and Law In Reproductive Medicine
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is primarily upon ethical, social and legal aspects of reproductive medicine, with particular reference to new reproductive technologies. The first part of the course focuses mainly upon ethical issues, relating to conceptuses, and fetuses, genetic engineering, pre-natal testing, genetic discrimination and commercialisation. The second part of the course looks at the legal issues associated with the regulation of reproductive technologies, with particular reference to access to assisted reproductive services, the use and disposal of gametes, surrogacy and posthumous reproduction.
learning_outcomes: Identify major ethical theories and principles related to reproductive medicine.
Describe the laws regulating assisted reproduction.
Discuss the social and political aspects of the law regulating reproductive technologies.
Examine and relate to your own moral commitments and decisions, in addition to those of others.
Apply skills of ethical reasoning and analysis to current issues in reproductive medicine and medical research.
Formulate critical responses to the existing regulatory framework.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reproductive, Perinatal Epidemiology and Biostatistics
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide an understanding of statistics methodology and clinical appraisal for students undertaking study in a reproductive and perinatal-health related program. This course is a core subject for the Programs 9014 Masters of Women's Health Medicine and 9065 Masters of Reproductive Medicine. This course aims to introduce students to research methodology and statistical analysis. Using examples drawn specifically from the field of reproductive and perinatal medicine this course will also develop in students the ability to critically analyse/appraise literature pertinent to that area. It is likely to be most relevant to those working primarily in a reproductive and perinatal health setting-in particular gynaecologists in training, sexual health physicians, primary care physicians and family planning practitioners as well as nurses, counsellors and scientists with a special interest in this field.
learning_outcomes: Perform statistical data analyses using SPSS software including calculating measures of disease occurrence and association, statistical significance tests in hypothesis testing, correlation and simple linear regression and proportion differences.

Distinguish between common study designs that can be used to address descriptive and analytic epidemiology research questions about health status, determinants of health and effectiveness of health services with particular reference to reproductive and perinatal medicine.

Critically appraise the quality of published studies in reproductive and perinatal health, demonstrating the ability to assess study design and methods of data analysis, as well as interpret study methods, results and conclusions.
Describe the concept ‘study validity’ and explain how factors could affect study validity, including selection bias, measurement error and confounding.
Describe key statistical concepts used in common epidemiological studies (including hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, study power and significance levels).
Describe key epidemiological issues related to reproductive and perinatal health (including infant and maternal mortality rates, perinatal terms and definitions)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Impact of Infections on Reproductive Health
syllabus_overview: This course, designed for postgraduate study, aims to examine the epidemiology, symptoms and management of a variety of infectious diseases from the perspective of their potential impact on reproductive health outcomes for both males and females.It is likely to be most relevant to those working primarily in a reproductive health setting-in particular gynaecologists, sexual health physicians, primary care physicians and family planning practitioners as well as nurses, counselors and scientists with a special interest in this field.
learning_outcomes: Describe in detail the range of public health strategies designed to minimise the impact of infections on reproductive health outcomes, including screening, immunisation and partner notification.

Discuss the potential impact of various infections, sexually transmitted and other, on reproductive health and pregnancy outcomes and apply this knowledge to situations likely to be encountered in clinical practice.
Discuss the investigation and management of sexually transmitted and other infections which impact on reproductive health and pregnancy outcomes.
Provide competent, evidence-based and balanced advice to patients/clients in relation to sexual and reproductive tract infections.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Child and Adolescent Gynaecology
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will examine the epidemiology, symptoms, and management of common gynaecological conditions in the child and adolescent with emphasis on implications for reproductive health. It is suitable for gynaecologists, sexual health physicians, primary care physicians and family practitioners as well as nurses, counselors, clinical psychologists, and scientists with a special interest in this field. You will study the normal development of the reproductive tract as well as disorders of sex development. The aetiology, pathophysiology, and physical and psychological management of common gynaecological disorders, including amenorrhoea and disorders of sex development will be covered. The following topics will be covered in this Course: When things go right…. Normal development of the reproductive tract Pubertal development When things go wrong (part one)…. Abnormal development of the reproductive tract Disorders of sex development – aetiology and pathophysiology Management of disorders of sex development When things go wrong (part two)…. Common paediatric gynaecological disorders Mullerian anomalies – aetiology and pathophysiology Management of mullerian anomalies To bleed or not to bleed……. Primary amenorrhoea Secondary amenorrhoea Psychological impacts of disorders of sex development and mullerian anomalies
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate normal embryological development of the male and female reproductive systems and develop an understanding of the potential impacts to normal development.

Critically appraise the practices of disorders of sexual differentiation (DSD) and Mullerian anomalies and develop skills related to communication, impact of language, approach to parents and patients for a life-long care plan within a multidisciplinary team.
Appraise the investigations and management of paediatric and adolescent gynaecological conditions and particularly the timing of these when development is abnormal (different than expected).
Evaluate medical management paradigms in patients with DSD with respect to genetics, molecular biology and the long term implications of the disruptions of sex hormones.
Compare the differences in normal and abnormal gonadal development and its resultant phenotypic development.
Critically analyse the investigations and management plans of paediatric and adolescent gynaecological conditions.
Appraise the psychological effects of DSD and Mullerian anomalies in adolescence and adult life, and the management of these, to aid patient adjustment.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Antenatal Care
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will examine the issues involved in delivering a high clinical standard of pregnancy care. This course emphasises critical evidence-based analysis of current systems of care, appropriate pre-pregnancy and antenatal investigations, and management of problems during pregnancy in order to optimise health outcomes for both the pregnant woman and her fetus/child. You will also examine the impact of pregnancy complications on ongoing maternal and child health. It is likely to be most relevant to you if you work in a reproductive health setting, such as obstetricians/gynaecologists in postgraduate training, primary care physicians, midwives, and maternal/child health nurses, as well as allied health professionals with a special interest in this field. The Course will cover the following topics: Pregnancy preparation/Pre-pregnancy care Early pregnancy care Antenatal screening The pregnant woman in society Late pregnancy care Complicated pregnancy: maternal Complicated pregnancy: fetal Pregnancy as a stress test for life/Developmental Origins of Health and Disease
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise and demonstrate understanding of current systems and components of pregnancy care.
Outline and critique current evidence-based best practice, with Australian focus, in pregnancy clinical care.
Explain the physiology of the different phases of pregnancy, and demonstrate understanding of how this impacts the development and management of common maternal and fetal complications of pregnancy.
Describe the lifelong impact of normal and complicated pregnancy and motherhood on a woman's physical, mental, and social health and wellbeing.

Outline the assessment of maternal and fetal risk in pregnancy, including risks arising from social determinants of health and inequitable access to care, and describe the indications and demonstrate understanding of appropriate referral pathways to appropriate medical, midwifery and/or allied health specialist care and support.
prerequisites: Women's Health Medicine program (7014 & 9014) or Reproductive Medicine (5508, 7379 & 9065) only

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cancer in Women
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will examine the epidemiology, clinical presentation, investigation and management of cancers specifically affecting women. A major emphasis of this course is examining the potential impact of a cancer diagnosis at varying stages of a woman’s life, including impact on reproductive health, sexual health and maintaining independence in old age. It is likely to be most relevant to you if you are working primarily in women’s health across the lifespan, either in a reproductive health setting and/or with older patients . In particular, gynaecologists and primary care physicians, as well as nurses, counsellors and scientists with a special interest in this field. The following topics will be covered during this course: Hereditary Aspects of Gynaecological Cancer Uterine Cancer Cervical Cancer Vulvar/Vaginal Cancer Ovarian/Fallopian Tube Cancer Breast Cancer
learning_outcomes: Analyse the epidemiology of various common women’s cancers in Australia and globally and demonstrate understanding of their clinical presentations.
Demonstrate evidence-based understanding of the main treatment options for the studied women’s cancers, and how to apply these to specific patient circumstances.
Discuss and apply knowledge regarding how to investigate women presenting with symptoms suspicious of gynaecological/breast cancer to confirm a diagnosis.

Evaluate how a cancer diagnosis may impact a women’s psychological and physical wellbeing, including sexual health and reproductive concerns, and how these impacts should be integrated into patient management.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Male Fertility
syllabus_overview: You might encounter issues relating to male reproduction and fertility almost daily in your practice. Yet most practitioners, when they first face these issues, have minimal knowledge of this subject. During this course you will be presented with a wide array of male fertility issues with a specific emphasis on common conditions, further investigative work-up and clinical management health. The course includes basic male reproduction and anatomy through to common medical conditions and ways to manage them. By the end of this course students are expected to confidently obtain medical history, examine and manage patients presented with fertility issues explored in this course.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate evidence-based management options and apply these to the development of management plans for a range of clinical scenarios
Explain and analyse spermatogenesis and factors impacting sperm production with respect to points of failure that result in infertility
Examine the aetiology of conditions that may affect male fertility and apply this to the design of relevant investigative approaches in the clinical setting
Apply evidence-based principles when preparing advice to patients &/or other professionals regarding aetiology, investigation and management of disorders of male fertility
prerequisites: For student currently enrolled in Reproductive Medicine programs (7379, 5508, 9065)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Reproductive Anatomy and Physiology
syllabus_overview: This course, designed for postgraduate study, aims to provide an in-depth understanding of the anatomy and physiology of the Reproductive system of both males and females. This course is a core course for 9014 - Master of Women's Health Medicine. The focus of this course is on the practical application of reproductive anatomy and physiology to common clinical situations. It is likely to be most relevant to those working primarily in a reproductive health setting-in particular gynaecologists in training, sexual health physicians, primary care physicians and family planning practitioners as well as nurses, counselors and scientists with a special interest in this field. The course will cover the following topics: Signals and targets-hormones, receptors and end-organs The female reproductive system Sexual differentiation, pregnancy and fertility Beginnings and endings - puberty and menopause The male reproductive system Sexual function and dysfunction
learning_outcomes: Describe the physiological processes which underpin fertility and infertility, and the major hormonal change which occur during pregnancy.
Describe the anatomical, physiological and psychosocial processes which influence sexual function and dysfunction in males and females.
Discuss the process which initiates normal puberty, and demonstrate an understanding of the mechanisms which may lead to abnormal pubertal development.
Describe the physical and hormonal changes, which occur at the end of a woman’s reproductive life - menopause and beyond
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the male and female reproductive systems, and the actions of the hormones that drive these systems.
prerequisites: Women's Health Medicine program (7014 & 9014)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Clinical Approaches to Pelvic Pain and Abnormal Uterine Bleeding
syllabus_overview: This course examines the epidemiology, symptoms and management of a variety of common gynaecological conditions that present to both primary care and specialists. The course explores the causes, diagnosis, and evolving management strategies for pelvic pain and abnormal uterine bleeding, highlighting both current practices and future directions in women's reproductive health. It is likely to be most relevant to those working primarily in a Women’s Health/Gynaecological Medicine setting - in particular gynaecologists, sexual health physicians and primary care physicians as well as nurses, counsellors and scientists with a special interest in this field.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate diagnostic methods and treatment options for persistent female pelvic pain and apply them to develop management plans across clinical scenarios
Explain the anatomy and physiology of the normal menstrual cycle and contextualise to situations where pain and/or abnormal bleeding may arise
Discuss the aetiology, diagnostic features, investigation and management of abnormal uterine bleeding
Describe the specific disease conditions that may lead to persistent female pelvic pain and the essential features in the clinical history that may aid in the diagnosis of these conditions
Explain the central and local pathways where persistent pain may be targeted for treatment
prerequisites: Enrolled in Women's Health Medicine programs (9014, 7014)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project in Reproductive or Women's Health
syllabus_overview: The project comprises enquiry-based learning in an area of Reproductive Medicine or Women's Health Medicine. Students are expected to demonstrate their ability to apply knowledge and skills gained in the course, through: identifying and defining a significant issue; systematically collecting relevant, up-to date information about the issue; analysing, interpreting and discussing the information; drawing conclusions; making recommendations; and writing a report in a manner consistent with academic standards at Master's level. The project may be in the form of a small-scale research study, a case study, or a clinical audit. Although candidates are advised to start planning early in their undertaking of the Masters Program, the project is normally undertaken in the last term of the Masters Program. Prior to enrolment, students need to identify a topic area, find a relevant and willing supervisor, contact the course convenor, fine-tune the project proposal, and ideally also obtain necessary ethics approvals. These are all time-limiting factors requiring 6-12 months of pre-planning. Please Note: It is a requirement of enrolling into SWCH9019 that students have achieved a Credit or higher in the SWCH9011 Introduction to Perinatal Epidemiology and Biostatistics course. Enrolment is by application, please contact Student HUB.
learning_outcomes: Write a report which is consistent with academic standards at Masters level
Identify and define a significant issue
Draw conclusions, make recommendations where applicable
Analyse, interpret and discuss the information
Systematically collect relevant, up-to-date information about the issue
prerequisites: A grade of credit or higher in SWCH9011 (Reproductive and Perinatal Epidemiology and Biostatistics)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Common Urogynaecological Conditions
syllabus_overview: This course provides a clinically oriented examination of the epidemiology, symptoms and management of a variety of common urogynaecological and pelvic floor conditions. The course will be of most benefit and relevance to those working primarily in a women’s health setting – in particular gynaecologists, primary care physicians, pelvic floor physiotherapists as well as nurses and counsellors. The following topics will be covered by this course: Urinary incontinence – causes, classification, diagnosis, conservative management and an overview of surgery Painful Bladder Syndrome – theories of aetiology, diagnosis and management Urinary tract infections – diagnosis and approaches to management Pelvic organ prolapse – risk factors, conservative management and an overview of surgical options Vaginal mesh – a historical perspective, modern controversies and complex management approaches
learning_outcomes: Integrate history taking and results of investigations to develop evidence informed diagnostic and management strategies for urinary tract infections.

Describe the features of painful bladder syndrome, appraise emerging and established treatment options, and apply these to the development of evidence-informed management plans across a range of clinical scenarios.
Describe and justify the initial approach to a woman with vaginal mesh pain or complications, including consideration of the clinical and psychosocial impacts.

Critically appraise diagnostic tools and classification systems for types and severity of various forms of pelvic organ prolapse and evaluate the comparative effectiveness of evidence-based treatment options tailored to diverse clinical scenarios.
Demonstrate an understanding of urinary incontinence, including its classification, aetiology, diagnostic features, investigations and management.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Postnatal Care of the Mother and Her Baby
syllabus_overview: This course, designed for postgraduate study, aims to provide up to date information on postnatal care of the mother and her newborn baby. A specific emphasis of this course will be on common conditions that affect the mother and newborn in this period, including screening and preventative health. It is likely to be most relevant to primary care clinicians, nurses and midwives, counsellors and obstetricians. The following topics will be covered during this course: Postnatal care of the mother Routine Care and Common Problems in the First Six Weeks Newborn Screening and Preventative Health Lactation & Breast Feeding Substance Abuse and Drug Use in Pregnancy SIDS and Sleep
learning_outcomes: Provide competent, evidence-based advice to mothers regarding the benefits of breastfeeding and critically evaluate the appropriateness of alternative sources of infant nutrition.
Recognise the serious and common conditions that may affect a mother and newborn after birth and confidently discuss methods of screening, diagnosis and management of these conditions.
Describe the potential impact of maternal substance abuse and drug use during pregnancy and breastfeeding and apply this knowledge to situations likely to be encountered in clinical practice.
Explain the risk factors for sudden infant death syndrome and outline the evidence for risk prevention strategies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Perinatal Psychology
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will examine the perinatal period from the perspective of psychological adaptation of both parents and infants to the new family structure. You will adopt a clinically oriented and evidence-informed approach to perinatal mental health and wellbeing. This course is likely to be most relevant to you if you are working primarily in a pregnancy, parenthood and reproductive health setting- such as obstetricians/gynaecologists, primary care physicians, midwives, nurses, and maternal/child health nurses, as well as family planning practitioners, counsellors and allied health care practitioners with a special interest in women, child and family mental health. The following topics will be covered by this course: Pregnancy and becoming a parent Optimising the birth experience and pregnancy related trauma The infant, attachment theory and developmental psychology Perinatal Substance use, domestic violence and complex post-traumatic stress disorder Mental health conditions in pregnancy and postpartum: adaptation/adjustment disorder, unresolved grief, anxiety disorders, mood disorders, eating disorders and psychotic disorders.
learning_outcomes: Discuss parenthood as a developmental process, and explain the major biological and psychological adaptive changes
Critically evaluate the evidence base pertaining to parent-infant bonding and attachment, including the association between perinatal mental health and infant physical and emotional health

Understand the impact of current and past trauma related disorders during the perinatal period, including trauma arising directly from pregnancy and birth events, and critically evaluate the immediate and longer-term psychological support and interventions

Understand the major psychological risk factors and protective factors in the perinatal period, including for perinatal mental health conditions; and describe the impact of perinatal stressors, critically evaluating common psychosocial clinical scenarios.

Explain psychological and developmental processes and changes that occur during pregnancy and early parenthood, and how these might impact on mothers/birthing parents, fathers/non-birthing parents, and families

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business and the Law
school: School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation
syllabus_overview: This course offers a foundational understanding of the legal concepts and principles pertinent to the business sector, tailored for those aspiring to roles such as business owners, client advisors, or other positions requiring proficient legal knowledge. It is structured to enhance your confidence in engaging with legal professionals and in discussions concerning legal advice and practice. You will receive a thorough introduction to the Australian legal system and its application within a business context. The course content encompasses essential legal domains such as contract law, consumer law, tort law—especially negligence—and includes an examination of laws related to competition, property, employment, and business entities. Each topic will be explored through a variety of learning and teaching methods designed to solidify your understanding and practical skills. These include ongoing case studies, structured debates, and assignments that adhere to established legal frameworks. The course content will be delivered through a blend of synchronous and asynchronous methods, ensuring a comprehensive and flexible learning experience. By the end of the course, you will have gained a robust grounding in the main sources of law and the roles of parliamentary, regulatory, and legal institutions in Australia, equipping you with the fundamental legal knowledge necessary for informed decision-making in the corporate world.
learning_outcomes: Confidently communicate complex topics in a professional manner both in effective group discussion and formal writing.
Combine and apply research from authoritative sources to support a position.
Apply legal principles via the advocacy for and critique of alternate legal positions using logical reasoning e.g. the IRAC structure.
Identify legal issues that arise in commercial situations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Must not be enrolled in Law single and dual programs and completion of 18UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Ethics and the Law
syllabus_overview: Society increasingly demands ethical and social responsibilty. This course provides an ethical dimension to the conduct of contemporary commerce in Australia. Although ethic exist independently of the law, legislative and common law developments are increasingly imposing higher standards of commercial morality. This course examines the conceptual basis of ethical behaviour, and the increasing attempts by the law to prescribe ethical behaviour, through a series of case studies drawn from disciplines within the Faculty's jurisdiction.
learning_outcomes: Experience working with others where teamwork is not separately assessed
Communicate ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
Understand the ethics of certain business practices and of corporate responsibilities; and the rationale behind codes of ethics for professional advisers.
Analyse case studies that raise moral issues in business.
Understand the role and function of regulatory authorities and codes of conduct in commercial life.
Apply critical thinking skills in the analysis of ethical problems and in determining appropriate courses of action; and analyse case studies that raise moral issues in business.
Identify and assess ethical issues in a business environment.
Identify and assess environmental and sustainability considerations in a business environment.
Construct written work which is logically and professionally presented.
prerequisites: Prerequisite:LEGT1710 or TABL1710 or TABL 2710 or 12 UOC offered by the UNSW Business School.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Law in Action
syllabus_overview: Law forms the basis of all business transactions and is essential to their proper understanding. This course examines the use and legal effect of contracts in a range of business contexts. Both negotiated contracts and standard form contracts will be studied. The role of terms in negotiated contracts will be explored as will the impact of insolvency of one party to a contract. Standard form contracts that are used in numerous business contexts will be explored in the context of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 Part 3 Australian Consumer Law 2010 (Cth). The common contractual themes will be highlighted, along with the different requirements attaching to the rights and obligations of parties to a contract governed transaction.
learning_outcomes: Understand the consequences of agreeing to be bound by a contract.
Identify any ethical, environmental or sustainability issues raised through specific contracts
Communicate ideas in a succinct, memorable and clear manner
Apply different perspectives to problems that can occur throughout the life of a contract.
Construct written work which is logical, professionally presented and which addresses specific questions
Understand the implications of social and cultural pressures on contracting parties.
Analyse the purpose and utility of contract clauses, the impact of legal events on the effectiveness of contracts and the application of relevant legislation to contracts.
Explain the benefits and disadvantages of using different forms of contract.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: LEGT1710 or TABL1710 or TABL2710

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Entities
school: School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive exploration of the legal frameworks governing business structures in Australia. It is designed for individuals seeking a deep understanding of the various forms of business entities, including partnerships, joint ventures, trusts, and corporations, with a particular emphasis on the modern corporate entity. You will engage with the core principles of the Corporations Act, gaining insights into the operational aspects of companies. The curriculum covers essential topics such as the formation of companies, capital raising, the management and issuance of shares and dividends, and the legal obligations and privileges of directors and management. Additionally, the course delves into shareholder rights, mechanisms for their protection, and the procedures involved in insolvency and liquidation. Through this course, you will acquire the knowledge necessary to navigate and influence the legal dimensions of business practice effectively. This includes understanding the strategic considerations involved in selecting appropriate business structures and comprehending the implications of corporate governance and regulatory compliance. Ideal for aspiring professionals and existing practitioners, this course equips participants with the legal acumen required to excel in the dynamic field of business law.
learning_outcomes: Analyse corporate governance trends in the context of their social impact on society
Collaborate effectively in a team by regularly sharing and evaluating ideas to produce a cohesive outcome.
Explain and apply principles of company law, including practical features of corporate and non-corporate business structures.
Analyse the business environment in which business structures operate and evaluate its use in a commercial context
Identify and assess legal and ethical considerations in decision-making in the management of business structures - for example, decision making by partners, trustees, promoters and directors
Succinctly communicate written and spoken ideas through logically and professionally presented work.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Not enrolled in Law single and dual programs, and completion of LEGT1710 or TABL1710 or TABL2710 or (COMM1100 and COMM1150) or COMM1900

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Tax Law
school: School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation
syllabus_overview: Become a highly regarded and trusted tax advisor to businesses and investors. Individuals and entities undertaking business and investment decisions require professional advice to make the most tax-informed decision. This course is the starting point for building your expertise in tax law. You will deal with real world facts and problems confronted by businesspeople and their tax advisors, which require solutions through the application of tax law. You will develop analytical skills in identifying and then applying the tax law to diverse commercial and investment transactions. You will focus on the taxation of typical tax-related commercial transactions, the taxation of key entities, the role of the tax regulator (Australian Taxation Office) and the obligations of tax agents and tax advisors. Key elements of fringe benefits tax, goods and services tax, some anti-avoidance rules, superannuation and international tax are also covered. The course is a core course in the taxation major in the Bachelor of Commerce, and an elective course for other majors. The course satisfies accreditation requirements of the professional accounting bodies (e.g. CPA Australia, CAANZ, IPA). It also satisfies the educational eligibility requirement for registration as a tax agent under the Tax Practitioners Board guideline for one of the two courses required in taxation law.
learning_outcomes: Conduct legal research with respect to taxation matters and develop your ability to critically analyse taxation law.
Analyse factual situations to determine tax outcomes on matters involving income tax, GST and FBT.
Construct oral and written work in a clear, succinct, and professionally presented manner.
Recognise the Australian taxation regulatory framework in existence and the policy considerations underlying taxation legislation.
Identify the need for anti-avoidance rules in the taxation legislation from an ethical and governance perspective.
Collaborate with other students effectively as a group in presenting oral and written solutions that provide tax outcomes.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: TABL1710 or TABL2710 or LAWS1052 or JURD7152 or (COMM1100 and COMM1150) or COMM1900 Excluded: LAWS3147, LAWS3751

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Competition and Consumer Law
syllabus_overview: The marketing and distribution of goods and services operates within a comprehensive regulatory framework. This course examines that framework within the scope of competition and consumer law. Topics include restrictive trade practices implications of distribution with special reference to collusive activity, exclusive dealing, resale price maintenance and abuse of market power; consumer protection and fair trading implications of sales promotion with particular reference to misleading or deceptive conduct and other unfair practices; advertising self regulation; product liability; protection of intellectual property; franchising, licensing and character merchandising.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend and apply issues arising from competition and consumer law in the context of the marketing and distribution functions of a business.
Identify and assess ethical issues in a business environment.
Construct written work, analysing the law, which is logically and professionally presented.
Apply critical thinking skills in the analysis of legal issues in competition and consumer law and determine appropriate courses of action; analyse cases that raise legal risks in business.
Be aware of intellectual property issues in the context of the marketing and distribution functions of a business.
Analyse legal cases associated with the marketing and distribution functions of a business; and analyse legal risks associated with marketing and distribution.
Communicate legal ideas in a succinct and clear manner.
Work in a group to address business decisions in the context of legal risk.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Tax
school: School of Accounting, Auditing and Taxation
syllabus_overview: This course addresses the complex landscape of international taxation, a critical area of study for those engaged in or aspiring towards careers in global business and investment. As barriers to international direct investment continue to diminish, tax-related challenges remain significant due to variations in national legal and tax systems and the often inadequate coordination between these systems. You will explore the fundamental principles of international taxation, with a specific focus on the Australian context to exemplify different international tax policy choices. The course also places a special emphasis on the practical tax issues that arise with international direct investments, which are pivotal for multinational companies and their tax strategies. Through detailed discussions and analysis, you will gain insights into how multinational companies navigate the international tax system, including strategies that have led to increased scrutiny and calls for reform in the way international transactions are taxed. Offered as part of the taxation major within the Bachelor of Commerce, this course aims to equip you with a thorough understanding of international tax rules, enabling them to competently handle and advise on cross-border tax matters. The knowledge and skills acquired are essential for effectively managing the complexities of taxation in a global economic environment.
learning_outcomes: identify and assess diverse outcomes resulting from various international tax planning strategies.
Utilise appropriate resources to analyze and address complex international business taxation challenges.
Apply Australian international taxation laws accurately to analyse and resolve specific tax issues.
Communicate logical and professionally structured written responses to international business taxation issues.
Identify and articulate the foundational principles and rules of Australian international taxation law.
Compare and contrast Australia's approach to international taxation with other OECD member countries.
