What does empirical research say about the effectiveness of these approaches to leadership? Finally, “Doing” empowers you to apply leadership across diverse contexts. Through real-world projects and exercises, you’ll learn to adapt your leadership skills to various situations and settings. This course is designed for undergraduate students who want to develop themselves as impactful leaders, regardless of their future career path.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the elements of leadership and how these contribute to developing leader capability.
Reflect on the integration of leadership behaviours in your day-to-day activities.
Examine empirical research into leadership and how this supports lifelong leader development.
Differentiate between the concepts of leading, managing and commanding.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZBUS1101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Governing Australia: Managing the Public Sector
syllabus_overview: The course focuses on strategic level management of the Australian public sector and comprehends setting objectives, planning implementation and marshalling resources. Students completing this course will understand how Australian public policy objectives are set, how public policy programs are implemented and how competition for limited policy resources is adjudicated. Students will be encouraged to evaluate the ADF's role in the policy process and to assess critically wider policy and management issues.
learning_outcomes: Analyse public management problems and issues; in particular: "wicked problems", competing priorities, limited resources, implementation challenges.
Apply a range of public sector management academic concepts, theories and frameworks to case studies and problems to determine how to create public value.
Construct persuasive oral and/or written arguments demonstrating analysis of public sector concepts, theories and applied learning.
Understand how institutions, governments, stakeholders and citizens interact in setting policy objectives and implementing government programs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Innovation and Organisation
syllabus_overview: Organisations are continually striving to develop their innovation capabilities, skills and culture. This 6UOC course aims to equip students with an awareness of the role, impact and challenges of innovation within an organisation, so as to reduce risk and increase effectiveness. The importance of innovation for all aspects of organisational effectiveness, not just new products or services, will be stressed. This will support students as they develop strategies across a broad range of topics and disciplines. This course will examine definitions of innovation, the importance of innovation in creating competitive advantage, how organisational leaders can support innovation and an innovation culture.
learning_outcomes: Apply different theories of innovation in a range of contexts to create more effective outcomes.
Implement organisational innovation processes.
Create strategies to overcome innovation implementation challenges.
Synthesise theories of innovation in ways that demonstrate their organisational potential.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Analytics and Visualisation
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to empower students with the essential skills needed to present data effectively to specific audiences for informed decision-making in business, community, and government organisations. It guides and supports the students to delve into the art of constructing communication through data visualisation, ensuring that their presentations are focused, accurate, compelling, and thematic (FACT). The students will understand that, beyond creating pretty pictures, data visualisation can navigate conversations with clarity, target diverse audiences strategically, and make a prominent impact in an evolving environment. In addition, students will work in groups and practice delivering real-world data visualisation tasks, simulating teamwork undertaken in their workplaces. Delivery of this course is non-technical, highly applied, and based on case studies, with various hands-on activities.
learning_outcomes: Discern the significance of “know your audience” in a data-driven communication and construct an effective data visualisation tailored to a specific audience.
Identify clutters in diagrams based on data visualisation principles and analyse the effectiveness of a visual in delivering a key message or insights.
Compare the key characteristics inherent in different data types and understand the specific questions each type is best suited to answer.
Assess and criticise data visualisation cases, and develop focused, accurate, compelling, and thematic (FACT) visuals from a given dataset to effectively influence a decision-maker.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Financial Management
syllabus_overview: This course deals with investment evaluation and finance. Standard investment appraisal techniques are introduced, and a range of issues in financial analysis are covered. Topics covered may include evaluation under conditions of risk and uncertainty for public and private enterprises. Financial topics covered include standard techniques such as discounted cash flow, financial statement analysis, capital asset pricing, security evaluation, optimal capital structure, and sources of capital from financial institutions in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication in relation to the synthesis and interpretation of accounting information.
Synthesise finance ideas, concepts and techniques to analyse financial investment opportunities.
Explain how theory informs practice in finance, and the relevance of both for finance decision making.
Critically evaluate financial management and risk decision making within a corporate environment.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZBUS1103

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Business
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to key theories and concepts of business and business activities in a regional and international context. Throughout the course, students will have the opportunity to critically examine the opportunities and challenges that arise from conducting business in different political, economic and cultural settings. Some of the topics covered in the course will include globalisation, International Trade and Payments, geographical, cultural and institutional factors, regional blocs and markets, international dimensions of marketing and strategic management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the ethical aspects of proposed solutions to international business challenges.
Reflect critically on the strengths and weaknesses of different business theories and concepts in an international context.
Demonstrate knowledge of social and cultural nuances, and how they pertain to international business practices.
Apply frameworks to identify and problem-solve business challenges in local, regional and global environments.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Research
syllabus_overview: Students will undertake a research project commensurate with Year 2 study, supported by a supervisor. Bachelor of Business CDF students will complete this course in Semester 1 of Year 2, in lieu of a Level 2 business elective. In this course, students will select their research topic and develop a research question or hypothesis. Students will also undertake a literature review and commence drafting a thesis.
learning_outcomes: Commence writing appropriate thesis chapter(s).
Design a realistic business research proposal and create a research plan.
Undertake independent literature searches and write a literature review that frames the research project.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in CDF Program (4462).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Research Project in Business 1
syllabus_overview: Students will undertake a research project commensurate with Year 2 study, supported by a supervisor. Bachelor of Business students will complete this course in lieu of a Level 2 business elective. In this course, students will select their research topic and develop a research question or hypothesis. Students will also undertake a literature review, choose a research methodology and appropriate methods relevant to their research project.
learning_outcomes: Develop a research methodology appropriate to the research project.
Design a realistic business research proposal and create a research plan.
Undertake independent literature searches and write and literature review that frames the research project.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in CDF Program (4462).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Legal Aspects of Risk Management
syllabus_overview: This course aims to broaden the understanding of the law and legal processes operating within a private or public (such as Defence) business risk management context. The course introduces students to a range of legal topics (including the management of information and data, privacy, cybercrime, property, assets, employment duties, exposure to financial risk and government procurement contracts). Such rules and processes underpin legally sound business decisions and actions in seeking to avoid or reduce risk.
learning_outcomes: Provide concise, accurate, clear and compelling arguments in the discussion and presentation of the results of legal reasoning activities.
Cultivate an awareness of legal issues affecting business in their dealings with third parties and recognise the strengths and weaknesses of current legal regimes.
Identify and explain the legal rules and principles affecting the operation and risk management of Australian business enterprises.
Use legal techniques to provide legal analysis of issues, and any solutions to problems, that arise in scenarios affecting enterprises.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Management
syllabus_overview: How can we avoid major disasters like the Deepwater Horizon oil spill and the Boeing 737-Max plane crashes? Key to solving these issues lie in the effective use of project management processes, including the critical role of project planning, execution and the ability of project managers to be agile and responsive to changing environments. Project management is the art of getting things done, one that follows proven tools and technique to effectively achieve valuable outcomes but also acknowledges complexities such as competing and sometimes conflicting, priorities, interests, norms and values that must be navigated and negotiated to ensure project success. At the completion of this course, students will learn how a wide range of tools and techniques can be used to plan projects and ensure success while developing the knowledge and skills to navigate complex and uncertain circumstances projects often encounter.
learning_outcomes: Apply key tools and techniques necessary in the realisation of a project in collaboration with others.
Describe the different types of project management approaches and tools and techniques that are relevant to ensuring project success.
Critically reflect and justify the management techniques required to lead a project to its successful completion.
Distinguish between the linearity of the project management process and the complex, dynamic practical realities that must be negotiated in pursuing project success.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Resource Management
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the theory and practice of Human Resource Management. It examines, as an important aspect of the management function, the management of people in the work place.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and critically evaluate scholarly literature.
Demonstrate knowledge of the concepts and techniques applied in human resource management.
Apply theoretical or applied insights to workplace situations and/or a case study.
Demonstrate effective written communication.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Capstone
syllabus_overview: This Capstone Course provides an opportunity for students to work in ways that replicate teamwork undertaken in industry, community, and/or government workplaces. Designed around a work practice project model, the course enhances students’ workforce readiness and employability by integrating academic learning with its practical application. It builds on skills of problem definition, analysis, and decision-making by showing how solutions may be identified in organisational settings and applies business frameworks to diagnose their strengths and weaknesses. Working with a client who has defined a project to be undertaken provides an opportunity for students to gain broad-based experience engaging with industry, community, and/or government organisations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the potential impacts of proposed solutions to change management and organisational strategy challenges within a workplace-based project.
Critically evaluate the use of appropriate frameworks in a workplace context.
Apply frameworks to identify and problem-solve performance and leadership challenges in public, private, non-profit, and international organisations.
Demonstrate leadership and teamwork skills in diagnosing and recommending solutions to address organisational challenges within a workplace-based project.
prerequisites: Completion of ZBUS3108 Business Strategy Implementation is assumed prior to undertaking ZBUS3104 Business Capstone (Work Practice Project).
Business Program (4405 or 4462) and ZBUS1104

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Illicit Business in the Modern World
syllabus_overview: Illicit business is an important area of study because it affects all levels of society. It distorts international trade, threatens the health and safety of consumers, and creates significant problems for regulatory and law enforcement agencies. Money laundering, tax havens, counterfeiting, conflict diamonds, terrorist financing, drug trafficking, arms smuggling, trafficking of wildlife, human body parts, and ancient historical artefacts, as well as human smuggling and the modern-day slave trade constitute billion dollar global industries that form an increasingly important part of the global economy. These illicit businesses and dark economies facilitate terrorism, war and conflict, corruption and present serious challenges to the national security of states across the world. This course introduces students to the dark side of international business in order to develop approaches to addressing the challenges they pose.
learning_outcomes: Apply frameworks to identify and problem-solve challenges posed by illicit businesses in global environments

Critically analyse and evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of theories and concepts that attempt to explain how and why illicit businesses have become a critical part of the international economy in 21st century
Demonstrate knowledge and application of economic, social and cultural differences, and how they affect the development of illicit businesses in discrete geographical areas

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business and Sustainable Development
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the principles of sustainable development and how they apply to business. Sustainability is a critical component of modern business practice with implications for risk management, decision making, and stewardship. The course provides an overview of key environmental, social and economic challenges, examines the concept of sustainable development and its inherent paradoxes, and interrogates the role of businesses, individuals and governments in sustainable development. Students will gain an understanding of current regulatory and corporate social responsibility drivers for businesses to address sustainability challenges such as modern slavery, climate change, and biodiversity loss. Students will develop knowledge and skills that will allow them to undertake a critical analysis of the setting and measuring of business sustainability targets and thus the capacity for sustainable development in the ‘real world’.
learning_outcomes: At the successful completion of this course students will have applied the principles of sustainable development to business strategy and operations
At the successful completion of this course students will be able to develop targets to measure the outcomes of sustainable development practices
At the successful completion of this course students will have demonstrated their understanding of the concept of sustainable development and the challenges in its application
At the successful completion of this course students will be able to recognise the trade-offs that need to be made in achieving sustainable development

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Making of Economic Policy
syllabus_overview: This course deals with the process of economic policy making and analyses the rationale for, and implications of, economic policies in open economies. Topics covered may include rationale for government activity and intervention; critiques of the size and economic role of government; public versus private ownership; production and provision; regulation and deregulation; competition and industry policy; implications of economic policy for economic welfare, and for security, defence and defence industry.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role that public institutions play in policy formation using the concepts of economics.
Prescribe public policy using the concepts of economics whilst being aware of the social and ethical contexts of those prescriptions.
Comment on public policy using the concepts of economics whilst being aware of the social and ethical contexts of those prescriptions.
Predict how public policy will work using the concepts of economics.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZBUS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Management and Governance in Developing Countries
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the role of the state in developing countries. It traces the emergence of the Third World and the concepts of development, development management and governance before examining the contemporary environment in which development takes place. Items include the pressing problems of weak states, widespread issues of law and order, and the challenges of rebuilding post-conflict states. The course provides an understanding of public sector management in developing countries as well as specific issues including decentralisation, planning, foreign aid and relations with civil society. Students will be equipped with the knowledge and skills to analyse and understand the context, practices and possibilities for development in different types of developing countries. The course uses a problem-oriented approach seeking practical solutions to pressing problems of development.
learning_outcomes: Explain the historical forces and events that have shaped the contemporary nature of developing countries
Analyse contemporary social, economic and political conditions in developing countries
Identify and assess the specific development problems and options for post-conflict countries
Apply concepts and components of the policy process and public sector management to key problems in developing countries

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Marketing and Communications
syllabus_overview: This course presents an introduction to communications and marketing concepts relevant to various organisations, but with a focus on the Defence/ Security context. The course will i) introduce a set of analytical techniques to understand stakeholders and other contextual elements, ii) present planning frameworks and methods, and iii) develop implementation approach that allow students to develop an understanding of marketing and communications. While using a common structure and core, students will be able to choose an emphasis for their studies based on their goals. Stream 1, the ‘communications’ stream, will focus on internal communications in terms of those key elements relevant to conveying messages at targeted stakeholders within the boundaries of an organisation, normally to facilitate large-scale change. Stream 2, the ‘marketing’ stream, will focus on ‘marketing’ or external communications, which involves conveying message to selected target markets to achieve commercial or social outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Develop compelling arguments regarding how marketing and communications contributes to the strategic development of an organisation in multiple industry contexts.
Describe key marketing and communications concepts, including major analytical techniques, and key implementation frameworks.
Develop insightful yet succinct appraisals of situations facing organisations.
Design and implement marketing and communications-related initiatives relevant to an organisation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Defence Economics
syllabus_overview: This course uses economic tools and concepts to analyse contemporary Australian Defence policy and management issues. Key themes include: The place of economic thinking in Defence strategy. The political economy of Defence budgeting and alliances. Military technological innovation and economic growth. Defence procurement and Defence workforce planning.
learning_outcomes: Apply simple models of market exchange and government involvement in the economy within the context of national defence.
Explain the economic arguments for and against a domestic defence industry and subsidies for the development of defence technology.
Use economic concepts such as technology spillovers, externalities, and public goods within the context of national defence.
Describe the economic context within which national defence organisations operate.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZBUS1102 Business Economics

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Strategy Implementation
syllabus_overview: It is widely accepted that identifying and developing a list of strategies is only one, albeit necessary, part of delivering effective business outcomes; effective implementation is also critical. In an uncertain and globalised business world, there are few ‘universal truths’ in the field of strategic management. What is clear are the different perspectives that can help senior managers and executives in the continuous process of analysing business situations and emerging industry and societal trends and gaining a clearer understanding of the implications of these considerations on the implementation of business strategy. In ZBUS3108, students are introduced to some of the recognised perspectives on managing the organisational dynamics of strategy implementation. The intent is to challenge you to understand and adapt one or more of these perspectives to develop your own approach to deal with strategic issues such as business uncertainty, resource constraints, personnel management, and cultural change. The focus is on translating theoretical frameworks into practice through the analysis of organisational case studies, using such analysis as the foundation to develop practical insights into strategy implementation.
learning_outcomes: Create strategic plans designed to address organisational challenges.
Synthesise strategy implementation theory and practice to demonstrate potential impacts on organisational outcomes.
Evaluate the potential impacts of management choices on business strategy implementation.
Identify and analyse key issues pertaining to strategy implementation and how they influence potential organisational success.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Logistics Management
syllabus_overview: This course gives an introduction to theories and practices of logistics and supply chain management, with an emphasis on learning and addressing the challenges associated with the movement of people, goods and services. The focus of the course will be on the process of logistics activities such as procurement, transportation, inventory management, Just-in-time strategy, warehousing, materials handling, information management and sharing and risk modelling, identification and quantification. In addition, the course will cover the latest trends, opportunities and challenges faced by logistics providers from the commercial and military perspectives because of globalisation. During the course, students will be required to apply their learning in the Australian Defence Force context to address problems in that domain.
learning_outcomes: Apply learned logistics management techniques to solve logistics problems
Analyse and identify different logistics issues and challenge both in defence and the commercial business environment
Prepare assignment reports by applying the techniques taught in the class to logistics services, operations and management
Demonstrate the understanding of key logistics concepts, theories and practices, as well as their application in a real world environment

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Entrepreneurship: Theory, Process and Practice
syllabus_overview: This course suits individuals looking to build their strategic abilities in entrepreneurship. It provides exposure to both the fundamentals of business innovation and the practical aspects of identifying, evaluating, and implementing new business ideas. Three methodologies of entrepreneurship will be covered in this course: design thinking, transformative innovation, and lean start-up. The course has four main sections: The first part of the course explores the theory of entrepreneurship in the 21st Century. The second part of the course explores design thinking and resilient entrepreneurship: from opportunity identification to the business model. The third part of the course examines how to plan and grow entrepreneurial ventures. The last part of the course will give attention to financial matters for entrepreneurial ventures. After completing this course, students will have a good understanding of all stages of the entrepreneurial process including: opportunity identification, developing a business plan, launching a new venture and growing a venture. Understanding what makes entrepreneurship and innovation work is paramount to future entrepreneurial success.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate innovation through opportunity identification in the start-up economy, the corporation and in the public sector.
Design viable entrepreneurial business ventures by going through the steps of defining, building, and presenting a business start-up plan.
Assess the characteristics of successful entrepreneurs in the start-up economy and public sector.
Display entrepreneurial thinking in private and public contexts.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Emotion at Work
syllabus_overview: The course will introduce students to the major theories and approaches to emotion, feeling, passion and affect with a focus on the organisational setting. Students will be introduced to the controversies in the field and encouraged to explore the intersection of emotion and cognition. This will give them a critical understanding of the theories of mind/emotion and how we might understand feelings. The emotional life of organisations – how the contexts of work structure feelings forms the second component of the course. Students will develop a strong understanding of their own emotional repertoire by the use of reflective engaged learning tasks. The theory – experience – reflection nexus is a core aspect of emotional management and as such will be utilised as an educative tool in the course. Students will complete the course with a strong understanding of the various theoretical approaches to emotion and how these can be utilised in organisational settings to achieve more effective management.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically assess the key theoretical paradigms that explain emotion/affect/passion.
Evaluate their own emotion management style and how this will affect those around them.
Critically apply the paradigms to problems of management.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

syllabus_overview: This course reconceptualises obligations for ensuring the health and safety of workers by helping students shift their attention from ‘work health and safety’ to ‘safe and healthy work’. Case studies will help students explore how WHS theories, principles and performance measures can be integrated into the processes and information systems that support strategic and operational decision-making by business leaders. Topics will include understanding the due diligence obligations of business leaders; recognising WHS risk within complex organisational systems; defining and evaluating WHS performance; supporting effective decision-making; and assurance and verification of safe and healthy work. The course examines both technical skills (designing evaluations, selecting methods) and critical perspectives, such as whose interests are served, what gets measured versus what matters and how power shapes evaluation processes. institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

syllabus_overview: This course suits individuals looking to build their strategic abilities in entrepreneurship. It provides exposure to both the fundamentals of business innovation and the practical aspects of identifying, evaluating and moving business ideas forward. Three methodologies of entrepreneurship and intrapreneurship will be covered in this course: design thinking, transformative innovation and the lean start-up. The course has four main sections. The first part of the course explores the theory of entrepreneurship in the 21st Century. The second part of the course explores design thinking and resilient entrepreneurship: from opportunity identification to the business model. The third part of the course examines how to grow and plan innovative ventures. The last part of the course will give attention to financial matters for innovative ventures. After completing this course, students will have learned all aspects of the entrepreneurial process, including designing venture creation, resourcing, strategy, management, corporate as well as public innovation, by drawing on group work, case study analysis and the development of individual business plans. Understanding what makes entrepreneurship and innovation work is paramount to future entrepreneurial success.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Business of Managing Projects
syllabus_overview: Projects play a central role in business. It’s important to understand how they impact on organisational objectives, the effect of organisational decisions on project success or failure, the organising principles of project governance, and the project manager’s role in managing stakeholder expectations and delivering project outcomes. These are dynamic processes because projects are complex activities that are performed by a range of people and that rely on relationships formed through social interactions. The course is about projects as activities that are conducted by people, who make conscious decisions about the types of tools and techniques that are used. All this means that, together with technical skills, effective communication including the ability to persuade, critical thinking, problem-solving, people management, and leadership are essential project management skills. It is the business, organisational, cultural, and social, or human, aspects of project management that are the focus of this course. At the end of the course, you will use key project management concepts to explain the interactions between people and processes in projects, formulate evidence-based solutions to complex challenges that projects face, and develop skills in communicating those solutions to diverse stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Develop written and oral communication skills by writing responses to tasks and/or presenting oral reflections.
Identify organising principles of project governance and supporting organisational capabilities.
Using a real-world project case study, identify, analyse and evaluate organising principles of project governance and supporting organisational capabilities and their influence on project outcomes.
Critically analyse the role of social, cultural, and soft skills in project management and their implications for decision-making, team performance, and project outcomes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

In an era of abundant data and competing perspectives, this course develops your capacity to distinguish reliable evidence from unreliable claims, evaluate the quality of arguments, and construct sound reasoning. This course extends beyond academic writing, it develops systematic analytical approaches to evaluate information critically in any context. Students learn to identify credible sources, recognise logical fallacies, and assess methodological rigour; skills that are crucial whether evaluating technical specifications, research findings, policy proposals or professional recommendations. Through structured practice in analytical reading and writing, students will develop the ability to synthesise complex information and articulate clear, evidence-based positions. These skills transcend disciplinary boundaries and remain relevant throughout one’s career, enabling better decision-making, more effective problem-solving, and the precise communication of expertise. Graduates gain an advanced understanding of analytical frameworks applicable to both theoretical concepts and practical challenges. In a world where discerning quality information is increasingly difficult, the ability to critically evaluate evidence and construct sound arguments represents not merely an academic exercise but an essential professional competency and a significant competitive advantage.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

This postgraduate course is designed for emerging and experienced leaders seeking to deepen their self-awareness, expand their skillset, and enhance their impact. Building upon your existing leadership experience, this course provides a framework for personal and professional growth, empowering you to navigate the complexities of leadership in the 21st century. We begin by exploring the core of your leadership identity – your “Being” – analysing how your values, experiences, and personal style influence your decision-making and approach to leadership. Next, we delve into the “Knowing” of leadership, critically evaluating established and emerging leadership frameworks and their effectiveness in diverse contexts. You’ll engage with cutting-edge research and real-world case studies to understand the nuances of leading in complex systems. Finally, the “Doing” component empowers you to translate theory into practice. Through simulations, action learning projects, and peer coaching, you’ll hone your ability to lead change, navigate ambiguity, and inspire high-performing teams.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

syllabus_overview: Business enterprises in the modern global economy are routinely faced with challenging ethical issues. Do corporations have “social responsibilities” beyond making profit for their shareholders? Is it morally acceptable to use bribery in cultures where it is normal and widely practised? Is the use of sweatshop labour exploitative? Is networking for career advantage a form of “cheating”? What counts as “discrimination” in the workplace? Must the most qualified candidate always be appointed? Is advertising to children and other vulnerable groups appropriate? What’s so bad about “insider trading”? This course will equip students with the analytical tools to anticipate, critically assess, and appropriately respond to the ethical challenges that arise in business and professional life, both in the private and the public sector.

Construct cogent, clearly articulated arguments where the premises rationally support the conclusion

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

syllabus_overview: This course is tailored to meet the requirements of the Australian Command and Staff Course - Capability Management (ACSC-CM). The course will provide students with various case studies to examine world’s best practice as well as physical asset management sustainment failures. institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

syllabus_overview: As a result of far-reaching economic and social trends, the Australian Defence Force relies on commercial contractors, not only for the supply of platforms and systems but also for the repair, maintenance and adaptation of those platforms and systems in-service. Effective management of the business relationship between Defence customer and commercial supplier across the full materiel life cycle is therefore a key input to Defence capability. The Commercial Skills in the Public Sector course is intended to help Defence managers develop the commercial acumen required to manage Defence business relationships with an eye to their wider Defence capability significance. To this end the course will address the interface between Defence-specific requirements and the wider principles of financial management, contract law, procurement and a strategic approach to negotiating with Defence industry.

It will explain the methods, tools and techniques on how to identify areas of losses, minimise and mitigate any financial, asset and human lives losses and help prepare the next generation of entrepreneurs or industry leaders for the changing business environments. The course introduces students to both academic research and industry practice. Due to the nature of global operations, and cooperation of multi-players, multi-operations and multi-systems, the course examines how risks are identified and projected from uncertainties, how it is assessed and what are some of the various different ways to manage the potential risks. It will also give an explanation of the practical, theoretical tools and methodologies which are currently used in Risk Management of business operations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the key concepts of risk, uncertainty and the effect that it has in the networked chain of global logistics
Critically understand the ISO standard on risk management, its different phases and importance in managing logistics operations
Apply risk management techniques for improved management of operations
Understand various computational methods and techniques for risk identification, qualification and management

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: People and Systems
syllabus_overview: The People and Systems course considers the role of people in delivering high performance and the impact of managers on outcomes. The concept of systems thinking and the role of people as part of those systems will be introduced. The course then considers and reflects on the way people will behave within the systems. You will be able to integrate systems thinking concepts, principles and practices to improve organisational systems and have a clearer understanding of the challenges faced by managers when taking responsibility for a team of people within an organisation.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise a range of theories about individuals and groups in order to evaluate a range of possibilities for implementing given strategies
Recognise the determinants of a high-performance system and the role of people within that

Explain to others how people fit into systems theory, assessing the implications for middle manager decision making and recognising the elements of the people system, which will create instability or support adaptability
Identify leverage points in systems and determine how people can shape systems’ behaviour

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Driving Performance
syllabus_overview: The successful implementation of business strategy changes must be underpinned by performance management and reward strategies that are aligned to the new aims of the organisation. This course integrates different aspects of managing people, including rewards, incentives and performance management in ways that will support change and the creation of high performing individuals. It equips managers with the knowledge and understanding of theory, concepts and approaches related to the utilisation of reward and performance management routines to maximise organisational outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Implement performance and reward management in a meaningful way which supports organisational strategy.

Synthesise theory and practice relating to both performance and reward, then develop performance, reward and compensation plans to support organisational performance, including for cultural inclusiveness.
Identify the key issues pertaining to individual and group performance management and how these influence organisational outcomes.
Understand how to evaluate the outcomes of choices made concerning reward and performance management strategies and techniques.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Developing Organisational Capability
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on how organisational capabilities can be developed through the careful management of key people resources, particularly human capital, knowledge and social capital. The important role of organisational routines in developing organisational capability is discussed, with a focus on human resource practices such as workforce planning and recruitment and selection in identifying and acquiring required knowledge, skills, attributes and other characteristics. It also covers the role of learning and development, including effective training needs analysis, the need to integrate experiential, social and formal learning to develop required knowledge and skills, and the need for effective evaluation of capability development interventions to ascertain return on investment. The role of rewards management in motivating employees to engage in routines and use their knowledge and skills to derive value is also discussed. The integrated nature of all aspects of people-based interventions and the need for all implementation plans to be developed in a holistic way will be emphasised.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a capability issue through integrating theoretical concepts such as human and social capital, knowledge management and intellectual capital.
Synthesise ideas from different disciplinary areas to analyse organisational practices.
Develop implementation plans to enable the effective utilisation of an organisational workforce.
Explain the concept of organisational capability and how it develops.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cross Cultural Management
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the knowledge, skills and approaches they will need to manage across borders and cultures. The course provides conceptual and theoretical frameworks for understanding cultural differences, as well as the challenges of cross-cultural communication for the dynamics of multicultural work teams and organisations at home and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Write and present a persuasive argument
Demonstrate knowledge of the issues, opportunities and challenges of managing people across cultures
Critically engage with the theory and practice of managing a cross cultural team
Identify major cultural characteristics, including communication styles, that characterise regions, nations, communities, organisations, groups and individuals

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Workforce Planning
syllabus_overview: Workforce planning impacts organisational productivity and outcome attainment through: analysing the key internal and external environmental factors likely to impact an organisation, developing alternative scenarios, and then systematically forecasting future workforce demand and supply to identify gaps. Important to this process is establishing plans to address these gaps. The course, which is designed for middle managers, includes: the importance of situating workforce planning in context, how workforce planning is used as a strategic tool, and the role of storytelling in effective workforce planning. It also covers the core elements of workforce planning: environmental scanning and scenario planning, the principles of workforce demand and supply, establishing workforce plans, and evaluating plans. Finally, key challenges and skills required for workforce planning are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Propose how the core elements of workforce planning could be applied to an organisational context.
Devise well-justified recommendations to address identified issues.
Critically analyse and synthesise data and information to inform workforce plans.
Argue why workforce planning is important for organisations and strategy achievement.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Strategic Logistics Management
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide students with an analytical, theoretical and practical understanding of logistics strategy. Case studies and simulation are used to allow students to experiment with different logistics strategies. Consequently, the course enables students to demonstrate their practical and theoretical understanding of supply chain strategy analysis and implementation. Students are encouraged to complete ZBUS8302 Logistics Management and ZBUS8313 Risk Management in Logistics before undertaking this course.
learning_outcomes: Analyse (and effectively communicate) an existing logistics strategy, focussing on theoretical and practical issues associated with its contribution to organisational performance.
Create a new logistics strategy that demonstrates alignment with desired organisational strategy.
Critique an existing logistics strategy in terms of alignment with stated or implied organisational strategy.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Managing Diversity
syllabus_overview: This course examines concepts and theories that enhance understanding of equality, diversity, and inclusion and the development of individual, team and organisational knowledge and skills. The unit highlights structural, organisational and individual factors which can impede successful diversity management, and provides students with a range of tools to ensure they can progress effective diversity management in their organisation. Topics will include: theories of difference, equality, diversity and inclusion; the business case for diversity management; the legal frameworks to prevent discrimination; bullying, violence and psycho-social safety at work; barriers experienced by various diversity target groups (including women, First Nation peoples, those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, older workers and LGBTQI+ workers); the construction of merit and operation of biases; organisational change; and inclusive leadership. The aim is to enable students to understand the complexities of diversity management so that they can create and maintain an inclusive and diverse workplace, and develop, implement and evaluate successful diversity management policies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the theories relating to equality, diversity and inclusion
Understand and evaluate the business, policy and social contexts of workplace diversity
Understand how diversity impacts on business practices and strategic human resources
Identify, develop, and communicate appropriate management interventions, actions and strategies in order to bring about effective change

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Business Analytics and Storytelling
syllabus_overview: This course integrates storytelling principles into data-driven decision making, empowering students with business analytical thinking and skills to transform data insights into narratives that are focused, accurate, compelling, and thematic (FACT). The course covers four types of business analytics - descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, and prescriptive - using real-world data and case studies. Within each type, students will learn techniques and tools to analyse real-life data analysis problems, effectively communicate results and findings, strategically target diverse audiences, and make an evidence-informed impact on organisational decision-making. This course offers hands-on experience with artificial intelligence (AI) and business intelligence (BI) tools that feature interactive and intuitive visual enhancements.
learning_outcomes: Implement storytelling principles to communicate data analysis to a specific audience.
Conceptually map data-related questions to suitable business analytics techniques.
Critically analyse real-world business data utilising AI or BI tools.
Analyse a real-life data-centric problem using the focused, accurate, compelling, and thematic (FACT) framework.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Workforce Planning Research
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will use workforce planning data to underpin a research project. In conjunction with supervisors, students will identify a specific Defence workforce planning issue that their data can help resolve. The research project will use skills developed throughout the Master of Workforce Planning (8561) to analyse and present the data in ways that will enable better decision making. This elective is only available to Defence funded students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to develop a clear research question and design that addresses a specific workforce planning problem area.
Demonstrate the capability to carry out investigated reasoning leading to applied research outcomes.
Report research findings in a way that will support effective workforce planning strategy and implementation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Asset Management
syllabus_overview: Asset management failures, such as the Dreamworld Thunder River Rapids Ride disaster of 2016, drive home the importance of organisations having a systemic approach to managing their asset portfolios. This course aims to equip asset managers with the insight, organisational approaches and cultural awareness needed to ensure their organisations can make the most of their assets to deliver their organisation’s outcomes in the most efficient and effective way. Students will critically examine a series of case studies to illustrate how a systemic approach, such as the international standard for asset management (ISO55000), can make a significant improvement to organisational outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Conclude how lessons learnt from a series of asset management disasters should change an organisation’s asset management practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of root cause analysis in an asset management case study.
Reflect on self and organisational biases toward asset management and how it may affect safe, efficient and effective outcomes.
Critically reflect on an organisation’s asset management practice and assess how it might change to achieve excellent asset management outcomes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Leadership, Change and Innovation
syllabus_overview: Defence business managers operate in a dynamic environment, with economic and technological changes combining with evolving policy, military and governance requirements. To be effective in this dynamic environment, defence business managers need to be able to articulate the kind of vision required to lead change and promote innovation. The course aims to assist Defence managers to develop the leadership and change management competencies required to influence stakeholders inside and outside of their organisation. To this end the course will explore leadership frameworks and the effect of leadership on organisational performance and the processes involved in managing a change intervention, in particular their capability to lead a Defence sustainment change initiative. In addition, the course examines the importance of innovation and explores how organisational leaders can plan and manage for innovation.
learning_outcomes: Communicate about and build effective relationships across organisations and teams.
Critically analyse leadership, innovation and change management practices in contemporary organisations.
Understand the different conceptualisations of leadership, innovation and change management and be able to apply the principles deriving from them.
Research and diagnose organisational practices to identify issues, recommend change management interventions and justify them.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Delivering Capability
syllabus_overview: This course seeks to establish robust conceptual foundations for the conduct of projects. The focus of the Course is on the project as a domain of investment decision-making rather than merely as a platform for the exercise of rules and procedures. ZBUS8912 introduces a rigorous theoretical framework from which are drawn a suite of supporting analytical tools. These are then used to explore a number of important contemporary issues in project management across the public, private and social sectors. The course is not methodology-based. (The PMBoK and PRINCE2 are touched on, but only as topics for the short research papers prepared as items of course assessment).
learning_outcomes: Devise the worth of a proposed project in business terms and assess its eventual success.
Deduce the selection criteria for an appropriate project delivery approach from an organisation's strategic objectives.

Critically assess the effectiveness of accepted project management methods and practices, including a critical reflection on leadership styles required of a diverse group of stakeholders, to deliver project outcomes.
Conceptually map the relationship between project outputs and business outcomes.
prerequisites: Currently enrolled in program 8399 Capability Management

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Platform Technologies
syllabus_overview: This course is tailored to meet the requirements of the Australian Command and Staff Course - Capability Management (ACSC-CM). The Platform Technologies elective aims to allow students to develop a high level of understanding of the identification and management of trade-offs related to the planning, acquisition, and in-service support of complex technology and systems. The elective combines introduction to elements of aeronautical and military vehicle performance, combined with naval architecture principles to assess the effect on vehicle and ship design and sizing. This will be viewed through the lens of standards and certification to understand characteristic behaviours and the impact on air, land, maritime, and joint operations. The elective will consider the impact of design on in-service support and sustainment to achieve capability requirements, along with some initial cyber security and protection considerations.
learning_outcomes: Critique key design and management considerations of a proposed asset acquisition taking into account the proposed operating environment, mode of operation (crewed, remotely operated or autonomous) including cyber threats.

Differentiate operating environment approaches to certification, assurance and verification regardless of acquisition methodology chosen such as zero-base design, commercial or military off-the-shelf.

Develop key functional and design requirements of a proposed procurement taking into account specification development, implications for platform performance recording and how the platform integrates into the wider ADF capability from a configuration and safety case perspective.

Evaluate the essential mechanics (or mechanical requirements) of a proposed asset procurement for the appropriate operating environment that are appropriate for the desired acquisition lead-time, organisation risk assessment and operational integration into joint, bilateral/multilateral forces.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Adaptive Leadership
syllabus_overview: Adaptive leadership is a practical framework to assist individuals and organizations confront and diagnose difficult situations and flourish in turbulent and challenging circumstances. It meets the needs to respond dynamically, creatively and respectfully to intractable problems, as well as emerging crises and ambiguous system and worldview changes. This course offers an additional tool to the mainstream leadership repertoire that relies on a heroic, visionary individual at the top of an organization to chart a course and marshal people along a path towards achievement of pre-defined solutions. The course meets the contemporary needs of practitioners from across Australian society who confront massive systemic challenges, shifting geopolitical forces and social movements, and significant domestic public sector reform agendas, all requiring new ways of collaborating and practising leadership as a collective endeavour. The course will equip students with practical tools to contribute to the advancement of Australia’s interests both domestically and in the Indo-Pacific region.
learning_outcomes: Leverage adaptive leadership practices in a live challenge to mobilise diverse peoples and perspectives towards progress
Identify adaptive challenges in system contexts

Deploy temperature regulation and holding container techniques to develop an approach for how you and your system/s will deal with any incurred losses associated with applying adaptive leadership practices
Understand and apply baseline concepts of adaptive leadership

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Developing Capability
syllabus_overview: The Department of Defence is often criticised for delivering late, over budget or not fit for purpose capability projects. Sub-standard outputs from capital procurement projects often stem from poor management and decision making in the requirements setting and development phases of the capability lifecycle. This course aims to develop students with leadership and management skills to address these matters, integrated with appropriate technical knowledge to ensure improved capability development outcomes. This course is tailored to meet the requirements of the Australian Command and Staff Course - Capability Management (ACSC-CM). Through the lenses of requirements, systems and mission engineering, students will examine a series of case studies from various defence forces where capability outcomes were not delivered in line with government, public and the end user expectations. The intent is to prepare students to lead and manage the development of capability to ensure timely, value for money and technically capable defence material that will equip the ADF for the future operating environment.
learning_outcomes: Oversee and lead the requirement setting for a capability project, program or portfolio to deliver outcomes in accordance with Defence needs, government direction and industry capability
Use advanced systems and grayscale thinking for problem solving and risk mitigation in capability development
Effectively communicate contestable operational concepts and high-level requirements across industry and whole of government, within regulatory requirements
Evaluate alternative capability solutions and acquisition strategies to deliver an integrated force in a timely manner, within budget to meet the operational capability need

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: People and Systems
syllabus_overview: The People and Systems course considers the role of people in delivering organisational effectiveness and high performance, in conjunction with the impact of their managers on the outcomes. The concept of systems thinking and the role of people as part of those systems will be introduced. The course then considers the role of people and reflects on the way people will behave within the systems. The key course outcome is to ensure that managers recognise their role in enabling and supporting others to achieve their goals, and the consequences of not doing this well. The course will take students through a number of real world case studies and present the challenges faced by managers when first taking responsibility for a team of people within an organisation.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise a range of theories about individuals and groups in order to evaluate a range of possibilities for implementing given strategies
Determine the drivers of individual motivation and engagement and apply this knowledge to develop implementation plans and create effective teams
Recognise the determinants of a organisational performance and the role of people achieving organisational performance

Explain to others how people fit into systems theory, assessing the implications for middle manager decision making and recognising the elements of the people system, which will create instability or support adaptability.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Public Service Implementation
syllabus_overview: It is widely accepted that developing good policy is only one part of delivering effective outcomes; effective implementation is also critical. In this course students are introduced to an implementation cycle, which stresses an end user focus, and the elements provide the basis for the curriculum. Topics include: the impact of internal and external context; ways of engaging with stakeholders; success identification; system level change; capability identification and development; risk assessment and mitigation; performance and accountability management; measurement review and evaluation; enacting implementation; and continuous review. The aim is to prepare students for the messy reality of implementation through introducing the range of issues involved, and the inevitable complexity of the interactions of different public service stakeholders and organisations.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse elements of context that shape successful implementation processes
Synthesise and apply a range of theoretical perspectives on implementation in order to critically evaluate implementation effectiveness
Recognise the interconnected nature of challenges and opportunities in implementation
Discuss the components of implementation processes and the capabilities required to support them

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Public Service Performance and Evaluation
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for those working in and around the public sector, at all levels of government, who wish or have responsibility for improving organisational performance. It will explore a range of performance monitoring and evaluation strategies, approaches and frameworks. It will examine the use of programme theories in public service evaluation and change processes as well as consider different types of available evidence and the contexts in which they are best suited. Qualitative and quantitative approaches to data collection including focus groups, interviews, surveys, and participatory research will be discussed. Students will develop skills in both designing and undertaking the analysis of data to create formative and summative evaluations, and skills in designing data collections useful for program managers to monitor program implementation including identifying emerging implementation risks.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between monitoring and evaluation and articulate their roles in the context of government policy and program implementation.
Create arguments to support and apply the strategic use of evaluation and programme theories of change using a range of evaluation and monitoring frameworks and techniques.
Analyse elements of context that are relevant to proposed change processes and develop appropriate evaluation designs.
Synthesise a range of data and mid-range theory sources to prepare an evaluation strategy ready to be communicated to inform implementation/change managers.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Defence Logistics Management
syllabus_overview: The United States Airforce has operated the B52 strategic bomber for over 70 years. It is expected that this capability will operate up to 100 years. The strategies, procedures and know how to operate such a high-end technical capability for so long demonstrate a bureaucratic discipline that has delivered great outcomes for the US Government. This course will provide students with a high-level overview of these types of strategies and how organisations are best placed to procure and sustain defence materiel to ensure the greatest capability possible for each taxpayer dollar spent. This includes bringing differing stakeholders on the procurement journey including non-defence related bureaucracy, defence industry and our political masters through the procurement process, ensuring best asset availability for minimal cost once the capability is online and ensuring a supply chain that can support these assets in challenging circumstances such as a warlike situation.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise and make practical contributions to the body of knowledge necessary for the establishment and operation of efficient and effective supply chains of defence materiel.
Reflect upon best practice for the procurement and sustainment of defence materiel through a thorough examination of an appropriate case study.

Critically appraise methods for the identification of maintenance, inventory requirements and configuration management inputs to defence materiel to ensure the efficient and effective asset availability in the sustainment phase of the physical asset life cycle.
Critically reflect on use of Life Cycle Costing (LCC) principles to manage defence materiel efficiently and effectively.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Business of Managing Projects
syllabus_overview: Projects play a central role in public policy. It’s important to understand how they impact on organisational objectives, the effect of organisational decisions on project success or failure, the organising principles of project governance, and the project manager’s role in managing stakeholder expectations and delivering project outcomes. This course is about projects as activities that are conducted by people, who make conscious decisions about the types of tools and techniques that are used. Effective policy leadership applies best practice from both public and private sectors in support of these decision. In complex policy networks and systems, policy leaders need to select and match the most suitable strategies. This course expands student awareness of public sector management strategies and encourages them to translate strategies from their previous MBAX studies. The Business of Managing Projects will focus on the key project management concepts to explain the interactions between people and processes in projects, formulate evidence-based solutions to complex challenges that projects face, and develop skills in communicating those solutions to diverse stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Develop written and oral communication skills by writing responses to tasks and/ or presenting oral reflections.
Reflect on the social, or human and soft skill elements of project management in organisational settings and be able to relate these to your own experience.
Develop analytical and evaluation skills by critically reviewing contemporary scholarship on issues in project management and proposing well-justified solutions supported by evidence.
Identify and explain organising principles of project governance and supporting organisational capabilities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Engineering Foundation, Theory and Practice
syllabus_overview: The Digital Engineering Foundation, Theory and Practice course is designed to provide a comprehensive foundation in digital engineering, focusing on the integration of theoretical concepts with practical applications. This course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate and lead digital transformation initiatives within various industries. The course emphasizes the interdisciplinary nature of digital engineering, bridging the gap between traditional engineering disciplines and modern digital technologies. It covers key areas such as systems design, development, implementation, testing, production, and sustainment, with a strong focus on data-centric, integrated, and model-based approaches. The rationale behind this course is to address the growing demand for professionals who can effectively implement and manage digital engineering practices. The objectives are to provide students with a deep understanding of the digital engineering lifecycle and its value proposition, equip students with practical skills in using digital engineering tools and methods and prepare students to lead digital transformation initiatives and assess digital engineering capabilities within organizations. Graduates of this course will be able to demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of digital engineering principles and practices. Also, they will be able to apply digital engineering tools and methods across the entire lifecycle of complex real-world systems to improve design, development, operation, and sustainment. This course is targeted at postgraduate students, particularly those with backgrounds in engineering, computer science, information technology, and related fields. It is also suitable for professionals seeking to upskill or transition into roles requiring digital engineering expertise. The course addresses a critical need in the industry for professionals who can drive digital transformation and innovation. As organizations increasingly adopt digital engineering practices to improve efficiency, reduce costs, and accelerate time-to-market, there is a growing demand for skilled practitioners who can lead these initiatives. This course aims to fill this gap by providing students with the necessary core knowledge and skills to meet industry and community needs. This course is aligned with cutting-edge industry needs, leveraging insights from leading technology companies and government agencies. Guest lectures and collaborative projects will enhance practical learning and industry engagement. This postgraduate course, which grants six (6) Units of Credit (UoC) with 150 hours of study and a learning journey. It builds students' foundational understanding of the approach for engineering ‘digital transformation’, including their holistic understanding of the capability elements essential for the implementation (i.e. data, people, technology, and processes).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the use of various Digital Engineering approaches and methods to deliver systems that effectively meet stakeholders' needs and requirements
Explain and use the fundamental principles, ontology, and other core concepts necessary to implement data-centric and integrated model-based digital engineering

Utilize advanced computing tools, including Model-Based Systems Engineering, modelling and simulation, and visualization within an integrated digital engineering ecosystem to deliver systems that effectively meet stakeholders' needs and requirements
Apply Systems Thinking to the Digital Engineering approach to create, coordinate, and exchange digital artefacts across the digital life cycle of contemporary real-world systems

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mission Engineering Capability Development for Socio-Technical Systems
syllabus_overview: Mission Engineering Capability Development for Socio-Technical Systems provides a comprehensive overview of mission engineering, emphasising its critical role in socio-technical systems and its significance across various domains. This course is meticulously designed to equip students with the essential knowledge and skills to make informed decisions and tackle complex challenges within their respective fields. Participants will gain advanced insights into mission engineering principles and tools, specifically designed to address the multifaceted challenges they encounter in their roles. This postgraduate course offers six (6) Units of Credit (UoC) and involves 150 hours of study, encompassing a comprehensive learning journey. The curriculum is structured to provide a transformative investment in professional development, empowering learners to contribute effectively to their organisations and address socio-technical challenges in any sector. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to understand the fundamental principles of mission engineering and its application in socio-technical systems, analyse and address complex challenges using mission engineering tools and techniques, enhance strategic and tactical decision-making capabilities, and apply advanced insights to real-world scenarios within their professional roles.
learning_outcomes: Utilise advanced software tools, including modelling and simulation, to enhance mission engineering and develop systems that effectively meet stakeholders' needs and requirements.
Evaluate the complete mission engineering lifecycle, from problem identification and definition to generating insights and supporting decision-making.
Employ advanced mission concepts and their relevance across all tiers of defence and National security decision-making.
Apply methodologies that underpin mission engineering to make informed and context-specific decisions with greater speed and confidence.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Engineering
syllabus_overview: The Data Engineering course grants six (6) Units of Credit (UoC) with 150 hours of study and a comprehensive learning journey. It provides a foundation in the principles and practices of data engineering. This course is designed to equip students with the skills necessary to design and build systems that collect, store, transform, and analyse large amounts of data from various sources. By focusing on the creation of reliable data pipelines, the course ensures that raw data is transformed into usable formats for analysis by data scientists and business analysts. Students will explore key areas such as data collection and management, data analysis, and systems architecture. The course covers the entire data engineering lifecycle, from the initial collection of data to its final transformation and analysis. By the end of the course, students will be well-prepared to tackle complex data engineering challenges and contribute to data-driven decision-making processes within their organisations.
learning_outcomes: Formulate data models to fit various consumer needs.
Design, automate, and monitor data pipelines, ensuring data flow and integration across various systems and platforms.
Demonstrate proficiency in building and managing scalable data infrastructure, including data warehouses and data lakes, to support large-scale data processing and analytics.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Engineering Governance
syllabus_overview: The Digital Engineering Governance course is designed to provide students with a deep understanding of the management practices and governance principles essential for the effective implementation and management of digital engineering projects within organisations. The disciplinary focus includes business needs analysis, identifying digital engineering challenges, implementing enterprise-level governance frameworks to manage risk, regulatory requirements, and ethical considerations, and ways for fostering effective team cultures. This course aims to equip students with the skills necessary to align digital engineering initiatives with organizational goals and industry best practices, ensuring successful and sustainable digital transformations. The rationale behind this course is to address the growing need for professionals who can implement and manage digital engineering efforts. The objectives are to provide students with practical skills in business needs analysis, problem identification, risk management, and governance frameworks, preparing them to lead digital engineering projects effectively. Anticipated graduate outcomes include proficiency in applying management and governance principles to digital engineering, the ability to align digital initiatives with business objectives, and the capability to foster high-performing, productive team environments. The target student cohort includes postgraduate students with backgrounds in engineering, computer science, information technology, and related fields, as well as professionals seeking to enhance their digital governance skills. The course addresses industry and community needs by preparing graduates to meet the increasing demand for skilled digital engineering governance professionals across various sectors, including technology, finance, healthcare, and more.
learning_outcomes: Formulate plans for effective implementation of digital engineering frameworks, including the role of human development

Create organizational artefacts (e.g. roadmaps, practices) for effective governance of digital engineering activities in line with the relevant standards (corporate, industry, national and international) and ethical principles
Formulate the value proposition for digital engineering through the analysis of business needs and objectives, including risk assessment
Apply systems thinking approaches to define the required change and constraints (i.e. processes, people, data, technologies) for effective implementation of digital engineering frameworks

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Modelling and Simulation
syllabus_overview: This course familiarises students with the essential concepts and practices of Modelling and Simulation. Students explore the foundational principles and methodologies that drive the development and application of models and simulations. Emphasising an iterative approach, the course guides students through the process of constructing, testing, and refining models to ensure accuracy and reliability.
