These fundamental questions of how human relations should be structured and managed have a long and important history, and continue to engage people today in the quest to overcome authoritarianism and tyranny. By focusing on some of the most important and influential political thinkers over the last two and a half millennia, this course will examine how they both introduced and addressed the fundamental questions of politics. We will see how these thinkers not only have an enduring legacy in the fields of domestic politics, security and international relations, but also how they have helped shape our view of the world today.
learning_outcomes: Have a basic knowledge and understanding of 8 key political thinkers
Be able to read and comprehend complex primary texts.
Apply normative political theories to some enduring problems
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Application of Air Power
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Air power is a relatively recent development in the history of conflict. Even so, in the century of its application the discipline has become integral to the conduct of war and is central to the national security strategy of many states. This course will examine the roles and characteristics of air power from its earliest years to the contemporary era, and the challenges of applying air power in current and future conflicts, especially those where force may not be the deciding factor.
learning_outcomes: Explain the principles of applying air power across the spectrum of conflict.
Describe the role of air power in national security.
Describe the relationship between the development of air power theory and air power practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Theory and Application of Land Power
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: For over 5,000 years, organised societies have used Land Power as the decisive means to dominate others. Land Power’s unique capacity to achieve sustained and persistent control and influence over the land, and the population that lives on it. Land Power continues to be a tool employed by contemporary societies in modern war. Therefore, the ability to fight and win wars remains important for nations and requires a significant investment in human, materiel, and technological resources. This warrants careful study to understand how the theories which govern Land Power and the means to wage it are applied. This course provides students with an understanding of the theory and application of Land Power. It examines various theories which contribute to thinking on the utility of Land Power in war. It examines the application of Land Power and the interplay between political, societal, and technological drivers on warfare. To do so it explores the development of the theories and application of Land Power across the major conflicts of the 20th and early 21st Centuries from World War One to the Russo-Ukraine War. This includes the various ways that Land Power is applied including Armoured, Airborne and Amphibious techniques. The course views Land Power from a global perspective, however; it focusses on its application through the lens of Western military experience. Students study the theory and application of Land Power in terms of: the principles, characteristics, themes and utility of Land Power, the unique nature of the Land Domain, the role, function, and forms of Land Forces, the application of Land Power in peace, competition, and conflict; and, the future of Land Power. This course is open to midshipmen and officer cadets of the Australian Defence Force, military students from select other nations and select others. The Asynchronous version of this course is a 6 Unit of Credit Course. It includes ten topics examined across six modules. Students conduct remote learning over the duration of a semester to complete this course.
learning_outcomes: Describe of the utility of Land Power across the spectrum of conflict
Explain the broad application of Land Power techniques across the spectrum of conflict
Demonstrate an understanding of the theories, principles and approaches which guide the application of Land Power in national security.
Describe the relationship between the development of Land Power theory, technology and application

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Politics of the Great Powers
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course studies the role of great powers - established and emerging powers - in shaping regional and world orders. The policies and strategies of great powers are examined as are the interactions between them. Attention is given to the theory and history of great power behaviour, the distinction between 'hard' and 'soft' conceptions of power, and the key issues confronting the great powers in contemporary global politics. The following themes and questions will be explored throughout the course: What role have great powers played in maintaining or destabilising order and justice in international society? What do we mean by 'power' and what makes one 'great': is it military strength, economic strength, or something more? How should great powers behave? What ought to be the rights and responsibilities of great powers?
learning_outcomes: Develop analytical and evaluative skills by critically reviewing contemporary scholarship on great power politics
Improve written and oral communication skills with peers and distinguished guests on great power politics
Reflect upon the challenges and aspirations of the great powers in the 21st century
Understand the roles of great powers and the relevance of several theories of international order.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZHSS1201 and ZHSS1202 or ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Great Clashes that Define Us: Ideology in Australia
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the great controversies of Australian politics. It will give you the opportunity to understand the debates, the history, and to decide where you stand. The course introduces the big debates through a historical approach. Most of the key divisions in Australian politics have evolved over many years. Whether we are debating democracy, the beliefs of the major parties, economic equality, free markets, unions, race, multiculturalism or feminism, there is a long history. We start at Federation and we follow the debates through, watching how they evolve to the current day. This allows you to follow the big personalities, the big issues and the big ideas through time. The course also takes a theory approach, introducing you to the major schools of western political thought that have driven these debates. It gives you an overview of the major schools of political theory and explains how they developed in response to practical politics. It allows you to compare these different schools of thought, explore the ideas in their real life context, and learn how the ideas played out in practice when reforms were rolled out in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Analyze the relationship between the historical events and the development of the key political ideologies/schools of political theory, including: Conservatism Liberalism Socialism Constructivsm Neo-Liberalism Neo-conservatism.
Identify key actors in Australian politics and how they have evolved over time
Explain the key crises and controversies that have shaped the evolution of Australian politics;
Interrogate political speeches and rhetoric for their underlying ideological commitments

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indonesia: State and Society
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course offers an exploration of Indonesia’s historical trajectory - from the pre-colonial period through colonial rule, decolonisation, and the formation of the post-colonial state - to the processes of democratic transformation, contemporary challenges, and Indonesia’s evolving role in the world. It integrates theoretical frameworks from humanities and social sciences to explore key themes such as political culture, nationalism, identity, and democratisation Since gaining independence at the end of the Second World War, Indonesia has experienced considerable turbulence in its pursuit of political stability, economic development, and democratic governance. Over the decades, the nation has experimented with diverse political ideologies and systems - liberalism, socialism, communism, Islamic state models, and various forms of democracy - in its ongoing effort to promote social welfare and maintain relevance within the global order. Predicted to become one of the world’s major economies by 2050, Indonesia has growing middle class, strategic geographic position (particularly in relation to Australia), and dynamic political, economic, and cultural landscapes. Understanding how the nation’s past has shaped its present, and where it might be heading, is central to grasping its significance in regional and global contexts.
learning_outcomes: Assess the current affairs against the foundational concepts and learned knowledge.
Identify and explain the key discussions/readings, historical events, and contemporary dynamics
Demonstrate the area’s characteristics (e.g. historically, politically, culturally, diversity etc.) in contrast to the leaners’ cultural background.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Development Policy & Social Contexts in Indonesia
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Due to steady economic growth, Indonesia has successfully grown to become a lower middle income country and a regional power in Southeast Asia. However, Indonesia was created out of anti-colonial nationalism and the fragile territorial boundaries and the artificial sense of belonging have led to the implementation of centralistic government policies for more than half a century. As a result a various socio-political tension has come into existence in contemporary Indonesian society, resulting in social exclusion and marginalisation. This course will critically analyse socio-economic development policies such as urbanisation, environmental management, public health and poverty reduction and nationalism in Indonesia. Students will gain an understanding of causes of the socio-political tension and its impact in contemporary Indonesian society.
learning_outcomes: investigate the specific factors and influences that shape the practice of development policies.
obtain foundation knowledge and general concepts to analyse significant socio-economic issues in the contemporary Indonesian society.
critically evaluate and analyse sources (e.g. media, academic reading, opinion) relating to development projects in general.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Japan and North East Asian Dynamics
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to contemporary Japanese society. By taking this course, students will acquire a fundamental understanding of the significant historical, political, social, and economic issues that have influenced modern Japanese society. The emphasis lies on the period following World War II up until the present, examining Japan's recovery from the aftermath of the war and its subsequent transformation into a prominent global economy and influential regional power. This course will examine the impact of diplomatic, political, and economic shifts on various aspects of society, including education, businesses, political dynamics, racism, food security, gender, family, and popular culture. Additionally, it examines Japan's pacifist ideology after the war and its impact on the future of nuclear weapons.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate an ability to develop an evidence-based argument using primary and/or secondary sources.
Identify stereotypical assumptions made about Japanese society, politics and culture in case studies and topics covered

Gain the understanding of scholarly works from a range of disciplines in social sciences related to Japanese society Demonstrate knowledge of scholarly works from a range of disciplines relating to Japanese society, politics and culture.
Communicate effectively in oral presentation or group work on topics relating to the course.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Indo-Pacific Societies
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The Indo-Pacific region is a large geographic area characterised by complex social structures and a rich cultural diversity. There are flourishing branches of major world religions such as Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam, and Christianity. However, the region is also home to the growing urban aspirational middle classes of Asia. This interdisciplinary course, which draws from the knowledge bases of sociology and anthropology, will focus on the foundations of the local society and culture. Rather than seeing the area as a static single entity, this course will introduce key analytical concepts and perspectives to understand such cultural and societal dynamics that affect everyday lives. By taking this course, students will acquire the fundamental knowledge and analytical tools necessary to understand the significant historical, social, and cultural issues that underpin the region's rapid social and economic change, which is accelerated by digital transformation. Religions, modernity, ethnicity, class, marriage and kinship, gender, power, and livelihoods will all be explored.
learning_outcomes: Identify stereotypical assumptions made about diverse societies, politics and cultures in case studies and topics covered.
Gain the understanding of scholarly works from a range of disciplines in social sciences related to diverse cultures and societies in the Indo-Pacific region.
Communicate effectively in oral presentation or group work on topics relating to the course.
Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate an ability to develop an evidence-based argument using primary and/or secondary sources.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1501 and ZHSS1502

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indonesian A
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Indonesia is a country of strategic importance to Australia. It is an emerging economy in the Indo-Pacific region. Engagement with Indonesia will require you to understand cultural differences between the ethnic groups of Indonesia as well as develop your Indonesian language competence. The course is designed to introduce the first session of elementary Indonesian language to form language acquisition skills. You will undertake study of written and spoken standard Indonesian language. Bahasa Indonesia is the official language in Indonesia while a closely related language, Malay, is spoken in Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei. No prior Indonesian language knowledge is required to enrol in this course.
learning_outcomes: Speaking/listening competency: you will be able to conduct basic conversations in Indonesian about issues related to everyday life
Reading and writing competency: You will be able to read and answer simple questions about short edited Indonesian texts, and translate simple sentences from Indonesian into English and vice versa
Socio-cultural and situational understanding: You will be able to understand and explain some of the historical, political and cultural foundations of modern Indonesia
You will be able to recognise sounds, writings, and expressions in Indonesian language and to compare its mechanics of language (e.g. grammar) with those of English (or other languages)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indonesian B
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This is the second session of the Indonesian language and culture course to further develop your competence in the Indonesian language acquisition and cultural understanding of Indonesian society. You will gain understanding of the important processes and social structure which are vital in contemporary Indonesian society. Students are expected to conduct a simple conversation in Indonesian related to daily activities.
learning_outcomes: You will be able to recognise sounds, writings, and expressions in Indonesian language and to compare its mechanics of language (e.g. grammar) with those of English (or other languages).
Socio-Cultural and Situational Understanding: You will be able to understand and explain some of the historical, political and cultural foundations of modern Indonesia.

Reading/Writing Competency: You will be able to read, write, and answer simple questions about short edited Indonesian texts, and translate simple sentences from Indonesian into English and vice versa.
Listening/Speaking Competency: you will be able to conduct basic conversations in Indonesian about issues related to everyday life.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS2510

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Practical Ethics for the 21st Century
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Constant changes in both the global environment in the 21st Century and the expectations placed upon the military combine to make new and increasingly complex ethical demands upon officers of the Australian Defence Force. This course introduces students to ethical theory and debate with reference to various issues they will face as future officers in the military and as citizens of Australia. Topics to be discussed in the course will be selected by the students and may include discussion of topics such as cloning, euthanasia, the environment, global poverty, terrorism, capital punishment, privacy and ethical issues in counter-terrorism.
learning_outcomes: Identify and investigate ethical issues critically
Use and explain the relevance of critical ethical thinking in everyday life
Apply these theories to a range of contemporary ethical issues
Explain the fundamental ethical theories
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Any 2 of ZHSS1201, ZHSS1202, ZHSS1301, ZHSS1302, ZHSS1401, ZHSS1402, ZBUS1101, ZBUS1103 or ZGEN2240 with Head of School consent.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introductory Business Ethics
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Business managers in the modern, global economy are routinely faced with challenging ethical issues. Do managers that sacrifice profits for the sake of mitigating social and environmental problems breach the trust of the shareholders that they have been appointed to serve? What are the moral requirements that marketing campaigns must adhere to? What rights do employees hold against their employers? Under what circumstances is it ethically appropriate to file for bankruptcy? Is it permissible to use bribery in cultures and markets where it normal and widely accepted? To what extent should free and voluntary commercial exchanges be coercively regulated by the state? In answering such questions, the law often provides little guidance. Students enrolled in Introductory Business Ethics will learn to apply traditional ethical theories and principles to modern-day business decisions in a wide range of contexts.
learning_outcomes: explain, discuss, and propose sollutions to the moral challenges confronting business organisations today
apply abstract ethical theories and principles to real-world situations
Identify the salient features of ethical problems in the business world
comprehend and critically evaluate the concepts and precepts of various approaches to ethics;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Humanities & Social Sciences Special Topic 1
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to offer students enrolled in the BA (CDF) an understanding of research and writing in the Humanities and Social Sciences, building upon what they will have learned in their first year of study. The course will be structured to introduce ideas and methodologies pertinent to a course that they have studied in first year or are currently studying and will enable students to define a related research topic on which they will complete an extented essay or project.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an in depth understanding of the relevant field of study.
Demonstrate the ability to research and write in depth and with clear focus.
Select, understand and utilise relevant discipline skills and scholarly literature.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in CDF Program (4461)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Humanities and Social Sciences Research Project 1
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students will undertake a research project on a nominated topic in a specific discipline area commensurate with their year of study. As one of the aims of the program is to further develop critical thinking and independent research skills, the project will involve 'hands-on' research experience in collaboration with a staff member or their research team. A supervisor, who will work closely with the student, will manage each project. The research project will be chosen after discussion between the student and the supervisor. Students will be expected to present a short introductory seminar on the topic by week 4 of Session. Final assessment will be based on a written paper and an oral presentation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to research and write in-depth and with clear focus.
Select, understand and utilise relevant discipline skills and scholarly literature.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the relevant field of study.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in CDF Program (4461)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Studies in the Media
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The media reporting of war plays a pivotal role in how war today is waged and understood. This course examines the history of this relationship between war and the media alongside various theories and practices of the communication of war from the nineteenth to the twenty-first century. The course will consist of selected theoretical readings that focus on various elements of the media reportage of war and its media forms, including the role of the journalist, the witness, propaganda, memory, truth, images, film and humanitarianism.
learning_outcomes: Understand key theoretical perspectives on war, the media and processes of mediatisation
Develop the skills necessary to apply current theories of war and the media to contemporary reporting in the media.
Understand the way in which media, genre and form determine and condition the representation of war.
Have a more expansive grasp of the history of the media reportage of war
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Classic Literary Texts
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this course students will be introduced to some of the major works of Western culture, works that have been characterised as 'canonical' texts. The concept of 'canonicity' will be explored through a selection of material that may include the Old and New Testament and works from the Greco-Roman tradition, modern European classics in translation, and major works of English literature.
learning_outcomes: Identify significant characters and myths, and describe some of the contexts and influences of literature and film in the Western traditions (cultural literacy).
Understand some key ways in which textual analysis proceeds methodologically.
Comprehend and analyse major literary and film texts in English (knowledge of the discipline area).
Apply critical and analytical skills to the close reading of literary and film texts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Literatures of the World
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines writing in English or in English translation from the formerly colonised nations of the world. It explores the rich literature generated by a confrontation with political and global forces, and the influence of more than one literary tradition on the formation of texts. The course examines literature, film and popular culture, within the context of local histories, politics and cultural patterns.
learning_outcomes: be able to assess and respond to texts from different contexts in a comparative frame
possess improved skills in undertaking and deploying independent research in literary studies
demonstrate advanced skills in reading and responding to complex forms of representation
demonstrate enhanced familiarity with writing and film from outside the English tradition
have some mastery of ideas and theories about the development of culture in relation to decolonisation, globalisation and conflict
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: War Literature and Film
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: War literature and film explores the human dimension of war, asking what it means to fight, to suffer and to remember wars. Focussing, therefore, on the personal experience of soldiers and civilians caught up in conflicts, this course is a study of selected war literature and films from the twentieth to the twenty-first century. It examines key questions about how war and its often terrifying violence have been represented; how authors and film makers have managed to convey the shifting character of modern war; and how texts about war portray the complex relationships between civilian and military worlds. Concepts and issues examined will include violence, pain and trauma, experience, the fragile body at war, military occupation, civilians in wartime, comradeship, masculinity, media forms and representations of the soldier and the enemy. The course is worth 6 units of credit in the English and Media Studies program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the way in which genre and form determine representation
Demonstrate an understanding of the literature and film of war
Explain some essential features of literature, film and popular culture from the eighteenth century to the present
Explain and apply current theories associated with the study of trauma, violence and war
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reading Theory
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: How does meaning work? 'Reading theory' explores the concepts underpinning our understanding of representation in texts, reading and writing. It surveys the major literary and cultural theories of the last century, examining and applying methodological approaches one by one. Questions raised include: How should we read? What is a text? Is it possible to arrive at a single correct interpretation? How are texts related to other texts? How are texts related to their historical and social contexts? What is an author? Does politics matter to culture or culture to politics? How does a reading of literary texts assist us in understanding the larger contexts of contemporary culture?
learning_outcomes: Understand some founding concepts of critical practice and literary theory
Know how to employ concepts and methods in literary and cultural analysis
Engage with the history of critical debates within the field of literary studies
Understand the role of theory and critique in literary studies
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Literature of the Modern
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The Literature of the Modern is a study of British prose and poetry from the industrial revolution of the early nineteenth century to the Second World War in the twentieth. This was a period in which the modern world took shape through an unprecedented series of technological, social and political changes, many of which first occurred in Britain. While progress came to be widely celebrated, many authors were also concerned that their contemporary world had become severed from its traditions and cultural heritage. A core element of this course will be to consider how literature of the period responded to the idea of being modern and to the cultural, social and political ramifications of modernity. The question was repeatedly asked – how should we understand progress? Authors examined include William Wordsworth, Charlotte Smith, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, Lord Byron, Thomas De Quincey, W.B Yeats, T.S. Eliot and Virginia Woolf.
learning_outcomes: Analyse literature by showing how genre and form determine representation
Undertake literary analysis that draws on current theories of the relation between texts and their historical contexts
Communicate awareness of the development of literary genres and forms since the eighteenth century
Demonstrate an understanding of key literary texts of the Romantic and Modernist eras.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1101 and ZHSS1102

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Preliminary Honours History: Methodology, Research and Writing
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed as a ‘capstone’ to a discipline major. It is open to final-year BA students with a high credit average in their major stream who would like to explore their discipline in more depth and to develop higher-level skills in methodology, research, and writing. It is therefore a foundation for those intending to apply for final year Honours or anyone wishing to pursue research in their later career. The structure of the course is based on two pillars. The first is the design, development, and writing of an individual research project. The student will shape a project that interests them, with support from me and their peers, and develop it through various research and writing stages from a proposal, ‘workshopping’ different elements, to submission of a research essay. The second pillar is coursework that explores discipline and research methods and the nature and use of different source material. The course invites students to shape their own learning and develop their capacity for creativity, self-directed and collaborative learning, critical analysis, and effective writing. The small-group seminar format aims to be an immersive and intellectually stimulating learning experience in which students gain a more nuanced understanding of their discipline and are rewarded by a deeper understanding of themselves as independent, rigorous, and reflective scholars.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate high skill levels in written and oral presentation, analysis, argument, and scholarly debate.
Explain and apply critical understanding to disciplinary texts, concepts, and methodologies and analyse various types of scholarly sources.
Construct and write a clearly expressed and logically organised research essay that gives evidence of initiative and self-direction in learning.
Critically and creatively employ disciplinary knowledge to define and develop a complex research problem.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: 24 units of credit in upper-level History passed at Credit level or higher; Corequisite: 6 units of credit in upper-level History.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Space: Security, History and Politics
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Australia has been involved in space since the start of the space age, launching its first satellite in 1967 and operating the world’s largest rocket range. Famously, Australia also helped put a person on the moon through tracking stations, some of which are still in operation. Today, space is a vital domain for Australia and influences every aspect of daily life, the economy and national security. This course aims to provide students with a foundational understanding of the space domain. It examines space from a broad perspective applying a range of approaches to understand the military, civil and commercial elements of space. Students will explore Australian and global space history, concepts of space power, military uses of space, legal and ethical considerations, and the commercial space economy. Space will also be examined through the lens of culture, drawing in science fiction and public imagination to understand how Australia has engaged with this new domain.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and analyze the key debates relating to the space domain.
Demonstrate an understanding of the drivers of action in the space domain.
Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate an ability to develop an evidence-based argument.
Identify and explain key theories and concepts that are applied to space.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Second World War
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will give the student an understanding of the greatest global conflict in history through the analysis of the military, social, political, economic, ideological and moral issues that shaped it. Students will study the strategic decisions, the major air, sea and land campaigns and the key turning points of the military struggle. The course also examines the impact of the war and mobilization on the home fronts, raising questions of leadership, morale and social change. Students will study life under foreign occupation and the difficulties this imposed on the defeated. The study of the Second World War raises many moral issues: amongst them, the barbarisation of warfare; the Final Solution; the choices of resistance and collaboration; the dropping of the first atomic bomb; and the trials and punishment at the end of the war. Students will examine different historical interpretations of these issues and engage in the arguments surrounding them.
learning_outcomes: Discuss and engage in the continuing debates surrounding continuing scholarly issues
Identify, contrast and interpret the different experiences and perspectives of combatant and occupied nations
Explain the course of the war and contextualise and explain its key events
Analyse and evaluate the forces that shaped the war
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1201 and ZHSS1202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Australian Military History 1788 to the Present
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide students with an understanding of the impact of war, the military, and defence issues generally on the development of Australian society over the two hundred years of European settlement, with an emphasis upon the period since 1899. While not neglecting the pre-Federation period, the focus of the course is on substantive issues arising from involvement in Australia's wars in the twentieth century and the periods of peace between them.
learning_outcomes: Enhance their understanding of the major historical processes that shaped Australia’s war experience.
Improve their academic and formal writing skills and the ability to express ideas and arguments in the written form
Develop or refine their ability to form coherent arguments and opinions relating to issues raised in the course

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Genocide: Crime of Crimes
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Genocide is known as 'the crime of crimes'. This course gives students an understanding of the history of genocide in the modern world from the early twentieth century to the present. Students explore the origins of the concept and its definition in humanitarian law (the United Nations Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide). The course compares several case studies to examine various themes: the changing face of genocide; motivation of perpetrators; moral dilemmas of victims and bystanders; the link with war and ideology; and how intervention, prevention and punishment challenge the international community. Students engage with many primary sources and interdisciplinary debates in a rich scholarship.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept of genocide
Develop effective academic skills in research and writing
Develop effective communications skills as a presenter, leader and contributor to discussions
Reflect on their own learning and understand their own learning processes
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1201 and ZHSS1202 OR ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Naval History and Sea Power in the Modern Age
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: We will study navies and sea power, on the international stage, c.1890 to the present, especially navies as a vital part of the wider context of twentieth-century history. The emphasis will be on strategic and grand strategic, rather than tactical themes, although these will feature in case studies (e.g. the Battle of the Atlantic). Topics will include Mahan and the classical maritime strategists, the world wars at sea, sea power and the British empire, the Cold War, the Gulf Wars, current issues and the future of sea power, naval command, and the personal experience of naval warfare.
learning_outcomes: Understand the historical development of navies and sea power in the modern era.
Evaluate relevant historiographical arguments and debates.
Analyse the writings of leading naval and maritime strategists and apply these ideas to historical and contemporary situations.
Construct and communicate sophisticated historical arguments in written form, informed by sound historical methods.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1201 and ZHSS1202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: First World War
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course considers the First World War as the first global war of the twentieth century. It will develop students' knowledge of this conflict by examining the causes of the war, the major military theatres of operations, the social and economic mobilisation of civil society, issues of loyalty and dissent, the relationships between the major alliance partners, and the effects of the war in Europe and in the rest of the world. Students will also analyse how the First World War has been variously remembered or forgotten in the nations that fought it. This course will give students an understanding how major conflicts can be catalysts for change for states, societies and individuals.
learning_outcomes: Understand a range of basic historical themes and concepts relevant to the First World War
Engage with wider debates over the causes and impacts of the First World War
Evaluate relevant historiographical arguments and the changing course of these over time
Construct and communicate sophisticated historical arguments in written form, informed by sound historical methods
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1201 or ZHSS1202 or with Head of School approval

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars, 1792-1815
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars between 1792-1815. It will detail the origins of these conflicts, their conduct both in Europe and globally, their social and political contexts, and their enduring influence on global history and the conduct of war. It will give students an understanding of key themes including the influence of social forces on the conduct of war, the relationship between European military systems and colonialism, and the growth of strategic and operational thought and practice.
learning_outcomes: assess critically, and deploy primary sources, informed by sound historical methods, to create historical arguments.
demonstrate understanding through a critical analysis, of a range of historiographical issues in the history of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars.
construct and communicate sophisticated historical arguments in writing.
demonstrate in-depth knowledge about this significant period of modern European history.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nazi Germany 1933-45
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Why do historians continue to debate National Socialism? Why do we continue to regard Hitler, Nazism and the Holocaust as the supreme examples of evil in modern history? This course will encourage students to consider these questions as we examine the history of Nazi Germany and key historiographical arguments and their significance to the broader understanding of modern history through a focus on three themes — the regime’s racial policies, the relationship between the German people and the dictatorship, and the relationship between the German military and the regime. This course offers history students the opportunity to undertake original research on the period by studying a source written by an actual participant in, or witness to, the Third Reich. It encourages an understanding of the strengths and weaknesses of various approaches to understanding this multifaceted historical phenomenon.
learning_outcomes: know more about this significant period of 20th century history and be able to:
understand, assess critically and deploy primary sources, informed by sound historical methods, to create historical arguments

understand a range of historiographical issues in the history of Nazi Germany, relating to Nazi Germany as a racial state; support, accommodation and opposition to the regime; and the armed forces' role in the regime
construct and communicate sophisticated historical arguments in writing.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Either ZHSS1201 or ZHSS1202, or both ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Winners and Losers in World Economic History
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The course presents a survey of major developments in world economic history and economic thought from about 1500 to today and arranged around the theme of ‘winners' and ‘losers'. It examines why the West triumphed in the early modern period and why at the same time great eastern civilisations such as India and China declined. It covers the West’s adoption of the system of slavery, the industrial revolution that began in Britain and extended to other European countries and the United States, and the development of capitalism. It looks into differences within capitalist countries and between rich capitalist countries and underdeveloped countries in the periphery. The course examines the contest between major economic ideas such as liberalism, comparative advantage and socialist ideas; the causes and consequences of the Great Depression of the 1930s; and the effort led by the United States to reconstruct the non-communist world after World War II. We discuss winners and losers in the Golden Age of capitalism and a world divided between rich western economies, a less prosperous and centrally directed communist bloc and the ’third world’ of under-developed countries. The course then discusses major developments in the late 20th and 21st centuries including the Global Financial Crisis, the rise of China, and the dominance of high technology companies. Finally, the course also pays attention to the question why Australia emerged in the two centuries after 1788 as a prosperous country.
learning_outcomes: Understand how economic power interacts with other forms of power;
Understand the main themes in world economic history from the late Middle Ages to the Present;
Become familiar with major debates and controversies in world economic history;
Clearly express ideas and arguments about world economic history in written form.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Secrets and Spies: Intelligence Activities Throughout History
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the activities of spies, spy-catchers, intelligence agencies, and the operations they have conducted throughout history to obtain or protect secrets. Cloaks and daggers, dead drops, surveillance vans, and electronic intercepts have all been used by state and non-state actors vying for an edge over their adversaries. Using case studies from across the globe – in times of peace and war – students will use historical material to develop an understanding of why intelligence agencies exist, what they do, and how they do it. Instances of success and failure will be analysed, requiring students to think critically about the use and misuse of intelligence, including the propriety, ethics, benefits and limitations of intelligence collection. The course aims to explore the shadowy world of intelligence operations, and through this further develop students’ abilities in using primary and secondary sources to research and examine important historical events.
learning_outcomes: Establish a broad understanding of the role of intelligence agencies and their activities throughout history
Engage with key debates about the use and misuse, and the benefits and limitations of intelligence
Demonstrate the ability to develop coherent arguments and clearly express them in formal academic presentations and writing
Differentiate between primary and secondary sources, and know how to incorporate both into your assessments
prerequisites: ZHSS1201 & ZHSS1202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indonesian 3A
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Indonesia is a country of strategic importance to Australia. It is an emerging economy in the Asia-Pacific region with a large Muslim population. This course will enable you to understand current socio-cultural issues of Indonesia through the study of the Indonesian language and culture. This is the first session of a third-year Indonesian language course, which focuses on oral competence in Indonesian as well as providing an understanding of Indonesian cultures and society. Students are expected to read and respond to authentic Indonesian materials.
learning_outcomes: Write reports, accounts and commentary with confidence using more complex language.
Express their opinions, thoughts and ideas by engaging in language exchanges with confidence using more complex Indonesian, on the topics covered in class.
Gain deeper understanding of Indonesian society and culture.
Read and comprehend more complex written Indonesian.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS2302

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Indonesian 3B
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Indonesia is a country of strategic importance to Australia. It is an emerging economy in the Asia-Pacific region with a large Muslim population. This course will enable students to understand current socio-cultural issues of Indonesia through the study of the Indonesian language and culture. This is the second session of a third-year language course, which focuses on oral competences in Indonesian as well as providing an understanding of Indonesian cultures and society. Students are expected to read and respond to authentic Indonesian materials with high-level grammatical complexities.
learning_outcomes: express opinions, thoughts and ideas by engaging in language exchanges with confidence using more complex Indonesian, on the topics covered in class
gain deeper understanding of Indonesian society and culture.
read and comprehend more complex written Indonesian
write reports, accounts and commentary with confidence using more complex language
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS3301

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Uses and Abuses of History
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course investigates the sometimes fraught and contentious relationship between historians and other stakeholders, such as governments, cultural institutions, the media and the public. Using a range of historical methods and materials, students will explore local and international case studies and examine the ways that the past is presented, interpreted and used by individuals, groups and communities. Key themes covered in the unit include the role of history in constructing national narratives, the challenges of exhibiting the past, and the politicisation of history and its consequences. The aim of this unit is to provide students with an understanding of how history has been used and abused and the connections, controversies and collisions between the past and present.
learning_outcomes: Analyse debates relating to the real-world implications of how the past is presented and used in local and international contexts
Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate the ability to develop an evidence-based argument
Demonstrate an understanding of how history is used and interpreted by individuals and communities in a range of settings
Identify and explain the key theories and approaches historians use to debate interpretations of the past
prerequisites: ZHSS1201 & ZHSS1202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Politics of Australian Security
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will examine current and future issues facing Australian national security planners. It will cover the major challenges relating to Australian foreign and defence policy, as well as broader issues relating to homeland security.
learning_outcomes: Graduates will demonstrate that they have acquired coherent knowledge of the underlying principles and concepts of the key elements in Australia's foreign and defence policies;
Comprehend the nature and role of intelligence processes and product in modern organisations;
Identify lessons to be drawn from recent Australian experiences and formulate solutions to complex problems with intellectual independence;.
Demonstrate cognitive skills that review, analyse, consolidate and synthesize knowledge regarding the contributions made by government agencies to the broader homeland security portfolio;
Demonstrate a broad understanding of a body of knowledge and theoretical concepts with advanced understanding in Australia's strategic relationships with other states;
Understand principal factors shaping the development and employment of Australia's?s defence capabilities;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Regional Security Issues
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The regional security environment is rapidly changing. This course examines the key elements shaping the Asia-Pacific security environment in the early 21st century. It will consider the nature and dynamics of a range of contemporary security challenges facing the region, the capacity of regional security structures to manage these challenges, and the influence of major regional powers on the evolving regional order. Particular attention is given to analyzing regional security flashpoints and to emerging non-traditional threats to security in the era of globalisation. The impact of key developments in regional security on Australia's national interests will also be examined.
learning_outcomes: At the successful completion of the course, students will be able to explain the nature and dynamics of key security issues in the Asia-Pacific region;
At the successful completion of the course, students will be able to analyze the relative contributions of different security structures to regional order;
At the successful completion of the course, students will be able to assess the impact of changing power relativities on regional security;
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Building Southeast Asia: Politics, Society and Culture
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Building Southeast Asia: Politics, Society and Culture is a broad survey course of the eleven political systems making up the Southeast Asian region: Brunei, Burma (Myanmar), Cambodia, East Timor, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. The focus is on the contemporary period. The course critically evaluates various frameworks that are employed by political scientists to understand the political process: democratic, electoral democracy, semi-democratic, semi-authoritarian, authoritarian pluralist, Leninist and military regime. Then the course examines in detail constitutional structures, the process of political change and transition, leadership, opposition, civil society, the political role of the military, political Islam, corruption and crony capitalism, and political violence and armed separatism.
learning_outcomes: Development of independent research skills to analyse and interpret diverse source material.

Enhanced understanding of the major processes of political transition and political change in contemporary Southeast Asia, including familiarity with the major analytical frameworks employed by political scientists to understand the processes of political transition and political change.
Development of effective academic writing skills.
Improved critical reflection and evaluation of required reading.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethnic Conflict and World Politics
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of ethnic conflict as a major challenge in contemporary world politics. It develops analytical skills in assessing the political dynamics of conflict management, resolution and reconciliation of specific case studies. Students will be introduced to the conceptual debates within the multidisciplinary field of ethnic studies and will be required to critically assess the political dynamics of specific case studies. Part I examines definitional debates about ethnicity and nationalism and considers the relationship between theory and policy. Part II compares and contrasts various political and social contexts where ethnic cleavages have become sources of conflict and those where communal differences have not led to conflict. In particular the claim that democracy and civil society offer some insurance against ethnic conflict will be scrutinised. Part III examines the international politics of ethnic conflict. Many contemporary ethnic conflicts have their origins in the legacies of imperialism. Modern forces such as globalisation have exacerbated or ameliorated the conditions for ethnic conflict. Part IV surveys strategies for the management, resolution and reconciliation between ethnic communities.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate efforts for prevention of conflict
Reflect on what have been the main challenges or obstacles for settlement and management of the conflict?
Examine the interdisciplinary debates surrounding ethnic identity and their implications for analysing ethnic conflict
Explain how international factors influence the causes of conflict?
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Complex Peacekeeping Operations
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Since 1948 the UN has authorised more than seventy peacekeeping missions, with tens of thousands of peacekeepers currently deployed around the globe. Many complex factors determine if a peacekeeping mission will be deployed, and if it will successfully be able to fulfil its mandate. This course considers the history of peacekeeping operations and how they have evolved over time. It examines current operations, including mandates, budgets and operational context. Finally it will consider the future of peacekeeping in the current geopolitical environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective skills in independent research and academic writing.
Demonstrate a broad understanding of peacekeeping operations, including their history and evolution;
Critically evaluate debates about key issues in peacekeeping, including political, strategic and ethical aspects;
prerequisites: Pre-requisites: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Topics in Political Philosophy
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The ideals of freedom, equality, and justice are commonly invoked. But what does it actually mean to be free? Or to be equal? Or to live in a just society? This course will examine these and other fundamental questions of political philosophy using both contemporary and historical thinkers. Topics to be addressed include: justifications for the existence of the state, political obligation and civil disobedience, freedom, private property, equality and justice, and whether we have obligations to those who live in other societies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrates the ability to understand, analyse and evaluate key arguments in relevant literatures
Demonstrates a knowledge of some of the major theories and debates in current political philosophy
Demonstrates the ability to develop your own views through careful consideration and analysis of the views presented in the course, and to do so with clarity and rigour
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401, ZHSS1402 or ZHSS2600

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Air Power in Small and Irregular Wars
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Almost from the inception of powered flight, Western states have found air power to be an especially useful means of dealing with irregular forces. Whether quelling rebellious tribes in far flung colonies or pursuing bandits across border regions, air power in its many forms has been an important component of irregular warfare. In this course our underlying concern is to explore the use of force in the international environment, particularly its use by states against non-state actors. The context for this examination is the use of air power in small, irregular and unconventional wars, since 1917. Wars against bandits, rebels, insurgents, terrorists and guerrillas. The course will investigate the historic use of air power through colonial and post-colonial settings to consider finally the challenges such wars pose for the employment of air power today. This course may be taken as an IPS or a History unit at stage 2 or stage 3.
learning_outcomes: Explain how air power has been employed in a variety of small and irregular wars since 1917.
Identify key insights regarding the effective employment of air power in small and irregular wars and in particular identify where the use of force has and has not achieved the desired outcomes.
Describe the unique characteristics of small and irregular warfare and the possible implications of these for the use of air power.
Analyse and evaluate the performance of air power as a form of military force in these conflicts.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: National Military Power and Joint Warfare
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students an introduction to the theories and guiding principles of National Military Power and the application of armed force via Joint Warfare approaches. It develops a student’s understanding of the relationship between National Defence Policy, and National Military Strategy and how this translates into National Military Power. To do so it explores the relationship between the government and the military, the legislature which authorises, commands, controls, and administers the use of force and the interplay between policy, strategy and joint capabilities such as intelligence, logistics, health, personnel and operations within the context of Australia’s National Security. It examines the theory and application of Joint Warfare through the lens of the Australian Department of Defence and the Australian Defence Force. This is achieved by exploring the various ways that National Military Power is applied across the Sea, Land, Air, Space and Cyber Domains during peace, competition and conflict.
learning_outcomes: Critique the relationship between National Defence Policy, Military Strategy and Military Capability.
Articulate the utility of National Military Power across the spectrum of peace, competition and conflict.
Argue the utility of National Military Power within the constructs of National Security and National Power.
Evaluate the broad application of Joint Warfare across the spectrum of peace, competition and conflict.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402 or ZHSS1201 and ZHSS1202

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Australia: Who really holds power?
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course gives students an applied, hands on, understanding of how the Australian political system works and how government policy making works in practice. The course takes a case study approach where students are required to pick an issue they care about and to follow it through the political decision making process. As we introduce each element of the political system, the student can see how it works in practice through their case study. Students are also required to engage with their peers' case studies giving them a breadth of insight into the major issues on the Australian political landscape and the different political dynamics that develop around different issues.
learning_outcomes: Apply the different theories of power and political decision making to analysing contemporary events in Australian politics.
Undertake research into an issue in contemporary Australian politics.
Identify and explain the key elements of the Australian government system and how they combine to shape government policy making.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Politics of International Human Rights
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the political struggle to develop and implement international human rights norms, which protect people against abusive states and support international peace and stability. After a critical introduction to the international human rights regime, the course turns to two inter-related questions at the heart of the politics of human rights: Why do states violate human rights, and what can “we” (the international community) do to stop them from doing so? This provides the students with an opportunity to "step into the shoes" of policy makers and actively engage in an effort to find solutions to a major international problem.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the human rights situation in particular countries, including the nature of major violations and their root causes;
Critically evaluate human rights policies of foreign governments and international organisations and advise decision makers on appropriate courses of action.
Explain what human rights are and their appropriate role in international relations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Politics and Ethics of War
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the ethical arguments, assumptions and principles that are used to prescribe and evaluate policies and practices in the context of contemporary organised violence. Moreover, and importantly, this course makes the particular political contexts of these arguments, assumptions and principles a central part of this examination. In other words, its starting-point is the necessity of studying the ethics and politics of war together. Combining these two categories sets this course apart from other courses being taught both within UNSW Canberra and at other institutions.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate current policies and practices given both relevant political factors and ethical constraints.
Demonstrate a clear understanding of the general normative theories applicable to conflict and international politics.
Analyse the impact of these theories on policy and practice in armed conflict and IR.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Security Studies
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to introduce students to contemporary security studies through a critical exploration of theory and practice. Traditionally, studies in international security have assumed that states are the primary actors in world politics and that the focus of security should be concentrated on conventional military threats. Contemporary security studies challenges both assumptions. The course evaluates debates between conventional and critical security studies by exploring how security is an essentially contested concept and examining this proposition in terms of the importance of non-military issues and non-state actors. The main schools of thought are reviewed to develop conceptual tools that will be used to analyse a range of non-traditional security issues such as energy security, environmental security, ethnic conflict and health security.This is followed by a survey of non-state actors such as private security companies, non-governmental organisations, AI/robotics and multinational corporations. Students completing this course will develop their analytical skills required for understanding complex security dynamics.
learning_outcomes: Assess the role that non-state actors play in contemporary global security
Understand the main schools of thought in security studies
Reflect on whether contemporary security challenges are fundamentally challenging traditional security concepts and policies
Evaluate why a range of non-military issues have emerged as important security concerns
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZHSS1401 and ZHSS1402

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Global Climate & Environmental Security
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Are we ready for the Anthropocene? Whether you are a citizen, a policymaker, or a member of the armed forces, you will have experienced environmental threats and disaster, and wondered how they came about and how they can be mitigated. ZHSS3436 Global Climate & Environmental Security considers the sources and consequences of major environmental threats and risks such as climate change, biodiversity loss, and competition for natural resources, and analyses their geopolitical, human security, military and ecological implications. It has a dual frame that introduces conceptual approaches and debates about security and the Earth system, along with the challenge of framing national policy and global governance responses.
learning_outcomes: Explain key processes, actors and drivers in climate change and other forms of environmental insecurity, and the ways in which they interact and combine.
Communicate and debate complex ideas, lucidly and ethically, capably using a variety of different media.
Reflect on how key national and international governance frameworks for security and the environment intersect (or fail to intersect) to address complex drivers of environmental change.

Explain the major observed and potential impacts of climate change, biodiversity loss, extreme weather and earth system change on states, human communities, ecosystems and biomes, and the ways that these impacts can be understood as forms of insecurity.
Describe and evaluate policy proposals and community actions to address environmental insecurities and propose integrated solutions.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Politics of the USA
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The United States is the world's superpower, and political decisions made by the US often have global ramifications. The US is also Australia's most important ally, with whom we have close strategic and defence ties. This course will enable students to develop a strong understanding of the political system in the US. It will examine the foundations of US politics, the role of key political institutions, and consider how power and influence functions within the system. It will also explore areas of foreign policy and foreign relations. Finally, the course will analyse a selection of contemporary issues and challenges faced by the US in the twenty-first century.
learning_outcomes: On successful completion of this course, students will be able to reflect upon the aspirations of and challenges likely to be experienced by the US in the twenty-first century

On successful completion of this course, students will be able to critically evaluate debates about key issues in US politics, from the past and present, demonstrating an ability to engage with a range of historical and contemporary influences on policy development
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate a broad understanding of key political institutions in the United States, including their historical development
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate effective skills in independent research and academic writing

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The United Nations in Global Politics
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: The United Nations (UN) has been central to global politics and world order since it was first established in the immediate aftermath of the Second World War to prevent another devastating war, and its responsibilities and activities today span many of the most pressing global security and development challenges. This course examines the past, present and future of the UN, focusing on how it shapes and is, in turn, shaped by broader global forces. It introduces students to the basic history, organisation and functions of the world organisation; it undertakes a critical survey of the efforts of the UN to prevent war, protect human rights and promote development; and it engages with key debates about how the UN may be reformed to remain relevant in a rapidly changing world.
learning_outcomes: On successful completion of this course, students will be able to describe the internal governance structures and principles of the UN.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the role of the UN in global politics and how it has evolved over time.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the UN as a vehicle for resolving major global problems.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to critically engage in current debates about UN reform and how to keep the world organisation relevant in the 21st Century.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Contemporary Islam: Community and Changes in Indonesia and Beyond
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Contrary to the prediction of the modernisation theory, Islam is the fast-growing religion in the world. Understanding of Islam, Muslim societies, and identity politics is becoming increasingly important in the professional life of our graduates. This course examines contemporary challenges faced by Muslim communities with a focus on regional perspectives and especially on Indonesia, which has the largest Muslim population in the world. It introduces fundamental knowledge of Muslim religious beliefs and practices, and their historical development. It also explores the relationships between Muslim communities and the state, and examines the challenging contexts in which Muslims have been placed to negotiate their identity and Islamic ideas.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate various challenges facing the Islamic communities.
Gain relevant disciplinary knowledge of Islamic Studies relevant to Southeast Asian contexts.
Achieve broader understanding of Islamic beliefs and practices.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Civil-State-Military Relations in Indonesia
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will critically analyse areas in which Indonesian people demonstrate their capacity to empowering civil society to reinforce their citizenship amidst the crucial democratic transition the nation has ever experienced. In particular, the future of Indonesia along the path of democracy, a success or a failure, would be determined by conditions in civil-state/military relations. The course will look into the practices of the state and the armed forces in relation to civil society activism, the everyday life, the practice of media, the political expressions in popular culture to assess the contemporary state of civil-state-military relations in Indonesia. The use of selected texts in Indonesian language may be used to allow students to gain an advanced understanding of the current state of democracy in Indonesia. Topics that are covered for this course, among others, are the state ideology, Indonesian armed forces (e.g. history, doctrine, culture, etc.), social activism, as well as political expression in popular culture and media.
learning_outcomes: On successful completion of this course, students will be able to critically analyse and evaluate the information relating to civil-state-military relations.
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to identify various factors and influences affecting the practice of civil-state-military relations; and
On successful completion of this course, students will be able to achieve a broad understanding of the contemporary Indonesian society;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Maritime Security and the Rules-Based Order in the Indo-Pacific
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the challenges Australia faces in safeguarding both its own maritime domain and championing the ‘rules based order’ at sea in a rapidly evolving Indo-Pacific context. These range from non-traditional security threats such as narcotics smuggling and illegal fishing, to maritime boundary disputes, to ‘grey zone’ geopolitical contestation playing out between coastguards and maritime militias instead of navies in the South and East China Sea. The course will provide an introduction to the rules-based order at sea and UN Convention on the Law of the Sea as the ‘constitution for the oceans’ governing both maritime law-enforcement operations and securing our sea lines of communication. The course will explore both the importance of adherence to international laws and norms governing maritime activities and attempts to re-shape that order for strategic advantage. This is significant not only in the efforts of China as a rising power to reshape elements of the maritime order but also, for example, in the campaigning of Pacific Island States to prepare for a future in which they may be de-territorialized by rising sea levels. By studying this course, you will gain an understanding of the legal, diplomatic, and operational aspects of upholding the rules-based order.
learning_outcomes: Explain theories of the ‘rules based order’ and what it means, its function in an age of great power contestation, and its application to particular case studies.
Understand the major principles of the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea and explain how they operate in context.
Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate an ability to develop an evidence-based argument using primary and/or secondary sources.
Identify non-traditional maritime security threats and analyse the effectiveness of national and regional responses to them.
