It will survey the key developments in naval and maritime technologies over the past 200 years, setting them into their broader contexts. This will provide a grounding for a more focused exploration of the historical, political, strategic, tactical, and cultural factors that frame decision making regarding Australian naval construction. The course aims to develop the students’ understanding of the contexts which shape the decisions over the design and construction of warships.
learning_outcomes: Engage with some of the debates over the conception, design and construction of warships
Demonstrate the ability to develop coherent arguments and clearly express them in formal academic writing
Demonstrate a broad understanding of the development of naval and maritime technology
Evaluate different factors which have helped shape technological progress

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Australia and International Rules-Based Order
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: International law plays an important role in the system of international politics: the rules-based global order. Australian defence and foreign policy is committed to upholding that order and being a regional leader in it. But what does that mean in a time when rising and revisionist powers may be re-shaping the rules-based order? The content covered includes topics such as: the core principles and concepts of international law; international law and the use of military force; the role of multilateral treaties in global governance; distinguishing a political from a legal interpretation of a treaty; the operation of international courts and tribunals; and the relationship between foreign policy formulation and international law with an emphasis on current case studies. This course focusses on the interaction of law and politics.
learning_outcomes: Identify the various ways in which politics and law are related at the international level and explain how this relationship operates and why it matters.
Explain the Australian contribution to international law and the uses of international law in small and middle power statecraft.
Understand some of the key concepts and principles of international law and some of the more important aspects of the contemporary system of international law.
Communicate clearly in written form and demonstrate an ability to develop an evidence-based argument using primary and/or secondary sources.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Nearest Neighbours: Asia-Pacific Literature, Culture and Communication
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This interdisciplinary course is a study of Australian engagement with the Asia Pacific region, using the high impact cultural form of film to explore both connection and conflict. The aim is to expand Australia’s often limited understanding of its neighbours, fostering regional security through cultural exchange. The course has two modules. Module one focuses on Australia in Asia, examining geopolitical accounts of Australian strategic engagement with diverse nations in South East Asia and East Asia. In this context, it employs a focused comparison of two Australian films about decolonisation and war in Indonesia and East Timor to examine changing popular perceptions of these strategically important near neighbours. Module two focuses on Asia in Australia, highlighting the experiences and cultural expression of Asian Australians through contemporary feature films, utilising this powerful form of transnational storytelling to illuminate regional identity. Students will gain critical insights into Australia’s place in the Asia Pacific region and acquire cross-cultural knowledge to advance cultural diplomacy and regional security. The course is relevant to students working in defence, security, intelligence, development, international affairs and diplomacy.
learning_outcomes: Develop skills in applied research methods, assessing and employing scholarly sources and interdisciplinary approaches to broad strategic issues.
Demonstrate sound contemporary understanding of a range of Australian geopolitical, social and cultural responses to its Asia Pacific neighbours.
Further develop advanced skills in communicating evidence-based analysis and effective arguments.
Contextualise understandings of regional strategy and security through analysis of the impact of national and transnational popular cultural products such as film.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Representations of War
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to key concepts surrounding the ways in which wars are represented, and hence how war comes to be known about in the social and cultural domains. Our key question, then, is how do we know about war? What are the ways that war is reported, analysed, mediated, commemorated, and spectacularised? Such questions about the representation of war have received attention from a range of disciplines because they are central to our understanding of war’s relationship to society. Can wars be waged without public visibility and hence public support? This course will introduce students to some foundational questions about war and its representation. Texts studied may range from literature, art, and commemorative practices that shape the ‘human face of war’, to propaganda, journalism, and social media, and on to broader considerations about war as a cultural event that is always at some level determined by beliefs, perceptions, and memories of war. With its emphasis on critical reading and writing skills, this course is ideally suited to supplement the pleasure and success you can gain from the other offerings in the Masters Programs.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of key concepts and debates required for the study of war and its cultural, media and social representations.
Demonstrate advanced skills in analyzing complex forms of representation, across a range of genres and media.
Undertake independent research into the relationship between war, culture and representation and effectively communicate research findings.
Understand the historical, cultural, social, ethical, and political contexts that shape processes of representing war.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: War and Memory
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the key concepts from the booming field of memory studies that allow us to explain why debates about the past can be so heated – what is at stake in these discussions? What enables, and indeed compels, us to “remember” conflicts that we did not experience personally? What are the ethical limits of such memorialisation? How do memories change across time? And what is “forgotten” in this process? In pursuit of answers to these and many other questions, we will pair our theoretical readings with a range of materials that memorialise some of the key moments of the 20th and 21st centuries, for example: the First World War; the Holocaust; the Cold War; and the recent conflicts in Iraq and Afghanistan. Materials studied may include novels, memoirs, anthologies of soldiers’ writings, documentaries, feature films and websites.
learning_outcomes: On successful conclusion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate a critical understanding of key concepts and debates from the field of memory studies as they relate to the study of war and memory
On successful conclusion of this course, students will be able to demonstrate advanced skills in responding to complex forms of representation, across a range of genres and media

By studying navies and sea power in the modern world, from the 1890s to the present, concentrating on various thematic issues, students will be challenged to analyse the role that sea power has played in shaping the modern international order and the historical evolution of the concept. syllabus_overview: This course examines genocide from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Beginning with the emergence of historical and legal concept in the United Nations Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, students will explore major case studies, including Armenia, the Holocaust, Cambodia under the Khmer Rouge, Bosnia, Rwanda, and questions of genocide in the contemporary world. The course investigates the political, social, cultural, and ideological conditions that enable genocide, while critically evaluating the difficulties of perception and intervention. Students will engage with contemporary debates surrounding genocide prevention: the role and responsibilities of states and international agencies; the political and strategic limitations that influence intervention; and the problems of punishment.

They will benefit from the skills developed in critically evaluating the causes, course, resolution and consequences of armed conflict and how it has shaped our world.

syllabus_overview: This course examines peace as a central ordering concept of international relations and introduces a conflict transformation approach to conflict and post-conflict analysis. Beginning with a critical survey of the field, the course develops an understanding of the complex policy challenges associated with peace negotiations and explores different approaches through consideration of protracted conflicts. The field of peace research has developed significantly over recent decades leveraging new technologies for measuring peace. Conflict transformation theory recognises the complexity of conflict dynamics (not having neat beginnings, middles, and endings) and observes that the challenge of ‘managing’ or ‘resolving’ protracted conflict through peace processes have themselves often been the source of deep resentment and justification for further violence. Transforming protracted conflicts requires more than the redistribution of material resources or reframing of positions into resolved outcomes. The approach builds upon a deeper analysis of identity of stakeholders, issues, historical grievances, structural factors, and divergent world views. We will consider the UN concept of peacebuilding and evaluate its effectiveness in addressing the root causes of conflict, promoting justice, and fostering reconciliation among conflicting parties

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Special Operations: Theory and Strategic Utility
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: A common distinction made between special operations forces (SOF) and their general purpose counterparts is that SOF are 'strategic' troops. But is this so? And if so, what does ‘strategic’ mean in this context? This course explores the strategic utility of Special Operations (SO) and the forces that carry them out, and examines the competing and complementary theories of SO. As a core course in the Master of Special Operations and Irregular Warfare, content is designed to give you a comprehensive and integrated understanding of special operations as a military instrument. As an elective in other Master programs, the course will develop your expertise in the study of strategy and security. You will study various strategic theories, including the notion of using SO to induce 'strategic paralysis', often associated with airpower theorists like Giulio Douhet and Billy Mitchell. These are contrasted with attrition-based SO strategies, such as that proposed by James Kiras. Influential 'kinetic' theories of SO, like that of William McRaven, are compared and contrasted with strategies of influence which emphasise the 'indirect approach' of SOF in unconventional warfare. Using this theory, you will analyse the current utility of Special Operations in the context of contemporary major-power competition. Via your assessments, you will be asked to explore a broad range of options, such as bureaucratic control of SO, modernisation requirements of SO, personnel development or selection requirements of SO, or the application of SO theory to other elements of Government (such as policing counter-terrorism requirements).

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethics in Special, Complex and Irregular Military Operations
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: “Conventional” military operations, in which the uniformed military forces of one state engage with an equivalent force of another state, have become the exception rather than the norm in contemporary warfare. Military forces now more often find themselves pitted against non-state (or hybrid) opponents who avoid symmetric military engagements, preferring to seek shelter among civilian populations while employing a range of asymmetric guerrilla and terrorist tactics in operations located in the 'grey zone' between war and peace. States are making increasing use of special operations forces and other unconventional capabilities (such as cyber/information warfare operations) to carry out 'grey zone' missions, and those same special operations forces find themselves fighting alongside and enabling irregular and non-state forces which employ a mode of warfare that is distinctly unconventional. These realities considerably complicate the existing challenges of conducting operations in a manner consistent with the ethical norms for the use of military force. This course students will give the student detailed knowledge of concepts at the heart of the ethics of war and an understanding of how to apply ethical frameworks in analysing the challenges that arise from military actions in the operational environment of special, complex, and irregular operations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyberspace, National Security and Law
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: How law applies to the cyber domain is presenting increasingly acute challenges for security and military perspectives. From a military perspective, cyber is now a fundamental component of physical operational domains of sea, land, air, and space. From a security perspective, the cyber domain and cyber capabilities also present democracies with significant challenges in balancing the imperatives of security with the protection and maintenance of human rights such as privacy. This course will examine the current state of the ‘law’ – both international and domestic – as it relates to cyber as a military and security capability
learning_outcomes: Understand key concepts and principles of international law that apply to cyberspace operations and the contested political interpretations that might apply to them

title: Military Game Changers in 21st Century Warfare
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: While the nature of war does not change, the character of war unquestionably does. During this course we explore four key disruptive capabilities changing the character of 21st Century warfare: special operations, cyber war, autonomous weapons systems and space operations. After learning the basics of each capability we will look at its impact on operational and tactical levels of the military, as well as discuss implications for international relations and the law and finally, the ethical considerations. The course will require students to hypothesise how these capabilities will combine and interact in potential future conflict.
learning_outcomes: Hypothesise how military capabilities will combine and interact in future conflict.
Discuss the implications, risks and opportunities of future capabilities on military efforts at operational and tactical levels;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Public Leadership
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: Public leadership is differentiated from other forms of leadership in that its principal focus is promoting the common good and pursuing the public interest. In brief, it is leadership that does not seek to preference or prejudice the needs or desires of any group at the expense of others or to advance personal or private aspirations and objectives to the detriment of the collective wellbeing of the entire citizenry. Public leadership is indifferent to polemical agendas and partisan goals, and transcends the practical preoccupations of administration and management. This course begins with interpretations of competing and contrasting definitions of the ‘public’; provides a basis for identifying and then differentiating ‘leadership’ from oversight, supervision and management; canvasses the elements and imperatives of reliable and responsible leadership; and, offers students a template for describing the possible objectives and outcomes of ‘public leadership’ in a range of professional settings. While the focus will be on research into general principles, the student will be encouraged to consider these principles within the circumstances of their own organization and in the context of Australia’s evolving public life. The course provides a theoretical foundation for the exercise of effective public leadership.
learning_outcomes: Develop and demonstrate the ability to independently research a topic in public leadership
Develop and demonstrate postgraduate level communication skills
Develop, and effectively communicate, in a focused manner, a well structured and well supported argument or counter-argument
Develop and demonstrate a clear grasp of the principles of public leadership
Demonstrate the ability to interact analytically and respectfully with the ideas of peers

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Space Cooperation, Conflict and Competition
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: More satellites have been launched in the last 15 years, than in the preceding 50, starting from the launch of Sputnik I in 1957. If the plans of just 10% of satellite operators proposing new satellites and constellations of satellites were to be realised, as many as 100,000 satellites will be launched in the next 10 years. What accounts for this exponential growth? Can and should it be sustained? The exploration and use of the space domain was born out of great power competition and under the spectre of conflict between the USSR and the US. Yet, over the early decades after the dawn of the space age, exploration of outer space was often characterised by cooperation. In the last decade, an increasing number of States, non-State and commercial actors have sought to exploit the commercial, strategic and scientific opportunities of this domain. Sometimes they cooperate, there is always competition, and the spectre of conflict in space itself looms larger than it ever has. Under-regulated conflict and competition could make Earth orbits and beyond unusable in the near future and for generations to come, with potentially devastating consequences. The course invites you to undertake a learning journey in astropolitics and to set your own personal learning goals. As a core course in the Master of Space Operations program it gives students a detailed understanding of the economic, strategic and political drivers of space activities. It facilitates the intersection of multiple disciplines – particularly in the humanities (history, public policy, economics, commerce, strategy, law, ethics and politics) – with the technical foundations of space operations. Students will gain insights into how these drivers influence planning, policies, acquisitions and operations in respect to space activities. As an elective in other Master programs, the course provides advanced knowledge of the factors shaping the strategic and security environment and policy challenges in the space domain. Students will gain insights into the emerging potential for conflict and about the impact of disruptive space technologies in both the space and terrestrial domains. Students will also gain an appreciation of how the space domain may support conventional and special operations and may be an arena for irregular warfare involving non-state actors, especially commercial entities supporting military activities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an applied understanding of the basic elements of select disciplines (science, history, commerce, strategy, law, ethics and policy) in relation to the space domain.
Synthesise knowledge across select disciplines to argue a position about cooperation, competition and/or conflict in the space domain (astropolitical situation).
Formulate an original idea about an astropolitical situation and demonstrate high level communication skills to advocate for the idea.
Demonstrate enquiry-based learning through critical reflection on, and integration of, new disciplinary and/or professional knowledge of astropolitical situations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Gender and Power in the Indo-Pacific: Key Debates
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines gender and power dynamics in the Indo-Pacific region, with a focus on nations with which Australia seeks to foster strong security and economic cooperation: Indonesia, Japan, India, and Korea. The course gives an understanding of gender-power dynamic as a key element of the social fabric of these societies and analyses the ways in which it influences state governance and its international framework. he course explores local expectations around gender norms and leadership, and how these influence critical debates towards achieving gender equality in the Indo-Pacific. The course provides unique empirical knowledge of the region and a foundation for engagement in gender and security work. It is relevant to students working in defence, security, intelligence, and development as well as in NGOs seeking to achieve UN Sustainable Development Goals.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Cyber-Security: Policy & Operations
syllabus_overview: Cyber security is headline news and a growing challenge for national and global security, while computer technology now pervades every aspect of the personal and professional lives of our graduates. This technology underpins enormous performance improvements but also brings serious vulnerabilities. The many forms of cyber-threats - such as data theft, surveillance, and system compromise - have become tools of activism, corporate and state espionage, warfare, counter-proliferation, and intelligence gathering. This course provides an indepth introduction to the strategic and national security challenges of cybersecurity, and provides students with the skills to defend their organisation and their personal computers from the most common forms of attack.
learning_outcomes: Practice appropriate levels of security in personal computing;
Demonstrate a practical understanding of the organisational, policy and national security contexts in which cybersecurity is important;
Identify organisational responsibility for elements of cybersecurity and evaluate the evolving legal, ethical and normative context in which cybersecurity is being discussed internationally;
Describe common cybersecurity attack threats, relevant defence methodologies, and apply them to an organisation cyber environment.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Engineering Materials and Chemistry
syllabus_overview: This course provides the foundation for understanding material and environmental properties and behaviour in engineering and technology. It includes electronic structure of atoms and molecules, intermolecular forces, thermodynamic driving forces for chemical reactions, chemical equilibria, electrochemistry, corrosion and redox reactions, solution chemistry, acids and bases, kinetics and rates of reactions, complex molecular structures in metals, polymers and ceramics, crystalline lattices, yielding and lastic flow, strengthening mechanisms in metals, phase systems and alloys, ferrous and non-ferrous metallurgy, mechanical behaviour and properties of materials.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Academic Practice: Critical Reading and Writing
school: UC School of Humanities and Social Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to guide students on a pathway into various master’s programs. Its focus is on building the skills essential for success at Master level. At the same time, it engages with one of the pressing conversations of our time: what is the future of war? In order to consider this question, we will explore the ways in which military theorists and historians, as well as writers of prose fiction and films representing war, have imagined the forms which future conflicts may take. Are you able to comprehend and synthesize new information from a variety of sources? Are you able to communicate that understanding clearly and persuasively? This course is intended to empower you by developing these attributes, through carefully scaffolded activities and assignments with relevance to your own real-world context.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, synthesize, and critically evaluate information to demonstrate problem-solving skills.
Develop and demonstrate knowledge, understanding, and application of conventions of scholarly enquiry at Master AQF Level 9.
Communicate ideas and arguments clearly and accurately in a range of formats.

syllabus_overview: This course is tailored to meet the requirements of the Australian Command and Staff Course - Capability Management (ACSC-CM). The course provides an overview of the technical factors that affect the military use of explosives and propellants, armour materials, guns, guided weapons and light weapons. Topics include military ballistics, gun design, gun fire control, warhead design (including guided weapons), terminal effects and the penetration of armour. This course is restricted to ACSC-CM members and guests.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Chemistry 1A
syllabus_overview: The course commences with chemical reactions, concepts involved in chemical equations and an introduction to nomenclature of inorganic and organic substances. The gas laws are presented and then the electronic structure of gaseous atoms is developed. This leads to the concept of an orbital and provides a basis for the later description of ionic and covalent bonding and molecular geometry. Intermolecular forces are introduced which then leads to the chemistry of solutions and their properties. Finally, the chemistry of carbon, organic chemistry, is studied. Sub-topics include classes of organic compounds and common functional groups.
learning_outcomes: Perform a range of chemical calculations pertaining to stoichiometry, composition and concentration
Become familiar with a range of basic laboratory procedures
Identify and classify organic molecules and determine the types of reactions they are likely to undergo

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Chemistry 1B
syllabus_overview: The direction in which chemical reactions proceed (thermodynamics) is studied. There is an introduction to the laws of thermodynamics and the concepts of entropy, enthalpy and free energy. In kinetics, the temperature and concentration dependence for rates of reaction are discussed. This includes the concept of rate laws, activation energy and mechanism. The degree to which a reaction proceeds (chemical equilibrium) is discussed and related to the change of free energy. Electron transfer is introduced as an important area of chemistry, together with the principles of electrochemical cells. Finally, some military chemistry is presented, including a brief introduction to chemical and biological weapons.
learning_outcomes: Relate thermodynamic data to reaction spontaneity and kinetic data to reaction mechanisms
Identify the oxidation state of elements in compounds and determine the direction of redox reactions

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geography 1A
syllabus_overview: Geography 1A sets you on a journey to exercise your geographical imagination. The course progresses through key themes in geography, beginning with an overview of the history and scope of geographic thought. Geography 1A shows how a geographic perspective links people and life with the environment, which helps us to understand our world and to think critically about what it might mean to improve it at a time of rapid ecological change.
learning_outcomes: At the successful completion of this course, students will be able to identify environmental factors that influence life, including humans, on Earth.

At the successful completion of this course, students will be able to recognise different theoretical frameworks of geographical knowledge-making and competing intellectual lineages within the discipline.
At the successful completion of this course, students will be able to apply appropriate theoretical perspectives to geographical phenomena.

At the successful completion of this course, students will be able to analyse key themes in geography and critically reflect upon their significance for understanding the relationship between people and their environments.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Geography 1B
syllabus_overview: Geography is the multidisciplinary study of both the physical and human worlds in which we live, and a discipline that variously rethinks the relationship between people and the environment. One of the things that makes Geography such an exciting and contemporary subject for study is its incorporation of heterodox ideas, methods, skills and techniques for engaging in the task of ‘Earth writing’. Straddling both the sciences and the arts, Geography is a subject that directly intervenes in many of our most pressing 21st Century problems: from anthropogenic climate catastrophe and mass biological species extinction, to the political production of the ecology, to environmental erosion and modifications to physical systems, to rapid urbanisation and growing levels of global developmental inequality. Geography 1B is a course that helps make sense of these problems and provides tools for rethinking the future of human-environment relations in innovative and exciting ways.
learning_outcomes: Outline reasoned judgements about matters involving relationships between the physical environment and society
Identify key components of human-environmental systems
Analyse contemporary environmental problems according to particular geographical scales

Statistics concerns the use of data to obtain information about real-life situations and problems. There are various statistical tools that help extract useful information from data. Topics covered are: measures of location, variability in data, histograms and distributions of discrete and continuous variables. The ideas and concepts of calculus of functions with a single variable are generalised to functions with two or more variables. Topics include: surfaces in three dimensions, partial derivatives, gradient vector, directional derivative and multi-variable optimisation.

ODEs, considers methods for solving some first-order and second-order ODEs, as well as applying differential equations to model populations and physical systems. Multivariable Calculus, introduces the student to calculus in two dimensions such as gradients, line and double integrals and basic vector fields. This course will use competency-based assessments

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Discrete Mathematics
syllabus_overview: Discrete Mathematics is an area of mathematics directly applicable to both practical and theoretical aspects of computer science. It is the study of mathematical structures that are inherently discrete, as opposed to continuous structures that are dealt with using differential calculus. The importance of Discrete Mathematics today lies in its numerous practical and relevant applications. It plays an essential role in modelling the natural world (e.g., the genome) and the technological world (e.g., the Internet), and in designing efficient solutions such as Internet routing protocols. It is commonly used in cryptography, computer security, electronic banking, algorithms, theory of computing, telecommunications, web search engines, to mention a few. Emphasis will be placed on developing knowledge of the elements of discrete mathematics of fundamental importance in the context of computing. Topics to be covered include: foundations of logic, propositions and predicates; the concept of mathematical proof, with a focus on proof by induction, recurrence relations and algorithm correctness; set theory and basic theory of graphs and networks, including optimisation algorithms.
learning_outcomes: Construct a valid proof of a true and provable mathematical statement

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Oceanography
syllabus_overview: This course is a broad introduction to the interconnected physical, chemical, biological and geological aspects of the oceans. Topics may include: physical and chemical properties of seawater, and what their distributions tell us about ocean circulation; the role of the oceans and ocean currents in Earth's climate and El Nino; an introduction to waves and tides; modern ocean measurement technologies such as robot gliders and satellites; plate tectonics and the formation and structure of the seafloor; marine biology and ecosystems; marine resources and environmental management, and Defence Oceanography. The fascinating interconnections between these different aspects of Oceanography are highlighted. Navy related oceanography knowledge is also part of the course. The course may also include a Virtual Field School, which allows students to "participate" in a simulated field school experience where they can deepen their understanding of concepts and approaches discussed in the course.

Understand the fundamentals of marine biology and ecology.
Understand the basics of physics of ocean waves and tides.
Develop knowledge of the geological features of the seafloor and the processes that create them.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)

ZPEM1503 explores the fundamental physics of mechanics, waves, fluids and thermodynamics which are essential to engineers of all disciplines. The course emphasises both conceptual understanding and quantitative problem-solving, tied to real-world applications in engineering and military contexts.

The course will introduce nuclear fusion, fission and reactor science, as well as the important topics of general radiation safety and regulatory frameworks as they apply to the Australian Defence Force.
