title: Explosive Ordnance Research Project
syllabus_overview: Students in the Explosive Ordnance (EO) Masters Program will undertake a research-based project as a capstone element of the program. As one of the aims of the EO Masters program is to develop critical thinking and independent research skills, the projects will involve research experience in collaboration with staff members and their research teams. A supervisor, who is a member of academic staff, will work closely with the student and will manage each project. The project will be chosen after discussion between the student, the supervisor and other members of staff. Students will generally take this course in their final two semesters of enrolment. Enrolment in this course is only open to students nominated by the Department of Defence. Note: This is a 12 UoC course. You will enrol in 6 UoC in each of 2 successive semesters with a result reported by a single grade at the end of the second 6 UoC course.
learning_outcomes: Develop a coherent research plan and design appropriate experiments
Analyse and interpret data collected.
Undertake independent literature searches appropriate to the project.
Write a substantial literature review of publishable standard.
Communicate the context, methodology, results, interpretation and implications of the research project in written and oral formats.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZEIT8512 and ZPEM8101

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counter IED and Forensic Investigation of Explosives
syllabus_overview: The course presents the fundamentals of improvised explosive devices (IEDs) and develops an understanding of how chemical analysis techniques are applied in forensic explosives investigations from field through to laboratory. It covers types of improvised explosives and devices, introduces students to the scientific principles and sampling methods for different types of chemical analysis relevant to IED detection, and provides an awareness of the strengths and limitations of each method. Enrolment in this course is only open to students nominated by the Department of Defence.
learning_outcomes: Develop an awareness of the advantages and limitations of various analytical methods in different operational situations.
Demonstrate an understanding of chemical compositions and structure and stability of EO in common IEDs.
Demonstrate an understanding of the general principles of analytical chemistry and instrumentation applied to the sensing and identification of chemical explosives.
Demonstrate an understanding of methods for collecting sample of bulk and /or trace explosive samples for subsequent forensic analysis

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Economic Geography
syllabus_overview: Economic Geography is invaluable in providing the operational context for strategic managers and those responsible for implementing business strategy. The constitution of urban settings can be better understood through an attention to economic processes and practices, from regimes of production to international divisions of labour, the changing demographics of the workforce, flows of finance, services and products and the institutions of governance that regulate business practices. Economic Geography offers to students studying the Masters of Business a way of understanding evident geographical variation in economic practices, at the global scale but also from the point of view of the diverse practices observed in different locations. An understanding of the geographic landscape via the theoretical frameworks and empirical studies of Economic Geography lends specificity to the study of business practice. The course complements Strategic Management (ZBUS 8101) and Organisational Behaviour (ZBUS 8102) as core units in the Master of Business, as well as such electives as Cross-Cultural Management (ZBUS 8318) and Economic Worldview (ZBUS 8148).
learning_outcomes: Analyse the major determinants of economic activity in the urban environment
Demonstrate an understanding of the contemporary context studied by economic geography
Apply economic geographic concepts in order to explain the relationship between diverse people and their diverse environments
Synthesise case study data and the scholarly economic geographical and social scientific literature to explain the location and practices of businesses and economic sectors.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human Factors and the Technological Interface
syllabus_overview: The increasing reliance upon technological innovation, from pervasive digital computing in everyday smart phone and smart infrastructures to new forms of intelligent materials and pharmaceutical augmentation, is changing the nature of human-technology relationships. These changes are in turn having a major impact on the nature of human behaviour and the ways in which governments, defence, policy makers and intelligence services understand, predict and transform collective and individual human action. Traditionally the study of human factors has centred on scientific questions but this course widens the focus to address the broader transformation of human behaviour in ways that bring together contemporary debates in anthropology, philosophy, behavioural science and technology studies through practical case-studies and application. This course focuses upon the human factors influencing effective decision-making in a range of technological interface scenarios to offer invaluable insights into how courses of action are chosen from within mundane, novel and complex situations. The proliferation of technological interfaces, both digital and biological, raises new questions about the autonomy and reliability of the human when the location and agency, the where and who, of decision-making is no longer clear cut. These questions shape contemporary concerns in politics, ethics and security. Looking at a series of technological interface scenarios the role of human factors in decision-making processes can be better understood through an attention to the role technology is playing in reshaping the context of human behaviour. Contexts will range from collective and team performance within hierarchical command structures to emerging spontaneous crowd behaviour, from augmented individual biological performance through skill and training to diminished mental and physical capability of stress and fatigue, and from the agency of code, digital mediation and matter to the spatial and temporal questions of architecture and duration. The social science of recent technological innovations will present students with an exciting opportunity to examine, evaluate and critique the emergence of new kinds of behaviour at the evolving interface of human and machine. The course is designed to provide students with an understanding of what human factors are, including habit, trust, team performance, individual mental and physical skill, affect and endurance, with particular attention paid to scenarios where technology has both an intensive and extensive influence on decision-making and behavioural change. Students will bring together information to analyse how human factors shape, and are reshaped by, technological interfaces through a qualitative social science perspective.
learning_outcomes: Apply social science concepts in order to explain the evolving nature of the relationship between humans and technology

Synthesise case study data with the scholarly social scientific literature and diverse social scientific methodologies, to explain the changing nature of human factors in the interface with technology
1. Demonstrate an understanding of the strengths and weakness of different theories questioning the nature of human factors in relationships with technological interfaces
Analyse the levels of human agency in decision-making through technological interfaces, including human-computer interaction from cyber-security to everyday internet use

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Development Geography
syllabus_overview: Development Geography will provide students with an understanding of how the global economy impacts on developing countries, or the 'global South', where complex challenges of global poverty and hunger are making ever greater demands on local, state and international institutions to 'deliver' development. This course will critically engage in 'development' thinking, strategies and ideology from the post-World War II period to the present. This course will have a particular (though not exclusive) focus on development issues in sub-Saharan Africa, where many countries did not meet the Millennium Development Goals (2000-2015). A solid grounding in theories of development and 'underdevelopment' will provide students with the analytical skills to engage in real world practical examples of development challenges and opportunities. Topics will include: the role of institutions of global governance, link between 'resource curse' and conflict, rural and urban livelihoods, international development aid, indicators of development and the post-2015 Sustainable Development Goals. Further information For MBus students this course will complement Strategic Management (ZBUS8101) and Organisational Behaviour (ZBUS8102) as core units in the Master of Business as well as such electives as Cross-Cultural Management (ZBUS8318) and Economic Worldview (ZBUS8148).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of development theories and their application in the 'real world'.
Identify the major institutions and organisations involved in development planning and practice.
Evaluate international development policy and its influence on uneven development.

Systematically assess development policy options for specific development issues in different contexts using case study data and the scholarly international development literature to explain the historical and contemporary contexts of international development.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Institutional Subjectivity and Ethics
syllabus_overview: The unit will combine conceptualizations of institutions from the humanities and social sciences with critical case study analysis to develop ethical considerations about institutional life. Social scientific theorizations of institutions have traditionally examined the ways in which social bodies gain structure and meaning through institutional regulations, policies, laws and cultural norms. It is increasingly understood, however, that institutions are sites and processes capable of not only regulating society but of actively producing the social by fostering diverse forms of ‘institutional subjectivity’ and therefore shaping how people ‘instinctively’ behave and conduct themselves. Institutions thus represent important sites for theorizing ethics and for posing ethical questions targeting their influence over societies and the forms of individual and collective socialization they produce. As will be examined in the unit, exploring the ethics of institutions is pertinent both because ethics provides a framework for evaluating social practices as they arise through institutional processes, but also because the formalization of ethical rules and regulations in itself constitutes a form of institution. The unit integrates scholarly texts with examples of institutions across a range of domains, histories, and geographies. Structurally in the course, these materials amount to a series of paired lectures, the first of which introduces theoretical work on the core concepts of institution, subjectivity and ethics, and the second of which presents a case study through which those ideas are put into practice. As part of each pairing, the course content and discussions aim at encouraging critical appraisals of the theories and empirical spaces studied as well as informed speculation about emerging institutional trends. The course will develop skills in critical thinking, and in synthesizing case study data with theoretical research. At the conclusion of the course, students will be able to utilize these diverse forms of knowledge to evaluate the ethical importance of institutions around us in the contemporary world.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the ethical implications of institutional subjectivity in relation to contemporary examples.
Identify and understand the importance of a range of formal and informal institutions in shaping society.
Analyse some of the ways subjectivity is produced through different institutional contexts.
Synthesize theoretical and social scientific literature on institutions with case study data to understand institutional practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Understanding Social-Technical Systems: Ideas, Spaces and Cultures
syllabus_overview: The increasing ubiquity of digital information technologies and systems – from smartphones and self driving cars to artificial intelligence and advanced robotics – is having unprecedented impacts on society and how we think about issues like privacy, security, responsibility, and trust in the future. The unfamiliar landscape inaugurated by new digital information systems also demands new ways of thinking and problem-solving within engineering disciplines. This course will introduce students to the intimate connection between ideas and practice - philosophical concepts and technological systems - in both historical and contemporary contexts. The questions the course poses are twofold: first, how have different genealogies of ideas about the human and the machine (such as cybernetics and complexity theory) fed into the evolution of today’s digital information systems?; and second, what is the broader significance of such systems and associated technologies in challenging conventional understandings of key concepts – including intelligence, autonomy, and responsibility – in ways that advance discussions about the political, ethical, and security issues associated with intelligent technologies? Drawing on the latest research across the social sciences, the course will unpack these questions through a range of exciting topics, including the rise of online social networks and the associated challenges to traditional notions of privacy and identity; new understandings of security and trust in blockchain technologies and cryptocurrencies; and new conceptions of intelligence from ‘Deep Blue’ and ‘Alpha Go’ to the ’Blue Brain’ project.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in conceptual vocabularies to support interdisciplinary projects across the physical and social sciences;
Evaluate the significance of ‘socio-technical systems’ as a unit of analysis that enables a more holistic, ethically-informed approach to problem solving within the context of technological change.

Apply social science concepts in order to explain the evolving nature of the relationship between theoretical concepts and the development of networked digital information systems in different cultural and geographical contexts; and
Develop a critical understanding of the ideas and assumptions that underlie your design practice;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Researching Behaviour: Creative Methodologies in a Digital Age
syllabus_overview: Cutting-edge social science research methods have never been more crucial than in our contemporary digital age, where developments in Big Data, Artificial Intelligence, and Machine Learning are raising vital questions about the balance between the quality and quantity of information across a range of different institutional contexts. Despite this, much research in behavioural science continues to be wedded to cognitivist and linguistic methodological frameworks of the past that are patently unable to account for the complex unconscious and technologically mediated nature of contemporary social life. This course is designed to address the question of how to research behaviour when the dualism between the human and technology is increasingly blurred. This team-taught course will be organized into four key thematic blocks (Experimentation and the Digital; Human Performance; Assemblage and Network Methods; Research Ethics in a Digital Age) which will give students the opportunity to put theories and concepts encountered in other core Behavioural Science courses into practice. Through weekly readings, online discussions, and practical activities, students will be introduced to cutting-edge methods and techniques at the forefront of contemporary behavioural and social science research, equipping them with the skills they need to produce innovative and timely research on the needs, attitudes, opinions, desires, and motivations of different communities and populations.
learning_outcomes: Construct well-defined research problems and identify the most appropriate research methods and techniques best suited to address these.
Develop skills in applying both traditional and cutting-edge methods to research human behaviour and socio-technical relations.
Demonstrate awareness of key methodological issues, challenges, and debates in contemporary behavioural science research.
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of various cutting-edge qualitative methods and techniques in relation to specific behavioural science research projects at the human-technology interface.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Analysis and Applications
syllabus_overview: This course provides a foundation in statistics for students undertaking further studies in many applied fields, including workforce planning. It teaches the fundamentals of data analysis with emphasis on the analysis of data arising from real-life situations across various disciplines. It focuses on the understanding of the concepts of statistics without overemphasizing the mathematical detail. The course teaches the principles of good experimental design, as well as the interpretation and critical evaluation of statistical information presented in the media and in published reports. It introduces a computer software package which is used for data exploration, presentation and analysis. Main topics covered include: gathering, organising and summarising data; using graphical techniques to present statistical information; measures of location and spread; probability; probability distributions such as the normal distribution; introduction to Markov modelling; confidence intervals and hypothesis tests; correlation and simple linear regression.
learning_outcomes: At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to use sample data to assess claims about unknown population parameters.
At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to solve life-related problems using probability distributions.
At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to model relationships between variables by using linear regression techniques.
At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to summarize and present data clearly in numerical and graphical forms.
At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to estimate the true value of parameters with confidence.
At the successful completion of this course, students should be able to interpret results of statistical analyses and present conclusions in clear non-technical language.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Crime and Ethics
syllabus_overview: Ethical and professional behaviour are the cornerstone of cybersecurity. This course provides students with fundamental ethical frameworks, applied to the cybersecurity profession. Students analyse topics and current and historic cyber events from ethical, professional, and legal perspectives. It also seeks to understand how computers and computing have created opportunities for crime and to analyse how they operate. The course equips students to recognise, effectively analyse, and respond to future ethical challenges as they arise, and to recognise new forms of criminal activity online.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the impact of cybercrime on government, businesses and individuals.
Identify and describe historical and emerging trends in cybercrime.
Identify and critically analyse abstract and real-world ethical challenges in the cyber security domain.
Describe the duties and responsibilities of cyber security professionals under current legal, professional, and ethical frameworks.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Oceanography Research Part-Time
syllabus_overview: Part-time research in Oceanography to meet the requirements of the University for the degrees of Doctor of Philosophy and Master of Science by Research.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate a sound knowledge of the literature and data sources in the selected subject area; understand in-depth the concepts underpinning the research discipline; competently use the techniques, investigative methods and instrumentation appropriate for research in this field of study;

understand the potential hazards associated with the research discipline and have regard for the relevant OH&S legislation; regard all relevant UNSW policy and procedures and adopt safe, effective, ethical and collegial work practices in accordance with the UNSW Research Code of Conduct.

independently analyse and evaluate the results of the research and the research of others in the discipline; devise, implement and complete research with limited supervision; communicate the processes and outcomes of the research, both in written and oral form, in a concise logical and coherent manner;

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Programming Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: This course develops the essential skills to write code that is not only correct but also readable and maintainable. Through hands-on exercises and practical examples, this teaches the fundamentals of a high-level programming language, enabling students to express ideas effectively and efficiently in code. This is the first introductory programming course, teaching the fundamentals of how programs are created, fundamental programming requirements, and initial concepts. This is a foundational block for future software development courses.
learning_outcomes: Use fundamental programming concepts, such as variables, data types, control structures, functions, and objects, to solve simple computational problems.
Use debugging and testing techniques to identify and fix errors in their code and ensure its correctness and robustness.
Write correct, readable, and maintainable code in a high-level programming language.
Apply programming best-practice techniques and conventions.
Design and implement modular programs that follow good software engineering practices, such as abstraction, encapsulation, and separation of concerns.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Information Technology and Networking
syllabus_overview: Introduction to IT & Networking provides students with a broad foundation of modern information technology systems that form the key components of most of today's information systems. The course introduces key concepts in computer hardware, operating systems, and networking. Through a mix of theory and practical lab work, students will learn the core functionalities of popular operating systems and will be provided with hands-on experience in navigating, configuring, and administering them using both graphical and command-line interfaces. Students will also develop a solid understanding of how core IT systems support the transmission and sharing of information between digital devices across networks and the Internet using intermediary hardware devices and networking protocols.
learning_outcomes: Analyse how data flows across network layers using OSI and TCP/IP models and identify the roles of key networking protocols in data communication.
Explain the principles of computer networking, including the hardware and the functions of various network devices, topologies and protocols.
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of IT concepts, including hardware and software components, and networks.
Apply historical and current context of Information Technology and analyse current trends and emerging technologies, and their potential impact on industry and society.

Apply networking concepts such as IP addressing, subnetting, routing protocols, VLANs, and NAT to configure and manage intermediary devices for efficient and secure data communication across networks.

Examine the key features of popular operating systems such as Windows and Linux and gain hands-on experience with key aspects such as system navigation, file and directory management, and software control using both graphical and command-line interfaces.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computer Architecture and Operating Systems
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide students with a solid understanding of the essential concepts and components that form modern computation, with a focus on the physical components, firmware, and operating systems. Specifically, this course provides an understanding of the underlying operating systems which students have implicitly relied upon when developing applications in other courses and will serve to provide practical outcomes for their future careers. This course also takes a security-specific lens for operating system functions and limitations.
learning_outcomes: Explain the design of modern operating systems: architecture components and services.
Analyse a system architecture and operating system behavior to identify and demonstrate potential vulnerabilities, propose and implement proof of concept solutions and justify them accordingly.
Communicate modern OS security implementations, threats, and controls including their use, limitations, and countermeasures.

Explore and explain the principles of modern operating systems such as process management, filesystems, memory organisation and hardware elements including stack, heap, registers, instruction pipeline, direct memory access, and their role in exploitation
Convey the differences between classical, virtualised, and mobile operating systems, and analyse their designs from a security perspective to identify potential vulnerabilities and areas of weakness.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZSPS1111 Introduction to Information Technology & Networking

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: Cyber security is headline news and a growing challenge for national and global security, while computer technology now pervades every aspect of the personal and professional lives of our graduates. This technology underpins enormous performance improvements but also brings serious vulnerabilities. This course provides an in-depth introduction to the foundational concepts of cyber security. This introductory course aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the fundamental concepts and principles of cyber security, exploring the various cyber threats and vulnerabilities that exist in the digital landscape. This course explores the importance of raising awareness and educating users about cyber security best practices, emphasizing the role individuals play in ensuring a secure digital environment.
learning_outcomes: Explain the historical context of cyber security, and current developments in the field, and so make reasonable assessments of likely future attacks and emerging risks.
Apply an understanding of human behavioural factors, human errors, and social engineering to cyber security contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship of cybersecurity to related fields.
Analyse real-world problems and apply theoretical cyber security frameworks to make decisions taking into consideration key factors such as cost, risk, and privacy.

Define and explain fundamental concepts and terminology related to cyber security, such as threats, vulnerabilities, risk management, and ethical considerations, to establish a foundational understanding of the field.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Structures & Algorithmic Knowledge
syllabus_overview: The primary objective of this course is to enhance student comprehension of data structures and algorithms, to understand their theoretical complexity, practical behaviour, and their effective utilisation in the design of software systems. The aim of this course is for students to become proficient programmers, equipped with knowledge of essential data structures and programming techniques. Students will be capable of constructing complex substantial software systems within a team environment, employing efficient data structures, widely used algorithms and sound programming practices. The concepts taught in this course apply to all programming languages and software development domains and will lay a solid foundation for further specialised studies in computing, empowering students to delve into more advanced areas.
learning_outcomes: Implement data structures and algorithms and analyse their performance.
Structure computer programs for scalability and decomposability.
Work collaboratively to develop scalable and efficient computer programs that solve complex real-world problems.
Justify the suitability, effectiveness and efficiency of selected data structures and algorithms to solve a given complex problem.
Articulate fundamental data structures and algorithms, their uses and when to employ them.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Knowledge Representation and Databases
syllabus_overview: In today's technology-driven landscape, the indispensability of large data resources in every significant modern computer application cannot be overstated. Consequently, possessing the expertise to effectively understand and manage these resources is important. This course aims to explore in depth the practice of developing database applications and the theory behind large data storage systems and models, including relational database management systems (RDBMSs), NoSQL, Graph, and Map Reduce paradigms. This course will equip students with the skills necessary to construct high-quality applications that exhibit correctness, efficiency, and usability, leveraging the potential of different storage paradigms. By engaging in comprehensive learning modules and hands-on exercises, students will develop a solid grasp of the fundamental principles and best practices required to build applications reliant on large data storage.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the benefits and use advanced features in different systems.
Develop applications that programmatically interact with different storage paradigms;
Articulate the different forms of data storage and the advantages and limitations of each.
Formulate queries to efficiently extract data from different storage mechanisms;
Develop accurate data models for multiple data storage forms, suited to different applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Web Application and Security
syllabus_overview: This course covers the fundamentals of developing and securing web applications and websites. Web applications are currently the major source of system vulnerabilities breached by complex cyber-attacks. This course will delve into the development of web applications and their security practices and standards. Students will learn web application vulnerabilities, and their exploitation and application security testing, authentication and authorisation, as well as secure web deployment. Students will also learn common types of web threats and how to protect against them in real-world case studies. Overall, the course aims to educate students on best practices for developing secure web applications and protecting them from potential cyber threats.
learning_outcomes: Analyse in-depth vulnerabilities of web applications and how to defend against them.
Learn fundamentals of web application developments, such as CSS, JavaScript and web sockets, and apply industry-standard security frameworks such as HTTPS and OAuth and JSON Web Tokens.
Architect and design secure web applications using best practices, such as encryption, secure coding frameworks, and access control policies.
Develop and evaluate a security plan for web applications taking into account user behaviour, threat modelling, and access control.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethical Hacking & Penetration Testing
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will delve into the dynamic and rapidly evolving field of penetration testing. This process involves systematically identifying vulnerabilities in computer systems and networks to enhance their security. Through a blend of theoretical knowledge, practical exercises, and real-world case studies, students will develop the skills and mindset needed to become proficient ethical hackers. By the end of this course, students will have a strong foundation in ethical hacking methodologies and techniques. They will be able to identify and exploit vulnerabilities, conduct thorough penetration tests, and provide actionable recommendations to enhance system and network security. Additionally, students will understand the legal and ethical considerations associated with ethical hacking, empowering them to apply their skills responsibly and ethically in a professional setting.
learning_outcomes: Explain how network attacks occur, including a comprehensive understanding of common protocols, and vulnerabilities.
Exploit network attacks and understand their respective aims, limitations, and when to appropriately employ them in offensive security testing.
Effectively communicate technical findings and proposed mitigations to both technical and non-technical decision-makers.
Use technical techniques to professionally carry out and document a penetration test in accordance with current best practice frameworks.
Explain the legal, ethical, business, and technical constraints of offensive penetration testing and its relationship to the discipline of cyber security.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Defence
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will gain both a solid theoretical foundation and practical technical skills necessary for protecting contemporary systems and networks from potential attacks. The course offers a comprehensive overview of modern attack techniques and explores a range of defensive measures and tools, highlighting their strengths and limitations. The course aims to equip students with the technical expertise required to design and implement robust security measures in modern systems and networks. Through hands-on exercises and real-world case studies, students will develop the practical skills and knowledge needed to identify vulnerabilities, assess risks, and implement effective security solutions to safeguard critical systems and networks. Overall, the course provides the foundational knowledge of cyber defence and develops skills in applying various defence techniques, procedures, and tools.
learning_outcomes: Articulate the core principles governing defensive system and network security mechanisms and demonstrate proficiency in their strategic deployment and, efficient and reliable operation, and reliable assurance.
Effectively communicate the advantages and limitations of different cyber security defensive tools and processes to technical and non-technical stakeholders.
Select, deploy and utilise systems, tools and techniques to detect, prevent, and respond to cyber threats. Analyse case studies and evaluate cyber security strengths and weaknesses.
Apply current security frameworks and best practices to assure the security of legacy and emerging technologies.
Critically analyse case studies to assess the strengths and weaknesses of proposed or deployed cyber security measures.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Mathematics and Applied Cryptography
syllabus_overview: Mathematics is a key enabler of computer science and cyber security. This course builds a foundation of mathematical concepts required by computing and cyber security graduates. The course includes foundation mathematics for computer science and cyber security and students learn various cryptographic techniques, including symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures and their applications such as blockchain. The course emphasises mathematical definitions and proofs as well as applicable methods as well as encompassing the fundamentals of cryptography and other applications.
learning_outcomes: Use appropriate terminology to communicate solutions to problems involving discrete mathematics techniques.
Articulate uses of mathematics in the field of cyber security and related fields.
Apply critical and logical thinking skills to solve mathematical problems, and understand their application.
Implement and validate cryptographic algorithms, and communicate how they work.
Identify and employ suitable discrete mathematics techniques to solve problems encompassing propositional and predicate calculus.
Explain fundamental cryptographic principles and analyse the strengths and weaknesses of cryptographic implementations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Enterprise Cyber Security Governance and Policy
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive understanding of the essential principles, frameworks, and practices involved in establishing effective cyber security governance and policy frameworks within organisations. In this course, students will explore the critical role of governance in ensuring cybersecurity resilience and compliance with relevant regulations and standards. They will also examine the formulation and implementation of cybersecurity policies to address emerging cyber threats and protect digital assets. At the conclusion of this course, students will have a solid understanding of cybersecurity governance and policy principles, enabling them to develop and implement effective frameworks within organisations. They will be equipped to address regulatory requirements, mitigate cyber risks, and establish a culture of cyber security awareness and compliance.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate different cybersecurity governance frameworks and policies, considering their applicability and effectiveness in addressing the evolving cyber threat landscape.
Evaluate competing risks and benefits against organisational culture.
Understand the fundamental principles and concepts of cybersecurity governance and policy, including their significance in ensuring effective cybersecurity practices within organisations.

Critically examine the role of stakeholders, including executive leadership, board members, and IT professionals, in shaping and implementing cybersecurity governance and policy, and understand the importance of collaboration and communication in achieving organisational cybersecurity goals.

Evaluate the effectiveness of cybersecurity governance and policy measures through monitoring, auditing, and continuous improvement practices, and develop strategies for adapting to emerging threats and technologies in a rapidly changing cybersecurity landscape.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Security Entrepreneurship
syllabus_overview: The field of cybersecurity presents numerous opportunities for entrepreneurial ventures. This course aims to equip aspiring entrepreneurs with the knowledge, skills, and mindset required to navigate the intersection of cybersecurity and entrepreneurship. This course will provide students with the tools and insights necessary to thrive in the cybersecurity entrepreneurship space. This course will teach students to identify market opportunities and develop innovative business ideas that address critical cybersecurity challenges. With a focus on entrepreneurial principles and frameworks, student will develop a robust business plan, considering market analysis, competitive positioning, revenue models, and growth strategies tailored specifically to the cybersecurity landscape. Understanding the legal, ethical, and regulatory considerations specific to cybersecurity entrepreneurship is paramount. This course builds on and extends work on data protection, privacy laws, intellectual property regulations, and ethical frameworks to ensure compliance and build trust with stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Apply entrepreneurial principles and frameworks to develop a comprehensive business plan for a cybersecurity venture, including market analysis, competitive positioning, revenue models, and growth strategies.
Identify and evaluate market opportunities within the cybersecurity industry, considering emerging technologies, market trends, and customer needs, to develop innovative business ideas.
Assess the legal, ethical, and regulatory considerations specific to cybersecurity entrepreneurship, ensuring compliance with data protection, privacy, and intellectual property laws and regulations.

Evaluate and mitigate cybersecurity risks associated with entrepreneurship, including identifying vulnerabilities, implementing appropriate security measures, and establishing incident response and recovery plans.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Machine Learning for Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: Existing cyber security solutions, such as firewalls, access controls, cyber threat intelligence and hunting, penetration testing, intrusion detection and prevention, and cryptography-based applications require automation and orchestration for achieving Intelligent Security in critical infrastructure systems and networks. Intelligent Security is a new trend in contemporary cyber security theories and practicals that develop artificial intelligence and machine learning for cyber security systems. This aims at devising intelligent methods for offensive and defensive applications, and the automation of the security processes to enhance efficiency and reduce human errors. This course covers the fundamentals of machine learning theories, their practical implementation, and their utilisation in cyber security applications. Students learn data acquisition, exploration and visualisation techniques for cyber security industry challenges. Students also learn descriptive statistics and probabilistic models as the fundamentals of developing machine learning algorithms. Moreover, students practically learn supervised and unsupervised machine learning algorithms to solve red-blue teaming problems, along with industry standards and best practices.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the use of Machine Learning in Offensive and Defensive Security, intrusion detection, to anticipate future trends and emerging risks.
Discuss the relationship between supervised and unsupervised learning techniques and their influence on automating cyber security tasks.
Apply Machine Learning models in real-world cyber security contexts to solve problems like detection of phishing, malware and other threat identification.
Analyse and interpret features from cyber security datasets, such as network logs or PE files, to extract meaningful insights for threat detection.
Explain fundamental concepts and terminology related to Machine Learning and Cyber Security to demonstrate a foundational understanding of their integration.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Deep Learning for Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: This course covers theories and their practical implementation of deep learning for cyber security solutions. Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that involves the use of artificial neural networks to learn and make predictions based on large data sources. In the context of cyber security, deep learning models can be used to analyse vast amounts of data to build offensive and defensive strategies, such as automated penetration testing, intrusion discovery, vulnerability and malware detection in real-time. This can help organisations to understand how cyber threats would occur, detect and prevent them before they cause significant damage and achieve cyber resilience. Students learn discriminative and generative deep learning algorithms, Autoencoders, and convolution networks for various red-blue teaming scenarios from the industry perspective.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop end-to-end learning pipelines for various cyber security tasks, such as malware detection, intrusion detection, network traffic analysis, and threat intelligence.
Analyse and evaluate the performance of deep learning models on cyber security datasets, and optimise hyperparameters for improving models’ performances.
Implement and deploy deep learning models in distributed and parallel computing environments, and benchmark their scalability, efficiency, and reliability.
Critically assess the ethical and legal considerations related to using deep learning for cyber security, and propose solutions to mitigate potential risks, biases, and abuses.
Explain the fundamentals of deep learning algorithms used in cyber security applications, and apply them to real-world problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZSPS2118 Machine Learning for Cyber Security

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Trustworthy AI for Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: This course covers advanced AI technology for cyber security, including explainable AI and adversarial machine learning algorithms. Trustworthy AI for cyber security involves the development of artificial intelligence systems that can operate securely and reliably in a variety of contexts. These systems are designed to detect and respond to various threats in cyberspace, such as malware, phishing attacks, and advanced persistent threats. To accomplish this, trustworthy AI incorporates a range of security measures, including encryption, secure communication channels, intrusion detection systems, and continuous monitoring and updating of threat intelligence, explanation and robustness of models. In addition, trustworthiness is also ensured through robust testing and validation processes that ensure the reliability and consistency of AI systems, and the identification and mitigation of potential biases or unintended consequences. In this course, students learn the mitigation strategies against adversarial machine learning and consider the ramifications of deep fakes. Students also learn the implications of explainable AI and how to achieve responsible AI models for offensive and defensive problems. Students will also learn the threats and mitigation for large language models (including GPT models), and their impact on cyber threat hunting and threat intelligence, and penetration testing.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and articulate the ethical considerations of deploying AI and machine learning models for cyber security.
Evaluate the generalisation and robustness of machine learning models used for cyber security purposes.

Critically evaluate the state-of-the-art literature and research in the field, and contribute to the advancement of new and effective strategies for leveraging AI and machine learning to enhance cyber security.
Identify and mitigate adversarial attacks on AI and machine learning models, improving the security and resilience of digital systems.
Design and implement trustworthy AI and machine learning models specifically tailored for cyber security applications.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZSPS2118 Machine Learning for Cyber Security

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Security Industry Project 1
syllabus_overview: This course prepares students with the necessary skills to effectively participate in work integrated learning projects, and the opportunity to apply learning from their programs to projects relevant to their career goals. Students will work with internal and in some instances, external mentors to identify project types, make project pitches, develop project ideas and understand execution processes as well as reflection.
learning_outcomes: Effectively apply strategic and effective communication skills to harness or deal with complex opportunities and challenges in the field.
Demonstrate initiative in engaging with industry professionals (where applicable) and apply learning in a practice environment
Demonstrate an understanding of a particular genre in your chosen industry and relevant administrative and policy guidelines to work effectively in such organisation.
Exercise critical judgement in relation to assessing possible solutions or treatments
Demonstrate the use and value of research and analysis in responding to potential or emerging challenges in that field.
Understand risks and mitigation measures when working in a new environment.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Human-Centric Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: This course covers a comprehensive approach to protecting and securing digital information and systems by focusing on the human component of the security equation. The course introduces theoretical and practical aspects of behavioural analysis in cyber security, including an analysis of business models and criminological theories designed to modify behaviour and exploit human factors. Students learn human behaviour as it relates to cyber security, especially the mental states of hackers and defenders. Students also learn the personality characteristics of victims, attackers and defenders, and with this knowledge, how policies, procedures and standards can be developed to reinforce an organisation's sustainability objectives.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate cyber security threats that exploit human factors.
Articulate human-centred approaches to cyber security, including the psychology of security and how to design end-user safety and security.
Utilise professional skills and practice to build efficient team building, negotiation and high-level communication through various industry environments.
Assess personality characteristics of victims, attackers and defenders, to develop policies and procedures that achieve organisations' sustainability objectives.
Apply risk assessment techniques and best practices to identify vulnerabilities in human-centric aspects of cyber security such as user awareness and training.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111 Introduction to Information Technology and Networking, and ZSPS1337 Introduction to Cyber Security

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Forensics
syllabus_overview: This course covers both the theory and practice of digital forensics. Students will learn to execute recent technologies of digital forensics in operating systems, and networks as well as implementing digital forensics principles using open-source digital forensic tools. Students will also practice various digital forensic approaches, advanced learning-based forensics methods, and how they relate to incident response plans and professional reports that would be employed to be admissible as evidence in a court of law.
learning_outcomes: Outline how Intelligent forensics techniques and their professional reports could be admissible as evidence in a court of law.
Develop data capturing, logging, and recovery techniques in various operating systems for analysing data for incident response plans and finding evidence.
Apply existing incident response playbooks and adapt them to specific environments and scenarios.
Demonstrate a theoretical and practical understanding of cyber threats and their relationship with the incident response and digital investigation processes, and their relationship.
Execute digital forensic methods in operating systems and their networks, describing in detail computer foundations, especially Data, Booting process, and hard drive.
Examine hard disks, including Master Boot Record (MBR), GUID Partition Table (GPT) in operating systems, and file system types such as FAT and NTFS.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111 Introduction to Information Technology and Networking, and ZSPS1337 Introduction to Cyber Security

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Internet of Things and Network Security
syllabus_overview: The course covers security theory and technical aspects of Internet of Things (IoT) as well as associated network protocols and architectures. Topics include identifying common network attacks targeting IoT systems, analysing how these attacks occur, and applying effective countermeasures. Students will design and implement technical controls across the OSI model to strengthen IoT network security. The course also introduces risk management strategies, intrusion detection and prevention techniques, and defensive measures against emerging threats to IoT environments. Overall, the course emphasises the secure integration of IoT devices into networks and examines relevant industry standards.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate security threats and vulnerabilities associated with IoT devices, and networks and associated protocols, and how to defend against them.
Compare and evaluate the effectiveness of various security mechanisms applied to IoT systems, networks, and protocols.

Develop and deploy a layered (defence-in-depth) cybersecurity strategy by applying appropriate defense mechanisms across all layers of the OSI model, incorporating risk management, technical, policy and education techniques.
Apply secure IoT architecture configurations and how they can be implemented to safeguard IoT devices and networks.

Investigate current trends and emerging technologies in IoT and network systems, and apply critical thinking skills, and problem-solving techniques to identify potential solutions to complex real-world problems.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Critical Infrastructure Protection
syllabus_overview: Critical Infrastructure operations increasingly depend on the fourth revolution of Industry (Industry 4.0), including the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) and automated Industrial Control Systems (ICS). These systems comprise human-machine interfaces (HMI), programmable logic controllers (PLC), remote telemetry units (RTU), and supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA) systems to offer smart critical infrastructure environments such as smart factories, smart healthcare, and smart grids. However, these systems suffer from various vulnerabilities and cyber attacks that attempt to compromise their critical infrastructure and achieve various attack motives. This course covers the underpinnings of theories and practicals of critical infrastructure and their security controls. Students will learn the fundamentals of Industry 4.0 environments. The student then practices the vulnerabilities and threats against these environments. Finally, students learn the security controls and protection methods, including standards, policies and frameworks to protect critical infrastructure systems.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical thing, problem-solving, and decision-making skills to design and implement comprehensive infrastructure protection plans that align with organisational objectives and regulatory requirements.
Design and develop various mitigation strategies and risk management to safeguard control systems.
Articulate the fundamental principles and concepts of infrastructure protection.
Critically assess vulnerabilities of critical infrastructure and how to mitigate them.
Critically review the deployments of industry 4.0 systems, such as HMI, PLC, RTU, and SCADA, and their security practices.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cloud Computing and Security
syllabus_overview: In today's rapidly evolving digital landscape, the cloud has become a fundamental component of modern computing. As organisations increasingly rely on cloud services to store, process, and manage their sensitive data, the need for robust cloud cyber security measures has never been more critical. In this course, students gain foundational knowledge of cloud computing, associated architectures and deployment models. By the end of this course, students will have a comprehensive understanding of cloud cyber security principles, technologies, and best practices. Students will also be equipped to secure cloud environments effectively, mitigate risks, and protect sensitive data stored in the cloud.
learning_outcomes: Contrast the different cloud paradigms and use-cases of their implementation, and their respective use-cases, advantages and limitations.

Analyse real-world case studies to identify cloud security issues, evaluate the effectiveness of existing cloud security strategies, propose improved solutions, and effectively communicate the results to key stakeholders.

Apply, configure and manage secure cloud environments using industry-standard platforms and security systems such as encryption, Identity and Access Management (IAMA) and MFA, while ensuring compliance with cloud-specific frameworks and security best practices.
Explain the technical and non-technical aspects of cloud-specific vulnerabilities and potential attacks.
Apply system, network, both current penetration testing techniques and apply cloud-specific penetration testing techniques to understand the security concerns of cloud implementations.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing
syllabus_overview: The Advanced Ethical Hacking course is designed to deepen the knowledge and skills in the field of ethical hacking. This course goes beyond the fundamentals and focuses on advanced techniques and strategies used by cyber security experts to protect critical systems and networks. It seeks to focus on more complex, multistage attacks, and to give insight into different actions on objectives.
learning_outcomes: Design and execute multi-stage adaptive cyber security attacks, encompassing various stages such as reconnaissance, vulnerability detection and exploitation, physical attacks, social engineering, and the development and deployment of customized tools.
Demonstrate proficiency in conducting advanced network attacks while adhering to professional, ethical and legal guidelines.
Illustrate the principles essential for stealthy infiltration, exfiltration, and persistence, while also possessing an understanding of potential detection measures and countermeasures.
Develop new programs to conduct offensive security operations.
Effectively communicate outcomes in writing to technical and non-technical audiences.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: ZSPS1111, ZSPS1337, ZSPS2113

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Risk Management & Incident Response
syllabus_overview: In today's technology-driven landscape, organisations face unprecedented challenges in protecting their valuable digital assets from cyber threats. Cyber risk management has emerged as a critical discipline that combines strategic planning, proactive risk assessment, and effective mitigation strategies to ensure the resilience of organisations against cyber threats. This course aims to equip students with the knowledge and skills necessary to navigate the complex world of cyber risk and develop robust risk management strategies. At the conclusion of this course, students will be equipped with the tools and techniques to assess and manage cyber risks, enabling them to make informed decisions to protect an organisation's digital assets.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective incident response strategies to manage cybersecurity incidents, address gaps in existing response frameworks, and foster organisational preparedness for potential risks and future incidents.

Justify the selection and utilisation of specific risk mitigation techniques by evaluating their compatibility with the organisational or project requirements, regulatory frameworks, and industry best practices.
Demonstrate an understanding of various forms of risk, their characteristics and implications, such as assessment of their likelihood and impact on an organisation.

Evaluate, compare and effectively communicate the strengths and limitations of various risk assessment methodologies—including their complexities, resource requirements, and suitability—to support informed risk management decisions.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZSPS1337

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundations of Organisational Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: In order to be an effective leader, it is critical to have a solid understanding of the work others in the discipline do. In cyber security, this means understanding a wide range of knowledge domains ranging from deeply technical fields through to legal and ethical considerations. Foundations of Organisational Cyber Security will focus on providing future leaders with a technical foundation to enrich their lexicon and enable effective communication with technical colleagues.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the impact of decisions made by cyber leaders across different organisational functions.
Demonstrate a working knowledge of foundational technical concepts in cyber security.
Discuss the real-world applications, historical context and evolution of the discipline of cyber security.
Describe the major principles and frameworks of cyber security.
Analyse the interconnectedness between cyber security and broader organisational concepts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Operations
syllabus_overview: Cyber Operations develops the theoretical foundation and practical skills needed to design, implement and evaluate cyber operations within complex enterprise environments. Students will explore both defensive and offensive security strategies used to protect, monitor and assess enterprise systems using best-practice frameworks, tools and operational processes. The course equips students will skills and knowledge to analyse and respond to threats, simulate attacker behavior, and communicate operational insights to both technical and non-technical audiences. Throughout this course students will gain insight into industry security roles and constructs such as SOC analysts, threat hunters, and red, blue and purple teams. Defensive modules include techniques such as threat intelligence, monitoring and response aligned to enterprise operations and cyber resilience objectives. Offensive modules focus on controlled and ethical activities including reconnaissance, scanning, exploitation and red team simulations used to assess and strengthen system security.
learning_outcomes: Communicate cyber operational findings and decisions clearly through written reports and/or presentations to technical and non-technical audiences, including enterprise stakeholders.
Analyse and interpret operational cyber security information to identify and prioritise threats and recommend or initiate appropriate mitigation strategies based on operational context.
Describe the objectives of cyber security operations.
Design, evaluate, or critique a cyber security architecture for an enterprise network that supports both proactive defence and ethical attack simulation capabilities.
Understand and utilise range of tools, techniques and technologies associated with cyber operations including security monitoring, logging, analysis, and threat intelligence.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Security Governance, Risk and Compliance
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) in the field of cyber security. Students will learn about governance structures, managing risk, audits for compliance, including legal obligations that organisations must meet. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the skills and knowledge necessary to effectively manage cyber security risk and ensure compliance with relevant laws and standards. The emphasis will be on understanding and implementing effective risk assessment and management processes to ensure the security and resilience of organisational systems.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the potential impact of different organisational priorities in the context of compliance.
Describe the effectiveness of risk assessment methods and apply these methods in real-world scenarios.
Communicate Governance, Risk, and Compliance concepts to a range of stakeholders, including technical and non-technical audiences.
Evaluate risk profiles and make governance recommendations that enhance cyber resilience.
Describe the principles and best practices of Governance, Risk, and Compliance in the field of cyber security.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Security Leadership and Strategy
syllabus_overview: This course on cyber security strategy and leadership aims to equip students with the necessary skills to lead and guide organisations in the constantly evolving field of cyber security. Students will learn how to evaluate and navigate the impact of new and emerging technologies in the organisation. This course will provide the tools required to inspire change, engage with executives, build teams, and create a strategy to drive the organisation's direction in cyber security.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to adapt strategic initiatives to different contexts.
Demonstrate effective communication appropriate to a range of organisations, inclusive of technical and non-technical audiences.
Apply concepts of strategy and leadership to cyber security.
Analyse the impact of emerging technologies on an organisation's cyber security strategy.
Analyse situations and trade-offs required for successful implementation of strategic goals.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Security Data Governance and Privacy
syllabus_overview: This course will explore data protection, privacy, and the law in the field of cyber security. Students will learn about the principles and best practices of data management, and how to navigate the complex landscape of privacy laws and regulations. The course will also touch on the skills required to navigate these complexities in the context of cyber security, data governance and privacy. Students will gain a deeper understanding of the challenges and opportunities presented by these critical issues in cyber security.
learning_outcomes: Identify the principles and best practices of data governance in relation to privacy and cyber security.
Apply knowledge of data governance to categorise and treat data according to privacy, security and regulatory requirements.
Describe the link between privacy and data governance, including ethical considerations.
Analyse the impact on data governance and privacy, within regulatory landscapes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Governance in Policy Systems
syllabus_overview: In order to be an effective policy leader, it is critical to have a solid understanding of how contemporary public policy challenges exist in systems. In multi-layered, multiple stakeholder, federal networks, a policy leader at any one level will not have the ability to direct policy at other levels, or in the private/not-for-profit sectors. Further, past policy leaders have addressed many of the policy challenges that respond to a single program, leaving today’s most pressing policy problems which are complex and multi-faceted. This means that policy leaders require a deep understanding of governance at the project, program, organisation and systems levels. Governance in Policy Systems will focus on providing future policy leaders with strategic insight and practical skills to provide stewardship of policy through complex systems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a high-level understanding of governance principles, practice and stewardship in complex systems.
Apply principles of policy stewardship and network analysis within a complex policy system.
Identify the differences between the principles of corporate, data, program and network governance.
Describe best practice skills in project governance and report their application through a practical example.
Articulate and apply the key features of network governance within the Australian Federal system through contemporary examples.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Assessing Data for Evidence-based Policy
syllabus_overview: Technological advance means that the range of data available to support policy leadership is constantly evolving. While professional experience will provide some knowledge of particular data types and possibilities, it is difficult to grasp the breadth or keep up with the pace of data advance. However, policy leaders need to know how to request, design and interpret data for its reliability, validity and relevance as evidence. This course will focus on the range of data sets currently available, how they should be interrogated and ways they should be presented to support policy and political decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Describe where data and modelling fits in evidence-based policy making theory and critically interrogate its practical relevance, integrity and use for policy.
Outline relevant national data sources, articulate how they can be accessed and used in policy work.
Demonstrate competency in the basic data visualisation principles/ tools presented in the course.

Critically analyse the strengths and weaknesses of emerging data tools (such as machine learning) for a policy example, as well as identify key questions to interrogate the utility and validity as evidence.
Demonstrate the ability to analyse commonly available statistical analysis (descriptive/ inferential) and how to assess for reliability and validity as policy evidence for decisionmakers.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Philosophy of AI
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course explores the philosophical and ethical questions raised by artificial intelligence. You will examine debates about consciousness, autonomy, moral responsibility, and technological risk. Through critical reading and writing, you will learn to analyse philosophical arguments that shape contemporary discussions of artificial intelligence. The course emphasises ethical reasoning and conceptual clarity as foundations for informed judgement about artificial intelligence in organisational and societal contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain philosophical arguments concerning the nature and possibility of artificial intelligence
Analyse and critique reasoning in philosophical and artificial intelligence-related texts and peer arguments
Evaluate ethical and social implications of intelligent machines
Communicate complex ideas clearly and persuasively

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Responsible AI for Business and Society
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in business operations and societal decision-making. While AI enables innovation and efficiency, its use introduces ethical challenges, organisational responsibilities, and broader societal implications. AI-enabled decisions influence fairness, accountability, transparency, employment, and public trust. This course examines the ethical, social, and organisational challenges created by AI-enabled decision-making in business and society. Students explore responsible AI principles and evaluate how organisations apply these principles in practice. Through real-world cases, students analyse stakeholder impacts, assess value-based trade-offs, and examine how AI reshapes accountability and organisational responsibility. The course emphasises ethical reasoning, societal impact, stakeholder analysis, and structured judgement as foundations for responsible organisational decision-making. This course aims to develop students’ ability to evaluate AI-enabled practices through ethical, organisational, and societal lenses; build structured judgement in assessing trade-offs and unintended consequences; strengthen organisational responsibility analysis; and enhance professional communication of responsible AI recommendations.
learning_outcomes: Explain how AI-enabled decision-making influences business processes, organisational accountability, and societal outcomes.
Apply ethical reasoning, stakeholder analysis, and value-based trade-off evaluation to assess AI use in real organisational contexts.
Identify organisational vulnerabilities and unintended consequences associated with AI adoption.
Develop and communicate structured, ethically grounded recommendations to support responsible and sustainable AI use in business and society.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: AI Fluency
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course introduces foundational artificial intelligence (AI) concepts, terminology, and applications for non-technical learners. Students explore how AI technologies are reshaping industries and work, develop practical skills in applying AI tools to enhance productivity, decision-making, and creative problem-solving, and build the analytical foundation needed to assess where and how AI can be applied effectively in business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key concepts, capabilities, and limitations of AI technologies
Apply AI tools to enhance productivity and decision-making in professional contexts
Evaluate the ethical, social, and economic implications of AI adoption

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Developing Strategy for AI
syllabus_overview: This course develops students’ ability to design and communicate strategies for artificial intelligence informed by contemporary strategy and digital transformation frameworks. The course focuses on AI as an organisational capability, covering how to identify, prioritise, and govern AI initiatives, and how to make and communicate strategic decisions under uncertainty. Students analyse real-world organisational contexts and case scenarios to frame AI and articulate strategic trade-offs to managers and non-technical stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Assess the strategic and operational implications of artificial intelligence
Design strategies for the development and deployment of artificial intelligence that enhance organisational performance
Communicate artificial intelligence strategy to diverse internal and external stakeholders, including senior leadership, boards, operational teams, and non-technical audiences.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Computational Thinking and AI
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course develops programming literacy and structured computational thinking for business contexts. Students engage with programming and related tools to understand how business problems are translated into data processes, logic structures, and automated workflows within organisational systems. The course introduces foundational concepts such as data representation, control logic, modular design, and process decomposition, enabling students to interpret how artificial intelligence-enabled systems are constructed and monitored. Students focus on evaluating, adapting, and validating code — including code generated with artificial intelligence tools — and assessing the robustness, limitations, and organisational implications of computational solutions. The emphasis is on understanding how software systems think and operate in practice, equipping students to collaborate effectively with technical teams and exercise informed oversight of artificial intelligence-enabled processes.
learning_outcomes: Communicate computational reasoning and system logic clearly to non-technical stakeholders.
Evaluate and validate computational outputs for accuracy, robustness, and organisational relevance, including when using artificial intelligence-assisted development tools.
Explain core programming and computational concepts relevant to business problem-solving.
Analyse how business problems are translated into structured code, data processes, and automated workflows.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Risk Management and Governance in the Age of AI
school: School of Risk and Actuarial Studies
syllabus_overview: This course examines organisational risk management and governance challenges associated with artificial intelligence adoption. Students apply established risk management frameworks, regulatory standards, and governance models to identify, assess, and mitigate artificial intelligence-related risks, with particular attention to compliance and accountability. The course emphasises formal governance structures, risk controls, regulatory compliance, and escalation pathways.
learning_outcomes: Identify and evaluate AI-related risks
Apply risk management frameworks to mitigate AI-related threats
Design organisational policies for responsible AI use
Collaborate to evaluate competing risk perspectives and produce joint governance recommendations
Analyse and compare governance models and regulatory approaches across jurisdictions

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Leading AI-Enabled Change
school: School of Information Systems and Technology Management
syllabus_overview: This course examines organisational change in response to artificial intelligence adoption and transformation. As artificial intelligence reshapes workflows, decision processes, governance arrangements, and workforce capabilities, leaders must design and sustain change that is strategically aligned, ethically responsible, and operationally viable.
