More importantly, this course highlights (i) the governance issues faced by startups in the heavily-regulated FinTech space, (ii) the competitive mass that is needed to enter into spaces already dominated by large organisations, (iii) the design of cost-effective marketing strategies to capture early adopters, when there is typically a narrow window to scale up, (iv) the cybersecurity and data privacy issues, which are specially crucial for FinTech firms, and (v) other issues, such as recruiting strategies, and tactics to create sustainable cash-flow profiles.
learning_outcomes: Appreciate the infrastructure required for, and the challenges and risks associated with, setting up and launching a startup in the FinTech space.
Design a commercial model for a FinTech startup.
Identify growth opportunities.
Evaluate the pros and cons of the various funding and scaling options available to FinTech startups.
Appreciate the possibilities and boundaries of technology in the financial services industry.
Define the problem to be solved by the FinTech startup.
Identify strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats in each FinTech subdomain
Decide on an exit avenue for the startup.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied FinTech Project
syllabus_overview: Over the course of your studies, you will have gained an appreciation for the vast range of opportunities that exist for innovation within the FinTech space at the intersection of financial services and technology. This capstone course provides students with an industry aligned framework for application of their cumulative FinTech skills to identify a real-world opportunity for an innovative FinTech application, and to then develop and pitch a methodology or an actual solution for implementation of that FinTech application. Students will exercise and develop their collaborative, creative, analytic and communication skills across this process.
learning_outcomes: Apply project design and data collection and analysis concepts, models, frameworks and tools to the specification of a FinTech application.
Interpret and discuss on how environmental, social, cultural, and ethical factors influence and, reciprocally, are impacted by a proposed FinTech application.
Develop and deliver a solution for an identified FinTech opportunity.

Collaborate with finance industry experts and peers to identify and confirm the viability of FinTech opportunities/needs, and observe and determine the role of collaboration in identification of FinTech opportunities.
prerequisites: Pre-requisite: in Master of Financial Technology (Online) and completed 48 UOC

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Portfolio Management
syllabus_overview: This course aims to develop a basic conceptual framework within which the modern investment environment can be understood. You will firstly contextualise learning by being provided with an institutional and product overview of the investment markets. You will then develop a more complete understanding of the risk-return relation in order to review alternative investment strategies and asset pricing models, with a focus on use for portfolio construction and valuation purposes. Real-world circumstances in which these models and strategies may or may not apply will be explored. The material will be taught in a way that focuses on how the theory applies to real-world situations and will aim to be as up-to-date as possible by emphasising recent developments in investment management.
learning_outcomes: Create an optimal investment portfolio by applying portfolio theory.
Identify the limitations of the models in certain situations and the resulting implications for designing investment strategies.
Utilise the models taught to interpret and analyse real problems in investments.
Describe the operation of financial markets and common financial products
Apply the standard models of asset pricing to measure, price and manage risk; value securities; and exploit mispriced securities.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Corporate Finance
syllabus_overview: This course explores the modern fundamentals of corporate financial decision making with a focus on making optimal investment decisions. Hence the course considers widely used methodologies for forecasting cash flows and determining an appropriate return on invested funds, incorporating analysis of capital structure policy, raising capital, and payout strategies. The course is a blend of theory and practice, drawing on prepared problem-solving activities as well as the real-time analysis of listed companies.
learning_outcomes: Present sophisticated analysis using proper finance arguments and frameworks for a professional audience.
Propose and justify relevant corporate capital deployment recommendations.
Explain key concepts and terms from corporate finance.
Apply modern methodologies for forecasting cash flow and return.
Recognise the different options available for capital raising and the processes involved.
Make credible recommendations about capital structure and payout.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: International Finance
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the knowledge required for the management of financial functions of multinational firms. In addition to building a rich theoretical grounding in international finance concepts, the course teaches you how to apply those concepts via real-world data analysis and scenario-based studies. The course begins by exploring international monetary policy and foreign exchange markets at the macro-economic level and moves on to a theoretical understanding of exchange rate determinants. We then shift the focus from the global- to the transaction-level and learn how to identify and develop hedging strategies to deal with risk related to exchange rate and interest rate fluctuations. With the core conceptual understanding of hedging instruments in place, we expand our knowledge to application and decision-making at the firm-level and students learn how multinational firms can invest and finance in international markets and manage related risks. At each stage of the student journey, learning material, as well as weekly activities and assessments, are designed to build a community of inquiry and to articulate theory through real-world examples, cases or data exercises. It is recommended to undertake this course later in the program, where possible.
learning_outcomes: Identify exchange rate risk and develop hedging strategies to deal with it.
Compare, contrast, and assess varying exchange rate systems in various countries and understand the determinants of foreign exchange rates.
Analyse and discuss the international macro-economic and political environments that are relevant to multinational firms.
Evaluate foreign direct investment and tax and regulatory arbitrage opportunities.
Apply the theories on exchange rate determinants and global portfolio models to real problems in global business using dynamic real-world data.
Construct professional and logical written work in the context of international finance.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Private Equity and Venture Capital
syllabus_overview: This course examines venture capital and private equity investments. In particular, it focuses on issues surrounding the funding of entrepreneurial firms that are financed by venture capital or private equity funds. The course departs from conventional investment approaches that examine risk and return of publicly listed securities, focusing on issues associated with financing and innovation intensive private businesses.
learning_outcomes: Explain the key determinants that drive the choice of IPO (initial public offering) versus trade sale when exiting and in investment.
Identify the risks associated with venture capital/private equity investments and explain how to mitigate them.
Illustrate the key differences between the private and public financial markets.
Explain and discuss how cultural and social aspects can affect decisions in a private equity/venture capital context.
Evaluate private equity and venture capital funds performance and their contribution to a portfolio.
Negotiate an appropriate investment structure, both from an investor and investee perspective.
Describe the responsibilities of directors of private companies, in particular, in a private equity/venture capital context.
Determine which valuation method is most appropriate depending on the context of the valuation exercise, the nature of the opportunity and the stage of its development.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethics and Professional Standards
syllabus_overview: This course describes why a high level of ethical standard is needed by those employed in the financial services industry. Initially, significant ethical theories are explored. Next, the six components of the Code of Ethics are addressed and each of the seven Standards of Professional Conduct examined in detail. The course also analyses the scope and key features of the Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS), the reason for their creation, to whom they apply, and how to verify GIPS compliance. The course includes interviews with leaders in the industry who reflect on the role of ethics in their careers.
learning_outcomes: Explain the ethical responsibilities required by the Code and Standards, including recommended guidance and procedures for compliance practices.
Evaluate ethical dilemmas through application of the Code and Standards (including sub-parts).
Explain the role Global Investment Performance Standards (GIPS) play in promoting an ethical framework for calculating and presenting investment performance history.
Identify the role ethical theories, including the CFA Code of Ethics, have in the financial services industry.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Equity Valuation
syllabus_overview: This course explores techniques, models and industry practices in equity analysis and valuation. Both quantitative and fundamental analyses are covered to illustrate the work and research behind the trade recommendation reports prepared by financial analysts.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the competitive advantage, industry structure and sustainability of return on invested capital of the subject company to determine the profitability of the subject company
Evaluate the debt management of the subject company using relevant financial ratios
Apply discounted cash flow, residual income and market-based valuation models to estimate the fair equity value of a listed company

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fixed Income
syllabus_overview: This course presents a foundational knowledge framework for professionals seeking understanding of the quantitative and qualitative characteristics of fixed-income assets (i.e. debt securities). Students firstly get an overview of various types of fixed-income assets before looking in detail at the financial calculations relevant to their valuation and risk analysis. A crucial element of the course is the development of students’ financial mathematics skills, which will be achieved with practical demonstrations and exercises linking course work concepts with real-world applications. The course is predominantly aligned with CFA Level 1, but also delves into more advanced topics such as yield curves, risk management of fixed income portfolios, structured financial products, and credit default swaps.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of additional debt security complexities such as accrued interest, floating rates, inflation, embedded options and structured financial products.
Demonstrate understanding of credit risk, credit ratings, and credit default swaps.
Demonstrate the relationships between a bond’s price, coupon rate, maturity, and market discount rate (yield-to-maturity) in spreadsheet calculations.
Describe government and corporate debt markets and their stakeholders.
Explain the concepts of duration and convexity and apply them to manage the risk of a bond portfolio.

Demonstrate the relationship between yield curves, and spot and forward interest rates in spreadsheet calculations, and demonstrate understanding of the relationship between yield curves and economic circumstances.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Decision Making in Analytics
syllabus_overview: Businesses deal with an ever-increasing array of data, in terms of volume and sources. This presents businesses with opportunities to harness insights from this data to support decision making. This course will introduce students to a range of decision-making techniques in data analytics. Students will be shown how to design and implement application systems to support decision making in organisational contexts. The course will also cover a number of modelling approaches (optimisation, predictive, descriptive) and their integration in the context of enabling improved data-driven decision making. Students will be expected to be able to calculate and manipulate data as well as interpret the results in order to derive and evaluate alternative solutions to typical organisational problems.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe complex analytical problems in a variety of contexts.
Develop skills in spreadsheet modelling to enhance decision making processes in real-life contexts.
Apply critical thinking to complex information, problems, concepts and theories of analytical tools.
Apply analytical tools and established theories in the decision-making process.
prerequisites: Prerequisites ZZBU6501 or ZZSC9001

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Derivatives
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for professionals or trainees who aspire to work in a managerial capacity in a contemporary global business environment as a manager in a financial institution/department, or an international business unit. This course will introduce you to topics such as forward, futures, swaps options and various structured product and markets that trade them. There is an equal emphasis on the practical and theoretical applications of these financial instruments. Through the progression of this course, you will reflect on future trends of the practical relevance of modern derivatives theory and realise that derivatives can be a significant and integral part of business transactions and corporate risk management practices.
learning_outcomes: Explain the definitions and uses of a variety of derivatives, e.g., futures, options, swaps, and options.
Communicate financial derivatives pricing and risk management ideas in a clear and succinct manner.
Use financial derivative instruments for managing and hedging portfolio risk.
Value derivative instruments using discrete time and continuous time valuation principles.
Construct written work in relation to applications of financial derivatives which is logically and professionally presented.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Strategic Leadership
syllabus_overview: Strategic leadership is critical to the effective planning and delivery of project portfolio outcomes that support long-term business and organisational objectives. This course develops participants’ capacity to lead effectively in complex environments by cultivating strategic thinking, ethical decision-making, and stakeholder engagement. Emphasising a theory-neutral approach, it equips students to evaluate and apply diverse leadership models, navigate governance and influence across organisational contexts, and design initiatives that align leadership practice with strategic goals. Through reflective practice and structured experimentation, participants will evolve their personal leadership philosophy and articulate strategies for ongoing growth as strategic leaders.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on personal leadership practice and articulate strategies for ongoing growth in complex organisational contexts.
Develop and articulate strategic leadership approaches that align with organisational goals and respond to complex environments.
Critically evaluate and apply diverse leadership approaches, grounded in empirical research, to lead teams effectively in dynamic organisational contexts.
Assess ethical dilemmas in leadership and justify decision-making approaches using ethical reasoning frameworks.
Understand and apply leadership approaches to engage diverse internal and external stakeholders and navigate organisational complexity.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Environmental, Social and Governance for Projects
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) principles within the context of project management. Students will explore how sustainable practices, stakeholder engagement, and governance frameworks influence project planning, delivery, and long-term value creation. Through real-world case studies and applied tools, students will develop skills to integrate ESG factors into strategic project decisions.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategies to integrate ESG factors into project management.
Evaluate ESG risks in complex project contexts.
Demonstrate understanding of ESG concepts and their relevance to project planning and delivery.
Apply relevant ESG frameworks to enhance project sustainability.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: The Business of Managing Projects
syllabus_overview: This course explores how projects align with business strategy, governance and stakeholder needs. Students develop leadership and decision-making capabilities by analysing the human, organisational and strategic dimensions of project delivery. With a focus on real-world challenges and opportunities, the course prepares students to navigate complexity, drive innovation and deliver value across dynamic business environments.
learning_outcomes: Develop written and oral communication skills by writing responses to tasks and/or presenting oral reflections.
Using a real-world project case study, identify, analyse and evaluate organising principles of project governance and supporting organisational capabilities and their influence on project outcomes.
Identify organising principles of project governance and supporting organisational capabilities.
Critically analyse the role of social, cultural, and soft skills in project management and their implications for decision-making, team performance, and project outcomes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Program and Portfolio Management
syllabus_overview: This capstone course provides students with the opportunity to integrate and apply advanced knowledge of program and portfolio management in a substantial, research-informed and practice-based project. Students will explore how organisations achieve strategic objectives through the selection, prioritisation, execution, and governance of multiple initiatives. The course emphasises benefits realisation, risk management, and the role of the Program Management Office in supporting strategic delivery. As a capstone, the course requires students to demonstrate high-level autonomy, initiative, and accountability by planning and executing a complex project that synthesises theory and practice. This project will address a real-world or simulated organisational challenge, enabling students to critically evaluate and apply program and portfolio management principles in a strategic context.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate program and portfolio management frameworks to support strategic decision-making in complex organisational environments.
Communicate project findings and recommendations effectively to professional and academic audiences.
Demonstrate high-level autonomy and accountability in managing project scope, stakeholder engagement, and delivery performance.
Plan and execute a substantial, research-informed capstone project that addresses a strategic challenge in program or portfolio management.
Apply advanced principles of benefits realisation, governance, and risk management to assess and improve program and portfolio outcomes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Change Management
syllabus_overview: Change management in the project context involves two interrelated dimensions: the strategic process of embedding organisational change and the operational controls that govern its delivery across the project lifecycle. This course examines both, integrating theory, research, and applied practice to equip students to lead change initiatives, respond to evolving project conditions, and deliver outcomes that are aligned with organisational intent. Through real-world scenarios and applied learning, students will develop the capability to diagnose change needs, engage stakeholders, and navigate governance structures in complex and dynamic project environments.
learning_outcomes: Assess change outcomes and long-term integration using metrics, feedback, and evaluation strategies.
Evaluate and apply change management approaches to design tailored interventions for project environments.
Critically analyse change drivers and organisational readiness in project and program contexts.
Develop and apply stakeholder engagement and resistance management strategies using targeted communication and influence strategies.
Implement and refine change strategies in response to project complexity and organisational dynamics.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Risk Management
syllabus_overview: Effective risk management is critical to the success of projects and organisations in an increasingly complex and uncertain global environment. This course provides students with a foundational understanding of risk management principles, frameworks, and best practices, with a focus on their application in project management and enterprise environments. The course discusses the complex nature of the words 'uncertainty' and 'risk', and how their many definitions and interpretations impact risk management. The course covers aspects of risk management including why individuals and organisations must manage risks; the identification, classification and measurement of risks; the fundamental principles and frameworks for risk management; the tools and techniques used in the risk management process; the important role of risk culture and communication in managing enterprise risks; and current issues in risk management.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate a case study application of project risk management theories, frameworks, and standards.
Conduct advanced qualitative and quantitative risk analyses and design integrated risk response strategies.
Explain and evaluate the impact of risks on individuals and organisations, and evaluate strategies to measure and treat them effectively.
Evaluate the effectiveness of risk governance, risk appetite frameworks, and senior-level governance oversight in aligning risk management with organisational objectives.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Administration
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with the knowledge and skills to analyse and manage the complex environments in which major projects are defined and delivered. The course emphasises the organisational, political, financial, and legal dimensions of project management, including corporate governance, project viability and contract law. Through real-world case studies, students will develop advanced capabilities in project governance, procurement strategies, financial evaluation, and risk management. The course also explores contemporary challenges such as government regulations, stakeholder engagement, and dispute resolution strategies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate legislative and common law provisions impacting procurement and develop strategies to address legal and ethical challenges in project delivery.
Analyse governance objectives, constraints, and delivery models to recommend effective solutions for managing project complexity.
Develop a comprehensive Project Execution Strategy that effectively manages project risks and aligns with governance frameworks.
Analyse the financial and economic aspects of projects and develop data-driven cost-benefit recommendations to support decision making.
Design project organisations and procurement strategies that optimise performance while balancing buyer and supplier objectives.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Management Body of Knowledge
syllabus_overview: This course explores the multifaceted challenges and dynamic conditions of project management in both public and private sector contexts. Focusing on the project manager’s role as a facilitator and enabler, it combines theoretical insights with practical skills in both technical and interpersonal areas. Students will engage with the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBoK) as a foundational framework, developing the capacity to apply its principles and processes to the planning, execution, and oversight of complex projects.
learning_outcomes: Apply the Project Management Body of Knowledge principles and processes in a complex project.
Explain the inception and requirement for a Project Management Body of Knowledge.
Demonstrate the value that a Project Management Body of Knowledge brings to successfully manage projects.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Project Schedule and Budget Control
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the knowledge, tools, and techniques to manage project scope, scheduling, budgeting, and control effectively. Students will learn to develop project plans and baselines using industry-standard techniques. The course emphasises the practical application of project scheduling and budgeting principles, resource management, and progress reporting. Students will also explore strategies for managing uncertainty and adapting to changing project requirements. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to plan, track, and control project performance to ensure successful delivery of time, cost, and scope objectives.
learning_outcomes: Analyse project performance using Earned Value Management (EVM) to evaluate progress and control deviations.
Develop project plans, schedules, and budget baselines using industry-standard techniques, such as PERT, CPM (AOA, AON), and EVM.
Explain the principles and processes of project scheduling, budgeting, and control, and their importance in project success.
Design strategies to manage project uncertainties and address changing requirements in project schedules.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Operations
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the theoretical knowledge and practical skills for designing, implementing, and defending modern enterprise computer networks. The course introduces students to security architecture for secure system design, security engineering for implementation and configuration, and security operations for managing, monitoring, and defending systems. The course has a focus on defensive technology, practical skills, and the activities that organisations undertake to assure their information systems.
learning_outcomes: Select and evaluate security controls for an enterprise network.
Analyse cyber security information, logs, and events.
Describe the objectives of cyber security operations.
Implement and configure security controls.
Design a cyber security architecture for an enterprise network.
prerequisites: ZZEN9201

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Data Security and Privacy
syllabus_overview: Security and privacy are related but distinct concepts; they are also some of the defining terms of the 21st century. This course equips student for handling data in secure ways, understanding the nature and principles of privacy, and how to securely identify manage and respond to privacy risks across large datasets and apply current best practice in a changing global environment.
learning_outcomes: Apply data security and privacy principles in security engineering design of software, systems, and policies.
Apply national and international legislation, ethical standards, and professional best practice to organisational practice and personal professional practice.
Demonstrate a critical understanding the nature and principles of privacy, and of the potential costs, benefits, and risks under societal, commercial, individual and governmental perspectives.
Explain historic data security and privacy failures and their causes and consequences.
Analyse the privacy implications of systems and processes.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Risk and Resilience
syllabus_overview: Cyber resilience is the organisational ability to deliver business or operational outcomes despite cyber attack. True resilience is a measure of both business and cyber understanding. This course provides students with the skills necessary to manage contemporary risks through gaining a systematic understanding of the principles and policies for developing the resilience of communities, businesses, and critical systems.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the results of risk assessments effectively to key stakeholders.
Explain different forms of risk, strengths and limitations of a range of risk assessment approaches, and when it is appropriate to use them.
Integrate cyber resilience frameworks into business needs.
Develop appropriate risk assessments and recommendations.
Analyse and develop a cyber risk profile for an organisation or project.
Apply current risk assessment best-practice and standards, and effectively apply them to new situations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cybersecurity Ethics
syllabus_overview: Ethics underpins everything we do in our professional life. The cyber industry presents unique ethical challenges, due to the rapid rate of change and the often-unknown future of innovations. This course provides students with an understanding of three framework concepts of ethics applied to the cyber profession. Students analyse real world challenges in cyber through an ethical lens. The course equips students with the tools to unpack and respond to future ethical challenges as they arise.
learning_outcomes: Explain cyber ethics and its relevance in the cyber industry.
Apply ethical principles to decision-making in the cyber industry.
Analyse three framework concepts of ethics as they pertain to cyber.
Evaluate real world ethical challenges in the cyber industry.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Transformation in AI
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the strategic integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in driving digital transformation within project environments. It covers key concepts in AI strategy, governance and implementation, preparing students to lead innovation-focused projects and manage change in complex, technology-driven settings. Students will explore how emerging technologies reshape project lifecycles, stakeholder engagement and decision-making. Through case studies and applied learning, they will develop the skills to lead AI-driven initiatives, assess digital maturity, and apply ethical and data-informed leadership practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the strategic role of AI in driving digital transformation across project environments.
Apply ethical and leadership principles to manage change and assess digital maturity in complex project settings.
Evaluate emerging technologies and their impact on project lifecycles, stakeholder engagement, and decision-making.
Design AI-driven solutions to enhance project planning, governance, and automation.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Management and Leadership Capstone Project
syllabus_overview: This course is the capstone for the Security Management and Leadership Specialisation within the Master of Cyber Security (Online) program. It provides a self-directed learning opportunity to work in a team to integrate the skills learned across the program.
learning_outcomes: Summarise and effectively communicate mastery of professional skills and capabilities, including analysis, problem solving, risk assessment, and ethical considerations in cyber security.
Apply cyber leadership and governance knowledge and skills in a real-world application.

Demonstrate the ability to work collaboratively and professionally in a team, identifying and addressing team issues, enhancing and supporting team effectiveness and applying cultural and global competence, in the context of cybersecurity.
Critically reflect on self-management capabilities, including communication, project management, and time management.
prerequisites: Enrolment in 8649 and 48 UOC completed

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Digital Forensics
syllabus_overview: Digital forensics is an under-represented area of cyber security. It encompasses the processes and technical understanding surrounding both the investigation of computer crimes and crimes where evidence remains on computing devices. This course provides a strong foundation for both those wanting to specialise in this area of cyber security, and those seeking to understand the processes for improved incident response. Students will be able to forensically analyse digital devices and understand the ethical, legal and self care issues associated with cybercrime investigations.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply a digital forensic mindset.
Communicate results effectively in professional reports and as an expert witness.
Synthesise and apply current forensic procedures and techniques regarding the identification, collection, preservation and custody, and analysis of digital evidence.
Perform analysis of acquired digital devices.
Explain the current theoretical principles that underpin the science of digital forensics.
prerequisites: ZZEN9217

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Management and Governance
syllabus_overview: Cyber Management and Governance equips you with the skills for weighing competing challenges for the management of cyber and related governance activities in an organisational context. You will learn how to develop cyber strategies, policies and to apply a critical eye to the cyber challenges facing organisations today. Building an understanding of how these governance tools impact people and the efficacy of cyber security controls and practices.
learning_outcomes: Integrate emerging directions in cyber management with existing norms to shape policy and strategic organisational aims.
Evaluate competing risks and benefits against organisational culture.
Produce executive level documentation that demonstrates ability to articulate complex concepts to non-technical audiences.
Make decisions and recommendations aligned with organisational objectives.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of impact of cyber policy and strategy.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber Threats and Crime
syllabus_overview: The Internet drives economic growth and enables new ways to connect and co-operate. As with most change, increasing our reliance on cyberspace brings new opportunities but also new threats. While the internet fosters open markets and open societies, this can also make users more vulnerable to criminals, activists, and foreign intelligence services who want to harm us by compromising or damaging our critical data and systems. Cybercriminal attacks against Australian organisations are not a matter of “if” but of “when”. In this new era of unavoidable attacks and breaches, cybersecurity professionals have to duty to ensure their organisations are resilient, and to be adequately prepared when an incident unfolds. This course outlines, from a holistic perspective, the current and emerging trends in cybercrime and how they are being countered from an Australian perspective. It also introduces students to contemporary trends in cyber security strategy and demonstrates how they can be used to increase an organisation’s resilience and preparedness.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the data and effect of online crime and the impact it has on government, businesses and individuals.
Synthesise current trends to predict future trends in cyber crime and terror, and effectively communicate appropriate actions and controls.
Critically evaluate the current legislation that impact on computer crimes and law enforcement and corporate responses to this legislation.
Identify and describe the different categories of both historical and contemporary computer crime.
Explain the strengths and weaknesses of current controls to minimise the impact of cyber crime and terror.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Foundational Counselling Skills
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the foundations of the therapeutic relationship and use of self in counselling. The course orients you to a humanistic, person-centred approach to counselling. Utilising the online environment, you will build your capacity to use counselling skills in digital contexts. You will apply First Nations knowledges (such as deep listening) while fostering reflective practice and critical self-awareness, through experiential and reflective learning. You will engage with experiential learning in small groups and roleplays to develop foundational counselling skills and practices, including the use of digital and online counselling.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of relevant therapeutic approaches
Articulate the components of the therapeutic relationship
Demonstrate core counselling skills
Critically appraise your counselling skills

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Ethics in Counselling Practice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the ethical foundations and professional standards, informed by the Australian Counselling Association (ACA) that guide your development as a counsellor and your counselling practice. You will explore ethical theories and decision-making frameworks while emphasising reflexivity as central to professional identity. You will consider key issues of ethical practice, including boundaries, authenticity, and cultural responsiveness in the therapeutic relationship. You will be introduced to supervision as a site of ethical and reflective practice and critically consider emerging issues such as digital ethics (including use of AI) in counselling.
learning_outcomes: Describe the use of supervision in ethical and reflective counselling practice
Evaluate the role of professional standards in counselling
Demonstrate an understanding of ethics, boundaries, authenticity, and cultural responsiveness in the therapeutic relationship
Critically reflect on relevant ethical issues and theoretical approaches in counselling practice

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Mental Health, Trauma and Resilience
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to a biopsychosocial spiritual cultural perspective on human development and health over the lifespan. You will analyse contemporary approaches to mental health, trauma and resilience, across diverse populations. You will utilise a range of interactive practice skills to develop skills and knowledges in trauma informed care, risk and counselling responses to mental health issues. Your reflections on your experiential learning build your skills and capacity for effective counselling practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse contemporary understandings of mental health, trauma, and resilience
Articulate an understanding of trauma-informed and responsive care
Explain key concepts of human development and relational processes across the lifespan

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counselling in a Diverse World
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course engages you in critical exploration of counselling practice within diverse personal, social, geographical and cultural contexts. Emphasis is placed on culturally responsive and socially just counselling practice, informed by First Nations knowledges, cultural humility, intersectionality, and emancipatory frameworks. The course highlights the role of humanistic and narrative traditions—including existential and meaning-making perspectives—in supporting clients’ stories and lived experiences. You will engage with online and digital counselling technologies to promote inclusivity. You will develop skills to engage with clients from a wide range of backgrounds and experiences including neurodiversity.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate integrative counselling strategies to promote inclusive, culturally responsive and socially just practice
Evaluate the role of digital technologies in counselling, including accessibility and inclusivity
Critically reflect on how social and cultural diversities shape counselling practices
Articulate how First Nations knowledges and relevant frameworks inform inclusive and socially just counselling practices

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Applied Counselling Approaches
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this course you will interrogate key frameworks informing counselling such as cognitive, behavioural, and mindfulness-based approaches. You will develop a critical understanding of the theory and skills base of these frameworks to advance your capacities in cultural responsiveness, reflective practice and the therapeutic relationship. You will participate in interactive tutorials and deliberate practice to build on and extend your foundational counselling skills via roleplays, small group exercises, critical reflection, class discussion, and feedback. Your reflections on your experiential learning build your skills and capacity for effective counselling practice. This interactive learning furthers your ability to use advanced counselling skills and apply relevant counselling approaches across a diverse range of client and counselling practice contexts.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate key concepts and techniques underpinning relevant counselling frameworks
Effectively apply counselling practices utilising ideas from a relevant framework
Critically evaluate the appropriateness of frameworks in addressing diverse client presentations.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, and ZZCO5004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Working with Couples and Families
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This elective course extends your counselling practice beyond individual work to include therapeutic engagement with couples, families, and kinship groups. You will develop an understanding of age-appropriate practice and critically examine selected systemic theories and approaches that underpin relational and multi-person counselling. The course explores the diverse contexts, dynamics, and ethical considerations of working with more than one person and provides opportunities to develop advanced skills for facilitating change in relational systems.
learning_outcomes: Integrate advanced skills and reflective practice in working therapeutically with more than one person
Critically analyse systemic and relational theories and practices relevant to multi-person counselling
Evaluate contexts, dynamics, and ethical parameters of therapeutic work with couples, families, and kinship systems
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, and ZZCO5004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counselling for Grief and Loss
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This elective course will equip you with specialised knowledges and skills to work with end-of-life, death, dying, loss, and bereavement across the lifespan. You will interrogate contemporary theories and models informing grief and loss and critically reflect on cultural and spiritual dimensions of grief. Learning will incorporate systemic and political dimensions of loss including contemporary challenges such as climate grief. You will engage with critical issues pertaining to death and dying and become familiar with key medicolegal and care frameworks, for example Voluntary Assisted Dying, palliative care, and the coronial system. Your repertoire will expand into advancing your counselling and reflective practice skills and working with complex issues in grief and loss such as intersections with traumatic stress, sudden and unexpected death, and prolonged/complex grief.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of dying, and bereavement across the lifespan including cultural and spiritual dimensions
Utilise advanced skills and practices in grief and loss counselling
Interrogate contemporary theories and models informing grief and loss
Articulate critical issues pertaining to grief, death and dying
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, and ZZCO5004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Counselling Practice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course builds on and extends your counselling knowledge, skills and practices to ground and prepare you for your first counselling placement(s). Exploring the counselling encounter with respect to diversities and contexts, you will develop advanced counselling practices that consider and apply professional standards, ethics and risk. The experiential learning in this course will extend your counselling proficiency to in-person environments. An in-person residential workshop will provide an in-depth opportunity to build your applied counselling practices and skills with your peers and guided by counselling practitioner teachers. This unique forum provides an interactive and collaborative opportunity to use deliberate practice to implement essential advanced counselling skills, including risk assessment. The workshop will also utilise innovative reflective techniques, to extend your capacity to form effective supervisory relationships, develop your reflective capacity, and attend to self-care.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective counselling skills in simulated in-person encounters utilising in person engagement.
Critically apply counselling knowledge and practices to the counselling encounter as a whole
Demonstrate an understanding of risk and risk assessment
Use reflection and feedback to enhance your development as a counsellor and your counselling practices
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, ZZCO5004, and ZZCO5005

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counselling Placement A
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: You will undertake a placement in an approved human services/counselling agency. Your learning experience is supported by clinical supervision facilitated by practising counsellors and clinical consultants at the placement agency and in tutorial classes. You will begin to develop your skills in giving and receiving feedback, both individually and in small groups with your peers, across the length of the placement. The placement provides an opportunity for you to reflect on your theoretical and skills-based learning in counselling settings, to develop your counselling approach and your self as a counsellor.
learning_outcomes: Effectively apply professional standards in counselling in a workplace setting
Utilise coherent case presentation skills and supervision to develop your reflective counselling practice
Integrate and apply counselling skills and knowledges in a real-world professional setting
Critically reflect on your professional development as an accredited counsellor
Identify links between relevant counselling theory and knowledges with practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5005 and ZZCO5008

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counselling Placement B
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: You will undertake a placement in an approved human services/counselling agency. Your learning experience is supported by clinical supervision facilitated by practising counsellors and clinical consultants at the placement agency and in tutorial classes. You will begin to develop your skills in giving and receiving feedback, both individually and in small groups with your peers, across the length of the placement. The placement provides an opportunity for you to reflect on your theoretical and skills-based learning in counselling settings, to develop your counselling approach and your self as a counsellor.
learning_outcomes: Utilise coherent case presentation skills and supervision to develop your reflective counselling practice.
Effectively apply professional standards in counselling in a workplace setting
Integrate and apply advanced counselling skills and knowledges in a real-world professional setting
Critically reflect on your professional development as an accredited counsellor
Identify links between relevant counselling theory and knowledges with practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5009

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Psychotherapeutic Frameworks
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: In this elective course you will engage with psychotherapeutic frameworks used in counselling, for example psychodynamic and interpersonal psychotherapies. You will critically examine theories and concepts informing human relationships across the lifespan, such as attachment, object relations and relational-cultural. You will develop your use of self, including awareness of the transference relationship, to deepen your capacity in the therapeutic relationship. The interactive learning in this course will extend your counselling skills and applied concepts and your ability to work psychotherapeutically.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate relevant theories and concepts informing human relationships
Utilise psychotherapeutic frameworks for work with individuals
Integrate advanced counselling skills and concepts in the therapeutic relationship
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, and ZZCO5004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Counselling Practice for Trauma, Crisis, and Violence
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This elective develops advanced counselling practices for working with people impacted by trauma, crisis, and violence across diverse contexts, including for example family and gendered violence, disasters, displacement, and intergenerational trauma. Interactive learning will orient to understanding the self of the counsellor, self care and applied skills and practices. The course builds and extends trauma-informed practice, integrating cultural responsiveness and intersectionality to recognise how social location, power, and systems influence help-seeking, and recovery. You will critically examine and apply risk assessment, counselling approaches and phased, evidence-informed frameworks including for example EMDR, and TF-CBT and the use of digital and online counselling technologies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse evidence-informed approaches to trauma, crisis, and violence, and their application across diverse contexts.
Integrate advanced skills and applied practice in working with trauma, crisis, and violence
Articulate an understanding of the contexts impacting trauma, crisis, and violence.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5001, ZZCO5002, ZZCO5003, ZZCO5004

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Evaluating Evidence for Counselling Practice
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to ideas about evidence and the role of research in the development of knowledge and in relationship to counselling practice. You will critically evaluate the use of digital technologies and the social and ethical contexts of evidence and research. Building on this knowledge, you will develop and apply skills in information literacy including locating, evaluating and using relevant information for the purpose of evidence-based counselling and research.
learning_outcomes: Analyse ethical practice in applied evidence and research
Locate, evaluate and apply relevant information literacy skills for the purpose of research and evidence in practice contexts
Articulate the role of evidence and research in counselling
Evaluate the use of digital technologies for evidence-based counselling and research
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5009

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Integrated Counselling Practice (Capstone)
faculty: Faculty of Arts, Design and Architecture
syllabus_overview: This capstone course will bring together your learning across the program to develop and employ your personal integrative counselling framework. Engaging with applied learning in interactive tutorials and webinars, you will develop your capacity to respond to challenges that arise in the therapeutic relationship. Utilising and applying knowledge and skills gained in the program to date you will expand your counselling repertoire by engaging with complex client presentations to formulate, plan and provide integrated and effective counselling. The course prepares you for your transition to work as a fully accredited counsellor, refining your capacity for reflective, ethically grounded, and contextually responsive counselling practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective counselling practice
Utilise family systems ideas in working with people over the lifespan
Respond effectively to challenges in the therapeutic relationship
Develop and articulate a personal integrative counselling framework
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZCO5010

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Programming
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This is a first programming course. It provides an introduction to programming in Python and covers the following essentials: Program design and implementation in a high level language, with procedural and object oriented constructs and some functional features. Fundamental programming techniques, data structures and algorithms. Debugging and testing. Simulation. Applications in different areas, including those involving graphical user interfaces and animations.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement algorithmic solutions to problems that require writing small to medium-sized programs.
Write code for a variety of programming tasks for a broad range of applications, in particular in analysing data, plotting data, and running simulations.
Apply programming techniques that borrow from the procedural, functional and object-oriented paradigms.
Apply a disciplined, rigorous, and methodical approach for program design and development, with special attention given to effective debugging and testing.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Principles of Security Engineering
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the principles of the emerging field of Security Engineering, applying engineering principles and practices to the design, operation, and assurance of secure systems. Students will engage in a systematic, analytic and reflective approach to designing and assuring reliable secure systems from unreliable insecure components, as well as understanding how systems can fail and the nature of the cryptographic components from which modern digital systems are constructed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the nature of characteristic cybersecurity attacks, including the nature and characteristics of the vulnerabilities they exploit, and analyse the range of mitigation measures possible.
Demonstrate an understanding and make appropriate judgements about when to apply the major principles of secure design operation and assurance, their characteristics strengths and weaknesses.
Analyse real world design, operation and assurance scenarios and then apply a security engineering approach to make appropriate decisions.

Apply fundamental cryptographic primitives (including confidentiality, integrity, and authentication) and protocols to achieve them and explain their weaknesses and appropriate use. Be able to apply information theoretic concepts such as information and work measures, zero knowledge, randomness, and privacy to design appropriate solutions for real world cryptographic and security problems, or recognise when no effective solutions are likely to be feasible.
Analyse their prior approach to security in everyday life, and reflect on how a security mindset changes this.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Advanced Penetration Testing
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course follows on from the introductory Penetration Testing course, which is a prerequisite. This course teaches offensive security. Coverage will be updated to remain current and includes topics drawn from advanced web application attacks, hand crafted multi stage and non-tool based attacks, layer 2 attacks, social engineering, stealth, exploit generation and delivery, physical attacks, insider attacks, negotiating appropriate rules of engagement and managing legal risk, reporting and ethical professional frameworks for advanced penetration testing and red teaming. assumed knowledge: Students are expected to be familiar with TCP/IP networking across OSI layers 2-7 and programming / scripting in python or equivalent.
learning_outcomes: Design and effectively conduct a multi stage adaptive attack including some or all of recon, vulnerability detection and exploitation, physical attacks, social engineering, and build and deploy custom tools.
Explain the principles required for stealthy infiltration, exfiltration, and persistence and an understanding of potential detection measures and counter measures.
Conduct advanced network attacks in accordance with professional ethical and legal best practice frameworks
Explain network attacks across at OSI network layers 2-7 and the common protocols across them including operation and packet structure and be able to manipulate packets as required for attacks.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZEN9213

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Security Engineering Capstone Project
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This Security Engineering Capstone course allows you to demonstrate your mastery of the security engineering discipline. This course will draw together everything you have learnt and requires you to apply it in a practical fashion; this includes technical knowledge, professional skills and research abilities. You will apply these skills in a real-world situation with several of your peers in order to participate in and complete a real-world exercise. While the exercise itself is simulated, this is one of many things a security engineer may be asked to work on, and the data you will work with is completely real.
learning_outcomes: Summarise and effectively communicate mastery of professional skills and capabilities, including analysis, problem solving, risk assessment, and incorporating ethical considerations, based on evidence specific to cyber security.
Critically reflect on self-management capabilities, including communication, project management, and time management.

Demonstrate the ability to work collaboratively and professionally in a team, identifying and addressing team issues, enhancing and supporting team effectiveness and applying cultural and global competence, in the context of cybersecurity.

Demonstrate the ability to scope and plan a medium-sized project relevant to cybersecurity, including identifying and articulating a real-world problem statement, identifying stakeholders and their needs, critique key issues, and effectively evaluate solutions.
Apply security engineering knowledge and skills in a real-world application.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Enrolment in 8649 and completion of 48 UOC.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Penetration Testing​
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides a theoretical background to the science and art of penetration testing along with an introduction to hands-on skills used in the process of carrying out a tool based penetration test. The course also provides an understanding of the legal requirements, professional ethical and self care issues, technical processes, limitations, and reporting requirements and communication skills for non-technical audiences.
learning_outcomes: Exploit common vectors of web application testing and network perimeter attacks and understand their respective aims, limitations, and when to appropriately employ them in offensively security testing.
Apply the legal, ethical, business, and technical constraints of offensive penetration testing to real-world environments and case studies.

Synthesise technical findings to provide effective information to both technical and non-technical decision makers on the current security state of the network, and make effective holistic recommendations for addressing weaknesses and improving security.
Use tools to professionally carry out and document a simple penetration test in accordance with current best practiceframeworks including attacking web applications.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cloud Security
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the rapidly growing field of cloud security. Aside from its significant commercial benefit, cloud infrastructure brings its own unique challenges to security. The course addresses the ways in which cloud paradigms change the strengths and vulnerabilities of infrastructure compared with traditional computing environments. The course covers paradigms for securing and assuring cloud based infrastructure at scale.
learning_outcomes: Contrast the different cloud paradigms and use-cases of their implementation, and their respective use-cases, advantages and limitations.
Effectively communicate security results to key stakeholders.
Explain the technical and non-technical aspects of cloud-specific vulnerabilities and potential attacks.
Synthesize and apply security mitigation to cloud environments.
Apply both current penetration testing techniques and apply cloud-specific techniques to understand the security concerns of cloud implementations.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Reverse Engineering
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This overall aim of this course is to examine the link between high level code written by humans and low level code executed by systems. An understanding of the ways in which these can differ is essential for developing exploitation skills, and for low level defensive design and testing. This course requires entering students to already understand higher level programming languages such as C and low level machine code for common microprocessors such as x86/x64 or ARM. Students learn software assurance and security analysis as well as basic malware analysis.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure and key elements of a compiled binary on common target platforms
Explain the characteristics of common vulnerabilities and able to identify potential vulnerabilities in binaries
An appreciation of how idioms in high level languages are compiled into machine code and the process of linking and be able to apply strategies to convert machine code back into such idioms.
Select and use appropriate tools such as debuggers and decompilers
Analyse and unpack obfuscated malware
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZEN9217

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Fundamentals of Coding: C and Assembler
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Learn how to program to C and low level assembly language. This course provides an introduction to programming in C and a low level understanding of the underlying operation of modern computers. C is introduced slowly and at each step we see how C programs are compiled into corresponding machine code and the details of how the computer actually then executes the program. This course is suitable for those who have never programmed before, or those who have programmed but are not familiar with C or assembly, or who would like a refresher from the point of view of cyber security.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of the principles of secure coding and given a C program be able to identify common security vulnerabilities in it.
Design, write and debug programs in C
Be able to write programs in a simple assembly language.
Effectively collaborate with others in accordance with modern software design practices including pair programming and team review.

Explain how C programs are compiled, linked, and executed including memory allocation, stack frames, system calls, the role of static and dynamically linked libraries and how to inspect this using a debugger.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Operating System Fundamentals for Security
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of modern operating systems including how they are attacked, their security mechanisms, and countermeasures. It provides an in-depth look at the services provided by modern Operating Systems, from a security perspective.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a system, identify potential vulnerabilities, and design and create simple proof of concept exploits.
Explain the design of modern operating systems: architecture components and services.
Explain the principles of modern file systems, memory organisation and hardware elements including stack, heap, registers, instruction pipeline, DMA, and their role in exploitation.

Analyse and describe the differences between classical and mobile operating systems, including on internet of things devices, and analyse designs from a security perspective to identify potential vulnerabilities and areas of weakness.
Communicate modern OS security implementations, threats, and controls including their use, limitations, and countermeasures.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZEN9216

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Database Systems
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: A first course on database systems. Data modelling; principles of database design; data manipulation languages; database application teachniques; introduction to DBMS internals. Prac work: design and implementation of a database application using SQL and stored procedures.
learning_outcomes: Develop accurate, non-redundant data models.
Implement stored procedures and triggers.
Analyse and improve redundancy in relational models.
Realise data models as relational database schemas.
Describe, at a high level, the internals and database management systems
Formulate queries via the full range of SQL constructs.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Big Data Management
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the core concepts and technologies involved in managing Big Data. Topics include: characteristics of Big Data and Big Data analysis, storage systems (e.g. HDFS), techniques for manipulating Big Data (e.g. MapReduce, Spark), query languages (e.g. HiveQL and Spark SQL), and typical applications (e.g. recommender systems, text analysis).
learning_outcomes: Develop efficient solutions for analytical problems involving Big Data.
Utilise the map/reduce paradigm to manipulate Big Data.
Explain the important characteristics of Big Data.
Develop an appropriate storage structure for a Big Data repository.
Use a high-level query language to manipulate Big Data.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: ZZEN9021

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Neural Networks, Deep Learning
school: School of Computer Science and Engineering
syllabus_overview: Neural networks and deep learning play a critical role in pushing the boundaries of what AI can achieve, making them indispensable for various industries and applications. Their ability to learn and adapt from data has revolutionised many fields and opened up new opportunities for solving complex problems. This course provides an introduction to and deep exploration of neural networks and deep learning principles and practice. Topics chosen from: perceptrons, feedforward neural networks, backpropagation, Hopfield and Kohonen networks, restricted Boltzmann machine and autoencoders, deep convolutional networks for image processing; geometric and complexity analysis of trained neural networks; recurrent networks, language processing, semantic analysis, long short term memory; designing successful applications of neural networks; recent developments in neural networks and deep learning.
learning_outcomes: Students will be able to analyse a solution to a neural network problem in terms of the relevant NN and DL techniques.
Students will demonstrate an understanding of a variety of NN and DL techniques.
Students will be able to program neural network and deep learning applications.
Students will have an awareness of the computational theory underlying the various NN methods.
Students will demonstrate an understanding of aspects of the social, intellectual, and neuro-biological context of neural networks and deep learning.
Students will demonstrate a working knowledge of one or more neural network simulation packages, and be able to use them to perform a range of computational tasks.
prerequisites: pre-req: ZZEN9021

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Law, Regulation and Ethics
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with a foundational understanding of the Australian legal system and the ethical frameworks within which businesses operate. Students will examine the nature of the Australian legal system, key institutions and principles, the evolution of that system over time and its place in the broader international context. Additionally, students will explore the main areas of law regulating business, environmental, social and governance (ESG) impacts and understandings of ethical business practice. Topics will include the sources and hierarchies of law in Australia, systems of government and the separation of powers, Australia’s federal system, and the role of courts, tribunals and regulatory bodies. Students will also be guided to develop legal reasoning, and in the application of legal principles to fact scenarios. The course will be delivered online through asynchronous modules, online forums and synchronous online classes.
learning_outcomes: Interpret legislation with reference to the rules of statutory interpretation and find and understand caselaw (PLO 2, 3, 4)
Evaluate the ethical frameworks for the conduct of business (PLO 3, 4, 5)
Articulate legal and ethical concepts clearly to a broad audience (PLO 4, 5)
Analyse the evolution and key components of law of the Australian legal system (PLO 1, 6)
Examine the sources of law regulating business (PLO 1, 2, 5, 6)
prerequisites: Must be enrolled in program 7301, 8431, 7413, 8436, 7430 or 5436

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Corporate Governance and Leadership
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: This course explores the primary legislative rules and legal principles that regulate the operation and governance of corporations, focusing on the legal responsibilities of leadership roles. Students will also be guided to develop legal reasoning, and in the application of legal principles to fact scenarios. Topics include foundational principles such as legal personhood and limited liability, the rights of shareholders and other stakeholders, decision-making, the appointment and removal of office holders, duties and remedies. The course also examines the community and regulatory context in which corporations operate and contemporary issues in corporate governance. The course will be delivered online through asynchronous modules, online forums and synchronous online classes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse key principles of corporations law and governance.
Evaluate the duties of directors and other leaders and the availability of remedies.
Interrogate the regulatory and social responsibilities of corporations.
Apply key principles of corporations law and governance to fact scenarios.
prerequisites: Must be enrolled in program 7301, 8876 or 8431

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Commercial Contract Law
school: School of Private and Commercial Law
syllabus_overview: Contracts are an essential part of the daily conduct of business. In this course students will examine key elements of contract law and practice, including how and when contracts are formed, terms (express and implied), performance, what happens when contracts are breached, how they can be terminated, and remedies. Focusing on agreements in a commercial context, this course also explores the relationship between regulation and contractual freedom, and the interplay between contract law and related forms of legal obligation. Through exposure to case law and legislation, students will develop an understanding of sources of law and how to interpret primary legal materials. Students will also be guided to develop legal reasoning, and in the application of legal principles to fact scenarios. The course will be delivered online through asynchronous modules, online forums and synchronous online classes.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the regulation of contracts in the context of business law.
Analyse the key principles of contract law as they relate to the conduct of business.
Identify the availability of remedies in statute, common law and equity.
Apply key principles of contract law to hypothetical fact scenarios.
prerequisites: Must be enrolled in program 7301, 8876 or 8431

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fully online - Standard (usually weekly or fortnightly)

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Cyber and the Law
school: School of Law, Society and Criminology
syllabus_overview: The goal of the course is to provide a legal orientation for cyber security professionals. Students are not assumed to have a legal background. The course offers an introduction to legal and policy issues in cyber security. It introduces students to relevant core legal concepts, including understanding the role of legislation and case law as well as other forms of regulation, including technical standards. It will guide students in understanding the ‘map’ of law and regulation relevant to cyber security and the role of these in Australia’s cyber security policy. The course helps cyber security professionals become familiar with legal issues they are likely to encounter and how to manage them in different circumstances - during normal operations, in responding to an incident, and in the aftermath of an incident. After completing the course, students will be aware of and be able to manage core compliance obligations as well as be in a good position to interact meaningfully with legal advisers in more complex scenarios. The focus is on Australian law, but comparative and international material is included where relevant, particularly where it impacts Australian industry.
learning_outcomes: Identify key legal requirements and how these and other forms of regulation impact on cyber security professional practice.
Discuss the limits of law, both generally and in specific instances, and be able to argue for reform in particular areas.
Explain the role of key players in regulation for cyber security and be aware of the circumstances in which engagement with regulators is required or advisable.
Analyse and respond to legal issues arising in the contexts of cyber security operations, incident response and incident fall-out.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Psychology 1
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the content and methods of psychology as a basic science, with an emphasis on the social bases of behaviour. The course will cover several specific topics related to the social aspects of human behaviour. Each week students will explore one of the following topics: development psychology, theories of personality, theories of emotion and motivation, cross-cultural psychology, health psychology and social influences on behaviour. In addition, training in the methods of psychological inquiry and in the critical evaluation of research is also provided. This course is appropriate for students with and without a background in science. The course content will be delivered via asynchronous (pre-recorded) lectures, synchronous tutorials, readings and self-paced modules and quizzes.
learning_outcomes: Find and evaluate literature in the field of psychology, with a focus on the scientific method and peer reviewed research.

Recognise fundamental ideas and theories about a diverse range of psychological issues including individual differences and their measurement, development of the individual, emotion and motivation, health psychology, social and cross-cultural psychology.
Cite information sources appropriately in written communication.
Recognise the importance of a culturally sensitive approach to societal issues and the value of research from diverse perspectives.
Formulate scientific arguments by contrasting, synthesising and applying competing theoretical and empirical perspectives in psychology research.
Communicate scientific arguments using theoretical and empirical evidence in written communication to expert and non-expert audiences.

institution: University of New South Wales (UNSW Sydney)
title: Introduction to Psychology 2
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the content and methods of psychology as a basic science, with emphasis on the biological bases of behaviour. The course will cover several specific topics related to the biological bases of human behaviour. Each week students will explore one of the following topics: neurobiology, animal learning, abnormal psychology, memory and cognition, perception, and consciousness. The course will explore a range of the basic phenomena within an area and the neural bases of these behaviours.
